I have two points that I want to take up from the speech made by the member for Auckland Central. One point was the facsimile and I ask him to table it. If what he says is true, it is a very serious matter that must be dealt with and addressed by the Government. Secondly, and personally, I have no difficulty with the Regulations Review Committee looking at the regulations and making some comment. We are validating regulations at this time of the year rather than later because of the very serious situation that the industry is in, and the need to put some security before the growers. There is no doubt at all that there are serious divisions within the industry, and they will not be resolved next week or next year. There will always be people who will strongly support the board and the single-market concept. There will also be those people who will continue to support the free-market style of individual exporters involved in the industry, as they were prior to . In the middle is a large group of growers who are not too sure, and who in recent weeks have backed both options because of their serious concern for their future outcome. It was important that the Government clarify the exact position by introducing this Bill to ensure that everybody knows where the Government stands so that the industry can go forward into the selling season. It is important because picking and packing are about to start. We are less than a month away from starting. There is no way that out of the blue we could suddenly decide that there would be a different method of dealing with the marketing of kiwifruit for the coming season. As the Minister said prior to Christmas, the Government said that the board would be in place for this season because there was no proper indication from the growers that they wanted to remove the kiwifruit board. It has been Government policy, and will continue to be Government policy, that if a substantial majority of producers come to the Government and say that they do not want their board any more and give reasons, and the Government determines that it is in the national interest to remove that board then after properly consulting the industry it would remove it. I have no doubt that the Government would do that should that course of action be taken. When the Kiwifruit Marketing Board was first set up the views of growers were asked for, and growers expressed their opinions, so it would be only proper, therefore, that a properly conducted referendum of growers should be undertaken before a change was made. The last season was close to being a disaster for many people. It has had very serious repercussions on families, and I doubt and would be most surprised whether anybody in the industry made a profit.

Earlier in the debate on the Bill the Deputy Leader of the Opposition said that she was pleased that this was the last time that we would be debating the matter in the House. I hope that it is not the last time that we will be debating this matter in the House, but I hope that for different reasons from those of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition. It is my view that the publicity that the Bill has created during the past few years has had the biggest influence on adult smokers who are giving up smoking. I think that it has had a far greater impact on people than any threats to remove sponsorship or the banning of advertising have had. The debate that has gone on in this Chamber and among the organisations that have been sponsoring one side or the other of the argument has influenced people. The media in all its forms have carried this debate well---the printed media, radio, and television. The dangers to health have certainly been highlighted. I cannot think of any other period in my life in which I have been aware of more adult people who are giving up smoking than in the past few years. I appreciate that the habit of smoking has now been declining in New Zealand for a number of years. But when the figures of what has happened in the past few years are revealed, I am sure that they will show a great decline. Whilst I have a different point of view from that of the member, I compliment the Deputy Leader of the Opposition on her campaign---if one likes---and the courage that she displayed during the whole of this debate. Earlier on, this debate was certainly not very easy, and I really appreciate her contribution. However, I disagree in principle with the banning of advertising of a legal product. To my way of thinking, a double standard has crept in, in which within New Zealand we have not been able to advertise, but we have been able to accept advertising from outside our borders---that is, from overseas. I feel a little bit uneasy about that. Of course, that situation will continue into the future until the world at large adopts different measures. The policy has also, in a way, stopped a process that had already started. Responsible bodies such as sporting or cultural bodies, which had some members who accepted and believed that smoking was bad and injurious to health, were actually looking for alternative sponsors. It was not easy, but they had started that process. I think that a stronger attitude against smoking in this country would have been cemented in if all those sports bodies, in particular, had been challenged by their own membership to find other methods of funding. They do not have to do that at present. Whilst that funding from the tobacco companies is ceasing, there will be other funding in place---at least, I certainly hope so. There are two groups of people involved in this legislation: the smokers and the potential smokers. I do not have any doubt that as far as the first group is concerned---the smokers---the publicity that has been generated through this legislation has been successful in reducing the number of adult smokers. Whether the sponsorship ban goes or stays, it has already had its impact. However, I hope that the level of publicity will be maintained, and that is why I hope that it is not the last time that we will debate the matter in this House. However, I am not sure that this legislation has had a great deal of impact with regard to potential smokers. Whilst I do not refer specifically to this Bill, I am a little bit disappointed that not enough publicity has been given to discussion and planning for the education of people, particularly our younger people, right through the schools. I know that some work is being done, but it has not been publicised enough, and more work is needed. We really have to get through to young people before they start to smoke because, quite frankly, they have no idea---nor has anybody who starts to smoke---how addictive the tobacco product really is. One must smoke for some time, and give up smoking, before one can really appreciate the strength of that particular drug. I have made my own inquiries about what affects young people who smoke. There is no doubt that a major factor is peer-group pressure. A small number of the students to whom I have talked accepted that advertising could have had some effect on them, particularly as it related to alternative brands. But I, like one or two other members who spoke this evening, did not find any young person who believed that sponsorship advertising had any effect on their starting to smoke. When I think back to my younger days, I have to agree with the findings. Two years will pass before the legislation expires, as it were. I hope that those sporting bodies that state that they oppose smoking will go out of their way to find alternative sponsorship. I believe that we must put a lot more effort into educational programmes that are aimed particularly at schools. If we are not successful in persuading people against smoking, we must consider stronger measures. Throughout the world people smoke. New Zealand does have the Bill of Rights . It would not be reasonable for Government members to say suddenly that they were going to ban tobacco as a product, because the law would be flouted and broken and there would be the same reaction that there was in America when alcohol was banned. There are a number of other precedents. If we are not successful in educating our young people not to start smoking, we should make smoking illegal for people under the age of years. I believe that that would be acceptable; there are messages that must be given to young people. If we really want to break the habit of smoking and to reduce the cost of our health budget, we may have to take that measure. I see no conflict in taking that strong action, if it is our genuine desire to get rid of the habit of smoking in this country. The Government cannot be accused of saying that although it does not want people to smoke it does not mind if they do because it is getting a whole lot of tax out of it. There does appear to be a double standard there. However, we can get over that problem. I believe that, if one has not started to smoke by the time one reaches one's early twenties, one will never start. There will be a lot more pressure in today's world for people not to start. But it is young people who are challenged by their peers, and who smoke to flout the rules because they are not allowed to do it at school. They take up the challenge and smoke. I say again that people do not understand when they first start smoking how addictive this habit is. Earlier in the debate the Deputy Leader of the Opposition mentioned that she was concerned about the statistics that showed an increase in the consumption of tobacco in Third World nations. I say to her that one has to look at those figures in a realistic way, because in emerging nations and Third World countries people start by smoking raw tobacco rolled in newspaper, and some of them smoke like that for their whole lives. There are never any statistics on that type of smoking, and it so happens that many of the countries that are emerging or that are Third World countries have a climate that can produce tobacco. It is only as those societies start to become a little bit more affluent that people change to what they call tailor-made cigarettes, and are able to give up smoking raw tobacco that is crushed and rolled in newspaper. When I made the change to tailor-made cigarettes, I know that I really appreciated the difference. The point is that the smoking of cigarettes that are not tailor-made does not show up in statistics, so that, although the statistics may show an increase in smoking in the Third World, that does not mean that those people are smoking more; it just means that they have changed from smoking raw tobacco that is wrapped in newspaper to smoking tailor-made cigarettes. They have made that change because those cigarettes are usually available at quite a cheap price, having been produced on the local market. I agreed with some of the comments about alcohol that were made tonight by the member for Hawke's Bay. We do need to target that particular drug.

I spent years of my life as President of the New Zealand Labour Party, organising an electoral machine that would outgun the much-vaunted, highly regarded, even feared, National Party election campaign organisation during the period to . We worked, we planned, and we organised meticulously for the day of reckoning, which turned out to be a little earlier than we expected---in July . It was an anticlimax when we found that the political enemy, for which we had thoroughly prepared ourselves, had evaporated before our eyes. The heavy political artillery was to drop a barrage on the political landscape, then the troops were to move in. Well, the barrage was there during the election campaign. The troops moved in, but they were all ours. There were no National Party troops. They had left either before the day of battle or on it. The election campaign was an organisational rout, and we are looking at the remnants of that rout tonight. The Opposition has said that it is opposed to the Budget---the Government's major financial statement---but it organised itself so abysmally that it gave away its speaking rights. The Opposition does not really care about the people.

I was critical of the member for Avon; I do not think that he is a woman. The NewLabour Party made submission on the Bill. Although the Labour Government's pay equity legislation is completely inadequate---and I have said that on previous occasions---the repeal of that legislation will leave a vacuum in pay equity legislation and employment opportunities legislation. If the Government wants to make some proposals it should do so, but it should leave the legislation in place until it has got its act together. The repeal of pay equity legislation as well as the repeal of equal employment opportunity legislation is similar to running a bulldozer into a house that needs maintenance---knocking everything down, but putting nothing in its place. Women's wages are lower than men's wages largely because they lack the industrial strength to negotiate for better pay. By hinging pay equity on negotiations between unions and employers, the previous Government was asking the very system that had brought about low pay for women to deliver equal pay, and the system was not up to it. That is the reason that the legislation was fatally flawed. I have a private member's Bill on the Order Paper that proposes that equal pay for work of equal value should be compulsory. Pay equity is a justice issue, and, as a matter of justice, the State has an obligation to deliver it. The State should not allow it to be negotiated. Pay equity will never be achieved if it must depend on compromise between women workers, particularly in the current economic climate, and their employers. The NewLabour Party opposes the outright repeal of the employment equity legislation. When the previous Government passed the employment equity legislation it knew that it would not deliver much to many women and that it came much too late in any case. The NewLabour Party opposes the repeal of the Act because to retain the Act would be something of a hollow victory for the supporters of pay equity as it is time to go much further and to deliver real wage justice for women workers. Equal pay for work of equal value is an idea whose time has come. However, it should be implemented independently of the industrial relations system. It should be the right of people who are employed in female-dominated jobs to claim the wages earned by those in male-dominated jobs that require the same level of skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. We believe that that right should exist, even if the Government makes the radical changes that it proposes in the wage-bargaining system. The pay equity legislation should be part of a raft of anti-discrimination legislation that includes the Equal Pay Act and the Human Rights Commission. The Labour Government was wrong to tie pay equity to the industrial relations system and wage-bargaining, as that has meant that discriminatory wages were acceptable as long as the unions and employers agreed to them. Wage discrimination is unacceptable in any circumstances. In a free labour market, women will need all the protection they can get against discrimination---and they would not have received it under the present Act, and they are not likely to receive it under anything that the Government is to propose. The bottom line is that people should not be paid less because they happen to work in sectors traditionally dominated by women. When it is shown that such jobs have similar value to male-dominated occupations that are paid at a higher rate, to allow those employers to pay less is to allow wage discrimination on the basis of gender. That should be unlawful, just as other forms of sex discrimination are unlawful.

I know that the Government would wish that it had President Clinton's problem. He has actually got the support of to percent of the American people for his domestic-led investment recovery programme---would that the Government had anything remotely like that! The gratuitous advice that the Minister of Finance has been giving to President Clinton should be followed by herself in terms of getting the deficit of this country under control, getting the overseas balance of payments deficit under control, and of developing some employment and the social and economic infrastructure in this country. Unemployment is the No. social and economic cancer that blights this country. I want to use my time in the general debate to ask three questions. What is the present situation of unemployment? What has caused it? What can be done about it? In an election year it ill-behoves any party in the House just to have a critical diatribe; we have to put up some positive alternatives. If we examine the present situation, the Minister of Employment said in the Waikato Times on February---just week ago---``The growth in jobs did not necessarily mean the level of unemployment would decrease. He estimated , young people were destined to leave school and go straight on the dole.''. The September figures show that percent of young people between and years of age are unemployed. The latest household survey figures show that there are , jobless---an increase of percent that has occurred during a time that both Labour and National Governments have been elected. That figure equals percent of the total workforce. I see that the Australian figures have been estimated to be percent of the total workforce. A study that was released this month showed that New Zealand had one of the highest youth suicide rates in the world and the highest female youth suicide rate in the OECD. A New Zealand study reported that suicide rates for the unemployed were . per ,, compared with . percent per , for people with jobs---in other words, suicide is about times higher among the jobless than among those at work. Any MP who is in touch with his or her electorate knows full well the anguish of young suicides in their area. The jobs that have been announced as having been lost this year, in the first weeks from January to February, mean that New Zealand is losing jobs at the rate of a week---yet we are told that there is an economic recovery. That figure does not include the people who will lose their jobs in the shellfish industry. How on earth did we get into that situation? First, we got into it because the monetary policy that was adopted by the Labour Government was idiotic in its application, and it fuelled speculation. There was the stock market boom then the stock market crash. The monetary policy was used to control inflation. The Government of the day was warned what would happen if monetary policy was used to control a single economic indicator such as that, but it did not listen. First, it used fiscal policy that was too loose. Funded deficits resulted in Government bond rates of percent; that was too tight and forced the collapse of the economy. The sequence of reforms was abysmal to say the least. Subsidies were removed from farmers before anything was put in place in terms of an overall economic policy for the agricultural sector. Manufacturers were hit by high exchange rates, and that meant that both exporters and import substitution industries were virtually destroyed. New Zealand is now trapped by an economy that is stagnant, and the growth rates that we have at the moment are abysmal by anyone's standards. A growth rate of percent is quoted as some kind of triumph when in fact it is a disaster for an economy that is trying to come out of a depression. If we ever look like getting a recovery, we suddenly face an immediate balance of payments deficit problem. That started to show last month with a $ million balance of payments deficit. New Zealand has appalling levels of investment. In the early s we were investing percent of the gross domestic product. We now are down to percent, which in effect means that we are investing $ million less in the economy than we were before. That means we are in an impossible position to have either a domestic-led or an investment-led export recovery. What should we do? Clearly, the investment sector and our productive base---agriculture and manufacturing---have to be given stable conditions in which to invest. There has to be a managed exchange rate that gives some confidence for the future, and gives investment stability and certainty. We have to create conditions for investment conditions such as lower real interest rates. I do not know whether members of the House have figured this out, but manufacturers and other businesses in this country that try to borrow money at to percent interest---if they are lucky; the good companies pay percent---against an inflation rate of percent are paying real interest rates of percent. That is not much of an incentive to invest. The kinds of problems that we face as a result include rising unemployment, lower infrastructural investment, and a lack of confidence in either the export or the import substitution industries. Surely people can see that! Some niche markets are doing well, but, overall, unemployment levels increase and social deprivation gets worse. Taxes have to be raised to finance this extra investment---which is what President Clinton is telling the people in the United States has to be done---not only to finance the investment, but also, of course, to constrain the balance of payments. If it is done just by borrowing, the balance of payments deficit will blow out. If it is done through taxation, we can strain expenditure from the affluent, invest it in the economy, and create jobs for those people who are desperately in need of them. I refer to research and development, and to the accelerated depreciation allowance. Our Crown research institutes---the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries as they once were---need to be given a boost, not to have all their scientists marching with their feet. National and regional development co-ordination is a programme to enhance opportunities for all sectors of the community. It would create jobs in health and in health education, and in catching up on waiting-lists---$ million invested each year for the next years would wipe out waiting-lists for hospitals. Who in the House would not like that to be done? The provision of community services for reintegrated psychiatric and intellectually handicapped people has to be funded if it is to mean anything at all. It cannot mean simply closing down institutions to save money. There are more jobs there for skilled and trained people. Restoring and improving our rural hospitals and our mainstream hospitals would create work and worthwhile social service opportunities. We should expand our hospice services, look after terminally ill patients and elderly people in the community, and research environmental health and all the things that would make the workplaces in our community safer and more healthy. In terms of education, smaller classes would mean more teachers. Special needs and gifted children should be given special opportunities. We say that we have mainstreaming, yet we leave schools to try to cope without the assistance that they need to make it work. Building maintenance should mean something, instead of our having deferred maintenance programmes of up to $ million for all of our schools as at present. I am pleased to hear that the Government is to announce extra assistance for skills training, but look at the mess that the training opportunities programme is in! The member for Yaldhurst mentioned that programme. Many of our talented people who have some skills and an educational background need an opportunity to further their chances of getting a job, but they are prevented from having skills training by bureaucratic regulations that make a farce of that kind of skills training programme. Instead of closing down public transport, we should be opening it up in most of our main areas---not clogging our roads and inner cities with cars. Multi-use forests and degraded areas should be replanted for catchment and conservation purposes, flood control, and erosion control. There should be tree nurseries on local and Crown land. In relation to pest control, there are problems in various areas with old man's beard, tussock, and with the removal of exotics from national parks. There are pests such as possums, rabbits, ferrets, deer, goats, and so on. Tens of thousands of younger people in this country could be trained for a different lifestyle and could make a real contribution. Research and development are needed to look at alternative industries for furs, pelts, and yarns, and at making pet and human food from some of the so-called pests in this country. Each year New Zealanders are killed on the roads. Surely we can make the roads safer. For every $ million that are invested to save a life, jobs are created on the road, yet the Government is cutting construction investment. There is also the matter of fisheries research into stocks, and so on. There are innumerable opportunities, and I urge the Government to take up some of them.

The only ones missing, which the Labour Party made sure it put in, are the Reserve Bank and Treasury, which under this plan are permanent members of the Enterprise Council. Within months the new Enterprise Council would produce a -year strategy. Why did someone not think of that before? That is all we need. The member says it is rubbish, but I have actually spoken to hospital managers who believe exactly that. They believe that the Government requires it of them. The level-crossing accidents are nothing to do with it---I see! Well, the Minister has not read the report. I can see that. In roading there is a strong tendency to overspend on city motorways despite worldwide evidence that commuter congestion cannot be solved by road building. On the other hand we underspend on the State highway system. Many accident black spots, which have been identified by systematic road safety research, have not yet been fixed due to limits on the income of Transit New Zealand. On many rural State highways there are still too many corners and undulations and too few passing lanes. So the road service in many areas is unsatisfactory. There is no question that as much attention must be given to that matter as to public commuter transport in our main cities. This is the proper way to address rush-hour congestion. Many ideas have been developed to improve city public transport but progress has been slow and disjointed, and the Minister has to take a good deal of responsibility for that. We have to give attention to providing covered car parks close to suburban train stations; faster speeds for commuter rail services, once we make them safe; smoother linking between the different transport modes of rail, bus, tram; and bus priority lanes. The only way that public transport can attract passengers back is for it to become quicker and more convenient for the motorist than sitting in traffic jams and slow-moving vehicle traffic. The use of fuels within our transport system must be looked at very closely. Yesterday I tabled in this House the details of what appears to be a very serious situation at the New Zealand Stock Exchange. The papers I tabled showed that the Stock Exchange did not appear to be paying withholding tax on a series of contracts with non-residents ranging in value from $, to $,. The tabled documents showed that contractors from Australia and Canada were brought to New Zealand for computer consultancy work. All these invoices were paid with no deduction made for withholding tax. The New Zealand Stock Exchange is required to deduct withholding tax from payments to non-resident contractors unless it has obtained an exemption certificate from the Inland Revenue Department. No exemption certificates appear to have been issued. In simple terms, tax was due and it does not appear to have been paid. I have referred the details to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue for his consideration. Today I have more evidence of apparent irregularities in tax payments at the Stock Exchange. I have here a restraint of trade agreement signed between the Stock Exchange Chairman, David Wale, and the Chief Executive, Bill Foster, signed in July . It is an agreement that Mr Foster will be paid $, over years, which it claims is in exchange for Mr Foster agreeing not to go and work for any other New Zealand Stock Exchange. It is a preposterous agreement because there is not another Stock Exchange for him to work for. The obvious reason that the restraint of trade agreement exists is to avoid paying tax. There is some very arguable law allowing contractors in some circumstances to avoid tax on the component of their contract which is a restraint of trade. That is questionable enough, but it is for contractors. The chief executive of the New Zealand Stock Exchange is not a contractor, he is an employee. Employees who have a restraint of trade component in their contracts have to pay tax on that element, otherwise tax law would be in chaos---everyone would simply declare his or her income to be mostly restraint of trade and stop paying income tax. But the restraint of trade agreement with the chief executive of the Stock Exchange is a sham anyway, not just because it is beyond belief that he would set up another Stock Exchange in New Zealand, but because it is not really a restraint of trade at all. The purpose of the agreement is to compensate him for not being paid enough in the past, in the view of the board, and to dodge tax in giving him such a special payment. The minutes of the Stock Exchange board meeting of October reveal that the so-called restraint of trade is a sham. The first item of the minutes reads: ``... the Chairman reported that the Exchange had entered into a Covenant in Restraint of Trade with Mr Foster. The consideration agreed upon reflected the terms of the Covenant and compensation for an inadequate salary package in prior years.'' Further down the minutes record that one board member raised the need to properly resolve the tax issues and said: ``... it might be appropriate to seek an indemnity for taxation if subsequently assessed.'' In other words, the restraint of trade clause was not for restraint of trade at all, it was a boost in his pay and it seems that no tax was paid on it.

So there is some nostalgia for older New Zealanders in the image of a young princess who would have remained young in their thoughts for a very long time. Just before we rose for lunch I was thanking Sir William Birch for his role in this legislation. Given that I know the Labour members love to hear people thank Sir William Birch for his role in things, I think I will probably pick up from where I left off. Sir William Birch has always been a Minister who has had vision and conviction in whatever it is that he has put forward. His track record, long after he leaves this place, will certainly be a demonstration of that. Of course, the Labour members oppose what he does because they totally lack vision. They pick on the energy programmes and things like that, which last year in Taranaki earned $ million for the province. That is the type of stuff one gets from the Labour Party. There are others whom I also need to mention. The Hon. John Luxton was clearly the one who started with this vision some time ago, and I have to say that I had some concerns about it myself. I thought that he was trying to push the industry further than where it wanted to go at that time. The reality is that the industry itself, after having been required to report back to the Government last November, came up with this proposal. This is an industry initiative. There are no heavy-handed tactics in this. The industry itself arrived at this position. The industry itself employed the McKinsey group, which identified a potential $ billion export industry for New Zealand. The question that has to be asked is how does that group think it will achieve that. The reality is that if one looks at the growth that has been in the dairy industry over the last years, one will see that it is possible because the dairy industry has been one of the fastest growing industries in this country. That is the reason we are here today on the eve of what will be the most monumental piece of legislation passed in this House, not in this decade, but during the term of this New Zealand Government. The dairy industry earns percent of this country's export earnings. It has a programme and a forward-looking plan to grow that industry to $ billion. So far its predictions and its track record are something that the Labour Party should take a look at. Several other issues have been mentioned during the discussions. One of them is that the mega co-op will be of no benefit to farmers. Well, the sorry news for the Labour Party and its Alliance coalition-bloc partner is that a survey was done on that, as well. It identified $ million in potential savings for the dairy industry by rationalising its manufacturing sites. There is a lot of politics in the dairy industry, and there have been a lot of mixed signals. Most of that has happened at company level. By rationalising it to one major producing company we will remove most of that. One of the other situations that has been discussed ad nauseam in this House and put forward by members of the various Opposition parties is that the farmers themselves are being railroaded into something they do not want. The reality is that this is enabling legislation. It goes absolutely nowhere, falls off the table, and is completely null and void unless it gets percent support from farmers. Unlike the Labour Party, dairy-farmers are not stupid. They will actually analyse the detail. If they do not like it, they will not vote for it. It is as simple as that. It is an open, democratic system, and one of the most robust in this country, with more political nous than I have ever seen in this House. They will not put the concept up unless they are confident they will get percent. Let us remember that this is an industry that has to have percent support--not percent like in this House. The arrogance of this place! We cannot get things through here with any more than about percent support, yet we would suggest that we have an overwhelming knowledge of how this industry should function, and its target is percent. To get their constitutions put together, some of the company mergers have had to have percent. The constitution of this company will have a target of something similar to that. That is yet undecided, but I am sure it will be a robust and solid voting bloc to get that constitution put in place. Those are some of the issues that the Labour Party will never understand, and that was made clear during the Committee stage of this legislation. Having said that, I should acknowledge that the Labour members on the select committee did, in my opinion, put up a very good argument right throughout. It was very balanced. But the irony of that was that Jim Sutton who really is in favour of deregulation to the maximum was on one side, and Damien O'Connor was often being reined in on the other side by his senior colleague because, being more conservative, he thought that we might be moving too far. That was an interesting little development. I thought the Alliance member made a very worthwhile contribution throughout the debate. The philosophical arguments that came out of that sometimes were quite beneficial, and some amendments were made as a result. I commend the members for the work that they did during that process. I also need to make mention of the chairman of the select committee. At times he had a fairly difficult task with some of his own colleagues as well as with the Opposition. He had a fairly difficult task to rein us in. He made a superb job of chairing that committee. He kept the thing on schedule, and got the legislation through with general consensus in most instances. The submitters who came before the select committee raised some interesting issues across the whole cross-section. It demonstrated to me the sort of polarisation that exists in any type of organisation, particularly the dairy industry. There were some bizarre submissions from farmers who are trying to hang on to what potentially is something that is no longer relevant today. They will eventually get out of the industry themselves. It was overwhelmingly obvious to me that commercially they will not be viable because of their approach to the farming system. The mandate for this measure will come from the dairy-farmers. If farmers are not satisfied they will not vote for it, and that is the bottom line to this process. Farmers have to be satisfied, otherwise it will not go anywhere. This is an industry that is percent export orientated and percent domestically orientated, and we have to get past the Commerce Commission problems that are associated with something like this. This is a sound piece of legislation and I totally recommend it to the House.
It will. I would like to move that this Bill carry on.

It is with a great deal of disquiet and unhappiness that I have to rise and speak against this legislation. It rallies against all of the basic principles of property rights that we have come to expect in this nation over years. Unlike my colleague who was the previous speaker I have not yet learnt how to be restrained when I see such draconian legislation enter this Parliament. Part of this legislation---clause , ``Land status may be changed by declaration''---sums up exactly why what is happening here today has made me a little bit grumpy. The worst thing about it is that this legislation attacks the very foundation of the people who formed the Labour Party. It goes right to the heart of the West Coast---the people who put the Labour Party in action in the first place. How can the modern-day Labour Party look at its predecessors' photographs on the wall when they walk into the caucus room each day, and look themselves in the face when they are passing legislation like this today? How can they do that? I am sure that Mike Moore would come back from overseas if he knew this was happening. Norman Kirk will be turning in his grave tonight at the very approach of this legislation---``Land status may be changed by declaration''---that absolutely flies in the face of democratic process. It flies in the face of what the Labour Party stands for, and the Labour Party, aided and abetted by the ``green on the outside, red on the inside'' Green Party, should be absolutely ashamed of itself in this Chamber tonight. I want to refer members now to the fact that one can actually change the status of land by declaration without consultation. That party, on platform after platform up and down Taranaki - King Country, said time and time again during the by-election, and then at the election: ``We won't be arrogant like the National Party. Oh no, we'll listen. We'll consult. We'll travel to every nook and cranny in the country and we will listen. But we won't go down the West Coast, oh no!''.

I take issue with the comments made by the member for St. Kilda. He said that the Labour Opposition's only reason for opposing the Bill was the accommodation supplement. He suggested that the accommodation supplement was unfair, unworkable, and did not do justice to people who need support in housing. I remind the House of the parlous state of the housing support system that was inherited by the Government, which it will address with the introduction of the housing supplement on July. The housing policy that the Labour Government introduced and worked with had , people in State houses and , people on waiting-lists, for goodness' sake! The new supplement and policy that the Government has introduced will support some , families. It is a fair policy, it is good social legislation, and the Labour Opposition does not understand that. It knows all about socialism, but it does not know about good social policy, or fair social policy, which is what the Bill is all about. The amount of money that will be spent on housing New Zealanders and on supporting them has not been diminished. It is the same amount, but it will be spread more fairly among those in need. Because so many people need support, the system prevailing before July creates waiting-lists, unfairness, and manipulation. Some people who cannot get housing support are on waiting-lists according to a points system that does not support or assist people in their housing needs. It is quite ridiculous for the Labour Opposition and its previous spokesperson on social welfare to say that the one reason that they oppose the Bill---which addresses the problem of manipulation of the welfare system and takes on the people who are manipulating the system---is that the housing supplement is not fair. That comment shows exactly where Opposition members are coming from. They would not know a good bit of social policy if they saw it. Social policy is about fairness---fairness in housing for New Zealanders, and fairness for those who need support and assistance. The Government's policy will advantage , families, and that is an enormous number of people who previously did not have any opportunity for support or assistance in their housing needs. The previous situation encouraged unfairness. It is an indication of the Opposition's lack of knowledge of fair social activity in housing that that member---who is now the Opposition spokesperson on finance, God forbid, and whose knowledge of financial affairs was reflected in the recently released Opposition finance package---suggested that the only reason that the Opposition was opposing the Bill was the housing accommodation supplement! Probably the most important issue facing most New Zealanders is housing. If New Zealanders can be supported and assisted to own, or to feel that they can own, their own homes, and given some feeling of security in their homes, that is an advantage for society and the country. When a socialist party, a unionist party, a party that gives us that sort of rubbish, stands up in the House and says that sort of stupidity about good social legislation I think that the country needs to be told exactly where Opposition members are coming from, exactly how shallow their promises are, and exactly how ridiculous their social policies are. The Bill before the House is all about the people who are manipulating the system. Again, I emphasise that the housing supplement policy is fair, it is good social policy, and it is good housing policy.

Has the member for Waikaremoana anything to say about Tomorrow's Schools? It would seem not. Good education cannot be obtained on the cheap. Has the member not looked at the Budget tables, which show an increase of . percent in funding for education? Expenditure on education as a percentage of gross domestic product has greatly increased and is the highest since the early s. I am proud to stand here and tell that to the member. The Government is honouring its commitment to enhance the education provisions for children. Opposition members have asked about pilot schemes. It appears that they are prepared to sit on the fence, put off implementation of the recommendations, and to delay. There is only one word to describe their actions, and that is that they want to obfuscate. Opposition members want to do nothing. I remind them that there has been the Thomas report, the Currie report, the educational development conference, the Johnson report, the McCombs report, and The Curriculum Review. I say to Opposition members that it is time for action. We cannot obfuscate any longer. We must implement the proposals. The Government is not prepared to go down that road. The Government has consulted and has listened to all of the people at public meetings. There have been public meetings attended by , , or people. In the Ashburton electorate people came. It was a stimulating and challenging meeting. The decisions have been made, and the Government is ready for implementation. I feel as though I have waited half a lifetime for this day---half a lifetime of commitment to education. I am right here in this place, and involved in the decisions that will do so much for the education system. The country is on the brink of the greatest reforms in education since the Rt. Hon. Peter Fraser implemented the education policies of the first Labour Government. This Government will provide an environment for excellence in both administration and the classroom. I can think only that the member for Kaipara and the member for Waikaremoana have revealed their ignorance in being unable to have a vision. They have no policy statements, let alone any ideas. All they could do was come up with criticism of pupils being represented on the boards of trustees. It is ironic that the first school to invite membership of a student on the board of governors in the mid-s was the school at which the member for Tongariro was the principal. What a development he set in train! That development is coming through in the recommendations made in the Picot report. Opposition members questioned the decision not to put in place the policy advisory group. It seems to me that they have not read Tomorrow's Schools, which points out that the ministry will establish specific task forces to assist in policy development for limited periods of time. I can only suggest to Opposition members that they do not believe in the efficient use and management of resources, nor do they believe that issues can arise from time to time that need an in-depth investigation to come up with the recommendations that can be adopted by the Government for implementation. Opposition members challenge the provisions for equity in Tomorrow's Schools. They want freedom of choice. How in heaven's name can one manage a system for children and provide a completely open choice in the provision of places in schools? This country has a concern and a commitment to community schools. They are the only way to ensure the effective management of resources and to provide access for children within a neighbourhood. The equity provision is an interesting one. It has come to light during the consultation process since the Picot report emerged in late May that people realise and understand that some schools are better off than others. How can the Government resolve that position and ensure equity? The recommendations coming through in Tomorrow's Schools will do just that. The adoption of the bulk funding proposals with weighted formulas to provide for rural schools and schools in the lower socio-economic districts will ensure that no school and no child will be impoverished in any way in the matter of educational provision.

I am rather pleased to be able to follow the Minister because it gives me the opportunity to expose some of the myths he tried to indicate to us before the dinner break. I am not embarrassed by, nor do I recoil from, the processes or the policy adopted by the Labour Government for the reorganisation of the management of education. The Labour Government did not engage in secret reviews. It did not, under any circumstance, sideline the professionals or the parents in an attempt to superimpose upon the system a whole raft of policies, the implications of which are now coming home to roost. They will haunt the Minister. The Labour Government did not, as the Minister asserts, create a dinosaur. Each of the agencies set up under Tomorrow's Schools and Learning for Life has done an exceedingly good job in a short time. Each of them has a precise function. The Education Qualifications Authority is working superbly, as is the Education and Training Support Agency and QUEST Rapuara. Wherever the Education Review Office people go to undertake reviews the people in the schools and on the boards of trustees are full of admiration for the comprehensiveness of the agency's work and the quality of its recommendations. However, the Government is cutting the agency's budget by more than $ million. The Minister carefully avoided saying how the agency will carry out its functions with a reduced budget. A reduced budget means that it will lose staff. We have not been told how many staff will go, but, if its budget is reduced by more than $ million, of course it will lose staff. That will mean that there will be no quality assurance for education and consequently no commitment, in spite of the Minister's rhetoric about wanting standards to be raised. No one believes him and no one respects him. He is rapidly becoming an ill-informed nonentity. Once again he trotted out the nonsense about an $ million blow-out in teachers' salaries. He ought to remember that under the Official Information Act he gave me information on how that $ million was calculated. I will not give the figures because it would take too long, but I shall read out the items: a calculation error in primary teachers' salaries, new policy omitted, roll drop less than estimated, secondary out-turn adjustment, a secondary roll drop that did not eventuate, and an upward trend in teachers' salaries. Why was that? It was because an insufficient number of people were coming out of the teachers' colleges to go into the positions available, and teachers who were already experienced came back into the system. In fact, two-thirds of the people recruited last year were experienced teachers, but they cost more, and that is where the Minister's $ million comes from. That is the only so-called salary blow-out. There was a wage round shortfall in and growth in . Those items contributed to the $ million. It was not a salary blow-out. I expect the Minister to start to tell us the truth. He also went on about unappropriated expenditure. Opposition members have refuted that time and time again by pointing out that the Minister and the Minister alone withdrew $ million of money earmarked from the Telecom sale and intended to fund deferred maintenance in schools. He also withdrew $ million from money put aside to fund open access to tertiary institutions. He cannot claim that it was unappropriated money. He removed it from last year's Budget. The Bill is about the biggest omnibus Bill we have seen for years. It has parts and it amends Acts. Not a single part needs to be passed under urgency. There has not been public consultation on any one of them. Not one of them will be referred to a select committee for public scrutiny. Instead, arrogantly, the Bill will be ramrodded through Parliament under urgency in a way that is reprehensible given the range of Acts being amended. Why are we being exposed to this kind of unbridled power? Why is the Government rushing headlong into legislation in this way? Why are we not engaging the people and involving them in the scrutiny of legislation? That was a characteristic of the Labour Government. What is the Government afraid of? It most certainly is not the fount of all wisdom. The mistakes made in the very short time that it has been in office are legion.

After listening to that gramophone record winding down during the past minutes, I really do have to ask why we are being exposed tonight to the sort of D team of the National Party; the also-rans. Where are the Ministers who will defend their Government's performance? The description of New Zealand that the member for Otara gave is of the New Zealand that the National Government of - destroyed totally. Here is a member who is deserting his own people and moving to another electorate, because he knows that he has lost their confidence and would not be re-elected in Otara. So, in order to give his Rolls-Royce and Cadillac an outing every now and again, he is shifting over to the affluent suburb of Auckland. The National Government is a Government of total failure. It has failed in both significant areas---that is, in its economic policy and in its social policy. I believe that that is so, and so do the people of New Zealand. That failure is of such dimension that the people are reeling from its impact. It does not matter whether one talks to the elderly, to families with young children, middle-income families, relatively affluent two-income families, or beneficiaries, one's heart goes out to those people because they cower with feelings of insecurity, inadequacy, and anxiety, all of which are engendered by the policies of the National Government, and which we have had to endure since October . The Government is out of control, it is totally uncaring, it is arrogant. It is so lacking in sensitivity that its own party this afternoon expelled one of its members and allowed him to hear that news over the radio. That is arrogance in the extreme. It has not occurred to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, or the ``Minister of Everything''---who is behind a newspaper---that those Ministers have ridden roughshod over their caucus as well as over the people of this entire country. Yesterday the member for Wanganui revealed a great deal about the tactics used by the senior bullies in the National caucus. How do they go about getting their own way in caucus? It seems that they simply ridicule or put down members, in order to get their own way and to have their policies accepted. No wonder the health and the education professionals were sidelined; how on earth could they contribute anything to the debates that went on all through and , if the Government of the day showed all the arrogance of that ``born to rule'' attitude that was written in their body language whenever they appeared in the House or in public? Well, as we know, it is election year. The people will speak, and no amount of good news, ``good news'' trips, bonhomie, or back slapping will save the Government, because the people have made up their minds. Along with those one-term members---and the member for the West Coast---who will go into oblivion, this Government will be consigned to history. It is true to say that there has been a decade of very painful restructuring of the economy, and we are still far from achieving the necessary rates of growth to reduce unemployment and to restore household incomes. The Government, with all its crowing, will not admit that the economic situation is still below the level it was at in , and our medium-term prospects are that growth will reach a level of only percent overall and that is insufficient to make even a dent on the levels of unemployment.

In spite of the hour and in spite of urgency I am extremely pleased that the legislation is being passed. It is landmark legislation, and the Opposition is extremely pleased to support it. It had a -year gestation before being introduced by the Labour Government in September last year, and over the past year it has been subjected to select committee scrutiny. In the Committee of the whole House Opposition members drew attention to a number of issues. The Minister attempted to answer them, but did not do so satisfactorily. It is fair to say that, although the select committee deliberated on the legislation over a long time and heard submissions from all the major parties concerned with it, we found that subsequent to the reporting back of the Bill on October the Minister engaged in further negotiations with some major players. That was reported on today's Order Paper, showing that not only has he met those people but at this late date their submissions have largely been responsible for the preparation of the further supplementary order paper that we have just agreed to. In the main the Opposition is not concerned about the content of the supplementary order paper. In most instances the amendments clarify the issues. They do give a significant further function to the Fire Service Commission, but, nevertheless, the submissions made by that commission, by the Building Research Association of New Zealand, and by the Cement and Concrete Association have resulted in a large number of changes to the Bill. In most instances they have significantly improved it. During the Committee stage the Opposition drew attention to the way in which the interim board had performed during the past year. It was ably led by Mrs Wyn Hoadley. In spite of the fact that some appointments to the board will come up for renewal or replacement in February next year, we hope that the wealth of knowledge and experience that board members have acquired will enable them to see through the implementation phase of the legislation. The Opposition also drew attention to the need for the board to be adequately funded. The Opposition understands that there is some question about that, and the Minister did not give a satisfactory answer. A couple of things included in the supplementary order paper, which will become part of the Bill, ought to be mentioned. The disabled persons community will be heartened I am sure by the greater clarity given in the new clause to the need to provide adequate and reasonable access to buildings to ensure that disabled persons can carry out normal activities and processes. They have made repeated submissions on the Bill to ensure that their people are in no way disadvantaged. It is interesting that the Minister has allowed the functions of the Building Industry Authority to be extended to provide that it shall consult the Fire Service Commission on all matters relating to fire safety and fire engineering practices, and also in any appointment of a fire certifier. This provision is in addition to the functions set out originally, and is clearly the result of deliberations that the Minister has had in private with this organisation. One or two other matters of importance that I had hoped the Minister would comment on relate to the use of buildings and the way in which the new clause clarifies the kinds of changes buildings could be subjected to. The changes to the new clause B to reduce the longstop liability to years will bring great relief to the whole of the building industry and will allow better insurance cover, and perhaps also give the consumer some benefits. I think that local authorities will also welcome the measures to give them power to avert immediate dangers and to rectify unsanitary conditions so that they are able to close buildings and to go to the district court in a way that releases them from liability when they have acted in good faith. This Bill is very important. It rationalises the present system of building controls. As the Minister has indicated, it brings together Acts into a single flexible building code. It means that the whole industry can become cost-efficient and also more cost-effective. It has the support of architects, engineers, and builders, and it will provide them with the ability to operate in a more flexible and innovative way. It is also fair to point out that the Bill will not address the severe economic woes of this country. It is interesting to note that the October report of the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research showed that more building plant is idle now than at any time since World War II, and that percent of building firms claimed that their profitability had deteriorated in the last quarter. However, the Bill will provide for opportunities for the building industry to be more innovative in its approach to the solution of building and structural problems, and, at the same time, ensure that it meets good design and performance standards. The Opposition welcomes the Bill and supports its passage.

How does the axing of the equal employment opportunities requirement of early-childhood centres square with the National Party's election promise to provide additional resources to promote equal opportunities programmes in the private sector that, of course, would include early-childhood centres?

That is not what Government members said during the Committee stage. The Associate Minister said that the Government was legitimising the donations that are already being made to kindergartens. Nobody is denying that, but the kindergartens have developed a very simple means of ensuring that the dignity of people is preserved when they make either a financial contribution or a contribution in kind. By making it even permissive the Government is actually leaving the kindergartens with no choice but to charge a fee. The Associate Minister said that the Government cannot afford to maintain pre-school education, and that it will not put resources into it. Government members tried to claim that private individuals are setting up a system they cannot preserve with public money. Where is the clear commitment that was made in the Government's election manifesto? The National Party stated that it was committed to early-childhood education and to maintaining that service. It is my assertion, and I say it openly and without any fear of contradiction, that in opening up the options by making such a provision there will soon be some communities in the country with superior kindergartens and early-childhood services resourced by parents who are well off and affluent. However, in the suburbs where people belong predominantly in the lower part of the socio-economic spectrum there is dearth of kindergartens. Those there will not be as well resourced, and there will consequently be ghettos, as in black communities in South Africa where the children are impoverished in their start in life. I dispute the assertion that has been made that there will be no wind-down in early-childhood education funding. That claim cannot be substantiated, as yesterday $ million was removed from early-childhood education funding. When one considers all that has been achieved in the past years to put in place and to implement the Before Five proposals to make sure that early-childhood education would be free and accessible, it is exceedingly disappointing that the Government has chosen to single out pre-schoolers as some of the recipients of its slash-and-burn regime. The Labour Government had proposed that funding would be provided by so that there was a real possibility that all children would have access to early-childhood education that would match that currently provided in kindergartens, and that it would essentially be free with open access to all. However, the Associate Minister of Education---the member for Matamata---now exposes the secret agenda whereby pre-school children are subjected to the user-pays system. The only conclusion one can come to from the introduction of the Bill is that as the fees are charged the funding from the public purse for early-childhood education will be cut to make way for funding in other sectors. We also have to ask whether the same principle will next be applied to primary schools, and, after them, to secondary schools. One cannot avoid arriving at that conclusion. That is true. The first point that I would like to make about this Bill is to agree with a couple of previous speakers who said that it shows a maturing of New Zealand's attitude. New Zealand historically has had a rather cavalier approach to personal security. I go no further than the example of Mr Lange, who from time to time, as large as his frame was, tried to dodge away from his personal diplomatic protection officer because he felt that somehow that officer's presence constrained him and was an invasion of his personal privacy. But as time has gone on, other unsavoury aspects of the world have come to New Zealand, and people do feel less secure about personal security in many areas. We have come to accept that personal protection officers, as they are called, are a fact of life. The second thing that I would like to agree with is that by having a clear and open process for the people who come here as personal protection officers for senior foreign politicians, we will have some certainty about what they are carrying and what they are up to. I accept the notion that if we said that, no, these people cannot carry any weapons in this country, they would do that anyway. I am not saying that we should change the law because people are going to flout it, but I think we have to accept, to a degree, some of those realities. I think there is an even more important reason that we should support this Bill. If we took the view that my parliamentary colleague Matt Robson put forward---that we have the resources to guarantee everybody's security, that the New Zealand Police and the New Zealand Army are all that is required---we would be saying that we absolutely guaranteed the personal safety and security of those foreign diplomats and politicians when they come to this country. If we said that we guaranteed their personal security, and we failed, then the responsibility would be absolutely ours, percent. I agree with this Bill from the perspective that if we agree that senior foreign politicians can bring their own personal protection officers with them, we are saying that the security of those people is a shared responsibility, and that if something goes wrong, New Zealand is not absolutely, solely, and only responsible. So I think that in that regard the Bill is quite sensible. We are sharing the responsibility. The second point I will make about this matter is that from my own reading and from discussions with other people---this is not from my own personal experience---I know that a quite strong rapport develops between the person who is being protected and the people who surround him or her. That is very important because the person who is being protected wants to be assured that the people offering him or her protection will do everything that they possibly can to guarantee the preservation of that person's life. It is an instance where people will genuinely put their lives on the line. The senior politicians coming from overseas want to make sure that they have that certainty, that the people assigned to them will do everything---and I mean everything---to protect their lives. We cannot give that quality of assurance to those people when we assign them staff whom they do not know. If we were to say to those people that we would look after their personal security, and that we would do so entirely with New Zealand staff, we would not be offering them the comfort of the personal security that they expect and demand. If we are to have the conference go well, we want people to feel secure in this country. Of course, we feel secure here because we live here. Unlike many other countries, people eat fish and chips for lunch on the lawn of Parliament. In many Parliaments members of the public cannot get anywhere near the front lawn. Quite often, when people come here they comment to me that they cannot believe that office workers and others sit on the steps of Parliament to eat their lunches. It simply would not be seen in some countries. We are relaxed about that, and so we should be, and it is something I am very grateful for---

I sometimes wonder if I was at the same select committee as the chairman who has just reported back on the Bill. The House should understand that that Bill was introduced well before the last election. It had a proposed implementation date of October . It has an expiry date of September , and now, almost months later, Parliament is being asked to consider it again. I do not believe that the chairman of the committee could honestly say that the submissions were supportive of the Bill or of the Government's thrust in unemployment. Indeed, the environment at the committee was one of great frustration that the Government had made totally inadequate responses to the very high levels of unemployment. Most of the submissions drew to the attention of the committee the point that since the Government had come to office unemployment had doubled and was increasing. Most of those who made submissions were very critical of the inadequate responses by the Government to those high levels of unemployment, and nobody was prepared to say in front of the committee that the Bill would contribute to an adequate response to unemployment today. In every submission there was, at least, strongly implied criticism of the Government's handling of unemployment. The reality is that the Access programmes were---theoretically at least---in place well before the Bill came to the House. The Government had set a programme of commencement dates for the regional employment and Access councils early in , and those councils were in a state of confusion at the time the legislation came to the House. Those who made submissions were equally confused about the aim of the Government in the matter of unemployment. Indeed, several of organisations that made submissions, such as the Salvation Army and the Young Men's Christian Association, had had their work programmes axed recently by the newly constituted regional employment and Access councils. Those organisations were critical of the Minister of Employment and the Government for the handling of the resources that had been built up in New Zealand to cope with the need for training in the private sector and after young people had left school. Many of those who made submissions complained that they had worked hard to build up the resources. They had implemented good quality training programmes that had been axed by the regional employment and Access councils, and had been forced to dispose of the equipment and resources that had been purchased to train young people. They found that policy difficult to understand. Some people asked why there was a need for legislation, because the councils had been established and the Government had made the allocation of resources, even though that allocation was hopelessly inadequate. The Government was doing all of the things that the Bill would require the regional employment and Access councils to do, without the legislation. The submission made by the National Council of Women queried whether it was necessary to enshrine the scheme in legislation. The council could recall no similar legislation, and, given the insistence of the Minister of Justice that there was too much legislation already, expressed some surprise. The fundamental question is whether it is necessary to legislate when the schemes the Government has brought together with a hiss and a roar are, theoretically at least, in place. The Bill proved to be window-dressing. It was an attempt by the Government to create the impression that it was doing something about unemployment when it was not. Many of the submissions contained widespread criticism of the lack of accountability. Members have already had the experience when asking the Minister of Employment questions about Access programmes of the Minister saying that the programmes had nothing to do with him, that he had washed his hands of them, and that members should ask the regional employment and Access councils. The Bill makes some important changes to the Survey Act . Some aspects of that Act concerned the Opposition at the time the Bill was before the House, and they are still of concern. Two clauses in the amendment Bill add to that concern. I shall raise a few questions and make a few comments on those particular clauses. Clause deals with fees and charges and clause deals with the powers of the Director-General of the Department of Survey and Land Information. The concern of the Opposition about clause is that, unlike the present legislation whereby fees are set by Order in Council on the recommendation of the Minister, the new Bill provides that the Director-General---or Chief Executive---of the Department of Survey and Land Information will unilaterally set fees for the department, which has monopoly powers in some instances. The department has a monopoly power to carry out its function of examining survey plans. The fees for that function will be set by the department. The Opposition is concerned about that matter and will take it up with the select committee. I distinguish between the functions of the department when it has a monopoly under the law in relation to the survey and title system, and the functions that it is empowered to undertake under the Act that are not related to its responsibility to examine survey plans. If the department is empowered to carry out a monopoly function the Opposition believes that this shift in the system of setting fees is bad; the department becomes less transparent, the Government becomes less answerable, and the department is delegating the function to a senior civil servant. There is no right of appeal and no sense of responsibility of the Government. That is the first point. The second point is in relation to clause . The Act was typical of many of the changes made by the Government whereby it empowered the apparatus of the State---if one likes to use that description---to compete with the private sector. The new Department of Survey and Land Information---previously the Department of Lands and Survey---has now within its competence, its statutory rights, the ability to compete with private sector survey firms. I do not like that position because it is not necessary in our form of economy; it is not essential for the State to set up in competition with the private sector, which can provide adequately the wide range of services that the public demands from the survey profession. The State, in its position of privilege, does not need to compete. The Opposition continues to object to the Bill because the Bill expands the powers of the director-general. A general authority is given to enter into contracts or arrangements with any other person. The Opposition would have no objection to the Bill if the powers and functions of the department were confined to what it should be doing---that is, working for the State and having a statutory role in examining survey plans and so on; but the legislation has been amended to give the department an unconfined role to compete in the private sector, and the Opposition does not agree that the functions and responsibilities of the department should be further expanded. The Opposition will consider that matter also during the select committee stage. Those are the Opposition's general objections to the Bill. The Opposition will not vote against the Bill at this stage. It may be that after hearing the submissions to the select committee the Opposition will take a stronger line. I should like to hear what private sector surveyors, and those who are competing with the department, have to say about the unilateral setting of fees as a monopoly, and the expanded opportunities to compete in the private sector. I know that my colleague the member for Awarua wants to say something about the matter, and I shall leave the other aspects of the Bill to be raised by him.
