I move, That the Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Amendment Bill (No. ) be introduced. The Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Act received royal assent on April , and the bulk of the Act came into effect from July that year. The legislation represented a major review and overhaul of the accident compensation legislation, which had been introduced in . There had been some reviews in the years before the introduction of the Act. Briefly, to bring the present amendment into context, the reason for it was that for years under the previous Government the accident compensation expenditure had been increasing at the rate of percent per year. Clearly, that was unsustainable, and put huge pressure on premiums and employer levies, and on the scheme itself. So it was reviewed, and the new Act came into effect, as I have said, principally from July . Now that that scheme has been running for almost year, the Government has listened to the experience of claimants and agrees that it is now appropriate to consider some amendments. These need to be made to ensure that the principle of fairness, which was the underlying principle of the review, is preserved through this legislation. In particular, those people who were high users of attendant care under the old accident compensation scheme will, under this amendment, have their entitlement grandparented for life. Workers who are injured and who are also eligible for national superannuation will no longer be compelled to choose between the forms of income but will be able to receive both for the first months. Changes are also made to the calculation of earnings for self-employed people to ensure that they are not disadvantaged. Those are quite substantial changes to improve the scheme and to make it fairer in respect of entitlements to people who have suffered personal injuries. Other major changes will be made for the benefit of low-income earners and self-employed people with a low income. There will be cover for clinical trials, which was a matter of debate; there will be teacher-aides and transport for children to school when parents have suffered personal injury; and there will be a reinstating of the proposal of trusts for payments for children in certain circumstances, which I will explain further in my address. In addition to those amendments, the opportunity is also being taken to amend the Act to reflect the provisions of the health reforms---that is, the new Health and Disability Services Bill. It is intended that the Bill will be referred to the Labour Committee to allow submissions on the amendments and to allow consideration and deliberation by the parliamentarians on that select committee. I turn now to the specific provisions of the proposed legislation. Clause excludes from the definition of ``accident'' any treatment that is provided outside New Zealand by a person whose qualifications are equivalent to those of a registered health professional. This treatment is already included in the definition of ``medical misadventure''. Clause amends the Act so that personal injury that results from a drug or clinical trial that has been approved by an appropriate ethics committee will be covered as ``medical misadventure'' under the scheme---and our hospitals will be pleased to hear that. Clause also makes a technical amendment to ensure that where a person has suffered personal injury by medical misadventure and sustains further personal injury by reason of an abnormal reaction or later complication, that later personal injury will still be covered by the scheme. The clause also extends the definition of a ``registered health professional'' in the Act to include a person with the equivalent qualifications to those of a registered health professional in New Zealand. Clauses , , and are amendments that will ensure that in the areas of gradual process, disease, or infection arising in the course of employment, and for victims of criminal conduct, the ``injury'' must have occurred in New Zealand or while the claimant was ordinarily resident in New Zealand. As there is a deemed date of personal injury for these types of injury, it is currently possible under the scheme for a person to have been a New Zealand resident on the deemed date of the injury, but not to have had that status at the date of the incident that gives rise to the cover, so that will correct that anomaly. Cover under section of the Act is also extended to those cases in which the employment through which the exposure occurred continued beyond April . Clause restricts the corporation's liability for designing individual rehabilitation programmes to those matters that are the corporation's responsibility. Clause provides that social rehabilitation regulations may include payment for teacher-aides, as well as for transport to school for children requiring special assistance. Clause amends the test of capacity for work so that it clearly applies to people who have cover as earners, or for loss of potential earning capacity, but who were not in employment at the time that they were injured. Under the Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Amendment Act, weekly earnings, for the purposes of weekly compensation, are the lesser of either of one fifty-second of earnings during the previous year or one-quarter of the earnings of the weeks prior to the incapacity. This has resulted in difficulties, particularly for people with seasonal earnings. Clause provides that weekly earnings for periods of incapacity after the first weeks will be calculated as one fifty-second of the previous year's earnings. This provision will be much fairer and will remove that anomaly as well. Problems have arisen with the calculation of earnings for the self-employed, particularly those who have been self-employed for only a short time, or those who have not yet filed their income tax returns for the taxation year immediately preceding their incapacity. Under clause , these people will be entitled to a minimum rate of weekly earnings as set out in the Act for the first weeks of incapacity after the first week. At present, they are often not entitled to compensation until weeks after the incapacity. This clause also allows the use of an earlier income tax return if the preceding year's return is unavailable. However, earlier tax returns may be used only for months after the incapacity, after which time the preceding year's return should be available. I think that, in practice, that will work well. Clause clarifies section of the Act to ensure that there is only a -week stand-down period in respect of each personal injury even where there are subsequent periods of incapacity arising from the same personal injury. Clause provides a more equitable approach to providing compensation for non-work accidents to those who pay the minimum annual earner premium. At present some people would be paying the minimum premium but may not be entitled to receive the minimum weekly earnings. Clause ensures that the assessments of capacity for work must follow the criteria set out in the Act. That clause covers a small crack that appeared in the legislation. Due to the way in which the scheme's abatement provisions are applied, it is possible for a person in part-time work after an injury to receive more than he or she was receiving prior to the injury, by receiving both earnings for the hours worked part-time and also the weekly compensation. Clause therefore provides a cap to the compensation to ensure that it is not possible to earn in total more than was earned prior to the injury. I think that would be seen to be fair, as well. Clause relates primarily to compensation paid for loss of potential earning capacity. The Act currently states that the capacity for work can only be assessed months after the incapacity commences. This clause makes it clear that the assessment can also be done more than months after the incapacity. Clause amends the current situation in which a person who is eligible to receive national superannuation, but who is also eligible for weekly compensation after an injury, must make an election as to which form of income he or she will receive. I have had a number of submissions on that point. I do not believe that it is too difficult to demonstrate that it is unfair if somebody is receiving national superannuation, is also in employment and paying both the employer's and the non-earner's premium, and has an accident but is not entitled to income-related compensation. The provision will now change so that such a person will be entitled to receive both forms of income for a period of year after incapacity. At the end of that year that person will need to elect which form of compensation he or she wishes to receive for the following months---national superannuation or the earnings-related compensation. At the end of months the person will then return to receiving national superannuation if he or she had previously elected to receive weekly compensation.

I take it from the interjections being made by the Opposition that it favours people being able to stay who are here illegally. The Government takes a different view. It takes the view that people need a permit to come to New Zealand and need a permit to remain in New Zealand. Migrants, like all others, should be required to obey the law. Given that those legal issues are themselves uninvolved and rarely contested, it is proposed to streamline the procedure. It is proposed to give the Secretary of Labour or an immigration officer delegated by the Secretary of Labour the power to issue a removal order in respect of any person when the Secretary of Labour or officer is satisfied that the person is not a New Zealand citizen, does not hold a permit, and is not exempt from the requirement to hold a permit. Those grounds for making a removal order are identical to those on which a district court at present is required to be satisfied before issuing a removal warrant. The new procedure will contain a number of important safeguards. In the case of a person on whom a removal order has been served choosing to leave New Zealand within days, the removal order will be cancelled. Alternatively, the person may appeal to the Removal Review Authority against the removal order within a -day period. If a person neither appealed against a removal order nor left voluntarily within a set period, a district court judge would need to endorse the order before it could be executed. Part II also makes provision for the establishment of an independent Removal Review Authority to consider appeals against removal. The authority is to consider appeals on factual or humanitarian grounds and to determine whether it is appropriate for an individual in New Zealand to be removed from the country. If an appellant is a New Zealand citizen or holds a permit or an exemption from holding a permit, the authority could cancel removal orders on factual grounds. On humanitarian grounds the authority could cancel an order or limit the -year period during which the order would normally be enforced. Part III concerns the right to appeal to the High Court on questions of law arising from a decision of the Removal Review Authority or the Residence Appeal Authority. Part III also provides for an increase in fines for carriers---that is, airlines---and persons in charge of craft where responsibilities under the Immigration Act have not been met. Events of recent times have clearly demonstrated that New Zealand lacks proper custodial provisions in legislation to cover security concerns about individuals arriving at New Zealand's border. That limitation has been shown up by, but is not confined to, individuals who arrive with no prior screening and without documentation but who then claim refugee status on arrival. The deficiency in legislation has been the subject of comment in the Court of Appeal, and also by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and other groups. The proposed amendments will ensure that, if security status cannot be determined on arrival, detention will be provided until an application for a permit or a claim for refugee status or security status itself can be determined---whichever is the earlier. Warrants of commitment will be issued by district court judges. Other amendments in Part III to powers of entry and inspection will remove the current limitation that those powers be exercised only in instances in which there is knowledge of a particular person being in New Zealand unlawfully, and will increase the level of general penalties for offences against the Immigration Act. Transitional provisions in Parts I and II would ensure that applications lodged before the enactment of the Bill will continue to be processed as before, and that rights previously held will remain unaffected for those applications. I want to make it clear that there will not be an amnesty for any persons who are overstayers at the time that the proposed legislation comes into place. The Bill does, however, make provision for persons unlawfully in New Zealand at the time to come forward and apply for a temporary permit or a residence permit as they can at present under the provisions of section () of the Immigration Act . This Bill will be referred to the Labour Committee. I expect the committee to look closely at a number of proposed changes. I also expect that it will invite submissions from parties with an interest in immigration matters. I pay tribute to the chairman of the working-party on immigration, Mr Bill Wilson; to members of the working-party, Mr David Brown and Mr Russell Davis; and also to the many individuals, including officials from the Department of Labour and the New Zealand immigration service, who have contributed to this new policy development. In conclusion, I reiterate that this Bill has been designed to maintain the integrity of New Zealand's proactive immigration policy and to provide a legislative framework suitable for New Zealand in the s.

It is no use blaming the Government for the state of housing, health, and education. Under the policies of the Labour Government those institutions were falling to bits, were being abused, and were ridden with inequities. Successive Governments have been borrowing to maintain the very large amounts of expenditure involved in health, housing, social welfare, and superannuation. Year after year, that policy was adding to the country's debt. When I came back into office after six long years in Opposition I found that the biggest change was that the level of debt had trebled. The cost of paying the interest on the public debt and of servicing that debt was the second largest item of Government expenditure, and it was rising rapidly. It was no longer sustainable. More than $ million a year was being spent on paying the interest on a debt that had trebled during the years that the Labour Government had been in office. The country could no longer afford to continue to borrow to fund social services and superannuation, but the policies had to change in any case because of the lack of delivery of services and of equity. I have long been a supporter of universality of national superannuation, which I believe is fair and equitable if the country can afford it. However, we cannot justify borrowing and increasing that debt burden to redistribute substantial funds or payments through superannuation to persons who have substantial resources of their own. Universality of national superannuation is the fairest system when the country can afford it. However, the Labour Government trebled the public debt in years, and that system is no longer affordable. That is the stark reality. As I said, the interest on the debt costs more than $ million a year. The Budget contains many bold and far-reaching decisions that had to be made. It is a watershed Budget that will establish a new foundation for the delivery of health, accident compensation, social welfare, retirement superannuation, housing, and education for decades to come. Much of the reform is designed to encourage greater individual self-reliance---which must be encouraged---and greater individual independence.

It gives me a great deal of pleasure to move, That the Tax Reduction and Social Policy Bill be now read a second time. This is an omnibus Bill, which implements the tax reductions and the social policy programmes announced by the Government on February. It is my intention at the conclusion of the debate to move that the Bill be referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and that the committee report the Bill back to the House on or before April. The background of the Bill is straightforward. The Government has dealt with the fiscal crisis inherited in . It has set New Zealand on a path of sustainable growth. At currently projected rates the economy will double in size by the year . Without alteration in tax rates, growth has substantially boosted Government revenue, creating new options for New Zealand that are the envy of many other Governments around the world. Health and education are top priorities for National. As a result of economic growth, we have been able to put an extra $, million into health and education since -. On top of that, a further $ million has already been committed to those areas in the next years. That is a total gain for health and education of $. billion over that period. Through growth and responsible fiscal management, we have dramatically reduced net public debt, which is now projected to fall from its peak of percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in to less than percent of GDP by June . But notwithstanding those large expenditures, the fiscal surplus was projected to reach $. billion by ----far larger than is required. Growth and good management now give us opportunities for major social and economic progress. After making provision for an ongoing surplus of at least percent of GDP, plus ongoing increases in the priority social spending areas, especially those of health and education, the Government is asking the House today to invest the rest of that revenue in an improved future for the low and middle income people in this country; in particular, in a better future for low and middle income families. So why does the Government have that clear focus? In any nation, low and middle income working people make up the vast bulk of the workforce. They are the engine-room of an economy. Without their energy, their commitment, their initiative, and their continuously improving skills, a nation is unlikely to grow rapidly. For some years now, low and middle income working people in New Zealand have, as I see it, been short-changed. Firstly, during recent years leading up to the change of Government, Government spending rose substantially as a percentage of GDP. Low and middle income families do not have a lot to come and go on. Expenditure and taxes at that level undoubtedly put a burden on those families. Secondly, since when the recovery began the overriding priorities of National have been employment and stability. The country has taken most of its gains in the form of more jobs---and there have been a lot of them---and less debt, and the Government has got the debt down. This has been a period when ordinary working people have worked harder, in many cases, and have contributed more to the economy than maybe ever before in their lives, and their efforts have been successful.

The Government has a balanced mix of policy objectives, which it will continue to achieve through this year's Budget. Among these policies is the repayment of public debt, which is still far too high. Tax reductions will not be considered by this Government until the debt approaches a more prudent level.

The Earthquake Commission Amendment Bill is a short Bill of only three clauses. Clause is the short title, clause recognises that the Minister of Finance can, and should, ensure that the Earthquake Commission exercises its investment and reinsurance powers in a manner consistent with the management of the Crown's financial position overall. In this regard, the Government's guarantee is crucially important. Given the guarantee, the Minister of Finance has the responsibility to ensure that the Earthquake Commission investment and reinsurance policies remain consistent with the overall management strategy of the Crown. Let me look at some of the public reaction and at some of the components that have made for a good reaction by the media and the analysts. I would identify three large segments in the Budget. The first are the economic and fiscal components. Those forecasts are amongst the best, if not the best, in the OECD. Very few economies around the world today can say that they are producing Budget surpluses, using those to repay debt, having tax cuts at the same time, and allocating resources for social priority areas like health and education. That is an extraordinarily great achievement, and the coalition Government continues to take it forward. In respect of microeconomic reform we have a very full agenda---which, if I get time in this debate, I might be able to develop in some detail---for the coalition both in terms of ongoing achievements like electricity now coming to fruition, and tariffs. We have been able to announce the changes in the tariffs, and some of the labour market changes are about to be announced. We have good ongoing reforms with imminent results and announcements, as well as a forward-looking agenda with reforms on accident compensation. We heard what Michael Cullen said about accident compensation. The reality out in the market place is that the employers want to have accident compensation reformed. They want competition, and they recognise that they will have to pay premiums that will fully fund it to make it competitive. Employers recognise that. It is no use Michael Cullen saying that the employers will pay more. They know that there is a price for getting accident compensation on to a commercial basis and for making it work better. In the longer term the costs of delivering accident compensation will be more competitive and cheaper. We can see the big benefits of some of those microeconomic reforms starting to come to fruition already. Today somebody announced the details of the reduction of new car prices. Medium-priced cars of $, are being reduced by $,. That is a huge drop in the price of a family motor vehicle that will now be available to New Zealanders. No wonder the Labour Opposition has nothing to say! The realistic effects and practical benefits of those changes to ordinary New Zealanders are everywhere for people to see, all across the pages of our national dailies. There are huge reductions in the price of cars. That is what the removal of the prohibition on parallel importing is about, as well. For some goods we pay a price that is above what we can buy them for in other countries. That is because of protection by prohibition of parallel importing. Removing the prohibition on parallel importing will make those goods cheaper in New Zealand. We can look forward to that. What are the electricity microeconomic reforms all about? There is only one objective for the Government in relation to electricity reforms, and that is to make sure that the producers of electricity are operating in a more competitive environment, that it drives down the costs of generating electricity, and that they sell it cheaper to the consumer. So over time New Zealanders can look forward to lower electricity prices. That is essentially what the microeconomic reforms are all about. Tax cuts were also confirmed in the Budget. On July---

The fact remains, and I think the Labour Party should start to recognise it, that Michael Cullen is a liability to the Labour Party. He has demonstrated that on a number of occasions and he continues to demonstrate it in the House. My advice to the Labour Party members is that if they do not like receiving back what they give, then they should take stock of their own position. The fact is that the Bill before the House today is a development---a consequence if one likes---of a very careful assessment by the coalition Government of the workloads of a coalition Government, recognition of the wide responsibilities of the Treasury Ministers, and the need to share power. That was expressed in the protocols very carefully brought together and negotiated, and now reflected in this legislation. My sincere belief is it will be a permanent development in the establishment of the executive Government. I have to say it does work well. The three Treasury Ministers, led by the Treasurer, including the Assistant Treasurer, John Delamere, and myself as the Minister of Finance, have brought together a lot of resources and energy on the seventh floor of the Beehive and we are now well advanced in bringing the Budget together. The process has worked well and will be very good in terms of economic and fiscal policy management. That I think is excellent. I invite members to go back and read the protocol document, which was publicly released after the coalition was formed in December. It is a shame that Labour Party members have displayed this ongoing arrogance. They were invited to have a briefing to actually get in behind the substance and merits of this proposal so that they would know more about it. But, no, they bring this supercilious, superior, half-hearted, jocular, arrogant approach, which is so characteristic of Michael Cullen's performance in the House.

The Minister produces all sorts of rhetoric, and counts all sorts of money and gets to a fancy figure, but the fact of the matter is that the Government declines to get enthusiastically behind the exercise and to ensure that a large number of New Zealanders, who traditionally have not had the part in the political system that they should have had, know of their rights, simply because the Government knows that most Maori voters will not vote for the National Party. This is a deliberate and cynical attempt---given that under the mixed-member proportional representation system (MMP) every vote will count---to cut down the anti - National Party vote. From the National Party's own crude political position, it has no incentive at all to encourage Maori to go on to any roll. Whatever rhetoric the Minister of Justice comes up with---and he has a reputation for being a fair-minded, decent Minister---on this occasion he has undermined his own credibility. The Government has spent money on all sorts of publicity campaigns, many of which have been extremely dubious. This occasion is an extremely important constitutional exercise not just for Maori but also for the credibility of the whole electoral system as we move to MMP. It is a complete failure on the part of the Minister in particular that the Government has declined to fund a decent publicity campaign that has some chance of being effective. That is the first reason, which I support in detail, that members should support the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition. Secondly, I shall address the matter of poverty. The Government recently held a caucus meeting in Nelson, and, at the time, I congratulated the Government on its excellent choice of venue. I sent a message to the National caucus via the Prime Minister, which I assume it got to know about. I welcomed the caucus to Nelson and pointed out that I hoped that caucus members would have time to enjoy the vitality, enthusiasm, innovative spirit, and diversity of the Nelson community---

Yes, the Minister, to defuse a very controversial issue, a week or so before an election said: ``Yes, I accept the recommendation, we will drop this particularly repugnant clause , which allows the Minister to lease out marginal strips.'' But against strong opposition from Labour members, clause has emerged virtually intact from the select committee and it specifically allows marginal strips to be leased. We think that is quite unacceptable. Yes, the select committee did hear a certain amount of evidence from the department but we were unpersuaded that the view of the working-group should be changed. We continue to subscribe to the view expressed by the working-group and which the Minister repeated in his press statement on October---a week before the election---that the whole principle of public access to marginal strips should not be compromised for a few cases. That is the position of the Opposition and I am sure it will be the position of the members of the working-group when they discover that basically they have been betrayed by the Government, which said ``No problem, we will sort out clause and drop it.'' They will now find that clause has been retained. I am sure that the Minister will have some explaining to do in that regard, in a little while. A number of other matters arise, and perhaps at this point I should mention the question of the West Coast Accord because I would not want to be entirely churlish. The work done by the committee on the West Coast Accord provisions was very good, and we have emerged with a much better set of provisions than those that went into the select committee. The Minister will find it a great deal easier to gazette the reserves than he would have, had the select committee not done that detailed work. I am particularly disappointed that the Government rejected the Queen's Chain Protection Bill. The committee heard submissions and in the light of those submissions I suggested some amendments. One submission suggested that guardians should not just be members of conservation boards, but also be members of local fish and game councils. I thought that was a good idea and I wished to move an amendment to that effect, along with a couple of other amendments, to improve my Bill. I regret to report to the House that I could not move those amendments because the Government had a predetermined mind-set to chuck out the Bill; we did not even get to put them in the Bill so the House could consider an improved Queen's Chain Protection Bill. The Government was not about to give conservation board members or Fish and Game Council members any kind of power of veto over certain ministerial decisions. Government members ran the argument that there was something constitutionally repugnant about it, but there is a direct precedent in the Conservation Act with provision for the guardians of the southern lakes. References elsewhere also state that the Minister cannot act---or he does so at great legal peril---unless he acts on the recommendation of a conservation board or the Conservation Authority. It was not such a radical provision. I would have hoped that the Government would accept it. I might say that Government members voted for the introduction of my Bill in September because they did not dare vote against it weeks or so out from an election. But now they are safely past an election, they thought they could dump it. They are proposing to dump it, and I think that is a matter of very considerable regret. There are a couple of other things I want to mention in this contribution. One other area that may well be controversial is the question of fish and game commercial hunting, and fishing guide licences. The proposal that went to the select committee that there should be provision for the Minister to require those guides to obtain commercial licences from the Fish and Game Council and pay appropriate fees has been dropped. The Opposition reserved its position on that particular matter, and it is certainly my view that we ought to reinstate that power. It is not very often that Oppositions want to give members of the Government increased powers but it certainly is our view that the Minister of Conservation ought to have that discretion to charge reasonable fees to commercial fish and game guides if he thinks that is appropriate. That is really based on the principle that those guides are deriving an income, a living, from using a resource maintained and provided by the Fish and Game Council, and it is therefore reasonable that they should make a contribution, as well as the contribution being made by their clients who, themselves, of course, take out fishing licences. One other matter the committee considered, and that is noted in the narrative report, is the question of a public process for mining access on conservation land. Currently there is no requirement for a public consultation process before the Minister agrees to an access arrangement in respect of the Crown Minerals Act. A number of people who submitted to us---the Royal Forest and Bird Protection Society and others---thought this was inconsistent. Broadly, I think, the committee agreed with them, but that is a matter we did not feel competent to deal with in the committee. But we have specifically written, or are about to write, to the Minister of Conservation about the matter. I would like to ask the Minister what he is likely to do and whether he might agree that we should deal with this anomaly now.

The Minister asks me to make up some more. That is the absolute truth. The Government has systematically dismissed career public servants in the Beehive and replaced them with party political appointees. That is a fact. That is an example of what will happen in the rest of the Public Service. I imagine that there will be jobs for the boys and the girls. One could conjure up a wonderful list of potential appointees. What about Pat Kelly for foreign affairs? Well, he might be straighter than the present one. What could Bill Andersen---New Zealand's leading communist---do? He could probably have the Ministry of Defence. Hone Kaa, that well-known journalist on television, could have the Department of Justice. Someone suggested Jim Knox for the Department of Education. Jim is not too well at the moment, and he may not be able to do the job. What about Dame Ann Hercus? Well, there is a thought. I suppose she could run the civil aviation division, defence of airports, and island tours. Syd Jackson could run the police. He is a well-known supporter of the police. If the Government wants to look after the Department of Labour and totally politicise it, why not put in old Ken Douglas? I am certain that Ken would like to do that job. If the Government really wants to bring intellect into the running of Treasury, a former Labour member of Parliament, Eddie Isbey, is available for the job. Someone suggested that a former Labour member of Parliament, John Kirk, could get a job---perhaps in the Department of Social Welfare, or a job relating to ``perks''. We may laugh, but let us consider the serious prospects. Under the Bill any one of those persons could be appointed to any one of those positions. There is absolutely nothing in the Bill to prevent the Executive Council from appointing any one of those persons to those positions. That is the position under this obnoxious legislation. Each and every one of those persons I identified has the necessary qualifications, because no qualifications are required to be appointed to positions I named---the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, the Department of Justice, the Department of Education, the Police Department, the Department of Labour, and Treasury. One could go through the list and put others underneath them of the same ilk and the same political persuasion. It is fascinating to know what some of the academics said, but Dr Walsh from Victoria University of Wellington summed it up best of all in the submission he made to the committee. He said that the Bill had been produced at great speed, and introduced in duplicitous circumstances; that its contents reflect lack of careful thought or wide consultation; that the select committee should recommend that Parliament should not proceed with the Bill in its present form; and that the Government should undertake to negotiate with the Combined State Unions on its contents. I agree with Dr Walsh. That is the recommendation that the committee should have brought to Parliament, but it is not too late for Parliament to be master of its own destiny. The select committee is but a servant of Parliament, and Parliament is master of its own destiny. All it requires is that the Labour back-benchers have the strength to vote according to their convictions, and that one by one they demonstrate that strength, and the strength to represent and reflect the views of those who elected them to Parliament. That is the challenge that finally is before Parliament, because Parliament cannot hide anywhere. It cannot run away from its responsibilities; it cannot blame the select committee; it has to make the final decision. It can make the decision in the second reading to vote the Bill down and out. That means that the existing State Services Conditions of Employment Act will remain in force until new and appropriate legislation is drafted after due consideration and due reflection on the issues, and brought to Parliament and taken through the parliamentary process. That is the challenge that faces each and every elected member of the Chamber, and I invite them one by one to explore their own consciences. Do they want to be part of a political party that will introduce into the New Zealand Public Service the potential for corruption---and therefore be part of introducing and passing legislation that they have been warned about by people at the highest level in their own party and other senior people involved and informed on the issue? That is what they will do if they vote in the Ayes lobby. They would be voting with their eyes open, because they have had advice from their party that the Bill would introduce not only total politicisation in the Public Service but the potential for corruption from top to bottom. I ask members to pause. It is easy to make gestures in Parliament, but it is important to stand and vote.

The laughter of his members shows how little they care for their former leader. What they are saying by their laughter is that they did not understand the pressure they were putting the Prime Minister under; that they did not have any appreciation of what the divisions and the backbiting were doing; and that, in the light of the long, detailed letters of self-aggrandisement that the member for Manurewa wrote to all and sundry, and released, they did not seem to understand that that was putting in place the eventual demise of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister had to perform many times and on grand occasions, and occasionally he had to acknowledge that he had failed. One of those occasions would have been when he told the public that the policies he was elected on had been subverted by his own team. That would not have been easy for him to say, but at least he had the honesty to say it, and he should have marks for that. Even the member for Hawke's Bay, whom I have mentioned, finally managed to summon up the courage to play Brutus and sneak in the blade that forced the Prime Minister to announce his resignation yesterday. I do not think that the Prime Minister would have made that announcement with great enthusiasm. He is a young man who would have preferred to carry through some of the programmes to reach some of the goals---but he was not permitted to do so. I say to the House on this historic occasion, when one Prime Minister makes a statement in farewell and hands over to another, that for New Zealand's sake I hope that Government members---having succeeded in replacing their leader, as they have assiduously sought to do for months, and elected a new leader and a new deputy leader---will, in New Zealand's interest, allow them---

On behalf of the Opposition, I associate Opposition members with that message of sympathy to the wife and family of Constable Umbers. They will extend to the family directly the sympathy of the Opposition, and I am sure of the wider New Zealand community. It may be eased a little by the fact that Constable Umbers died honourably in the course of duty, and it is hoped that New Zealand will learn something from his death. The Deputy Prime Minister said that the Opposition was concerned about policy. I find it fascinating that in the first imprest supply debate of the new parliamentary session the Government did not call upon one of its five Ministers with responsibility for finance to lead the debate. Instead, it chose the Deputy Prime Minister who, demonstrably, is an ignorant member of the team on financial matters. The House has had to put up with the growth of the Executive. For many years before the Deputy Prime Minister entered Parliament he was critical of such growth, yet today he gets up to defend the Government, instead of one of the five Ministers with responsibility for finance. During his gloating about the lower consumer price index for the September quarter---which was close to my prediction of . percent---he said he wanted a debate on the fundamentals. I shall examine the fundamentals. There has been no economic growth, and the forecast is for a minus growth rate. Three years and three months after the Government was elected the economy will get smaller. That is a basic fundamental in terms of opportunity and employment. Interest rates have been at record levels and are increasing to higher levels. New Zealand leads the world with its high interest rates, and that is another fundamental that I want to consider, and that the newly appointed Government finance spokesman, the Deputy Prime Minister, should consider. The level of investment indicates confidence or a lack of confidence in the future. There is no investment in manufacturing, agriculture, horticulture, or forestry. I ask whether there is confidence in the future, and the answer must be no. I turn to another fundamental: people and jobs. There is no job growth in New Zealand. Last year full-time jobs were lost. That is another fundamental that I invite the Deputy Prime Minister to consider. He should not gloss over those facts, and he should not gloat that the Government has achieved a great breakthrough. I expect the Government to respond to the fundamentals that I am raising. I shall turn to the future confidence of the country. Is such confidence expressed by a surge of people coming to New Zealand, or is it expressed by a tail wave of New Zealanders leaving the country? The record numbers of New Zealanders leaving New Zealand indicate that people see no future in their homeland. That is another fundamental that the Government should consider. Would the Government consider honestly the matter of the internal deficit? I do not mean the fiddle, but a genuine measure of the total Government sector borrowing, which would include the borrowings of the State-owned corporations and institutions such as the Rural Bank and the Housing Corporation. If those borrowings are taken into account the result will be a continuing massive deficit of billions of dollars, not a surplus. That is another fundamental of the economy. I turn to the fundamentals as measured by the exchange rate and the impact on the export sector. The Deputy Prime Minister will acknowledge that the message is one of disaster. The debate should be on the fundamentals, and the economic debate should deal with the issue of people. I shall not draw on comments made by Opposition members, academic critics, or overseas critics, but on comments made by the person who aspires to be---and the rumours are that he will be---the next president of the Labour Party, the secretary of the engineers' union, Rex Jones. In a speech last week he said that a continuation of the Government's economic policy, which he described as ``Rogernomics'', would inevitably end up with the wealthy protecting their property and their homes by building walls around them and placing guns on top of the walls to ward off the hordes of disadvantaged people outside. That comment was made by the man who will probably be the next president of the Labour Party. He dealt with the fundamentals. Predictably, the member for Wellington Central forgot to mention that she was a Minister in the outgoing Labour Government that pursued the policies that put more than , New Zealanders on the dole. She stayed there and voted for those policies that put New Zealanders on the scrap-heap of unemployment. She then has the audacity to come into Parliament and say that she is concerned and that she feels for those who are out of work; for those who are distressed; for those who are hurt; for those who cannot pay their home mortgages; for those who do not see a future; and for the young people who do not know what they will do after they leave school. She says that she is concerned. Where was she for the past years? Was she deaf? Was she blind? Did she not see what was happening? Does she not understand that when her Government spent more than the country earned the overseas debt was doubled; that the Government's debt was more than doubled; that there would be a day of reckoning; that New Zealand has one sacred cow it must deal with; and that the legislation and the announcements made in Parliament yesterday dealt with that sacred cow? That sacred cow means that as a country we cannot continue to spend more than we earn. For too long we have seduced ourselves into accepting that we could continue to spend, spend, and spend, when we did not have the money. The day of reckoning is finally approaching. The new Government has the courage to face up to that day of reckoning. Sure, it would have been easy to say ``Yes'' to every spending priority, but Government members of Parliament---most of whom are new to the Chamber---had the courage to consider the facts and to agree with Cabinet that we had to deal with those issues. Opposition members would claim the mantle of Michael Joseph Savage, but they should remember one thing that Savage said: ``You can't spend money before you earn it.''. That is what Savage said at the commencement of the welfare State. He knew, with the clarity of a person who had worked---and very few Opposition members have---and earned his wage, that he could not spend it before it was earned. For the past years the Labour Government has worked on the presumption that someone would provide. Even if New Zealand did not earn the money, somehow we would borrow it and go out with a beggar's bowl and borrow some more. New Zealand has borrowed from the world time and time again. The country has been great at spending the savings of the rest of the world. It is time that we fronted up to the fact and to the hard reality that the country has avoided for too long. I am sure that the member for Sydenham, who wants to follow me, thought that we should spend more, just as the member for Wellington Central and other Opposition members thought that we should spend more. Each and every one of them thinks that we should spend more. That is the only message that has come out of the debate from Opposition members. They simply say: ``Spend more''. We cannot do that. The member who preceded me in the debate, the member for Wellington Central, was in Cabinet when the documents were signed. Those people are the ones who committed the money. Government members are prepared to face up to New Zealand's sacred cow of recent history---that we spend and spend and do not earn. The Government wants to earn more. I tell the Opposition that the overriding goals of the Government are to maintain strong economic growth, then to make certain that we can build a greater measure of social cohesion and stronger communities the length and breadth of New Zealand. No one can stand in this House tonight---certainly neither I nor my colleagues---and suggest that New Zealand has no social problems. Nobody is going to make that vacuous statement, because we know there are social problems. But we are working to resolve those social problems through the education system, through the way in which we deliver the welfare system, through providing the opportunity to families to own their own home, and through ensuring that our police service is properly resourced to do its job. This is all part and parcel of dealing with the social problems that a society like ours has in the middle of the s. These problems are different from those of the s, the s, or the s. We know that. I do not pretend, tonight, that this Budget has solved every one of our social problems, but I do say that we are now in a position to direct resources more aggressively towards solving those problems. That is what we are in a position to do, and that is what we have committed ourselves to do in this Budget. I would like to think that that is something the Labour Opposition could agree with, and that it could agree that that is going in the right direction. Labour Opposition members would want to address those social policies. I know that the Labour Opposition has difficulty with this Budget; it is so good that it is difficult to criticise. Let us face it. What can be criticised on economic grounds? Can it be the deficit? That does not exist. Is the surplus too big? Are the growth rates too strong? The Budget cannot be criticised on those grounds. Labour Opposition members cannot criticise those matters. They cannot criticise their own Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. They want to make a bit of a fuss about the Employment Contracts Act but they are not so stupid as to say that it does not work, because they know that it does. They opposed the Fiscal Responsibility Act, but they know that it is right. The important component of that Act is that never again will any Finance Minister from any political party, of whatever political persuasion, stand up in this House and deliver a Budget made up with mirrors, as happened in when the then Labour Minister of Finance claimed he had a surplus of $ million but there was a $. billion deficit. He will never again be able to do that. Because of the Fiscal Responsibility Act, no political party in the future will be able to go to the electorate and mislead it as to the true state of the nation---as happened prior to the election. The Fiscal Responsibility Act rules out all of that. It means that New Zealanders can vote on the fact, not on the fiction. They can vote on the substance, not that which a series of mirrors seeks to create. That, again, puts substance into New Zealand and into New Zealand policy-making and debate. We have done something else that has altered two very important components of our achievement. One is to build on what was introduced by the Labour Government in the reform in the State sector area. We have been able to achieve very substantial improvement in the delivery of State sector services---Public Service---support, to the country. We are doing it in a way that is far more efficient and far more beneficial, and at a substantial reduction in cost. That is another positive for New Zealand's growth that is often overlooked by commentators, but it is very, very important, indeed. The final and most important point of all is that nothing I have talked about in terms of the success of New Zealand has happened by accident. It is all because of our clear strategic approach to the responsibilities of Government that we engaged in at the commencement of our term of office. We set out to put in place the framework that would deliver the results in the Budget that was presented last Thursday, and that I have been talking about tonight. It is no accident that we are doing so much better. Quite simply, this Government has set out very clearly---in Path to , and, in fact, in an earlier document that National put out before the election, together with The Next Years, which I released about or weeks ago---the corporate plan for New Zealand, which enables everybody, large and small businesses, employers, and employees, to know the focus and the direction of the Government's strategic thinking and policy and to know where we will put our investment. Then the Budget comes along and fills out the detail of the strategy that has been articulated earlier. We will continue to do that---to give substance and coherence to the development of policy in New Zealand. In we set out very ambitious goals for New Zealand, and we restated them in . Yes, we have had our critics. A number have said that the goals would not work; I quoted specifically the leader of the Labour Party tonight, but she was certainly not alone. We went through the political pain, the anguish, and the abuse that our policies caused when they were first introduced, because we were convinced it was the only way that we could deliver a better New Zealand on a sustainable basis. We could have backed off, taken some softer options, tried to garner some additional political support, or whatever, but we confronted all the political downside---and it was considerable. We were convinced that the responsibility rested on us, and if we did not turn round the New Zealand that we knew---the New Zealand we inherited as a Government---this country was for ever going to underperform. Never again would we get the chance to turn it round, because we would have fallen too far behind. We caught New Zealand in time. We are now back at the top of the growth stakes, although not in relation to the gross domestic product per head of population. We are still a long way behind others, because we had fallen so far behind in the past years. I would not want anyone to believe that we have passed the United States, Japan, or even Australia in terms of growth per head of population, because most certainly we have not. We are about half way there with the top two---Japan and the United States---but we have now commenced the climb back up the ladder of a modern developed society with a social conscience that is building and providing for the future. That is what this Budget is all about. It builds on the Budgets of , , and . I thank both the present Minister of Finance and the previous Minister of Finance for the work they put in to bring those Budgets together. I thank my colleagues in Cabinet and caucus for having the raw political courage to see it through in the difficult days. They thoroughly enjoy the right and the opportunity to go forth in this Budget debate to point out the success that they collectively, working with New Zealanders up and down the country, have achieved for New Zealand.

Ngai Tahu rau rangatira, t~en~a koutou. I want to apologise for being a few moments late into the House to hear my colleague and friend the Minister in charge of Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations open the debate. It would be unkind for me to say I was waiting for the Speaker to count the votes of the previous debate, but it was true. I was waiting for that to happen. The process that we heard enunciated by the Minister and supported by the remarks of Jim Sutton a few moments ago traversed but a little of the extraordinarily complex relationship that we have had to try to distil and find answers to in the last years during which the Crown has, in this era, been seriously negotiating to try to find a settlement to the obvious grievances of the Ngai Tahu. I say to those who believe that somehow or other we rush into this Parliament and recklessly offer solutions with other people's money that this was preceded by the tribunal having or years of extensive research to determine the history. It uncovered parts of that history that were, perhaps, less well known or not known. I looked up---and I want to put this on the record of the House---the members of the Waitangi Tribunal who heard the Ngai Tahu claim, because they do not sound like a bunch of left-wing radicals to me: Judge Ashley McHugh, who was the acting Chief Judge of the Maori Land Court; Bishop Manu Bennett, former Bishop of Aotearoa; businessman and the former secretary of the Whakatane trust board, Sir Monita Delamere; the Taupo lawyer and now member of Parliament, Georgina te Heuheu; Professor Sir Hugh Kawharu of the University of Auckland; emeritus Professor Gordon Orr of Victoria University; and the then Chief District Court Judge, Sir Desmond Sullivan. They were the people on the tribunal who heard the case. I read their names into the record just to remind the House that even the most biased observer would have to say these people who went over the history of the relationship between the Crown and Ngai Tahu---before they wrote the report, which was long and extensive---were people of substance, mana, learning, and scholarship. Once the report was delivered we started on the long journey of negotiations. They were long, protracted, and difficult. This occasion will almost certainly be the last time I speak on a piece of legislation in this Parliament. This afternoon I want to place on record my thanks for the leadership of Ngai Tahu in the person of Sir Stephen O'Regan. Steve, I thank you for never losing the faith that we could find a solution; that it was possible, despite all the difficulties, disagreements, phone calls, and meetings, we would finally reach a stage where we could shake hands and say: ``That is as good as we can do.'' That is what we are seeking. The word ``fair'' is an elusive one. The word ``full'' is an impossible one when we look at what history shows us. So, with goodwill, we seek to determine what we can do to remove the hurt, acknowledge the wrongs by apology, determine the size, the quantum, of the redress, and, in particular, focus on that which had a particular significance and a spiritual connotation for the Ngai Tahu people. Pounamu was an obvious early start, but then we had to do the mahinga kai, and go to the Crown Titi Islands, and so on. We had to look at some aspects of the conservation estate. In the end, of course, far more land has gone into conservation. The fear people had was that, according to some mad people, we were going to do all sorts of things and take all the conservation estate and give it away to Maori---terrible thought. At the end of the day we put more land, tens of thousands of hectares more land, into the conservation estate in the negotiations. So in acknowledging the leadership of Sir Tipene, I want to acknowledge the extraordinary support and wisdom of Charlie Crofts and Sid Ashton, whom I describe as the front row---with some feeling, I might say---of the negotiating team. It was a formidable front row, and it never buckled. It may have held its ground at times when we would have liked to move it a little. There were a few attempts---dare I say it---to screw the scrum occasionally to see whether some advantage could be achieved, but at the end of the day I think we had a straight scrum and we were able to get the agreement that we are putting forward for the House's consideration in the legislation the Minister in charge of Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations spoke to a few moments ago. The issue of how wide we should go was clearly one of the greatest importance. The question is how one looks at something that is so large, then determines what component part is sufficient in the circumstances, because that is really what we had to do. In that we were supported by the officials on both sides. They did an extraordinary amount of work. Belinda Clark led the Crown officials. Before her it was Mary-Ann Thompson. The chief negotiator, Brian Roache, and Anneke Goodall from Ngai Tahu were others. Each and every one of them was probing, seeking, and searching for what at times looked to be an elusive answer---an answer to which we could finally put our agreement and decide was correct. But despite all that hard work, all that effort, and all the publicity, a letter came into my office just this day that tells us that, sadly, in the minds of many---maybe some, maybe a few; I should not be harsh---we still as New Zealanders have some journey to go. The letter states: ``Mr J Bolger, Prime Minister (deposed). I would like you to receive this letter while you are still in Parliament. I have written to previous PMs and have always had personal replies. I will be surprised if you reply.'' I say to Mr Brian T Rankine, Kelvin Grove Road, RD , Palmerston North, that I will reply in public. I will not read all the letter---I do not need to; members will get the flavour. Halfway through his one-page letter, he states: ``Your continued attempt to appease this minority group at our expense has cost you your job. Your sell-out to this group of mixed parentage; your slobbering, disgusting nose-rubbing antics with the New Zealand Maori party, are the absolute pits. The facts are that the Maori population in New Zealand do not enhance our lives in any way, you are welcome to them.'' It is great that he is giving them away, is it not? This is the sad bit, and it is why I am reading it publicly: ``As a schoolteacher for the last years''---what extraordinary damage has this man done in that time---``I am well positioned to make rational judgment.'' I suggest that Mr Brian T Rankine represents the sad, sad component of New Zealand society. What I say to this Parliament is that we have to move much beyond that. Why I draw that to members' attention is that there will be the temptation to try to make party politics out of this, and I thank Jim Sutton for not doing so. But there may be others. I say to ACT: ``There is a by-election in my old seat, but do not try to make party politics out of something that goes to the core of New Zealand---the two races that dominate this country, the Maori people and the European people; and many others have come now. Do not try to drive a wedge through it. Do not become a Mr Rankine.'' That is what I say. I leave this House with a great sense of satisfaction about the many things I have seen that have been good in the years I have been here. Yes, we have had bad patches, but I believe that nothing has been as satisfying to me as to see this Parliament in the last few years face the daunting challenge of addressing Maori grievances. If we had walked away---and the politics would have said to walk away---we would have compounded the grievance. We would have created real anger, and the possibility of even more divisive confrontation and even violence. We can avoid all that by honestly and openly admitting the wrong of the past and doing our best to resolve it. I conclude by thanking my good friend Douglas Graham for the extraordinary contribution that he has made to the process. I say without question that if he had not been there to carry the burden through the long days, then we would not have made it to the end of the journey. That is the tribute I pay to Doug Graham. To Sir Tipene and his team, I just say: ``Thank you, thank you, thank you.''

It would pay the member for Napier just to listen, because sometimes we can learn from history. I would have to say that Parliament, because it operates on a -year cycle, ignores the lessons of history. Increasing the dependency of New Zealanders on the State has been nothing short of a national calamity. More than half the people of this country suckle on the public breast in one way or another. We have removed their independence; we have removed their ability to have more control over their lives. We have imposed a great weight of responsibility and fiscal debt on those who have remained in a job and have looked after themselves. One cannot help the poor by destroying the rich. Successive Governments have done that by taxing the very heart out of New Zealanders.

The member for Christchurch North may well laugh. He was part of it, and for the life of me I do not know why he feels ashamed of it now, because the policies are producing the results that at least the Wall Street Journal and many people in America see quite clearly. ``In that period New Zealand has largely shaken off its suffocating dullness and dreary provincialism.'' Those are not my words. They are the words of the Evening Post, written not long ago, at a time when it observed that the social fabric of this decade of radical change had not been ``rent by the disappearance of hundreds of cosy but inefficient post offices. Overseas travel is no longer a bureaucratic exercise governed by daily currency limits, and shops are now stuffed with all manner of competitively priced goods.'' Opposition members are trying to run away from these things. New Zealanders actually like these things. Why do Opposition members want to run away from them? There is no doubt that in that -year period---and it includes years of a National Government---we did not get it all right. The years of the cup of tea that Labour enjoyed, or, at least, imposed on us, really did a great deal of damage in New Zealand. The loss of momentum and the loss of direction caused much unnecessary hardship, which we are having to grapple with in this Parliament right now. Unlike the last speaker, who concentrated on whether the Waitakare bus timetable was available to someone who was looking for something out of the New Zealand health system, we in this House should be concentrating rather more on providing real leadership and direction and a better understanding of what is happening in the rest of the world. I dare to say that far too few members in this House really understand the huge upheaval that has gone on in the rest of the world---and here as well---which will ultimately drive what we do here. We like to kid ourselves in this Parliament that somehow or other we can change the world, or at least New Zealand. Well, we cannot change it. We in this country, we in this economy, are driven by things much bigger than a little New Zealand. That message has not got through even remotely to members of the Alliance Party. We have seen changes in the world economy that have been far more radical than we have seen in any decade this century. What is more, it will not stop simply because the Alliance, or indeed anybody in this House, wants to get off the world. We will be faced with things that perhaps we do not understand, but we in this House must concentrate on the bigger picture when looking at what is best for New Zealand. I venture to suggest that too often we concentrate on a tunnel vision view of really quite minor problems. They are big problems to us individually, or to many of our constituents individually, but they are minor in the sense of the issues we in this Parliament have to deal with. We ought to examine every member in this Parliament to ask just how well we all understand the impact of technology and information changes going on in the world. They will be the driving force behind the things we will have to react to in a policy sense in the future. Technology and the way in which information is transferred around the world will radically change the social organisation in New Zealand in a way we had better try to understand very quickly. In New Zealand we are now at something of a crossroads. We are teetering---and the teeter will happen at the next election---on a choice of whether we go ahead and match what is happening in the rest of the world, or at least try to match what is happening in the world, or whether we go backwards in a way that some members in this House would have us go back to rapidly and without an understanding of what is happening around us. Most of us know in our personal lives---when we change a job, when we get married, when we get divorced, when we do things as people---that the last thing we can do is go backwards. The sense of forward momentum is something that is deep in the human condition, and for that reason, it is no different from New Zealand society. I say to the Alliance that if the choice it is offering New Zealanders is to go backwards---and it surely is---it will condemn this country to a standard of living that will fall faster than we ever achieved post-war, in the years in which we took our eye off the big international ball. I only wish that the Alliance would have the honesty to try to understand the bigger picture before it tries to tell us that we should go backwards. The choice is not between Left and Right in politics any longer. The Alliance might well be committed to the past. Labour is dithering; it does not know whether to own up to and be proud of what has happened over the past years, and in which they played an important part. But for all that, the Labour Party is dithering. It does not know what direction to go in. They do not know whether to go forward; they do not know whether to go back. But Labour members, along with every other party and members of Parliament, will have to make up their minds about where we go in the future. I am proud to belong to a centre Right political party, because there is nothing surer than that the centre Right in politics is the only progressive wing of the political movement in this country. That is because it is based on a realistic view of the world. Unless we understand the bigger picture, we are going to get it wrong. The one thing that we have to accept, it seems to me, is that New Zealand is still a vulnerable country. It will be, simply because of our size and geographical distance---which we can do nothing about---and our dependence on a narrow range of products. We will still be vulnerable for many years to come. Whatever policies are followed in the future, we must reduce our economic risk, because unless we reduce our economic risk we will have no show in the world of dealing with our social problems---none at all. If there are members in this House, and perhaps people in New Zealand, who believe that we have made a great deal of progress in the past or years then I ask them to dwell on one or two facts. The first is that our wealth base depends on our ability to export, and our ability to export depends on our selling products that people abroad want to buy. What we are capable of doing---and have continued to do and will continue to do better than anyone else---is to export agricultural products. Yet, in the past -odd years, we have managed to reduce our dependence on agricultural exports---in whatever form---from percent in down to barely percent now. That is not a huge development; it is not a huge change in the past -odd years. If we think we have made progress---and somehow or other it is bound up in the sort of country we are---let me simply say that in terms of the vulnerability rankings, in other words the ability of an economy to reduce its economic risks of relying on a small economic base, Ireland has done dramatically better than us. Yet I suspect that most New Zealanders continue to think of Ireland as a relatively poor country, but ``they ain't as poor as us''. What is more, it has reduced its vulnerability. So I simply say to members of this House that we have a long way to go to reduce the risks both to our economy and to our social fabric. That means that we must continue on the path we are on, partly because we do not have any choice: the rest of the world will largely determine what we can do, how fast we can go, and how we do it. Another risk that we have to deal to is debt, and I am pleased that for the first time in years it was dealt something of a blow in the Budget. We have to ``deal to debt''; it is an awful phrase. But debt remains one of our largest risks. It is still percent of gross domestic product. In it was only percent, and virtually nil prior to that. It is the largest risk because of the fact that exchange rates can move against us. It is made even more risky by the fact that we depend on such a narrow range of agricultural products for exports. Furthermore, we are vulnerable because debt is dependent on interest rates, and, as much as we would wish otherwise, interest rates are not within our control to a significant extent. The rest of the world will influence our interest rates, although we can play a major part in ensuring that our rates are at or below world standards by the consistency of the policies that we run. Lastly, in the debt area I have to say that the largest risk of debt is to future generations. We have no right in this House or in this country to pass on a level of debt that constrains the ability of future generations to have choice in what they do. We need to dwell also on the benefits that will flow from GATT. There is no doubt that that has created an opportunity. The estimates vary: anything from $. billion to $. billion a year in additional benefits. The one thing that will happen as a result of GATT is that other countries will take advantage of the benefits they have. If we think we somehow or other have had this magic wand of $. billion or $ billion waved at us for ever, we should forget it. A lot of other countries that are now reacting to the additional free-trade elements provided by GATT, will react in a way that quickly reduces the benefit to us. We cannot stand still in relation to the policies that we adopt. Our challenge is to better understand the changes of all these intertwined factors that are forced upon us: the change of technology, radically changing world markets, security issues that we do not even understand. What is happening in Russia and in parts of Asia will provide new security risks that we have to be aware of and deal to. We have, of course, continuing risks from our economic and social structures; irrespective of the progress that we have made in the past few years, we still have a considerable way to go before we can feel comfortable that we can face any shocks in the future. In the remaining moments I want to touch on another issue, which I think will radically change the way in which politics operates in this country. We tend to see the ideological battle as one between the State and the individual. But it will not be like that in the future.

I move, That this House note the passage on October of a New Zealand - sponsored resolution condemning the resumption of nuclear weapons tests by France and China at the th conference of the Inter-Parliamentary Union at Bucharest, Romania, the text of which is as follows: Recalling the commitment made by all Governments, those of China and France included, at the Review and Extension Conference of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, to exercise the utmost restraint on nuclear weapons testing, and therefore profoundly regretting the further nuclear weapons tests conducted on August, September, and October by those two States; Hoping that these tests will not complicate the already difficult negotiations under way on a comprehensive test ban treaty and make it more difficult to achieve a truly comprehensive and internationally verifiable treaty; Noting with approval the undertakings of the Governments of China, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, and France to support a comprehensive test ban treaty, which prohibits all nuclear weapons test explosions; Recalling that the Inter-Parliamentary Union has a duty to promote the cause of international peace and security, nuclear disarmament, and the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons; Recalling also recent resolutions of the Inter-Parliamentary Union on nuclear disarmament and the elimination of nuclear proliferation, especially that of the st conference---Paris, March ---entitled ``The importance of adhering to the obligations specified in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons''; Recalling finally the horrific effects of the use of nuclear weapons of war years ago at Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Convinced that the right of all to life, health, development, and a clean environment now and in the future is compromised by the existence and continued testing of nuclear weapons; . Appeals to the Government of France to abandon its current series of nuclear tests in the South Pacific, to the Government of the People's Republic of China to put an immediate end to its nuclear weapons testing programme, and to all Governments with nuclear weapons testing facilities to close them permanently; . Calls on all States that possess or have the potential to possess nuclear weapons to abide by a global nuclear testing moratorium until this is superseded by a comprehensive test ban treaty; . Urges all States, especially those with nuclear weapons, to work for and actively support the conclusion and signature, at the earliest possible date and by the end of at the latest, of a truly comprehensive and internationally verifiable test ban treaty prohibiting all nuclear weapons test explosions; . Calls on all Governments to work for the regulation and eventual elimination of all production, stockpiling, trafficking, and transfer of fissile material used for the production of nuclear weapons; . Urges all members of the Inter-Parliamentary Union to give their strong and unequivocal support to the early conclusion of a truly comprehensive and internationally verifiable test ban treaty as an essential step towards preventing and curbing horizontal and vertical nuclear weapons proliferation and attaining the ultimate goal of total elimination of nuclear weapons; Note that it was passed by the substantial majority--- votes to ---of the delegates from the countries represented; and note with appreciation the very strong support of Chile, Japan, Australia, South Africa, Mexico, Indonesia, Estonia, and Norway in securing passage of the resolution.
