I move, That the House take note of a matter of urgent public importance. Yesterday we saw the latest in a long list of reports about dysfunctionality and disruption in the Army and the New Zealand Defence Force. The Carruthers report was the sixth of seven reports that have been prepared, or investigations that have been undertaken, into some clearly quite inappropriate and unacceptable behaviour, particularly in the Army. I have to say I am disappointed in the Carruthers report, but I do not hold Mr Carruthers accountable. I say that for this very simple reason: in every situation that has arisen on defence matters in the last or years, the Government has deliberately attempted to cover up a series of problems. In the Carruthers investigation it rigged the terms of reference in such a way that Mr Carruthers, with the best will in the world, would not be able to get to the bottom of what was going on---particularly, in the Army. In spite of that gerrymandering by the Government, Air Marshal Ferguson chanced his arm and in his report he lays the blame where it should lie. I have to say that the most revealing thing in that report, and in the statements made by Mr Ferguson yesterday, were about the culpability of the then head of the Army, Major General Dodson. Mr Dodson is an extraordinary person. Undoubtedly, he has had a long and distinguished career as an officer over many years. None of us in this House could or should take that from him, but in terms of his role as head of the Army he clearly displayed, on a number of occasions, a lack of judgment on very serious issues. Some time ago he was accused of inappropriately using his financial authority to grant money to an institution led by Piers Reid at Massey University in Palmerston North. Mr Dodson was found guilty of shredding documents that should not have been shredded. In the report released yesterday he was found guilty of having inappropriately accessed Ron Mark's personal file for purposes that were never fully explained by Mr Dodson, either to the Carruthers inquiry or to the public of New Zealand. The only revelation we have from Mr Dodson is that had he known that his actions would create such a furore, he ``would not have touched it with a -foot bargepole''. That is not good enough. Mr Dodson also stands accused of spending public money on a public relations campaign in the Army, which was judged by Air Marshal Ferguson to be utterly inappropriate because it advanced the Army's cause at the expense of the other two defence force services. Today, we heard Derek Quigley on National Radio say that Major General Dodson, while head of the Army, sought to influence Mr Quigley by discussing privately with him, when he was chair of the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, what Mr Dodson thought should be done. That was well outside the normal channels of communication, either within the defence force or in terms of proper behaviour within a parliamentary select committee. Lastly, and perhaps most critically, the report severely criticises Mr Dodson for his lack of leadership in dealing with the culture within the Army---a culture of divide and conquer. That culture is set out clearly in the so-called Gordon letter. I make those points for one reason and one reason only. Mr Dodson was head of the Army at a time when some very important decisions were being advised to the Government with regard to re-equipping the Army and, indeed, the New Zealand Defence Force as a whole. Much of this activity we know took place while the Labour Party was in Opposition. Although it will be very difficult to prove, those in the know are aware that certain senior army officers were advising the Labour Party Opposition---the present Government---about what they thought the Army should get---but that was at the expense of the other two services. We also know that the judgment exercised by Mr Dodson was contested very rigorously by the proper processes---something that Ministers of Defence in any Government ought to have confidence in. Mr Dodson was not doing that; he was trying to go around the back. He was creating a dysfunctional relationship with the then Chief of Defence Force, Air Marshal Adamson. He was creating a divisive environment, which the Carruthers report criticised, and attempting to suborn the public through the inappropriate expenditure of money on a public relations campaign. I have a question for the Government. How can the Minister of Defence have any confidence at all that the decision to purchase $ million worth of light armoured vehicles was correct? How can he have any confidence that Colonel Gordon's proposal---and, we now know the proposal by certain army officers to get rid of the air-combat wing---was the right decision, in terms of the defence forces of this country? Those are major questions that have to be answered, and the Opposition will be holding the Government to account over the next few months. This litany of behaviour at senior level in the Army enabled it to get what it wanted, at the expense of the Air Force and, to a lesser extent, the Navy. So how can this House, and how can the New Zealand public, have any confidence that the Government was properly advised---and that is being charitable---and, ultimately, made the right decisions on the re-equipment of the Defence Force? I do not think that any reasonable person in this House would believe that the Government received the right quality of advice about what the Army needed, given a leader like Major General Dodson, or in terms of the decisions that were ultimately made to make a major change in the structure of the New Zealand Defence Force. This whole sorry, sad situation shows that the Minister of Defence should not have tried to cover up this situation, as he has done time after time again over the last years. He would not agree to any public investigation. He would not allow the people who were to give evidence to the various inquiries to be required to do so under oath. He would not allow the public to have access to hearings in public. He has done nothing but try to cover this up. I say to Mr Burton that it has not worked. It has not worked, because this report shows that the Minister received advice from people who have been severely criticised for lack of leadership, shredding documents, inappropriately engaging in accessing the personal files of members of Parliament---God only knows for what reason!---and inappropriately spending money on public relations campaigns, just so the Army could get its way. I want to know from the Minister of Defence whether he will go out and convince the New Zealand public that the decisions that the Labour-Alliance Government made to gut the Air Force, to downgrade the Navy, and then buy light armoured vehicles for the Army, which many officers in the Army say are not needed and are inappropriate, were the right decisions. Those are the questions that this Government has to answer. I also want the Minister to consider whether the processes that this House has been exposed to for years, in terms of major defence policy decisions, are appropriate, because, speaking as the previous Minister of Defence, I now know they are not. I suspect that even Mark Burton, if he takes a deep breath and does the right thing, will conclude that the process of white papers, of officials-only considerations of major defence changes, and of special one-off reports---that do not see the light of day and do not have any public consultation---have led to the wrong decisions being made for the defence forces of New Zealand. That has happened for the last to years, and it sure as hell happened on this last occasion, when the Labour-Alliance Government took the advice of an Army chief and a lot of his own people. But that person has now been shown utterly to lack leadership ability, and to have engaged in practices that are the subject of severe criticism by the present Chief of Defence Force. I hope that when I leave Parliament I will see a commitment from this House that any proposed major defence policy changes are subject to wide-scale public consultation---and I do not mean select committee hearings; they are just a bodgied exercise under MMP. I am talking about a wide-scale public consultation process, such as those followed by the Australians and the British. The public is owed that duty by this House. We owe it to the country to make the right decisions and to have faith in the people who are advising the Ministers of the day as to what sorts of major changes should be made in the structure of our defence forces. We have made mistakes in the past, and I know that the Deputy Speaker, who is in the Chair, will accept this. He is a man with a military background. We have made mistakes, and I still do not think we have it quite right. The Carruthers report, as inadequate as it is, in some ways shows us very, very clearly---as, indeed, did the Auditor-General's report on the purchase of light armoured vehicles---that something was wrong. Clearly, that decision was wrong, yet we are left with the consequences of decisions that involve billion-dollar expenditure on defence purchases, but the person who gave that advice to the Government of the day has been shown, by this report, to have had no leadership qualities, at all. That sort of thing is wrong, and has to be changed in the future.

The last weeks have seen a very confused public debate about the community services card. The best thing about it all has been that the issue of whether we as a society should have targeted entitlements is back on the public table. The worst thing has been the revelation of the cloud of unknowing which seems to permeate the highest levels of policy advice to Ministers. I am sure that this Labour-Alliance coalition Government did not set out deliberately to create a new class of some , people who could not access the community services card, whilst others on the same income could. But, somehow, when the Government increased all benefits, including superannuation, by the rate of inflation at April, the fact that a whole new group of losers would be produced just slipped it by. Having created this new anomaly, the Government continued to operate on false information. For example, public statements were made early last week about raising the limits for beneficiary access to cards, when it has always been the case that community wage, transitional retirement, domestic purposes, widows, independent youth, invalid, and veterans beneficiaries automatically gain access to the community services card regardless of their actual level of income support. This debacle has been a stunning example of what happens when neither Ministers nor their advisers are aware of the operational details of the legislation and regulations that they are supposed to be overseeing. It is heartening to hear the Prime Minister calling for heads of departments and others to sharpen up their act. The whole area of the interface between benefits, wages, and taxes, and associated entitlements such as the community services card, is a nightmare mosaic that has grown like Topsy in the last years. That even the most senior Government officials do not seem to understand aspects of it makes a serious review of all impacted areas even more urgent. If it is hard for chief executives and ministerial advisers to comprehend the rules, we can imagine what it is like for beneficiaries and low-wage workers applying to the State for support. It is high time that the Government began the essential and long-overdue process of completely overhauling all legislation and regulation around targeted income support and other entitlements for beneficiaries and low-wage workers. The community services card was introduced in by the National Government, following the benefit cuts and the introduction of the Employment Contracts Act. The card fitted in very much with the National Party ideology of that time, which focused on making benefits as low as possible so that people would be encouraged into paid work, no matter how poor the wages and conditions, at the same time as ensuring that such assistance as was provided was targeted to the maximum extent. The community services card has never been automatically indexed, and therefore does not automatically rise with an increase in inflation, wages, or benefit levels. However, since its introduction its income limits have been increased a few times. For example, in and the thresholds were raised to accommodate changes to family support. Since , the card threshold overall has been increased by some . percent for singles living alone, and by percent for married couples with no dependants. New Zealand superannuation has increased by percent, and average wages by around percent. However, in low-income employment categories, such as the low-wage service industries, wage increases are typically below average. This year, when the Government increased all benefits by the rate of inflation, officials advised them---somewhat belatedly, it now appears---that this would result in around , superannuitants losing their eligibility for the community services card. Cabinet then decided to raise the threshold for this group only, to accommodate those particular superannuitants. The Government apparently had estimated that if it increased the threshold for low-income workers to the same level as it had done for superannuitants, then some , people who currently do not get the card would be eligible for it. It worked out that this would cost an additional $ million per year, and that is what a lot of the debate over the past week has centred on. Technically, the Government is correct in saying that no individual will be worse off than before, but what has happened is that we now have a new inequitable situation, where there are different eligibility criteria for two groups of people on the same income: superannuitants and low-income workers. This raises another, deeper issue that we are about to confront in a much bigger way in the debate on the pre-funding of superannuation, and that is the weight we place on different groups of people in society. Do we put the majority of the resources of society, in a prioritised way, towards the older generation, or do we have a fairer distribution of the resources of society between age groups, between the needs of older people, people raising families, young people, and children? What has happened in the past week with the Government's creation of a new group of , wage workers who will not benefit from a rise in the community services card limit illustrates clearly the whole injustice and inadequacy of targeted support systems. As soon as there is any change in a targeted system, new groups of winners and new groups of losers are created. A small number of superannuitants have won in this matter, and a much larger group of low-wage workers have lost. One of the most difficult things about this is it has accentuated the poverty trap that people fall into when they move between benefits and work. It is bad enough as it is, but this policy means that people who move from a benefit into work that gives them an income of about the same level as their benefit, or even less, will lose access to the community services card. That is one of the reasons I took this issue so seriously. Anything that makes the move between a benefit and work harder is sad, because it is hard to make that transition, anyway. If one can see very visibly that one is going to lose something of as much benefit as the community services card, it makes the transition even more difficult. In response to Mr Anderton's question earlier, I tell members that I have always opposed the community services card. The unemployed workers' movement demonstrated against the introduction of the card in . We saw it very clearly as part of the whole move to cut benefits, cut entitlements, and deepen poverty traps. The Green Party is very pleased that the Government has now promised to speed up its review of the community services card, and hopes that the Minister and others will maintain ongoing consultation with us as to what will happen with subsidies in the area of primary health-care. We, along with colleagues in the Alliance and the Labour Party, would like to move to a system that had much more universality, where everyone was treated the same. As some members will be aware, my own background for the last years has been in running one of the larger community medical centres in Auckland, through the three People's Centres there. We have used a capitation system in that practice, along with many other community, union, iwi, hap~u, and pan-tribal medical centres around the country, and we have found that we can keep health-care costs down to a very low level for our members. In our centres, members access medical care for free if they are beneficiaries or low-income workers. The cost to people who are not beneficiaries or low-income earners is kept down to $ a visit. I think that is an example of the kind of equity that can happen if we move to a different kind of support. We believe that moving to a capitated system, especially when it is applied only to not-for-profit health-care providers, is the way to go. We look forward to working with the Government on that. At the same time, we would also like to stress that we need benefit reform, and fast. There are poverty traps in all sorts of areas. There are poverty traps at the interface where people start earning money when they are on the benefit, and at the interface between students leaving university or polytech and going into the workforce. They face huge costs through student loan paybacks, and that is combined with what happens when they start paying tax. There are a whole lot of questions that need to be addressed, and I hope the Government will be speeding up the work on that, as well. The Green Party and the Government both agree that the community services card must go. What we have disagreed on in the past week is the short-term measures that should be taken to increase eligibility for the card, until the review is complete. This week's events have demonstrated very clearly the flaws in the community services card system. Forty-eight thousand people fell through the hole this week, but the bigger picture is that this system, which is supposed to be a safety net for all low-income workers and beneficiaries, is full of holes. There is no way to plug those holes now, so any meaningful review will have to call for the scrapping of the community services card altogether. I believe that the Government could find the money in the short term to level out the threshold so that low-income workers would be treated in the same way as superannuitants. The Government has said that it would cost $ million a year. If it had to cover that for only the next months, until the review was completed, it would cost half of that. I think it is a bargain price to pay to restore some equity and to restore low-income workers' faith in the Government, especially as today is May Day.

The Bill will empower the Napier City Council to hold licences under the Sale of Liquor Act . There are only two short clauses. The legislation will be called the Napier City Council (Sale of Liquor) Empowering Act and it will enable the Napier City Council, which runs the Kennedy Park motels in Storkey Street, to hold on-licences and special licences under the Sale of Liquor Act. I join the other members in congratulating the chairman of the select committee, which has facilitated what could only be called a rapid return of the Bill to the House. It is appreciated by my constituents and by the local authorities in Napier. I thank the chairman and the committee. Napier is very fortunate to have a local authority that in decided that it would have a motel complex. The Kennedy Park complex is very large. It covers more than acres and it consists of motels, tourist units, caravan sites, camp sites, and standard cabins. It has been upgraded recently and has a very large restaurant that can hold more than people. It is used not only by tourists but also by service clubs and is a great asset to the city of Napier. It also has a very proven track record in tourism. It is a sort of springboard for tourism throughout the whole of the Hawke's Bay region. It is a very valuable asset, and granting authority for the local authority to have a licence will improve the facilities that can be offered. I will not detain the House for much longer. I thank the chairman, the committee, and the House. This is an important Bill for the city of Napier. I know that there is one former member who will be delighted that it has come through---a Mr Gordon Christie, a very old friend, and a very valuable man who served many valuable years in the House. In many ways Gordon Christie was responsible for the establishment of the Kennedy Park motels by putting a local Bill through the House. I thank the House. Bill read a second time.

Their compassion for the small people, for the families that lose out, and for the communities, all sounds very good, but there have been umpteen areas of concern in this country whilst National was in power from to last year that have not been addressed in any way, shape, or form. People suffered and the community lost out when National scaled back superannuation, for example. There is massive casualisation in this country right now. It is all brought about by the National Party in Government. The Wages Protection and Contractors' Liens Act was repealed in . What did National do about it in the years it was in Government? Precisely zilch! Now National members stand in this house and say they are concerned about communities and the effect that this type of action in the contracting industry has on families and communities. I represent a party committed to private enterprise, to a competitive environment, but we believe in a level playing field. If a playing field has to be slanted at all, it has to be slanted in favour of New Zealanders, not overseas people and others who want to exploit this country and the people in this country. I think the thrust of this bill is going in the right direction. I accept the comments made by Mr Worth that it might not be as all-embracing as it should be, but I have no doubt at all that the select committee will address those shortfalls, and the bill will come back to the House tightened up, and will address the concerns that both he and, perhaps, Nick Smith raised. I do not have a great deal to add to the substance of the bill except to say that it should have been instigated years ago. It should have come before the House years ago to address the problems of the construction industry. I look forward to this bill going to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, coming back, and going through with the support of all the House, so that one segment of New Zealand society is better off for it.

First, I would like to take this opportunity to welcome everybody, particularly the new people, to this first Parliament in this new century. I hope they have a stimulating and enjoyable time. The Governor-General, Sir Michael Hardie Boys, in his Speech from the Throne on Tuesday, December , said that people had voted for change in economic and social policy. I am not totally convinced that that was the case. Certainly voters did shift their political allegiances in some cases, but let us not forget that we still have a minority Government, and a marriage between two distinctly different parties was required to patch together that marriage. There was no overwhelming mandate for any party to introduce the reforms that they may wish to make. Indeed, we have a compromised Government, and policies will no doubt be tempered to ensure the support from a number of parties. Compromise will be required and therefore final policy may not in any instance reflect solely the views of the Labour Party, or, indeed, solely the views of Labour and the Alliance. I am certain Labour Party and Alliance colleagues are well aware of that. The Governor-General went on to suggest that the role of this new Government in providing evidence that MMP can work in the best interests of all New Zealanders was also a responsibility. That is a very important responsibility. I therefore urge that extremes of political direction are not adopted, as such actions will undoubtedly undermine MMP. MMP should, if it is working correctly, allow all political parties and those they represent to give vent to their views, and should not commit the views of others to languish because arrogance overrides principles.

Earlier this year an attempt was made to rush this legislation through. I did not know it was as rushed as Ian Ewen-Street from the Greens told us---namely, that the Government wanted the three stages to be passed in one day. I cannot recall that, but I accept that what he said is true. The Minister wanted to get this legislation in and out of the House in a hurry. To be honest, there was no obvious good reason. From my reading of the Scott-Gorman report it has raised some concerns. At one point they say that their findings relate to the licensing system, which they describe as ``dangerously defective''. That, I presume, is why the Minister wanted to push this legislation through the House in such a hurry. In my opinion, Scott and Gorman did themselves a disservice. I believe they overstated their concerns. There was no real factual evidence that planes were about to drop out of the sky or crash, because of issues with the medical certification of pilots. As Ian Ewen-Street has suggested in his findings, there is a big, fat zero of incidents in this country, and I think he said one had occurred in Australia. So there was no obvious need to try to push this legislation through as rapidly as apparently thought necessary in the early days. Indeed, the evidence at the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee showed that the pilots and aviation doctors were behaving very responsibly. They took the attitude that, despite there being much friction between participants in the industry and the Civil Aviation Authority, they would address this bill in a responsible manner. The issue that concerns me, and I do not know that anybody has touched on it, is that the Civil Aviation Authority has a legal requirement to consult the industry on matters of safety. Apparently, this was so important that the authority decided it did not have to consult at all! However, having said all that, Scott and Gorman did identify some areas of concern as being potential abuse and, dare I say it, potential corruption. For example, aviation doctors were passing pilots as fit for flying, and the authority's audit system was, if not non-existent, effectively non-existent. There was concern that the system could be abused. The select committee heard those sorts of facts, and I personally was quite warm to the idea of moving to the American system. Initially, the legislation was drafted to use the Australian system. The Civil Aviation Authority and the Minister wanted to introduce a system that was more centrally controlled, and, for convenience, the Minister wanted to move to the Australian system. But when the members of the committee learnt more about the American system they were keen to change things to the American system---the Federal Aviation Administration system. That system is quite different from the Australian system. Put simply, aviation doctors in America pass a pilot through the medical system as fit for flying. The Federal Administration Authority has to amend or revoke that licence within days, otherwise the licence stands. In the Australian system the doctor gives a temporary clearance, for want of a better term, for a pilot to fly, and the Civil Aviation Safety Authority endorses that or otherwise. We thought it was a significant move to go to the American system. One reason I am keen for us to adopt an internationally acceptable system is that young pilots training in this country spend a lot of money getting their qualifications. In large part, their qualifications count for little when they go to the UK or America. They have to do the whole darn thing again. We train our pilots to world-best standard. It makes sense that both the medical and the licence itself should be up to world-best standard. I would hope that, in the longer run, a pilot who is deemed fit to fly in this country will be accepted anywhere in the world, without question. That, I would suggest, is an aim that we, as politicians, should target. There could be significant spin-offs for New Zealand if we adopted that sort of attitude: if we trained our pilots for the commercial airline industry on a worldwide basis with qualifications that are totally accepted elsewhere in the world. I am talking specifically about Europe, Britain, and the USA. With regard to the select committee, I do think the process was handled very well under Harry Duynhoven's chairmanship. Members examined just about every piece of evidence in detail, and challenged just about everything that was put before us. I compliment the officials on their efforts. We asked them repeatedly to go back and talk to the industry, and get its views on this and that. As a result, we changed the legislation quite significantly. Indeed, changes were made as it went through its second reading last week. That says a lot for the attitude of the committee members, MPs in general, and the officials, in particular. They had their work cut out for them on what is really quite a small bill, from the public's point of view. I believe that this bill is probably as right as we will get it for what we want to do. I think that is praise indeed for members of the select committee, particularly the chairperson, Mr Duynhoven, and the officials. I was pleased to be in an environment where MPs basically identified the issues, sorted them out, and did not play party politics. A concern I had, and I think it was shared by all members of the select committee, was the gap---for want of a better term---and the friction that existed between the Civil Aviation Authority and industry participants. Since that time there has been a massive change of personnel in the authority, and I am hoping that the friction between industry participants and the bureaucracy will disappear. I am hoping that in the near future, if not immediately, we will see a very good relationship between aviation people and the administrative organisation---the Civil Aviation Authority. I am hoping that under the leadership of the new director, who has an excellent reputation in the industry, we will get an improved climate between all parties involved. I am pleased to see this bill finally go through the House, and I am hoping it will be the start of a positive regime between the industry and the Civil Aviation Authority.

I will not take a long call. In fact, I did not intend to participate in the debate but after listening to the speeches made by Rodney Hide, Lockwood Smith---and indeed, the senior Government whip, in the debate on the Singapore agreement---I feel I have to stand up and comment. We have heard much about free trade, and free access for goods coming into this country, but we have not had one word about what Singapore does when it subsidises its own companies. Indeed, the select committee report says, and I will quote it because I would like it recorded in Hansard: ``Singapore operates a system of subsidies granted to domestic industry. This may place Singaporean companies at an advantage over importers into the Singaporean market. They may also be used as a means of cross-subsidising Singaporean businesses competing with New Zealand firms for international business.'' I would be more accepting of these arguments from Rodney Hide, Lockwood Smith, and Rick Barker if they addressed both sides of the issue. Subsidies have the same net effect as tariffs. One makes internal goods cheaper; the other makes external goods dearer. Here in New Zealand we are now talking about maintaining a modest percentage tariff on goods coming into this country, but there is not one word from the free marketeers of any concern about Singapore subsidising its domestic economy, its domestic goods, and the possible effect of cross-subsidising goods on the international market. I say that that is not good enough. It is not balanced reasoning or balanced rationale. New Zealand First will support this bill because its members are consistent. We would like to see free trade, but we do not believe that this country should be the guinea pig for free trade. When everybody else wants to go down that line, we will support New Zealand going down that line. I refer to a comment made by my leader in the earlier debate, when he said that the Singaporeans are for Singapore, first, second, and third. I am proud to be a member of a party that says exactly that about this country. New Zealand First is for New Zealanders and this country, first, second, and third. We will support this bill, as long as it is balanced and as long as it gives some support to New Zealanders. If there is a tilt in the playing field, let it be in favour of this country, not somebody else. After years of Labour and National, the people out there, the people who will pay with their jobs and higher prices, are saying to balance the fairness. I will sit down now but I say that New Zealand First will support this bill. We hope Labour will take our concerns on board.

It is a point that I want you to clarify. With due respect, I think an underlying unfairness is coming through. Mr Hide is saying that this commencement date should not come into place because of the problems of introducing technicalities in terms of the governance board and what have you. He is illustrating that by mentioning the difficulties that Mr Tim Barnett had with a trust. That is a worthwhile example for this Committee.

In some respects we welcome the Supplementary Order Paper in Margaret Wilson's name, but I have to say that it is with a great deal of disappointment and I urge the Committee to vote for my amendment. I want to point out a few things. I want members to imagine that it is o'clock on a nice Sunday morning when parents are going out for a drive with their family, and the manager of a bus company gets a telephone call to say that buses will be on strike in hours' time---that at o'clock on a Monday morning they will be on strike. How many of those families will know that those bus drivers will be on strike at or o'clock when they take their children to get on the bus? Will the bus driver tell them? I do not think so. Will there be time for the bus transport company to advise the parents through the school? No. This is a sham. I say to the Minister to put bus transport where it should be, on the essential services list, and give a proper time of notice--- days. I quote: ``The operation of meat inspection services associated with the slaughter or supply of meat for domestic consumption.'' Those people have to give their employer days' notice under this amendment. We are not going to have kids going to school with just seconds' notice, and, in some cases, no notice at all. The Greens say they have had a success. God, I would hate to see a failure! I am disappointed in Lockwood Smith, and I have told him that tonight, because he stood and in some degree defended the Greens. The Greens did not once vote to put this issue on the essential service list at the select committee, and when it came to the last vote---I am sure Dr Lockwood Smith will agree with me---they abstained. My God, what kind of guts is that!

I raise a point of order, Madam Chairperson. Earlier on, I asked the Chairman specifically whether we were being confined to debating the title. He said that he had announced at the beginning of the debate that it was wide ranging, and he would let people have a free-range of speech on the whole bill. Now, Madam Chairperson, for you to confine it to the title---
What increase will superannuitants receive this year?

I want to make just a couple of comments on the short title, and to take on a few of the points made by the previous speaker. The first and most important point is that members on this side of the Chamber certainly have no intention of changing the commencement date of this Bill, simply on the basis that members on the other side of the Chamber live under the delusion that after next year's November election they may be in Government. If any Government ever decided to take that sort of action, and to be moved by an Opposition simply saying: ``Don't do anything because we're going to undo it.'', then there would never be any progress in this country at all. This is a good Bill. It sets out to provide cover for New Zealanders who have accidents. ``Cover'' indicates there is some sort of insurance involved. Therefore, the short title of this Bill, the Accident Insurance Bill, is most apt. Implicit in the word ``insurance'' is that there are some entitlements, and those entitlements are enshrined in the Bill. What is more, most New Zealanders understand that. They do not expect to go along to their insurer and buy house insurance, and to be told in the title exactly what it will cover. It is implicit in the contract. It is implicit in this Bill that rehabilitation is a major part of it. It is also a nonsense to suggest that changing the date to the year , as opposed to , should be done because the industry cannot write sufficient number of policies. We also heard that the large groups that represent various employers will mop up a very significant number of those small employers inside contracts that will be drawn up for their industries. They will have the choice of accepting or not accepting contracts that are industry specific. They will have the choice of a contract that is industry specific, or they can go to a broker and get a contract themselves. We heard from the brokers, who said that they had the capacity to work with this Bill, and they asked to be enshrined somewhere in the Bill as the mechanism that will allow employers to go out and get their insurance. We rejected that because we think it is obvious that they have a role to play and that employers will go to them. I conclude by simply saying that this short title is most appropriate. The Bill, as I said before, sets out to give cover to New Zealanders who have accidents. Therefore, it is an insurance Bill. Implicit in insurance is the acceptance and expectation that there will be some entitlements, and this Bill is very specific in saying that they relate to accidents. So the title ``Accident Insurance Bill'' is ideal for this Bill.

I support this legislation. I support the legislation because it is clear, defining legislation that separates this side of the House from that side of the House. I can also say that this legislation very clearly will deliver benefits to people in my constituency. As someone who comes from a city that has a problem with getting clean air, that needs cheap electricity, I am pleased that this Government is about the business of lowering electricity prices for New Zealand consumers. Some of those people who may or may not be listening out there today, some of the people who have followed the debate in the last few days, would be extremely confused by the position being put forward by the Opposition. Very, very confusing bits and pieces are being put into the argument, and all they really do is to confirm that whenever a Government tries to engage itself in micro-reform of the economy at some level or another, it is difficult because we are attacking or taking away some privilege in the community held by that group. This legislation is about returning to New Zealanders their right to get a good deal from the electricity assets that they own. The first Opposition speaker this morning was Mr Hodgson, who is the Opposition spokesperson on energy. He said that the Bill purports to achieve gains for consumers but he questioned where they would come from. He further went on to say that the select committee process was not something that he was at all comfortable with in this particular case. Those two statements simply serve to confirm that the Opposition has been having trouble keeping up with such a complex piece of legislation and recognising what the core, important part of it is. Mr Hodgson attacked the Minister---a very competent Minister---a Minister who has impressed me throughout his ministry with his willingness to listen to what people have to say to him, and with his willingness to act when people put a proposition to him. The member attacked that Minister for talking to players in the industry. What a crime that is! What a crime it is when people in the industry come to the Minister and say: ``We have some concerns about this. We want to talk to you.'', and the Minster talks to them! The member is saying that is not the way to go. Well, I congratulate the Minister on what he has done. I state again that this is a complex piece of legislation, in much the same way as some of the legislation was produced in the glorious years of the Labour Government----. I do not like to praise it, but when we look back in history we can always find something good about everybody. In those years there were a number of complex pieces of legislation that many members over there might now say they did not understand but was good for the country---and this legislation is the same. I want to pick up on a couple of points. First, I want to read out a little statement that I think clarifies what the major part of this legislation is about: ``The combined retail line companies that operate in most areas of New Zealand are, in effect, monopolies. This means companies have no incentive to pass on lower prices to small businesses and domestic consumers. And because they control the lines, the companies can also discourage other retailers from coming in and offering a competitive service. They can make line access difficult or use their profits from lines to subsidise retail activities, presumably at the cost of their consumers. Separating line companies from retailers will stop this from happening, it will open up opportunities for other retailers to come in, and offer cheaper electricity prices to New Zealanders.'' I congratulate the power company in my own area, Southpower, which has announced an accommodation between itself, United Electricity, and Enerco. United Electricity and Southpower are South Island companies. Enerco is largely a North Island company. Those companies have understood what this process is all about, and they have taken action to ensure that they will be well positioned when this legislation comes into effect. In that regard, I take issue with some of the comments made by Mr Swain. From as far back as , power companies in this country have known that this legislation was coming. Southpower would be one of the few that has taken the sorts of steps necessary to ensure it is well positioned beyond the passing of this legislation, and that will be good news for all its consumers. The company states that the new arrangement will be able to achieve significant economies of scale and will be in an excellent position to negotiate better prices with generators and other suppliers, and that will mean lower energy prices for consumers. I congratulate John Gray, the chairman of Southpower, for the work that he has done with his colleagues in United Electricity and Enerco, and I look forward to the gains that they promise Canterbury consumers. In the second part of this Bill there is the provision to further separate ECNZ. I think this is where the Labour Party has got itself in a real bind. I quote the Opposition spokesperson on energy---this is so appalling that it upsets me to say it---who said that he predicted a percent increase in the wholesale electricity prices as a result of ECNZ splitting away from Contact Energy. He predicted a percent increase in prices---that is what he said. The Opposition spokesperson on energy said: ``If you split ECNZ and you make two corporations---ECNZ and Contact Energy---you will end up with a percent increase.''

I want to speak briefly to this Bill this morning, which is very well supported in the House. It is technical in many ways but the actions it enables cannot be described as technical. It will enable social services to be more appropriately, shall we say, devolved to organisations that can deliver. It makes better provisions for the placing of children who find themselves in difficulty. As I said, the Bill is very well supported. I am pleased it has been brought to the House. I congratulate the Hon. Tau Henare on the efforts he has made over a long time to persuade the Government to introduce it. He has been very persuasive in his argument, as has Manu Alamein Kopu in her representations to the Minister. To take any more of the House's time would, I think, be a waste and I suggest it would probably try the patience of the Deputy Speaker a little too much. On that note I will finish.

I am delighted to follow that first post - maiden-speech given by the member for Waimakariri. I think it was a very good speech. I think it was extremely well delivered, and I am sure the Labour research unit was listening, and will say: ``That's the man for us. He can do what he's told. We're gonna write more speeches for him. We're gonna give him a few more chances.'' I think one of the great luxuries of being in Opposition---if there is a luxury in being in Opposition so close to having been in Government---is that one still knows how reaction in Government is portrayed in the House. What we have seen today with the hot-air, windbag speeches from the Labour Party directed entirely at Mrs Shipley, is an attempt by a party whose morale is completely shattered and strewn across the floor of this House to pull itself up by trying to find a focus for its vitriol. Well it has failed. It has failed miserably, because, if it were to succeed, it would in fact find itself in deep, deep trouble. I am now, after all these hours in the House, completely uncertain of where this line is leading me, to a point where I simply have to say to the Labour Party: I do not want to relitigate the Dover Samuels stuff, but there we are---I cannot help myself. What we have seen over the last wee while, in this whole sad case of a party turning on one of its own, is the destruction of a man for very, very spurious reasons, I suggest. That is a sad thing, particularly when it is one's own team that turns on one. I would have thought if anybody could give a speech today that might help salve some of the difficulties the other side of the House is having at the moment, it might be Clayton Cosgrove. Because he was, and is, a good friend and strong supporter of the Rt Hon. Mike Moore, and he knows how terrible it was when that party turned on that great New Zealander. We have heard in the last couple of days some sordid tales about how the Labour Party went out to dig the dirt on Dover Samuels. My colleagues have recounted the story of Chris Carter---everyone heard it on the news last night---where he left a message on the tape to a fellow called John, asking whether he knew of any spurious connections with supposed underworld involvement that this fellow had in the past with Dover Samuels. The interesting thing is that he described himself there as a detective. We have to ask what sort of detective he was. Was he a Sherlock Holmes? Was he a Hercule Poirot? Or was he perhaps a Maxwell Smart? I have to tell members he is no Sherlock Holmes, he is no Hercule Poirot, and he sure as heck is not smart. No detective worth his salt would leave a message on an answerphone like that. No detective would work like that. Imagine if the criminal investigation branch (CIB) of the New Zealand Police worked like that, and someone rang up the local crim and said: ``Hello, it's Chris here. I'm the local CIB detective, and I understand you've done a bit of burglary. I'd like you to give me a call back to talk about it.'' That man over there is being maligned by any suggestion he is a detective. There is absolutely no possibility of that at all. But this does highlight how hopeless and hapless the Labour Party is. It highlights how deeply sectionalised it is, how deeply factionalised it is, and how willing the current Prime Minister is to draw the hatchet on anybody who gets in her road. She would be the most controlling politician this country has ever seen, without doubt. It is a sorry spectacle when politicians are handed warrants by the Crown, but then find they have to look over their shoulder all the time, in the hope that the Prime Minister will not second-guess them on something and consequently white-ant them. Where is her mandate to do that? Today we have seen the release of the police report on the Waitara incident. That was a very sad and sorry incident, where the Prime Minister quickly went out and blamed racial tension for the problem. There was none. There is none. And her actions were quite out of order.

I raise a point of order, Madam Speaker. It may have been a ``go in peace'' sign, but down in Canterbury it means something quite different, and I tell the House that I was extremely terrified by the advances that Mr Clayton Cosgrove was making. I am quite unaccustomed to that sort of advance.

I am very pleased to make a contribution. I am not pleased at the effect of the bill, but pleased to be making a contribution. Some months ago when the bill was brought to the House, Labour, Alliance, and Green members packed all the empty seats in this place. Their friends packed the empty seats we see now to be part of the celebration that marked the beginning of this bill's passage. We have had many months of delays, many months of changes, many months of trying to reposition, hours and hours in the select committee, and, finally, over hours in the Chamber in debate. I have a question for my colleagues. Does that look like parties revelling in the joy of parliamentary triumph? Those members know that this is a bad piece of legislation. The time taken to pass it through the House exceeded the time it took to pass the marathon Maritime Transport Act. It took twice the time it took to pass the Employment Contracts Act and twice the time it took to pass the bill in that occasioned the previous time the House had to sit on a Monday. Why? Because it has been easy to sustain high-quality debate attacking the weaknesses of this bill. When we came to the third reading, would members not have thought the Government might put up some speakers who would revel and triumph at the moment they are about to pass a bill like this? What do we get? We get Margaret Wilson, the architect of the bill---the honourable member who has supposedly been in charge of the passage of this bill through its various stages---coming in here saying that the members of the public out there who are terrified of the consequences of this bill are terrified because of what the Opposition has been saying. I have news for that Minister: the Opposition will not stop saying it. The Opposition will be going up and down this country pointing out to people what this bill will do for them. I want to let the Government know right now that from our perspective the fight for workers' jobs in this country is not over. The reason is that this bill directly threatens the availability of employment to the New Zealanders at the bottom end of the scale who most need jobs. I want to pick up on the comments made by Alliance member Willie Jackson. Fancy coming into this House and making a statement like: ``There is no mana being at the end of a mop.''! Let me tell that member that there is no mana to be had sitting on one's backside while the mop lies idle in the corner. If that member thinks for one minute that I do not have respect for the people who use the mop to make my life easier, he is wrong. That member betrays his own people by refusing to recognise that there is dignity in all work. As for his song---well, it is best he does not give up his day job. We have asked throughout the process of this legislation being before Parliament whether this bill is about jobs or about unions. At the end of the day, all we can conclude is that this is about putting unions back on the map in New Zealand. It is a bill that disenfranchises workers in the workplace. No longer in a workplace where a collective contract is in operation can a worker negotiate directly with an employer. This bill entrenches conflict between employers and employees. That will never be good for industrial relations in this country. A bill that takes away the right of anybody to discuss their work situation with their employer is a bad bill, and will quickly be seen to be so. I now to turn to the comments made by the Hon. Dr Michael Cullen. His speech in the House today was a plea for moderation. Effectively, he asked for Opposition parties to lay down their opposition to this bill. He also suggested that unions need to modify the expectations that they might have as a result of this bill passing. The sad thing is that no one will listen to him. The unions will not listen to him because they believe that, after years, they have an absolute right to assert themselves in the New Zealand workplace. Most other unions that came to the select committee said: ``This is about utu.'' If Mr Jackson thinks that casting a vote in this House in M~aori is offensive, that is how offensive it is that a parliamentary select committee should be threatened with that sort of comment from a union.

I support the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition subsequent to the Prime Minister's statement. He called on this House to express no confidence in the Labour-Alliance Government, as a result of what the Prime Minister had to say and the publication of the statement, Growing an Innovative New Zealand, which is little more than a cynical deception, a rehash of jargon, and political spin. With its lack of certainty it can only be described as confirmation that the Labour-Alliance Government has no capacity whatsoever to lift this economy into a growing position. The way the Government has handled itself in the last couple of days tends to show just how incompetent it really is. It would have been a very simple matter to circulate this document to all members of Parliament so that they could have had it in the House, listened to the points the Prime Minister was making, and referred to the particular programmes described in it. We cannot bring computers into the House, and it is unacceptable that the Government is able to get away with not distributing information to members of Parliament, by saying the information is available on a website. I rang staff in the Prime Minister's office this morning and asked for this document, but I was told they did not have any copies. I said I was sorry, but they did, because they gave them out to the media yesterday. I said I understood they were mailing them out to people this morning, and told them I wanted one. They said they did not have enough for their mail-out. A short discussion ensued, after which I had a copy made available to me. The Prime Minister's answer---surprise, surprise---is: ``Let's get a growth package going for New Zealand; let's lift New Zealand to the top half of the OECD.'' Well, what is her proposal for that? It is a whole pile of committees, a whole lot of discussion, but not one concrete decision in the announcement made yesterday. Just to put it in some context: later in the day we had the Treasurer saying: ``We think we'll need to have growth of percent - plus.'' But this country had growth of percent - plus, when the Labour Government came into office. This Government has ripped that in half, during just two short years. Further, to put it in context, this country would have to have, year on year, growth of percent - plus, just to get us up to th position, from th position, on the OECD, in years. It would take years of growth at percent - plus, to achieve the Prime Minister's objective. She thinks it can be done by simply talking about setting up committees, and peppering her speeches with the words ``private sector partnership''. She is talking about the fundamentals of the New Zealand economy being sound. But as long as the Government is spending, and effectively controlling, over one-third of our gross domestic product, the fundamentals are not sound. As long as we have very low thresholds for our highest tax rate---and our tax rate is one of the highest in the Western World, the highest in the OECD---we do not have the fundamentals of our economy going well. That speech yesterday was very, very sad and retrogressive. Mr Prebble was able to say to us that much of the content seemed to come from the National Party manifesto. What New Zealanders need, and what the New Zealand economy needs, is a greater degree of freedom so that entrepreneurs can do the things they are good at, without the Government getting in the road; without the Government being insistent on the entrepreneurs paying very high taxes; or without the Government insisting that it be involved in all aspects of the economy. I ask the House whether a group of bureaucrats could ever have decided to go with VHS instead of Beta. Could a group of bureaucrats have ever decided that PCs are a better bet than Macs? Could a group of bureaucrats, even if they were creative people, have decided that the Beatles were on to something bigger than the London Philharmonic Orchestra? None of those things could have been done by those groups. All those decisions were made because entrepreneurs had the sort of freedom they need to do what they are good at. The Prime Minister made a sad little statement yesterday when she said that some still hanker after lower tax rates and further deregulation as the key economic prescription. Well, I will put my hand up for that; so will anybody who wants this country actually to achieve a position in the top half of the OECD. The Prime Minister then, in her own arrogant way, said that she believed that many more are seeing the strategic focus the Government is adopting, and the policy of intervention that accompanies it, is better. That is why this package is in trouble. That is why it will never get off the ground. That is why it will never fly. The total contradiction that we saw yesterday was the list of legislation that the Government is posing this year. Here we have the Government saying: ``We want business to grow, we want this country to grow, we want a better standard of living for our people, we want to get into the top half of the OECD.'', and the legislative programme says that the Government will be bringing in paid parental leave and more bureaucracy for tertiary education, will increase the minimum wage, bring in more compulsory holidays for people, give the power of general competence---the ability to raise local taxes---to local bodies, and put a moratorium on the most exciting science that will be seen in this century. Finally, the Government is going to ratify the Kyoto protocol. We got a ``weasel words ''sort of answer from the Prime Minister today about exactly what she means by saying: ``We're going to sign up in September of this year, but we don't have to do anything until .'' Only two of our major trading partners---in other words, two out of the top trading nations that New Zealand needs for its economy to be dynamic---have signed up to this protocol. The rest are out in the cold. So why on earth would we punish ourselves by going ahead at this point? The Prime Minister knows that that is true, so says, quite cynically, that we will sign up, but do nothing. Anyone who believes those words is foolish. This Government will turn the economy on its head.

I intend to object to clauses and in Part , and, as well, to support the opposition of my colleague Jeannette Fitzsimons to clause in Part . The reason for opposing clause is that the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act was passed in . Three years later we have not seen the enactment of any of the provisions applying to hazardous substances. We have seen an orchestrated litany of foot-dragging over actually getting control of hazardous substances and their importation into this country. The commentary to this Bill states that its purpose is to make it less restrictive to bring into this country hazardous substances, particularly innovative substances for agricultural, veterinary, and medical use. Yet it is precisely these substances that that Act, after the full process of Parliament, was introduced in to actually control. So how do we have this subversion of the parliamentary process through a trivial Bill---which is supposed to simply tidy up---that introduces major substantial changes that will prevent the full control of hazardous substances from being introduced into our agricultural environment? In the preamble to the Bill, we are told that it makes such innovation easier. Yet we are told that it will exempt substances of the same type from applications for use without adequate definition of what ``type'' means. I believe that the impact on our hazardous substances legislation will be highly detrimental. Let us actually get that Act implemented in this country, and let us start to do something about the toxins that we are constantly introducing into our environment rather than start to change, weaken, and liberalise its provisions through the back door before we have even begun. I object to clauses and in Part . Clause is simply an enabling of clause . But clause prohibits the public from finding out substantial amounts of information concerning the records, reports, information, and returns relating to mining operations in this country---the mining of minerals. Why should the public have its right to know proscribed in this way? All we are told is that there is a paramountcy of commercial interest. Why should accountability to the public be overridden in this particular way? Surely reports can be made in such a way that they can be made public without hiding behind the screen of commercial sensitivity. More and more of the activities that have a major long-scale impact on our environment and society are hidden from public view and accountability behind the screen of commercial secrecy. This Bill will simply extend that to the mining area. Two particular areas will be put out of reach of public scrutiny. One is that if we want to introduce, in the future, ecological taxes, taxes on the exploitation of minerals or on the production of pollution, it will be very much harder to introduce taxes when we do not actually know the amount that is being extracted. Why should the public not know the amount and value of minerals being extracted from this country, particularly when it is left with the toxic effects of that mineral extraction? The public has to pay long after these secret companies have left the country. Members should look at the effects of the tailing dams. Surely we should know just how much profit has been made from those toxic exercises so that we can know just how much the public should also charge those companies to clean up their dirty acts. We do not want to extend more secrecy.

It may be seen as boring, but the initiatives will go to the very heart of the capacity of New Zealand to compete in economic terms. I suggest that they are amongst the most important issues that New Zealand will face in the next months and they will lay the foundation for whatever economic recovery the country can hope to achieve. I am deliberately dealing with what I see as matters of particular importance. The closer economic relations review will deal with services in which it is hoped to see a considerable liberalisation. The Government regrets that the previous Government did not succeed in achieving that. The review will deal with investment. It is extremely important to have a national treatment that unifies both countries' investment regimes. The review will move on trans-Tasman shipping, which has remained one of the major bottlenecks to allowing the liberalisation of trade between New Zealand and Australia. We still have the most expensive piece of water anywhere in the globe. Those are particularly important considerations. The review will deal with the harmonisation of quarantine laws, and, once again, I have no illusions that the Opposition is more than familiar with the problems that New Zealand had about those matters under the previous Administration. The harmonisation of standards will also be considered. The Government is very conscious that the Australian industry assistance measures have created lop-sided opportunities for the Australians. The Government expects to achieve considerable further progress in business law, taxation, and tariff policy. Our criticism of the previous Administration is not that it did not commit itself to closer economic relations, but that it gave way on so many issues, so that New Zealand ended up with a very lop-sided relationship with Australia. New Zealand was weak, vacillating, and ineffective in its negotiation techniques. The fact is that by the time the National Government took charge the Australians, in many respects, had all the benefits and New Zealand had very much the second-hand position. The Australians were enjoying advantages well above what we had. The Government hopes to achieve an equality of opportunity as a consequence of the present closer economic relations review. It appears that we will succeed in achieving that aim. Therefore the closer economic relations review that is coming up next month remains an extremely important document. I expect to achieve a great deal more than the previous Administration achieved in the past years. In addition, we have reopened initiatives with Asia. In this respect I regret that the previous Government saw fit to ignore Asia in favour of other priorities. The reality is that New Zealand's trade is moving dramatically into the Asian sphere as we see a greater proportion of our trade being absorbed in that region. In this respect, I am very happy to inform the House that a considerable spin-off appears to be emerging from the seminar that was held in Singapore earlier this year. Similarly, I can inform the House that initiatives taken in Korea and Japan are likewise attracting the possibility of a dramatic increase in Asian investment in New Zealand. I can easily start to make dramatic claims of the order that were made during the previous Government's time in office, but which never transpired or were never delivered. What we can say is that there is the prospect of a dramatic improvement in this regard, and that we can look to a significant increase in Asian investment. The importance of that particular source of investment must not be underestimated, as New Zealand is increasingly a part of the Asian sphere of economic influence. Without that investment and without that confidence in this economy, I doubt very much whether New Zealand will achieve the increase in living standards that we so desperately need. The European Community is still an important market but, whether we like it or not, the European Community post- will become a unified market that will be that much more difficult to penetrate. We continue to have very close bilateral negotiations with the European Commission so that we enjoy our special access arrangements---they are important, and they will not be ignored. To that extent I can inform the House that certainly in New Zealand will continue to address that priority. The Government is very proud of the initiatives that it has taken. It knows that it took over at a time when there was a complete loss of confidence between the private sector and the Government. The Government simply had not won the confidence or the respect of the private sector. We had a disastrous stand-off. We have moved to re-establish co-operative and productive relationships between the Government and industry. In that respect we have been most successful.
All that the projections take into account is that the industry is doing remarkably well and is something that the country should be proud of.

He described them as ``those who play an important part in strengthening communities'', and I agree, they most certainly do. I have mixed feelings about the mixed-member proportional representation system (MMP). When the referendum was held last year, the citizens of New Zealand voted for change and MMP was the preferred system of government. Since then many people in New Zealand have been waiting for the findings of the select committee. I congratulate the committee on the time and effort it has put into the matter. It has been a very hard job to do because different factions in New Zealand have been lobbying. In the end, it was no mean feat to come up with something that will be a happy result for all. Anti-MMP groups have been lobbying vigorously throughout New Zealand during the past few months. Members of Parliament who believe that MMP is the best option for political reform in New Zealand have also been lobbying and pushing for their own interpretations. People are very confused; most of them do not know who they should believe or how they should vote on electoral reform. I hope that all of those who are concerned about the future of our country are listening to this second reading debate as the Bill passes through the House. I feel that the people want open, democratic government that they can be a part of. I believe that the first priority should not be electoral reform, but, rather, parliamentary reform. Aspects of the Westminster system should be changed so that the passage of legislation through the House cannot be hijacked by the Executive elite. Select committees should have more power in the decision-making process. Cabinet Ministers should sit on the appropriate select committees. The Minister must be accountable to the portfolio he or she holds, and, more important, that should happen through open forums, with concerned citizens and lobby groups having their say. The role of this House is really to be accountable to the citizens of New Zealand. That, combined with citizens-initiated referenda, will make for more open Parliament. Binding citizens-initiated referenda would give the voting population more input into the policies of New Zealand and make the Government more accountable, especially on more controversial issues. I believe that reform within Parliament is urgently needed. We are putting the cart before the horse if we introduce electoral reform before parliamentary reform. Over recent years we have seen huge changes in New Zealand. At the same time, people have not been consulted and promises have been broken by all parties. People expect their members of Parliament to be more accountable and answerable to their electorates. A binding referendum at the next general election will enable the introduction of MMP. The people's choice should be decided by more than percent of actual voters only, not of the number on the electoral roll. It is unacceptable to me to allow non-voters to be counted as votes for the status quo. If one does not exercise one's vote one cannot participate in the future of our country. If MMP is to become law the citizens will get two votes, the first for a local member and the second for a member from a party list. I shall support the amendment to the Bill that requires democratic candidate selections by supporting open regional lists. The public's interests must be protected. There must be credibility and integrity in the political process. A closed party list would only encourage party toadies and persons who would not be accountable. That is not what the people want. Nor would closed party lists encourage Maori participation. I believe that under MMP the four special Maori seats would no longer be necessary and should be disbanded. New Zealand is made up of many multicultural and ethnic groups, and, through MMP, that will enable those groups to put forward their parties or organisations and have the right to stand in Parliament. In areas of high Maori population the Maori will be able to contest elections in their own right. However, that will be possible only with a system of regional party lists. Since New Zealand is made up of many cultural groups, all ethnic groups would be able to have their own representatives.

When the Minister replies he might care to tell the House what on earth the proposed new section (A) that is referred to in the new clause () amounts to, because the key issue still is whether there will be a structure that will be attractive to new investment. I defy the Minister of Agriculture to demonstrate to the House that we do have such a structure. There are two key elements when it comes to examining the structure of producer boards: one is their capital structure; and the other, which is allied to it, is their monopoly powers of acquisition. This matter does not amount to an attack on the board. There really is a problem if one cannot discuss fundamental issues that really affect the country's economy without having accusations of treason, as it were, thrown around the place. That does not help anybody. I acknowledge that the Dairy Board has moved a considerable way. It regularly now gives permission to exporters who want to export speciality dairy desserts or speciality cheeses or ice cream, which are important products. However, that clearly is not its attitude towards its core products, and I think that that is a problem. It is a problem for new investors and for our dairy-farmers in particular. The other obvious problem that the dairy-farmers have is in assessing how good the board is. If about one-third of the board's sales are of products that are not even dairy products at all, or that are produced in countries other than New Zealand, how can dairy-farmers know that their efforts are being sensibly rewarded when they get a single price indicator? That single price indicator--the amount that they receive for their milkfat--may well be going up in value not because of their efforts and improved performance but because of increased sales of non-dairy products somewhere else, or because of the sale of dairy products that did not come from New Zealand. Indeed, the single price indicator may be going up because the dollar has devalued, which was the point being made by the Minister of Housing in the remarks that he gave in May of last year. I think that fundamental questions ought to be asked about the producer board structure. In that respect at least, Porter was absolutely right. The Bill does not do that; it does not begin to do it. The Bill does less than the original Bill that was introduced by the previous Minister of Agriculture did. I regret that. The defence that has been offered--perfectly straightforwardly--by the chairman of the select committee is that the amendments that have been made are what the industry wanted. That is absolutely true, but it amounts to saying that we have written a blank cheque and handed our jobs over to somebody else. The industry was asked what it wanted.
