Something important has been added to the Bill during the course of its progress through the select committee, and that is a revision of the power to recall. I think that properly strengthens the law. I do not know that it is very helpful to describe it as tough, but it is a strengthening of the powers of the Parole Board, and, indirectly, of the courts, in a way that I think is useful, and, perhaps, even important. Some other features of the Bill that attracted criticism, not just from the Opposition but from outside the House as well, have been remedied. Most noticeable was the withdrawal of the Government's original intention to bring back into the law the power to veto decisions of the Parole Board. I am very pleased that has gone. I regret that the Government ever raised the issue. I think the truth is that when the previous Government abolished the system the National Party, in Opposition, rushed in with a promise somewhat too early. I think it was at that stage that the National Party expressed itself rather too quickly on that subject and promised, somewhat cavalierly, to bring back the system without allowing a little time to pass to see whether or not it did damage.

I could identify those matters, but let us not take away from the satisfaction of seeing common sense prevail. I think it is a good thing that we are leaving the Parole Board in quite this way with a discretion that is not interfered with. It is also important, I think, to observe that it is not as though the Parole Board acts entirely on its own. The Government is perfectly able, and properly able, to influence the decisions of the Parole Board. Indeed, in the Bill the Government's power to do that has been extended, compared with the present situation, because we have widened the categories of offences in respect of which the Government, through the Minister, may give directions to the Parole Board. Such directions will have to be tabled in Parliament. Indeed, I do not think that the power to give directions has ever been used thus far. But I believe that it is quite proper to have that power there. It is not proper to have politicians sitting in judgment around a Cabinet table trying to work out whether or not individual prisoners should be released. The previous Government got rid of that system for two reasons that I think have already been recorded, but may as well be repeated now in case people have forgotten. The Government got rid of that system for a reason of principle and for some practical reasons. The reason of principle is that the only additional perspective that politicians can bring to that decision is a political one, and, frankly, I do not think that is a proper consideration. Cabinet had no fresh evidence. Cabinet had no additional psychiatric evidence that had not been before the Parole Board. Members had no additional specialist advice or knowledge of their own. They simply reviewed material, and exactly the same material, that had been before the Parole Board. Either it was rubber stamped, which seems pointless, or it was interfered with on a basis that is almost certainly improper, if not unfair. None of that seems to make sense. The other practical consideration that weighed with us, although it is not as important, was that to do a fair job of reviewing a Parole Board decision was quite time consuming. Typically, a lot of papers are before the Parole Board when the decision to release a long-serving prisoner is made, and, when all things are considered, I really do think that it is a case of the Cabinet having better things to do and the Minister of Justice probably having better things to do than to go back over such material. That is the background and I am pleased that with those kinds of considerations, or whatever other considerations weighed with the Government caucus, we finally reached consensus on that. It is also pleasing that further thought has been given to the wish of probation officers to retain that title and not to be called community corrections officers, or some other piece of what certainly sounded to most people like jargon and terminology that would have taken a long time to take root. Probation officers and wardens will still be called by those names, which was their wish, and it reduces the prospect of confusion to the public. Personally, I regret that we have even adopted the ``corrections'' terminology within the department, but if we had to do that then at least let it be confined to that area. I am also pleased that the decision has been dropped to include, within the Bill, the possibility that parole might be denied based on a prisoner's reluctance to attend particular courses. On reflection, and a number of witnesses picked up this point, it seemed wrong that inmates should be coerced into attending courses. They are more likely not to co-operate, or to take seriously the training---or whatever is being offered to them---if they are there merely because failure to attend might cause them to be denied parole. Finally, in what seems like quite a long list of things that have been done---some more important than others, but ultimately with support from both sides of the House---the Opposition strongly supports the changes that have been made in relation to reparation. Opposition members think it is a good thing that the courts are being given a signal from Parliament that underlines what I think we have tried to say before; that reparation ought to be considered in every case, and what we understand to be the current practice is now to be given statutory authority. That is to say, making reparation should take priority over the payment of any fine in terms of the use made of moneys paid by offenders. I say again that the select committee was given to understand that that is the current practice. It is certainly not the widespread view of victims that they get first bite at payments. It is entirely appropriate that they should be assured that that is the law and that they have that priority. Having said all that---and I do not wish to qualify everything that I have said---this is a measure that carries into law a number of worthwhile reforms and avoids a number of mistakes that would otherwise have been made. Regrettably, there is one significant exception---the matter I identified some minutes ago, a matter that Opposition members identified their disagreement with when the Bill was introduced, indeed, when the Government first gave notice of the intention to increase the penalty for rape. I regret that that is happening, and I regret it for a number of reasons. I regret it because I do not think that it will make any practical difference. It is not right that Parliament should go through the motions of pretending to the public that it is doing something that is unlikely to make any practical difference. I regret it to the extent that it may make any practical difference---though I think for the most part that is unlikely---which is that sentences are already getting longer. That is the key point. The Bill is not likely to make a major difference in the behaviour of the courts, but, to the extent that it does, there is a very grave risk that it may do harm, indeed, serious harm. While this argument is to some extent hypothetical, it is an argument that has been made outside the House with conviction and real concern. The specific argument is that someone who sets out to rape a woman may then go beyond that and commit murder as well because there will be little practical difference between the punishments for the two crimes.

The Prime Minister chose to describe the address made by his colleague the Minister of Finance outside this House today as a defining moment. One might describe the Prime Minister's address to this House a moment ago as a defining bluster. It turns out that what we have had from the Minister of Finance is the same old story that the public of New Zealand has often heard---from more than one Government, I think it might be said. The announcement turns out to be ``jam tomorrow''. The Prime Minister said that the news today was that New Zealanders are to get the rewards from the stronger economy, but when we look at the details it turns out that not all New Zealanders will, and the rewards will not be equally distributed, so it is jam tomorrow. For some it will be a considerable helping, and for some it will be a mere scraping. What Government members hope is that the reward New Zealanders might get will be unequally distributed in their benefit so that they will get the rewards in a political sense, which is their real hope. And, it seems to me, some of them are quite cognisant of the financial reward as well. They have taken to describing their programme as a hand-out programme. Certainly they are going to be handing it out. Let us accept this---I ask the next speaker, who I think might well be the Minister of Finance, to deny what I am about to assert---is it not the case that under the tax hand-out programme he announced in general terms, and is responsible for initiating, no one will benefit more than the Cabinet Ministers themselves? Is that not the truth? I invite the Minister of Finance to deny that, because I believe that is the case. Many who need it far more---indeed who need it whereas the Cabinet does not---will benefit far less. The Labour Party would change that tax programme. Why would it not? Would any self-respecting Government allow itself to have the tax schedules dictated by the previous Government? That is what this Government thinks it can get away with. This Government thinks it can cut taxes not just next year but for as well, have an election in between, and still have those tax cuts sacrosanct, delivering to people like themselves on the highest incomes the greatest benefit. No, a Labour Government would not stand idly by and allow the tax rates to be dictated by the previous Government. I will tell members what this Government intends to do. It is quite clear. It has announced enough details to make it clear. It intends to drop the middle tax rate---not the bottom one, not the top one, but the middle one. The Minister of Finance nods in confirmation. It might adjust the tax thresholds a little bit as well, though that is not the critical issue. If the middle tax rate is dropped, and nothing else is done, then the greatest benefit from dropping that middle tax rate will be earned by those on the maximum income. If it is just the middle tax rate that is dropped then the benefit accrues to everybody on that rate, and everybody on the top rate as well. The greatest benefit occurs to those paying the greatest tax. There is a very simple answer to that. All that needs to be seen, to avoid what is obviously a silly outcome, is that those on the very greatest incomes are not those in greatest need. Plenty of social needs in this country are not being addressed, in education, in health---weekly, if not daily. We hear of needs in the social areas that this Government is not addressing. Here it is proposing to give money away to people who clearly do not need it. It is not as though it is not easy to work out what to do. All that needs to be done is to put in another tax step that takes that money back from the people who do not need it. Their tax rate does not need to be put up by any more than the benefit they would have got from the reduction in the middle tax rate. Only that amount can be clawed back. They can be left in exactly the same position if it is wanted. It is not hard to do. It has been done before. The only reason that this Government would not do it, the only reason that the Prime Minister pretends that it is somehow impossible to do, is presumably that Government members are looking forward to the benefits, if not for themselves in a financial sense then for the political benefit that they expect will come from people like them: high-income earners getting an unnecessary benefit. The Labour Government elected next year would not stand by to see our social services deprived of money they need while those who do not need a tax reduction, those who do not need a tax hand-out, get it, and get more than those on the low and middle incomes that this Government says it is trying to assist. That is the difference. I do not know that I would describe that as a defining moment. I think it is a very simple choice. It is a very simple difference of values. We have the health system in disarray. We have the education system crying out for more resources. We have the Government acknowledging it is collecting money that it does not need, being prepared to hand it back. And it proposes---and today's announcement confirms this---to hand the most back to those who need it least. You bet there is a stark difference in priorities! I want to remind the Minister of Finance of something that he participated in some years ago. Was he not in the Government that temporarily put up the tax rates from c in the dollar at the very top to c. Did he not do that? Did not the Prime Minister vote for that as well?

I want to say a couple of things about the report back of this Bill. A number of speakers on the Labour side have said that this Bill demonstrates in many ways that the Government is in considerable difficulty. The Bill itself as introduced was a mess, and much of what the select committee has had to do has been in response to that. I will not debate at length something that is not here, but I can illustrate the point I have just made by reference to the decision of the select committee to delete what was originally Part VI, which, the House might recall, related to the Crown's decision to try to grab ownership of geothermal wells, thereby overriding a decision made only days previously by the Maori Land Court. It is odd that, having withdrawn from that decision for the moment---that portion of the Bill has merely been parked in the select committee, not abandoned---the Government now adds provisions to this Bill that seem to have the effect of overriding another court decision, this time to do with fisheries. The decision is known as, I gather, the Robinson case. Fisheries is an area in which the Government has almost perpetually been in a shambles. I will need some persuading that the Government needs these provisions, and that it is not acting in a way that is improper and, in effect, overriding proceedings that are currently before the court. The main matters that I want to address are the provisions in this Bill that deal with the subject of superannuation. Those provisions respond to a recent decision of the High Court that is known as the Coburn case, named after, I think, one of the plaintiffs. The case effectively dealt with the legality of one of the largest private superannuation schemes in New Zealand at present---the scheme run by New Zealand Steel. It had implications for a large number of private superannuation schemes and, indeed, for the Government Superannuation Fund itself. The Bill picks up certain findings of the court but, interestingly, goes well beyond those findings. Yet it does not deal with certain issues that the select committee identified and that Opposition members on the select committee sought to have addressed. In essence, the Coburn decision found that many private superannuation schemes---in particular, the New Zealand Steel scheme---are in breach of the Human Rights Act, and were probably in breach of the Human Rights Commission Act that preceded it, in that they provide benefits for spouses of deceased contributors but no corresponding benefits for contributors who have not been married, although the contribution rates are typically the same. The implications of providing similar benefits for unmarried contributors as are provided for the spouses of deceased contributors are very considerable. The cost would run to many hundreds of millions of dollars---indeed, possibly thousands of millions of dollars if one added it up across the whole of the private sector. Some figures were offered to the court---and are recorded in the Coburn decision---of exactly how much money would be involved. The Government has proposed by way of a supplementary order paper to the Finance Bill (No. ) that companies be retrospectively relieved of that obligation to provide equivalent benefits, but in the future---from, I think ---schemes would have to offer equivalent benefits and to comply with the Human Rights Act in all respects. So far, so good, except that I echo the point made by, I think, the member for St Kilda earlier this afternoon that this seems, to say the least, a very rushed response.

The member for Sydenham should produce the correction. He should tell the House how he came to be quoted as saying that. That statement does not indicate a long and genuine interest in employment equity for women. Members are told that the fundamental difference between the Bill before the House and the Government legislation is that the Government Bill was about promoting an idea and this Bill is about action. The action that the member for Sydenham has in mind is unbalanced, unfair, and does not consider the balance of interests that have to be considered in industrial legislation. The Government has often been critical of the attitude of the Opposition on industrial legislation because its approach is unbalanced; it is too much one way. The Government has hung its hook on the balanced Labour Relations Act. That idea of balance has been carried through in the employment equity legislation. The position of the employer is considered and the Government does not impose completely unreasonable requirements for making rapid advances towards employment equity that could damage employment itself. Under the Bill, once an employment equity assessment is conducted it would have to be written into the award by the Arbitration Commission. That blunt, inconsiderate, and impractical instrument was ruled out of consideration by the Government. It is not on for the assessment to be written straight into the award by the Arbitration Commission. The member for Sydenham departs a long way from the principles of the Government Bill that recognise the important role that unions play in negotiating the pay and conditions of their members. The Employment Equity Act clearly puts as the centrepiece the role of the union, its coverage of members, and its rights to advance their interests. This Bill goes much further in relation to individual claims. It suggests that individual women should take an employment equity claim. Latest figures indicate that there are more than , women in the work-force. To lumber an employment equity commission with the possibility of individual claims from hundreds of thousands of women is ridiculous. I recollect, and perhaps the member who chaired the select committee might pick up on the point later, that evidence from Great Britain, where it is possible to advance individual claims, showed that virtually no progress had been made in moving towards employment equity for women. Taking claims one by one does nothing for the great collective of women who are discriminated against in pay-setting. That is but one of the Bill's many faults. The member for Sydenham must recognise that legislating for employment equity is a different matter from legislating for equal pay. Equal pay is quite obvious---when a man and a woman work next to each other and do the same job, the same rate ought to be paid. That is measurable; it is obvious. Even when that simple and obvious legislation went through Parliament in ---and I have always acknowledged the role of the National Party in promoting that---it had a -year phase-in period. It was simple, but it was gradual. Employment equity comparisons are another matter. It is a difficult exercise to evaluate the worth of one occupation against the worth of another. To suggest that one should go from the assessment stage straight to writing into awards is much too casual an approach to a complex exercise. Again, when the Government considered how the exercise should work in principle, it considered the role of unions and employers in negotiating pay rates. It said that the assessment done by an employment equity office ought to become something that the parties in the industrial relations scene could negotiate. If they could not come to an agreement the matter would go to arbitration. At least, it should go through the normal industrial relations procedures. The Bill side-steps that, it side-steps the legitimate role of the union, and it side-steps the legitimate role of the employer to raise objections to the assessment, to the way in which it was done, and so on. For that reason, I have no hesitation in saying that the Bill is biased and that it could be destructive of jobs while aiming to be good for women---which it is not. It did not surprise me that the member came up with the Bill. I have noticed the odd piece in the newspapers from the New Labour Party candidates, who state that the Government did not go far enough. The New Labour Party wanted it done yesterday, and it wants the assessments and the pay rates tomorrow. They describe the legislation, and the member for Sydenham did again tonight, as non-interventionist. Not one employer in the country would believe that the Employment Equity Act is non-interventionist, because it is. I have never shrunk from that label, but it is responsibly interventionist in that it sets up a procedure that can be managed and afforded. It is important to apply that criterion. The member for Sydenham complains that, perhaps as a result of the Bill, the pay gap will close by only to percent. The Bill's object never was to try to close the pay gap by more than the gender discrimination that had been found. The object was to identify the gender discrimination that existed---estimated to be in the range of to percent---and to set in train a procedure by which that could be overcome. To suggest that that short-changes women leaves much to the imagination about how the member for Sydenham works out those matters. Other problems exist in the Bill. Clause ()(a) states: ``The public service shall establish the relevant equal employment opportunities programmes within months of the commencement of this Act.''. The - year was one of public debt hitting a record high under that Minister---a year in which the money owed by every man, woman, and child rose by $ a head. It was also a spectacular year for the breaking of other promises by the Government. We had been through a campaign when time and time again the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance repeated the fatal words of George Bush: ``Read my lips: no more taxes.'', and categorical assurances of that kind. The truth of the matter was that in the financial year under consideration the Government introduced a new hospital bed tax, new accident compensation taxes on earners and on petrol, a new tax on gaming machines, a new regional petrol tax, and announced a tax to cover the casinos---if we ever see them---a new housie tax, and a new capital gains tax. This was a year of shame for her. It was not only a year of shame for the Minister of Finance, but it also was certainly a year of shame for the countless numbers of health Ministers that we have---one does tend to lose count. That has meant nothing to the Minister of Labour, who has gone on with a pre-arranged agenda that was written by elements of the employer community in order to destroy, one after another, any little bits of help from the Government that might have advanced workers' interests. That is the history of the Bill. It has to be seen in its context as one of a long line of measures that starts with the repeal of employment equity and ranges through the repeal of back-stop arbitration, the introduction of the Employment Contracts Act, and the changes to accident compensation. Now there is this legislation. Legislation on redundancy is to follow later this afternoon. This legislation is part of a concerted attack on workers. For the member for Tarawera to say that the Trade Union Education Authority is ``no longer appropriate to a vigorous, expanding New Zealand economy'' only proves to me that the authority must be totally appropriate, because there is no vigorous, expanding New Zealand economy. There is an economy in decline; an economy that is struggling to get back on its feet. This is an economy that needs workers who are in a position to do something to promote economic growth. The work of the Trade Union Education Authority was very much geared to bringing unions, delegates, and workers up to date with what was happening in the broader economy, in their enterprise, and in their industry. If that facility is taken away, they are left disempowered when they try to make an effective contribution to what is happening in the work-force. The member for Tarawera mentioned the work-place reform conference that has been taking place in Rotorua. It has been a very successful conference, and he used that as evidence that other initiatives were going on, independent of the Trade Union Education Authority, to educate workers. I find it somewhat ironic that the Government and some employers, who are totally unsympathetic to workers' collective institutions, are falling over themselves to embrace that conference. Their embrace is absolutely meaningless, because unless there is the back-up of strong workers' education, such as that through the Trade Union Education Authority, people will go away from that conference and, unless they belong to a union that is one of the few left that is well resourced and can itself afford to pay for workers' education, absolutely nothing will happen. The reason that an Act such as the Union Representatives Paid Education Leave Act, which is being repealed in this Bill, is needed--and the reason such an authority is needed--is that in this country many workers are not members of large unions, and, without a requirement by the State, those workers cannot get access to paid education leave. Now, in the trend of voluntarism that has come through in all of the legislation of the Minister of Labour, something that would have helped is scrapped and, again, the strong will benefit, because their unions will do something for them, but the weaker unions will not have the resources to help their members. The Government is fond of quoting the recommendation from its latest review team, which stated that, given the existence of the Employment Contracts Act, perhaps the Trade Union Education Authority was not appropriate any more. I was unable to attend the meeting yesterday when members of the review team gave evidence, but I have very full notes from colleagues who were there. I am told that Mr Jackson, the former Secretary of Labour, advised the committee that the terms of reference given to the review team led it to its conclusion. Because of the way in which the terms of reference were set up, committee members could draw no other conclusion than that the Trade Union Education Authority could go. That point was made from the outset by the Labour Opposition and the trade union movement. When the terms of reference for the latest review were looked at, we knew that the Trade Union Education Authority could not survive. The result was cooked before the review started. None the less, Mr Jackson and Mr Trotman were bound to report back that the Trade Union Education Authority was well managed, that it had performed well, that it gave good value for money, and that it had made a significant contribution to New Zealand. That is a vote of confidence, but it was not enough for the Minister, who had made up his mind to scrap the education authority. He set up terms of reference for a hand-picked committee that could not fail to report back that the Trade Union Education Authority should be scrapped, then he went ahead. One would think that if a statutory authority is chaired by a man who also happens to be the president of the Council of Trade Unions there just might have been some consultation about what was happening. I want to tell the House about the evidence that the president of the Council of Trade Unions gave to the select committee. He was able to spell out, in chapter and verse, the lack of consultation that the Minister of Labour had had with him. In fact, I think that there has been almost a complete breakdown in relations with the Minister of Labour, who was unable to look him in the eye and tell him what he planned to do. The president of the Council of Trade Unions told the select committee that he had not been given any indication that repeal of the Act was on the agenda. The Minister of Labour had not been able to bring himself to utter that simple truth to Mr Douglas. Eventually he was told when he was asked to the Minister's office about another matter. At that time the Minister told him that the announcement of the repeal was imminent and he asked the Council of Trade Unions to think about what it wanted to do with the Trade Union Education Authority. I might point out that the authority is a statutory authority--not a creature of the Council of Trade Unions--that reports to this Parliament. That was the consultation. The president of the Council of Trade Unions, who was also the chair of the Trade Union Education Authority, was told that that decision would be announced. He was never asked for his views on it. Of course, the authority was notified the next week, only shortly before the decision was made. I find that absolutely disgraceful. I am sure that that is the way in which the Minister of Labour customarily operates. What is more disgraceful is that there was no consultation about what then might happen to the Trade Union Education Authority. A sum of half a million dollars was announced as being available for the education authority either to carry on or to wind up. The Trade Union Education Authority could not carry on in those circumstances. It had an infrastructure, staff, overheads, and commitments. The sum of $, was not enough to cover those costs. The authority could not carry on in the hope that it might get contracts from a contestable fund; I am sure that the Minister of Labour did not go to all the trouble of destroying the authority in order then to hand over the bulk of its contestable fund to the people who had been running the authority. The people from the Trade Union Education Authority and the Council of Trade Unions were dealt with shabbily from start to finish on this matter. A very good authority, such as the Trade Union Education Authority was, that emerged intact from every review that was ever conducted of it, had to be wound up at great speed in order not to leave staff in a very very difficult position. I suppose that the Minister of Labour would have welcomed that outcome of his disgraceful actions. There has been a mean-spirited, vindictive, and cowardly attack on an authority that was working extremely well. Those who were to be the victims of the attack were not consulted at any stage, nor were they given any hint that repeal was on the agenda; they were simply told when it happened. I find that absolutely incredible. We heard from the authority itself and from its director, who is an educationalist of some distinction. I still do not think that the Minister knows what he has done.

The Prime Minister dodges responsibility; he is not up to it, and he will dodge it in relation to anything that affects the people of this country. Of course, the Prime Minister wants the credit for the ``dead cat'' bounce-back from the recession that his Government created---it was all its own work. Everywhere I hear people saying: ``What good news? We're worse off; we're paying more tax; we're even paying new taxes; we're paying new charges; our wages are frozen.''. People are saying: ``The Remuera recovery isn't helping us. Who is it helping, because it is not helping us?''. It is hard to find what this Government takes responsibility for. It is silent on the issues that count or it pushes them away on to somebody else, but in the end the responsibility goes back to the Prime Minister---a Prime Minister who talks tough and acts weak. Remember last year and earlier this year when Electricorp talked about putting up prices? The Prime Minister talked very bravely about that one; it was far too much to ask; he wrung his hands; he jaw-boned away---but the prices still went up. We did not hear any more about it for a while. Now, when the country faces black-outs, when old people face a cold winter, and when small babies face the prospect of a cold winter, that position has nothing to do with the Prime Minister. I am telling the Prime Minister that a power shortage has everything to do with him and his Government. The public thinks that. The public knows that the Government is the only shareholder; the public knows that the Government is grasping for every last cent of dividend that it can get from Electricorp; the public knows that the Government is wringing the dividend dry; and the public knows that Electricorp has run our hydro lakes down to unprecedented levels in order to pay those dividends.

No one is so stupid as the Minister of Youth Affairs. As the Minister of Youth Affairs one might think that he would speak up for children that he knows are the victims of tobacco advertising. He should put his own addiction to one side and think of children in this matter. The Associate Minister of Health, and a couple of other Government members, took the view that we should not be taking a stand against tobacco sponsorship here because not every other country had. Well, it is really incredible to take the view that New Zealand should be the last to adopt a policy of banning sponsorship. If every other country took that attitude no country would ever take the first step and tobacco would continue to have its message paraded around sports fields for ever in the countries of the world. I remind the Associate Minister that we were not the first country to take this step. We were well down the track. Other countries are considering banning sponsorship, and even the Minister's own leader, the Prime Minister, had said that he thought the issue would soon die because Australia was about to ban tobacco sponsorship and the trend was away from that. The Prime Minister is right, but I say again that he would be respected more if he were part of keeping New Zealand in the vanguard rather than saying that we should just have a ``me too'' policy when everybody else has done it. New Zealand can stand out in a leadership position and should do so. In the Committee stage the misleading arguments about parallels with the exemption for craft in yachting races were again run before members. I repeat in very simple language that the original Bill was not a matter of the Whitbread round-the-world yacht race being favoured over others. I put it to members that a yacht race, using New Zealand as a port of call, is totally different from having a multinational event staged entirely in New Zealand in a sports field that is utterly bedecked with tobacco slogans that appear on television hour after hour. Government members know that that is the truth. They know that that is why the yachting races were treated differently, but they have persisted in misrepresenting the original very narrow exemptions. The original very narrow exemptions in no circumstances allowed for a whole event to be staged in New Zealand backed by tobacco. It was a very narrow section and one that should have been maintained by the House. In the Committee stage very frank accounts were heard from some members who had actually been induced to take up smoking as a habit by advertising and by the images portrayed through it. I thank those members, because their testimonies got to the heart of the issue---that sponsorship is advertising that aims to sell a deadly product. It takes a lot of people in. The addiction is hard to buck, and for many addicts an early death will be at the end of the road. The effect of the Bill is a victory for Benson and Hedges. Tobacco wins again. The Government in the long term will be the loser. Debate interrupted.

It is by percent a week--down from $ to $--and the Minister will not return to Dunedin to look John Kaye in the eye. It was the former Leader of the Opposition, who is now the Prime Minister, and his deputy. Mental health was always an area that was starved of money by Governments in the past. However, it finally got its dues in the Budget. It was the first up for the chop. The Government falsely claimed that the money promised for mental health was not provided for in the Budget. It is clear from the Budget that money was provided. It was provided for in the Budget tables. It was provided for in the supplementary estimates. Health and education spending were identified separately from other supplementary estimates. Health spending was part of the fiscal out-turn for which the former Minister of Finance budgeted. It will not wash for the Government to say that that money was not planned for. At the weekend I sat at home and played back some of the old television programmes I have recorded on the video. I came across the ``Frontline'' programme of Sunday, October, on which the member for St. Kilda and I appeared with the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Social Welfare. A young woman in the audience, who was a representative of Psychiatric Survivors, asked the Deputy Prime Minister: ``Can you assure me that the full $ million will stay in community mental health?''. He said: ``Yes''. That was one of the first items to come up on the block for chopping by the Government. The Associate Minister of Health made very foolish statements about this area of budgeting. She told the doctors' magazine that she thought that a small proportion of the allocation for mental health had already been committed by boards. I shall tell her about the plans that some of the boards have. I shall mention the Northland Area Health Board, because I know that every Northland seat except Northern Maori is held by Government members. That board put up plans to me when I was Minister of Health, which I approved for its share of the money---from $,---to establish and develop a community mental health centre in Whangarei, to establish and fill a position of psychiatric social worker or district nurse in Hokianga, to establish and fill a position of senior psychiatric social worker located in Whangarei, and to purchase vehicles to help them do their jobs. The list goes on and on. The board was told that the money was available, and that the money was programmed for in the Budget. However, this Government wants to whip it away after that work. It will not wash for it to say that that money was not budgeted for. I shall not spend time tonight talking about cervical screening, but a minor scandal is brewing as a result of the chaos caused to that programme by the statement made about it by the Associate Minister of Health. I turn to the claims about the pharmaceutical budget. As my colleague the member for St. Albans said before dinner, the Government has a bad case of the ``Sir Humphreys''. The Department of Health has been told for some years that it must do better with the pharmaceutical budget. The Labour Government capped pharmaceutical expenditure, and was successful from the - financial year in bringing down the level of pharmaceutical spending. It had planned to do so again this year. Of course it is difficult to bring it down, but the Government has released the Department of Health from any obligation to try to do so. I can tell the House that the department had a strategy, but I do not suppose that it will need it now that the Government has gone soft on that matter. I wonder what has happened to the work that the firm of Coopers and Lybrand was commissioned to do on the strategy. What has happened to the priority projects to bring down costs? I was told that each of those projects had the potential to attract savings or revenue and thus to contribute to the savings required. Quantifying work was done. The Government has taken the easy way out. Perhaps it plans to increase prescription charges and thereby not to make the other hard decisions that might hurt vested interests such as the research medicines industry. In today's New Zealand Herald the research medicines industry rushed to the Government's defence and said: ``The last Government didn't budget for the extra pharmaceutical charges that would come from lowering the cost of going to the doctor.''. That is wrong, also. Of course it was budgeted for. The Labour Government was not so stupid as to provide for more people to go to the doctor and not to realise that more drugs would be prescribed as a result. The money was written in. I was interested that the research medicines institute ran to the Government's defence. The Government's soft attitude on pharmaceutical spending helps the drug industry. It is also very clear to me that a new pattern has crept in in dealing with health issues. The Government is set to appease a whole new set of vested interests such as the research medicines industry. That industry has the Government's ear. I have seen the minutes of meetings between the research medicines industry and the member for East Coast Bays and the Deputy Prime Minister, in which they schemed on cutting off the grant for the Public Health Association from the Department of Health because the research medicines industry did not like its work. The tobacco industry has the Government's ear. It has had the ear of the Deputy Prime Minister for some time. The alcohol lobby has the Government's ear. The first tax increase on which the Government reneged was the indexed one for putting up the alcohol tax every months. The alcohol lobby got to the Government. Of course, the New Zealand Medical Association has had the Government's ear for a long time. That association puts its own petty interests ahead of the public's interests to lower doctors' fees. That association will agree in dark corners that the Smoke-free Environments Act was the most important thing that could be done for health, yet does not say anything when the Government, which pays it out, proposes to repeal the Act. Vested interests have the Government where they want it in regard to health. The debate tonight would be an appropriate time for the Minister of Health to come clean on what he intends to do with the Health vote. What other vested interests does he have to pay off? Will he stand by the Prime Minister's election pledge not to take a dollar away from health? Will he stand here tonight and say that the Health vote has not been touched? Is it to be the most spectacularly broken promise early on in the National Government's term? Of course the Minister will not do so. He is co-operating with the razor gang. Health is on the blocks. It is a sorry tale in order to pay out tax rebates for favoured industry sectors, in order to put extra police on the beat, and in order to pay out on the superannuation surcharge. In the end, Government budgeting is all about setting priorities, and the present Government's priorities are transparent. Its priorities are unfairness and privilege, and that is a disgraceful start for a new Government.

I, too, should like to thank the officials who worked extremely hard on the legislation for over years. Government members know full well that the Opposition will not support the third reading of the Crown Minerals Bill. There are three major reasons, all of which were rehearsed during the Committee stage. First, Opposition members strongly believe that the provisions for the allocation of minerals should be in the main resource management law reform legislation. We think that because those provisions will be stuck out on the side in separate minerals legislation a different ethos will be brought to the issue of the allocation of minerals from that which will govern the general treatment of other resources. My fears on that score were heightened when I listened to the Minister of Energy, who introduced the third reading, because he gave one of those incredibly pro - mining industry speeches that I have heard from Ministers of Energy ever since I came into the House. His speech evoked the spirit of the s and the reason that gold-miners had representation in Parliament. It was wrong then, and it would be wrong now, but I think that to put that part of the legislation under that Minister---whoever the Minister of Energy is---is not right, and will keep that privileged place in New Zealand law that mining has had for so long. The second reason for opposing that part of the legislation is that Opposition members are very concerned that there is no requirement that national policy statements on minerals be prepared. The review group did recommend that. We believe that it is the Government's responsibility to spell out its views on minerals and their usage in national policy statements. The Opposition moved an amendment to that effect but it was not accepted. The third major issue is the landowners' veto. I have heard all the arguments, and I may well accept that the legislation is tougher than it has ever been, but it is not tough enough. I believe that farmers should have the right to prevent their way of life from being destroyed by a mining company coming on to their land. I strongly believe that. I do not believe the Minister of Transport when he says that the chances of obtaining an Order in Council are in ,. I think that they are much greater. I know the resources that a mining company can bring to bear when it is up against a farmer, who is probably heavily indebted and cannot afford to fight that company. I am very concerned about that. I have looked very carefully at clause E of the original Bill. It will be numbered somewhat differently now that the legislation has been separated out. I know the process; I know that if a miner is not satisfied because, although he has a permit, he cannot gain access, he can trot off to the Minister of Energy. An application will be put in and the Minister must consider whether there are sufficient public interest grounds to support overriding the landowner's veto. If the Minister thinks that, prima facie, there is that interest, he will serve on the farmer a notice in writing of his preliminary views that there are public interest grounds. The farmer will have months in which to give in then and there and negotiate access, or to cave in and agree to an arbitrator's settling the question, or to fight it and to try to argue to the Minister that there are no public interest grounds for the mine to go ahead on his or her land. Remember that the farmer cannot argue his own private interest as a landowner and his interest in wanting to farm his land undisturbed and to live in his home undisturbed by heavy machinery and explosives from a mining company working around him. I cannot see that he can do that; the way that clause E is worded he can only argue the public interest. I think that his private interest is a legitimate interest, and I support it. Three months after he has put the case to the Minister, the Minister for the Environment and the Minister of Energy could determine that an Order in Council would declare that an arbitrator was able to determine access. I think of the farmer who has written to me several times. He is from Opito Bay, and he has been fighting off miners for years. He is not in a particularly strong position. I am very concerned that clause E does not define public interest. Will ``public interest'' simply be some suggestion that the mining company will dig out gold that is worth millions of dollars? I still do not think that we have struck appropriate rents or royalties for that. Will ``public interest'' be determined as simply being the fact that the company has promised to create a few short-term jobs? Mining jobs are normally short term. Will ``public interest'' be defined to protect the company, which, of course, will argue that it has, in some cases, spent millions of dollars getting to that point, and that that money will have gone to waste if it is not granted access? I think that that will end up being a very strong ``public interest'' argument, regardless of the fact that the company may have insulted and offended the farmer to the point at which he does not want to have anything to do with it. I believe that, if the Government were really interested in protecting the interests of landowners, ``public interest'' would be spelt out in the legislation so that people would know what they were fighting when they tried to fight an application for an Order in Council to determine access on the basis of public interest. I also wonder whether public interest will vary a great deal depending on the region of the country that we are talking about. For example, what will ``public interest'' mean on the West Coast? We heard the views of the member for West Coast a little earlier. I do not agree with any of them, at all. If the Minister for the Environment wants to assure me that that will not be the definition of ``public interest''---

I move, That the House take note of miscellaneous business. This afternoon the Opposition wishes to raise the issue of the closure of rural schools and the manner in which those closures are being carried out. We wish to invite the Minister of Education to reconsider the decision that he has come to, in principle, in respect of schools, and to ensure that those schools are given the opportunity to go through a full process of consultation with their communities about what is best for them. Before going into the substance of the issue, I will comment on the importance of schools in the rural community. The school is a focal point of a rural community. I grew up in such a community, and often the community is characterised only by the school and the hall, which are a focus of community activity. Nobody says that small schools should not ever close, but there are processes. Those processes are set out fully in the law of the land---in this case, the Education Act---and it is very important that those processes should be observed. It is important because the processes give the communities time to come to terms with decisions made about their future. When the boom is simply lowered from Wellington, as has been the case with these closures, communities are not given the dignity of being able to work through their own future. I have been in contact with a number of these schools where the common feeling is one of betrayal.

Just before the lunch adjournment I was making the point that the total number of intellectually disabled offenders who are potentially dangerous is not high, and I wonder whether a mountain may be being made out of a molehill in respect of the facilities that New Zealand needs to get in place to deal with that small category of offenders. I note that on previous advice from the Society for the Intellectually Handicapped we were told that there could be, at most, to people in New Zealand of all ages in that category at any given time. It seems to me that it is not beyond the wit of our criminal justice and intellectual disability services to come up with an appropriate facility that ensures that, in future, people in that condition are not inappropriately detained in mental hospitals. I come back to the main problem that I see with the Bill, and that is that, in effect, the mental health Act has been run through a word processor to apply to intellectual disability. That has some rather bizarre effects when one looks to, say, clauses and , lifted straight out of the compulsory care and treatment sections of the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act and purporting to apply to people with intellectual disability. Those clauses state: ``Special provision relating to electro-convulsive treatment'' and ``Special provision relating to brain surgery'', and, as in the mental health Act applying to mentally disordered people, it states that no patient shall be required to accept either electroconvulsive treatment---or electric shock treatment as it is more commonly known in the public mind---or brain surgery unless he or she consents to it. The problem is that I cannot see anywhere in the modern world that anyone would suggest that an intellectually disabled person should have either brain surgery or electroconvulsive treatment for his or her condition. That is an example of how absurd it is simply to lift the provisions of one Act and apply them to a completely different situation---namely, to those who have an intellectual disability. The advantage of the Bill now having at least seven weeks' study in the select committee is that very significant redrafting should be able to be done. I say, for my part, that I would like the select committee to come back with a completely redrafted Bill for the intellectually disabled offenders, which gives them their own provision in legislation, because the approach taken in the Bill being considered today does corrupt the principle of the mental health Act. Indeed, the whole Part II of the Bill, which is dealing with those offenders who require detention but are not mentally disordered, is to impose on them a medical model. I know that that is something about which people working in the intellectual disability field have long had concerns. That was why there was concern about funding for disability support coming into the health system last year. People feared that inappropriate medical models would be applied, and when one sees in the Bill that the responsibility for special patients who are intellectually disabled will rest with the director of area mental health services, one can understand the concern, because the intellectually disabled are not mentally ill. I submit that the director of area mental health services is not the right person to be taking responsibility for their compulsory care---certainly that is the right person in respect of someone with a mental disorder, but not the right person in respect of those intellectually disabled offenders. Again, if we are looking to appropriate legislation we need to start with the responsibility for that group going to a designated person who is not part of the mental health system, but whose authority flows through disability support and people who specifically understand the needs of those particular offenders. The whole debate on the Bill has thrown up the complex interface between the health, disability, and justice sectors. Again, I say that we did not see the disability support people in the briefings but we did not see the representatives of the Department of Justice, either.

Come back to Tolaga Bay---an invitation from the member for Mahia to the new Treasurer. What a rapid socialisation! What a good pupil for Treasury! The ink was hardly dry on the coalition promises before the Government started to back away from them. The Labour Party has done its sums and we know that all those promises cannot be paid for with the money that has been allocated. We have issued figures that no one has seriously disagreed with, that for the - year they are about $ million out; for the - year they are almost $ million out; and from to they are almost $ million out, not allowing for any fiscal slippage or the effect of uncosted initiatives. Scarcely was the ink dry on the coalition agreement before duty Ministers started shedding some doubt on whether the policies could be paid for. Perhaps it was a mistake to leave the new Minister of Labour, Mr Bradford, in charge over the summer because he told the truth. He told the truth about a number of things. He said some policies would have to be postponed to stay within the self-imposed spending limits for the Budget. In fact, Mr Bradford was frank, not only about the problems of paying for the promises. He also let the cat out of the bag on the secret privatisations. Labour will be supporting the passage of the Bill---not because the Bill is perfect; it is not perfect---because we wish to see the settlement effected between Ngai Tahu and the Crown. To see the Bill lose in the House now, I believe, would be a betrayal of all those who have put years of their lives into seeking justice for Ngai Tahu, and of those generations of Ngai Tahu who have gone before, who sought recognition of the wrongs done to their people over a period of almost years. A defeat for this Bill would mean more years going by without justice being done to Ngai Tahu for those historical grievances. The history of the issue is well summarised in the Bill's preamble. In Ngai Tahu signed the treaty. In the years following, the Crown sought the transfer of land from Ngai Tahu to it. There were ten major purchases, and we know them to be shady. >From an early time Ngai Tahu pursued claims against the Crown---claims of unfair purchase practices and breaches of the deeds of purchase. There have been a number of inquiries into what went on. Some have been outright dismissive. Others have found validity to the Crown. But until now no appropriate action has been taken to address those grievances. In the fourth Labour Government made it possible for claims under the treaty going back to to be examined by the Waitangi Tribunal. On August , exactly years to this day, the Ngai Tahu claim went to the Waitangi Tribunal. Hearings were held in and , almost a decade ago. In , the tribunal reported on the claim and found substantially in Ngai Tahu's favour, and also recommended the passing of a statute to create a representative tribal body for Ngai Tahu. The Crown accepted the thrust of that report and entered negotiations with Ngai Tahu in September , almost years ago. Te Runanga o Ngai Tahu was recognised by law years ago as the legal representative of Ngai Tahu. In October , heads of agreement for the settlement were entered into, and, in November , the deed of settlement was signed. This Bill, introduced in March this year, gives effect to certain provisions of that deed of settlement and provides for an apology by the Crown to Ngai Tahu. Labour is committed to the process of settling grievances and claims made under the treaty. We restate that basic commitment in our support for the passage of the legislation, knowing that all over this country Maori wish to settle through due process and we must support that process. We do not see supporting the Bill as indicating any general confidence in the Government. We have none. But what we do acknowledge is that there have been years of patient negotiation between the Crown and Ngai Tahu, and that has been carried out in good faith. It would be wrong to see that work scuttled now for any short-term political objective, and we will not do that. I also wish to record my personal appreciation for the dogged efforts of the Minister in charge of Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations in the way he has pursued these matters. While there is room for considerable debate about the approach taken to this settlement in particular, and to treaty settlements in general, I would not for one moment underestimate the personal commitment and contribution that he has made. I do want to comment on the difficulties that Parliament is placed in when legislation of this kind comes before it. This is no ordinary Bill. I see its presentation to Parliament as akin to the presentation of an international treaty here for ratification. That, I think, is a procedure we should be following with treaties that the Government enters into using its executive authority. A treaty entered into by a Government acting with that authority, and then brought to this House for ratification, could not be amended, nor could it be in any country by a national legislature. A legislature in those circumstances must vote the treaty up or down. Apart from technical amendments, that is precisely the position we are presented with in this Bill. I believe that the select committee's report states that succinctly, and I quote from it: ``We accept that it is Parliament's task to determine whether to give effect to the settlement that has been agreed between two parties, but not to substitute a different settlement. It is also Parliament's task to evaluate whether the provisions in the bill do give proper effect to the negotiated settlement. In this way, it is within our power to recommend amendments that will ensure that the bill's provisions work in a technical sense and that all necessary provisions are included, or changed to correct errors of fact or law.'' That is the task the committee has undertaken. The select committee report also notes that the deed of settlement negotiated between the Crown and Ngai Tahu is a contract between the parties that is conditional on the passage of the Bill in a form acceptable to Ngai Tahu. We can, of course, debate whether this is the way in which treaty settlements should be handled in the future. I do appreciate the frustration of members of the committee and of those who made submissions who wanted to see change. The plain truth to me is that it is not possible to make significant changes to this Bill without wrecking the settlement. That does not mean the committee or this Parliament are being asked to be a rubber stamp to the legislation. We are being asked to vote yes or no on the merits of the issue. Feeling the weight of history on our shoulders, Labour will vote yes and will not support amendments that would scuttle the Bill were they to be passed. When the heads of agreement for this settlement were entered into in October , I recall saying that it was a proud day for Ngai Tahu. But one of the issues that has gripped the committee throughout is who are Ngai Tahu. Who is covered by the Bill and whose future claims are extinguished by it? I acknowledge the sincerity and good intentions of all those members who have advanced the case for Waitaha and others to have their identity acknowledged as separate from that of Ngai Tahu. Frankly, the evidence presented has been contradictory. It may be that further consideration should be given to those issues, but to give that consideration now cannot be done without doing an injustice to a far larger group who wish for the speedy resolution of this settlement after almost years of injustice. I would urge Te Runanga o Ngai Tahu to seek to be as inclusive as it can be in ensuring that all those entitled to participate in its affairs and benefit from the settlement can so participate and so benefit. In this respect, I do draw attention, as the select committee report does, to the accountability mechanisms in the charter of the runanga. They are critical. They can be legally enforced. Further, decisions of the runanga are open to judicial review and the Ngai Tahu charitable trust may be scrutinised by the Attorney-General under the Charitable Trusts Act. If the rules established for accountability are honoured, then what follows from this settlement and the passage of this Bill will in my view have integrity. I conclude by wishing Ngai Tahu well as they go forward from the passage of this Bill to realise the dreams of generations of their people, who sought that apology from the Crown and who sought to redress grievances. They will see the passage of this Bill as meeting their aspirations and giving them a new basis on which to move forward as a people.

I move, That this House note with sadness the death of Her Royal Highness The Princess Margaret, Countess of Snowdon CI, GCVO, and that it extend to Her Majesty The Queen and members of the royal family its deepest sympathy. It was with sadness that I learnt late on Saturday evening of the death of Princess Margaret. Princess Margaret never visited New Zealand, yet, because she was the Queen's only sibling, New Zealanders knew a lot about her. When I was a child, Princess Margaret was a beautiful and glamorous young woman. Her life was not always a happy one. While materially wealthy, she lived within a system of constraints that most of us would find intolerable and that led to her putting royal duty and constitutional convention ahead of her first love. As a key member of the royal family Princess Margaret was associated with many voluntary and charitable causes. As a child who did not attend school, her association with the Girl Guide movement provided her with contact with other children, and she repaid the Guides' friendship with lifelong support for the movement. Princess Margaret's many years of involvement with the Order of St John and with Barnardos were appreciated by their branches in New Zealand. The princess was also a longstanding supporter of the creative arts, especially the ballet. In recent years Princess Margaret suffered poor health, but none the less the sudden news of her death came as a shock. The Government conveyed a message of condolence to Buckingham Palace on behalf of New Zealanders on Saturday evening. Flags were flown at half mast at Government House on Sunday, and at Parliament and Government buildings yesterday, as a mark of respect for the princess. They will fly at half mast again on Friday, the day of the funeral. A condolences book is available for signature in the parliamentary foyer. Our sympathies this week are with Princess Margaret's children, Lord Linley and Lady Sarah Chatto; with the Queen and the Queen Mother; and with all members of the royal family. May Princess Margaret rest in peace.

The reason the country got into trouble was that a Cabinet of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member froze wages, but did not do anything but permit benefits to be indexed. The present Leader of the Opposition acquiesced in the intervention of the right honourable gentleman from Tamaki, who was the Prime Minister at that time. There is no sense in arguing about that. The present Leader of the Opposition did not have the ability to say that he would not do it, as did Mr Quigley, the former member for Rangiora---he stood up. I give the member for Selwyn full marks. She crossed the floor one night. I saw the man called Jones from Auckland cross the floor. I give full marks to people in this place who have the courage and integrity to follow their principles, but not to the people who, with some degree of cynicism---I am not allowed to use the word hypocrisy---condemn the Government for a poverty trap that they created themselves. It is a difficult thing to get out of. I accept wholeheartedly that one of the tasks for the Government is to encourage people to break out. The worker who does his or her hours or more is entitled to a higher benefit as a result of that work than the person who elects to stay at home, either because of force of circumstance or because of the economy. There must be an incentive to get out and work. One of the troubles is that the wage structure is too low. The unions are right when they say that it is too low, but they are wise enough to know that at present they cannot demand excessive wage claims from manufacturers and transport operators, who cannot afford them. In the recent round they have shown a restraint that is commendable. I know of the problem. I am with the member for Remuera on the problem; I agree with him. It is not a problem of this Government's making. It started with the intervention in the economy by the right honourable gentleman who imposed a wage freeze. It could not operate. I am willing to say that the member for Selwyn, the member for Raglan, and some of the others at least tried to distance themselves from that.

I am convinced that a good healthy interest in any form of sport or vocation is good for New Zealanders. If the races continue to be held in the afternoon there is nothing to prevent or restrict anyone from observing the religious matters that they want to be involved in, and that is their business. I say seriously to those who from a religious point of view take a conscience vote against me that I understand their position. The thoroughbred breeding industry is a good industry. The country will probably sell between $ million and $ million of livestock off shore this year. It will also import many horses. To me it is not just the export of thoroughbred livestock; it is also the fact that Australians recognise that it is something that New Zealanders beat them at. New Zealand has won about of the past Melbourne Cups. The latest Melbourne Cup was won by Empire Rose, which is a wonderful mare. If she were human she would be ft in. and almost as big as Joel Garner. She is a wonderful mare, and it gave me pride as a New Zealander to see her finish in the McKinnon Stakes as Kiwi did years ago, and to see her hang on with all her courage against the colts and the geldings coming at her. It gives me pride as a New Zealander that the thoroughbred industry can throw up a champion such as Bonecrusher, even though he ran a disappointing race in the Japan Cup recently. Any New Zealander who watched Waverley Star and Bonecrusher race down the straight at Moonee Valley in the Cox Plate in the past few years would have stood up and cheered for New Zealand. There are many knockers in this country, but we can be proud of our racehorse industry and our breeders. People from around the world come to New Zealand to buy the best. They are prepared to pay a fortune. We are able to raise good horses because of the limestone country, the good grass, the fact that New Zealand farmers---not just the big studs---breed horses, and because New Zealanders love horses. In the end that means that as a small nation of people we can be proud that the rest of the world recognises us as the breeders of some of the greatest thoroughbred stock in the world. As the member for Waitotara said, New Zealand can compete with the rest of the world and do well with horses such as Balmerino and others. I remember saying to the late Joe Walding one day: ``Let's get ourselves a filly. We'll breed her off shore, off time''---because one has to go off time---``and we'll will win the Oaks in Britain. I'll make the speech and you'll get the cup. I'll tell them that we rode out and got the slowest horse in the brumby herd, and that we are going back next year to get a fast one.'' The speech made by the member for Maramarua was one of the saddest speeches I have ever heard in the House. His body language was so strong that his speech was also the most unconvincing speech I have ever heard in the House. The member purported to support the interests of women, but it was quite clear that it was the interests of the employers that he actually had in mind. His speech was probably the worst anti-women speech I have ever heard. Basically, he said that women could not be trusted under the Bill to ensure that their needs and requirements were met. He was saying that the National Party knows better than the women of New Zealand. If he were really concerned about women he would allow the Bill to go through and let women themselves decide whether they would take pay equity claims, but no, he made the usual patronising speech. Government members are completely sick of the Opposition's attitude that it knows best. On the contrary, I am pleased to speak in the third reading of the Employment Equity Bill. The Bill is an important part of the Government's plan for social policy reform. The Bill has had a long gestation period, and is the result of three reports in the same number of years. It is interesting that the Bill is being passed today when five Ministers are women. It is a historic fact that women in a Cabinet of is the best number that any New Zealand Government has managed to achieve. We owe those women a debt of gratitude for making sure that the Bill came into the House and that it would be passed tonight. What does the Bill do? First, it insists that discrimination against workers, whether based on gender, disability, or ethnic origin, should play no part in the employment scene. It paves the way for employers to plan and monitor programmes that eliminate barriers to the employment and promotion of women, disabled people, or Maori and Pacific Island people. The Bill makes it absolutely clear that all workers should enjoy equal opportunities for employment. The select committee amended the Bill by inserting a new definition of ``opportunities'' in order to make it absolutely clear that opportunities must be based on merit. Women would do much better in the hierarchy of New Zealand employment if merit were the basis on which promotions were made. The Bill states in a nutshell that all people should be treated according to merit, and should not be discriminated against because of gender, disability, or ethnic origin. I cannot understand why anyone could possibly object to the equal employment opportunity part of the Bill. During the Committee stage Opposition members spent practically no time at all talking about that part of the Bill. The member for Marlborough said that he supported that part of the Bill, then---as is the wont of Opposition members when voting as private individuals, and as they always do---he trooped into the lobby and voted with the Opposition en bloc. At no time did Opposition members explain---and I have not heard an explanation today, either---why employers should not be required by law to remove the discrimination that operates at present against the more vulnerable members of society. Opposition members complained that the Bill was a sop to women. The member for Maramarua suggested that the Government was passing the Bill only to show that it cared about women. The public can work out from that statement, and from the way in which Opposition members vote, exactly how much they care about women. Opposition members also showed very clearly that they have no respect for the women in their caucus. The member for Waipa was once an enthusiastic and vocal supporter of the Bill. When Parliament received petitions last year asking for the Bill the member for Waipa, day after day, called out from her chair: ``About time, too'', and ``When will the Government do it?''. The petitions were considered by the select committee and were reported back to the House unanimously in support of the Government's giving the Bill favourable legislation.
