The episode clearly shows that the whole issue results from an error or bad planning on the part of the Government. It is now March---less than weeks from the end of the month. Members have been pulled into the House under urgency to pass tax rates for the ensuing year. Any Government that was organising a tax programme properly and carefully would have had the legislation passed well before this time. The matter of some urgency being required for some measures in the Taxation Reform Bill (No. ) was raised several times, but the Government ignored the need to get on with the job and pass those measures. Since I became a member of Parliament I have noticed that Government members claim much credit for referring taxation Bills to a select committee---a procedure that did not happen before. That is a good procedure. They claim great credit for it, but it is not happening today. That is particularly important in relation to clauses to . On Budget night a proposal was put forward that pay-as-you-earn tax be paid twice---on the fifteenth and the fifth of the following month. It was a big change from the previous requirement that it be paid on the twentieth of the month. A threshold of $, was included that would have allowed people to pay on the fifth of the following month only. That threshold was raised to $,. As a result of an advice from the Waugh committee on tax simplification, it has been decided to charge businesses that pay less than $, pay-as-you-earn tax a year on the twentieth of the month. In the ordinary economy that would represent a firm with about nine employees. If a firm has nine employees it is entitled to pay its tax on the twentieth of the month following the month in which that tax was collected from the employees. If that firm has $, the tax has to be paid twice a month on the fifth and on the fifteenth. There has been no investigation of the link between that threshold and the dates on which pay-as-you-earn tax is paid. When that one-payment scheme was introduced the Government decided that a logical cut-off point would be nine workers. In the Opposition's opinion the cut-off point should have been $,, which would have cost about $. million a year in cash-flow delays---practically nothing in terms of overall Government expenditure---and would have relieved the burden. As there will be no select committee hearings the Minister should explain why, out of all the matters considered by the Waugh committee, the Government has chosen this one point to force through in legislation in this way, I suspect that it is because there has been such an enormous eruption of resentment at the compliance cost caused by that thoughtless measure, which would have gained very little revenue but would have put an enormous ongoing burden on all businesses. In response to that eruption of resentment the Government has decided to change that provision, and that provision alone. It should be referred to a select committee so that members could consider whether that is the correct threshold, now that it has been decided to return to the payment date of the twentieth of the month. Provision has been made to enable donations to the Cyclone Ofa Relief Fund to qualify for the income tax rebate. The Opposition supports that provision in principle, and I can understand its being agreed to. There will not be any concern about it from the business community or from anyone else who has to pay tax. It is giving away a benefit, and that should be done. One clause will allow local authority trading enterprises, port companies, airport authorities, and so forth, to have their taxation treatment confirmed to allow them to carry forward losses from port operators and suchlike. Why is it so important that that provision be passed by March? When the Minister introduced the Bill he carefully went through its provisions and explained what it would achieve. He said: ``It will do this, this, and this'', but he did not justify the urgency in passing the Bill. I accept the point about rates. Under a well-planned programme that measure would have been introduced some time ago, but no justification has been given for a lot of the clauses that are being introduced being passed in such a hurry. What about the proposal to raise the charitable succession exemption from $, to $,? That is one of the recommendations in the report to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Social Welfare on the taxation treatment of sporting bodies and charities. It is the only recommendation to have found its way into law. I know the reason for its being included, and it is sensible. It brings the treatment of donations and charitable exemptions into line and makes them consistent with each other. Why was that measure the only recommendation of that report to be picked out as having to be passed urgently? It is the only measure that is not to be referred to a select committee. The Bill should be examined by a select committee to consider whether the submissions received are in accordance with the proposals in that report. That whole matter should be reviewed to make it tidier so that taxpayers can clearly understand what they are and are not permitted to do under the Act. The point has been made. This is an abuse of parliamentary procedure by a group of members who call themselves the Government yet cannot organise the passing of tax rates until days before the end of the year. That Mickey Mouse way of operating is not good enough. Sitting suspended from midnight to a.m. (Thursday).

I also think, as the previous speaker said, that it is good that there has been some bipartisanship on this Bill. As the Attorney-General has pointed out there are probably some reasons for that happening that go back into the history of how the Bill came about, and that is not to be criticised. I think that it is important that we have this issue in front of us. I do not know whether the Bill will go quite as far as we need to go---and that is an issue that I want to address. It is a good idea to have a privacy Bill. The technology improvements that have occurred make the sharing of information far easier than it used to be, and I imagine that it will get easier still in the future, and as it does the pressure on departments---such as the one for which I am responsible---to disclose information that they have and hold and collect for the use of other departments will also increase. I have never shared the cynicism that some people have about the State, and I think that the argument advanced by the member for Christchurch Central that one always impinges on someone else's freedom when one takes one's own freedom is a valid argument. One individual's freedom will end when it interferes with another individual's freedom. In the case of information-sharing of, say, income information that could be used to stop benefit abuse, it is easy to accept the valid argument that in overprotecting the freedom of the individual to have the information supply checked one is interfering with the freedom of other taxpayers who have to be taxed at a higher level than they would otherwise have to be to fund what is an erroneous claim on the State. There has been some discussion about identity cards. Identity cards bring out quite strong emotional feelings because people see them as being -ish and they worry about departments of State having little cameras in the corners of every room supervising people's every move so that no person would be able to conduct his or her day to day affairs without being supervised by the State. No one is trying to move to that position. An identity card can only establish a person's identity. I know that is a self-fulfilling truism. There are many ways to establish a person's identity, and on its own it does not prove anything of terribly great value. It may prove that a person applying for a benefit was the actual person and that it was not somebody coming in as name No. or name No. so that they could get many benefits; that is as far as it goes. Information-sharing is the way to know whether the application details themselves are correct. A person's income information and employment information need to be known to make the system work, and that is the way in which this kind of legislation is important. New Zealand has a self-assessment or voluntary system of paying taxes. We profile taxpayers to provide a sufficient presence of policing so that people know that sooner or later they will be checked, but they know that the department does not maintain a big enough structure to check every person every year. We look to match data that are collected already using such systems as PAYE. The employer pays it in and at the end of the year the taxpayer puts in a return, and the department matches the two. Source deduction payments have added to the certainty, that not declaring income will be discovered, but by and large we rely on people to declare their incomes honestly. That is as it should be. Because it is a self-assessment system it is important that when people give the department information they can feel confident that it is being used only for the purpose for which it was intended. Clause lists information privacy principles, which I think constitute the core of the Bill. I have read through them and I have to say that in the light of the knowledge that I have on this subject I think that they need to be more comprehensive. The guidelines on what is admissible information to pass from one person or department to another person or department or any official making a check need to be more refined. We need to have narrowly circumscribed instances of when State information is permitted to be shifted from one department to another. It is important that it is done in that way because under its Act the Inland Revenue Department has very substantial powers that are not normally available to most Government departments. The department has the power to inquire into a person's banking and financial affairs. I often fear that one of the reasons that information-sharing is called for is not so that one department can access information collected by another department---thereby avoiding duplication of the collection agencies---but so that one department can step in and use the important and very extensive powers already legally granted to another department. They are powers that Parliament has given in the past to one department because of the importance of obtaining that information to enable that department to carry out its own activity, which is to ensure that all taxpayers pay a fair and correct contribution to New Zealand's revenue. For that reason the principles in clause will have to be gone over to remove their generalised content, and specifically to circumscribe the activities that are permitted by particular departments. I refer in particular to the Inland Revenue Department, because I would be concerned if the powers provided under section of the Income Tax Act were available to other departments by virtue only of their right to access information from another department---hence my concern that information-sharing rules in the Bill are not sufficiently circumscribed as to the information that is permissible. The final point that I should like to make is that we have not been particularly effective in New Zealand at letting people know what information-sharing is currently allowed. I have seen various surveys that have been conducted that make me aware that many people in the community believe that the Inland Revenue Department already shares information with other departments. However, it does not; it cannot; and it is prohibited from doing that by its legislation. I know that the Leader of the Opposition raised as an important election issue that the department should be able to share information in order to avoid benefit abuse. I think that that is something that will have to come about so that the Government's revenue can be properly protected from abuse by wrong claims, and from people who put in dishonest claims for the resources of the State when they are not entitled to them. The Bill is a useful first step. I am pleased that it will be referred to a select committee, and I congratulate the member for Ohariu on bringing the issue forward. I am sure that the Bill will have to be developed considerably more before it will be able to be used, but at least it sets the ball rolling on an issue that will be important for New Zealand.

I move, That the Government Superannuation Amendment Bill (No. ) be introduced. The Bill we are about to introduce reflects a recent Cabinet decision to defer the closure of the Government superannuation fund for a year. The Bill makes two simple but important changes to the Government Superannuation Fund Act; first, the Government superannuation fund general scheme, which is the scheme to which most State servants belong, will now be closed to new members from July , not , as applies in the principal Act, and, second, the provisions which would have required the Government to start funding the scheme's future liabilities as they accrue are being repealed. The Government will continue, as successive Governments have for many years, paying its share of the cost of benefits as the benefits are paid. The Government is deferring the closure of the Government superannuation fund general scheme because it believes in building a community that saves and is self-reliant. As an employer the Government has a responsibility to its employees to encourage them to save for their retirement. We do not see the present Government superannuation general fund scheme as filling the needs of the Government as an employer or of its employees in the long term. Deferring the scheme's closure by months will provide time for adequate replacement superannuation arrangements to be put in place. Such arrangements have not been put in place through the State sector in the past months. It is clear to us that the previous Government did not think through all the issues involved in this very complex question. It is also clear that departments have not made sufficient progress to ensure that schemes are put in place to fill the gap. The next months will be used to ensure that those needs are adequately reviewed and the replacement schemes are in place. Importantly---and this relates to something that was absent in the previous case---this process will include consultation with the interested parties---something that was sadly lacking last year. During the same period the special schemes in the Government superannuation fund will be reviewed and the needs of the employers and the employees will be assessed, also in a consultative framework. The closure of the Government superannuation fund general scheme is covered in clause of the Bill. Clauses and deal with the way that the Government funds its subsidy as an employer. At the present time the Government pays its share of the cost as benefits are paid to people who belong to the scheme; that is as they retire and earn their pension. Under the legislation that the Bill repeals, the Government would have started paying its contribution into the Government superannuation fund along with its employees' contributions from July . The Government does not see this change as being necessary. It adds nothing at all to contributors' security, and that is the usual reason employers fund schemes. It would simply add a further burden of $ million for present taxpayers.

I move, That the Public Finance Amendment Bill be now read a third time. The Bill is a small Bill without a great deal of importance, I suppose, in the narrow sense. It relates to the fact that the definition of a ``Crown agency'' and the way that Crown agencies will be consolidated into the balance sheet of the Crown for the purposes of the annual accounts of the Crown have yet to be established. The Public Finance Act was introduced in , and, as a result of select committee consideration of that legislation, it was felt at that stage that the definition of a Crown agency was too unclear for Crown agencies to be ready to be included in the consolidated accounts of the Crown. It was therefore decided to refer that matter to the Finance and Expenditure Committee so that it could come up with a definition of a Crown agency for the purposes of the Public Finance Act, and also come up with a method by which those accounts would be consolidated into the Crown's accounts for the purpose of the Public Finance Act. That was years ago, and I have to report that during the Committee stage of the Finance Bill there was some criticism from the Opposition about things not having been achieved in that regard. I have to say that most of the fault would have to rest with the Labour Government, because it was during its term that the issue sat for years before a select committee. However, as a result of the concern that was expressed I spoke to the chairman of the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and I was told that several actions have been taken that will have the effect of speeding up the process of coming up with a definition. It appears as though a subcommittee of the Finance and Expenditure Committee will be appointed and given specific responsibility to conclude the matter. The effect of the Bill is to extend for a year the period in which the Public Finance Act will not apply to Crown agencies. In that year it is hoped that the definition and the way in which it will be consolidated into the Crown's accounts will be finalised. That is the purpose of the Bill. The Bill is not of great size. It merely gives the Finance and Expenditure Committee time to complete its inquiry to enable the necessary legislation to be prepared and the way in which it will be incorporated to be decided, and to have the legislation passed through the House so that by April the Crown agencies will be brought into the accounts under the umbrella of the Public Finance Act.

I want to conclude by briefly covering issues of special importance to me in terms of my portfolios. The first portfolio, which I have been associated with for some time, is that of revenue. The main point I want to mention is the progress that we made in that we have introduced a new form of policy making. The Rt Hon. Sir Ivor Richardson has done a very good piece of work that will be concluded shortly, in the review of the Inland Revenue Department. He has recommended that we need to look at the process by which we make tax policy so that there is more consultation, more consideration, and a better understanding of why tax policy is as it is. I say that with the member for Tauranga present, as I know that the tax area is one of his areas of special concern. I make the point that, as I look back in Hansard over time, I notice that whenever Governments have introduced sensible but fairly tough and hard policies---and I read that the member for St Kilda, as an Associate Minister of Finance, had to introduce one himself in ---the Opposition has jumped up and the speeches have been exactly the same, regardless of the party of the members in Opposition at the time. They criticised the Government for exactly the same things. Tax policy is by nature complex. Tax policy is by nature difficult. But tax policy and tough tax policies are, by nature, necessary. If we do not have them our tax base will very quickly walk away from us. The gap between and that allowed all sorts of rorts to develop is at the heart of the problems that we have been discussing so much in this House now. Finally, I should like to mention the employment portfolio. It is an area in which we are now starting to see real progress. I am fortunate to be the first Minister of Employment who has been appointed when unemployment is actually falling. The rest of them have had to go out and explain ever-increasing unemployment figures. It has always been something of an illusion to try to get around the statistics that were there. Thankfully, unemployment is on the way down. We now have to focus our employment policies to assist those who have been caught up in the group that we refer to as the long-term jobless, and to assist those in the younger age-group to ensure that, whatever else happens, we have training programmes and assistance programmes that will ensure that they, too, will not end up in that pool of long-term jobless. If we can achieve that within this term, while I have responsibility for that portfolio, we will have done a great deal of good for New Zealand. It involves some refocusing of the New Zealand Employment Service on helping the long-term jobless, but that is what that service should be there to do.

Clauses and of the Bill seek to validate a number of rating irregularities in one or both of the - and - rating years. I have been going through a list of measures in this Bill that are reducing the compliance cost of taxpayers---a long list of measures. If the member read the Bill and knew what these things were I think she would very quickly realise that it contains a number of measures that reduce the compliance cost to firms significantly. One of the main ones, of course, is the binding rulings themselves. During the select committee process an amendment was made to correct a drafting error made in the income tax amendment legislation in relation to provisional tax relief: ``Relief from use of money---Interest has been restricted to those cases where the tax law of the commission or its policy is changed on or after the first day of the actual month in which the instalment of provisional tax is due.'' The amendment ensures that relief will be available from the first day of the preceding month---again a change that will help in relation to the compliance costs to taxpayers. The Bill tightens the rules relating to deductibility of expenditure incurred in providing fringe benefits. A small change in the fringe-benefit tax rules was recommended at the select committee level to put absolutely beyond any doubt the position relating to shareholder employees. The Bill exempts from gift duty transfers from local authorities to community trusts set up with the proceeds of the sale of shares in port companies. This kind of measure has been necessary in relation to a number of changes that have occurred in the structure of port companies and in what previously were local government trading operations. The Bill also amends the Local Government Act to require community trustees to be approved by the Minister of Local Government in consultation with the Minister of Revenue. The Bill has been amended to allow local authorities to transfer the earnings or the proceeds of the sale of port company shares to their community trusts. Provisions have also been made for earnings on these proceeds to be transferred free of gift duty before a certain date, to be set by Order in Council. The Bill introduces a new provision that is designed to stop deemed dividends from arising from the transfer of company property when it transpires that the consideration provided in respect of the property did not represent the correct market value of the property and at the time of the transfer the taxpayer had taken reasonable steps to value the property. Again, that is a measure that will introduce certainty into the tax legislation and is an important change in the provisions. The Bill contains several minor amendments to the Income Tax Act that flow from the company law reform legislation of . In particular, it provides for the tax consequences of the collapse of a financial arrangement on the amalgamation of a holder and an issuer. Several minor changes have been made to this provision at the select committee stage, the most important of which is that the relevant section now applies to all amalgamations, not just to qualifying amalgamations. Two consequential changes have been made to the Bill as a result of the decision to remove casual agricultural workers and election day workers from the income tax withholding payments regulations and to make them subject to PAYE at c in the dollar. The Bill gives effect to the first group of recommendations of the Richardson committee concerning the functions and objectives of the Inland Revenue Department. These, too, are very important changes. The measures proposed in this Bill clarify and confirm the current functions and obligations of Ministers, the Commissioner of Inland Revenue, and officials. As a result of submissions to the select committee, the provision that confirms the scope of the power of the Minister of Revenue to elect the commissioner in performance of certain functions has been clarified. The new subsection will confirm that directions may not be given concerning the tax affairs of individual taxpayers or the interpretation of tax law, and I have no difficulty with that change. This was a recommendation from the Richardson committee. Although it was not intended that it would be used for that purpose, the fact that the statute drives the point home is a good idea. The Bill contains amendments to stop tax avoidance opportunities relating to Niue's becoming a tax haven last year. That is an important measure in relation to the fact that the tax affairs of the Pacific Islands and the way in which those islands organise themselves have been something of an issue in New Zealand over recent times. The Bill introduces a provision enabling the Commissioner of Inland Revenue to monitor the flow of general insurance and reinsurance premiums flowing to insurers resident in the Netherlands and Switzerland. This measure is necessary because of our double tax agreement. A number of other measures are associated with this very long and very thorough Bill. I think the Bill demonstrates how well the generic tax policy process is working in that it has had a smoother passage than most tax Bills since I have been around this House, partly because the consultation recommended by the Richardson committee before Bills actually get into the legislative system allows a lot of the problems to be identified in a way that was not possible in the past. I have explained why progressive pricing is wrong. It is anti-environment, and it is anti-conservation. It forces consumption up. It means that we will have more stations than we need to have. I think it leads to inefficient use of power. In the absence of any logical way to attack the policy of introducing competition into generation the member for Dunedin North has engaged, in my opinion, in extreme exaggerated speculation---there is that word again---predicting huge price rises. He simplistically connects the price of power to the valuation of assets. Prices do not follow the valuation of assets; prices follow what one can actually earn for something in the market. But the member for Dunedin North does not seem to accept that. The lapse of understanding of the commercial world aside, the member's alarmism about the price of power is not supported by independent commentators throughout the community. The Consumer Coalition, a group representing electricity users, as reported on Morning Report on November, is of the view that the split will encourage competition between wholesale electricity suppliers, and the price of electricity will go down as a result. That is precisely the point. History has shown that competition actually works. Can anyone in this House remember what air services were like prior to the introduction of Ansett into the domestic aviation scene? There were no air bridges. There was no quality consumer service prior to the introduction of competition into air services. A monopoly will always be less sensitive to the interests of consumers than will competing firms. Competition clearly delivers benefits. The split of ECNZ is a key first step towards a strong, vibrant, competitive electricity market. The explanation I have given of the difference between long-run marginal cost pricing and progressive pricing indicates the ideological divide in this House on this particular issue. No amount of special pleading that they believe in microeconomic reform will alter that. Those are hollow words; crocodile tears. They do not actually believe in it. If they were honest in their beliefs, and I think they should be, they would both come out and say that they agree with progressive pricing, and that is what they are going to work for for the future. I am unashamedly in favour of competition in electricity generation.

The Ministry of Health is aware of the seriousness of the meningitis epidemic in New Zealand and is committed to preventing deaths from it. No vaccine currently on the market would be effective against the serogroup B strain of meningitis that is causing most deaths in New Zealand. The development and trialling of vaccines is a long and involved process with demonstrated safety and effectiveness being of the utmost importance. New Zealand is moving as rapidly as possible towards trialling a vaccine for the serogroup B meningococcal disease. The Ministry of Health has recently received replies from three vaccine institutes in Norway, Cuba, and the Netherlands, which were invited by the ministry to prepare information for assessment on current and future vaccines. The ministry is meeting the New Zealand vaccine research team this week, and will continue to do so to ensure progress in the next steps in the trial design. I am advised that a trial is possible for next year, provided good progress is made.

I know people can be silly about it, but the point is that race relations is a very serious issue for New Zealand. I remember Doug Graham talking about the Taranaki Waitangi Tribunal report, and he did have concerns about the language that was used in that particular report. It is important, though, that we take note of the type of personality Doug Graham was, in recognising that we solve problems in this country through the shared future that the M~aori King Tawhiao called for way back in of everyone working together for the common good of New Zealand. When I spoke on the reporting back of the Bill it had the allure and interest of a study of the third names of eighteenth century Hapsburg princes! When I reconsidered, I thought that that was an extreme form of flattery. When I went through the Bill more carefully, it was really hard to understand that more than a tiny number of people would have any great interest in those matters, but the truth is that a lot of people do have an interest in it. There is something in this Bill that is rather a sad commentary upon the nature of our national life and, indeed, the organisation of our economy. A great many of the matters that are dealt with in the Bill and that concern the consolidation regime and the like relate to the problem of why we cannot have a simple regime in relation to company tax. The only reason is because some highly complex, intelligent persons would drive very large trucks through it and no money would be collected. So we are engaged in an endless game of cops and robbers, or Inland Revenue Department and tax accountants or tax lawyers. Soon we will be up to the introduction in the House of the Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. ), one of a long sequence of never quite successful attempts to close loopholes and to ensure that the Inland Revenue Department gets what is owing to it, and that there is a decent and fair taxation system. If somebody could come up with an idea for either replacing company tax---that is, apart from a financial transactions tax---or, better still, fencing off companies from individuals in a totally impermeable fashion so that companies could be abolished and all taxation would rest upon the individual who received the profits and the dividends from the companies, that would be worth a very large ex gratia payment from Treasury. That idea would save an enormous amount of public administration. It would probably lead to a more highly efficient economy and to a greater level of revenue for the Crown at the end of the day, with much less agony. But the truth is that we will not be able to do that. I cannot join in entirely with the New Age, caring, ``love fest'' of bipartisanship that has been going on in the debates. While I appreciate the ``importance of planet Earth and the solar system beyond'', to quote the Alliance candidate for Wellington Central, my karma does not tend to bend itself in that direction. I want to highlight one or two matters on which there is some disagreement and that present some problems for the Government. The first relates to a matter that both the member and his Minister skated over very lightly indeed, and it is the matter of the changes to the Goods and Services Tax Act in relation to casinos and gaming. A number of moves in the Bill are designed to extend the taxation that has been imposed, and that is in contravention of the clear promise that was given that there would be no new taxes or tax increases during the life of this Parliament. We all remember the famous Morning Report interview in which the presenter said to the Leader of the Opposition of the time, the present Prime Minister: ``Sir, we've heard `no new taxes and no tax increases' in your first term'', and the Leader of the Opposition said: ``Where . . . but we've . . . yes you have.''. The presenter asked: ``That's in concrete?''. The Leader of the Opposition said ``Yes''. And of course there was that famous speech in which he asked whether anybody could think of any new taxes, and unfortunately got a reply that he has proceeded to implement ever since. The new casino tax, which is the new gambling tax that this Bill extends, is one of a very, very long list of new taxes that the National Government has introduced during this term of Parliament, and it is one of the clearest breaches of promise. I raise that matter only because the member for North Shore quietly slipped in---in a sort of sotto voce fashion and surreptitiously, while complimenting me---the fact that the Bill fulfilled a promise. That sparked me off, because the word ``promise'' tends to make me look through my notes to find whether, in fact, the existing legislation might involve some breach of promise. Indeed, I am afraid that the Bill incorporates a further, shall we say, ``sophistication'' in terms of breach of promise. It does not breach the promise de novo itself; it just adds a little bit more to a previous breach of promise that has occurred on the part of the Government in terms of ``no new taxes''. There is a lot of interest in the consolidation regime but I shall leave that aside for the moment and come to the issue of petroleum-mining taxation. That issue, like that of taxation of forestry, has been the subject of argument between the National Party and the Labour Party in the House over the past few years. It seems to me that there is a different issue in relation to the petroleum-mining taxation regime, and that is whether we essentially create an opportunity for not tax evasion but simply a light tax regime that is quite unnecessary in relation to other activities. It is important to note, as my colleague the member for Ohariu pointed out, that the Petro Consultants' report concluded that in New Zealand the fiscal regime, which covers taxation matters and others, is basically quite a relatively favourable petroleum fiscal regime by comparison with those regimes of other countries in the region. In other words, the reason that there is not a lot of exploration in New Zealand is not because the naughty Labour Government decided to tax petroleum mining out of existence; it is because there is low prospectivity in New Zealand. In fact, there is not a very high chance of major new oil or gas finds, and surprise, surprise, what the major oil companies use as their main criterion for looking for oil or gas is the expectation that they will find it! I realise that for those people who are buried in taxation law that might seem a peculiar reason for doing things; they might think that the reason people do things is the nature of taxation law, but, at the end of the day, Shell and BP and all those companies actually want to find oil and gas. They do not want merely a small tax concession for wasting a lot of money in not finding oil or gas, because looking for oil and gas still would actually cost them money, however favourable the taxation regime might be. So there must be some prospect of finding oil or gas, and it seems to me, therefore, that some of the arguments that have been put forward are a little irrelevant. However, being a person who can see two sides of the same issue, I say that there is an argument on the other side, because it really does not matter whether the petroleum-mining regime is a little too loose in terms of taxation. If there is a prospect, eventually the companies will get round to looking for it, and if there is not a prospect they will not bother, so the tax regime becomes rather irrelevant. In other words, the major determinants are the prospect of finding oil and gas and the price of the oil and gas relative to the probability of finding it. If the price is high, and if the price of oil is going up, one sees a great deal more exploration taking place worldwide. If the price is low, oil companies wind back their oil exploration worldwide. That is the most important thing that happens, and it has been happening for the past years or so in many ways. The taxation regime---contrary to the arguments of the member for New Plymouth, who would argue vehemently for the largest possible contributors to his election campaign funds---is not particularly important to those companies in deciding whether to explore. Of importance is whether the resource is there. That is why, when they do look for it, they look for it close to the electorate of the member for New Plymouth. They do not look for it close to my electorate, because the chances of finding oil and gas in the St. Kilda electorate are extremely low indeed. One would have to have a taxation regime that paid companies to look for oil and gas, for there to be the likelihood of any great exploration taking place there. So what I am saying is that as long as we find that the new regime does not lead to the unnecessary exploitation of resources---that is, the unwise use of resources---and does not lead to forms of tax avoidance, and I do not believe that it will, I do not see any great point in continuing to kick the issue round into the long-term future. The other issue that determines where prospecting takes place is the issue of political risk, and that has two dimensions. The first dimension is whether there is the chance of slightly loopy things taking place in terms of a change in the Government of a very strange people, and the codicil to that is whether one could buy off the very strong people. That is why countries with quite unstable political regimes still have lots of exploration; the oil companies work on the principle that at the end of the day the people in power could be bought. So as long as one is changing from one bunch of predictable crooks to another bunch of predictable crooks, it does not really matter. The real problem is when one has unpredictably honest people who might decide that they do not want exploration at all---such as some extreme version of the Green Party getting into power and deciding that there should not be exploration for oil and gas. That is not an issue in New Zealand. The more important issue is whether there are likely to be major changes in the taxation and related regimes that introduce a level of uncertainty into the area. As I said in relation to the forestry regime, there are much more difficult arguments, because already it is clear that some of the forestry partnerships have less to do with promoting forestry than they have to do with chasing a potential tax advantage in the short term. Nevertheless, one ought to strive for consistency and continuity in relation to regimes for these areas because, if one does not, one is putting at risk the economic prospects of the country. Opposition members are not about drawing dividing lines on these issues just for the sake of drawing dividing lines. In our view, an ounce of economic growth is worth a tonne of fiscal purity, and it is a pity that the Minister of Finance has not learn that lesson when it comes to the issue of the international tax regime. She is determined to get a tonne of purity---or, in her case, an ounce of purity---and will drive away growth in the New Zealand economy and drive away investment for the sake of that purity. I really hope that she starts to take a more pragmatic approach, as the Minister of Revenue does. We know very well that he takes that approach in the internal arguments of Cabinet. This Bill requires the Minister of Finance to pay off her National Party deceased persons in the form of repealing death duties by imposing an entertainment tax on living business people, and shearers, and people involved in the darts room at work, and all kinds of similar places---

It may be prepared to print money. That may well be true, and may well pay for some of its promises in the short term, and, of course, the country will pay for them in the long term should inflation be carried over. I come back to the Bill. It is an important Bill. It is the only formal parliamentary opportunity each year to debate these particular orders that have increased things such as war pensions and social security benefits. Parliament has the opportunity of this Bill to debate these matters at any length only because, while regulations are referred to the Regulations Review Committee, by the nature of things---barring the refusal by the member for Tauranga to grant leave for the House to rise at . p.m.---select committee reports are not usually reached within the parliamentary process, and remain undebated. Indeed, there is no matter for the Regulations Review Committee to report upon in this respect, because this Bill covers policy matters, which do not come within its purview. This Bill is not a question of the exercise of powers; it is a question of policy matters that normally are not matters for the Regulations Review Committee to consider. So this is an important debate. It is a chance for the House and the Government to front up to its failure to fulfil its promises. It is a chance for Government members to rise to defend the reason they have retreated from their pledges on the decent society. It will be interesting to see whether any Government members do rise to defend their Government on this matter. It will be very interesting to see how many Government members want to put their heads through the noose of receiving target mail by saying why they were prepared to break a cast-iron guarantee to superannuitants in relation to annual indexation of their pensions. That guarantee was given in full and open knowledge; it was repeated immediately after the election, and was broken only a matter of weeks later as the Government proceeded down its disastrous track. That matter has to be addressed by the House. That matter has to be addressed by Government members as they defend their sorry record in this regard. I have no apology for being somewhat bitter about it, because I well remember when I was Minister of Social Welfare the endless promises that were trailed before Grey Power. I well remember having to front up to those meetings with a policy of sanity and realism, and I make no apology for still defending a policy of sanity and realism in that regard. This side of the House has argued the issue with courage and consistency for years. There is only one football team kicking around the political football on this issue. In the past it has been the National Party political team. It is sad to see the Alliance political team now getting into the football game and making equally unfulfillable promises in that regard. The Alliance team is getting into the issue in the same way. The House has a very, very real problem facing it in terms of its credibility as a consequence of the Social Security (Rates of Benefits) Order , which cannot be lightly swept aside as a minor matter in politics.

The Minister of Revenue interestingly uses the example of a bank, but a bank has a whole range of prudential requirements and other requirements that solicitors are not required to meet in terms of these other areas of their activities, which are now being removed from coverage by the solicitors' fidelity guarantee fund. The Minister needs to grasp the point that there is a difference here that needs to be explored somewhat further. As my colleague has suggested, we may be ending up with an unsatisfactory half-way house. It seems to me that, if the coverage by the fidelity guarantee fund is to be withdrawn from a range of activities, at the end of the day it is best to say that solicitors do not engage in those activities, or, if they do, they do not engage as solicitors. In other words, when a solicitor is handling money in any sense---is engaged in investment in any sense---he or she is not doing that as a solicitor but simply as any other individual is free to do. When a person goes to a solicitor and places money with that solicitor for investment, I am not sure that the distinction could be drawn of the trust account versus the other accounts that the solicitor may be offering. I do not believe, for example, that the average elderly person, who is the main source of investment in solicitors' accounts, draws such a clear difference of that sort. When the select committee hears the evidence the end point arrived at may well be that it is best to banish the nominee company - type of operation entirely and to confine the activity of solicitors to the job of being a solicitor---which is not that of being a form of investment banker or indeed any other form of financial operator of that sort. If we arrive at that conclusion we will arrive at a sensible situation that will also avoid honest solicitors and accountants being put at enormous financial risk as a consequence of the actions of very, very few---a number of whom on occasions have had to assist the member for Glenfield and the member for Birkenhead with their inquiries.

I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I refer to the opening words of the Minister's reply. Every reply that the Minister gives to every question starts with a sarcastic, ironic reference to the member who has asked the question. Why does he have to start by saying ``Let's get things straight''?

He will speak very strongly against that provision. I have questions about a number of parts; first, Part I, in relation to the Accident Compensation Corporation. How much of a Budget fiddle is there in this part? How much is Part I simply there to reduce, just for year, the payment due from the Inland Revenue Department to the Accident Compensation Corporation by delaying payments during this particular financial year? It looks like the classic, one-off fiscal fiddle: how to transfer money from this year to next year to make this year's deficit look slightly better. This looks to me like a measure that the Minister of Labour has come up with, because the Minister of Finance did not come up with quite as many fiddles as she might have done. I want to go to Part XV. It is a little beauty. It covers income tax, but it covers one particular element that is close to my heart---the abolition of the surcharge. Today, the member for Hawke's Bay has put out a statement saying that he is confident that the Government will reduce the level of the income test on national superannuation before it comes into force. Already Government members have got wobbly round the knees as their electorate offices have been inundated with phone calls, as the delegates turn up to the National Party conference, ready, sharpening up the diamond cutters---that National Party superannuitants use at home---to use on their parliamentary representation. The House knows---it was explained by the Minister in his introduction---that the administration of the income test will be complex and intrusive. Every year, every single superannuitant---for example, an -year-old woman living alone---will have to fill in a form stating what her projected income will be for the coming year. At the end of the year she will have to have an end of year round-up to make sure that she has got it right. Twice a year every single superannuitant will have to fill in a form that is very complex.

The Minister of Justice agrees: ``My electorate is littered with -year-old lawyers who will carry on working for nothing in the future out of the goodness of their heart. They have been watching LA Law for too long, and identify themselves with those who work on behalf of the dispossessed within that particular firm.''. Do not talk garbage about such matters! I have received letter after letter, and they tend to start off in a very similar way: ``I have for many years been a loyal supporter of the National Party, but not any more. I am years of age and my husband is years of age.''. The wife does not qualify until she is aged years and months. Her husband has a small business that returns a small annual profit of $ and she has a nursing position that returns $, a year. At present her husband receives $ a year in guaranteed retirement income payments. The wife will give up work and the husband will give up his business. It will cost the Government not $ a year, but near enough to $, a year in extra payments by the time that the lost tax and the increased payment are taken into account. I have received letter after letter from people in that position. What were the costing assumptions in the scheme? They were that not one person would have to adjust his or her earning circumstances because of the effect of the income test---and that people would blithely carry on working for nothing at all out of the goodness of their hearts to get the deficit right so that the Minister of Finance could go to the Big Apple and live it up with the New York financiers. That is rubbish to the nth degree. People are changing their investment circumstances. Those savings will disappear, and the Government should say that it not only made a mistake in its promises, but made a mistake in its panic reaction to those promises. The Government should repeal all the Budget night legislation and go back to a surcharge regime, which means that for nearly percent of superannuitants the entire intrusive form that they have to fill in would be a single tick in one box in one form at the end of the year saying no. The other form referred to by that member is precisely the form that one needs when there is a tight social security income test. That is why it is there. It is why the Government does not have the same kind of form. Everybody will escape from that income test except those who cannot alter their circumstances, and, by and large, it will be people with superannuation schemes who cannot alter their circumstances. What an absurdity!

If we can get growth we will get growth, because the Minister does not know how to get it. Then today she had to do a little mock trial; she had to go before the news media to explain to them how the Budget deficit had doubled. The first thing the Minister did was a trick. There is a new Pol Pot style of economic memory going on over there. The Budget deficit started in December last year, not July. That data that came from the Minister compared the Budget deficit today with the December revision of $. billion, not the Budget-night deficit of $. billion. ``Oh, no,'' she says, ``it has not gone up that much---not quickly---it really has not gone up much at all.''. The revision of the deficit between December and April of this year---just those months---was blamed on a Labour Government, which went out of office at the beginning of November , over a year ago. Nobody in the press gallery believes a word of it. I must say to the Minister that not one single person in the press gallery believed a word of that press conference. The Minister said that this deficit was a different kind of deficit---it is not a kinder, gentler deficit; it is not a George Bush deficit; it is a tougher, harsher deficit; it is a $. billion tough, harsh deficit as opposed to a $ billion Labour soft deficit blow-out. Were Government members not reading the press statements? Did they not know that a full-scale recovery was under way? Did somebody forget to tell them, so that they felt better off and paid more taxes? No, the Government engineered a reduction in economic activity. This Government slashed benefits and wages, then stood back and said: ``Oh my goodness, economic activity has gone down, the Government's income has gone down.''. Treasury forecast, the one that caused the panic, that caused bits of underwear to flutter all over the floor---there was a deficit projection of $. billion, and after all of that it is down to $. billion. What is the projection for next year? The Minister would not tell anybody today; she refuses to release a deficit projection for - because, of course, then the markets really will react. The markets know that she has lost the battles in Cabinet committees; her proposals for this year's Budget have been defeated, one by one by one. She will come to the House with a deficit projection far, far higher than that in last year's Budget, a deficit projection that is not even remotely balanced, a deficit projection that will promise increasing indebtedness for the country. At the end of the day all that the Minister can promise is the hope of a level of growth inadequate to raise living standards and inadequate to reduce unemployment. There has been a history of failure--- years of chest-thumping, of tub-thumping, of boasting, of prattling, and of lack of performance.

The select committee on the Bill learnt many things while it was meeting---not least that it expected the driftnet fishing Bill to be reported back first. The departmental report on the Bill was extremely interesting, because it made clear that the Department of Social Welfare opposes the Bill. When the department was asked why certain relativities were set, and when it was asked why a certain level of benefits was set, it did not give a reason. Departmental officers, being good, faithful, loyal, public servants, as I know they always are, stated that the Government's view was that that was the appropriate thing to do---not that there was any evidence and not that there were any facts, but that the Government's view was that that should be done. The start of the department's report on the submissions stated that the department would comment on those matters when relevant. The final pages of that report consisted of reasons that the benefit cuts should not occur. There was not a single word of comment from the Department of Social Welfare in response to those reasons. When I asked Mr Alan Nixon why there was no comment he quoted the introduction and said that it did not seem relevant to comment because the Government had made up its mind. The select committee has been through a farce, with people on the edge of desperation, in tears before a select committee---and I have never seen that before, either--- I hope that the member for Otara continues to interject. The select committee learnt from the Human Rights Commission that the Bill may breach the United Nations covenants to which New Zealand is a signatory. I raise a point of order, Mr Acting Speaker, in relation to the ability of members to participate in divisions and to hindrances that may be placed in the way of members being able to do so. At this time the Planning and Development Committee is meeting on the Lake Pukaki Water Level Empowering Bill. It has long been a convention in this House that, when a select committee is meeting while the House is sitting, members of that select committee are able to participate in divisions. It is absolutely crucial that that is so, because to act in any other way is to provide a barrier to members being able to participate in divisions. The Government has arranged that its members on the select committee need not vote in divisions and may remain in the select committee, and the select committee continued to sit during that division. That leaves Opposition members of the select committee in a similar position. They cannot come down to vote; we have seen that this Government is perfectly prepared to deliberate on a Bill in the absence of Opposition members---it has done that already this week. It is a farce in relation to the powers of members of the House to participate in divisions if the business of a select committee is arranged in such a way that Opposition members are precluded from participating in a division. I suggest that it would be highly desirable if a message were sent immediately to that select committee to advise that its hearings and business should be suspended during a division. All members of the select committee should have the right to participate in a division. It is not a matter of granting leave for some members of the committee.

``What a good little destroyer am I!'', says the Minister of Finance. ``I pushed up the cost of the guaranteed retirement income to less than half proportionately of what the Germans now spend.''. Eighteen cents in every income dollar goes on their pension scheme compared with c in New Zealand and we are told that our scheme is unsustainable at our present level. How is it that Germany, which spends percent of its gross domestic product on income maintenance, health benefits, accident benefits, education and training benefits, and pensions can afford to have low inflation, high growth, high employment, and a stable economic system, but, somehow or other, on much less, New Zealand cannot afford it? Who cannot afford it---the multimillionaires who sit on the front bench of the Government? Almost every one of those front-bench members is a multimillionaire. The member for Fendalton is one of the richest men in this country. The Minister of Finance is a multimillionaire. The Minister of Labour is a multimillionaire. One person after another in the Government says: ``We're going to be courageous by cutting the pensions of those who have no other income. We're going to take those particular decisions, we're going to cut their incomes and be brave, but we'll never, ever do anything to lower our own incomes. We'll never, ever raise tax rates on higher incomes, because that can't be afforded. That can't be done by this Government.''. That is what the National Party says now that it is in Government. She laughs at the fact that the cast-iron guarantee for the elderly is broken. She laughs at the fact that a promise to repeal the surcharge is broken.
Does the statement that the ``imposition of the surtax was the single most serious act of ageism that has ever been witnessed in New Zealand'' represent this Government's policy; if not, why not?

She is human? Well, that is news to the public of New Zealand. I should like to see that put on the front page of the next National Party pamphlet; the Opposition will romp in as Government next time around. It is about time that that Minister started talking to the people who produce the goods and services in this country, instead of doing her ``mirror, mirror on the wall'' act down at the National Bank and talking to one or two other financial sector economists. She does not even bother to read the forecast. Let her read what it states: ``Growth profile is modest''---which is more than the Minister of Finance is---``Government's political situation still weak''. That is what the report states. Even an optimistic report on New Zealand's economy forecasts a mediocre performance, which is projected out beyond the next election. What does that say? It says that, at best, there will be percent ongoing growth, and that will not deliver a rise in the standard of living, will not deliver a sustained reduction in unemployment, and will not deliver the growth and the jobs that this country needs. After all the prattling and all the boasting the Minister has settled for mediocrity, and it is no wonder that her next Budget has really been written by the Minister of Labour. New Zealand has come to the end of the ``year of boasting emptily'' and we start on the new ``year of doing nothing smugly''. That is what the - financial year is going to be about. The Minister of Finance is not only out of touch, but out of her depth. The ``Remuera recovery'' that she goes on about is not felt by ordinary New Zealanders. She should come down to south Dunedin, go to Ponsonby, go to almost anywhere in the country outside of a few favoured circles, say to the people: ``Are you better off? She would be lucky to get out of the door alive at the present time. That, in fact, is what the position is like. She cannot even get her sums right. Remember Budget night? There was a $. billion deficit, which was $. billion by December, which was $. billion on April, and which now is back to something under $ billion. The Minister produced a forecast when National came to Government, and thinks that she could convince anybody. On April Treasury was still $ billion out in its deficit projection for the first months of this year, yet members are supposed to believe its projections for years out. Who believes Treasury in relation to those matters when it is under this Minister? It makes up the numbers to suit the case. Every year when there is a Budget round Treasury projects a deficit blow-out, and, lo and behold, when the Budget round is completed, the numbers come back to what they were at the end of December. What an amazing little miracle of financial management that just happens to be! It now has occurred a number of years in a row. The Minister's job now is merely to dance prettily for the financial markets. The memories of the Budget that the House is now finishing are surreal: the Minister in a tracksuit, jumping up and down on the road somewhere or other in Wellington, and prattling on about the ``mother of all Budgets'' and a ``spine-tingling Budget''; and the Minister of Finance in the House, giving a well-practised flutter of her eyelids at the television cameras as she went on and on about guts and courage. Tonight's announcements demonstrate our resolve to control, reduce and eliminate the budget deficit over three years.''. When will that happen, Minister? And then again in that speech: ``We have arrested the drift of decades, looked out over the span of a generation, and charted the path for the future.''. The Labour Opposition will be voting in favour of the report back of this Bill and its further passage through the House later on. It comes back to the House at a very convenient and, indeed, interesting time in international banking and in relation to banking supervision matters, as the saga of the Barings collapse unfolds before us. It is important to begin by saying that this Bill relates to only one of the two functions of the Reserve Bank. New Zealand's central bank, like a number of central banks throughout the world, has two different functions: one is the control of monetary policy; the other is the supervision of the banking system. This Bill relates solely to the supervision of the banking system element of the functions of the Reserve Bank, and bears no relationship at all to the issue of the control of monetary policy. As the member for Tarawera has indicated, the Bill changes very substantially the supervisory roles of the Reserve Bank. On the face of it---and crudely, if one was not to take notice carefully of what is actually done---it would seem to be a deregulation of the banking system. In practice that is not so, and I think I should try to explain that. The present system that New Zealand operates, which is similar in many respects to those operating in a number of countries, essentially holds out a promise that cannot be fulfilled. The supervisory system essentially involves the bank in attempting to supervise a number of internal matters of banking operations and gives the impression, as a consequence of that, that the Reserve Bank is in effect guaranteeing those banking operations and guaranteeing the security and soundness of the bank. That is not the case. There is no such guarantee either explicit or implicit in the present supervisory operations of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. Therefore it is very important to note that the Barings-type situation is not one that would be averted by the present, much more detailed, regulatory system operating within New Zealand. Rather, as we learnt in the select committee, the Bill provides for a system of disclosure that is very detailed in terms of the information that has to be disclosed by the bank. For example, it includes its asset quality and provisioning, its income statement and balance sheet, and, perhaps most importantly, information on its exposures to related parties, information on the number of exposures banks have to individual counter-parties, sectoral exposure information, and detailed information on the bank's capital adequacy and the bank's market risk exposures. Indeed, assuming that Barings had, in fact, operated proper internal controls and the directors were aware of what was going on---and the more information that comes out about Barings the more it seems that the knowledge was actually well up the information tree within that bank---then those kinds of risk exposures found in the Barings case should have been and would have been revealed under the disclosure requirements, which are really implicit within this particular piece of legislation. In other words, the Bill is predicated around the principle that if there is full and adequate disclosure of the risk a bank is exposed to, then that is the best protection the public may have regarding the soundness and security of that bank. When banks can keep secret the highly risky enterprises they are engaged in, in which they are exposed to very high levels of risk---as indeed occurred in the Barings case---that is when a bank is liable to collapse, and no amount of supposedly detailed internal regulation covered by a non-existent form of bank guarantee from the central bank will save that bank in the outcome. The truth is that if there is a totally dishonest bank run totally dishonestly, then that bank will get away with this supervisory regime---as it will get away with any supervisory regime until the principals are finally caught up by one means or another. But the truth of the matter is that the Bank of New Zealand (BNZ) situation in the late s, whilst it was morally improper then, would now be legally improper in any case under the Companies Act , because what the directors were involved with at that time would not be permissible under the Companies Act and the risk that the bank was subject to at that stage would have been disclosed under the requirements of the amending legislation, which is now in front of the House. In my view, this legislation provides better protection against a repeat of the BNZ type of situation than the present regulatory regime would do, and in that respect, therefore, the Labour Opposition is happy to support the passage of this Bill.

Like the previous member I welcome the increased funding for the Education Review Office, but I hope that some of that funding will be used in a more sensitive fashion than it has been at times over the last year or so. Some schools have just about had their morale destroyed by the way in which the Education Review Office has operated. I particularly look forward to a reasonable report emerging on Forbury School in my own electorate. I want to raise a couple of issues. In particular I want to reinforce the point made by my colleague the member for Dunedin North about the issue of normal schools. This has to be one of those issues where ideology is triumphing over practicalities to an extraordinary extent. In Dunedin we have a situation where the college of education clearly wishes to continue the use of the existing normal schools, and the existing normal schools wish to remain normal schools. Both sides want to have the ongoing continuity that designation as normal schools will give. What is the Ministry of Education proposing to do? It is proposing to remove the designation of normal schools and then to force some kind of competitive tendering to be supervised by the college of education. The college is far too busy to want to get into that particular piece of competitive nonsense. It is the best college in the country, the schools are excellent, and there is no reason that there should be any change at all in our area. Secondly, I want to plead with the Minister yet again to try to stabilise the funding for the subsidisation of the school bus services in the Dunedin area, particularly as it relates to the Otago Peninsula school bus service. There is no question that there cannot be any major shift to other forms of transport for children living on the Otago Peninsula. It is a road that is simply unsafe for cyclists to be on in any large numbers. As a person who drives up and down that road a number of times each week, because my house in Dunedin is on the peninsula, I know very well that meeting any cyclist, and particularly trying to overtake any cyclist, is a highly dangerous manoeuvre on something like percent of that road. There are very, very few safe passing areas on that road. The third point I want to make is that I hope that the Minister will consider carefully the submissions we will be making to him next week about Highcliff High School, as it is popularly known. It is a school for children with behavioural difficulties that is not just a facility for the use of kids in the care of the Department of Social Welfare, but which is used by schools to reference out children with behavioural problems. It has an outstanding record of success. Finally, I plead with the Minister to use his common sense, because he does have some common sense---unlike his predecessor, who was particularly prone on educational issues to what one might call ``Lockie blockies''---to look again at the issue of the imposition of a rigid unit standards framework on academic subjects in secondary schools and later. I have been looking at the fifth-form history unit standards proposals and, as a PhD in history, I have to say that I could not understand two or three of the questions being asked. They were meaningless, they had no relevance to the nature of history as a discipline, and they simply proved that the whole subject has been taken over by bean-counters, who do not seem to understand what an interpretive discipline like history or English is about in practice at senior secondary school level. We are in very real danger of destroying the integrity of some of our academic subjects at secondary schools by imposing upon them a model that is highly relevant and worth while in the vocational training area, but which is of limited use when it comes from academic subjects.

It is not for me to name people who might think that but that is certainly a view that has been expressed along those lines. First, I want to say that I do not agree with that view. I think there is a problem when there are very, very minor changes to legislation that have tended to accumulate, that do not incorporate any major principles but are not entirely non-controversial changes of the sort we have in the Statutes Amendment Bill, and that are worthy therefore of going to a select committee for some consideration and debate but perhaps are not worthy of introducing a whole raft of separate amending Bills to go off to separate select committees for separate hearings and the like. I think there are problems with that. The first problem, obviously, is whether those who are interested in the matters are always fully cognisant of what is contained within them. If legislation has a title that indicates the nature of its contents then that tends to alert members of the public that this is something they ought to be taking note of, and if they are experts in the field perhaps they will make a submission and assist Parliament in its deliberations. Something called a Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill tends to look as though it is concerned very much with the sorts of matters that used to be considered by the old Statutes Revision Committee and now the Justice and Law Reform Committee. But in fact, of course, when we turn to the Bill we find that the first area of legislation is the Customs Act, which is not something that comes within the normal purview of the Justice and Law Reform Committee. It is a quite different set of issues, a quite different set of expertise is required, and one cannot be quite sure that those who have a useful contribution to make in submissions to the select committee have, in fact, been able to make that submission, because they may not be aware that the legislation has been going through Parliament. I want to come back to that in the context of what is within that particular part of the Bill. The second matter that causes concern, and is much more legitimately a matter for public and parliamentary objection, is when a Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill comes in as a sort of train with a certain number of carriages, and a whole set of carriages are added on by way of a supplementary order paper or, even worse, by way of supplementary order paper to the Committee of the whole House without any chance of public input. That has been a growing practice over recent years---indeed, over the last or years. It is something that Parliament ought to take very strict note of. We ought to look at ways in which we can, at the very least, strongly limit the inclination to use law reform Bills as a train, something to which we can attach a whole set of other carriages. One of the good features of this Parliament, contrary to an extraordinarily expensive recently published private book, is the fact that in New Zealand we have a very, very much higher level of public input into the parliamentary process than is characteristic both of our own past---more distant---and of some very similar kinds of parliamentary systems. Even in the United Kingdom the Westminster Parliament does not have the same level of public input into legislation that is characteristic of the New Zealand Parliament. We have discovered over a long period of time now that that input is extremely useful. It often saves us from making some fairly simple and fundamental errors, and it often improves legislation very, very significantly indeed. But it also does something else. It enables people who have a particular interest in legislation, and who perhaps at the end of the day hope to have some ownership on what emerges out of the parliamentary process, to feel part of the process. In other words we are not seen in that respect as totally standing in opposition to public interest or public knowledge or public concern as it may be. In my view it is very important that we preserve the public input that has developed over the last years, particularly in New Zealand in terms of the select committee processes. There is always a danger that if the Law Reform (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill or the Statutes Amendment Bill, or the Finance Bill---which seems to be the worst of the three in that regard---becomes something that is sort of smuggled in with about two carriages and comes out the other end with about carriages---

Could I first of all begin by congratulating the Minister responsible for the Bill. Of course I refer to my good friend the Hon. Bill Jeffries, who introduced the Bill in . Might I say that I have come somewhat late to this Bill in one sense, but in fact it is nearly a quarter of a century since I began research on the origins of the Civil Registration Act of England and Wales that was passed in so I am not unfamiliar with births, deaths, and marriages legislation. The Bill is a complete rewrite of the existing Act; it is not simply an amending Act, thereby in effect it repeats in a somewhat unaltered form much of the existing material contained in the Births and Deaths Registration Act. The area is significantly new, which perhaps to some extent accounts for the rather long delay in the passage of the legislation. It relates to the difficult matter of the registration of the gender of people who are transsexuals, who having been registered in one gender---normally they are registered as males---subsequently undergo changes that reflect their own identity and how they see themselves, end up as females, and wish to change their birth certificate to reflect that fact. There are many such people in both our own society and overseas. One of the most famous travel writers in the world today is a transsexual who has been through the full process in terms of the surgical procedure. The present legislation is inadequate in that regard. It provides a situation that does not recognise the nature of some people in our society who wish quite naturally to be able to give full expression to who they are. In a society that thankfully has become a good deal more liberal in these matters and a good deal more all-encompassing about people's differences, it is very pleasing to see this legislation being passed today. There were some arguments in the select committee. I want to pay tribute to the Minister of Justice for the way in which he came round, in one case after a good deal of debate, to accepting some changes within the Bill. I might also thank the Associate Minister of Health, the member for Waipa, for her assistance. If the registrar-general has the duty of providing a record of deaths registration that occurred in, say, the case in Queensland that my colleague raised, then there is no particular reason that the birth of somebody overseas who particularly regards himself or herself as a New Zealander should not also be able to be recorded within the New Zealand register in a similar form. It would be very helpful should that be done at some future date. The other matters that arose were matters in relation to the ability to access records with the limitation in terms of years as a sort of presumption of death, which the Minister has now agreed to change to years, recognising increasing longevity within our society. I trust the Minister receives his just reward in that regard. Perhaps he will be able to proceed to the full ton. One trusts that members of this House will do rather better than New Zealand batsmen in the recent cricket tests in that regard. Our record of achieving centuries was not too good. We hope to do better in future. My colleague the member for Hamilton East raised an important matter relating to the registration of the occupations of parents. Probably all members of the House have looked at their birth certificates and noticed their father's occupation is entered---at least I assume all members have. In my case there is a rather lengthy inscription about the Royal Air Force of February . The occupation of one's mother is not entered. The Minister has assured the House that with the new regulations we will have the capacity for the occupations of both parents to be entered, as they ought to be. Having made those few comments, I think we have achieved an excellent Bill that is proceeding through the House on a fully consensual basis and merely emphasises, once again, that we did not need electoral reform to have consensual legislation.
