In we had the big promise to tertiary students. National said it would remove the toll-gate on knowledge. At the National Party conference on July the present Prime Minister said: ``We are going to tear down that toll-gate of tuition fees. The tertiary fees will go.'' It is true that the Minister of Education keeps saying: ``What I said was that Labour's tertiary fee would go.'' Labour's tertiary fee did go. It is true that, just like the surcharge, the Minister of Education put a bigger and brighter tertiary fee in its place. But that is not what he had said. I have here the pamphlet the National Party circulated amongst students in tertiary institutions in . It is true that the present Minister of Education, the then opposition spokesman on education, said: ``A National Government will scrap the fee.''---an interesting little indication of a hidden agenda. But that is not what the front of the pamphlet stated. The front of the pamphlet stated: ``What National will do for you: No Fees.''---no ifs, no buts, no maybes, no fees. Is that what tertiary students got up and down this country? That is not all that the National Party promised. It also promised to raise tertiary student allowances to the level of the unemployment benefit. It also promised in the same pamphlet to abolish the means testing of parents' incomes in assessing tertiary students' living allowances. What did the National Government do? It increased the means testing so that a -year-old is now subject to means testing of his or her parents' income. We now have a regime such that by the time people have finished paying for their children's tertiary education---if they are unwise enough to have children bright enough to go into tertiary and postgraduate education---they will have about to years left, at best, to save for their retirement under a National Government. If people are unwise enough to save during those to years, then the Government will flog the lot off them by way of the surcharge when they actually retire. This is called rewarding enterprise and creating opportunity for New Zealanders under a National Government. National Party members said: ``We will scrap the fees.'' That promise was not written in blood, because blood is red and the Minister of Education hates red, even red balloons. He has a pathological hatred of red balloons. I suspect he probably had some unfortunate experiences as a child with red balloons, which may explain a great deal about the Minister of Education. But he said: ``I, MP,''---now a cattle farmer and hence known as Cocky Lockie---``hereby pledge to tender my resignation as Minister of Education if the National Party, having become the Government in , has not implemented the majority of the National Party's education policy. In particular, I pledge to tender my resignation if the $, tertiary tuition fee has not been abolished by this time.''

Clause provides the basic rates of income tax for the - financial year. Can the Minister confirm that the Government has had a legal opinion from the Clerk of the House, and possibly from other quarters, stating that notwithstanding the passage of this clause now, the Government---whoever the Government is---should it choose to proceed with these tax rates, will have to re-legislate for them subsequently; that it is not possible simply to legislate for the tax rates in advance and not repeat those, because there has to be a confirmation of the annual tax rate; and that confirmation cannot occur at this point in time for the - tax year? Can the Minister confirm that a legal opinion to that effect has been received by the Government? It is my understanding that that is the case. It would certainly make the job of the incoming Government easier. I have to say in that respect that I do trust that the Prime Minister changes his tactics and strategy fairly soon, so that the nature of the incoming Government is somewhat better formed than might otherwise be the case. I come to the nature of those basic rates. In effect what we have here are the - rates that incorporate further changes in tax rates. The second tranche comes in on July , and the result is to incorporate the new rates with the large reduction in the middle tax rate---the previous c, c, and c rates. The Minister of Finance is trying to make much of this marginal tax rate, and I want to dwell on that argument for a moment. There is very, very little empirical evidence indeed, in fact there is no present empirical evidence at all in New Zealand or any other country, to suggest that lowering a marginal tax rate from an already fairly low level of c in the dollar to c in the dollar has any great impact upon incentives or human behaviour. That is not surprising. Turn it round the other way and the difference between keeping c and c in the dollar is actually not very large in terms of the implication for effort. For people on salaries of course, it is totally irrelevant. If the Government really meant this, then it should certainly exempt members of Parliament and Cabinet Ministers for a start because none of us earns an extra dollar by working an extra hour. We are on a salary; our salary is fixed. It does not matter whether we work or hours a week as most of us do, or or hours a week as Paul East and Don McKinnon do; we end up paying the same tax rate on whatever our salary may be. We are talking about hourly-wage workers. They are the people who might be encouraged to work a little more by a change in that middle tax rate. It does not have much effect on the wage-benefit gap---I invite the Minister to think about that fact. It is actually lowering the bottom tax rate, which increases the wage-benefit gap, because benefits are set in net terms, not gross terms. If the Minister really wants to widen the wage-benefit gap, lowering the bottom tax rate does a great deal for that without any other moves being made at all. I invite the Minister also to think that those hourly-wage workers will work harder only if the work is there, and, for most, the opportunity to work considerably longer hours will not be there. It is far from clear that we want to distribute increased employment by having the people already in full-time employment work more, as opposed to having people not in work get a job in the first place. It is far from clear why the change in the marginal tax rate would have that effect. For many New Zealanders we have to look at the other elements of the total wage-benefit system to see what their true marginal tax rate is in any case. National proposes to keep a c abatement rate for family support, cutting in at $, a year, under this package. It means that under National there would be a higher effective marginal tax rate for many families on $, to $, a year than there would be under Labour's proposals, because we would be lowering that marginal tax rate down to percent on the family support component. That means that our total marginal tax rate would be percent, whereas National's would be percent under this particular clause. So members have to look at the total impact of the Government's provision and not just the base tax rate elements if they want to understand what the marginal tax rates are. I come back to the fundamental point that there is very little evidence indeed that, beyond a certain point, changing marginal tax rates has much impact upon incentives and efforts. If we have a c in the dollar marginal tax rate we will have huge avoidance and evasion opportunities, and certainly massive disincentives to work harder.

I was not going to take a call in this debate but a number of the statements made in the Treasurer's speech, which I have gone away and thought about a little bit more and have done a little bit of research on, have moved me to rise to speak on this matter. Also we have made rather more rapid progress than was expected, or perhaps than the House ought to make, on a measure of this importance that has caused such divisiveness in New Zealand's politics over the last years. The surcharge was introduced by way of legislation immediately after the reading of the Budget in . The second reading of the Bill to introduce the surcharge was moved by the Hon. Richard Prebble, who now describes the surcharge as iniquitous. As the senior Government whip I had the somewhat dubious pleasure of being the only back-bencher to speak at any stage in support of the introduction of the surcharge in that legislation. I might say that unlike Mr Prebble, unlike Mr Bolger, unlike Mr Peters, and unlike a number of other members of this House I do not resile from what I said on that occasion or from the necessity for that action to be taken at that time. What I said at that time was very clear. New Zealand was in an economic mess left by the Muldoon-Birch-Bolger Government, with the deficit running at percent of gross domestic product. In modern dollar terms, the deficit of - was equivalent to over $, million a year. In that situation every section of society had to be expected to make some sacrifice. National has always taken the view that when the going gets tough, the tough get going by booting the weak. National prides itself on always attacking those who can least defend themselves. Under that Budget we applied a rigour to superannuation that affected the top one-quarter of superannuitants in income terms. The bottom three-quarters were not affected at all by the introduction of the surcharge. Only the richest one-quarter of superannuitants paid the surcharge when it was first introduced. They, like many other New Zealanders, were expected to make some sacrifice to bring under control the appalling economic and fiscal mess left by the Muldoon-Birch-Bolger Government in . In a blue, blind funk its members ran from office, unable to put together a Budget. That was the real reason that they went to the country early. When we came in to office in July there was no Budget under preparation for -. The previous Government could not put that Budget together. What has happened since then? First of all, for years the National Party made endless, ruthless, opportunistic play of the existence of the surcharge, culminating in that infamous speech of June in the Wellington Town Hall, when the then Leader of the Opposition, the Rt Hon James Brendan Bolger, promised to remove the surcharge---``no ifs, no buts, no maybes''---sorry, on June . Get it right, indeed; I got it right and he got it wrong, because he broke his word. He did not do it immediately, not after opening the books and saying, shock-horror probe, my projection for the deficit was in fact accurate---he had said on Budget night that the deficit would be $. billion. In , in the speech from the throne read by the then Governor-General, after the books had been opened and after the Treasury briefings, National promised once again to remove the surcharge. Who was in that Cabinet that resolved not just to keep the surcharge but to do something much more iniquitous than that? What happened then was that National decided not only to remove the surcharge but to replace it with a very tight income and asset test that would affect many more superannuitants, and would claw back full superannuation from much more than the percent who had previously lost their superannuation. In that Cabinet that took that decision, and that simultaneously froze the pension for years, was the Hon. Winston Raymond Peters. Mr Peters, who in the House this afternoon yet again paraded himself as the only man of virtue on the surcharge issue, voted in Cabinet to freeze the pension for years, and voted to replace the surcharge with a tight income and asset test. He has no credibility on this issue in the House, either. Why have we decided to proceed to this point where Labour supports removing the surcharge? There are three reasons. Firstly, let me say that I am growing increasingly resentful of the Prime Minister's inability to tell a single factual story about superannuation correctly. Labour's policy before the last election was to remove the surcharge and to put in place a new, higher tax rate for those on more than $, a year. The income from that would have paid for the abolition of the surcharge. It would have met the requirements of clause .. of the accord on superannuation. If it did not, neither did the Alliance's policy ever meet that requirement, and that consideration was never raised by the Prime Minister in . The truth is that Labour did not break the accord. Labour's policy was consistent with the accord of . We stood by the accord right the way through the election process. The second reason that we have decided to remove the surcharge is that, bluntly, it has become indefensible in fiscal terms, and that is for two reasons. The first is that an increasing proportion of retired New Zealanders will be arriving at retirement with surcharge avoidance schemes. The income from the surcharge would go down dramatically over the next few years in any case, because it basically captures people in old, defined benefit schemes, and people carrying on employment after retirement. There seems little point, therefore, in penalising some elderly people while others on higher incomes get away scot-free and do not pay the surcharge. That would become more and more the case over the coming years because of surcharge avoidance schemes. The second part of that issue is that we are no longer in a fiscally desperate situation. A surcharge introduced for fiscal reasons, when $ million a year---in present terms---was required to try to address a fiscal imbalance, cannot be justified when the Government is running a surplus. It is a different situation. The justification for the surcharge in was always a fiscal justification. The subsidiary justification was social equity in terms of sharing the sacrifices that had to be made. I do not resile from the position I took at that time, because I still believe it was the right position to take in the situation we were in in . In , with the Government projecting fiscal surpluses, it is very hard to justify a differential tax rate on the elderly that is no longer required fiscally, that is easier and easier to avoid, and that in the long term is a clear disincentive to saving. But the real question is why National is proposing to abolish the surcharge when the Prime Minister tells us that if the referendum leads to a defeat for the Peters' scheme we will have to have income testing of superannuation. The latest poll says that percent of people will vote ``No''. After ACT said it was in support of the scheme, support for it halved immediately. In the first poll to come out post ACT saying it supported the scheme, percent say they will vote ``No''. Defeat is certain. Therefore why is National removing the surcharge? It seems to me that the Government is the group that is in an absurd position in this regard. ACT can vote to remove the surcharge because the surcharge affects the well-off elderly the most. The Alliance can vote to remove the surcharge because it believes in a fully universal pension system, paid for out of current and more progressive taxation. Labour can vote to remove the surcharge because we believe that it is no longer fiscally necessary, and because it does not fit our policy of a dedicated tax and fund regime, which is not consistent with targeted payment of superannuation on retirement. But National is the one party that has no reason to vote for the surcharge. Its leader says we have to income-test superannuation, yet like sheep its members will go through the Ayes door today. Presumably, in months' time they will go through the Ayes door again to reimpose some form of surcharge. Finally, let me say that I reject Mr Peters' assertion in his speech today that six out of seven superannuitants who do not pay the surcharge at the moment are lazy, are non-savers, and are bludging off the rest of the community. The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed. Bill to proceed.

There was some truth in what the senior Government whip said, but it is also clear that the Chair required Mr Samuels to provide an interpretation, and the Chair cannot do that. The right to use Maori is absolute under the Standing Orders. It seems to me that what has to happen in this kind of case is that the Chair has a perfect right to request the member to provide a translation, because if the Chair is not fluent in Maori, as most of us are not, there is a slight problem. Even the wisest and most Solomonic of Chairpersons would have some difficulty at that stage, if he or she does not even know what the point of order is. It seems to me that the Chair has a perfect right to request a translation. There are only two people who can give that translation: the member who spoke in Maori or an independent interpreter. It does not seem to me that another Maori speaker in the House can be expected to provide a translation, because it may not accord with what the original speaker actually said, and therefore we would get into arguments about interpretation and translation, which is not a very good way for the House to proceed. It seems to me that if the member who spoke declines to give a translation, the Chair has no choice but to defer consideration of the point of order until he or she is able to get an official translation. Clearly, it would be in the interests of the general order of the Committee of the whole House if a translation was provided straight away, because points of order become fairly pointless after a fairly short space of time.

I move, That the House take note of a definite matter of urgent public importance. The matter we are to consider today is a very serious matter, and I shall begin by saying that it is raised by way of allegation in a book that is yet to be seen in full, from which excerpts have been published in newspapers over the weekend. Therefore, we are dealing with a matter where a charge is made by one person that affects a senior member of this House but also affects the integrity of the Administration of which he was part. That Administration, of course, was the coalition National - New Zealand First Government. The Serious Fraud Office Act of provides under section that ``() Notwithstanding section of this Act,''---which defines the responsible Minister, the Attorney-General---``in any matter relating to any decision to investigate any suspected case of serious or complex fraud, or to take proceedings relating to any such case or any offence against this Act, the Director shall not be responsible to the Attorney-General, but shall act independently. () Nothing in this section shall limit or affect any power exercisable by the Attorney-General in relation to any proceedings.'' Section is clear that the Director of the Serious Fraud Office is independent in carrying out his or her functions in terms of investigating any suspected case of serious fraud. The House will be aware that matters involving Mr Tukoroirangi Morgan, a member of Parliament of this House, were referred to the Serious Fraud Office by a number of people and that those related to the Aotearoa Television Network and to associated matters at that time. The suggestion was that Mr Morgan had, in effect, been misusing moneys that had been given to Aotearoa Television Network and that were, in effect, part of public broadcasting funding. Those matters were investigated by the Serious Fraud Office and a report was produced, not by Mr Sturt, who by that stage, for reasons of health, had resigned as the Director of the Serious Fraud Office, but by Judge Jamieson, who was the Acting Director of the Serious Fraud Office. Judge Jamieson, in a very carefully worded conclusion, arrived at the belief that there was no evidence to back the accusations that had been made. I say ``very carefully worded'' because Judge Jamieson's report did not in fact clear Mr Morgan, did not say that he was innocent of the charges that were laid, but stated much, much more carefully that evidence had not been found in that respect. If I may quote from some parts of that particular report, we find in relation to the issue of the secret interest in Aotearoa Television Network, which was one of the issues that was considered at that time---the issue of whether Mr Morgan had retained a shareholding interest in the company---that there was a conflict of evidence, and that there was a lack of documentation. The Judge Jamieson report concluded that ``this office has been unable to resolve that conflict, although the absence of any signed declaration of trust tends to support Mr Morgan.'' Judge Jamieson went on to say: ``In the event, I have been unable to find any evidence of criminal behaviour in regard to this matter.'' In his general conclusion he stated: ``It is my carefully considered view, after weighing all the material available to me, that the evidence here falls short of establishing any serious or complex fraud on the part of any of the persons associated with Aotearoa or its associated company, Pumanawa, to justify criminal charges.'' At no stage in the report was it stated that Mr Morgan was innocent; it was stated merely that there was a lack of evidence to demonstrate his guilt---and indeed, even somewhat less satisfactory, I would think, from Mr Morgan's respect in that regard, the conclusion was in regard of ``establishing any serious or complex fraud''. The nature of the fraud was itself qualified as not being ``serious or complex''. The report did not in fact find that there was no fraud at all---it meant that there was no serious or complex fraud. What occurred over the weekend was something very serious in relation to that investigation. Mr Sturt, of course, was a man who underwent serious illness at the time of the commission of inquiry into the wine-box affair. Many members of the House will recollect the sight of Mr Sturt on the witness stand, unable to recollect major details of that affair, and, indeed, major aspects of the principal matter under investigation at the time. It is now clear from Mr Sturt's autobiography that he was very seriously ill at that time, and in fact unable to recollect clearly, not because he did not know what he was doing, but because of the nature of his illness while he was on the witness box. He should never have been examined at that time in the state that he was in. It was not fair to him and not even fair to the integrity of the inquiry either. Now he has gone to the stage---and this is where I think the matter becomes very serious---that in effect he stated in his autobiography that he was approached by the Attorney-General at the time, Mr Paul East, who wanted to stress that, according to Mr Sturt: ``I was not to continue with my direction of the Aotearoa Television investigation.'' It is not clear why Mr Sturt makes that claim---whether that claim was a direction that the investigation was to be hobbled completely, or whether it was merely a direction that Mr Sturt was not to continue with the investigation, personally, but to be sure that other people carried out the investigation. This is a very, very serious matter indeed. If the Attorney-General at the time was involved in actually trying to stop the investigation, the credibility of the whole investigation must come under scrutiny. Moreover, it is clear that Mr East was acting totally improperly, and outside the framework of the Serious Fraud Office legislation. I would go further than that, and say that if Mr Sturt's accusation is correct, Mr East has really very little choice---now that he has already been dismissed as a Minister---but to resign from Parliament forthwith. I believe that there are not many more serious accusations that could be made against a law officer---in this respect a parliamentary law officer---than that they improperly interfered in an investigation. That would be true of a police investigation by the Minister of Police or a Serious Fraud Office investigation by the Attorney-General. Of course, it raises a further issue. Mr East was close to the leader of New Zealand First, the leader of the party of which Mr Morgan was a member. If Mr East, in fact, made this direction---gave this call---to Mr Sturt, the question has to be further raised: ``Who was Mr East acting in concert with?''. I find it difficult, knowing Mr East well---and having some respect for him as a long-term parliamentary colleague---to believe that Mr East, if he had done this, would have done this on his own initiative without any discussions with any other persons within the Cabinet, within the ministry at large, and particularly with those people who might have some degree of interest in the matter. The people who had the greatest interest in the matter were the New Zealand First Cabinet Ministers led by Mr Peters. At the end of the day the National Party had a limited amount to lose from Mr Morgan coming under attack in the way that he was under attack.

I withdraw. Let us be clear that the Government has put the boot in on the amendment. It has said to low-income New Zealanders with families, with kids, with students at university and polytech, that it is ``no go'' for them, that they will have it offset by their tax credit, and that it will not really work for them at all. At that point this Government has killed the taxation of life insurance and superannuation fund savings scheme. Let us not have any garbage about who is responsible for not lowering tax rates for lower-income kiwis. The taxation of life insurance and superannuation fund savings scheme is dead because Mr Birch has got the pricker and will not accept a sensible amendment that we have argued for at every stage through the select committee. If he had just one little bit of flexibility---some ability to recognise the flaw in the scheme he put up---he could have got that legislation through with Labour Party support today. I told him last week and I have told him earlier that if he supported that amendment we would support---despite our reservations---the taxation of life insurance and superannuation fund savings scheme in other respects. He will not do it, he has killed it, he has ensured that the scheme is dead, and it is totally his responsibility. But, of course, the Government does not have the fortitude to make this a confidence issue. It will not say that the Government stands or falls on this major aspect of taxation and taxation changes. It will go down to mewling, puking defeat today because of its own stubbornness.

Does the Treasurer believe that he was acting wisely in issuing a press statement yesterday that could have been interpreted as trying to influence the Reserve Bank; if so, did he consult the Minister of Finance before issuing it?

It has clearly been a hard night's work preparing that speech. Whoever thought that the successor to ``think big'' would be ``speak easy''? These two Bills represent votes of confidence in the Government. This Government does not deserve the confidence of this House as it has lost the confidence of this country. The Minister who has just resumed his seat has seen his party's support go from percent just over a year ago to percent in the latest opinion polls, and still he sneers arrogantly at other parties within this Parliament. He has seen his support drop very, very nearly percent in the space of year. He is headed for oblivion. The first reason that this Government does not support the confidence of this House or this nation---and Labour will be voting against these Bills---is that this Government, under this Prime Minister and this Treasurer, has demeaned the whole nature of government and of the political and parliamentary process. This is a Government seen rightly by the public as a Government of sleaze, of incompetence, of arrogance, of rudeness, and of ignorance. It has long since gone past the simple piece of farce involving one or two members of this House. The truth is that if any members over there talk to any of their constituents at the weekends they will find that the public believes that we in this House are crooks, at worst, or charlatans, at best. That is what the public believes of politicians after or months of this Government. If New Zealand First members were accused of winding back the odometers on their rental cars, the public would believe it. If parliamentarians from any party were linked with those pathetic, disgusting, perverted paedophile rings being shown up around the world, the public would believe it. From a low base in the last months, this Parliament and all of us in it have sunk into a cesspool of disrepute. We are swimming in sewage because of this Government and the way it has behaved. It has gone past just being a matter of those pathetic circus warriors in New Zealand First who think that smart suits and wraparound sunglasses are some kind of status symbol and some kind of assertion of their manhood and their intelligence. It has become the style of this Government, a cross between Trainspotting and Leaving Las Vegas, without the elegance and style. That is the way the public sees us in politics this day. That is the way we are seen, and it is demeaning to every member of this House that we cannot go back to our electorates and face our constituents with some sense of honour about the job that we do. In my own caucus there is a sense of deep unease and dissatisfaction about being in the business of politics in . Labour is riding high. In the polls, we have more than both Government parties put together. We are still rising and they are still falling. In that situation, one would expect members on this side of the House to be feeling good about the business of politics. But I doubt whether many of us could say honestly, looking in the mirror in the morning, that we actually feel good about the job we are going off to do during that day, because we have all been demeaned by the sheer unprofessionalism of this Government. It is a disgrace to a business that ought to be one of the highest callings within New Zealand. Still Mr Peters cannot bring himself to apologise to the House for his own behaviour within the precincts of this Chamber. We expect children in schools to behave better. We preach about bullying in our schools, what we will do to fix it, and we have a Treasurer who cannot apologise for his own behaviour within the precincts of this Chamber. Mr Morgan scarcely apologised for his behaviour. What he actually said was: ``I'm sorry for any embarrassment I've caused.'', not ``I'm sorry for what I did.'' That is the apology one gives when one is caught out; it is not the apology of a man standing up and accepting that what he did was wrong. I have never heard him say here, in front of his peers, so that the nation could hear: ``I apologise to Parliament for what I've done to the reputation of this House and the members within it.'' He stays on in this place doing that appalling imitation of Marlon Brando on Mogadon, which passes for his style of politics. He makes the Ingham twins look like the very model of loquaciousness. Indeed, he is to politics what the Ingham twins are to travel: an incompetent freeloader. Secondly, this circus---and the Treasurer is the chief ringmaster---would not be so bad, would not be so demeaning to the Government, if there was at least a plentiful supply of bread as well. The Government seems to have forgotten that if a Government is being run based on circuses then it is meant to be bread and circuses, not just the circuses. Well, the bread is not there for many people. The reality is so different. The kind of smug, overpaid, financial-sector economists that the National Party and New Zealand First---of all people---now like to quote, have no idea of the world out there. Over the last week the New Zealand Herald has been running a series on the way in which many of our young people live and are treated in the supposedly rich and bountiful community, and it summed up in just one headline. Before the Prime Minister witters on about social capital---a fancy way of saying: ``Look after yourself.'', invented by American sociologists---let him read that headline. How does that fit with his theology, his philosophy, and his belief in life? The headline reads: ``Cards stacked against the poorest kids.'', and this Government continues to act like a circus and to demean the business of politics while the cards are stacked against the poorest kids in our community. We are raising a generation, many of whom are bred in despair and hopelessness---people heading nowhere in the new, open, competitive economy. It is no good worshipping the joys of an open, competitive economy if our people are not being equipped to compete and be in that economy in a way that gives them fulfilment. The other side of the coin has to be there, or we breed despair and hopelessness. We breed a generation who will look at the rich, who will look at those who are doing well, and who will wreak their revenge by means of violence and crime throughout the rest of their lives. We are building up a social deficit in this country at such a rate that it must frighten anybody. I say to the Prime Minister again that wittering on about social capital is no answer to the pressing needs of so many young people throughout our community in this country of ours. The Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Service is in a disastrous state. The service is underfunded, its staff are undertrained, and there is too much incompetence. Too many children are being beaten and abused, and intervention is not occurring to protect them. Too many children are going hungry. Too many children are missing out on what they need in terms of housing, health, food, and education. What will the Government do about that in this Budget, when nearly everything it spends will, by and large, go on the better-off? We are under-investing in education. Reading-recovery programmes in schools in my electorate are being closed down, because those schools cannot afford to run them. Where will those children go in the future? Will we blame them and lock them up when they become adults? Will we have to get into a ``three times and you're out'' approach to those problems, instead of dealing with the issues at an early stage? Industry training for many of our people needing to adapt to the new economy is in chaos. The Government has made a complete mess of industry training. Tertiary education, in many respects, is in a mess. The quality is declining, there is a lack of clear focus, and a lack of relationship to the skills needed to be produced for this economy if we are to succeed. Growing poverty all around us is evident up and down this nation of ours. More and more people are badly housed. More and more people are in bad health. More and more people are missing out on the fundamentals of life in a decent and civilised community, and reflecting that in part is rising racial tension. How can we fix issues like treaty settlements, and how can we do justice in Maori issues, if at the same time so many of our people are suffering such deprivation that they cannot see the relevance of those great historic issues to their immediate needs? We cannot do one without the other, because it simply will not work. Then we have an overmanaged, under-resourced health monster, entirely of National's making, failing to deliver services of the most basic variety. How did the Prime Minister look at himself in the mirror when he heard the managers of this new system say that there was a -year waiting-list for a woman suffering severe pain from varicose veins, because those things are no longer being done in our public health system? What did the Prime Minister think when he looked at the New Zealand Herald this morning and found that our spending on health per capita is between Portugal's and Spain's, and we are left in the rear by every genuinely developed country in the Western World? What did he think of that as he praises himself for miserable tax cuts on July next year, which are going largely to the better-off in any case? I ask the Prime Minister how that fits in with his wittering on about social capital? How does that fit in with some view of New Zealand, which says to ordinary New Zealanders: ``You are treasured and valued.'', and which says to New Zealanders left out in the structure reform process since the early-s: ``But yes, now is your time to catch up, now is your time to be included.''? It is not: ``Now is your time to be left further behind, as we congratulate ourselves on giving ourselves a little bit more while you get absolutely nothing out of this growing economy.'', that the Treasurer prattles on about and praises himself for, when none of it is his own work in any case, and he opposed every aspect of the economic reform process that made it possible for this country to be more competitive and more efficient. I challenge the Prime Minister as to whether the vision to be announced in this Budget on June is a vision that says to the bottom third of New Zealanders in particular: ``You are our top priority. Improving your standard of living is our top priority. Improving your access to the health system is our top priority. Improving your children's performance in school is our top priority. Making sure your children from birth get the services they need to get a proper start in life is our top priority.'' What will be done about all the evidence that most people's life chances are locked in by the age of ? Will we congratulate ourselves that there is still a fiscal surplus, despite the fact that there is a falling one? Will we fool ourselves by rosy Treasury projections of growth that will not occur to years down the track? Will we say that it has all been for the best in the best of all possible worlds? Will we yet again get nonsense about ? I say to the Prime Minister that that is what we will get, is it not? We will not get a Budget that says to those who have missed out the most that they are the top priority for Government action in the next few years. That is why this Budget will be a failure. Finally, I say to the Prime Minister that it is time for him to act like a leader. It is time for him to take control of this sleazy, nasty, mucky little Government and to send to the people of New Zealand a clear signal that enough is enough, that being demeaned in this job, being demeaned as a representative of the people, has to stop, and that we will improve our act---we will improve what we are doing for the people of this country because they pay for us; we do not pay for them.

I will explain to the member how she gets that number. Mr Sowry might be interested because he is the one who is being attacked by the member in this regard. In New Zealand superannuation was not part of vote: Social Welfare; it was part of vote: Senior Citizens. The $ million a day in , just over $ billion a year, was social security expenditure excluding New Zealand superannuation. The $ million a day is not excluding New Zealand superannuation, and it includes some other social services that are not part of income maintenance. She is not comparing like with like at the present time. She is comparing like with unlike, which is a typical Mr Prebble trick. He has never launched a ``Save Truth'' campaign during this campaign, but no doubt he will launch other things. There are many fundamental errors, but another fundamental error that Mrs Newman made in that speech was to posit that essentially the State and the community sector were alternatives. In areas of social delivery such as this, the State and the community sector are not alternatives; they are essential partners. If they do not work together, it is impossible to achieve the best results that may be available. It is all very well to praise community groups; of course they do a good job. But she might care to think that this Bill makes it possible at the end of the day, in effect, for various community groups to access Government funding, apart from anything else. The vast proportion of the money is still going to come from the Government, not from the community. Contrary to the sort of mad books from the Institute of Economic Affairs in London that ACT members read and cite in footnotes, it is not true that the private sector and voluntary sector in the th century managed to solve the problems of poverty and community need. They did not even scratch the surface. That happens to be my expert field of historical research---th century social history. Let me assure her that until the Government came along, got active, and started providing massive funding and structural frameworks, poverty was rampant amongst a large proportion of the population. Let me also say that she makes a fundamental error about the domestic purposes benefit. The number of young women, particularly young women who have never married, who go on to the domestic purposes benefit is less now than it was years ago. Far from going up, the proportion has gone down. The people on the domestic purposes benefit now are, overwhelmingly, people who have been in a relationship. These days a relationship cannot be measured by the partners having been married, because many people now do not go through a formal marriage process, or do so many years after their relationship begins. In old-fashioned language, the vast majority of children are now illegitimate---the language that was used or years ago---or there is another word, based upon William the Conqueror and various others, which we will not mention in this House. Today that is not the case. We do not have that view. We recognise partnerships and relationships. Marriage is one of a continuum of possible forms that those partnerships and relationships take. As I say, the vast majority of the people on the domestic purposes benefit, of whom I think percent are women, have been in a relationship. They are not simply serially having it off in the back seats of cars with somebody they do not know, then collecting the domestic purposes benefit to go home and spend it all on Lotto and booze. Finally, I note in that respect, having praised the Australians, that the Australian level of support for sole parents is much higher than it is in New Zealand. The Australian equivalent of the domestic purposes benefit is significantly higher than it is in New Zealand. More is paid, in that respect. What she has to learn is that her simple world of so-called personal responsibility basically means that people of her type can abdicate responsibility. That is what it really means. It means that those who are lucky and those who are better off can simply wash their hands of social problems in the rest of the country and say: ``We leave it to you. You've got to haul yourself up by your own bootstraps.'', and, occasionally: ``I did so myself.'' That is the underlying tone that comes through. But most people in that position actually do not do that. I am always amused when people whom I talk to who have been to various posh schools around the country and have had all the advantages in life tell me: ``The problem is that people in this country don't want to work hard enough and aren't prepared to try to improve themselves in the way that we did.'' Of course, they did not; they just happened to be lucky in their choice of parents. There was another fallacy in her speech, and it was a fairly serious one at that. She seemed to think that there was some huge relationship between solo parenthood and children being abused either physically or sexually---that somehow or other physical abuse and sexual abuse were a mark of a social underclass. There is some relationship there, but it is equally true that abuse occurs across a very wide variety of families from the very richest to the very poorest. Indeed, it can occur within long and stable marriages where a relative may engage in the abuse. There is no necessary connection. Indeed, those people who prattle on most about families---and we see this most clearly in the United States---are often the people who are least prepared to give actual and practical support to families that are actually and practically in need. Referring to the family is often simply a cover for saying ``I don't care.'', or in the old-fashioned language that I was brought up with: ``Blow you, Jack; I'm all right.'' That is what some of that prattling about families all too often means. The other point I want to make today is that I welcome the Bill. I think the Minister of Social Services, Work and Income will probably agree that in some ways it is a slightly muddled compromise to a rather difficult issue that probably requires a slightly muddled compromise. There is no neat and aesthetically pure solution to how one classifies groups in this area and makes sure there is some equality of funding and treatment. But remarks made earlier seemed to me to misunderstand what the principal Act was about, and what the problems of failure in its administration are due to. There seemed to be some suggestion that the Act was about, in effect, handing problems over to social workers, who were then unable to solve them for the families in need. That seems to me to be a fundamental misunderstanding of the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act, which is very much about how the State can facilitate and cooperate with families, whanau, individuals, and community organisations to try to ensure responsibility is taken for the protection of children and for their care and upbringing, and to try to achieve appropriate outcomes in terms of a range of options and possibilities that may be available. The whole family group conference mechanism is not meant to be a means of avoiding problems; it is meant to be a means of ensuring that people actually face the problems, and start talking about taking ownership of those problems and seeking solutions that may work well in practice. The alternative model was a heavily professionalised model of people taking kids away from family networks, taking ownership on the basis that professionals knew best. In my view, that solution does not work effectively in practice and is never likely to do so. The real issue is that we need to invest more in this area. We need to invest more in these early-intervention programmes, because if we do not we will continue to have arguments with people in Northland about where new prisons go. We will continue to have arguments about where police stations go, and about how we will find more money for police, courts, and prisons. If we found some more money for early intervention and for proper care and protection, perhaps those people would not end up in the negative mores of the criminal justice system in any case. I do not know why Mr Gresham hates the yet-to-be-selected National Party candidate for Taranaki - King Country so much. To get up in this Chamber and say this Bill may lead to less compensation than the existing Act--- ---and he says: ``Yes, it could.''---seems very extraordinary in the run-up to a by-election in the Taranaki - King Country electorate. It is not merely: ``Beware of Greeks bearing gifts.''; it is: ``Beware of Nats coming in to take money back from you.'', by the sound of things in this particular case. Are we seriously to believe that, with months yet to run on the option that the farmers have at present, the Government has to get this Bill through today under urgency, without select committee scrutiny, without going through the meaning of the actual wording in the Bill itself, and without making sure that this time the legislation will actually work properly---that it has to do all of that today in order not to increase the level of compensation to lessees, with a by-election coming up in which this issue will be a potentially major difficulty for the Government? Are we seriously meant to believe that so noble and so dutiful is this National Party - led Government that it will actually take back from the farmers in the Taranaki - King Country electorate some of the compensation that they might have got under legislation that is yet to be properly printed and distributed throughout the country? It is simply not credible that that line should be put forward. This Bill is about trying to fix up a sore point for National in the by-election campaign. It is about kneecapping ACT. It is about stringing up New Zealand First in terms of its position for the future. The beautiful point---the true ``Birchism'' about this---is that it is not even Mr Birch who has brought in the Bill; it is poor old Mr Henare who has to bring in a Bill that says to his colleagues' constituents: ``You don't get an extra brass razoo, but the lessees who have been using your land do.'' I am proud to say that the only candidate in the Taranaki - King Country by-election who has had the wit to turn up to Parliament to find out first hand what is going on so that he can report back to the electors is Max Purnell. He is the only candidate in this by-election who realised what was happening and got down to Wellington in time to find out exactly what is going on in the Chamber, to listen to the argument, and to find out what the National Party is up to. I am not saying where he is; I am looking very carefully at you, Madam Chairperson. He is certainly in Wellington at this time, listening closely to the proceedings in the Chamber, and ready to report back to the electors of Taranaki - King Country. Of course, now that Labour has selected a dairy-farmer we have neutralised that issue as far as the National Party is concerned. It will have to select a trade union official if it is to match the Labour Party in that regard. Labour is going to fight the Taranaki - King Country by-election on this issue as well, because I do not believe that this Bill gives certainty at all. The only way of giving real certainty is to start the clock for compensation at the start of when the values began to drop, and to stop the clock at January when the process of this Bill is completed. Then we can actually say precisely what the drop in values has been, and, what is more, the compensation can be given in a reasonable time-frame after the loss in value has occurred. Mr Prebble is right. Why should farmers have to wait until the year for compensation for losses they have now incurred? Why should those farmers have, in effect, another years of lost value as a consequence? The compensation should be occurring now. But the Government, having given more money on one side, has now also got to balance the equation. If the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Act is finely balanced, then this Bill cannot be, because it gives more money to the lessees. It has to be matched by better compensation for the lessors, the landowners. Introducing legislation that is now fundamentally unbalanced destroys the balance of justice that is supposedly implicit in the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Act. This House went through those issues very carefully only months ago. Then we were told the balance is fine; now we are told the balance is fine even though it is being upset.

I could reword it in a much more vulgar way. I thought I had used the kind of technical grown-up language that we use around this place. We did not really find that a very pleasant process, and it is not the way in which we usually deal with matters in that select committee, in relation to officials. I want to talk about another matter. It is one of those little by-ways and highways that I come up with every year or two because it does interest me, and practically nobody else in this Chamber. It is the way that we express formulae in legislation, which is now done very frequently in taxation legislation. It did not used to be; it used to be spelt out in words, and it is now done by means of formulae and definitions. If the Minister cares to turn to new section EH in clause , he will find a set of definitions that are expressed in terms of y and z, then the same y and z, then u and v, then w and x. That suggests that somebody who is slightly dyslexic or whatever is moving backwards through the alphabet but could not quite remember what the order was, because we come then to a, b, and c, which is why it looks to me as though, in a circular fashion, we are going backwards. Then we suddenly start going forwards again to d and e, etc., applying to various matters. If we go back to new section EH we find a whole set of separate definitions on a number of pages where a, b, c, and d are used for different things. In other words, in each separate section or subsection, a, b, c, and d have one definition, then in the next clause within the same part, a, b, c, and d have a different definition. That is, in my view, quite difficult to follow, because one has to keep switching off what one understood ``a'' to mean only a page previously because ``a'' has now become something else. Whereas, in the grammar and syntax used mathematically in the other example, people moved on to using a different set of letters for the definitions, which, in my view, is a preferable way of proceeding. There is also a rather peculiar thing. I have never understood how the Inland Revenue Department decides whether it will put things in brackets. If we look at the definition in new section EH() in clause , we find the formula a b c + d, and if we look at the definition in section EH() we find the formula a (b + c). Mr Hide will be able to follow this because he has done enough maths, science, and economics to be able to do so. The formula a (b + c) is the same as a b c. It happens so often in tax legislation---and I sometimes wonder whether somebody randomly splatters the brackets around---that sometimes brackets are used and sometimes they are not. The logic for using the bracket in new section EH() would be to calculate b + c first then subtract it from a. That was the only real reason for putting it in brackets in that form; otherwise one would express it as a b c. If the reason is that tax practitioners would be working in this way, then they would add b and c, whereas under new section EH() they would be working sequentially through from a to b to c to d.

Despite the rather strange choice of select committee, the Labour Party will be supporting the second reading of this Bill. I suspect that the Bill should have gone to the Finance and Expenditure Committee since it comes solidly within the areas of that select committee's work. A Bill in the name of Mr Winston Peters called the Banking and Insolvency (Netting and Payments Finality) Bill is an open invitation to the Opposition to have something of a field day for the next hour or so, particularly in terms of the insolvency part of the Bill, but we shall decline the opportunity at this stage. I understand that the Government caucus is being stocked up with coffee now ready for the consideration of the latest round of legislation to do with energy, so we will not delay them very long. My colleagues Mr Mallard and Mr Robertson, and perhaps a few others, may choose to speak but the Government caucus will get there by about midnight or so to consider, hopefully, the latest supplementary order paper it has drafted. I also have to say that this Bill is now long overdue. It is very strange that we are dealing with the second reading under urgency, but the truth is that this Bill should really be passed by now because the real-time gross settlement system came into operation in March this year and since then we have been exposed to some extent to an unnecessary level of risk, which this Bill in part is designed to deal with. If I can put it as simply as I can, at the moment we have a situation where the amount of financial transactions going through the New Zealand banking system every day equates to something close to percent of New Zealand's annual gross domestic product. It does not take much to recognise that a relatively small difficulty within that system can cause a systemic problem. If present laws were enforced, even a bank that is quite solvent could find itself, at some particular period, in serious difficulties under a real-time gross settlement system. Previously, before the introduction of the real-time gross settlement system, accounts were settled at the end of the day, not during the day. The whole point about real-time gross settlement is that transactions are settled during the day on a continuous process. That is highly advantageous overall. It makes a great deal of sense, now that we do not need to collect up physically the cheques and the money at the end of each day and swap them around, which is what used to occur until recently. Now that these things can be done electronically, it makes sense for settlement to take place in real time and therefore for the balances to be running the whole time. But it does mean that, given the present situation in relation to netting and its relationship to insolvency, where there are complexities of laws that relate to different forms of settlements and what may occur, the general thrust is that fundamentally the resolution of any such matter, in terms of winding up, occurs at what is called zero hour. That means---putting it as simply as I can---that settlements that occur on a real-time gross settlement basis could be unwound. Essentially, this motion is the same as the previous motion. The member Sue Kedgley took some offence at my suggestion that there was collusion between the Greens and the National Party on this matter. I suggest that she read the two proposed amendments. They are identical, with two minor exceptions. One exception is that the National Party amendment has no reference to ``significant variation to an existing treaty or agreement''; those words are added in the Green's Supplementary Order Paper . Secondly, subclause () of clause F on the National Party's Supplementary Order Paper , in relation to district health boards, does not appear on the Greens Supplementary Order Paper. In all other respects the two amendments are absolutely identical, word for word, with one further exception, a cross reference mistake in the Greens proposed amendment. So if the member did not engage in collusion, I suspect that somebody did on her behalf. If that did not happen, I suspect that there has been an enormous coincidence, a level of coincidence around which even Charles Dickens might have had difficulty constructing a plot in terms of trying to explain the denouement of a particular novel. It is absolutely clear that a jack-up has gone on here between the National Party and the Greens. I come back to the essential point. The member says any amendment should be considered on its merits. My answer is no, if it is outside the scope of the bill. That is why this motion has had to be moved---because the amendments are outside the scope of the bill. It is not appropriate to suggest that any old amendment that one feels like putting should be considered just because one feels like putting it. Parliament is not a demand-fed institution. It has rules for a particular purpose. Secondly, and most important, I repeat what I said before. Changing the way that we treat international treaties is not to be done by ambush without proper consideration and without the matter going to a select committee for full consideration. This proposal completely changes, for example, the present Standing Orders treatment for various kinds of international treaties. It has never before been suggested that international treaties require prior approval by Parliament before they can be signed up to. That is a totally new suggestion coming through here. Mr Creech, as the previous Deputy Prime Minister, ought to be ashamed of himself for suggesting this ambush of the parliamentary process. He is making a joke of himself and a joke of his party. It is no wonder the business community is once again saying there is no point in it putting any faith in the National Party. It is dog tucker for years to come. The National Party will not be seen for ages to come in terms of being in Government. The same arguments apply to this motion as applied to the previous one. I trust it will suffer the same fate.

As other members have indicated, the Bill was introduced in December . Submissions were called for, and closed on January . I think that it is incredible to report to the House that it took another months for the Bill to be reported back from the select committee. It is only a small Bill, as has been mentioned, but it is part of a wider package. Unfortunately, the progress of that package through the select committee has been delayed. That is unfortunate in many respects, because this Bill did not receive the kind of scrutiny that it should have received. It is important to remind the House that committee members were forced to deliberate on this Bill because of an urgent requirement from the Government, as the Government did not have its entertainment tax legislation ready to be dealt with on the particular day in question. This Bill is part of a package of company law reforms, and this part of the package has not received universal support. The member for St. Albans quite properly described the Bill as constitutionally inappropriate. It is important for the House to remember that on this occasion members are delegating not insignificant lawmaking powers to the Accounting Standards Review Board. I think that it is fair to raise that issue in the House this afternoon. The member for St. Albans also described the Bill as a piece of political window-dressing. I am always concerned when legislation purports to do something, or to protect people from something, when, in a practical sense, it cannot achieve that objective. I do not want a false sense of security to develop because of the Bill. Financial reporting standards do not prevent companies from getting into financial difficulties, nor do they of themselves protect investors from losing investments from time to time. However, with those comments in mind, I should like to turn to some of the detail of the Bill as reported back from the select committee. The first point relates to the application of the Bill. The committee received a number of submissions that were concerned about the definition of ``issuer''. A number of submissions advocated that the Bill should apply to all reporting entities---that is, all those bodies that are required by law to prepare financial statements for use by third parties, for whatever reason. The concern was expressed that, by the adoption of the approach envisaged under the original Bill, two sets of accounting standards that differed in content and subject-matter would evolve. The reality is that that will happen, but one of the changes that was made by the committee was to include a reference to the Companies Act in the new clause (a). That will ensure that the jurisdiction of the board is extended to include the approval of standards for so-called ordinary companies. The basic distinction between issuers and ordinary companies will remain, and not all standards that apply to issuers will automatically apply to ordinary companies. Standards would apply to ordinary companies only if the board had made a conscious decision that they should do so. I think that that distinction is a practical distinction to draw. My next point relates to the question of the role of the Accounting Standards Review Board itself. A consultation provision was included in the Bill as reported back from the select committee. No consultation mechanism was in place in the original Bill. Although the Minister made some comment about the consultation mechanism, I must report to the House, as I did in the reporting back, that the Opposition voted against the clause that had been inserted in the Bill simply because of the addition of paragraph of the new clause A, which states: ``Any failure to comply with subsection () of this section shall not affect the validity of the approval by the Board of the standard or the amendment.''. Basically, that paragraph states that, if there is no consultation, that does not make any difference, so the Opposition was not able to support the clause as a whole. Opposition members do support consultation. An alternative was presented to us that we would have supported. It would have made it mandatory to comply with the consultation mechanism. A number of submissioners felt that the Accounting Standards Review Board should of its own initiative be able to present draft standards. That did not find favour with the select committee, and the position is that under the provisions of the new clause the New Zealand Society of Accountants and any other organisation or person may submit financial reporting standards, or amendments to any approved financial reporting standards, to the board for approval. That was an issue of concern to some submissioners, who felt that generally there should be a wider role for the board itself so that it could initiate some of that work. When the committee discussed those issues with some of the organisations---for example, the Reserve Bank---that had made submissions on that point, the fact that of their own volition they could raise the matter directly with the board was felt to be sufficient in terms of addressing the concern that had been raised. Another matter to which I want to refer is the application of the Regulations (Disallowance) Act . Under the Bill as introduced, only sections to of the Regulations (Disallowance) Act were to apply to the determinations of the board in approving financial reporting standards or revoking an approval. The select committee tidied that up, but that was solely because one of the members of the Justice and Law Reform Committee is the chairperson of the Regulations Review Committee. He is a very good member, and I am glad that the Minister has acknowledged that fact across the House. But it is not good enough for the committee to have to rely on an occurrence such as that to pick up discrepancies in legislation. To be blunt, if the member for St. Albans had not attended that meeting the matter would not have been resolved, and an amendment would have been required either in the Committee stage or by way of a supplementary order paper. I do not think that that is good enough; it would be much better if more consideration were given to those matters prior to their referral to the select committee. I do not want to dwell any further on the particular detail of the Bill. I am concerned that it will create an atmosphere that will tend to make people feel that somehow they have better protection. Some protections are offered by those standards, but they have been overstated, certainly by the Minister in his comments on the Bill. The Opposition will not oppose the progress of the Bill through the House. Bill read a second time.

I am simply commenting to the member for Invercargill that he was the member who said that there would be lengthy and considered deliberation about the option for privatising our prisons. What I am saying is that that simply cannot happen in the time-frame that the Minister has allowed the select committee by the commencement date contained within the Bill. Government members have tried to draw a comparison with the privatisation of some State-owned assets in the past, and I want to address that point because there is no question that the privatisation of prisons is quite a different issue from the privatisation of businesses operated by the Government. It is quite separate, and I think that it is wrong for Government members to draw any comparison between the two. Running our penal institutions is a core State function that should not be contracted out to the private sector. Imprisonment is the extreme to which the coercive powers of the State extend. I believe that contracting out coercive powers to the private sector away from the State is fundamentally wrong. It is quite wrong and it is one of the primary reasons that I oppose the Bill tonight. The Bill is being introduced to pave the way for a -bed remand centre adjoining Mount Eden Prison, and a -bed medium-security prison in south Auckland. There is no question that remand facilities need to be upgraded. I am extremely unhappy at the situation in which people on remand are being held in police cells. I have referred a particular instance to both the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Police and have had a less than satisfactory reply from the latter but a more considered one from the former. The reality is that some people are spending days on end in cells that are not designed for humane containment. That is a simple reality. There are no outside exercise yards and they do not have the range of facilities that are available in other penal institutions. It is clearly a situation that must be resolved. The point I am making is that this Bill is not the way to go---to hand over the remand facility completely to the private sector. We have a problem, and it was one of the very clear consequences of the new bail laws introduced by the Government about years ago. At the time, Opposition members predicted that remand prison space would become a problem, that it would be at a premium very quickly, and we were right. What has been the quid pro quo? There is absolutely no evidence that the rate of offending while on bail has been reduced one bit. All we have done is jail people, a third of whom will never be convicted of any offence, and for what benefit? What has been the return? The only thing is that the private sector will now have the opportunity to be involved in developing a prison to deal with the additional people within the system. All we have done is end up with more people in prisons and in police cells. It would be better to look at the reason that New Zealand is jailing more people than just about any other country in the world, with probably the one exception of the United States. Given that, why on earth is New Zealand Americanising its prison system? Maybe the Americanisation of our health system was such a good idea that the Government thought it would Americanise the prison system as well.

I want to take a relatively brief call on this legislation in order to support some of the comments made by my colleague the Minister of Broadcasting, particularly in relation to privacy matters. They are really the areas that I want to deal with. This bill provides for an extension to section ()(e) of the Broadcasting Act. Under that section there is provision for the Broadcasting Standards Authority to develop and observe codes of broadcasting practice amongst broadcasters that are appropriate to the type of broadcasting undertaken by them. The particular areas on which the legislation has focused in the past are the protection of children; the portrayal of violence; fair and accurate programmes, and procedures for correcting factual errors and redressing unfairness; safeguards against the portrayal of persons in programmes in a manner that encourages denigration of, or discrimination against, sections of the community on account of sex, race, age, disability, or occupational status, or as a consequence of legitimate expressions of religious, cultural, or political beliefs; restrictions on the promotion of liquor; and, lastly, presentation of appropriate warnings in relation to programmes, including programmes that have been classified as suitable only for particular audiences. This bill now extends that list by an additional provision that provides specifically for the privacy of an individual. The reason for needing to address this issue was quite appropriately described by the Minister as resulting from an awareness that there had not been a proper basis for the consideration of a large number of complaints that had come in. This amendment strengthens the Broadcasting Act. It will enable the Broadcasting Standards Authority to have a jurisdiction more in line with what I think most New Zealanders are looking for now. They are looking for laws that do reflect their right to privacy. Television is probably the most invasive form of medium. It is able to do quite considerable damage to the reputation of individuals and, therefore, the issues of protecting privacy are really important. I want to comment briefly on the decision to restore to the bill the mandatory requirement to consult the Privacy Commissioner. This is a matter that was subject to some debate in this Chamber during the Committee stage---I think it was probably the issue that attracted the most debate at that stage. The real issue was a conflict of opinion as to whether consultation with the Privacy Commissioner should be mandatory. I got the sense from the debate that there was a view that consultation ought to take place, and also that people felt it would take place. I think that the real difference between us was simply over whether consultation should be compulsory---whether it should be written in the bill. My recollections of the debate are that a number of other bodies, commissions, etc., were identified that might have an interest in providing input into the development of other codes under section ()(e) of the Act. The question then arose as to why we were singling out the Privacy Commissioner in relation to the privacy of individuals, as opposed to, for example, writing in a mandatory requirement to consult the Commissioner for Children on issues relating to the protection of children, the portrayal of violence, and those sorts of matters. I think that members opposite who raised those concerns did so in a genuine way, and I do not think that there is any great significance in the difference of view between us. The reason I do want this bill to contain a mandatory requirement to consult the Privacy Commissioner on individual privacy matters really stems from the different nature of the jurisdiction of the Privacy Commissioner. I believe that the way in which his role has developed under the Privacy Act puts him in a unique position to strengthen the process of developing these codes. Members opposite will, of course, be aware that the Privacy Act provides specifically for the commissioner to be involved in the development of codes of practice relating to privacy issues. He has worked with health professionals, and with a whole range of different organisations, to develop specific privacy codes in order to protect rights in quite specific circumstances. I believe that the role of the Broadcasting Standards Authority will be strengthened by the mandatory requirement to consult the Privacy Commissioner, because I believe that the expertise he will bring to that process will improve the end result. I do not think that there is an enormous difference between the parties on this matter, but I do think that the bill itself is strengthened by the decision of the select committee to restore the mandatory requirement to consult. I think that the requirement is in line with the Privacy Act, the very special role of the Privacy Commissioner, and the wealth of experience that he has developed since the enactment of that Act. I believe that will be of great advantage in this area. Finally, I want to make the point that under the Privacy Act, the news media are excluded from the ambit of that Act in relation to their news-gathering activities. Sometimes I feel that the news media have not quite worked out that not all of what they do is a news-gathering activity, and that they are required to comply with the provisions of the Privacy Act in respect of things that do not amount to news-gathering activities. The fact that the Privacy Commissioner will now have to be brought into a consultative process with the Broadcasting Standards Authority will be a good thing. So I congratulate the Minister on her work in bringing about a conclusion to the passage of this bill.
