It was disappointing to have to listen to the Alliance again. On principle the Alliance opposes everything, and given half a chance it would oppose the creation of life itself. But that is the nature of the beast. Listening to Mr Donald is like saying: ``Let's go back to the State-run oligarchies.''---which the Soviet Union got rid of not so long ago. ``Let's set up `New Zealand Incorporated' and put everything under the control of the Government, because that's the way to go.'' That is what Mr Donald is saying. He wants to know who will benefit from this Bill. Well, it certainly benefits the people of New Zealand and the farmers of New Zealand. Mr Donald would do well to listen to the Hon. Jim Sutton and the Hon. Lockwood Smith. He would learn something and would not need to go to Massey University, either. If he sat around and listened he would learn that this move should have been taken many years ago---and I think Mr Sutton was alluding to that, in hindsight. Hindsight is a wonderful thing, and I think Mr Sutton would have liked to introduce this Bill himself back in . Getting rid of section is good for the country. At the end of the day---as both Mr Smith and Mr Sutton have said---this issue is about cross-subsidisation, and that is what we were doing here in New Zealand. I agree with Mr Sutton that it would be a bit rich for New Zealand to take on Canada, when talking about cross-subsidisation. Even though we do have open markets there is always a threat to other countries. Mr Sutton was fairly correct in his assumption that there is a bit of a deterrent for people from other countries, such as Australians, to come into New Zealand with dairy products, knowing that at any time the Dairy Board could use section to subsidise local prices. So why would one go to the huge cost of setting up an infrastructure to import dairy products---milk, cheese---and other products into this country, when the Dairy Board could use section to quite legally undercut. I am glad that the Hon. Lockwood Smith has introduced this Bill to remove section to stop that price-equalisation or cross-subsidisation, which is effectively what it was. We need to tackle Canada on its scheme, which is locking out our dairy-farmers' exports to that market. But we certainly cannot go to the international forum and demand that Canada not do that when we have a scheme that could be manipulated to do something similar. I acknowledge and congratulate Dr the Hon. Lockwood Smith on bringing this forward. I am sure that the House will pass this Bill through all stages today, even if it is clause by clause. I see Dr Cullen has arrived, so I gather from my experience last week that it will be comma by comma. Be that as it may, it will be good to get this Bill through. The domestic dairy market will finally operate under the normal rules of competition. Perhaps we will see the Australians coming into the market, because the repeal of section means that the threat that our products will be subsidised by export no longer exists. We may well see other people coming in. We do have an open market, but this Bill will ensure that the market is a lot more open, and truly open. If we do not do this, it will be disastrous. The Canadians may be seen by the European Union as an appropriate model. We could have greater problems with the European Union coming together and working together on a number of areas. They already have enough subsidisation and we do not need further protection of their dairy markets. We need to take this to the international forum to ensure that the Canadian system is outlawed, because it would have a huge detrimental effect on us. At the moment it restricts us from going into the Canadian market. I have just come back from the USA and have seen some of the effects that subsidisation and protectionism have in that country.

On the motion to appoint Doug Graham to this committee, I want to say that I have no problems with Doug Graham's ability as a lawyer. I think he is an exceptional lawyer who would make an excellent contribution to a select committee of Parliament considering this Bill, but I do not believe that he should be appointed to the Intelligence and Security Committee, because, as the Rt Hon. Winston Peters pointed out, this committee is a two-party closed shop. National has three members on the committee, yet it got only percent of the vote at the last election. Labour has two members on the committee, and it got about percent of the vote at the last election. The rest of us have no representatives on the committee. Mr Mapp quoted from section of the Act, which tells us about how the committee is set up. Indeed, two members are nominated by the Prime Minister after consultation with the leader of each party in Government. I would be interested to know whether the Hon. Tau Henare was consulted on this, and whether he is the leader of a party in Government, because it is hard to know whether his party has been registered. Either way, there is nothing in this Act that precludes the Prime Minister from nominating somebody who is not from the Government side of this House. So there is every reason for her to have left Winston Peters on the committee, or to nominate somebody from the Alliance, or even Peter Dunne, who volunteered to go on the committee in the first place. I think that the very fact that we are having this debate today points to the fundamental issue before this House, which is that we are giving away our rights and responsibilities and following a process that occurred years ago when we considered the establishment of this committee in the first place. The Bill establishing this committee, which allows for the appointment of the Rt Hon. Doug Graham, was introduced into the House on December . The original submissions were due to close at the end of January, only working-days later. What do we have now? It is exactly the same situation. Mr Graham is being appointed to sit on the committee to consider those submissions. At least the Prime Minister says that the Rt Hon. Doug Graham will be hearing some of those submissions in public, whereas years ago there was grave doubt over whether that was the case. However, we still have the fundamental problem that Doug Graham has been appointed to a closed statutory committee, which I believe is highly inappropriate in a democracy. It is a committee that should not have been set up by this House, and it should be abolished.

I am committed to middle schools and I am a strong advocate for them. Middle schools can provide an education that is specifically geared to the developmental stage of emerging adolescents--- to -year-olds. This is a time when students are moving from being children who are dependent upon parents to being young autonomous adults. They still need boundaries in the way that younger children do, but they are struggling to become unique individuals in a more adult sense. Schools that particularly cater for students in their developmental phase of emerging adolescence can concentrate on the special needs of their pre-adolescent students without having to deal with the distractions of demands of younger children or older adolescents. It is important that we make available schools that offer an educational recipe catering for the unique developmental realities of this age group of students. This legislation will not impose middle schools on communities that do not want them, but it will certainly make it easier for those communities that do desire that form of schooling, to have it. I have had personal experience of how difficult it is under current legislation to form a middle school. My old school, Whangarei Intermediate, applied to the Ministry of Education in to become a form I to form IV school. It was, I believe, the first school in New Zealand to do so. However, because of the way the legislation in existence at that time worked, we could not get anywhere with the application. In essence, the ministry did not know what to do with it, because the legislation was far too restrictive and did not allow for that form of schooling. We surveyed the parents on two occasions. Between and percent of those surveyed wanted form I to form IV education and a school to develop in that way. Even though the parents wanted that structure, there was no way we could move towards it, because of the restrictive nature of the legislation at the time. This Bill will also replace the current two-stage process with a single-stage process. However, the Bill also makes it easier to establish other school structures such as senior secondary schools, which naturally complement middle schools. But it gives much more power back to the community to have the structure of schooling it wants rather than structures that have developed haphazardly over time and because of historical reasons. Quite rightly, there has been a considerable amount of concern in recent years over children who simply disappear from the system. They just drop through the cracks. In the old days of education boards there was a very tight system of control. Unfortunately, that disappeared with the introduction of the Tomorrow's Schools policy. It was one of the things that Labour overlooked in its haste to put this new system in place. Under the current system, children can fall through the cracks, especially when they move from one school to another, such as when they move between their primary school and intermediate school, their intermediate school and secondary school, or when they move to a school in another area. Many of these children just completely drop out of the system and they get no education whatsoever. Therefore, a national and consistent enrolment record that will follow children and allow them to be found more easily if they do drop out has to be applauded. I believe that this is one of the very worthwhile aspects of this Bill. The converse of children who drop out are children who could do with some time out. Under the existing suspension rules, only one short-term suspension is allowed per year. This is extremely restrictive. The two new concepts introduced into the suspension process---stand-downs and exclusions---give schools more flexibility when dealing with problem students. The Bill allows for a student to be stood down for up to days a year, which gives, once again, a much greater degree of flexibility. But it also means that conditions are attached to the student returning to school, and it puts in place measures to lessen the educational impact of a student being stood down. This means that schools have to help children and parents through various programmes and ensure that they get some guidance. It also recognises students' rights by giving them the right to be heard by the board of trustees. The powers given to the Secretary for Education to publish rules on this will also protect students' rights. Sometimes, however, problems in schools lie with the people responsible for running them rather than with the students. At the moment the options of the Minister of Education are limited when a board of trustees is not performing well or is not undertaking or fulfilling certain responsibilities. Essentially, the Minister has a choice of sacking a board or doing nothing, and clearly this is not satisfactory. There are times when a board that is not working very well certainly needs help but will not seek that help. Even if it is given a review by the Education Review Office that suggests that certain things should be done, those recommendations are ignored in some cases. This Bill is a step between those two extremes. Boards of trustees that are not meeting their responsibilities to their communities can be obliged to do so. The best interests of the children are at the heart of the matter in this provision. If boards of trustees are not looking after the children, the Government will have a means of ensuring that they do so. I just mention that the Bill also allows for the reviewing of home schooling, which once again is something that was in the coalition agreement and that the Labour spokesperson congratulated the Government on reinstigating.

However, quite contrary to the point Mr Shirley was making that the bill should go back to another existing select committee, we say ``No''--it should be set up as it is, for two reasons. The first reason is that it is such special and important legislation and it is absolutely critical that it is right because it will have so much impact not only upon the nation as a whole but also upon so many individuals if it is wrong. The second point I make is that as a result of the composition of this select committee, we are able to offer the expertise, the diligence, and the worth of a person of the calibre of Peter Brown. I noticed that Margaret Wilson spoke about the contribution that Peter Brown had made to the accident compensation legislation, and I see that Graham Kelly is nodding there. I believe that whilst there were some people within our organisation who said: ``Listen, you're not going to get many brownie points for this.'', Peter Brown basically took the viewpoint that it was important legislation, and he was going to give us his absolute all. That is to the extent that when I had to go into the select committee one day to find out from Mr Brown how we were supposed to vote on a particular bill that was going through, he was so concentrated in his effort that I could not get his attention. I got Mr Brownlee's attention, and he then passed the message on. But Peter Brown was totally focused upon the work. I can assure the House that Peter Brown will continue to be totally focused in this area. He comes with great experience of industrial relations. Mr Brown reflects, essentially, New Zealand First's philosophy towards industrial relations, and that is that any legislation that is put in place in this regard has to be fair, has to be flexible, and has to be politically neutral. I remind the House that there was a stage in our country's history when we went without a strike for about years. It was the years immediately following the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act of , which I think was put through by William Pember Reeves. The reason our industrial relations were so good at that time was that the Act was so balanced. It was only when the Government of the time started to stack the court with employers' representatives that we started to get strife. So it is critically important that we get this legislation right. We have to say from the outset that we do not think the Employment Contracts Act is all bad. We believe it has contributed greatly to growth in jobs and to a number of other factors, particularly flexibility, but we do believe that it has weaknesses. If this bill can overcome some of those weaknesses and get a fairer and more balanced approach into our industrial relations, then the House can be guaranteed that our representative, Mr Peter Brown, will be ensuring that that is what takes place. There were some concerns in the Committee on the Accident Insurance (Transitional Provisions) Bill that there was a conflict of ideologies between ACT and National, on the one hand, and Labour and the Alliance on the other; between privatisation and the single State-provider. Peter Brown came in from a totally different point of view and said: ``What I'm here for is to look after the victims of accidents, and to ensure that they get a fair go and get the best deal out of it.'' Similarly, in this case, Peter Brown will not be taking the side of the employers over the employees, or vice versa. He will be there to see that what comes out leads to an environment of fairness: fairness to the employers and fairness to the employees. A lot has been made of the fact that one side of this ``imbalanced'' select committee has been made up of trade unionists. All I can say is that I know Graham Kelly and I know Mark Peck. They are living proof that not all trade unionists are bad. I am sure that other members of the committee will take an objective viewpoint. If there are elements of the bill that are not sound and not good, then they will move to ensure that those things are modified to get the best possible industrial relations environment. We certainly do not want to go back to the days of massive strikes. I come from Northland, and I know the effect the Marsden Point debacle had. So we have to make sure that we do not get into the situation where a few possibly irresponsible unions hold the country to ransom, and, as Sue Bradford said, do not necessarily look after the needs of all the workers. I was very pleased to hear the comments made by Sue Bradford; that she was coming in independently and that she would take a look at the bill not only in terms of how it affects workers, but also some of those workers whom the Employment Contracts Act has dropped out at the bottom of the pile: the unemployed and the casualised labour. I can tell the House that New Zealand First is very concerned about the effects of the Employment Contracts Act on the process of casualisation, and the very unfair practices that have often been created towards casualised labour. The New Zealand First position is very much reflected by the concerns of our member on this select committee, Peter Brown. Therefore members can be assured that Peter Brown will be going in bringing a personal philosophy and also New Zealand First party philosophy into the discussions that take place in this select committee. Mr Brown just mentioned to me that if there is one negative feel about the matter it was that he felt there was a sense of a lack of open-mindedness in the Committee on the Accident Insurance (Transitional Provisions) Bill. It was a sense that two parties had gone into their corners and were not really prepared to view the matter as objectively or intelligently as possibly they should have. Therefore I urge the members of this select committee--and I have every faith in the members on this select committee--to go in there with an open mind, to ensure that what comes out in terms of the legislation is the best possible industrial relations legislation that we can get, so we can get back to a situation like that in . The aim of this select committee really should be to end up with an environment where there is fairness, where there is flexibility, where there is political neutrality, and in which businesses can flourish and grow, and in which workers can be provided with the best outcomes for themselves in the levels of safety and all of those sorts of things. New Zealand First will be voting against the amendment and will be voting for the motion. We will certainly be providing all the support we can to Peter Brown and the other members of this select committee.

I am really pleased that the Government has decided that it will support the amendments to clause and clause put in by Lianne Dalziel. We were particularly disturbed that this Bill did not make any attempt to regulate the activities of immigration consultants, given that the actions of such people regularly get into the newspapers as they do their work in a way that disadvantages and rips off the people whom they are supposedly helping. So it is good to see that the new subclause in clause will help in that direction, even though it does not go as far as Labour would have liked. We would have liked to have seen registration of such people by a proper professional body, so that their activities would have to be carried out in a totally professional manner. But it is good to see that the amendment will be supported, and it will help. The Labour Party will vote against the section on bonds. The previous speaker spoke about our concerns about all the fees that are in there. It is interesting that in section B in clause there is a new subsection that states that ``Different levels of bond, or different methods of determining levels of bond, may be determined or prescribed in respect of different categories of person, including categories of persons determined by having regard to the different regions of the world where their countries of origin or nationality are situated and the cost of travel or repatriation to such regions or countries.'' One would suppose that it seems reasonable to have the level of bond determined by the region that the person comes from, if it is meant to ensure that he or she can travel back to that particular area, but that is not the only reason. The different levels of bonds are in respect of different categories of person, including the categories determined by where a person comes from. In other words, it allows a discretion for the bonds to be differentiated for any reason whatsoever. I think that it does not reflect well on the New Zealand Government to have a provision like that in the Bill. It gives carte blanche to any sort of discrimination to be invoked, and the Labour Party is not in favour of that. We do not like the idea of bonds at all. As I said before, good government is a balance between economic management and quality of life concerns. I want to talk about one area in which I am specifically involved---the care for our environment. This Government has undertaken more in the way of reform in that area than any other Government, not just in the history of this country but in the history of the Western World. The people will not be hoodwinked again, and Opposition members, by playing the kind of burlesque games that the member for Rotorua and the member for Raglan embarked upon this afternoon in the absence of a policy debate, know that their time is running out. New Zealand will not fall for them again.

I support the reporting back of the Consumer Guarantees Bill. I also support what the Bill seeks to do, but I have very severe reservations about whether it will be able to achieve its purpose. The reason for my reservations lies in an area that was touched on by the Minister in her contribution. The Bill, which is a consumer Bill that deals with the rights and responsibilities of manufacturers and other suppliers towards consumers, is not to be administered by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs. Technically, it is a matter for the Department of Justice. While I believe the Minister when she talks about her commitment to honouring the Bill's provisions, I am far from convinced that the departmental structure will enable that to be the case. Debate has been going on for some years about the appropriate roles of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs vis-a-vis consumer legislation, and of the Department of Justice vis-a-vis commercial legislation generally. I am one of those who say that it is time the matter was resolved. It is time that consumer law was clearly made the responsibility of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, that the ministry was given not only the authority but also the status to act in support of that law, and that the hidden debate that is going on at the moment about whether the ministry should even exist was laid to rest. This is an important issue. I say that we cannot be confident that the Bill will work while the other matter remains unresolved. The Minister made another point, which I think is a good one about which we ought to be thinking---not just in the context of the Bill but also in the context of the wider issue of consumer protection. In my view there is a danger in investing all our faith in the consumer guarantees legislation to provide the ultimate degree of protection for people. Other measures also need to be addressed. I am concerned about the ongoing relevance of the Sale of Goods Act. I know that it is old and applies only in certain circumstances. We need to start looking at what its future might be. The Minister's point about the need to move on consumer credit legislation is also important. The issue of some of the changes that, for instance, the Fair Trading Act might undertake is also important in the context of ensuring that the Bill, which has been the subject of very lengthy consideration and examination, can achieve the objectives we are all talking about today. One other element relating to this matter bears being reported to the House. The submissions received were, on the whole, of extremely high quality. The one submission I was most taken with---and this is not to derogate its quality in any way---was the contribution made by the Association of Citizens Advice Bureaux. Unlike the people who came from a narrow professional or managerial perspective, the association clearly came from the consumers' point of view and gave the committee a great deal of practical advice on the way in which the law might work and might be seen to work. I want to record my gratitude and the gratitude of my colleagues to the people from the citizens advice bureaux for the effort they put into advising the committee and ensuring that we have good legislation. In addition to the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, the Department of Justice, or whichever department in the bureaucracy, it will be voluntary agencies such as that that end up dealing with the bulk of people's questions, complaints, and concerns about legislation of this type. It was important that the people from the citizens advice bureaux be involved and listened to. Opposition members certainly gave them that consideration. I concede freely to being one of those people who, right from the outset, were sceptical about the intention to include services within the ambit of the Bill, because I knew that in a number of cases those services were covered by their own legislation. I am happy to say that, having heard the evidence and having had the opportunity to debate the issues with colleagues and within the committee, I now believe that the approach the Bill takes is correct. I further believe that the professional services that felt their power might be demeaned or reduced by the passage of a statute of this type do not have a great deal to be worried about. I believe that once we come through the education programme that the Minister talked about, and the change in public attitudes takes place, those concerns will be further allayed. Motion agreed to.

I come back to the point that the member for Te Atatu made: if tourism is to be a jewel in our economic crown we need to recognise its potential for employment creation. I am disappointed that no reference has been made in the objectives to that potential role for tourism in New Zealand. I am also concerned---following the same line of argument---that, in the objectives, consideration has not been made to the export-earning potential of the industry to New Zealand. I do not know whether the Minister intends to take a call, but if he does I would be interested in his comments on those provisions. Clause sets out the board's functions. Again, I have no difficulty with the general thrust of those provisions, but I am concerned that they do not go far enough. One of the opportunities that will arise from the further promotion of tourism in New Zealand will not be just in service to visitors, but in providing tourism-related businesses within New Zealand the opportunity to create new opportunities, new ideas, and new ventures. I would have thought that that would be a role for the New Zealand Tourism Board as it has that function. Because the board will bring together a wide variety of expertise and talent from the tourism industry---as members have already been told---I would have thought that there would be a role under the functions of the board for it to be required to take a more active part in the promotion of tourism-related businesses in New Zealand throughout the regional economies of New Zealand. I am disappointed that a change has not been made to take that factor into account, as a result of the evidence at the select committee. Given the rising interest worldwide in what is called green tourism, and the potential role that New Zealand can play---as an environmentally attractive nation---in attracting environmentally aware tourists, and in view of the comments made by Mr Plimmer recently on the same theme, I am somewhat surprised that no reference has been made to include that issue in the objectives of the board. That will be an important issue in the future. It will contribute to the point made by the member for Te Atatu that tourism can be a jewel in the economic crown of New Zealand. That being so, I would have thought it appropriate to broaden the functions of the board to include reference to that particular issue. Given the intention of the Government to promote tourism as an industry I would have thought that some attention would be given to carrying on the training work that is now undertaken within the industry. Good work is being done, and the Kiwi Host scheme comes to mind as an example, but there is clearly a need for further training and for an improvement in the quality of service and for an ongoing upgrading of that effort. I would have thought that that should be a primary function of the New Zealand Tourism Board, and I am surprised that no reference has been made to that in the functions set down for the board in the Bill. Clause ()(b) states that the board shall deal with the industry on all matters relating to the development, implementation, and promotion of such strategies, but I do not believe that that is sufficiently specific to deal with issues of the kind that have been raised. If New Zealand is to achieve the potential that the member for Te Atatu quite rightly draws to our attention, the board, which is a useful addition to our infrastructure, needs to have the clear direction of the House to put such operations into practice. Given that the industry has a flagship role, the Government should think again about how these objectives and functions have been crafted, and whether they meet the true potential of the industry. Clause arouses some interest because it states that the board should comply with Government policy and provides that the Minister can from time to time give written notice to the board about certain aspects of Government policy---and I would be interested to know from the Minister or a Government speaker whether some of the issues I have just canvassed are intended to be addressed under that provision, or is it intended that the Government might use that provision to give official direction to the board from time to time? If that is the case, the potential of the board to achieve its role will be compromised. Motion agreed to.

I am delighted to take part in the general debate, spurred by the Opposition, on the theme of middle New Zealand families, because a particular concern of mine for some time has been the way in which successive Governments of New Zealand have overlooked the plight of those people. I am pleased to see that the Opposition is now aware of that theme and is working constructively on behalf of those people. However, I have to say that the response from the Government this afternoon indicates that it is clearly a long way from coming to grips with the plight of middle-income New Zealand families. The response from the Minister of Fisheries---namely, to chant through a series of statistics and tell us about a few oyster farms as though that were a panacea for desperate middle New Zealand families---shows that there is a long way to go. The reality is that outside of Parliament there are people who are not interested in those general statistics; they are far more interested in, and driven by, the reality of their daily lives. Successive Governments have failed them because they have not taken any notice of the reality that those people see, but rely far more on some ``external'' reality. That is why we get the sort of nonsense in the House that was talked by both that Minister and the Minister who preceded him this afternoon---that is, that somehow there has been some great fall in interest rates over the past few years that has resulted in a decrease in people's mortgages---when the reality is that, although there has been a nominal decline in mortgage rates, the real situation still has not changed significantly because of high real interest rates. There is still a disincentive for those people. In addition, as a result of the efforts of the Government in the past months, we have now seen those people pay not less tax, but more. They pay an accident compensation levy; they got a petrol tax of c a litre in last year's Budget; now there is a proposal for them to pay more in that area. They had increased charges for alcohol and tobacco should they choose to indulge in those things---and some of them do, if only to relieve the stress. They have increased education charges and increased health charges. The list goes on and on. We have seen a recent report that tabulates the net effect of that---namely, an effective tax rate of c in the dollar for those people earning about $, to $, income. All that those people have to show for that is an increasing sense of alienation, of disillusionment, and of sheer disparagement because of what the system has to offer them. It is no wonder at the moment that there is a massive clamour around New Zealand for substantial change in the political system, if only because people see that as the way in which their aspirations, which have been mistreated for many years, will at last be given some recognition. The Government is nowhere near recognising the depth of that anger, the depth of that disillusionment, and it is nowhere near having the constructive solutions to deal with it. All that the Government seeks to do is to transfer the cost from the Crown's liability to the liability of the individual, in some sort of book-shuffling exercise. Then we get the smug and pious explanations of economic policy such as we got this afternoon from the Associate Minister of Finance---the member for Timaru---who said: ``We've got expenditure under control; we're doing very, very well. We're not doing so well on the revenue side but we're doing well with expenditure.''. He gave middle New Zealand families a great new excuse to get to the bank manager. I wonder how many of those families will succeed when they go to their bank manager and say: ``We're following the `McTigue formula'. Our expenditure is OK, Mr Bank Manager; it's just our income that's the problem.''. Any credible bank manager would laugh at them; and that Minister deserves to be laughed at, as well. We face a situation in this country where the depth of middle-class disillusionment with the political system will demand radical solutions in the future, and the Government has shown itself to be clearly incapable of even thinking about what those issues might be. I want to put forward some suggestions this afternoon, in a positive and constructive way, about some of the areas in which a Government might move that would give some sense of comfort to middle-class New Zealand families that there is some group that has their best interests at heart. We need to look at a philosophical point, and we need to balance what we all claim as our ``rights'' from society against our responsibilities to society. There is no sense of shortage of compassion, but sometimes we go overboard on the ``rights'' side and we are too light when we claim back the ``responsibility'' that any Government or any society has to demand of its citizens. I suggest that for practical and other reasons the health charges that have been imposed, which are a major burden on middle-income families in particular, ought to be abolished. They are not working in terms of the revenue they have been designed to generate. Certainly they are not working in terms of the argument of the Minister of Health that the charges are all about changing behaviour. The charges are simply fuelling resentment and bitterness; people feel that the health system they thought they were paying for exists simply to drain them of more tax. A number of the same points can be made in respect of the education system. When middle-income, middle-aged families are now struggling to finance two or three children through university because their income puts them over that income test limit, how can the education system be considered just? At the same time they have been told that, because of the profligacy of earlier years of which they were not part, they are now responsible for their own superannuation. It is happening at a time when employment policy means that anyone in that age group who becomes redundant has a minimal chance of re-employment. What is just and fair about that? How can that be held out as an encouragement to middle New Zealand? The short answer is: absolutely nothing; and the Government has no idea of or interest in how to deal with those matters. We need also to look at our education system. A huge number of administrative and policy changes have been made over the years. But I believe that one of the essential objectives of that change---namely, to take the emphasis away from administration and turn it into delivery---has not succeeded and that the old education bureaucracy has merely gone away, regrouped, and come back stronger than ever. As a result, we find that parents and teachers, who thought that they were going to have a greater input through their boards of trustees, now feel more frustrated than ever---as a result of change and of finding that they do not have the direct control and direct input that they thought those changes would give them. That is why large numbers are not coming forward to serve on boards of trustees this time round. We also need to introduce a much greater sense of stability and certainty into New Zealand's political process. We have to get away from this ongoing personality cult approach to politics, and , instead, go for a system that is based on the substance of the arguments put forward, the credibility of the policies put forward, and the ultimate integrity of the people who put them forward. The sense of disillusionment and betrayal that middle New Zealand has felt over the past few years now means that any one of us---forget which party we belong to---who stands up to speak on that group's behalf is immediately subject to suspicion because of the failures of the political system of the past. The activities of the Government over the past years have not contributed at all to any reduction in that sense of alienation---in fact, it is quite the opposite. The sense of bitterness that had hitherto been in the system has been extended to a new art form. I say to the Government, on the eve of its second Budget, that it will be judged not by whether the statistics continue to flow along mellifluously---as the Minister of Fisheries might like them to do---but by the extent to which the Budget addresses the sense of betrayal and disillusionment felt by middle New Zealand. This country faces a situation where, unless radical change of that nature is introduced, this political system will literally crumble and those of us who work within it will go with it, as well. That is a serious situation. It is not being addressed in current policy---quite the opposite. In fact, it is being fuelled by the deficiencies of that approach. Until we can get to a situation where: firstly, the tax burden on those people is reduced in real terms, not just in an indirect sort of way; secondly, people feel that they have got some stake in the decisions that Parliament makes about their future; and, thirdly, politicians can act with integrity and credibility on their behalf, then and only then will we be able to say---as the Prime Minister boasted on election night---``We have the politics of inclusion in New Zealand.''. The record of the Government in the past years suggests that we have no hope of achieving those goals while the current direction and approach to policy remain. I say to the Government that in the Budget next week it has a chance to rectify some of those matters. If it fails to do so, it will certainly be a one-term Government, but, more than that, it will have to take the responsibility for what might happen subsequently.

This has been a rather peculiar debate, right from the time of the introduction of the Bill through until today, on what is essentially procedural legislation regarding the way in which applications for overseas investment in this country are processed. Even the Labour Party, as the party that has led from the Opposition side the attack against this Bill, has demonstrated---from the speech made by the member for St Kilda on the day the Bill was introduced, through to the speeches made in the second reading by the Deputy Leader of the Opposition and the member for Henderson, and indeed through to the speech from the member for West Coast that we have just heard---that its opposition is not really to the content of the Bill but to the way the matter has been progressed. In their speeches, Labour Opposition members say constantly that their principal objection is one of process, of inadequate consultation, and of the public not being taken sufficiently into the confidence of this Parliament in resolving the issue. Yet if one listens to the other Opposition parties---New Zealand First and the Alliance---it will be found that their opposition has been far more intense against the whole principle of this legislation and, indeed, as far as New Zealand First is concerned---I am not so sure about the Alliance---that it is an opposition to the concept of foreign investment itself, which is something that is certainly not shared by the Labour Party, let alone those that support this Bill. What I want to say, therefore, is that this Bill has had a peculiar history. It has been a combination of people arguing about process and others trying to inject a dose of completely irrelevant, unnecessary, and misplaced xenophobia into its consideration. It is very easy to whip up hysteria about the notion of foreign investment. We saw from the member for Tauranga this afternoon how easy it is---and, indeed, how despicable it can become. The reality right through this debate that no one has seriously challenged is that we live in a country that has been built on foreign investment over the last years or so. Right from the time that European whalers started to come here, from the development of the meat trade, it has been the input of foreign investment that has helped this country to grow, to prosper, and to develop. The issue that we debate today is not about that, despite the attempts by some to whip it up into that; the issue is one about process, and about how we have an adequate and fair regime both for the determination of applications in the future and for ensuring that the rights of New Zealanders are taken adequate account of as those matters proceed. That is what this debate is about. I find it extraordinary that the member for West Coast should talk about being sad that the Bill has gone this far. The sadness I would have, and what I find extraordinary about this Bill, is that an argument that really comes down to---to use his words---severe reservations and suspicions, and not much else, has been sustained for as long as it has been, and so much unnecessary twaddle has been whipped up in support of what is a very tame opposition to the provisions of this Bill. That is where this Parliament lets people down. That is where this Parliament gets people feeling that it is out of touch with their reality. I want to talk about the position that United New Zealand adopted in respect of this Bill. We started from the position that foreign investment was a necessary part of our history and our process for economic development in New Zealand. We started from the proposition that we wanted to ensure we had rules that encouraged that investment but also safeguarded the interests of New Zealanders---rules that ensured we prospered from such development. We were not satisfied with the Bill as it came back from the select committee. We had six broad areas of objection. All six of those areas have been dealt with satisfactorily, from our point of view, in the Committee stage. Let me run quickly through them. The first was the obnoxious clause . It is the one thing that everyone in this House was united about. It was the provision that would have exempted this legislation from the provisions of the Official Information Act. The clause was removed by the Committee of the whole House. That was entirely appropriate. It was utterly wrong that the clause be there in the first place. We were also pleased that the Government adopted the proposal to tighten up the provisions of new clause A of the Bill---the criteria for consent---and to make those criteria mandatory rather than just advisory, as they were in the Bill that was reported back. But even at that point, with those two amendments only, United New Zealand was not satisfied that the Bill was sufficiently acceptable. We therefore prevailed upon the Government to insert four more amendments, all of which were adopted by the Committee of the whole House and all of which are now in the Bill. The amendments to the Bill achieved the objectives that I set out before as being what we desired. There is now an associated persons provision in the Bill to prevent collusion by individuals to overcome the land-size requirement in the Bill. We could have had a situation, before that amendment, whereby a group of individuals could have conspired to each buy . hectares of land as individuals; they could then have come together as a partnership after the event, and thereby thwarted the provisions of the Act. The associated persons provision, inserted as an amendment to clause A, overcomes that. An amendment has also been made to clause . In effect it brings in the concept of ``user pays'' in terms of the operation of the Overseas Investment Commission. The people making the applications to the Overseas Investment Commission, and not the taxpayer of New Zealand, will be the people who cover the compliance costs, the monitoring costs, and any other costs that might arise consequential upon those changes. We have also seen an amendment inserted in clause that now gives the High Court the power to order the disposal of land in cases where people thwart the conditions of the approval, as opposed to the previous provision where there was just the possibility of only a $, fine. Considering the monetary value of the land concerned, that was a pretty puny consideration. We now have a much stronger provision in respect of that. We also have an amendment made to the first schedule of the Bill that ensures the protection of areas of special conservation or historical interest. I was thinking of this as the member for West Coast was talking, because the situation he outlined from his constituent would in fact be covered by the amendment that we have achieved to the first schedule. At this stage I want to put on record the approach that we take to dealing with amendments, because it did arouse some controversy in the Committee stage---misplaced and unwarranted controversy, I might add, but it was controversy nonetheless. We have been absolutely clear on the stand that we will take. We will consider amendments proposed by other parties, but we are not prepared to consider them if they appear on tatty bits of paper or if they are bright ideas dreamed up at the time. If people want our support for amendments to legislation, then they should do what the Alliance did. We happened to rejected the proposals of the Alliance, but it at least had the good grace to circulate them to us in advance so that we had time to consider them. I say to the Labour Party and to New Zealand First that if they want our future support for amendments, give us the courtesy of advance notice. Let us have a chance to see whether we are prepared to support them and let us have a chance to give a proper response. We will not support amendments that are just wheeled up---often for the sake of form, often just for the sake of disrupting procedure---and are clearly to make a political point. Someone during the Committee stage---from memory, I think it was the member for Northern Maori---asked why they should do that when United New Zealand had been to the Government and had talked about what it wanted in the Bill. He asked why United New Zealand should not go and talk to all the other parties. I say that the message to those parties is that we went to the Government because we had things we wanted inserted into this legislation. If other parties had things they wanted inserted, then they should have tried to persuade the Government, and, if that was unsuccessful, given the numbers that we hold, they should have come and talked to us. It is not our responsibility to go running around after them to find out the nature of the amendments that they want. I put that on the record because it is an issue that did come up during the Committee stage and will, I suspect, arise in the future. I believe that the outcome of this Bill has been positive in terms of process, which was a concern that the Labour Party had. It has also been positive in terms of content. We now have a consolidated, clear, and unambiguous overseas investment regime. We also have clearer controls in terms of the conditions under which licences can be approved and the penalties that will apply for breaches of those conditions. Given the fact that most people in this House say that they favour foreign investment and that it is something New Zealand ought not to shy away from, I find it extraordinary that there are still a number of members who, given that admission, do not then want to say that this Bill is a great improvement on the two previous Acts, and on the Bill that was introduced into this House late last year, and that has been amended through the select committee process, and through the Committee of the whole House, and that is now about to be passed into law. I believe we now have a regime that is robust, that is solid, and that will serve this country well in the future.

I want to speak to page , volume II, of the estimates vote: Prime Minister and Cabinet, and I want to draw attention to output class D and particularly to the reference in relation to the provision of constitutional policy and procedural issues for the Governor-General, the Prime Minister, and Cabinet. In that context, I want to draw the Prime Minister's attention to the report of the Government Administration Committee, particularly in regard to preparation for an MMP Government that was considered by the committee when it examined the Prime Minister's officials as part of its estimates inquiry. The report notes that the committee spent some time working on the matter of the role of the department with a coalition Cabinet in an MMP Parliament. I know that some of that work is now replicated in the work of the State Services Commission report that was released last week. I want to ask the Prime Minister whether the work that his department is involved in this year will include any consideration of the size and structure of a post-MMP Government Cabinet in terms of the number of ministries and the changes in the machinery of Government that are necessary to achieve that, whether there is some consideration being given to a wider re-examination of the structures of Government departments, whether he is looking at the concept of inner and outer Cabinets, and all those sorts of things. I also want to know whether the advice he has been receiving is highlighting the difference between operating a formal coalition Government of one or two partners of a major party in Government and operating a minority Government, such as we have at the moment, which is supported by other parties on a day-to-day basis on particular issues. Are the rules that govern the way in which Cabinet operates being reviewed in the light of either of those two possibilities? That does raise another issue that has been the subject of some debate of late. I do not want to enter into that debate, but it relates to the rules governing the conduct of Ministers. Is the Prime Minister requesting advice of his department about how adequate current rules are in relation particularly to issues such as conflict of interest and general rules of behaviour and how relevant they will be in an MMP Government---particularly a Government that could well be a coalition of one or more parties? I also want to know about the relationship between Ministers who are in the majority party in the coalition and Ministers who are in the minority party, particularly in respect of their relationship with other Cabinet Ministers or with departmental heads. There has been some speculation about this, and I think that the State Services Commission report refers to it to some extent. Is the work that his department is doing this year including an examination of those options and some of the potential conflicts that lie within those areas? The next issue I want to refer to is the upkeep of viceregal residences. Given the current debate about republicanism, which the Prime Minister has some sort of a leading role in, I want to know whether there is any review under way of the cost of maintaining our viceregal residences, whether there is any review under way about the need to maintain an alternative in Auckland to the official residence in Wellington, and whether there is any work being done by his department about the cost-benefit, if one likes, of the current residences. The next issue I want to raise relates to the crime prevention unit, which was discussed in the select committee. I want to acknowledge the positive role that the crime prevention unit is playing, but it occurs to me that there is scope for this initiative to be expanded further and to include not just crime prevention in the big and grand sense, but also crime prevention in the local community sense. There is scope for much greater integration between the work of the crime prevention unit and the local community policing councils and groups that are being established. I would be grateful for some comment from the Prime Minister about what is intended in terms of the further development of that work during the year under review. There is a widespread wish in the community for a much closer involvement in affairs relating to the prevention of crime in those localities. I want to know whether it is intended that the work of the crime prevention unit will be expanded to become not just a unit that is operating at a national level, but which is also providing advice and input into local community activities---particularly into the work of local support groups such as Neighbourhood Support and others. I would be grateful for some answers to those questions.

I was right here actually, in this very Chamber, and I will be here for a while to come, I hope. I say to the Minister that harmonisation between Australia and New Zealand is important, as he is well aware, because of the tremendous synergy---I suppose that is the right term---that can occur between the two countries in terms of products being sold in each other's market, and the springboard that gives for further work overseas. That is what closer economic relations are all about. That is what a whole pile of agreements between the two countries have been about---harmonisation in every industry. Industries are aiming towards that. Today we see New Zealand companies---engineering companies in my electorate, for example---because of their work in gaining quality standards, in upgrading the way they do things, being able to compete in Australia with Australian companies on their home turf. That sort of thing is important because it provides ongoing jobs and ongoing opportunities for New Zealanders. This harmonisation issue is a very important one. I remember standing in the House in the other building years ago when we were doing exactly the same as we are doing now. I quote directly from Hansard: ``To deal with the issues, this Bill needs to be passed in the time-frame we now have---a helluva rush---in order to keep faith with the memorandum of understanding that has been signed by the New Zealand and Australian Governments. This memorandum is aimed at reciprocity between the countries with regard to ...''. In that case it was air travel, the single aviation market. We did exactly the same thing. A Bill was introduced at the last moment and was scrambled through the House, in order to try to get the Australian Government not to pull out of an agreement already signed by the New Zealand Government. I hope this Bill is a lot more successful than that one was. Air New Zealand and other New Zealand airline companies absolutely rue the day they ever heard of this Minister of Transport, and what happened with the single aviation market. What we have here is the single food market, and it is also in danger by the look of it, because at the last minute a Bill is being scrambled through the House. Just as the Opposition spokesperson on health, Lianne Dalziel, said earlier, Labour will help to get this Bill through the House in a quick time-frame. We will assist the Government to do that, because we recognise the importance of it and because the Associate Minister of Health, Katherine O'Regan, has consulted and has asked for our help. Unfortunately, the Minister of Transport did not do that until the very last minute. We had a briefing literally before the House sat. Thankfully, the Associate Minister of Health has worked very closely with the Opposition, and her practices in terms of this Bill have been very good. I would like to congratulate her on doing that. As a result she has the full co-operation of the Labour Opposition to get this Bill through the House. We realise the importance of it. The single aviation market was about lining up the two countries so that they could trade in each other's market. That proposition was quite different from what happened with the Maritime Transport Bill, which gave away everything. We can now have a win-win situation for the two countries on this issue. I think that is really important. The Bill will give legislative recognition to food safety programmes developed and implemented by food operators, by allowing the Director-General of Health to grant exemptions from the requirements of the Food Hygiene Regulations. That matter will result in some concern from consumers, I guess, about food standards. But as long as we can be assured of the quality---and quality is something that New Zealand is renowned for---then we will see benefits to both countries. We must ensure that those quality assurance mechanisms are in place and are understood by both countries. Certainly that has been the case in other industries that have already gone down this path. Therefore this harmonisation process will be very important. The Minister for Trade Negotiations spoke earlier about the trans-Tasman mutual recognition agreement. The Minister of Police spoke several times about various agreements, because I think he wanted to take his full minutes. I am not going to do that. What I will say, though, in reply to the Minister is that I hope we have the standards regime right. The reason I say that is that he mentioned tradespeople. I am one of the very few tradespeople ever to be in the House. I was originally an electrician. I tell the Minister that I hope the situation today is a good deal better, in terms of the standards of the two countries being the same, than it was when I was an electrician. To be really blunt, I came into contact with a few electricians from the other side of the Tasman whom we had to subtly re-educate in order to get them to do things the way we liked them done. I hope we can now be assured that we can keep up our standards of quality. Anyone who has travelled around the world will know that New Zealand makes the best ice-cream. The Italians claim to do it, but those of us born in New Zealand and used to New Zealand ice-cream know that we make the best ice-cream.

The member for Christchurch North was very active in promoting the single aviation market. I do not think anyone in the Opposition would argue with that. But what I am saying to the Minister is that if these negotiations should take place, according to the Minister, on an equivalent commercial value basis only when they are in the best interests of New Zealand, and no other legislation governs them, why has he not agreed to that amendment, which he previously said would be agreed to, or that he would consider, and accepted the principle of? Now he says he does not need it because some yellow, mellowing, aged, aviation policy document has, luckily for him, been found. I say that is not good enough.

For the benefit of the member, I will say that I understand that I was actually top in New Zealand, but we will leave that topic. I was one of those who at the age of had had enough of the secondary school system, and by half way through the sixth form I was ready to leave. I think I was an average student but by halfway through the sixth form my teachers realised it was unlikely I was about to go off to university in a year or years' time. A much different course was suitable for me. Accordingly I did an apprenticeship in the electrical trade. I am very proud of that. I enjoyed myself. I worked hard. It was a very good company. I say to the members opposite that most countries in Europe would consider that what has been done to the apprenticeship system in New Zealand is an absolute crime. We have an apprenticeship system that has been totally--I was going to use an impolite word there and I do not want to do that--emasculated by the Government. We have a system that to all intents and purposes has ceased to exist. Right now, today, in spite of the continuing comments from members opposite--and especially the Minister--that we have a marvellous upturn in apprenticeships, we have the lowest number of apprentices that has ever been recorded in New Zealand's history.

I thank the Minister. I am sure his speeches on local Bills will be equally rivetting. We have a fine community facility in New Plymouth in that stadium. It is a multipurpose stadium---the venue for everything from rock concerts and basketball to vintage car shows, etc. The whole gamut of community activities take place there. But the provision of the community stadium led to a problem. The problem it led to was the definition of the area that the stadium occupies, and, of course, the development and further redevelopment of the racecourse. What has occurred in the time since is an agreement to relinquish part of the racecourse amenities area to the community stadium. That agreement was, if one likes, offset by an agreement that the district council would resolve to amend the Act to allow an increase in the allowable racing days up to . The agreement was made to compensate for that land use by increasing the number of racing days. Partly, I am sure, this will cater not only for the fact that some of the other racecourses in the area are not used so much any more and may be closed in time but also for the fact that racing clubs around the country are finding things a little more pressured, I suspect, and that centralisation is occurring. I am sure my colleague Damien O'Connor will have more to say about that. However, what has happened since is that a deed of agreement---overseen by Mr John Eagles, a solicitor in New Plymouth---was signed in September of last year. It reflects the change in circumstances and clearly sets out the current status of areas on the reserve. So what we now have is the resulting legislation, in my name---a local Bill, intituled: ``An Act to provide for the use of the land described in Schedule of this Act, and to repeal the New Plymouth Recreation and Racecourse Reserve Act ''. The short title of the Act will be ``New Plymouth Recreation and Racecourse Reserve Act''. Basically, it validates the deed of September that was signed between the Taranaki Jockey Club represented by Mr Carey Hobbs, Mr Brian Mason, Mr Neill Wolfe, and her worship the Mayor, Clare Stewart, representing New Plymouth District Council, and Mr Kinsley Sampson, the Chief Executive of the District Council. These people all have a long association with this very fine facility. Although the Act is short, with just two pages and six clauses, the schedules are considerably longer. The reason is that these detail the agreement, the deed, and the previous documents relating to this reserve. Basically, the areas that have been changed by the deed will be the definitions of the variety of areas of the community facility, the number of racing days, and the various rights, responsibilities, and limitations that have changed as a result. So the lease and the amendment for the community stadium, controlled by the TSB Stadium Trust Board, deal with the occupancy of the stadium area as defined in the jockey club deed, and it spells out the rights, responsibilities, and limitations for the stadium to occupy that part of the reserve. The amendment clarifies issues that have resulted from the TSB Stadium lease. I might pay a tribute to the Taranaki Savings Bank Community Trust; also to the TSB Bank for its tremendous role in enhancing facilities in my area. Clause of the jockey club deed, which acknowledges that part of the land that has been historically developed as a part of Pukekura Park and excluded from the provisions of the deed, should also be noted. In closing, I would especially like to thank Mr Jellyman, who is the community services manager from the New Plymouth District Council who first brought this issue to my attention, advising me of the need for a Bill, and I would be very pleased to help the House. I give notice that I will move that this Bill be sent to the Internal Affairs and Local Government Committee for consideration.

I am interested in the Minister's closing comment because I went over and had a chat with him earlier and almost walked off with his notes on the Bill, quite by accident, and he would have been in real trouble because this Bill, as Stan Rodger was fond of saying, ``is a small technical amendment'', as we were told by the Minister. Well, as a result I have had a bit of a look into this Bill and it has the potential to be more than a small technical amendment, but I agree with the Minister that it is on technical issues. One clause I have looked at is clause , which is about alterations to ships and the need for surveyors, and so on. When one tries to find out what clause refers to, one eventually winds up with the Ship Registration Act of , which has numerous references from the Maritime Transport Act, and when one looks at the definition of ``surveyor of ships'', which is what clause of this Bill is all about, it states that a surveyor of ships means a surveyor of ships appointed or recognised as such under section D of the Shipping and Seamen Act . When one tries to find that Act in the lobby it does not exist, so there is some difficulty in tracing all these things. These are exactly the sorts of measures that were talked about by myself and my colleagues during the passage of the Maritime Transport Bill. There were many amendments, as I am sure the Deputy Speaker will be aware, and as the member for Birkenhead at the time he was well aware of many of those amendments. As a result we spent a lot of time in this House examining that legislation in some detail. What we see today on the Order Paper are five Bills, four of them maritime Bills, and each of them could really have been dealt with by the Maritime Transport Act when it was passed. However, the Government chose not to listen. Why this particular clause has become important is that as a result of the Maritime Transport Act a rules process was to have been put in place by the Maritime Safety Authority of New Zealand. That rules process was supposed to have taken out a number of the old and antiquated provisions and replaced them with rules or regulations put in place by the Maritime Safety Authority. I am not quite sure why that has not been done in the interim, but I understand that there has been some delay with some of those provisions. A number of technical difficulties have been experienced in the administration of the Ship Registration Act. In the Minister's prepared speech he referred to the registration of ships on Part B of the register, and the changes that will be allowed there. When I looked up this Ship Registration Act, Part B has quite some requirements, and we are amending some of those in this legislation. I wonder whether the reason that we are amending those is that we no longer actually have any large number at all of New Zealand - owned ships. In order to retain some as New Zealand flagged ships, I guess we have to make some changes to the legislation. I wonder whether in a few years time we might be amending the legislation further, to state that any ship that has any beneficial ownership by a New Zealander shall be deemed to be a New Zealand ship. One of the things that is not spoken of in this new amendment Bill is the difference between a New Zealand flagged ship and a New Zealand - owned ship. That does not appear to be one of the items that is covered. I thought this would have been an excellent opportunity to address that issue and to look at what has actually happened around the New Zealand coast in terms of the number of ships that we could call New Zealand - owned ships operating for New Zealand companies that are left. I will bet that the Minister will rightly jump up and down and say that his legislation has been a wonderful success. Sadly, it is not ``rightly'', because it has not been a wonderful success. The Maritime Transport Act did not, as the Minister said it would many times in the House, provide more jobs, more manufacturing opportunities, more markets for New Zealand, cheaper shipping from the South Island to the North Island, or any of the other things that it was designed to provide. In fact, one of the leading proponents of the change, from Federated Farmers, a member of the board of Southport at Bluff, Mr Stewart Collie, was very vocal. He went around the country---as I did---convincing Federated Farmers and others that they should thoroughly back the maritime transport legislation of the day; that that was absolutely essential to reduce the shipping costs between the South Island and the North Island, to increase the opportunities for New Zealand primary producers and exporters, and to increase the jobs available to New Zealanders. What has happened? We see fewer services, fewer New Zealand ships, and fewer ships of any sort calling at Gisborne, Bluff, Timaru, Nelson, Picton, or New Plymouth. Manufacturers in those areas are actually losing markets as a result---not to mention the effect on New Zealand shipping companies. I know of one company that has cancelled one ship and diverted two others, while another company has amalgamated with it. New Zealand's largest company, Union Maritime Services Ltd, is now part of the Union-ANZDEL Line---a French and New Zealand combination, which is a difficult combination at best, I would have thought. But the Minister tells us that this has been a wonderful success.

I commend the speech made by my colleague Nanaia Mahuta a few minutes ago. I think she made an excellent speech outlining the issues very carefully. Everyone associated with this issue, right from the beginning of it some years ago, has stated he or she does not want one injustice resolved at the cost of setting up another injustice. Today we are addressing one injustice to a degree---that of the lessee farmers---but the lessors, the Maori landowners, are left out. Some of the lessees live in my electorate. Every lessee whom I have spoken to over the last years---it may well have been longer than that---was absolutely determined that there should be fair compensation from the Crown to the Maori landowners. Initially they felt that there was no reason for them to be involved, that it was a straight matter between the Crown and the Maori landowners who had had their right of access to the land removed in legislation passed by this House years before. The Maori Reserved Land Amendment Act, which was passed at the last minute just before Christmas, developed as a result of the previous National Government's effort initially to solve the ownership issue at no cost to the Crown. That was the initial aim. The aim was to have some sort of agreement between the Maori landowners---the lessors---and the lessee farmers to commercialise, modernise, or whatever, the lease arrangements at no cost to the Crown. A huge effort was made to sell that idea, and to try to arrive at an agreement between the lessees and the lessors. Of course, it was going nowhere and was creating real tensions, especially in Taranaki. As a result, we saw the compensation model developed---compensation to the lessees for increased rentals payable to the Maori lessors. This Bill is an attempt to right one of the wrongs put in place by the Act passed just before Christmas that Labour objected to and tried to amend, to solve. When one looks at what finally occurred in that legislation, and the reason for that last-minute change to the legislation just before Christmas, one sees it was all about the pressure being placed on the Government in that last sitting week of Parliament. We had an overnight, middle-of-the-night, sudden change to try to adopt the principle applied by Mark Peck, to try to get it into the Act. Unfortunately, the Government changed the dates, and that is what this Bill is about. This Bill is a further amendment to an amendment Act. This Bill has come about because of the pressure that has gone on the National Party in a lot of ways. There was a particularly rowdy National Party south Taranaki branch annual general meeting about a fortnight ago. The previous Prime Minister, Mr Bolger, was present, and got a very hard time from lessee farmers who said this issue was unfair and explained why very carefully---in very blunt terms, I am sure. Also, a by-election is coming up, and National can see its support draining. It can see ACT stomping up and down the Taranaki area and generating heat on this issue. We have a very simple situation. We have another knee-jerk reaction in the middle of the night, and it has not been done very well. It cures one injustice, but does not cure the injustice for the Maori landowners. It does not cure their longstanding injustice, which all the lessee farmers acknowledge and are very keen to have resolved in order to take the heat right out of this issue. I repeat that it is a pity that the select committee could not spend some time on this Bill. It is a pity that the Government was not prepared to accept some of the amendments to the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Act that were put up in the Committee stage. They would have resulted in a permanent solution to the problem, a permanent solution to the ownership rights issue---probably at less cost, and certainly with less of the public's time being taken up by debates in Parliament on the issue. They would not have resulted in any ongoing injustice. I refer to a solution that would have resulted in payments by the Crown as the farms came up for sale during the period. I hope the Peck amendment to clause will be accepted by the Committee. I imagine it will have support.
