That contribution is not worthy of response. It is so insulting, after the contribution that was made from across all political parties in a very constructive way during the select committee process. We had major but different concerns in the committee, but at least we gave each other the respect of listening to the arguments and considering them. That member was on another planet in my view, and I hope that she stays there and does not beam back into this Parliament too often. That sort of contribution is very undermining of the constructive process that can go on within this House. There are not many people with whom I disagree more on policy than Rodney Hide, but during the select committee process I always listen to the contribution he makes, consider it, then disagree with it. I always listen to it because I think that if people have been elected to this Parliament by the public of New Zealand, then we should respect the public's view---misguided though it was at the time to elect those people to Parliament---and give their contribution the consideration that it deserves. The contribution that Mrs Bloxham made was minimal. It does not require much consideration because it was so shallow and so minimal, but it is an unfortunate way of treating what is a very important issue. Labour opposes the passage of this legislation with reluctance, only because during the select committee process the amendments that were made did not address our fundamental concerns that we raised not only at the select committee but also during the second reading of this Bill in April. That is some time ago. The concerns that we had at that time are on the record of this House. They were raised not only by Labour members but consistently by people making submissions to the select committee. It was the Government's view that the legislation should proceed basically unamended. The only changes that have been made are improvements of a technical nature, and even some of those are not sufficient. But those are not the issues we are talking about. We are talking on behalf of low and middle-income earners who will be severely disadvantaged by the Government not considering other options to achieve what it describes as the purpose of the Bill. I have to express some concern at the comments made by the chairman of the committee that no other options were put forward. That is not the case. We received submissions. That is quite an astonishing number really, because the title of the Bill would not necessarily attract one to make a submission. It is called the Taxation (Tax Credits, Trading Stock, and Other Remedial Matters) Bill. A wide range of submissions were received from people who know the savings area well, who understand the importance of the Government encouraging savings, and who understand the effect that this legislation would have on that intent. We heard consistently from those submitters that this legislation had major flaws in the treatment particularly of low and middle-income earners. I want to take a punt at why I think that message was not taken on board and responded to in a positive way by members of the Government. It is because they do not understand the insecurity and the inability for future planning that many low and middle income earners now have. The Government talks---and I noticed the Minister of Finance doing it when addressing the Bill earlier today---as though people can all have a -year plan of their life that will not change, and have control over their income and their expenditure. Tragically, that is not the case. Many people are not able to plan in that way because they do not have control over, for example, the very basic issue related to income, and that is employment. Many people are now in casual employment. They do not even have the security from one week to the next, let alone from year to year, to know what their income will be. What is the advantage to those people, and what is the disincentive of this regime that we are currently making a decision on? The disadvantage is that people cannot plan, and if people cannot plan they cannot make a fully informed decision about what is better---whether to opt in or to opt out. When one is speaking of a difference of c for every dollar that is quite significant. So for those people this is a major concern. A lot of people do not have complete control over their expenditure. People living in rental accommodation are very vulnerable to the whims of the market because rental increases are common and can take a significant part of their disposable income. If one has children attending tertiary institutions---universities or polytechs---that makes quite a difference to one's ability to plan for the future. It even makes a lot of difference to one's ability to plan what might be in the refrigerator next week. But more important, control of income and expenditure is not there in the way that is needed for this legislation to be delivered. The idea of the Government encouraging people to save is to be applauded, and of course that principle is shared across this Parliament. But this regime does not deliver it. Other options were considered at the select committee---options that were put forward by people who know this area well. They came from people who work in the area, and who know far more about the subject, I would venture to say, than any individual member of the select committee. It frustrates me that those people take the time and trouble to read the Bill, to read the book put out by the Minister, to talk to officials, to put forward a submission, to come to Wellington to have that submission heard, and then to have it ignored. Why are Government members so scared of listening to people who know what they are talking about, and changing their minds? Why is the Government still so insistent? Being wrong in the beginning is not a bad thing if it can be proved during the process of deliberation that we can learn from people who know better. That seems to me to be one of the biggest lessons from MMP that the National - New Zealand First - United - sometimes Alamein Kopu coalition has missed out on. That is a lesson that needs to be learnt from this Parliament. No member of the public minds politicians saying: ``We were wrong but we have learnt.'' It would be a huge advantage to the credibility and the accountability of this process if that was taken on board by the Government. I know that some members of Government would like to do that. That is why it further frustrates me that they are all bound by silly whipping on select committees when, obviously, the facts are against what they are doing. Labour has put in an amendment to the phase-in period of the Bill, and I hope that that will be considered in a more favourable way. However, I come back to where I started. It is with reluctance that Labour is opposing the progress of the Bill, because the principle of encouraging saving is one that we share; so is the principle of having cross-party agreement on issues on which the fundamentals are agreed. But the fundamentals in this Bill are not agreed on. The technical amendments that have been made are an improvement, but I support the concerns and the views put forward by my colleague Mark Peck that this will not be the last time we see this sort of Bill, and that it will require further amendments. I conclude by reading out some advice the select committee was given, which shows just how poor it is when this sort of advice is not listened to: ``The absence of structural amendment is disappointing. The committee has been advised, on the authority of those well qualified to form a judgment on the matter, that the current proposal will have a very limited uptake in the context of existing funds and probably a nil uptake in the context of employer-subsidised funds, and will lead to prejudicial consequences to significant numbers of electing members in terms of social assistance programmes external to the Income Tax Act, and is likely to occasion prejudice to electing members in terms of tax rates applicable to aggregate income for internal income tax purposes.'' For low and middle income earners, employer superannuation schemes are, in the main, the only opportunities that those people have to get into superannuation schemes. Yet here the best advice the committee received was that this would disadvantage those people. For the industry itself, the compliance costs and the disincentive for people to move into them will have a serious negative effect. I urge the Government to give those fundamental concerns further consideration.

I have a couple of questions that I would like the Minister of Energy to address in relation to Part , and they deal specifically with clause , ``Directions by shareholding Ministers'', and, more specifically, subclause (). I really want to know where the role of Government starts and ends. For what other breach of the law would the Minister then change the law to make sure that only some people did not breach it? What is the Minister trying to achieve? I will tell the Minister what I think it means, and I would like him to answer the questions I put and to clarify whether my view is correct. Clause states that the shareholding Ministers will give directions to ECNZ, but subsection () states: ``No director of ECNZ is in breach of, or liable to any person under, the State-Owned Enterprises Act ,''---replacing the words ``principal Act''---``the Companies Act , or any other Act or rule of law by reason of any act or omission reasonably believed by the director to be necessary or desirable---''. So if a Minister directs ECNZ to do something that breaches the Companies Act, the directors of ECNZ are not troubled by that, because this provision removes them from coverage by the Companies Act. Why do that? Why would Parliament say it is OK for the directors of ECNZ to breach the Companies Act? In fact, with what the Minister is requiring them to do they will have to breach the Companies Act. Why do we not do this properly? Why do we not do any part of this Bill properly? Why did the Minister of Energy not first propose an amendment to the Companies Act? If he decided that part of it was shonky, or that part of it was inconsistent with his drive, then he should have proposed changing it. We could have that debate out in the open. I am surprised that the Minister shows some nervousness about debate, because it has always been my view that if the Government is clear about where it is headed, if the Government is prepared to be open and honest about it, then it can go through a proper process of debate. The Government does not have to ram things through a select committee. National does not have to con the members of its coalition partner with weasel words. It can be up-front and honest about it. I do not think clause () in particular is up-front and honest, to be frank. I think it is a very strange way of requiring directors to do something that breaches another law. It breaches that law because it is bad practice, in the Government's view. Why are people appointed by the Crown to be directors of organisations such as ECNZ? It is because they are considered to be good directors. Now the Minister is saying that in this instance we will require them to have bad business practice, but we will exempt them from the Companies Act. This is really shonky. This is a crazy way of saying that we want efficiency, that we want to lower prices, and that we want to deliver a better service to people. This part should talk about security of supply, but it is not there. Nowhere at all in this part is there any mention of security of supply, which has been of such concern to people in our country in other times. Nor does it talk about any environmental considerations, when we have situations such as a drought that are contrary to increasing supply. Perhaps the Minister has watched the news over the last couple of days, has realised it has been raining outside in the real world, and has said: ``The drought is over. There's no problem.'' Let us try to get beyond the view of the o'clock news and ask how, with New Zealand's weather conditions of extreme cold and heat---which obviously have adverse and contrary reactions as far as demand and supply go---we can guarantee supply and can ensure that environmental considerations are taken into account.

I appreciate the Minister's comments. Like my colleague Mark Peck, I also feel that despite the fact that there were highly commendable submissions on the Bill, and that select committee members worked very progressively together in a most constructive way, I do have some concerns. Those concerns are the same as those raised by Mark Peck---that is, that these issues have not been completed with this Bill. I feel that there are a number of outstanding issues that we will be revisiting in the future. I guess that that is the way in which we might always have to operate in Parliament, but I have to say that it is less likely to be the case when the select committee looks at the issues seriously and considers them along with the very helpful submissions and the extremely high level of advice we received both from officials and from the select committee's tax adviser, Lindsay McKay. That combination certainly made the process less likely to incur relitigation of issues in the future by this Parliament. But there was one issue I would really appreciate the Minister commenting on. The select committee rightly rejected the proposal in the submission from Mr John Pallot, who describes himself as an innovations consultant from Christchurch. The Minister might want to reflect on the underlying points that he made, even though it was not appropriate for the select committee to take on board the issues he raised. I think that the philosophy he was asking us to consider is worthy of some further discussion during the process of this Bill. I noticed yesterday that some of the contributors in this debate said that perhaps it was not appropriate that an inventor was making a submission on this Bill, but given the title---the Taxation (Remedial Provisions) Bill---and the fact that the submissioner did put to the select committee that this was an area where tax law was lacking, I think it is entirely appropriate that Mr Pallot made his submission. I believe that we need to take up the points he made further in this deliberation and in other debates. The basis of his submission is that inventors in New Zealand do not have a fair go compared with the way they would be treated if they lived in other countries. That is a pretty basic point. In New Zealand we are after innovation and supporting new enterprise. We are looking at the future of our country being at the cutting edge of such developments internationally. The point made by Mr Pallot is that basically the Government gives no help at all to inventors such as himself, and he is not the only one. I do not believe that the suggestions he made for assistance are at all appropriate. I certainly support the fact that we rejected his specific proposal. I know that the Minister has in the past expressed an interest in employment issues, and in developing enterprise in New Zealand. That is a different Minister of Police from the one members saw a few months ago talking in tough terms about what he intend to do. It is a different Minister of Police from the one who was chastising his Cabinet colleagues and saying that they were wobbly at the knees. Today, he has given us his ideas about the law and order problem. He began by saying that it is the fault of the post-war baby boom. Most of the people born in that boom are in their late thirties or early forties. Hardly any of those people are appearing before the courts, let alone appearing for violent crimes and sexual offences. The second explanation the Minister offered to the House for sky-rocketing violence under the present Government was that women had to ask themselves why men did not hold them in more respect. That is an assertion that the Opposition rejects totally and without qualification. I hope that every other Government member will take the opportunity of similarly rejecting that assertion as an argument for the increase in violence and sexual attacks in our community. I remind the House about the Government's record on violent crime. This is the Government that voted against Opposition measures to increase the penalty for rape from years to years, to send a clear signal to the judiciary that the level of penalty imposed for rape is inadequate. The Government voted against that proposal. The Government voted against a similar proposal, to increase the penalty for murder so that people could not be paroled so early after being sentenced to life imprisonment. The Government trampled over the constitutional judicial process and released to liberty two French agents who came to this country and committed the violent act of manslaughter by killing an innocent citizen. Those agents were brought before the court and sentenced to years' imprisonment by the Chief Justice. However, those offenders were let loose by the Government. What example is it to New Zealand's lawbreakers when the Government is prepared to sell out on the principle of upholding the sanctity of the law? What kind of example is that to the Mongrel Mob or the Black Power gang, when the Chief Justice had sentenced those people to years' imprisonment, and the Government let them go because of a little diplomatic pressure from the French? That is a disgrace, and nothing that the Government says on the issue of law and order will be taken seriously again. The Government has removed the ministerial responsibility for the release of prisoners sentenced to life imprisonment or preventive detention. Once upon a time the Minister of Justice had to acknowledge ministerial responsibility for the release of those prisoners, but he no longer has to do that. The Government voted out the legislation introduced by the Opposition to control gangs. However, it spent $ million of taxpayers' money on the ``rub out the crim'' advertisement. Why was that money not given to the police, which is the service that really needs it? Do members know that representatives from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research went to the Police Department and sought permission to employ four more analysts to carry out forensic work to bring murderers and rapists to justice? That request has yet to be approved. It has been sitting for months on the desk of the Minister of Police or at police headquarters. The DSIR does not have the analysts it needs to bring offenders to justice. Close scrutiny should be brought to bear on the allegation that the exhibits taken in the Teresa Cormack case were unable to be analysed properly because analysts were not available to do the work. The Minister should check out that allegation. If child murderers are loose in the community because the Government does not give appropriate resources to the DSIR it is the Government that must bear the ultimate responsibility. The Minister of Justice has said that one of the greatest contributors to violent and sexual attacks is racism. Who is responsible for racism in New Zealand? The signs already exist that in the matter of race relations is likely to be a major election issue. The Government is responsible for that, because of its half-hearted, bungling attempts to handle race relations. Innocent people in Te Puke have been killed by louts who drive cars without lights on the wrong side of the road, and an -year-old widow was brutally raped. Nobody could help but be moved by the television programme on the violence that that town suffers from. However, the policeman who tried to speak out about that matter was the subject of an investigation for making racial comments. Have we not gone too far when that is the way the scales are tipped, and those who are trying to restore law and order to the community find themselves under the spotlight, while gang members create mayhem? A gang member was sentenced to months' imprisonment for killing an innocent woman in Te Puke. A family has been left without a parent, and months' imprisonment was the penalty imposed by the court. It is time that Parliament said that that approach is inadequate. It is time to get tough. We need a Government that acknowledges that there is a real problem. Opposition members do not want any more Neville Chamberlain tactics from the Minister of Justice. He must acknowledge that it is a serious problem. We do not want any more Mr Micawber from the Minister of Police---he is sitting back and waiting for something to turn up. Innocent New Zealanders are being raped and killed while Government members sit on the sideline and do nothing. There are several respects in which the Government should act. The debate is about an increase in violent crime of . percent in the past year and an increase in sexual attacks of . percent in the past year. They are the highest statistics in recorded history in New Zealand, and this is happening under a Labour Government. Let us face up to the fact that we have an enormous problem and that this Parliament should do something about it. First, there are the police, who need the manpower and resources to bring those people to justice. The police have been asking for those resources, but they have been denied. The greatest deterrent to crime is the fear of being caught. However, when the police service is so short staffed that it cannot investigate burglaries and other offences but can concentrate on only the really serious offences, there is trouble, because eventually those minor offenders move on to committing more serious crimes, and the statistics grow. There is the matter of penalties. Government members should stop voting against the Opposition's measures. Let us send a clear message to the judiciary that the penalties are too light. The prison system must work as a deterrent. Let us overhaul the prison system. Let us not allow the Mongrel Mob and the Black Power gang to run wings at Paremoremo Prison; let us say that that position is not to be tolerated. Prisons are a deterrent and offenders go there to be punished. There is the matter of parental responsibility. Let us get back some responsibility for parents. We should not have a social welfare system that pays benefits to street kids wandering the streets, or to parents whose kids are in video parlours all day long. We should make parents responsible for their actions. There is the matter of unemployment. Why should we pay the dole to young people to do nothing? They get into trouble because they have time on their hands to wander the streets. Let us give them work; let us get them working, and offending will be reduced. Let us take those young people who are at risk and put them in work schemes. Now I refer to the education system. How can there be hope for young people when they leave school unable to read or write? At the first argument they get into, they do not have verbal skills so they pick up a lump of four by two and hit the other person. That is a direct reflection of the fact that the education system has failed them. Under our health system there are children who cannot hear because they have glue-ear, or cannot see the blackboard because they do not have glasses, so they are put at the back of the class and left to rot in our education system, and leave school unable to read or write.

I listened with interest to my colleague the member for Fendalton, who clearly outlined the reasons that the Opposition has the considerable reservations about the legislation that it expressed during the Committee stage. I shall address myself particularly to the new dissident Government members, who are obviously trying to hold to the view that New Zealand should have a market economy. I hope that some of them will take the opportunity to participate in the debate. They will realise, as the Opposition demonstrated in the Committee stage, that the legislation is really a knee-jerk reaction to years of bad news for the Government in relation to the economy, and, in particular, to a year of bad news in relation to sharemarket activity. The Government has recognised that the New Zealand sharemarket has performed worse than any other sharemarket since the collapse in October . The Barclays index is less than half of what it was a year ago---it is hovering around , but it was double that figure in October . The volume turnover on the Stock Exchange is one-third of the turnover a year ago because there is absolutely no confidence on the part of investors. As the Opposition said in the Committee stage, there are three reasons for that lack of confidence. First, the December economic announcement has still not been finalised, and that has left an enormous amount of uncertainty---particularly amongst institutional investors, who have had no rules to guide them since December last year. Secondly, in the past year---ever since the sharemarket crash---the Government has failed to spell out clearly its economic policy. Thirdly, investors have no confidence in fair and honest dealings on the Stock Exchange---a matter that the Government has tried, belatedly, to pick up with the Bills before the House. The Government has finally realised that the reason New Zealanders are not investing money in the market-place to provide capital for businesses to expand and to create jobs for New Zealanders is that they have no confidence. What has the Government done? It has wheeled in the measures before the House, and has said that it will be against the law to sell shares when people have inside knowledge. When one examines the detail in the Bills it is easy to say that inside knowledge is against the law, but who will take a case to court? Will it be the poor person who has been ripped off? I ask the Government how many New Zealanders, having lost their life-savings because they have been ripped off by an insider trader, will obtain the wherewithal to tread across the shagpile carpet of those corporate law firms, retain them at thousands of dollars a day, and go to court to try to obtain some of that money back? No one in his or her right mind would do that. First, those people would have been cleaned out, and would not have the funds to go to court. Even if they were not cleaned out it is a matter of once bitten, twice shy. When people have lost the $, or $, they have saved up---their nest-egg that they have saved up for retirement---will they risk what little else they have left to pay some high-paid lawyer to try to claim back some money? Not in a million years will they do that! The Government knows that it has failed. The Government knows that it has established a kind of Claytons measure that it hopes investors will feel warm and comfortable with and will make them rush back to the sharemarket. The investors have known about the legislation for a month, and I ask my colleagues whether the market has risen in anticipation. The market has fallen because the investors know that the legislation will not do anything. They are not as dumb as that. They know that there are no rules in the market-place, that it is the survival of the fittest, and that there is nothing there to protect them. The sharemarket has been a haven for rip-off merchants. They have seen the flag waved pathetically around the countryside by the Minister of Justice, who has been saying: ``I'm going to save you.'' What has the response been? Nobody can see those merchants for dust and small stones. They are running away from the market faster than ever, and with good cause, because the Bills will not save anybody. Until we have criminal laws that wheel some directors into court, put them into the criminal dock, and deliver them stern sentences, there will be no honesty in the market-place. I have said to the Minister of Justice time and time again that he is hitting the wrong targets. To get confidence back into the market-place we need to catch the directors who have ripped off shareholders by selling assets that they own at a vastly inflated price to their own companies, or by grabbing hold of companies and stripping the assets to the detriment of the shareholders. Either those directors sell their own assets to a company, at three or four times the amount the assets are worth, or they obtain the company's assets cheaply themselves and sell them at a vastly inflated value. Either way, they double, treble, or quadruple their fortunes without putting anything at risk. Such transactions have gone on month after month and year after year, and still those directors have not been taken to court and held to account. Some of them should be in prison, but the Government and the Department of Justice have not had the political will to move. The second move the Government should have made, but has failed to make in the legislation, relates to the point that for the past years people could say what they wanted to about their companies. They could stand up and say, ``Our company is brilliant. Here are the annual reports with auditor's queries and conditions all over them, but forget about those. Here are our revaluations. We're worth billions.'' In actual fact, the company was worth nothing. The Government has sat on the sideline while New Zealand company directors have presented their companies as being worth billions of dollars when, in fact, they have been worthless. The tragedy is that innocent New Zealanders have taken along their life-savings to the sharemarket and have lost the lot. Those innocent members of the public are pointing their fingers at the Government, which has failed to protect them. That lack of protection is the reason for the lack of confidence in the sharemarket, and the legislation will do nothing to help the position. During the Committee stage it was pointed out that the Bills will do worse than nothing. In fact, they will act in the opposite manner to that which is intended. Instead of having a fair market we now have the capacity for the legislation to be used and abused by every player in the sharemarket. If members want an example of that potential use they have only to turn to clause of the Bill as introduced, which states that a substantial security holder---a person with more than percent of the shares of a company---will be liable under the Bill if, having knowledge of a deal, he or she makes a profit at the expense of somebody else. For example, if my company is about to be taken over, and I have a larger shareholder than I feared, what do I do? I go straight to that large shareholder and give him or her some price-sensitive information so that the shares cannot be sold and are locked in; the shareholder then cannot trade those shares, because he or she will be liable if they are sold. It is a heaven-sent opportunity for a target company in a take-over to use the legislation to its own advantage. When in the select committee I questioned the reason that the provision applies only to public companies, I was fobbed off on the basis that private companies are not really in much of a position to rip off shareholders. When I asked about that, and when I did some research, I found that most of the major shareholders in New Zealand companies are not other public companies but are institutional investors who are not publicly listed on the Stock Exchange. The biggest company in New Zealand is the AMP Society. The legislation does not apply even to that company, and that makes the measures worthless. That company does not have to worry. Anybody working for the AMP Society can use the insider knowledge gained about another public issuer without any risk, because under clause of the original Bill that person is not a public issuer. We have been told that the legislation will be tidied up next year. Why was the legislation not tidied up and introduced in a proper state in the first place? The reason is that the Minister of Justice was in a political jam on the corporate fraud issue. He had had his reputation shattered; he was a broken man; and he was trying to restore that reputation by being seen to do something in relation to dishonest practices in the sharemarket. Therefore he whipped in some legislation as fast as his little legs would carry him, and he now finds that the legislation does not do the job that it is supposed to do. The Law Commission is investigating corporate law reform, but the Government has not waited for the commission, because it would not be fast enough. The commission would not restore the Minister's reputation in time, so legislation that is doomed to failure has been wheeled in.

I want at the outset to join those other members of the House who have expressed their sympathy and their condolences to the families of those who lost their lives in the Cave Creek tragedy. I think it is appropriate that the House debates this commission of inquiry report at the earliest opportunity, so that the country, and, more particularly, the survivors and families of those who lost their lives, are aware of the importance in which the Government and the Parliament hold this matter, and that, indeed, all steps are being taken to ensure that such a tragedy can never happen again. The families and the survivors need and deserve to know that the Government is moving with all possible speed to ensure that this tragedy can never be repeated. It is a tragedy that has had an enormous effect on our country, and I am sure many people looked for a report that clearly outlined where the responsibility lay for the tragedy, and that named individuals who were culpable. It was a matter of surprise and of concern to many, I am sure, when they realised the report did not do that, and, indeed, did not hold any individual responsible. That is the controversial element of the report, but it is a report that the Government accepts. The Government established the commission of inquiry to ascertain exactly what happened and what was behind this tragic accident, to establish those causes, and to make recommendations to ensure it could never happen again. Judge Noble has provided a thoroughly independent assessment, having listened to all the evidence. He has searched hard to find explanations as to why this tragedy occurred. The Government, following the release of that report, has immediately set up a process to examine and respond to the judge's recommendations and observations. Many of those recommendations can be actioned almost immediately; some will take a little longer. I hope it is of some comfort to note that even in the report itself the judge states that the Department of Conservation has moved, after the accident and prior to the release of his report, to remedy a number of the shortcomings that the judge found in the activities of that department. So the two main points of the report are, first, no individual was responsible---and the judge could easily have named an individual, including the Minister or the chief executive---and, second, despite the failures of the Department of Conservation that are identified in the report, the judge has acknowledged the work the department has undertaken to remedy the faults that have been ascertained, and has not suggested that any other department or agency should step in and take over its administration, at least in the meantime until we can all be satisfied that every action has been taken to remedy the faults outlined. To me, the report endeavoured to look forward rather than to look back and cast blame. The report outlined remedial action that should be taken. That is acknowledged, and the department has moved in some areas. The report also made some suggestions with regard to changes to legislation. That will be a matter for the House, but those recommendations particularly related to whether the Crown, by way of a Government agency, should be able to be prosecuted under the Building Act and the Health and Safety in Employment Act. Those matters raise certain constitutional issues about Government departments being prosecuted within the courts. Already there is the ability to get a declaration, as I understand it, under the Health and Safety in Employment Act if a department should act unlawfully. However, we are conscious of the consideration the judge has given to this matter. I will certainly be discussing it further with the Solicitor-General, the Crown Law Office, and the Ministry of Justice, but ultimately it will be this House that determines whether indeed the law should be changed in that respect. The judge also made some observations with regard to the State sector reforms, particularly on page of the report. They were not recommendations. They are perhaps best described as observations. He expressed concern about the accountability that now flows in the public sector following the imposition of State sector reforms, particular the State Sector Act and the Public Finance Act. That is another matter that the Government takes extremely seriously. It is not clear from the report what particular amendments or suggestions the judge has in that regard, but we will examine thoroughly the evidence that was presented to that royal commission, and where there is a need to strengthen accountability, where shortcomings are shown in the evidence that was put before the tribunal, the Government will act. Indeed, the State Services Commissioner has already been charged with that responsibility, and has been asked to report back to the Government as quickly as possible. As the House is aware, the department itself has carried out urgent and comprehensive reviews of management systems since the accident. Indeed, since the publication of the report the State Services Commissioner, under section of the State Sector Act, is to carry out a full review of the operations of the Department of Conservation. The commissioner acts independently of politicians in that regard, under the terms of the State sector legislation. I note that he has decided to seek the assistance of what can only be considered to be an experienced and capable group of people. Mr Michael Morris is the former senior partner, as I understand it, of KPMG Peat Marwick, and the present chairman of the Land Transport Safety Authority. The two other people who will assist are Michael Collins, a former Director-General of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, who is well experienced in public services and in matters relating to conservation and the environment; and Joan Fleming, a former assistant secretary of the Department of Labour and deputy general manager of the Iwi Transition Agency. That team is required to advise the State Services Commissioner of what they see as shortcomings within the Department of Conservation, and to recommend steps that can be taken to overcome them. The terms of reference have been made public. They are there for all to see, and that is as it should be. It is the job of the Government, having accepted responsibility for this tragedy---because it is a matter of the actions of a Government agency, and the Government must accept that, and must be responsible for the actions of a Government agency---to move as quickly as possible to ensure that that review is undertaken with all possible speed, and to ensure that the public, particularly the families and the survivors, understand and appreciate the steps that are taken in terms of reviewing the Department of Conservation so that this accident can never happen again.

There is nothing wrong with that, but I want to say that I do not like this sort of sanctimonious claptrap. The member is trying to get every political point he can out of it. I ask that honourable member opposite how he would have felt if it had been his mother or his brother whose personal medical information had been bandied about through the news media. How would he have felt if it had been a member of his own family whose medical records and whose state of mental instability became public knowledge to million New Zealanders? I think that most members of the House would agree with me that there are sound reasons for patient confidentiality, and I am sure that Neil Pugmire himself does also. That is why he certainly did not expect the name of a patient to become the public property that it did. I now turn to the legislation that is before the House. I believe there is certainly a role for an agency of State to be available for those who wish to bring to the attention of an officer of State that which they consider to be corruption, or serious misdemeanours, or matters that are of considerable risk to public life or property. There should be some neutral place to which such a person may go. I may say with regard to this legislation---and I will certainly vote for it to be considered by a select committee---first, I can see a real need for it in terms of the operations of Government, including State-owned enterprises, Crown health enterprises, and Crown research institutes---the broader public service---but I think we should be reluctant as a Parliament to set up new rules, requirements, and mechanisms for the private sector without any consultation or discussion at all. I am sure the honourable member for Roskill will confirm that---certainly to the best of my knowledge---there has been no discussion or consultation at all with the private sector, which it is intended to make subject to this jurisdiction. I can see that here, perhaps, is a case in which we should start with the public sector, see how effective the legislation is---as we have done in some other matters such as equal opportunities and other matters---then move it into the private sector. I have been attracted, from the time this discussion commenced, to the idea of utilising both the Chief Ombudsman in the Office of the Ombudsmen, and the State Services Commission. They are bodies that already exist. They are well proven, and they have excellent track records. I am sure that all members of the House would agree with that. It is my view that rather than set up another quango---a whole stand-alone, separate organisation to which people may go to bring information of importance with regard to the issues of crime, corruption, neglect, public safety, or the like---or State agency, as is envisaged in this document, we should build on what we have. In that regard, the State Services Commission and the Chief Ombudsman provide the very facilities that the public already has confidence in, and that can be built on to provide the very mechanisms that the honourable member is seeking. I would not have been distracted in the way that I was at the beginning of my speech if it was not for the manner in which the honourable member introduced the legislation. It is an important subject, and to have some form of mechanism to which such complaints or information could be taken would certainly be for the overall good of New Zealand and all New Zealanders. Any discussion on this issue requires a careful assessment of a number of issues that, no doubt, the select committee will wish to address. These issues in particular include the activities that are to be covered by the legislation, what organisations are to be involved, who should receive the disclosures that are made, and what protections should be provided for the person who is bringing this to the attention of the authorities. The honourable member, in his introduction speech, mentioned the Ohakea air force base. If we were drawing a line between the public and private sectors, the test would not be whether the person worked for the public sector or the private sector---and I talk about the enlarged public sector, including State-owned enterprises, Crown health enterprises, Crown research institutes, and the like---but where the culpable behaviour was taking place. For example, if it was in the armed services then one would expect the facilities to be made available to the person who wished to bring that to the attention of the authorities. So the distinction, as I see it, is not between whether one works for the public sector or the private sector but where the harm is being done---and the State has an overriding responsibility to deal with the issues for which it is directly responsible. I and, I am sure, my Government colleagues will vote for this legislation to go to a select committee. The misgivings I have expressed are simply whether we should we impose this on the private sector without consultation, discussion, or consideration. Should we take that step? Should we set up a completely new quango---a whole Government agency---to deal with these matters, or should we build on what, in my view, are tried and trusted agencies within the system of New Zealand Government---the Chief Ombudsman and his office, and the State Services Commission? With what I hope are the relatively minor misgivings that I have outlined, and putting to one side the motives that one or two members might suspect prompted this member to bring the legislation before the House, I do commend him for the work he has obviously put into the legislation, and I hope it will be considered by the select committee at the appropriate time.

The problem I have is working out which is which. When the Government was first elected we saw a brave new world of real free-market economics---``the devil take the hindmost'' in its rawest form. As a result of the implementation of those policies we have seen lower inflation and lower interest rates, but I have to say that the landing has been very hard---as it is phrased in economic circles---very hard indeed. It has been too hard for an enormous number of New Zealanders, many thousands of whom have had their lives ruined by it. At the previous election all kinds of promises were made, and some of them were about economic recovery. Unemployment was going to be reduced. It was going to be halved by election time . All of that has been thrown aside. What has happened instead has been an absolutely obsessive implementation of free-market economics. When I consider the matters that Government members trumpet as being great successes of their economic policy, such as low inflation and low interest rates, I have to say that, as I said earlier, they have achieved some things that some people thought that they would never achieve. What we do know is that those results have been achieved well ahead of target. If the well-documented ``Lusitania principle'' is applied, and such targets are achieved well ahead of time, the amount of fuel required---in this case, human suffering---becomes that much greater. I am pleased to speak in support of the second reading of this Bill. I wonder whether we are not getting the debate somewhat out of proportion. The public health issue in relation to immunisation is not whether it is a good idea---although some people debate that---it is how we actually get to immunise the children who need it the most. That is the public health issue with immunisation, not whether people can get someone to tell them it is a good idea. We need to keep in mind that the Public Health Commission put out a number of good publications. It stirred debate. But it is hard to point to measurable appreciable achievements in public health. Given that the Public Health Commission was there for only a short time people might not expect that. We need to keep in mind that public health of itself as a term means almost anything. I just want to take up the issue of funding that Opposition members raised in respect of material they had seen in official papers. Hawke's Bay is also the place where the campaign has been run to the effect that Crown health enterprise expenditure is not subject to audit and that the Audit Office has not been able to audit billions of dollars of expenditure, therefore the expenditure is outside any public scrutiny. I have to say that that is complete nonsense. In Hawke's Bay the problem is not a lack of public scrutiny of Crown health enterprise spending. The problem is that some of the local politicians do not like the results of the scrutiny of public expenditure in Hawke's Bay. There is no doubt at all that if members looked at the hospital set-up in that part of the country they would see that there should be one well-equipped regional hospital and other facilities spread around the populated areas. Opposition members have something of a problem with the use of the word ``privatisation''. In the case of the Opposition spokesperson on health it is because she does not quite understand. I know that the Leader of the Opposition knows what it means, in the health sector, to privatise something, but I do not think the Opposition spokesperson on health does. It is true that some Crown health enterprise services have become quite contestable. For example, in my own part of the country something of a controversy is brewing because the local Crown health enterprise has been given a contract for promoting immunisation around the area. Some of the local general practitioners have taken great exception to this. That is an example of contestability. One of the benefits of the regime that now applies for Crown health enterprises is that we do not draw the same arbitrary distinctions we used to between public and private. That means resources can flow to those who can best provide the service. Another area where there has been substantial change is, for instance, in the home support services, which in my part of the country, and other parts of the country, have moved away from the Crown health enterprise and into the hands of other operators. Regardless of whether members would call that privatisation or whether we think that every service that used to be provided by an area health board has to be provided by a Crown health enterprise, it seems to me to be a fairly illogical position. There was nothing obvious about the things that area health boards did. Certainly, to run a base hospital was the preserve of area health boards, but a lot of the peripheral services they ran in terms of community services, even mental health services, do not logically have to be run by a large public provider. That is certainly the case now. Crown health enterprises know that they have to sharpen their pencils on a lot of those services, and so they should. In relation to the salaries issue, the Minister will have had the advice that in the public health services, just over people are paid over $, a year, or paid at that rate if they are part-time employees.

At present the Government is still correcting decades of mismanagement by putting in place management and financial disciplines that are pure common sense to everyone except Opposition politicians. Gains could be made through some of the following measures that are occurring: closer co-operation between Crown health enterprises, and the streamlining of management and administration systems. In some places---such as Health Waikato and Canterbury Health---there have been quite substantial turn-rounds in performance, but I point out that our hospitals must provide the services that are purchased by the regional health authorities, and that is what determines the level of services. The Government will be vigilant in pursuing the costs of delivering those services.

The funder/provider split is still in its early stages and it will be some time before there can be a complete evaluation of it. But it is reasonably clear already that it gives us a better way of evaluating alternative service provisions, and it means the purchaser can make more objective decisions for the benefit of the population because it does not own hospitals and employ health professionals.

I move, That the Public Health Agencies (Redesignation and Taxation) Bill be now read a second time. Although the urgency motion for the Bill was that it go through all stages, the Government did indicate its intention to refer the Bill to the Health Committee. At the end of the second reading I will move that the Bill be referred to the Health Committee, with an instruction for it to be reported back by June so that it can be implemented by July . This Bill has two parts to it. The first is the redesignation part. A number of clauses in the Bill change the names of the regional health authorities and the Crown health enterprises. The Bill will change the designation of four regional health authorities named in the Bill to the Health Funding Authority for New Zealand. This reflects the coalition Government's policy to move from four regional agencies that have the function of purchasing health services to a Health Funding Authority for New Zealand. The other part of the Bill redesignates the Crown health enterprises as hospital and health services. This is consistent with the Government's policy of abolishing the Crown health enterprises and moving the new organisations, hospital and health services, on to a not-for-profit basis. There have been a number of operational policy changes pursuant to changing to a not-for-profit objective. Not all these policy changes are embodied in the legislation. A number of them are best expressed in operational policy---that is, particularly in the statement of the owner's intentions that is communicated to the boards of what are still currently called Crown health enterprises. I point out to the House that this will be a cheap name change because only two of these organisations use the term ``Crown health enterprise'' in their trading name or letterhead. Most of the others do not. The change in the legislation will officially bring to an end the terminology ``Crown health enterprise''. I might say that at the public functions I have attended since that announcement, there has been something of a feeling of relief that that will be the case. The taxation issues are slightly more complicated. The Bill does two things. One is to obliterate the accumulated tax losses of our Crown health enterprises. These amount to many hundreds of millions of dollars. The abolition of the tax losses is contingent on what is called the deficit-switch, which is a rather technical process that we are going through. I will not explain it to the House in detail. But the Bill provides for the tax losses to be abolished contingent on further decisions that Cabinet will be making. The second issue is related to the capital charge. The Bill calls it a specified health payment. The capital charge is consistent with the policy to move to a not-for-profit basis. Capital charges have been levied on Government departments for some time, and the charge will apply to the Crown health enterprises in the same way as they apply to a Government department. What the Bill does is make that capital charge tax deductible. The Government has made a policy decision that the Crown health enterprises will remain taxable as a simple base maintenance measure, but the Government did not find it acceptable that the capital charge would be recorded as a profit. So it is being made tax deductible, and therefore designated as an expense in the books of our Crown health enterprises. Any surplus over and above expenses and the capital charge will be recorded as a surplus and will be retained by the organisation. A key part of moving to the not-for-profit objective is that the Government as an owner gives up the right to take any dividend from these organisations. This legislative package is a pragmatic and low-cost way of implementing the components of the health policy developed by the coalition Government. It is a small piece of legislation, but I believe it sends a strong signal to the health sector that the coalition agreement is being implemented and that the profit motive is now a thing of the past. As I have said to the House, there are a number of operational policy changes that back up this piece of legislation. I expect there will be some fairly arcane debate over the next few weeks about taxability, surpluses, and so on, but I think those debates will not contribute much to the ongoing progress of the health sector. What is more important, particularly with our hospitals and our funding authority, is that we have a greater degree of collaboration between the two---and that is certainly being effected right now---and that we have a greater degree of transparency, both in the mode of operation of our hospitals and in the contractual arrangements that they have with the funding authority.

That is right, I agree, they did not listen to me. They listened to Dr Cullen and Jim Anderton. I bet that this morning Dr Cullen did not get quite the same warm reception at the Auckland chamber of commerce that he got months ago, when the chamber listened and believed what he said. It has found out that this Government has introduced every single policy that it can to make business harder to do. So the claims for this bill are enormous: to close the gaps between regions, and between M~aori and P~akeh~a; and to create jobs for all New Zealanders. We could end up supporting this bill in this debate if the Government can show that the bill will achieve those objectives in any way. If the Minister and the Government can show that this bill will close the gaps between M~aori and P~akeh~a, then we will consider voting for it. The other reason this bill is in bad faith is that it is the result of a tawdry deal within the Government. Dr Cullen and Labour said: ``How can we deal with Jim Anderton?''---now known, I am told, in the Civil Service as Fred Flintstone---``Well, we will put him in a playpen in the corner with a ministry and $ million, and he will go away.'' Now a lot of people in New Zealand thought that was pretty smart, because they were just as worried as the Labour Party about Jim Anderton. But it has turned out that the Labour Party is worse. Jim Anderton has not actually done much damage to the New Zealand economy, because the strategy has worked. Fred Flintstone is over in Bedrock, and his officials are up in ``Club MED''---as the Ministry of Economic Development is called---with their feet up on the desks. There are advertisements in the papers for big, high-paying jobs. The advertisements say that the first role for the new policy manager of ``Club MED'' relates to developing an overview of how economic policy contributes to the Government's goals. Why does the Government need to pay someone to do that? It is because no one else has worked it out, and the Government does not know either. The message that the Government is getting from the people who actually undertake economic development is that the Government has no idea what drives economic development. So it needs to pay someone at ``Club MED'' to tell it. That is another reason this bill is in bad faith. This bill will not buy off the wealth creators of New Zealand. They feel hammered by this Government---particularly by the Labour Party. They had believed the Government would be moderate, because Dr Cullen told them so time and time again, and they have found out it is left wing. They feel hammered, the bridges have been burnt, and the Government is hoping that this bill, and the investment and savings incentives that we know are going to be in the Budget, will buy off business. That is what Dr Cullen says about building bridges for business. At least he has recognised that the cold shoulder he got today was not just from the Auckland chamber of commerce; it is coming increasingly from New Zealanders across the business spectrum. There is another reason this bill is here in bad faith, and that is to do with the issue of the year in : golden handshakes---payouts. This is the first Crown entity that the minority Labour-Alliance Government has formed; the first one. Every New Zealander knows that the big problem with Crown agencies, Crown entities, State-owned enterprises, and similar organisations is golden handshakes. The Prime Minister said, when Television New Zealand got it wrong, that heads would roll. Not one head has rolled. Not one! Labour said that they would do Christine Rankin in. Where is she? She is safer in her job now than she has ever been. The Prime Minister has now said that she is angry about the payouts at Airways Corporation. She will be unable to do anything about those payouts. This bill gave the Government a chance to change the law. The Government had the opportunity to write into the bill some mechanism by which there would be no payouts to people who were made redundant from, or who performed incompetently in, Industry New Zealand. And the chances are that there will be plenty of incompetent performances there. I had a look at the provisions in the bill regarding terms and conditions of employment. This Government did not do a single thing to reduce the probability of payouts when it was writing its own law itself for its first Crown entity. That is not just bad faith, it is incompetence. For months we listened to expressions of moral indignation from those parties. The public believed that they would do something about payouts now that they are on the Government benches. They could have done so in this bill, but they have done nothing. In fact, they have made matters worse. The chief executive and the board of Industry New Zealand can do what they like---the Government is just employing them. It is not saying that if they do not perform there will be no payouts. In fact, when the Employment Relations Bill is passed this chief executive, like Christine Rankin, will have a job for life. But it is worse than that. Employees will be able to transfer to Industry New Zealand from ``Club MED''---and why they would want to leave ``Club MED'' for this body, I do not know---with all their service entitlements. Let us say that after months one of them is not performing. Let us say that one of them is telling the Minister the truth, and gets the Kit Richards treatment---the Government wants to get rid of him---and let us say that he has been in the Ministry of Commerce for years. He would get a payout of half a million dollars. There is nothing in the bill that will stop any of the things the former Opposition railed about for months and months. Absolutely nothing! I think the Prime Minister should explain that. She was quoted in the media just yesterday, saying that she was angry about Airways Corporation payouts. She knows that she cannot do anything about those payouts, and is trying to reverse a bad poll from a bad fortnight. Here is a bill in which she could do something about the issue, and there is nothing in the bill. Maybe we are missing something. Maybe it is just something that Labour says when in Opposition. Maybe it is just what Labour says when it cannot do anything about the issue. If we look at the objectives of this bill, we see it is a pathetic attempt to close the gaps between M~aori and P~akeh~a, between the regions, and to create jobs for all New Zealanders.

I conclude on the issue of the past by inviting Government members to consider what is happening to the people in their electorates---to consider the lack of investment, the debt they are themselves accumulating, people's confidence, and whether the Government's policies will lead to greater or fewer social problems in the community. Government members have only to consider the unemployment figure to realise what the conclusion will be. The Bill is interesting because it shows the Government's change of heart. When the Bill was introduced in December the Government talked about turning the Development Finance Corporation into a company, and that is what the Bill finally does. Only one little clause hinted at the asset sale, because the Government had not made up its mind at that stage to sell assets. It was still saying publicly that it would not sell off assets. Clause is critical, because the proposed new section in that clause allows the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Industry, at any time---not after consulting Parliament, not after an election manifesto that tells the people the truth, but at any time---to sell or otherwise dispose of any shares or other securities in the capital of the company, including shares subscribed for by those Ministers, under section of the Act. That provision continues with more legalese. Clause shows the way the Government was converted on the road to Damascus. However, I remind Government members that the conversion is very recent. In this instance the Government is selling the Development Finance Corporation for the wrong reasons and for the wrong price. The Labour Party's manifesto stated---I shall not quote it exactly, but shall quote from the kind of speeches that Government members made---that the Government had to play a role in assisting small businesses. Until the Labour Government took office the Development Finance Corporation had been very successful with such assistance over the years. The Government then assisted large businesses, because its most successful investment has been in the corporation's treasury division, with foreign exchange dealings. When one considers the economy, that is about the only successful venture there has been in the past years---there has been virtually nothing else. The Development Finance Corporation has made a considerable amount of money out of trading in securities internationally---that is, supplying the financing of those securities---and by all accounts has a very efficient Treasury operation. What is that doing to New Zealand? It is exposing New Zealand overseas in an unprecedented way. This country's very reputation is at stake. We are very vulnerable, as the New Zealand dollar is about the ninth most frequently traded currency. The reason for that is the dollar's volatility and the high real interest rates---and the Development Finance Corporation has been in the middle of all that. Its assets have been sold for $ million to a couple of shareholders---one of whom is an overseas owner, and one of whom, the National Provident Fund, is a New Zealand operation. The sale may help the Government for a short time, but if there is any deficit in current account spending and in the external accounts it will be dissipated very quickly. The policy of asset sales will not work because New Zealand is losing its ability to earn funds overseas and to supply taxes to the Government. The Government can sell off as many assets as it likes, but it will have nothing left if it sells off the country's productive assets either by running them down or by not giving them the chance to work at a profit. Tomorrow night the Minister of Finance will introduce a Budget that will include more asset sales in an attempt to balance the books. The result may well look like a profit. The Development Finance Corporation will be one of the sales that will help the Minister's Budget deficit, surplus, or whatever. However, the selling of the assets must be done for the right reason---that is, so that they can be run more efficiently. Opposition members believe that ``privatisation'' is worth while for that reason, but not just to pay the grocer, not just to make certain of making money out of paper-shuffling at the expense of investment in productive assets and gaining a return on them, which is what I talked about earlier when I said that the debt was so high under previous Governments. Under the present Government the debt is building up to sustain and maintain the economy, not to invest. The country is building up private sector overseas debt to a point at which the reputation and image of New Zealand might well be ruined. When the New Zealand dollar finally does crash---and it will---public companies will go down like ninepins because of the way they are exposed overseas. The Development Finance Corporation, ``privatised'' or not, will sustain some major losses internationally because all of its international loans are not fully covered. That exposure is one reason the Development Finance Corporation was sold at a discount. People in the financial sector---the kind of people I met last week in Hong Kong---know full well how vulnerable the New Zealand dollar is. They know that it is being traded up on speculation. They know that the New Zealand dollar is the ninth largest currency traded by volume; and that New Zealand has people, with a gross domestic product at a fraction of that of most countries. They know that it is based on a speculative float, on the Government's monetary and economic policies, which are holding up interest rates when our basic economy, our real production, is going downhill at a rate unprecedented since the great depression. I want to close on a couple of points.

If that is the position, Parliament will be guilty of passing complex legislation that was drafted in a couple of days. The legislation gives enormous powers to a department of State and leaves members in the position in which they cannot judge the issues properly because they do not have the information. The letter continues: ``I understand that the matter was taken to Cabinet on Monday by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. Cabinet's decision was that it preferred to pass the necessary legislation on Budget night''---I have already referred to that matter---``and the current situation would be met by you giving me a letter of comfort undertaking to pass the legislation as drafted. I can understand the wish of Cabinet to handle the matter in this way.''---I bet he can, and so can Opposition members; the Government wants to bury the matter on Budget night---``Unfortunately, it is not an option available to me.''. The Minister said that the Attorney-General had said that it was not a matter of urgency. However, earlier paragraphs in the letter stated that the Solicitor-General and the Prime Minister agreed that retrospective legislation was not an available option. The Attorney-General, who happens to be the former Prime Minister, has one opinion. However, what about the Solicitor-General? He is the Government's official adviser, and it is apparent in the letter that the Prime Minister agrees with him. The plot starts to thicken when the Minister of Agriculture gets up in the House and says: ``Well, the Attorney-General told me that it didn't matter.''. The Attorney-General happens to disagree with the present Prime Minister, a professor of law, and with the Solicitor-General---at least that is what members can deduce from the letter. The Government must give a better explanation of what is going on. If Government members sit in silence for the next half-hour while the House goes through the Committee stage without offering any explanation, legislation that gives the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries enormous powers will pass through the House without proper debate or proper disclosure of why it was necessary. When Parliament passed the reforming Bill of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries last year the select committee discussed---and the Associate Minister will remember this---whether or not to accept the recommendation of the Legislation Advisory Committee to give the department the powers of prerogative. That is really a common law power under which a Minister may make a department responsible to him or to her, and those functions can be conferred on the department by the Minister. The matter was discussed in some detail and the department said: ``No, we don't think that's a good idea. It's not necessary.''. Parliament is doing that tonight, because it is simpler than trying to list the powers. That department of State even has its own travel agency---goodness knows what else it has! The Government will try to pass legislation that involves a major step in a new direction without scrutiny. As far as I know, only the Department of Survey and Land Information, which is not a major department, has been granted similar prerogative powers---and that was done by the select committee, of which I am a member, as an experiment. The ministry is involved in protecting the security of New Zealand's agricultural industry---a most important export industry. It is involved in joint ventures with dozens of different companies, and competes with the private sector. Problems of all kinds in the administration of the ministry have to be tackled, and they will be tackled by a National Government. Parliament is going through the process of passing legislation under urgency when it has not been given the chance to interview the officials and the select committee has not had the chance to hear submissions from the Legislation Advisory Committee. I certainly should have liked that committee to consider the legislation, because the report released on October by the present Prime Minister, who was the Minister of Justice at the time, stated that there should be some major concerns about the way the powers being exercised by the department were being administered. The report detailed some of the Australian experience. The Australian Gazette is used regularly to keep the public informed about what a department is doing. The point is that the Bill before the House allows the Government to use powers that go back to when New Zealand had a slump that was followed by a war, and when the department of State was expected to become involved in everything it possibly could. The Minister is trying to enact legislation under urgency, without a select committee hearing and, according to the letter to the Prime Minister from Brian Tyler, the Controller and Auditor-General, against the wishes of the Solicitor-General and of the Prime Minister. It is not good enough, and Opposition members will vote against the second reading of the Bill, its Committee stage, and its third reading, and will do their best to make sure that Parliament has the opportunity to scrutinise and understand the legislation. If possible, members on this side of the House will wake up members of the news media and let them know that something is happening that should not be happening.

The Bill is the Survey Amendment Bill (No. ). The Minister of Overseas Trade and Marketing should stand up and say that he is not prepared to allow the department to indulge in predatory pricing; that he is not prepared to allow it to use its cost structure to charge consumers too much for a service on which it has a monopoly; and that he is not prepared to allow it to develop into a fat department rather than a lean one. He should ensure that the department applies the best method. The Department of Survey and Land Information fits in with the Department of Conservation. Department of Conservation officials have gone around and looked at the countryside. They have said that if there is a minor subdivision anywhere near a river or a coastline they will take all of that coastline---mile after mile of it---and set it aside for a reserve. I have a particular case in my electorate. I hope that the Minister will grant an exemption, because about or hectares of land on the coast are being subdivided. The Department of Conservation will make the landowner set aside as a reserve an -mile strip of land to which people already have access. Then, for about another or miles up the river--- It is the old story of the man who wanted to take the coastline stips on rivers and streams. I shall talk about that in a minute, because it is funny. I remember a friend of mine who was going to lose the front room of his house simply because the Minister decided that he wanted to take strips alongside all rivers and streams. However, in this case the Opposition has the chance of obtaining from the Government a clear undertaking that it will not let the department adopt predatory pricing or cost-plus attitudes, and that it will ensure that the flexibility given to the department by Parliament is clearly accountable for the benefit of all New Zealanders.
