He loves to grind into the dust the people that he milked; the people he took money from when he was a lawyer; the people he now describes as pretty poor businessmen, anyway. I invite the Minister to speak in the debate if he wants to; let his prejudices flow so that we can really hear how he feels about the agricultural community. I want to talk about the restructuring of the Rural Bank, because that is what the Bill is about. It is not about the economic viability of agriculture; it is about restructuring the Rural Bank to turn it into a company. The Bill was introduced earlier in the year on the basis that the Government believed that it could turn the Rural Bank into a company without having any effect on the bank's portfolio. The principal reason the Government has run into trouble is that the Rural Bank has had a Government guarantee on its borrowings. It is in trouble as a bank because the Government has forced it to repay Loans Account borrowings---borrowings the bank has made over the years from the Government and on-lent to the agricultural community---not just to farmers but to commercial interests, and so on. The Rural Bank has built the nation's kiwifruit industry; it has built the nation's prosperity in wool; and it has built the nation's prosperity in the dairy industry by being a financing operation that has encouraged development in industries that are earning the country billions of dollars each year. An examination of the problems the Government has with the Rural Bank at present shows that the bank has had to borrow substantial sums of money overseas because the Government has forced it to repay more than $ million of debt to the Loans Account in the past years. By and large that money is covered for foreign exchange risk---in other words, international investors have taken the risk. They have been prepared to take the risk that they will not lose money by lending to the Rural Bank. One of the reasons they have been prepared to do that is that the Government had a guarantee on the funds that the bank borrowed. Therefore the investors knew that, even if the exchange rate went all over the paddock and they lost money, they would be paid back because of the Rural Bank's Government guarantee. However, the Bill takes away the Government guarantee on new borrowing, and it potentially allows the Government to sell off the Rural Bank to the highest bidder. If the Government's track record is any proof, it will sell the bank very quickly---as soon as the bank is turned into a company. That means that the foreign investor is vulnerable. There is no doubt that the Rural Bank has some vulnerability, particularly if the funds that it has borrowed overseas are called up, and when the prices of land are falling by the day. According to the general manager, more than farmers are in arrears to the bank, with a further in serious trouble with percent of their mortgages in arrears. After the Government introduced the Bill it found that the Rural Bank had to renegotiate all of the international loans. The Opposition wrote to the Controller and Auditor-General and told him that it was concerned about the viability of the Rural Bank, about the taxpayers' liability, and about the position the Rural Bank would find itself in with the loss of the Government guarantee. I quote from the reply of the Controller and Auditor-General to my letter: ``Whether or not the change in funding arrangements would put the Rural Bank in jeopardy would depend on striking an appropriate balance between the rate which the Government-funded capital had to be replaced with private capital.'' The purpose for which the Minister of Finance wants ``privatisation'' is to make the Government's books look better. When it required the Rural Bank to fund more than $ million for the Government in the past years that money went into table as a miscellaneous item financing investment earning, and that has contributed to a reduction in the deficit. That $ million has made Roger Douglas's deficit look better.

No I did not; my horse came last. I had a very slow polo pony that I thought was a fast one. It did not do very well, so it was retired to stud soon afterwards. Many people train, breed, ride, and race horses as a hobby. If they choose to take part in their hobby on a Sunday, so be it. It is clear from the New Zealand way of life that many people indulge in very expensive sports on a Sunday that involve much more money---such as powerboat racing, international yacht racing, and motor racing. The Bill does not provide a vast liberalisation to cause people to descend into dens of iniquity and lose their life-savings. Some people may spend their life-savings on a boat that stops after going over the starting-line, or on a yacht that sinks. People who are interested in the sport of kings should have the opportunity to race on Sunday afternoons and, if they want to do so, to spend a few dollars on a little bet. I know that most people do not spend much more than $ or $. That is fairly cheap. It is one of the few pursuits that has not kept up with inflation. It is a little bit like the game of golf, on which people still bet c, or $. The House should provide a limited opportunity to allow people to indulge in the sport of kings. There is also a commercial reason. People have said---and the point was raised in the Committee stage---that some individuals might be exploited because of the extra days of racing a year. The people who say that are ignorant about what is required to look after an animal such as a horse. A horse must be fed or times a day, somebody has to ride it, to lead it out, and to muck out the stables, and those people work days a week, anyway. They would not be exploited if they had to get into a float and take the horse to the nearest racing club and see their friends and have a social day. They may be able to take their families, particularly when the pressure on Sunday racing days will not be the same as that for major meetings such as the Wellington Cup. Racing will have a chance to develop a new image. When the New Zealand Racing Conference first wrote to me asking for my support in the matter I wrote back and said that I might not be percent in favour, because I was worried that the change might recreate Saturday circumstances on Sundays, and not involve families. I believe that Sunday is one day on which families should be able to be involved in the sport. Racing, of all sports, gives that opportunity, if it chooses to take it. Racecourses have some of the best facilities in New Zealand. There are parks, reserves, and areas for children to play in. However, most racecourses do not have facilities for families. I challenge the clubs that are interested in running Sunday meetings to provide facilities for children. Parents, who might both work during the week and not see much of each other, may choose on a Sunday to go and indulge in their sport and recreation, and should be able to take their children and look after them properly, at least for a couple of hours. They may not necessarily want to play with their children all the time---anyway, as we all know, one cannot spend all of one's time playing with one's children, even if one wanted to. If racing clubs were able to provide facilities for families that would bring those families together, perhaps at lunch, afternoon tea, or in the evening, it would provide a way in which the racing fraternity could become more integrated with families. The racing industry has not looked after the members of the younger generation whose parents are involved in the sport. If racing can be given an image of a more family-orientated sport it would be to the good of that important industry. There are full-time and part-time workers in the racing industry. It earns about $ million a year in export earnings, and is New Zealand's most important thoroughbred industry. The Government has done its best to stop that. The only decent thing that the Govenment has done for racing was introduce the Bill, which is fairly minor. The Australians have changed the livestock tax system for thoroughbred breeding, and have improved their laws to make it harder for New Zealand breeders to compete. However, that is a little irrelevant to the Bill. If the industry is to be encouraged in this way we also have to consider other factors that the Minister of Overseas Trade and Marketing is interested in, because that industry, which could be exporting more, is losing investment to Australia. In the process of liberalisation members should consider other factors, such as tax legislation that prevents investment from coming into New Zealand when it could be coming in, and that is encouraging New Zealanders to send their mares to Australia, where the tax provisions are more favourable for the industry. The Opposition has some reservations about that major extension. However, I do not have such reservations. There could be a greater liberalisation, and many racing clubs that meet on Saturdays and during the week could meet on Sundays---it would probably be more productive for the country and more fun for the families, and racing would be the better for it.

The Opposition is relaxed about Part I, but it has some concerns about Part II, particularly about clause ()(e), but I shall come to that in a moment or two, and shall ask the Minister a few questions about it. The Bill is the second part of the system providing supplementary minimum prices for wheatgrowers. In the middle of the election campaign we heard about a grant of $ a tonne for every tonne of wheat grown in New Zealand. That is because the Government suddenly got worried about the Waitaki electorate and thought that it had better give wheatgrowers a subsidy. The Bill is the second part of that political bribe---it gives a compulsory levy to wheatgrowers so that they can fund their political activity. That is the part that concerns the Opposition. It is not concerned about the research levy, which is not new, but about the United Wheatgrowers Ltd levy, which can be spent on activities that that body regards as fit, with the exception of marketing involvement. Part I has only one new aspect compared with the original levy system, and that involves a levy of up to $ a tonne on imported wheat and flour. Why is wheat coming into New Zealand not levied? Why are growers required to pay a $ levy towards a research account on which they have only a couple of representatives out of members, yet importers who bring in wheat, process it into flour, and then sell it to bakers, are required under the Bill to pay a maximum levy of only $. It seems to me yet another example of the Government's being prepared to kowtow to the Australians. We have the levy of $ a tonne because the Government was not prepared to front up to the Australians about the subsidised grain coming into New Zealand---something that the Customs Department has clearly shown is happening. According to my reading of the Bill, and I would stand corrected, it is another example of the Government's being prepared to levy only wheat and flour coming into New Zealand, or to levy the flour---not the wheat. It is possible for subsidised grain to be imported from anywhere in the world under the deregulated environment, for the wheatgrowers to be wiped out and no levy to be paid for research and development, and, as a result, for the necessary research and development effort not to be funded on the same basis as if the wheat had been grown in New Zealand. Can members imagine the Australians doing the same? They would probably double the levy on imported wheat and make sure that the imported wheat was paying a much bigger share, rather than a smaller share. Why has the Government done that? Why was it not prepared to make the Australian imports of ``raw'' wheat---for want of a better term---subject to at least the same levy that New Zealand wheatgrowers are paying under Part I for research and development? Clause ()(e) relates to the expenditure of the levy. I certainly have no quarrel with the imposition of a levy when an organisation such as United Wheatgrowers Ltd is working internationally on behalf of all wheatgrowers, just as the Meat Producers Board and the Wool Board do for their growers. Perhaps even a little expenditure on promotion is not so bad, because it may be necessary to make sure that that industry has at least some cohesion. At present the chairman of United Wheatgrowers Ltd, Mervyn Gray, is in Australia negotiating with its Wheat Board to try to develop sensible arrangements between New Zealand and Australia. That is something the Government should have done before allowing imports to disrupt the whole industry earlier this year. It finished up, of course, making a $ million bribe. The Opposition has no problems with that, but the clause states: ``The money received by United Wheatgrowers in respect of the levy imposed by section of this Act may be expended by that company for the promotion, development, and improvement of the wheat growing industry.'' That is not bad, until one gets to the subclauses that list the general areas of expenditure. The first is the funding of the dominion office of Federated Farmers. In fact, Federated Farmers fund that office on a user-pays basis, and the Opposition does not have many problems with that as long as that organisation is doing work for all growers that is not political. The second item relates to the entering into insurance contracts to protect wheatgrowers against loss of or damage to crops. That is really compulsory insurance. One has to ask what happens if a grower wants to opt out and get a cheaper rate of insurance from, for example, Lloyds of London. Is there any provision for the Minister or anyone else to allow an exemption, as there is under the provisions of compulsory unionism? That is what this is. What is the position if a grower wants to get a better deal?

This Chamber echoes with the voices of men and women who have changed our democratic perceptions and pushed the boundaries of representativeness. Only when Parliament contains people who have known poverty, injustice, discrimination, and violence will it ever truly address the needs of those for whom these are daily realities. It is a case for celebration and hope that this House contains more women than ever before, more Maori, a wider ethnic representation, and list members whose task is to represent nationwide constituencies, which have never been concentrated geographically. It is a great privilege to join my colleagues Sandra Lee and Jim Anderton and to stand alongside other new Alliance MPs. We find ourselves in the late th century struggling with global realities that threaten to overwhelm us. A generation ago it became apparent that the world economic system was in a new crisis and this had major impacts on New Zealand. It had many faces: loss of traditional markets, geopolitical control of oil, growing overseas debt, rapid technological change, and a breakdown of the post-Keynesian consensus. A growing social alienation was fuelled by the Vietnam War and questioned the post-war ideals of progress and materialism. People are still searching for meaningful values beyond just economic growth. In response, New Zealand embarked on a series of rash experiments to try to shore up the previous world order and to make the world safe for the continued growth of international capital. First there was ``think big''---a failed attempt to grow the economy through large debt-financed and resource-intensive engineering works. Much of my early political work was focused on opposing and finding alternatives to these projects. In a second experiment, New Zealand led the world in economic rationalism, the ``casinofication'' of financial markets, the dismantling of the State, and the concept of the public good. It depended for its perceived success on a vicious game of winners and losers, where a huge gap was forced between the successful and the marginalised. Neither experiment improved the lot of ordinary people because neither addressed the real nature of the problem. Human numbers and human economic demands had reached the point where the free goods of the ecosystem---the air, water, and soil we take for granted---were no longer freely available.It costs more and more to produce less and less. Economic growth can destroy more well-being through pollution, stress, ugliness, and scarcity than it creates in new goods and services. Human beings are dwarfed and alienated by the scale of their technologies, which have left most of us with no apparent place in the production process that we have been taught to see as the reason for our existence. In the Union of Concerned Scientists issued a warning to the world's people. It was signed by , leading scientists, including Nobel laureates. They said: ``Human beings and the natural world are on a collision course. Many of our current practices put at serious risk the future that we wish for human society and the plant and animal kingdoms, and may so alter the living world that it will be unable to sustain life in the manner that we know.'' They continued: ``No more than one or a few decades remain before the chance to avert the threats we now face will be lost and the prospects for humanity immeasurably diminished.'' The warning catalogues loss of topsoil and forests, rising population and carbon emissions, falling per-capita agricultural productivity, eroding genetic diversity, and dying lakes, reefs, and rivers. It links poverty and human misery closely with environmental degradation. That is borne out by the million environmental refugees---a number that exceeds the number of all refugees from other causes and is growing by , people each day. Just because New Zealand is travelling first class on this planet does not mean the ship is not sinking. As the scientists say, no nation can escape from injury when global biological systems are damaged. Even as we speak, New Zealanders are sitting in ancient rimu forests to prevent a State-owned enterprise from felling them. Even as we speak, the lethal waste products of the nuclear industry are steaming towards New Zealand waters, but they are not doing so unopposed. Even during those two decades of failed experiments and social turmoil, the seeds of a new way forward were being sown. Like many new movements whose time has come, they occurred in several countries at once, and spread rapidly to more than . The first green parties in the world, the United Tasmanian Group, and the New Zealand Values Party, were formed in . They said: ``The key question was not whether centralised industrial capitalism should be controlled by the State or by private enterprise, but rather the unsustainability of centralised industrial capitalism itself.'' Values proposed a common-sense economic philosophy based on the principles of ecological sustainability and social responsibility. It sought production for real needs, the primacy of local communities rather than states, an internationalism of ideas, knowledge, art, hospitality, and solidarity with the poor, but the localising of economic relations so they are controlled democratically. Above all, it spoke of the politics of enough; that humans should stop when they have enough so that other living things can survive; that affluent humans should stop when they have enough so that others may have enough too. I was part of that party and helped to shape its policies. I voted for it from Europe in , on the strength of two press clippings. My father, who sent me those press clippings, is in the House tonight, and at is probably the oldest member of the Greens in New Zealand. As I voted I was thinking of the future for my first child, then a lively toddler. He is here tonight too, and in was the youngest candidate in the general election standing for the Greens. During that period Values had combined with local green groups to form the Green Party, which is now proudly a constituent member of the Alliance. We are now in contact with Green parties around the world on all continents, part of what Senator Bob Brown, leader of the Australian Greens, calls the thin green line around the planet. Hundreds of Greens have been elected to national and State Parliaments and to local councils. They are in the European Parliament and in most national Parliaments in Europe. In Finland they are part of Government and hold the foreign affairs portfolio. Many have visited New Zealand. I remember with particular affection the inspiration of the late Petra Kelly, then leader of the German Greens. Green parties are mushrooming in the tiger economies of East Asia, called into existence by human rights abuses, rampant nuclear power programmes, slave labour wage rates, lack of health and safety protection, and non-existent environmental standards. Their founding principles are remarkably similar to those of the New Zealand Greens: ecological wisdom, social justice, appropriate decision-making, and non-violence. I recently re-read Blueprint for New Zealand, the Values manifesto. It sounds surprisingly modern. It speaks of the destruction of the quality of life and especially of the need for livable cities, and of the need to humanise and share work. It laments that economic growth, seen as necessary to stop unemployment, is producing much that is of questionable value and destroying much that is of great value. It attacks militarism as obsolete and deplores the application of the corporate model to areas of human life where it is not appropriate. In some ways its predictions are uncanny. It foresees a Parliament of members with the extra elected via a party list on a two-vote system. It calls for the lowering of the voting age to , the passing of a freedom of information Act, increased use of referenda, Maori focused pre-school education for Maori, and homosexual and abortion law reforms. So we have made some progress in years, particularly in the field of human rights and the evolution of our parliamentary system, but in other ways we have gone terribly backward. Recognising that our society was on the brink of unheard-of levels of unemployment, the blueprint calls for a -day week, and worker-owned cooperatives, and says: ``Governments may have to create jobs directly and selectively''. We in the Alliance would echo that today as we would the later statement: ``Need should be the only criterion for receiving health care.'' The blueprint deplores any lack of social control over new technology. Since then, the threat of nuclear engineering has largely been replaced in New Zealand with the threat of genetic engineering, but there is even less democratic control than there was in the s. So we return to this Parliament and its role in the s. In a world where of the largest economies are corporations rather than nations, where our ability to decide how and with whom we will trade is policed by an unelected group of nameless officials in the World Trade Organization, and where most of the people's assets have been sold to private corporations, elected national Parliaments have less power than ever before. Some of this power they have chosen to give away, without a mandate from the people. Some could be taken back by developing new ways of working with other nations. Some power has been devolved to local communities and I welcome that, provided that local communities are empowered to strengthen their democracy and are resourced with the information they need. But I believe that Government cannot shirk its role as defender of the common good. Governments have allowed, encouraged, the huge gap that has opened up between rich and poor and they can and must close that gap again. Governments have aided and abetted the commercialisation of every aspect of our lives: not just business but health, education, and our public attitudes to the natural world. Three years ago Sandra Lee said in this House: ``The needs and desires of ordinary people have been suppressed by a political philosophy that recognises only commercial imperatives and the corporate model.'' That is even more true today. New Zealanders, like people everywhere, are crying out for a way of life that cherishes those values that corporatism denies. They are asking for protection from chemical trespass. They want to be able to swim and gather shellfish where they cannot now. They want better public transport and more human-scale cities. They want to buy food that is not contaminated with chemical residues or created by genetic manipulation. They want worthwhile work that contributes to human happiness rather than destroying it. They want their children to grow up knowing the rich diversity of living things that they have known. Untrammelled markets will not deliver these things. To the extent that Governments can enable people to achieve them and to build a more human existence for themselves, they have no more important duty. I have worked for these ideals as a community activist, and as a teacher, writer, and researcher. I see my work in Parliament as just another way of working for green goals, neither more nor less important, and I hope to continue to work with old friends who are still in those other fields. To quote a slogan of the women's movement: ``The personal is political.'' It is a real challenge to come from the Coromandel hills and the Kauaeranga River, from my eco-house and organic farm, to live in this overprivileged place in accordance with my personal beliefs of simplicity, walking lightly on the earth, and continuing to care for family and friends, but I intend to try. There is a different way of doing politics where the processes and the human relationships are important as well as the end. In fact, they are ends. We become empowered when we have a sense of being part of the ecosystem, when we start to make connections between our decisions and the cheap labour that furnishes our homes and tailors our wardrobes, between the fuels we use and rising sea-levels and tropical storms, between the rubbish we throw away and the mountains of waste we expect our cities to absorb. Change towards a better understanding is possible and local action must be backed up with parliamentary action. In this task I seek the blessings of my forebears---women like Rachel Carson and Petra Kelly---and courage for those who will follow.

In the Committee stage I referred to the , women who are currently on the cervical-screening register. Only about percent of women who ought to be on it are on it. This evening we are making sure that there will be an opt-off provision for women who will go on to the cervical-screening register, as a result of the changes. At the moment it is an opt-on provision. Unless a woman knows about the register or is told by her doctor, she does not get on to it. Now women will automatically go on to the register, unless they choose to opt off for cultural or other reasons. There was criticism about the delay. Any delay was the result of trying to accommodate the different needs of cultural groups and sensitivities to ensure that every woman in New Zealand--whether Maori, pakeha, or of Pacific Island descent--chooses to be part of that register, because it will eliminate the large numbers of women who are dying from cervical cancer. Because of the issue of cervical cancer, I would like to express my real anger at the slur that has been made in the House on some of the people who have been appointed to regional health authorities. I think of women in Auckland--such as Denise Henare, who has worked extremely hard for women's health, and also Lesley Mack, who is committed to the health of young children. They are the types of people who are on the Government-appointed boards that we have been discussing this evening. Those women have a commitment to ensuring that there are not deaths from cervical cancer. I am very proud that women such as that are being appointed to Government boards in New Zealand.

On a personal level I was delighted with the result of the referendum held on September. I am on public record as a supporter of MMP (mixed-member proportional representation). For me, it was really exciting to see people voting positively for something; I do not think that we have seen that in this country for a long, long time. I think that it is great to see something positive happening. I came into Parliament favouring change; I spoke of it in my maiden speech. That view has not changed in the time that I have been here--if anything it has become a little more extremist. I think that we must have change if New Zealand is to move forward socially and economically. However, there is one thing that we should have learnt from watching both this Government and the previous Government over the past or years, and that is that if the public is not taken with a government on any particular aspect of change people will be utterly confused. I have some real reservations about this Bill, in that it will further serve to confuse a public that is still reeling with some degree of confusion over the other options that they had to face up to on September.

I am proud to speak on the introduction of such a progressive and visionary Bill---the Electoral Poll Bill. I support this Bill without reservation. In my short time in Parliament as a back-bencher the work that I have been permitted to be party to on the Electoral Law Committee and also on the Government caucus parliamentary and electoral reform committee has been the most personally rewarding---certainly the most stimulating. I have enjoyed seeing the conjunction of the inquiry into the general election and the work that has generated from that, and also having an input into the contents of the Bill. I want to express my personal commendation to the Minister and also to the chairman of the committee. The committee has met regularly and members have had the opportunity to express their viewpoints. As a member of the committee I did not feel at any stage that there was a sense of urgency and that the Bill was being rushed through. Plenty of time was taken to explore the options and the concerns that the member for Ohariu expressed to ensure that the Bill was not too complex. Those concerns were well thought through and, as a relatively young and newer member, I was grateful to be given the privilege of working through this legislation. One of the advantages---perhaps the only advantage---that new back-benchers have over longstanding parliamentarians is that we can still view the electoral process in the same way that the public and the voters view it. No one who has spoken today disputes that the public does not consider that the existing system is very fair. As a back-bencher I have had plenty of time to reflect on what is required of me as a member of Parliament. First, I am required to represent my constituents---that goes without saying; second, to represent the nation as a whole; third, to provide effective government; and, fourth, to enact legislation and to scrutinise the actions of the Executive. It is fair to say that the public has not always felt entirely happy about the degree of scrutiny of the actions of the Executive, irrespective of which party has been in office. As a back-bench member, I say that our present crop of back-benchers has done well in endeavouring to fulfil that role. I am glad that we have done so, but I still feel that further work needs to be done on this matter. Like the member for East Coast Bays, I feel that this is only part of the solution to our problems. We must look at parliamentary reform as well---the sitting hours of the House. Members do not make sensible decisions when they are tired. I am told that the number of continuous sitting hours during the Budget debate was the greatest since . That did not make very good use of the parliamentary system, but I accept the need to work within the structures to achieve sustainable change, and I understand the need for party discipline. As a member who has crossed the floor on occasions, I accept that that is not appropriate for motions of Government confidence, but as back-benchers we are obliged to consider that scrutiny of the Executive---especially with the deteriorating economic climate and the vulnerability in world markets---and we must think clearly about attracting to this parliamentary structure people of vision who have clear and creative ideas about the way in which members should be addressing the future of this country. Some of those visionary people are the ones who are least likely to be able to work within the present two-party system. Those people would not last very long and would not be patient enough to wait to implement some of their ideas. The public has felt frustrated and disillusioned with the political system. Therefore I am pleased that this Government has honoured its promise to introduce the Electoral Poll Bill. I believe that we have seen on the part of our young people a loss of a sense of the value of the democratic system. I think that they feel, rightly or wrongly, that the integrity and the democracy has been lost. Before the election the electoral roll centre resorted to trendy advertising of all kinds to attract young people to go on to the roll. That is absolutely outrageous, given that there is a legal requirement that they register to go on to the roll. A small fortune was spent on having young people jumping up and down on ladders on television to try to attract those young people to be part of the democratic system. Given the developments in Russia in the past hours, those young people were not choosing to exercise their democratic rights. It is a tragedy that young people feel so disfranchised from our system when their Russian counterparts are expressing their willingness to fight oppression. It is absolutely tragic, and I hope that those young people will see the introduction of this Bill as a progressive measure towards a greater sense of purpose in our present parliamentary system. I draw the attention of members to a recent political questionnaire that was conducted in Eden. There were questions altogether, one of which was: ``Do you agree with the Government's intention for a referendum on electoral reform?''. In the replies to that question, percent said ``Yes''; percent said ``No''; percent said ``Maybe''; but there were very few blank spaces. Further down the questionnaire I asked whether there was support for a mixed-member proportional system or for preferential voting. There was a space for ``Yes'', ``No'', or ``Maybe'', and a blank space. Most of them, while expressing interest, did not understand the options that were available to them. They understood very well that they did not like the status quo and that they wanted a change, but they did not feel that they knew sufficient about the options to be able to express an opinion. I commend the Minister for the work that he has done in ensuring the setting up of an independent committee made up of the Clerk of the House, the Chief Ombudsman, the Law Commissioner, and the chief executive officer of the Ministry of Women's Affairs. Those people will try to get the message to the public about what options are available and what the political implications are for the country. I have heard some criticism from members about the appointment of the chief executive officer of the Ministry of Women's Affairs, and I say to my collegues that, in relation to the proposals to reform Parliament, women hold dear to their hearts the opportunity to express their feelings on that matter, given that until the time of the election there had been only women members of Parliament as opposed to male members of Parliament. I think that that shows that the status quo has not worked in favour of women in terms of political representation. Therefore I commend the Minister for his vision in ensuring adequate representation for women on that committee, which will be conducting the educational side for the public. We have gone to much trouble to ensure that the ballot paper is not too complex. I think that it is a good ballot paper. It will never be perfect, but I think that we have reached the best possible compromise in terms of presenting the options fairly. I believe that it is understandable, and I again express my support for the Bill and the delight that I shall have in being part of the select committee that will scrutinise it. I look forward to working with Opposition members on that committee. I see it as a constructive thing for New Zealand at this time, and I thank the House for the opportunity to speak in the debate.

I am delighted that this Bill is receiving the support of so many members of Parliament today. It is important legislation. For those members outside Auckland who think that this is an Auckland sort of Bill, I draw to their attention that every single time we have had legislation amending what were the assets of the Auckland Regional Services Trust, which is now Infrastructure Auckland, it has bought not just a regional benefit but, indeed, a national benefit. The first occasion was the amendment to release funds for the America's Cup. There is general consent amongst all parties in Parliament that the investment that has been made using Auckland assets in the America's Cup will bring about many national benefits. Infrastructure Auckland---the amendment that was made there---may not on the surface appear to bring benefits to the people of Dunedin or the people who are living in the far north, but the reality is that if we can use those funds to tackle the whole vexed issue of congestion and the costs associated with that that are affecting the whole of the country, then national benefits will accrue. With the establishment of this trust, there will again be national benefits. I could go on and on, in looking at the arts and culture organisations that will be the beneficiaries associated with this trust, and I think particularly of all the energy that is there: the Auckland City Art Gallery, the Auckland War Memorial Museum, the ballet companies, the theatre companies, the youth choirs, and the chamber music, and I could go on and on. There are so many very substantial arts organisations in the Auckland region that have so much to offer, not just in terms of New Zealand and Auckland's growing sense of identity but also looking out into the future and the opportunities that it affords and the enterprise in an employment sense. These groups need to be nurtured. This fund will go some way towards achieving that, and through that, grow the whole issue of employment and employment opportunities throughout the whole country. I am delighted that parties across Parliament have been prepared to reconsider this matter, and that we are now seeing the Bill progressed today. When the legislation was passed last year and $ million was allocated for the territorial local authorities, Auckland was afforded $. million at the time: Manakau City $. million, North Shore City $. million, Waitakere $. million, Rodney $,, Papakura $,, and Franklin $,. It is fair to say that Papakura, at the time, did not wish to participate in the establishment of a trust. Probably for that reason the legislation was not passed at that stage. But with what was passed it specifically prohibited the cities coming together in a way that I think everyone would agree is common sense, and we are now correcting that today. I thank members because it is my hope that the funds can be used to establish a significant fund that can grow to a much greater level of arts and cultural activity in the region. They are a vital part of a creative and vibrant place, and the Bill provides the chance to create a base of funds that can be grown to produce a substantial increase in the development of arts and culture. The cities are really looking forward to working together. I have met the mayors of North Shore, Manukau, Rodney, and, of course, Waitakere. We believe that there will be wonderful long-term ongoing benefits associated with that. We see the trust being able to use moneys to leverage additional funds for a substantial capital fund, but without this ability funds are more likely to be used for local rather than regional projects of significance, and they are more likely to be exhausted on a one-off basis. I would see that as a waste and a squandering of a really special opportunity. The submissions that were received on the issue from the arts community were overwhelmingly in favour of establishing a trust for the region. The call for the art sector was one for councils to think about and to apply funds regionally, rather than locally. First, the legislation has to be amended. That is what we are doing, and I am very grateful to the Minister for achieving that, and to the Prime Minister for her intervention in this matter. It is envisaged that the trust funds will provide the basis for the development of a substantial capital base. Once it is large enough and the base has been achieved, the income can be distributed on an ongoing basis. The purpose of the trust is to distribute funds in accordance with the requirement of the Act---that is, significant projects in the region in the areas of arts and culture. Specific criteria will need to be developed to define what constitutes this definition. I commend the Bill to all members of Parliament and thank them for their support. It is necessary to give Auckland territorial local authorities the opportunity to form this trust, which will make a huge contribution to regional arts and culture in the long term, and, as I said before, to other members outside of Auckland. Along with that will be benefits that will be felt nationally when we get this right. What is good for Auckland is good for the rest of the country. I thank all members for their support.

Following on from those points I want to draw attention to the fact that one can never have choice in a rationed situation. We have been dealing with a very flawed situation for the last years and I applaud the fact that we are finally seeing this issue trend in the right direction. I do not suspect that we will get it percent right today, but I think that if we look at all the individual measures that have been taken and put them in the context of what we are doing, it is a damn sight better than what we have had. When we get policy wrong, everybody pays. Do members know that according to a report tabled in the House from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, percent of the traffic congestion in Auckland is the result of parents crossing town to take their children to school. We need to get the policy parameters right. I believe that we are on the right track. It is not perfect, but it is on the right track. Another comment I want to make follows on from what I have heard in the debate about ``little Johnny at Auckland Grammar School''. Today, in Auckland it is not little Johnny ``the brown Maori face''; it is little Johnny from Taiwan and Hong Kong who is being excluded. We do not want to talk about it---it is not politically correct to talk about it. There is a very strong anti-Asian sentiment in what has been taking place. I believe in the package of measures that we are looking at---and they have been hard fought for and have taken one helluva long time---and there are some significant changes. For instance, I refer to clause , ``Exemptions from enrolment schemes in exceptional cases''. We in Epsom wanted to see the removal of the word ``exceptional'' because we were dealing with these cases all the time and we did not view them as exceptional cases. We are really saying: ``OK, where enrolment schemes have to be in place because these schools are full, let's make sure that the community is consulted. Let's make sure that the schemes will be coordinated.'' We are now looking at a whole range of provisions that wreak of common-sense. I do not want to get into too much of the legal argy-bargy because at the end of the day the Minister has his lawyers and Trevor Mallard has his lawyers. I am only interested in trying to see some certainty coming into the situation for parents and children. I have spent years of my time as a constituency MP, and there is also the time my electorate agent spends, facing little people who ask: ``Why am I being excluded?''. Parents want certainty. In my area it mostly takes two incomes to meet mortgage payments. The mothers are working their butts off, and the least that people can expect from their taxes is that they will have the right to get their children to school. What we are doing today is terrific, and it is trending in the right direction. I will take issue with one or two of the debaters that somehow the schools are being painted as the bogies. The schools in my community---and I have got a representative of the board of trustees of one of the popular Epsom primary schools---are not the bogies. They are being asked to face up to an unmanageable situation where there are simply too many people for the number of schools. So I hope that, in the debate that will continue, some common sense can come into this. I think that we are trending in the right direction. I just want to remind those who are new to the House of some of the heroes in this. Margaret Austin should be remembered in this debate today for what she has done. I am sure that there has been a certain amount of collaboration across the House, which was well before MMP and in the spirit, I hope, of MMP, but I would like to acknowledge Margaret Austin for the role that she played in actually getting the debate to this point. Locally, I would like to acknowledge Pam Knowles, Bob Demler, and my electorate agents. We were talking about electorate agents being heroes today. My heroine, in this case Lorraine Campbell, has now retired and gone on to a legal career, but she used to field call after call from parents who were just in absolute agony. I would like to remember Reg Lockstone, Gae Griffiths, and Ann Gluckman who took part in the education development initiatives that we had. But, really, I hope that we can see these measures being adopted today, because, although they are not perfect, they will provide a significant improvement over what we have had. At the end of the day, let us come back to first principles. This is about children. This is about New Zealand and affording our children quality education.

I join in with the many comments that have already been made about the two features that need to be debated in this bill: first, the process or procedure; and, second, the substantive question. I should say at once that ACT would expect to support a bill that reinstates for as many people as possible the benefit of the law before the Government changed it. However bad the process, unless something comes out in the examination we will get over the next few weeks, we would expect to support some kind of remedy that limits the damage done by this Government's new law. If that limitation is only in time---in other words, the damage starts from a later date than would otherwise be the case---then we will support it. We will be hoping that the Government learns something over the next couple of weeks: that there are alternatives to something as naked as reversing a Court of Appeal decision---a four to one decision by our highest New Zealand court; a decision that, in my opinion, accords with what I believe the rhetoric around this bill said Parliament intended. When officials advised on whether there should be a transition regime in this bill they focused on getting it operating as soon as possible. They said, quite glibly, that everyone knew it was coming and that the lawyers had had time to look at it. They said that businesses did not need to know exactly when the bill was coming in because they could take the bill into account and make adjustments for it. What the officials told the Government---or what the officials were asked to tell the Government, I cannot tell; I do not blame the officials, because I know now that they may often, privately, have different views from what they are obliged publicly to report---was: ``Don't worry about a transition provision, because people know this bill is coming, and if we do have one, it will delay its application.'' That is exactly what the Court of Appeal has said---that the application of the legislation was to take effect at the earliest available opportunity. Government members are now coming into the House and saying that there is uncertainty and that we must remove it. There is no uncertainty once four judges of the Court of Appeal have said what the law is. They have made the law certain. The Minister's bill will be saying: ``I want it to be more uncertain. I want it to go back, and although I said that what I was doing was important, although I said that this was a protection necessary for New Zealander consumers, and although I went on and on about increasing the threshold, I just don't want it to apply quite as quickly as the law made it apply.'' It is perfectly easy for ACT members to support this bill. We said that the section changes were wrong. We looked at the substance. We looked at Australian law and at the difficulty Australian courts had with it. We looked at the difference in size, and we recognised that nearly all significant acquisitions in New Zealand will mean a substantial lessening of competition. It is such a small market within an Australasian economy, or even within a Pacific economy, that it is almost certain that many New Zealand transactions will substantially lessen competition. ACT stands for integrity in the law. Because ACT members want the law to mean what it says, we said that the Government should not put through a law that will force the Commerce Commission to start finding tricky ways of avoiding its application---because that is what the Commerce Commission will have to do. The Commerce Commission, when applying new section , will not want to interfere with nearly every sensible rationalisation. It will have to start saying: ``Although these words may mean this in Australia, they do not mean that in New Zealand, because in New Zealand we will have to allow business to carry on.'' Instead of harmonising the law, we will, because of section , end up with a law that looks ridiculous and with reason for contempt. There will be contempt from New Zealand business people who will say: ``Why can't I just see what the courts have said in Australia, and apply it? They are the same words, and they have been there for many, many years. Surely it is intended to be the same?'' But no, the New Zealand Commerce Commission will be forced into tricky deals to disguise what it is doing. There is only one set of beneficiaries out of that: the lawyers and the consultants---the people who have to come along and give evidence, the people who have to provide the camouflage for the commission to show that the public interest justifies drawing conclusions from this new law that are not dictated by the words, and the people who create the sophisticated arguments and rationalisations to make the words deceitful, making the bill mean something other than what it says. They are the ones who will benefit, and it is business that meets the expense. The Minister now has an opportunity to do a proper fix of this. We would have supported it today. A proper fix here is not the Government saying: ``In effect, the Court of Appeal got it wrong, and we will simply reverse it.'' A proper fix says: ``We made a mistake. We now recognise that we do not mind the transactions that were caught on the cusp, straddling the introduction date. We want them to go ahead. We do not want the commission to have to go back and apply the new test to them because it might have to stop them. We recognise that that is undesirable.'' The Minister now has a chance to say: ``I've given this thing a test run. It was very obvious that, right from the start, it wasn't working.'' The Minister can fix this by saying: ``Let's repeal the silly changes we made in May. It's automatically fixed.'' There is one remaining thing that someone of principle would have in mind. An organisation, a cooperative of New Zealand grocers, has spent money to uphold its view of the law, and the Court of Appeal has said it was right. I do not know what the members of the cooperative have spent, but if we add in executive time, evidence gathering, and lawyers' fees, it was probably something like half a million dollars---or they have probably lost half a million dollars in a lost opportunity, because there could have been something better that they could have been doing. This Parliament should not reverse a decision obtained by those people in good faith, without compensating them for at least their out-of-pocket expenses. That will be one of the first things we will be pressing for when this is reviewed, as a matter of principle. To reverse a court decision should have us looking ashamed. It is appalling for the rule of law to have Parliament even looking as though it could contemplate a reversal of a decision a day after it is released. What kind of evaluation can the Government of New Zealand say it gave in a day? What kind of urgency can the Government claim? I have spoken to the representative of four of the people this legislation is supposed to rescue. They understand that as long as they know it is coming, and provided they will be able to rely on the longstanding law New Zealand evolved over years, it is not going to cause enormous loss. There is one party for whom delay may be problematic, and who may lose the deal. Progressive Enterprises may find it cannot arrange its funding, and that may be horrific for the company if it cannot be sorted out. The Minister may like to know that, interestingly enough, the Consumers Institute was bewailing the fact that his new law would not apply in terms of the Progressive Enterprises case. Others were concerned that the Minister's new law would not apply. There may well be people coming before the select committee who will say that, although from their perspective there needs to be an urgent revisiting of the impact of section in relation to the Progressive Enterprises case, there may need to be some amelioration. Something far more specific may be needed than the very crude instrument of this bill, which was introduced---as the Minister said---to create certainty, but in fact does the opposite. This is an embarrassing day for the New Zealand Parliament. The Minister has been rescued, I believe, by ACT's objection, by the Speaker's refusal to be stampeded into accepting extraordinary urgency, and by the Greens saying that they, too, would not allow this embarrassment to go forward. The Minister should be grateful. The best thing to do would be to reverse the original bad decision, and make it a principled fix.

I have so many amendments, and minutes in which to cover them. Plainly, I have to prioritise. I could spend minutes talking about the complete contempt for free speech, as shown in this bill. An example is the situation at Ocean Beach, where ultimately the corrupt union executive had to be displaced by management. They had to explain to the workers just what was going on, and how they could defeat it. That could not happen under this bill, because disclosure of that information would be undermining the union---as, indeed, it had to be. So truth is no defence. I could spend the time talking about the threat to people in business when information has to be given to the unions for multi-employer agreements, and then that information can be used against the business or its competitors. I see there is no provision for penalties where knowledge of that information is misused. I understand the drafting difficulty of that. The provision intends the misuse of information. It is intended that it will be used by unions as a ratchet against employers: when they say they cannot do something the unions can use the information against them by comparing them with their competitors. Instead of talking further about that, I want to go to the base thing in this bill: the Orwellian misuse of language, the abuse of the term ``good faith'' in relation to provisions that, in fact, encourage the opposite. Good faith is a matter of conscience. It is how one feels about something. It is a matter of one's beliefs. It is not a matter of conduct. What we have in this bill is the elevation of process, as the courts or the authority struggle to discern what someone is feeling, from his or her overt conduct. What is the consequence when we get this sort of slogan law? The sly and the smart get the advantage. Straightforward people, blunt people, people who are used to going straight to the bottom line, get trapped when they are not sly enough to go through the rituals of process. What will be the advice from prudent lawyers? What is the advice from those sorts of people already? I see here seminars advertised by a law firm that is charging $ to teach employers how to cope with the unions. These are the sort of things they say: ``Do not make blunt statements.''; ``Do not be straightforward.''; ``Do pretend to reflect carefully, however outrageous the demands.''; ``Always think about it.''; ``Take the demand away for further consideration.''; ``From North America it's quite clear that if you react quickly and intuitively you're probably disadvantaged.''; ``Start high; don't go anywhere near where you expect to end up. You've got to leave room to compromise.'' Both parties, of course, have to play the same idle game. They must start as far apart as possible so that in this ritual dance they can both show they have made concessions; they have moved toward each other. That is what the courts have to do to find good faith. Employers must learn the ritual dance of offer and counteroffer. They should make sure they leave enough time. Part goes to great lengths to ensure that the times are specified. That at least will protect some innocents, who might otherwise have gone directly to their bottom line, what they could afford, and then been trapped by failing to demonstrate good faith. Above all, employers should remember that this is about a state of conscience, and, since no-one can see a person's conscience, they should learn to display it. One of the Marx Brothers summed up good faith in perfect terms. ``If you can fake sincerity, you've got it made.'' That is what we will be doing to change the culture in New Zealand. Laws do not make good faith. Good faith comes from people who know what their obligations are. But this law does not tell them. It comes from people who are in a market where there is a labour shortage, where the interests of the low paid are best dealt with by giving them the bargaining power that comes from the fact that there are not enough of them. It does not come from destroying jobs. I turn now to the specifics. For example, clause (c) states that the object of this part is---``(c) to recognise the view of the parties to collective bargaining as to what constitutes good faith;''. How is that view recognised? That is done by appointing a couple of representatives of peak organisations to go through a dance---probably like the Heart of the Nation report---give it back to the Minister, the Minister ``recognises the view of the parties to collective bargaining as to what constitutes good faith'', and does that by rejecting that view and imposing her own. That is the approval process. How does a collective agreement vary? It is certainly not by going back through consultation, not by asking for representatives of the true parties here. Of course, the true parties do not come into this. This is all about unions and peak employers. This is nothing to do with the , or ,, or however many employers there are.

I rise to support this bill. The previous speaker is perfectly correct. I understand that the Government of New Zealand, in terms of the Labour Party and the Alliance in this Parliament, will be supporting this bill. I want to compliment the member opposite on the work that she has done to date. This is a good example of when an individual member of Parliament can help to make a difference. The member will forgive me if I refer to the letter. I too got a letter. It had two photos on it. It had one of the Hon. Marie Hasler, and it had one of a dog called Max. I will confess that I looked at the two photos, and, as much as I respect the member opposite, Max won the day. I just say to the member opposite that if she wants to convince this member of other bits of legislation, she should get Max to write to the Government, because she will then have a good chance. In fact, Max gave me lots of licks, and I appreciated that. I take the opportunity to quote from Max's letter. Max was writing on behalf of Hearing Dogs for Deaf People in New Zealand, which is a charitable trust set up for the purpose of providing dogs for hearing-impaired people. I want to emphasise the kind of uses that dogs, when properly trained, will have for hearing-impaired New Zealanders. For example, it was interesting that the letter went through the things about monitoring a trained response to the telephone or fax ringing, an alarm clock, a baby monitor, a cooker timer, a knock at the door, a door bell, and a fire bell. The thing that alerted my attention, and to be honest it was not something I had given a huge amount of thought to, was the smoke alarm. It was very interesting to read an article entitled ``Partnership in action'' from the magazine Communicate in its Autumn edition. It was about smoke alarms. Smoke alarms are wonderful things. They protect our families and homes. I will refer to the article, because I think it is a very relevant part of this debate and why this bill is important. Smoke alarms protect our families and homes. They improve our sense of security. They are fairly cheap, costing about the same as two tickets to the movies, but for many deaf New Zealanders and hearing-impaired people, this simple lifesaving device is inaccessible. How does a deaf person hear the sound of this lifesaving device? Smoke alarms for deaf people are available at a cost of about $ each. They are times more expensive than smoke alarms designed for hearing people. It states in that article that a simple proven solution is a hearing-ear dog, and, indeed, a nudge on the arm by this warm-blooded ``hearing aid'' lets many deaf people know that a sound has occurred that they cannot hear. I was very interested to read that hearing-ear dogs are specially trained, obviously to become the ears of a deaf or severely hearing-impaired person. When it hears a sound that it has been trained to respond to, the hearing-ear dog alerts its recipient by pawing the person and, where appropriate, leading him or her to the source of the sound. Of course, that can be very important, particularly in the case of a fire. This bill also alerts, shall we say, our consciousness in this area. To be honest, it is something that I as an individual New Zealander had not given too much thought to, but obviously what this bill intends to do is to convey to dogs specially trained to assist the deaf, the same situation as applies to specially trained dogs who assist sight-impaired New Zealanders. I take the opportunity to compliment the organisation, Hearing Dogs for Deaf People in New Zealand, on the excellent work that it has done. I notice in a New Zealand Herald article online the example of the case of Gavin and Suzette Poyner who want their new dog Bilbo to lend them his ears, and indeed that is what he does. I quote from the New Zealand Herald online article: ``The -month old is a hearing dog for the Tauranga couple, who were both born deaf. Bilbo has been settling enthusiastically into his new home this week, with trainer Johanna Brens helping him to acclimatise. The couple say Bilbo will make their lives easier by alerting them to a knock at the door, a page rolling off the fax, and the alarm clock and smoke alarms.'' I note that the article, which is very interesting, says that as well as being eager to please, the dog is also tuning into their sign language and reading hand signals and body language. This dog apparently is the third officially trained hearing-ear dog to be placed. Others have been placed in Napier and Nelson, and were also selected and schooled by an Auckland trust---Hearing Dogs for Deaf People in New Zealand. Indeed, after years of voluntary work to establish a hearing-ear dog programme, Ms Brens, from Hearing Dogs for Deaf People---who is hearing impaired herself and schooled her own dog---became a full-time trainer last year. I just want to commend Ms Brens, and I commend this charitable organisation. This is a wonderful start, and I think New Zealanders should support this excellent organisation. The programme was set up years ago by Ms Brens and Hannah Samuel. Meeting international standards, they select a range of breeds and crossbred dogs from animal rescue centres or pounds, as mentioned by the previous speaker. It is interesting that Ms Brens also estimates that about , dogs could meet the criteria and become hearing-ear dogs, but at present there is not enough money, staff, or time to train dogs for the several dozen people on the waiting list. But at least a small but very significant start is to get the legislation right, and through the process of legislation this will go a huge way towards raising public awareness. We take it for granted when we see a guide dog accompanying a sight-impaired person. That is a feature, and thanks to this bill---because I think it will have a speedy passage through the select committee-we will see more dogs helping hearing-impaired New Zealanders. Finally, I want to compliment the Hon. Marie Hasler. I would have voted for the bill, anyway, but the one that really swung it for me, I have to tell members, was Max. He convinced me. It is not often that a politician gets licked, certainly, and praised. But I say thank you to Max and thank you to the Hearing Dogs for Deaf People in New Zealand. The Government supports this bill. I support it going to a select committee, and, hopefully, not before too long, it will become law and the organisation and hearing-impaired New Zealanders can start to realise the benefits and advantages of having hearing-ear dogs.

The member for Waikaremoana mentioned the word ``equity'', which is one word that the Opposition spokesman on education will never mention. He did not mention, however, when he talked about students from low-income families who might be affected by fees, that those very students are exempt from the fees. University students from low-income families pay fewer dollars in entrance fees than they did under the old regime. Low-income students pay $ a year, and many of them have had their student income support more than doubled. It is an indictment on the member whose name is on the Bill that he has pledged publicly that he will cut the income support for low-income students and students over the age of years. That is how much importance a National Government would place on equity. It would cut student income support to students who come from low-income families or older students with a spouse or dependants when that family is living on a low wage. The Opposition has never stood for equity. Its promises to students and superannuitants have nothing to do with equity, but much to do with giving more to those who have and taking away from those who already have very little. The Bill would allow higher tuition fees to be imposed on students without the Government's being seen to be responsible for taking that action. In the Bill there is nothing whatsoever to stop any tertiary council from introducing the full user-pays principle on any courses that it likes, or from charging much higher fees on any or all students. The Bill introduces open slather. It takes the responsibility from the Government and puts it on the council. It tells the council that it can charge full fees to anyone it likes. The Bill removes the present protection that the Government gives by way of fees exemptions to -year-old and -year-old students, to those studying courses at or below a seventh form level in a tertiary institution, to those teenage students from low-income families, and to those students with spouses or dependants and a low family income. It allows any fee whatsoever to be charged, and it removes the protection that low-income students have. The Bill is a ``Pontius Pilate Bill''. It allows the Government to wash its hands of any responsibility for the level of tuition fees imposed on students. The Bill would make students worse off than they are at present. They certainly would not be better off. If fees are introduced by the Government as an elected body the students themselves can hold those elected representatives responsible for their action. If the fees are imposed by a council that is not elected at large the student population has no come-back if an unreasonable level of fees is imposed. The Opposition is revealing its secret agenda. We all know---and the member for Selwyn admits it---that the Opposition has promised $. billion in revenue cuts. In addition, it has promised hundreds of millions of dollars in spending. The figure for the superannuation policy alone was $ million or $ million. Opposition members have never been able to explain to New Zealanders where the money will come from---in other words, how a National Government would bridge the deficit between the reduced revenue and the increased spending. My ministry has costed the Opposition's promises in tertiary education alone at $ million. If a National Government kept the promise to remove tertiary fees $ million of that would have to be found elsewhere. The fact is that that $ million is not there. The member for Selwyn, the Opposition spokeswoman on finance, knows that well. In the past year an extra $ million has been spent on increasing student income support---in particular, targeting that support to students on low incomes. Another $ million has been set aside so that next year, for the first time in New Zealand's history, the Government can fully fund the growth in student numbers and allow any tertiary institution to take in anybody who is qualified to attend that institution. There is no way that a National Government, if elected, would be able to find $ million without slogging the taxpayers.
