I am not convinced that the mechanism by which a District Court judge can be sued for gross negligence or carelessness, which is by way of excessive jurisdiction, is the best way of ensuring judicial accountability. But I do know that the people of New Zealand expect all categories of professional people in this country to be held accountable, and judges are certainly not an exception to that rule. Before we deny the ordinary citizen of this country a remedy against gross negligence or carelessness, we need more than this sort of clause smuggled into this sort of Bill to justify doing so. I believe that we have to have accountability. I believe that it is a nonsense even to think about bringing in a clause of this nature---the more so when that wider issue has been referred to the Law Commission and is awaiting a report of the Law Commission. The Opposition was successful in the committee at getting the Government to drop that clause out of this Bill, and rightly so---it should never have been there. The Opposition was not successful in having that clause discharged altogether, which was the appropriate response to a piece of legislation that was ill-thought-out, opposed by the Law Society, opposed by the Legislation Advisory Committee, and it should never come back before this House. In looking at the Bill as a whole, there are a number of measures here that are likely to improve the effectiveness of the justice system, and we will ensure that those measures are facilitated in their passage through the House. We would want to see the remainder of this Bill passed by the House at the earliest opportunity. The reason for that is there cannot be a member in this House who was not disgusted to see a dozen cases dropped without evidence even being heard, where serious criminal charges have been brought against individuals because the justice system had failed. Those cases had been hanging around for in excess of months and the court ruled, in accordance with the Bill of Rights, that those cases be dropped.
That's just keeping up with the cost of living. What is the Minister talking about?

The Bill sets out that if a DNA profile cannot be gained from that, then the High Court judge required to provide a compulsion order can take account of that and may order the blood profile anyway. In the first instance, if a person has a genuine objection to giving a blood sample, that person can provide a sample from a number of hair follicles or from a mouth swab. We looked at the accuracy of DNA. DNA profiling is not a perfect way of determining a unique characteristic of an individual. In other words, it is not like a fingerprint. There is the possibility of a chance match but, according to the Institute of Environmental Science and Research scientists, that possibility is as low as one in several million. What DNA does, without any doubt at all, is provide powerful corroborative evidence that the person whose DNA profile matches the sample left at the crime is the person who has committed that crime. In the case of the serial rapist, DNA profiling was essential. In the second case that was recently before the court---the murder of Janine Law---again, DNA was essential in the gaining of that conviction. This was a murder-rape that was committed years ago, but on the provision of a blood sample by James Tamata that matched the DNA profile taken at the time of the murder, it was clear that the sample had an identical DNA profile. On the basis of that evidence, James Tamata pleaded guilty. The point I want to make is that in both these cases the DNA profile was gained by consent, without the requirement of this Bill. But without the sample, should either of those men have denied the police a sample of blood or other tissue, then the chances of arresting and convicting those men would have been reduced accordingly. That is not to say that they might not ultimately have been arrested, but the task of doing so and the certainty that the court had the right person would have been reduced. As the significance of DNA profiling becomes better known, in terms of providing powerful evidence for the conviction of an offender, it is possible---indeed I would argue likely---that offenders over time will become less likely to volunteer a sample. Certainly the person who knows he has committed the offence and knows that the provision of a sample will convict him is the very person who is not likely, by consent, to provide a sample. Even now, a smart criminal would not provide a sample voluntarily. Had Tamata or Thompson refused to provide that sample, that would have lessened the chances of their conviction. Those who are opposed to compulsion as the ultimate resort for gaining a blood sample, argue that if a suspect refuses to give a sample, then an inference can be taken from that and an inference can be drawn in court to a jury that the accused has something to hide. That may be well and good. However, if insufficient evidence means that the charge cannot be laid in the first place, then the use of the inference becomes irrelevant. Further, one could argue that the prospect of justice being done in court is much weaker if conviction relies on more subjective factors, such as the memory of witnesses, the alibis, or the skill or otherwise of a lawyer, which too often depends on what the defendant can afford to pay for that lawyer. What I like about DNA evidence is that it is much more objective. It provides greater certainty that the right outcome has been achieved. This benefits the innocent and reduces the possibility that the guilty will escape conviction. I am in favour of there being an ultimate resort to compulsion to gain a body sample, but the Bill sets down important prerequisites that must be met before a High Court judge will order that a sample be taken. Those prerequisites include limiting compulsion to a range of serious offences such as sexual violation, manslaughter, or murder. Another prerequisite is that the result of the DNA profile must be likely to prove guilt or innocence. Thirdly, and most important, the High Court judge must believe there is good cause to suspect that the person being asked to provide the sample did commit the offence. Those are important prerequisites. They rule out the prospect that compulsion could be used, for example, as a fishing expedition to take blood from a large number of people. There must be good cause to suspect. That judgment is made not by the police; it is made by a High Court judge. As a result of the proposal put forward by the Opposition, the judge will also take into account whether the suspect has been given the opportunity to provide a sample other than blood. I believe that is also an important factor in overcoming the small number of cases in which there may be religious or other objections to giving blood. Where the order is made that a sample be taken by compulsion, that sample cannot be a venous sample. It must be by way of finger-prick, and that limits the intrusiveness of this measure. We know that where ultimate resort provides for compulsion to be used, in fact the reasonable force allowed under this Bill will very rarely, if ever, have to be used. In in the state of Victoria, similar legislation to this was passed. In the years that have elapsed since that time, force has never had to be used. There is already ample evidence that where there is no provision for compulsion to be used as an ultimate resort, some serious offenders simply will not be brought to justice, and the select committee looked at examples of this. I want to give the House just two examples. In the first case, the complainant had gone to bed intoxicated and was asleep. The offender entered the room and raped her. The victim could not identify the offender because of, first, her state of intoxication and, second, the fact that she was asleep. The offender admitted to the police that he had indecently assaulted the victim but denied the rape. A medical examination proved without doubt that the woman had been raped, but because the offender refused to provide a blood sample the only charge that could be brought against that man was the lesser offence of sexual assault. In the second case, a man by the name of Pira in robbed a dairy, assaulted the owner and his wife, battered the woman, and raped the woman. Pira was identified as the suspect, along with other gang associates. He alone, however, refused to provide a blood sample. There was insufficient evidence to charge him. Eighteen months later, again approached by the police, Pira agreed to provide the sample, a positive match was made, he pleaded guilty, and he was sentenced to years' imprisonment. Compulsion clearly does involve the individual giving up an element of that person's rights. Such individual rights should not be intruded upon lightly. However, within the parameters laid down in this legislation, I believe that the surrender of some individual rights in these circumstances is justified by the broader public good that is achieved. A finger-prick is a small intrusion to achieve justice within the context of the massive intrusion represented by rape and the damage done to and the denial of the rights of the victim by the offender. While I support compulsion as a last resort, I do acknowledge that that view is not shared by others. Indeed, submissions before the select committee opposed the use of force, including submissions made by the Law Commission, the Medical Association, and the Privacy Commissioner. I respect the stand taken by the member for Tamaki, who said that he will vote against compulsion, and I know there may be others on this side of the House who will join him in this as a matter of conscience. Speaking personally, however, I am not prepared to leave a massive loophole by not adopting compulsion as the ultimate sanction. The guilty will most certainly take advantage of such a loophole, knowing full well that providing a sample for DNA purposes would clearly confirm their guilt. It has to be taken into account, too, that compulsion is not unique to this legislation. Arrested persons, for many years in New Zealand, have had compulsorily to provide their fingerprints. That is a clear parallel. Suspected drinking drivers must, as a matter of law, provide an evidential breath analysis or a blood sample. Again, we have made the decision that there are times when individual rights must be subordinated to the overall good of the community. This legislation does not break new ground in that sense. Turning broadly to another area covered by the Bill---that of providing a sample by consent---it is, of course, possible even now, without legislation, to gain a blood sample by consent. This legislation makes very clear the procedures that must be followed by the police and the safeguards that must be provided to the person asked for a blood sample. In most cases, those asked to provide samples will be innocent of the offence and it is important that people asked for co-operation should be fully aware of their rights. The Bill provides that people must be given oral and written information about the request, they must be informed that they are free to consent or to withhold consent, and they must be informed of the right to consult a lawyer. The person must be told that he is free to withdraw his consent at any time before the sample is taken. These safeguards, I believe, are as good as can be provided in legislation. There must be, however, proper monitoring of the use of consent requests to be equally sure that the safeguards are being applied in practice by the police. The problem in terms of voluntary consent here is not the inadequacy of the legislation, but to ensure that the constable on the beat who is asking for the sample is following the procedures set down. Last, I come to the third major issue in this Bill, and that is the issue of the DNA profile databank, which is established under the legislation. The Bill makes provision for the taking of blood samples, either by consent or from offenders who are convicted of certain serious offences, for a databank in which the DNA profiles of those persons will be stored for future investigative purposes. In the case of those convicted of serious offences, the offences in the schedule, the police may apply to the sentencing court for a compulsion order to place the DNA profile of offenders on the databank. Consent will be given in those cases by the High Court judge as a matter of course. However, other people may be asked to provide a blood sample so that their DNA profile can be placed on the databank as a matter of consent. They may subsequently withdraw their consent and, if they do so, their profile will be destroyed. However, along with the Department of Justice, the Privacy Commissioner, and others, I have concern about the scope of the databank. The databank concept was sold as being an offenders databank. Yet the Bill as currently drafted places no restriction on anyone's profile being held on the databank provided they give consent. I question the wisdom of mixing up in the databank the profiles of the innocent and the guilty alike. I question the need for profiles of innocent people to be held at all. I, therefore, will be proposing in the Committee stage an amendment limiting the databank to the holding of the profiles of only those who have been convicted of an offence punishable by imprisonment. It is clear that the police would prefer the databank to be wide open. However, they acknowledged in the committee that they could live with my amendment and that that would not significantly impede the purposes for which they are likely to want to use the databank. In conclusion, I support this Bill strongly. I endorse the safeguards that are laid down for blood samples taken by voluntary consent. I acknowledge the need for compulsion as a last resort in specific circumstances to gain a sample. I support the databank but I believe that it should be confined to being an offenders databank.

I will come to that in a moment. We gave the Minister every opportunity to justify why prisons should be privatised. He said they were not being privatised. Some of the members of the Government said that they were. What it comes down to, however, is that a core function normally operated by the State has been taken from the State and put in the hands of the private sector in a way that has not been done before, and, therefore, this legislation establishes a new landmark for privatisation. We did debate this at considerable length---it went through weeks of Committee stage. It was opposed at every point by the Labour Opposition, and, on the rare occasions that the third parties were here, they opposed it too. I thought it was a little bit rich for the Alliance leader to say, over the weekend, that more should have been done to oppose the Bill. I asked the Whips a moment ago what the voting record was on that Bill during the Committee stage, and, of the first votes, the leader of the Alliance missed and her previous leader missed even more. They were out of the House. The votes during the Committee stage were often as close as a four-vote margin, yet in those votes this very evening, had the four members of the minor parties been here, this legislation could have been stopped. We opposed this Bill in Committee because the Government failed to make a case for privatisation. It failed to make the case for a core State function being transferred to the private sector. We argued that the deprivation of liberty and the removal of normal civil rights from an individual are part of the State's core functions. Ethically, the deprivation of liberty has not, in New Zealand, been deemed to be a suitable function to put in the hands of the commercial sector, to be market and profit-driven. In the Committee stage the onus was on the Government to prove that there were advantages from doing so that overrode the assumption of the vast majority of New Zealanders that imprisonment is a role of the public sector. Government members failed to provide any hard evidence at all that there were major benefits to be achieved from privatisation. They implied, from time to time, that there would be cost savings, but they could not actually demonstrate that cost savings had been achieved by privatised prisons overseas. Nor could the Government guarantee that, if cost savings were to be made by privatising prisons, this would not undermine operational standards. The truth is that the Government, throughout this debate, has lacked a public mandate to proceed with this legislation. The uncertainty of the Government in proceeding with the Bill following the result of the last election is clear evidence of that fact. The Minister of Justice, himself, conceded that it would not be the end of the world if this legislation did not go through. A year later, when the Government's promises of consensus have faded and have now been broken, this Bill is back here. A recent public opinion poll, as we debated in the Committee stage, showed that there is support for this Bill from approximately one-third of the population. There is support from only one-third of the population; two-thirds opposed it or remained unconvinced by it. Nearly half opposed the measure outright. The other point raised in the Committee stage was that this Bill should have been referred back to a select committee. As introduced, the Minister disclosed in this Bill only part of his agenda. He later added the provision about privatisation of prison escort services and court custody, without the opportunity for the broader public to make submissions on that part of the Bill. We then had a further supplementary order paper dated June, which was pages long. It sat around for months when it could have been looked at by the select committee, but it was not looked at. I can only take from that that the Minister did not have the strength of conviction that this Bill could withstand that scrutiny. In the Committee stage the Government failed to put forward evidence to justify privatisation or to demonstrate its advantages. Even on cost savings---the Government's bottom line---the evidence was lacking. Reference was made to the work of Dr John Pratt, who is one of our foremost experts in prison policy in New Zealand. He has said recently that recent research shows little cost savings from privatisation. That is from an objective and well-informed outside source. A recent report from Britain, again referred to in the Committee stage, showed that the first privatised prison in Britain---the Wolds---had a million overrun in the last year.
Given the reported percent increase in serious crimes committed by young offenders since , what has he done this year to prevent the surge in juvenile offending?
Has he been advised of any examples of fire services which have been privatised, and have any of the current Fire Service Commission visited any such services?

This is really a curious evening. The House is sitting after o'clock on a Friday night. The last Bill that we took under urgency had been drafted / years ago, but for some inexplicable reason had taken / years to be introduced, but it was still brought in under urgency. This legislation is being introduced, in part, to change a piece of legislation that is years old. It has taken years to decide that we need to change this and we have had to do it with such a rush and in such urgency that it had to be brought in under extraordinary conditions on a Friday night. It suggests to me that this process tonight is an absolute farce because we are dealing with legislation that does not need to be debated under urgency. We are dealing with a slack Minister, who takes a long time to bring legislation into the House, and we are having to deal with it at o'clock on a Friday night. The extradition law, however, is an important piece of legislation. It is important legislation because extradition means the surrender by one State, at the request of another, of a person who has been accused or convicted of an offence committed within the jurisdiction of the requesting State. It creates some obligations for New Zealand to pass across its citizens to some other regime in some other part of the world to be tried and punished for an offence that that person is alleged to have committed. That is a surrender of sovereign rights. We would not normally do that lightly but, in contemporary society, we must broaden the provision for extradition because it is in the interests of every State that crimes acknowledged as such do not go unpunished. We are now living in an international community, and in the community of nations clearly we should give every assistance to bringing people, guilty of crimes, to justice in whatever nation those crimes might have been committed. So the Labour Party supports this legislation. It supports the procedures that are set down within it and it also supports the safeguards that are put in place to ensure that we will not be sending New Zealand citizens to countries where they may be subject to procedures that would not be regarded as just in this country, and to a punishment that we might not regard as acceptable. In that regard I would like the Minister to explain the situation that applies where a person is being considered for extradition to a country in which, if convicted of the alleged offence, that person may be subject to capital punishment. I understand that the procedure is that the Minister must agree to that before extradition takes place.

We did not oppose the Bill. This Bill is in the House today as a reaction to a draft member's Bill that I was threatening the Government with. I was telling the Minister years ago in the House, when he was denying there was a problem, that these measures were needed. The Minister should not come into the House now and say that this was a great idea of his, and ask why the Opposition did not have something constructive to give. The Opposition has been entirely constructive. For years it has been promoting measures to recognise and deal with the major problem of drug and alcohol addiction in prisons. It has taken the Minister and his predecessor as long as that to come up to par on the issue. I want from the Minister an attempt at least at an explanation of whether he is committed to concepts such as a drug-free unit. I want to know that he is committed to a realistic sum of money being spent to reduce the level of drug and alcohol addiction, in order, in turn, to reduce the level of criminal offending by those addicts when they are put out in the community. I tell the Minister that for every dollar we invest in a programme that can be proved to be effective, we are saving a huge economic and human cost to the community. If there is any reason for this Parliament to exist at all it is to work on behalf of people in the community. It is to put in place things that we know will be effective in improving their day-to-day security and in protecting them from the ravages of criminals in this society---most of whom suffer from drug and alcohol addiction problems as a contributing factor to their offending. The Minister knows---and I understand that the Chairman certainly knows---that if we put a person into prison we might keep them off drugs for the year or years that they are there, but if the craving for alcohol and drugs is not reduced, and if a change is not produced within that person to control that craving, then nothing has been achieved for the safety of the community when that person is released back into it. What I am asking the Minister for is very straightforward. Has he, together with his officials, a commitment to a realistic level of expenditure on effective substance abuse programmes? Will drug-free wings be opened up along the lines of the most effective programmes overseas, such as the therapeutic community? Is the exercise that we are indulging in today a key part of a much more effective strategy to address that problem, or is it simply so much political hot air to take the pressure off the Minister, because the public recognises the drug problems that exist in the prisons today?

According to the analysts, the social policy expenditure that is voted in this Budget is overwhelmingly to the benefit of middle and upper income people. Measures such as the abolition of the surcharge do not benefit people at the bottom of the heap. Those measures benefit people on relatively high incomes. We had some token expenditure directed at, for example, improving education in some of the low socio-economic areas. But essentially this Budget does nothing to reverse the growing entrenchment of a social underclass in New Zealand. By failing to confront social disadvantage, and by failing to confront the problems of dysfunctional families, this Government is condemning a growing proportion of our young children to lives of dependency, of anti-social behaviour, and of criminal offending. Every child who grows up with a poor start, who grows up poorly educated, with ill health or with major social problems, represents the waste of an individual's life. But more than that, it represents an enormous cost to our society as a whole. That individual who is neglected from birth, with the failure of the Government to intervene in the way that it should intervene to ensure that every child gets a good start in life, goes through life to become poorly educated, unemployed, and has a much greater chance of becoming a criminal offender with major social problems. Such people make no contribution to the economy through their productivity or taxation. They are a cost to the economy. Yet again in another Budget this Government has failed to learn that social prevention is much cheaper and much more effective than cure. Where is the vision in this Budget that will do something to intervene to ensure that children get the start in life that they deserve? I want to go on to another major scandal. I invite the next Government speaker to comment and give us his or her explanation of why this Government has failed to address the need of New Zealanders to be protected against a growing crime rate. I quote from a statement made less than a year ago. It states: ``The rate of criminal offending has escalated. Violent crimes spiral ever upwards and large numbers of law-abiding New Zealanders live in fear. The uncomfortable truth is that crime is out of control. Our thin blue line is losing the battle against crime.'' That was a quote from July last year. It was a quote from the now Treasurer, the Hon. Winston Peters. What has changed in the year that has passed since he made that comment? I will tell members what has changed. He has become the Treasurer, and he is now in a position to do something about the problem that he described so fiercely last year. He has failed. He has cut the police budget. Despite the efforts from this side of the House, the Minister of Police has failed to ensure that the people whom he should be representing around the Cabinet table got a fair slice of the action. The police budget has been cut by over $ million, notwithstanding the fact that each year half a million crimes are being committed, notwithstanding the fact that the crime rate in this country has increased by over percent since this Government assumed power in , and notwithstanding the fact that violent crimes are up by percent on . There are now , burglaries each year---, cases of people's homes being broken into and their property stolen and desecrated. What percentage of those criminals are convicted? Fifteen percent! People who are crims who go out and knock-off somebody else's home know that they have an percent chance of getting away with it. What is there in this Budget that protects people against that sort of desecration of their property? The answer is nothing! Earlier this year I exposed a Treasury paper that stated in fairly frank and blunt terms that if we give the police more money the problem is that they will go out there and catch more crims, and if they catch more crims it will cost us more money to put them through the justice system and jail them. That is absurd. There would not be a member in this House who would stand up to defend that statement. But this Budget is evidence that the Treasury position prevails. I repeat that the total funding for the police in this Budget is down by $ million. The promise of extra police is an illusion, a deception, and a lie. The force is already members down. The extra officers do not even cover the existing shortfall. Worse, during July the jobs of police officers will be cut to compensate for the cost of the police computer, the integrated national crime information system, notwithstanding that the computer system does not come into effect for months. It comes into effect in December , but we are taking police out of the ranks now to pay for it. Even the Minister of Police admitted that when the computer is up and running there is no guarantee that it will produce the efficiencies claimed for it. That is a nonsense, and this side of the House will continue to expose the lunacy of that action until it is reversed. Worse still, we might be getting new recruits but it is estimated that we will lose experienced officers this year--- experienced officers to be replaced by raw recruits. That does not make sense. It is time for the Government to live up to the rhetoric of its coalition document and give the police the resources to do the job of protecting New Zealanders against the growing rate of crime. This Government has failed. That Minister has failed. They should both go.

Let me address the points made by Dr Mapp. I have looked at the National Party proposals in terms of ``life means life''. What do those proposals mean? They mean that for the next years nothing will happen, absolutely nothing. In years' time we will lock up two extra people a year for life, and what does it mean to lock them up for life? It is exactly what the United States is starting to move away from at the moment. It has been found that when people in prisons are in wheelchairs and walkers it costs three times as much to keep them there. On average it costs $, a year for people who constitute almost no risk to society. If we are to spend money to protect society, we spend money dealing with those violent offenders who do pose a risk. The money is put into prevention and put into policing. That will make a difference, but National's proposal is purely politicking and it will get the National Party nowhere. The statement made by Bill English was entirely discredited. The member talks about risk. There is one person I am aware of---in the last century---convicted of murder who, on release, murdered again, and that was Dennis Luke. As far as I am concerned he should be locked up until he is in a wheelchair---he has murdered twice. What is really good about this legislation is that, for the first time, it recognises that there are different circumstances in relation to murder, and some murders require a person to be locked away for a very long time. The previous minimum period of sentence for those atrocious murders was years. Under this bill it is up percent to years, and that is only the starting point. Under the principles of sentencing in this bill, for the very worst Karla Cardno - type murders, the judge could decide to lock people away for , , , or years if that is required because of the nature of the offender and the nature of the offence. The characteristics of those who will be locked up for that period of time are set out clearly in the legislation. This legislation makes the penalties for those guilty of the worst forms of murders with aggravating factors much, much tougher. It should have come in, years ago. The National Party, supported by ACT, should have brought it in years ago. It did not. It was happy with years for the entire three terms of its parliamentary life, and now it is saying that what we are doing is not enough. The National Party did nothing for years, and now it is saying we are not going far enough, when we have nearly doubled the minimum sentence for that category of murderers. It is a bit of a farce. A lot of other provisions in this part make life tougher for those who constitute a risk. Preventive detention is expanded in three ways. It now applies to those who are as young as , because, regrettably, people at that age are capable of committing offences and being a huge risk to the community. They should not have to wait until they are to get preventive detention. Preventive detention should apply from age . Secondly, there is no longer the prerequisite of already having previously been convicted of a serious offence. If people are deemed to be dangerous to the community to the extent that they justify preventive detention, then they should be given it without the need for that prerequisite and without the ability of somebody like Taffy Hotene to go out and do it again. That is a major change. Thirdly, we are widening the range of sexual and violent offences for preventive detention, which means, effectively, that a life sentence can be applied. Mr Franks raised the question of the minimum period. Yes, the minimum period for imprisonment under preventive detention is years, which is the minimum period that will apply, perhaps in those sorts of cases that previously would not have been given it. But I can guarantee to the member that the average minimum period a judge applies will be much, much longer than that. I can guarantee that to the member. The legislation is tougher in that regard. Finally, the provisions for reparations are also strengthened under this part. We want to ensure that in every case the judge has to consider reparations. That is why the judge, in open court, must give a reason if reparations are not imposed. I believe that reparations should be imposed whenever there is the prospect of getting money out of the offender. I oppose the amendment by Dr Mapp, because it states that reparations will always be imposed. It is useless imposing a sentence that will never be carried out. That is why we give the discretion to the court, but it is also why we require the court to state its reasons in open court if reparations are not set. That strengthens the presumption that reparations will be required of offenders whenever there is any chance of those offenders paying the money.

I want to address a couple of issues that have not been specifically brought up yet. The key issue that has been brought up is the right of little Johnny to go to the school next door to him, and I do not think that is the most contentious issue in this legislation. It seems to me that the issue that we need to address, and the one that needs to be resolved by this legislation, is the fact that since there has been a huge tendency of people to ``choose'' schools, where they can do so, in socio-economic areas that are higher than the ones in which they live. Although there have been some counter-tendencies, in general across the country all the research has shown that that is the direction in which so-called choice has moved. In other words, those schools that are in wealthier areas are, by their very nature, for some reason or other more attractive to the parents of children. And going along with that has been the tendency of those schools to take advantage of that situation by creaming off the most talented children---those of a high academic or sporting standard---from the less-advantaged areas of towns and cities. We have seen that very strongly in relation to Christchurch, with one or two very notable exceptions. Marian Hobbs' role in breaking that tendency in Christchurch has been long acknowledged, and I salute her here now. In recent years schools in the north-west of Christchurch have filled up not because there are a huge number of extra children living in the north-west of Christchurch---because there are not---but because they have attracted children from all over the city. Fourteen schools in the Ilam electorate, which constitutes most of that area, have enrolment schemes, which is the highest-equal number of any electorate in the country. Epsom is the other that also has schools with enrolment schemes. Unlike Epsom, in which most of the schools already have a home zone---I think out of the ---the Ilam electorate has only four out of its schools with a home zone. Ten of those schools deliberately choose not to limit their catchment. I can hear the sort of argument that Tony Steel is making about reasonable convenience, already being made by the principals of all those other schools, including those in the press release that Trevor Mallard has already referred to. These arguments are going to be made in order to maintain the competitive advantage that comes with being able to have an enrolment scheme, and those schools will continue to cream off students, and there is nothing in this legislation that will stop them. There is nothing, for example, to give parents power. We hear a lot about consultation. Parents know about school consultation: they get consulted, then they get told what is actually going to happen. In fact, many parents are sick of consultation. What they want is some power on their side to say: ``This is what our needs are.'', and local schools should be forced to listen to that. There is nothing in this legislation that will give power back to parents to decide whether their needs are being met by legislation. One of the strange effects of enrolment schemes is that the ministry's school property policy has followed choice as well. So we have this odd situation in Christchurch whereby although most children are being born in the east and south, one still sees classrooms of children whizzing across from east to west in the city to fill up already packed playing fields in the north-west. We have smaller and smaller grounds in many of those north-west schools, whereas in the east we have bigger playing fields, because classrooms are whisked off to popular schools as policies of ``choice'' come into play. There are many schools in the north-west that are very full. This is not a good policy. What we want to do is to ensure that wherever children live they can go to effective schools. We do not want to see our children forced to travel across the city. Unfortunately there is nothing in this Bill to stop that from happening. The last issue I want to raise at the moment relates to children with special needs. Last Friday I was at the meeting of parents of children of Manurewa Central School, whose unit is closing next week. Those parents have all been told to tootle off and go back to their so-called local schools. There is nothing in this legislation to protect the rights of children with special needs. Under this legislation the children who were happy at that one school will be uprooted and sent to another.

It is rest home workers, people who clean the toilets and the floors in hospitals, people in private hospitals, in the health sector and the caring professions, who get their holidays taken off them. As the two previous speakers have indicated, the changes we have seen repeal the Harbours Act . A number of those issues have been dealt with in this Bill and in the other Bills that are part of the package. Although it was not the most interesting and exciting work that one could do on a select committee, nevertheless there are some issues that I think the general public will take an interest in. It is also worth noting some of the more important aspects of the Bill as we go through its third reading. As the Minister indicated with the repeal of that Act, we now have the maritime transport legislation, this Bill, and a couple of others, and then the legislation will be tidied up. In relation to this Bill, the Local Government Amendment Bill (No. ), the first issue I want to touch on is the ability of local authorities to delegate. Regional councils will be able to delegate to other public authorities and, in a limited way, to the port companies. That is, as the Minister said, in essence the result of the port reform. In doing that, it is important for some issues to be highlighted. I was on the select committee and we did consider, for instance, submissions from councils that did not wish to see the Minister's approval sought before land was sold. But the committee did decide, for a number of reasons, one of them being the interests of iwi, to continue with that even though it is in a limited form. The powers of councils are outlined in the Bill. One of the provisions that I think is important in terms of public information is the appointment of people such as harbourmasters and enforcement officers. On the committee we heard from people from different parts of the country. In the city of Auckland, where I come from, there may be no real difficulty in appointing harbourmasters and the like, but clearly in some of the smaller harbours throughout New Zealand the ability to have a full-time, paid harbourmaster just is not there, so there is the ability in the Bill to appoint honorary officers and enforcement officers where those smaller areas do not have the financial wherewithal to pay a person to do that as a full-time job. An area in which I was also interested was that of workplace safety and the control of dangerous goods. With the changes from the old Acts we will see other pieces of legislation like the Health and Safety in Employment Act and the Maritime Transport Act taking over from where the old Act used to be. The committee was interested to make sure that nothing slipped through the cracks in terms of the safety of people who work on the wharf in the loading and unloading of ships, or who work on the ships themselves. It is important to make sure that we protect the safety of workers in what is a potentially dangerous work activity. We will watch with interest to make sure that this legislation does achieve what it sets out to do in protecting those people. The next issue I want to touch on, which was the one spark, I suppose, amongst the submissioners who came, is the whole question of jet skis and the registration of those machines because of the potential danger and nuisance that they have become, particularly to communities in the Auckland and Northland area where we heard a couple of submissions. We grappled with this whole issue of registration of pleasure craft, and the arguments are very compelling on both sides. What we were able to do, and I am pleased that the Government members of the committee did agree to some small change, was to enable regional councils, where they see fit, to have by-laws that would require registration of what most people would call jet skis but what we have had to call personal water craft, I think, as a definition. As I have already indicated in previous speeches on this matter, regional councils can require the marking and identification of personal water craft, and there is a definition of them, as we cannot use the term ``jet skis''. But, as Mr Duynhoven has already pointed out, the concern is that whilst one regional council may decide to do this, others may not. Unless there is uniformity, it does make it rather difficult to enforce. This matter also came up in the Maritime Transport Amendment Bill, which we dealt with earlier this evening. There is the very vexed question of how we enforce all the safety regimes that these Bills have in them if we cannot identify the people who are doing wrong. I do not know how we can take one set of rules on the road and say that it is perfectly acceptable to New Zealanders to have things such as photograph identification, registration plates, and a whole system of keeping track of the cars in New Zealand, but we cannot start to grapple with a similar problem on the water. Of course, there is not as great a cost in terms of loss of life on the water but, nevertheless, there is a growing problem there. I think that Parliament will have to try to deal with that issue in the future because it is a growing problem. I do not think there is an easy answer. Certainly, we looked at the various arguments about the registration of pleasure craft. I still do not know what the answer is, but it is an issue that we will have to continue to work on. At least we have given the option in this clause for the marking and identification of these jet skis to see whether that offers some answers to those many people who made submissions, and who showed the committee video evidence and gave all sorts of clear indications to the committee about what a nuisance these jet skis can be to local communities. I think that we have at least kept some good faith with those people in putting through this amendment to the Bill. One of the other submissions that I thought we needed to deal with, and the Committee put some changes into the Bill, was the fees and charges that regional councils may have to recover. The regional councils are charged with a big responsibility in making sure that the waterways in their areas are safe---that they have proper navigation aids, and that they enforce the laws, the by-laws, and the regulations. The regional councils then had to try to figure out who would pay for that. Collecting this money is not a simple matter because a great many New Zealanders never have the opportunity to get out on to the harbour and, therefore, never contribute to incurring those costs. So the Bill does give flexibility to the regional councils and the way in which they may charge---and they may exempt people from charges. The regional councils asked for flexibility, and I am pleased to say that in the select committee work we did grapple with the problem and, hopefully, we have given them the words that they wanted to deal with that issue. It is a non-contentious Bill, apart from that one aspect of registration of pleasure craft. It was an interesting process to go through, none the less, to see how older pieces of legislation are put to one side and left in the past, and new legislation is drafted to take care of all the necessary contingencies. I was pleased to be part of the select committee. The officials played a good role. It is one example, I guess, of members of the Transport and Environment Committee being able to work together very constructively on non-contentious legislation such as this.

We have appointed a lead negotiator to enter into discussions with Air New Zealand and associated parties to develop the details of the various proposals and to report back to us. In addition, we have met representatives of the Australian Government and a joint officials working-party has been set up to consider the issue.

When Housing New Zealand bought these properties from the Department of Corrections late last year they had been empty for at least years, had been extensively damaged due to vandalism, and were unsuitable for Housing New Zealand needs. In the short term, until long-term decisions on the future of the houses have been made, Housing New Zealand leased them for year to Te W~ananga o Whanake Rangataua, which agreed to make them habitable again. The lease will cease at the end of the year.

I am looking at Part , which has two clauses. In relation to the commencement date, as previous speakers have indicated there is a Supplementary Order Paper that shifts the date out until next year. That is self-explanatory. Some people might like to read that, and the next part, because they keep on talking about retrospectivity. If they read the Supplementary Order Paper they might realise that having worked with the parties around this Parliament, we have a Supplementary Order Paper that deals with that. I want to start by thanking the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. This is an issue on which I would expect most New Zealanders could expect Parliament to rise above the politics of the situation, which is about the safety of the travelling public. We do expect that there will always be a bit of give and take in a debate of this nature, and I am big enough to accept that the bill that we put up originally was not thorough enough. So I thank the select committee and all those members from all parties around this Chamber who have worked so hard. I thank the chair and deputy chair of the select committee, and those many people who have contributed to this bill. I thank the people from the industry---the doctors, the pilots, and everybody else. It is about putting together a piece of legislation that will ensure we do have a safe system, one the travelling public can rely on, and one that stands up internationally. Some members might like to think about reading the Scott-Gorman report. If they do not agree with the conclusions or the figures, then they should read some of the history about what happened within the Civil Aviation Authority and the medical system, about the lack of auditing, and about what the Scott-Gorman report says on public safety. They should then look at the judgment, as I have---and Mr Hide has quoted it---and find out what the judge actually says. He said: ``The amended Act, on my reading, appears to address the concerns raised in the context of this review hearing.'' That is what Parliament is for. It fixes up problems in the law that have been created in the past. It is my job as the Minister responsible for civil aviation to take the best advice that I can, to act upon it, and to ask the select committee to do a thorough review. Yes, I was advised that the legislation should be done more quickly than normal. It was introduced in the normal way---not under urgency---but with a shorter period of time for the select committee to report back. I was advised that Parliament should deal with the matter urgently---not under urgency; there is quite a big difference.
