I am taking the somewhat unusual step of seeking a second call because I do not believe that the Government members who have taken part in the debate understand the importance of the point that Opposition members are trying to make. They seem to have treated the matter with some flippancy and with a certain arrogance that does them no good at all. What is about to happen is that two State-owned enterprises will be established. The Opposition raises no violent objection to that. It does enable a Minister of the Crown, the sole shareholder, to appoint directors to control those broadcasting arms. So be it. But at present there is a prohibition on ministerial interference. That prohibition is to be repealed, and the argument is that there will be more legislation towards the end of the year---after the appointed day for the two new State-owned enterprises to start broadcasting. Members have been told that that legislation that will go to the select committee and might come back to the House some time next year is meant to deal with the very important provisions in section of the Act. That position is quite unacceptable. When the question was put to the Minister and to the Minister of Tourism they simply replied that the select committee could consider the matter, yet the Minister agrees that there was no more important provision in the Broadcasting Act than section . Why has that provision been left out of the Bill? If I were really cynical, I would say that it was a deliberate omission. I hope that it is not. It is not good enough for that provision to be repealed. There will be a hiatus period with the possibility of political interference. The matter is as simple as that. Nothing that Government members have said in the debate gives me any cause for comfort---I feel the opposite. They are saying that, while the provision may have been left out, perhaps it should have been left in; they hope that the select committee will consider it; and, in any event, they will bring in another Bill soon that has not yet been drafted, and if the select committee overlooks it they will try to remember to put it in that new Bill. They acknowledge that they appreciate that that might happen months after the event, so there may be a period during which political interference is possible. I cannot make the point strongly enough that that position is totally unacceptable. I am surprised that Government members whom I consider to have some constitutional ability have not raised their voices in opposition to that omission.
Was the appointment formally approved by the Cabinet?

That is not how I read it, but I accept that the Minister is trying to make it say that. No doubt the select committee will struggle with that point. This is not the time to ask questions across the House and have some kind of friendly chat. There is no point in boring the House any further. The sooner the Bill is sent to the select committee the better.

The member for Eden says: ``That's all right.'', but I do not think it is justified that parties cannot purchase any time. If they do not qualify for free time they could be allocated a time that they are entitled to purchase if they want to do so, but to deprive them of a right to be heard at all is in breach of that fundamental freedom that was included in the original Bill that the Government introduced. That is the first objection. The second objection was raised by the Opposition in the Committee stage, and it relates to the Government's ability to spend large amounts of taxpayers' money on propaganda for the Government during the election campaign period. The Opposition moved an amendment to try to prevent that from occurring. The amendment was voted down by the Government, so the position remains that during the election period there is nothing to prevent the Government from spending large amounts of money, as it has done in the past, on ``Mrs Mops'' and bouncing babies to try to convince the public at its expense that the Government is worth having. It did not work in the past and I do not have the slightest doubt that it will not work in the future, either. It is wrong in principle, and I am surprised that the Government has reserved the right to itself to do that. The third point I shall raise relates to the matter raised by the member for Sydenham. That matter deserves serious consideration by the House. It is generally agreed that there is a need for greater Maori representation in the House of Representatives. After all, Maori form about percent of the population, but they are certainly not represented in the Chamber in that proportion. The concern of the royal commission was to try to design an electoral system that would enable greater representation of Maori people. Indeed, it went to great lengths with a form of proportional representation to try to achieve that. But that does not seem to be likely, and there does not seem to be any doubt that only one party is truly Maori---Mana Motuhake. All members respect that political party for its deep concern about Maori issues. We acknowledge the efforts that Mana Motuhake has put in regularly year after year to try to ensure that Maori concerns are known. I understand that six is the highest number of seats that that party has ever selected candidates for. Normally it has candidates standing only in the four Maori seats. It was not surprising, then, to hear from the member for Sydenham that the leader of Mana Motuhake had written to the Minister of Broadcasting suggesting that some special consideration be given to a political party that in every other respect qualifies for some free time but that has candidates standing only in the four Maori seats. During the Committee stage we were told that the Minister responded to Mr Rata to the effect that he was sympathetic to that suggestion, and asking Mr Rata to confirm that that was the wish of Mana Motuhake. I have sighted those letters in the House tonight. A reply that came from Mr Rata, the leader of Mana Motuhake, the same day stated: ``Yes, that is the situation. Thank you for your consideration. We look forward to the amendments.''. There are no amendments. Why is the Minister of Broadcasting now reneging on an undertaking or an understanding that clearly he had reached with Mana Motuhake? I am sorry to say that the only explanation is that the Maori members who hold the four Maori seats believe that their necks are on the political block. Therefore they went to the Minister of Broadcasting and said: ``We don't want Mana Motuhake to be able to challenge our seats.''. Despite the Minister's letter and the compact that he had reached, he backed down. Again, I am sorry to say this, because I have much respect for the Maori members who represent the Maori electorates, but they are clearly more Labour than they are Maori. That is a great shame, because historically those members have spoken in the House on Maori matters in particular. They are now not prepared to allow their own people even to challenge. The member for Sydenham pointed out the absurd position that if there were to be a by-election in Northern Maori, where Mana Motuhake is particularly strong, although it might be the second most popular party it would not have access to free time in the media. I also think that that is absurd and I suggest that all members think it is absurd. The Maori members are keeping other Maori people out of the House. One can imagine that that would be par for the course for Europeans, but I am surprised and bitterly disappointed that that is the attitude of Labour Party members for Maori seats. It means that there is little chance of Mana Motuhake having representation. There is less chance of that happening now than at the previous election, when at least that party was given some time on television and some time on radio. It will not now have any time unless it can field double the number of candidates that it has ever fielded in the past---an unlikely event. Despite being strong in the North, despite being a party that is concerned with Maori issues in particular, and despite having a leader who is a former Minister of the Crown, that party will not be heard of during the election campaign unless it can somehow or other find more candidates, or arrange for some funding and buy time before the election campaign begins, or find enough money to promote individual candidates. That is most unfortunate. It does not seem to be of great concern to the Minister of Broadcasting or to Government Maori members, but it is of concern to Opposition members. Justice will not be done the Maori people if the legislation is passed in its present form. For that reason and for the other reasons that I have mentioned I will be voting against it.

The difficulty with the Minister is that he tends to exaggerate, and when Opposition members try to work out exactly what he is saying it is a little difficult to differentiate fact from fiction. The amendments being debated by the House relate to the Electoral Act, and, as such, I think that it is generally agreed that they are important. The House is debating a Bill that was Part III of the Local Government Reform Bill, and that makes three specific amendments to the Electoral Act. The first amendment relates to the place of residence of voters, which is a very important matter; the second relates to the supply of specified information; and the third relates to the supply of computer lists and tapes. All of those amendments are of the greatest importance, and I doubt whether any members would gainsay that. When important changes are made to fundamental democratic principles one would expect amendments to the Electoral Act to be introduced so that everyone had notice of them. However, that was not done. Indeed, the first time anyone would have known of the amendments to the Electoral Act was when a supplementary order paper appeared a month or two ago. However, that supplementary order paper related to the Local Government Reform Bill---in which most people perhaps have less interest than they have in national elections. Not only were the amendments introduced through the Local Government Reform Bill, but they were contained on page of a substantial supplementary order paper. Even with the best will in the world the most assiduous member would have found it difficult to wade through all of the other amendments to local government legislation to find the proposed amendments to the Electoral Act. I am not too concerned about whether the Minister understands what was going on, although I have some doubt about that, and I am not too worried about whether I followed it exactly all of the way through. However, I am concerned about the public. Did people know about it? Were they told? When the supplementary order paper that related to the question of residence reached the House it was referred to the select committee, and it is true that the select committee called for submissions. On an important electoral matter the select committee received several submissions, four of which referred to that clause. A submission received from the Legislation Advisory Committee stated that it had no jurisdiction. Submissions were also received from a local body, from the National Council of Women, and from one other group. On such an important issue, I would have thought that receiving such a paucity of submissions would have put the select committee on inquiry. Members of the select committee may well have asked themselves whether they had drawn attention to that fundamental change as well as they might have done, and why the select committee had received only four rather vague submissions. The select committee apparently proceeded; it subsequently reported back to the House, and the matter proceeded from there. However, it transpired that the select committee had no right to consider in any way the amendments to the Electoral Act. Two days ago another supplementary order paper was introduced that also referred to the residential qualifications. At that stage many members looked, and found the residential qualification clause for the first time---because the supplementary order paper was in their Bill boxes. It is true---and I am the first to acknowledge---that many members, including myself, were unaware of the earlier supplementary order paper. Supplementary order papers are not normally introduced that repeat clauses contained in earlier ones. That is unusual. Therefore it is not surprising that some people did not know of the earlier incident.

The Minister who has just resumed his seat spoke with much more enthusiasm than did the Minister of Finance in his -hour diatribe tonight, which sent everyone into a deep sleep. At least the Minister seems to be enthusiastic about the sale of anything that moves, and that point is worth noting. Urgency has been taken on the Bill, and I have looked carefully through it to see what clauses need the urgent attention of the House. I cannot find any. None of them seems to be so important that we have to debate the Bill through the night. All of them could be passed later. No one will go and take advantage of the position to make money. Perhaps the classic clause of all time is clause , which repeals the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation Amendment Act . There is no such Act. The Bill has not been passed. The Bill before the House is repealing a measure that has not yet been passed. What kind of a shambles is that? This afternoon the House debated the second reading of the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation of New Zealand Bill. We have not even reached the Committee stage. We have not had the third reading, yet the Government is repealing it. It must get an A for trying, but it is pretty trying for everyone else who has to put up with such a shambles. By and large, the Bill sets up some of the Government trading arms with a view to sale. Most people would say that someone who had extensive debts would eventually have to do something to reduce the debt burden, or bankruptcy would follow. The problem for the Government is that in it set out not only to hold Government trading activities but also to expand them. It went to the country and told everyone, as one would expect from a Labour Government, that it saw a very important role for the State in trading activities. When the Government moved to set up the State-owned enterprises people began to get a little wary. They thought that that might be ``privatisation'' by another name, but we were all assured that it was not. The Government would have State-owned enterprises, and they would be commercially accountable---we have heard it all before. We were told that they would be owned by the State, and that the State would be not only allowed but encouraged to compete against the private sector. So the Land Corporation went out and became the State farmer, Forestry Corporation became the State forester, and so on. Those of a socialist bent decided that perhaps it was not so bad after all, and the fact that one or two of the new enterprises paid out $ million in redundancy payments was ignored. They did not worry about that---it was too bad. We were told that the corporations would become more efficient. Those who feared that the Government might have breached its principles and would ``privatise'' sank back and relaxed. The true position has now come out. The Government has managed to assuage some of the fears. It has decided that this is the time to proceed as originally intended. It has decided to ``privatise'' the lot, sell everything that moves, because New Zealand is so far in debt. When the Government came into office overseas debt was at about $ billion; it has increased remarkably. If the debt was as high as the Government claimed it was, and as much of a burden---and Government members go on endlessly about ``think big'' and all the debts the National Government created---why did it not do something about the matter before? We are in the fourth year of a Labour Government. If the debt was so serious why did the Government not do something about it straight after its election, by selling assets and repaying the debt? It did not do that; it misled the people by saying that it would not sell assets. What is worse, it built up the debt---in fact, it doubled it. On both counts the Government gets a D. The Bill states that the Bank of New Zealand will be sold off. I think that is a jolly good idea. I do not have any great love for the Bank of New Zealand. It should be sold, and the sooner the better. However, it is unfortunate that only some Government members agree with me. The Minister of Revenue certainly does, and one or two members on the front bench certainly do. It is unfortunate for the Government that not all of those who are away up at the back in the ``Himalayas'' do not. At the end of the Budget speech a classic comment was made that was meant to evoke tears and have the violins playing. I hasten to add that by that time the listening audience had been reduced to those people who were paid to listen---that is, members of the House.

When the Minister introduced the Bill I felt a pang of considerable sorrow for you, sir. The period after dinner is difficult at the best of times, but I found it almost impossible either to hear or to understand a word of what the Minister said. The second Government speaker was no better. It was not until the Minister of Conservation spoke that anyone in the House, or anywhere else, had the faintest idea what the Bill is about. I am sorry that the Minister of Revenue has disappeared, because he might have been able to lift the standard. The Bill vaguely contains an important issue. I have a horrible feeling that I may become as boring as other members when speaking about the Bill, because the topic is not very exciting. Nevertheless, it contains an important principle, so I will labour on. The Ministry of Works and Development is to be divided into two parts---a commercial part that is to be a State-owned enterprise, and a non-commercial part. It is obvious from today's news that the State-owned enterprise arena will become exciting. All State-owned enterprises are to be sold off. That is not such a bad idea, and the sooner it happens---particularly in relation to the Ministry of Works and Development---the better. The non-commercial part of the Ministry of Works and Development is dealt with in this Bill. It seems that the Government has considered what it will do with the other functions of the ministry, and it has decided that it will just dish out those tasks. It seems that the Government started at the top of a list of Cabinet Ministers, and asked who wanted what. It decided that anything that is vaguely related to land will go to the Land Corporation, anything that has wheels on it will go to the Ministry of Transport, and down the list it went. The Government had no idea whether the new department would be able to cope or knew anything about the matter, at all, and as a result most of the ministry's activities will be palmed off on to the Minister of Trade and Industry. The Department of Trade and Industry is a fascinating animal. It was doomed to head for total extinction about months ago when tariffs and import licensing were being dismantled. The department suddenly found itself with nothing to do. However, under this Bill the Government has given it something to do. The Department of Trade and Industry is to be responsible for architects, clerks of works, engineering associates, engineers' registration, and geothermal energy. The Historic Places Trust will also be palmed off on to the Minister of Trade and Industry, who will also be responsible for quantity surveyors---about whom he knows nothing. It seems incredible to me that on the Bill's introduction Ministers have not bothered to explain to the House whether the Department of Trade and Industry will carry out those responsibilities or ignore them. When that department is abolished---and that is likely---will those responsibilities fizzle out, or will they be transferred to another department---if any still exist? The presentation by Ministers has been lamentable. The House has not been properly informed. From what can be gathered from the speeches---and the quality of them left much to be desired---it appears that no work or thought has gone into the Bill. It seems to be a panic measure. One or two clauses need some comment. Clause , which relates to the Department of Trade and Industry, is intituled ``Additional functions of Department''. It states that the department shall have and undertake the following functions: to provide and carry out advisory work; and to undertake the performance and functions necessary for the due and proper administration of the Act. Without limiting the generality of that clause, it means that the department can prepare reports, tender advice, assemble and disseminate information, and promote research. One might consider that that is unremarkable. Whether the department will ever fulfil those functions is another matter. Clause relates to the powers of the Minister, and provides that he shall have all such ancillary powers as are necessary, conducive, or incidental to the performance of the Act. One might say that that is fair enough. However, the clause states: ``Without limiting the generality of subsection () of this section, the Minister, for the purpose of exercising any of the functions specified...shall have the power---To direct any activity or undertaking, whether a public work or not, in relation to the orderly and efficient use or development of natural resources.'' In other words, the Minister of Trade and Industry, for the purpose of exercising his functions under the Act, shall have the power to direct the private sector in the orderly and efficient use of natural resources. Is that what is intended? If so, it is wrong. I appreciate that clause appears on page of the Bill that was introduced today, and that many members have probably not read up to page ---I am not certain how I made it to page . Fortunately, the Minister's powers as set out in statute are of interest to me. I invite the next Government speaker---if there is one---to explain why it is necessary to give the Minister such wide powers to direct the efficient use and development of natural resources in the private sector. What has that got to do with the Minister of Trade and Industry? I have said enough. The Bill as it is introduced shows a lack of preparation and the kind of desperation that Opposition members expect as news breaks daily---almost by the hour. I suppose that if I pick up tomorrow morning's newspaper I shall find that the Government has yet again changed its mind, and that this Bill is not the Ministry of Works and Development Abolition Bill. Perhaps it will become the retention Bill. The Government is in such chaos, and the market is so confused, that nobody knows what is happening.

What consideration should be given to the legally binding contracts that so many people have entered into? The answer is no consideration. What about the taxation of life insurance companies, which are paying what is, in effect, a capital gains tax on share trading? Where is the neutrality for life insurance companies in comparison with other banks and financial institutions? A different tax regime exists between the two, yet the Government does not recognise that. What about the costs of the revenue? The costs have been set at $ million and then $ million.

He was saying that the gang problem will be solved only when there is better education, and better social conditions for gang members. I think the point is that, by and large, New Zealanders are just not prepared to wait for another generation to come through that is better educated. They see -stone louts lounging round the streets, and they want some action now. This is a three-pronged attack on that type of behaviour, which has been going on for much too long. I am sure that every member of the House is hopeful that the Bill will help to control that kind of activity. By all means get the sociologists and the psychiatrists, and all of the others, to try to work out why society has gone wrong, but in the meantime let us clean up the streets---that is the call from the public. I hope that the Bill will do something in that regard. The Bill is not a long one. It is said to have three main purposes---a new offence of disorderly assembly is introduced; there is the power to impose a non-association order; and there is a right to impose conditions of bail. I do not want to talk to the non-association order proposal, because it seems to me at first glance that that has great merit, and I think that it is long overdue. Nor do I want to refer to the conditions of bail. However, I do want to refer briefly to the disorderly assembly provision, because in that regard lawyers really enter the field. On the one hand, there is a contest between the laws that restrict individuals in their right to walk the streets---the laws that preserve the very basic freedom of association and freedom of assembly. For centuries, the first have been enacted to try to preserve an orderly society for the benefit of all of its members. Those laws exist and they are likely to remain. On the other hand, there is the conflict between those laws that control activity and the very freedom of individuals to assemble when they so desire. In the common law no offence or crime is committed until some overt act has been committed by somebody with a guilty mind---in law, mens rea. There have to be the two elements before a criminal act is committed; intention to commit a crime has never been enough. It is not enough for a person to stand in the street and think: ``I will burgle this shop''. If nothing further is done there is no offence. Once the attempt is made, that may be an offence. Once the burglary is committed that is the overt act that, together with the guilty mind, creates the offence. New Zealand has a very real problem with gangs. The problem is that so often the people who assemble together and who are members of gangs commit violence shortly thereafter. It is sometimes quite frightening. One need only read the article in the Dominion on April describing an incident at a gang party in Ngaio, Wellington---I shall read briefly from that newspaper article: ``In yesterday's incident police were confronted with pitchforks, bricks, bottles, to petrol bombs, and a chain-saw, when they tried to close down a noisy party. One policeman was stabbed, and an armed offenders squad member fired a warning shot over the heads of two gang members who advanced on police while threatening to throw Molotov cocktails.'' It is hardly surprising that members of the public have had enough, and are saying that those people must be stopped from congregating and that laws must be introduced to ensure that those events do not occur. The point is that this Bill has the rather unusual feature in that it is creating an offence when one has not yet been committed. That is quite a novel and dangerous precedent, and the House ought to be very careful before it supports such a measure. The Bill provides that people---gang members---who have lawfully gathered in the street are committing an offence, although they may have no criminal intent at all, and have done nothing wrong whatever. Nevertheless, because they are there, and because somebody who is not a party is frightened and has reasonable cause, as he or she sees it, to be frightened, an offence is committed even though those gang members have done nothing. Is that right? Should that be an offence? The person who is fearful for his safety, or fearful that violence might ensue, may be wrong. It is true that the Bill provides that the people have to have reasonable reason to suspect. That is a subjective judgment that will be tested later in court, and the objective test then applies: was it a reasonable fear that a reasonable man might have? The answer is: yes, it might be; or, no, it is not. If it is yes, we might be saying that those people then are guilty of an offence punishable by imprisonment even though they have committed no offence, and had no intention of doing anything wrong. They may have been about to disperse of their own volition, but, because somebody else was fearful for his or her safety, that is enough for an offence. In that event, not only does the case arise that there is no guilty mind---the mens rea---but there is also no overt act in the normal sense. So neither of the normal ingredients of a crime are present, and that is a very wide-ranging and novel approach to the criminal law. I have, of course, only just read the Bill for the first time. I can understand the dilemma the Minister of Justice found himself in when trying to design a law to cope with the problem; it is not easy. All lawyers in the House, and, I am sure, all members of the House even without legal training, would want to take great care before they expanded the role of the police and the authorities. Parliament has to decide whether, because the criminal activity of gangs is so prevalent, it justifies that expansion of the law. I see that under the Bill a warning has to be given, so that if the police, who have been summoned by the person who is fearful of violence, go to the scene and ask those who are there to disperse, and they do, then that is the end of the matter. If they do not disperse an offence is created. The police were not there when the activity complained of took place. By the time the police actually arrived it could be that either half of the gang had gone or those who were left were doing nothing very novel at all. Be that as it may, the warning has to be given, and that is a very proper provision. We ultimately have to satisfy ourselves that the mischief that is aimed at in the Bill is such that it justifies a wide power being given to the police and a novel expansion of the criminal law. Despite my very serious concerns, and my being a lawyer, I think that the provision is now justified. I am sorry that I have to say that, because I am one of those people who tries hard to preserve the liberty of the individual. I shall always fight to try to make certain that if there is to be an infringement on individual liberty it can be justified in only the most extreme cases. There is no doubt in my mind that gang activity in New Zealand has now reached the stage at which drastic measures must be taken. For that reason the Minister of Justice is justified in bringing the Bill with its new provision to the House. I recommend that it goes to the select committee for further study.

The Bills have the support of the Opposition, and Opposition members do not intend to waste the time of the House. The only matters I want to raise were discussed during the Committee of the whole House. One member raised the matter of his concern that as a result of the setting up of the State-owned enterprises there had been some discussion about whether members of the territorial force would be free to attend their courses. The Minister in the chair gave an explanation. I think it proper to place on the record of the House that some concern has been expressed. Opposition members are obliged to the Minister for having said that if there is a problem with any specific State-owned enterprise the Minister of Defence would contact the State-owned enterprise involved and make sure that the statutory requirements to release those territorial soldiers were complied with. Another matter mentioned in the Committee that may be of some interest to the public was the brief reference to the possibility of New Zealand forces serving in the peace-keeping force in Afghanistan. Whether that possibility comes to fruition remains to be seen, but I consider it only right that the public is made aware of the possibility. The fact that now appears to be established is that the Minister of Foreign Affairs has had some discussion with Sir Geoffrey Howe in London in relation to that possibility. I move, That the Electoral Poll Bill be introduced. This short Bill of clauses sets the scene for what could be the most major constitutional change in New Zealand's history. It is entirely right and proper, therefore, that any such change should be made by all New Zealanders. New Zealand has enjoyed a stable democracy for more than years. It is a record that few countries can match. Although parliamentarians have always been, and are likely to remain, the natural target for anger and frustration, and are often pilloried as a result, New Zealanders can take great confidence in the lack of corruption in the parliamentary system, and in the fact that successive Governments have never questioned that ultimately sovereignty rests in all New Zealanders who are eligible to vote. It is they who, by casting their vote, mandate a Government to act in the best interests of our greatly blessed country. The importance of that must never be underestimated. As Winston Churchill told the House of Commons in October : ``At the bottom of all the tributes paid to democracy is the little man walking into the little booth with a little pencil making a little cross on a little bit of paper. No amount of rhetoric or voluminous discussion can possibly diminish the overwhelming importance of the point.''. No one would suggest, however, that any parliamentary electoral structure is perfect. From time to time there are calls for change, and it is appropriate that the Government should respond to such calls. In New Zealand two issues have arisen in recent years that now require attention. The first issue relates to the way that members of the House of Representatives are elected. For more than years members have been elected using a plurality or first-past-the-post system. That means that a member can be elected on less than percent of the votes cast. A more compelling criticism is that in the aggregate the views of the population may not be properly represented in Parliament. That point is of critical importance to third parties, which may have substantial support but, because that support is spread thinly across all electorates, are unlikely to win the number of seats proportional to their support. That is perceived to be unfair. The second reform sought from time to time, proposes greater controls on the Government or---as it is frequently called---on the potential abuse of Executive power. While our present party system provides for strong Governments capable of responding quickly to events as they arise, there is undoubtedly some disquiet over the lack of checks and balances. After all, New Zealand has only one House of Representatives and the governing party is rarely, if ever, defeated. Some proponents of proportional representation believe that with the advent of more third parties in the House there would be some greater constraint on the Executive. Opponents maintain that the end result would be inevitable coalitions, with confusion in the public mind about who, in fact, would carry out whose policy. The Government in its manifesto before the election concluded that the time had come to seek direction from the public on these issues. The Bill fulfils that manifesto undertaking. The first issue, therefore, is the fairness of the electoral system and whether there should be a change in the way in which members of Parliament are elected. The second issue is whether there is a greater need for constraints on the Executive, and, if so, whether that should be done by the creation of a second Chamber or senate. Both issues are to be put to the public by way of referendum. For the past months the Government caucus committee on electoral reform has been meeting regularly and has had the benefit of advice from the Hon. Mr Justice Wallace, the Chairman of the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform; from Sir Kenneth Keith, President of the Law Commission and member of the royal commission; and from Professor Colin Hughes of Queensland University, who was formerly a member of the Australian Electoral Commission. I am indebted to members of the committee and to their advisers for their endeavours. I want to state immediately that the Government is determined that the issues to be put by way of referendum will be put fairly and without bias. The Government itself will not be promoting any particular option, and it will be open to all New Zealanders, whether individually or in groups, to debate the issues. I hope that the debate will be constructive and rational. At the end of the day it will be for all New Zealanders to decide what is to be done. I shall now explain the procedure that will be followed and the reasons for it. The Government has taken into account four factors in setting the procedure. The first is that in accordance with its manifesto undertaking the Government considers that on a matter of such constitutional importance, and one involving a number of systems that could well be suited to New Zealand, voters should have a choice of more than one alternative method of electing members of Parliament. Having considered the royal commission's report, the Government has concluded that there should be three reform options. They are the mixed-member proportional system, the supplementary-member system---both of which were seen by the royal commission as the best reform options---and the preferential system of voting, which is used in Australia. For a referendum on electoral reform to be binding it is necessary under the Electoral Act to put a ``proposal'' in the referendum itself. The advice received by the Government is that such a proposal needs to be set out in considerable detail. Indeed, it should be done by way of draft legislation so that if carried it can be enacted without major refinement. Thus a proposal for mixed-member proportional representation would need to set out how many electorates there would be, how the South Island quota would be affected, how electorate boundaries would be drawn, how the list of members of Parliament would be prepared, whom it could include, and how proportionality would apply. Draft legislation would also be required for the proposal for the supplementary-member system and for the preferential voting system. It is not a matter, therefore, of simply putting the options and working out the details later; rather, it is a case of working out the details and then putting the options. I am sure that the House will appreciate---even if perhaps some more strident reformers do not---that to draft such complex legislation for three quite different options would result in a very long delay. It is also quite impractical because only one of the options at best would ever be actually adopted. There would therefore be a necessary delay and a waste of effort for the two rejected reform options. Therefore it was decided to offer the three options in an initial indicative referendum, which would then narrow the options down to the ones most preferred. The draft legislation for that could then be put in place in time for a second binding referendum. The second factor is that the Government considers that all voters should be able to express their preference for a reform option even though they may favour the status quo. If it were otherwise, a new system could be imposed on them without there being an opportunity for them to express their views on it. The third factor is that it is clearly desirable that as many voters as possible take part in the referendum. It would be quite unacceptable to have a major constitutional change with a voter turn-out of, say, percent, of whom only percent were in favour of the option. It follows that the obvious time to have a binding referendum is at the time of a general election when historically there has always been a high voter turn-out. The final factor is that, when voting for or against a senate, voters should be able to take into account any change to the method of electing members to the House of Representatives. The reason for this is that some may support a senate if the status quo in the Lower House remains, but oppose a senate if there were a form of proportional representation in the Lower House. It follows that the question on the senate should be the last question to be put, and so it will be. Taking those factors into account, the procedure for the referendum of electoral reform will be as follows: an initial indicative referendum will be held in September pursuant to the Bill. The schedule to the Bill sets out the ballot paper, in which there are two questions. The first gives the option to vote for either the present first-past-the-post system or a change to the voting system. The voter simply ticks his or her preference. The ballot paper then explains the next step in the following words: ``If a majority of the votes cast in this poll are for the retention of the present first-past-the-post system, no further poll on the voting system will be held. If a majority of the votes cast in this poll are for a change, a further poll on the voting system will be held at the time of the general election. That poll would offer a choice between the present first-past-the-post system and the reform option that receives the most votes at this poll. Indicate which of the following reform options you wish to see as the alternative to the present system if a second poll is held.''. The voter then moves to question and is given the choice of the preferential voting system, the mixed-member proportional system, and the supplementary-member system. To ensure that there is no bias in favour of any one reform option, the order on the ballot paper for the options will be determined by lot by the chief electoral officer. The September indicative referendum will be preceded by a publicity campaign to explain to voters how each of the reform options would operate, with arguments for and against each option. Once again, to ensure that the material prepared and presented to the public is impartial and unbiased, a small committee of four will be appointed to approve or reject the material. That committee is likely to consist of a law commissioner from the Law Commission, the Chief Ombudsman, the Clerk of the House of Representatives, and the chief executive of the Ministry of Women's Affairs. The result of the September indicative referendum therefore will either confirm the status quo or require a further binding referendum to be held at the next general election. I now therefore turn to that second referendum. If a majority of voters support a change to the method of electing members of the House of Representatives, the second referendum to be held at the time of the general election will be conducted pursuant to further legislation that will be introduced in early . Two questions will be on that ballot paper. The first will offer voters the choice between the present first-past-the-post system and the reform option that received the most votes in the indicative referendum. In other words, there will be a run-off between the existing system and the most preferred option for reform. It may be argued that the first-past-the-post system is being put up again, and that this might create a bias towards it. However, on balance, the Government believes that a system that has been in place for more than years should be one of the options at the binding referendum as of right, and, in any event, as I have already indicated, it should not be set aside unless that is the wish of individual New Zealanders taken at a poll when there is a high voter turn-out. That is more likely at a general election. The legislation authorising the second binding referendum will be prepared in sufficient detail to be a proposal under the Electoral Act, and will therefore be binding. The second referendum will also include for the first time a question on the creation of a senate. The voter when voting on the senate question will know that the electoral system for the House of Representatives will be either the first-past-the-post system, which is the status quo, or the system referred to in the previous question on the ballot paper, which would be the most preferred reform option. Therefore the senate question will be worded in such a way that the person voting can vote for the creation of a senate whichever system is used, or only if the present first-past-the-post system is retained, or only if the preferred reform option is introduced. Alternatively, the voter can simply vote against the creation of a senate. The final form of that ballot paper will be included in the schedule to the legislation authorising that second binding referendum. Again, there would be a publicity campaign in the months before the general election, setting out the case for and against any change to the method of electing members of the House of Representatives, if that question is to be put, and the case for and against a senate. If the indicative referendum of September results in the retention of the first-past-the-post system, the only question put in the second binding referendum will be on the senate. I turn to the provisions of the Bill. Clause is the short title. Clause provides that the Act shall expire on March . Clause provides that an indicative poll of electors on proposals for electoral reform shall be taken on a Saturday not later than September . Clause applies the Electoral Act to such a poll. Clause provides that the electoral rolls for the time being in force shall be deemed to be the rolls of electors for the purpose of the indicative poll. Clause refers to appropriation. Clauses to provide for the appointment of scrutineers. Clauses to refer to the issue of voting papers and the method of voting. Clauses to are largely technical and apply to the poll matters usually required for a general election. Clause creates offences. Clause authorises the promulgation of regulations. This Bill is the result of a good deal of careful consideration. It represents part of the reform on electoral matters that will be introduced by this Government, and that will include the introduction of a citizens-initiated referendum Bill in the very near future. This Bill paves the way for electoral reform if that is the wish of electors. I am confident that New Zealanders will respond to the challenge, and I hope that they will make themselves familiar with the various reform options. At the end of the day it will be for them to decide. That is how it should be. I commend the Bill to the House.
Why couldn't they do it on Saturday, like everybody else?

The law of defamation is a relatively complex one. Many members of the House, including indeed the right honourable member who interjected, have some extensive experience in such matters, and I wish him well in the various matters that he has pending. There is no doubt that, whatever we do, there will be some people who will disagree. Defamation will always be with us, and the media have always shown a great skill in putting their retractions. I recall the case of the politician who found to his horror that he was named in the obituary column. When he remonstrated with the newspaper, the editor did file a retraction, but in the following words: ``We regret that the story of the death was not true.''. That seems to me to show that the wit of mankind is still not at an end, and that, no matter what we do, we will find that litigation still comes in the area of defamation. The Bills are very worth while; the legislation clarifies a lot of the law. I commend it to the House.

I move, That the District Courts Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is small and technical, and tidies up a few matters arising from the Courts Amendment Bill that was passed in July. That Bill restructured and reallocated the jurisdiction and business of the court system. It increased the civil jurisdiction of the district courts from $, to $, and in order to prepare the district courts for the impact of the increased jurisdiction it has been necessary to review the existing district court rules of procedure. That review has been under way for some time and is now almost complete. Several matters arose that required amendments to the District Courts Act . Most of them were incorporated in the Courts Amendment Bill in its passage through the House. However, it has become apparent that several other amendments will be necessary if the district courts are to have suitable rules of procedure for the proper conduct of their new business. Clause will allow rules to be made specifying the powers that are to be exercised by registrars, as opposed to deputy registrars. Members will recall that provision has already been made for the introduction of the summary judgment procedure in district courts. Clause will allow the transfer of interlocutory applications for summary judgment from a district court to the High Court. Clause allows questions of law to be removed to and heard in the High Court. Clause will amend the District Courts Act to enable district courts to order discovery of evidence against the person before the issue of proceedings to assist in the formulation of the intended plaintiff's claim. Clause will also allow orders for discovery against a person who is not a party to the proceedings. Clause will provide a mechanism for ensuring that orders for discovery against a non-party can be enforced. Clause sets out the rule-making powers necessary to give effect to the amendments to the Act, including the circumstances in which a court may appoint an expert witness. Finally, clause is a transitional provision. I commend the Bill to the House.

There were two points that I did not have time to cover before the dinner adjournment. One related to the rather difficult question of job security for jurors when there is a trial of exceptional length. The purpose of this Bill is to deal with a trial that is expected to last days. Not only will that cause considerable inconvenience to the jurors who are summonsed, but it may well impact on their salaries. I explained before the dinner break that the Chief Executive of the Department for Courts has discretion to pay greater than the scale, and I expect that is precisely what he will do in that case. As to remuneration to try to ensure security of work for jurors, that matter will be dealt with by the Law Commission in its review of juries, which is under way. It is about to embark on a sort of exit-poll survey of jurors over the Christmas period. The reviewers will be reporting in about March to the Law Commission, which hopes to have the juries report done by about July-August. That will be one of the issues covered, along with majority verdicts and a whole lot of other matters relating to juries. I think we need to wait and see what it comes up with. I appreciate that will not be helpful for the Rewa trial, but I will be talking to the chief executive about that, in any event. The other matter related to a possible review of this legislation, once it is passed, after a period of time. The argument goes that it is quite an important measure---I do not doubt that---it has come into the House quite quickly, for obvious reasons, and it is being passed quite quickly. I hasten to say that the Law Commission has commented on the Bill and supports the concept of it. Nevertheless, I think it is a good idea to review legislation, particularly legislation like this, so we would want to have a review in years' time, anyway, to see how many times there were exceptional circumstances that justified applying the measure in this Bill. However, I do not agree that reviews ought to be put in legislation. I think that is unnecessary and undesirable. Legislation should declare what the law is, rather than requiring a review of an Act of Parliament at a given time. There are occasions when that is appropriate, particularly for very wide-reaching laws such as the privacy laws, but that is not appropriate here. This is quite a simple issue. Important though it is, I do not think there is a need to put in the Bill that there will be a review. The Government would not support any such amendment.

No, just a moment. It was the intention of Ngai Tahu and the Crown to protect Mr McSweeney and his rights, and the rights of the bach owner, who had been there for a long time. The best way to do that was to create a historic reserve. Both parties agreed that that would be appropriate. The consent of the Minister of Conservation is still required to chop down trees on a historic reserve, and all that sort of thing. In making it a historic reserve there is a slight change in emphasis, but there is protection of ecological values as well. That seemed to be the best thing to do. The alternative would be to have the land go back to being a scenic reserve, and to have a specific exemption for this particular reserve, for the bach owner. I do not think that is an appropriate way of handling these matters. So what is the loss to Mr McSweeney? I cannot see that he has any loss, other than, perhaps, the Minister of Conservation authorising that trees be chopped down. I do not think that is very likely. Mr McSweeney's rights are preserved. They are not preserved because Ngai Tahu are granting them; they are preserved in the deed and the statute. If Ngai Tahu or any other operator or individual wants to object to somebody's concession, or to the renewal of a concession granted by the Minister of Conservation, that is his or her right. People should be able to go along and say: ``I object. I don't think it is in the interests of the country to have a concession over to Milford for the monorail.''---or whatever it is. Anybody can do that. The issue is whether Ngai Tahu have some sort of special preference. The answer is no they do not. Throughout all the negotiations the Crown has made sure that Ngai Tahu are in the same position as any other New Zealanders in terms of their right to object, their right to seek a concession themselves, and their right to compete. Why should they not have those rights? Why are they all of a sudden being accused of trying to ``heavy'' somebody? They can make some suggestions as to what Mr McSweeney or anybody else concerned with concessions might do about taonga or something like that, but they cannot enforce it.

It was never the Government's intention that the Human Rights Act would have a status that would permit it automatically to override all other legislation. To do so would accord the Act a primacy that is inappropriate. Even the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act cannot do that. In New Zealand, legislation is the means by which the people's representatives in Parliament decide on competing values and priorities. Parliament, with this in mind, also decides whether particular legislation should amend or otherwise affect the interpretation of other legislation. This is not an unusual approach in Western democracies. The general status of our legislation, as interpreted by the courts, is intended to benefit all New Zealanders.

There will be an involvement of the New Zealand Law Society and the District Court bench, as well, in those matters.
Yes, I would consider they should be remanded in custody. They probably are, and if they are not, sometimes it is because the police have not brought it to the attention of the judge.

I welcome the opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon. I listened with interest to the first Opposition speaker---the old backroom brawler, the member for Auckland Central. I thought: ``Here we go! Stage ; shift the ground; into the battle.'', and away he launched. I listened to his speech for minutes, and I noted that not once was $, mentioned. When the same backstreet brawler came into the House last week his speech was all about $,. Hello! What has happened? The member found that there was nothing in the story, so this week he has shifted ground once more. I noted with some interest that the member for St. Albans was very strongly in support of the member for Auckland Central last week. The Leader of the Opposition came down to the House last Wednesday. The front row was there to be involved in the debate, and I noted with some interest today that the member for Auckland Central had been hung out to dry. He has been the only speaker from the Opposition to continue to launch this spurious campaign, and I noted with some interest that the member for St. Albans was not involved. That is because two reports from the Serious Fraud Office have cleared the member for Bay of Islands, and I think that without any doubt the term ``Honest John'' will stick around for some time yet. That is the same member that the country had the misfortune to have as its leader for days prior to the election. That member, from one of the Christchurch seats, for some years has led campaigns up and down the country trying to build in the minds of people wonderful concepts about super-cows, lamburgers, and, recently, frost-free tomatoes. That same member who is leading that particular political party was, back in in the heady days of the Labour Government, the Minister of Tourism. There were only two members of that Government who claimed that they had an understanding of the business world. The other one was the member for St. Albans, who claimed he had once run a business involving a sum of about $ million, if I remember rightly. I remember well when the National Opposition checked that out and found that in fact he had been in charge of a business---
Have any changes been made to the interim charging regime since last July that affect users of hospital services?

I take the opportunity to speak on the reporting back of the Southland Flood Relief Committee Empowering Bill. As does my colleague, I have a particular interest in this matter, and I want to take the opportunity, first, to thank the committee for the work that it did on this legislation. As the member for Invercargill said, it seemed to be the most practical way in which to deal with a fund---$, or so---that has been sitting around for some time. The difficulty was that all of those who had made a claim on the fund had been paid out, therefore there was no other way of dealing with the money. I also want to take the opportunity to thank the many people throughout New Zealand who rallied around at the time of the flood, because the money did not necessarily come from Southland but from all parts of New Zealand. The original fund had a substantial amount---just over $. million---that was distributed not only in the city of Invercargill but also in the surrounding rural areas. I think that this is a good example of the House's using its power to provide legislation in relation to a fund such as this and I thank the committee, and especially the committee chairman, for the work that was done during that process. I think that it is an innovative step to close off the fund after years, and, as a member who may still be here in years' time, I shall be pleased to see the fund finally wound up at that time. Motion agreed to.
The member has said that four times now. Does he want to move on?

I have had some interest in the Bill since the time of the original legislation, introduced by Sir Geoffrey Palmer, a former Prime Minister---
Has the Minister received any reports that show what has happened to the number of liquidations or receiverships over the same period?

The Minister looked me straight in the eye and said: ``Nonsense!''. He should read some of the articles in national magazines to find out what is thought about the Minister's character and the conservation principles he has tried to put into legislation. If it had not been for the Opposition the Government would have got away with it once again. Those are statements that were put before the Government at the select committee, and that is the reason for the Opposition's concern. I want to refer to my electorate, because I have a particular concern at present. It is hoped that Lake Dunstan will be filled at some time in the future. The Lake Dunstan Boating Club wants to build a complex around the shore of the lake, but it is not permitted to do so because no one will say what the level of the lake will be. The Minister is shaking his head.
That is an interesting interjection. I can tell the public that only half a dozen Government members are in the House at present.

The Minister of Commerce is yapping away again and trying to blame the National Government. That tells the House that such a Minister has never made a hard decision in his life. He would not even know how to get on to a boat and go out fishing. He does not understand what the working men of New Zealand are all about. He sits in the House and tries to make rules. I challenge the Associate Minister to stand up and show statistics that indicate that family life has improved over the past years. I ask her to prove to me---

The Minister has given an assurance that he will highlight in his reply the clauses that cover the protection of the rights of way. I withdraw that comment. The member for Hawke's Bay did not reveal that during the next years the regional councils in my area are expected to find $, for rabbit control. They are contributing handsomely towards eliminating the problem---the Government is not providing all of the money. The member for Kaimai was correct when he said that pest destruction councils are concerned not only with rabbits but also with deer and possums. It is fortuitous that I have recently expressed concern in my local newspaper about the tremendous increase of tuberculosis in possums. There are areas in my electorate in which it is difficult to find a beef herd that is not affected by tuberculosis. The implications of that disease must be considered, and a long-term solution must be found. I hope that the Minister will give the House an indication of the way that possums will be controlled in New Zealand. The Bill provides for the privatisation of factories that make poisons. Members must be concerned about the statements that people who purchase New Zealand beef are making about the problem of tuberculosis in beef. Many reports have been written about the implications of tuberculosis in New Zealand's beef herds. It is horrific that reports state that if the present spread of tuberculosis continues amongst our beef herds it is realistic to expect that by the year every beef animal in the North Island will be affected by tuberculosis. I do not know how those statistics have been compiled, but they are frightening. The Bill basically establishes a State-owned enterprise to look after a factory in Wanganui and another in Waimate. Members must ask about the quality of the product. Are we absolutely certain that some kind of poison will be produced not only to control the rabbits that are increasing in such magnitude but also to kill possums? The sale of possum skins in Dunedin has been cancelled in recent weeks because the value of the skins is such that young people no longer want to spend their winter days catching possums. That is sad, because many young men started small businesses throughout New Zealand by trapping possums and selling the skins, which had a high value. It is only a few years ago that more money could be obtained for possum skins than for old ewes. The whole picture has changed.

Members have listened for the past minutes to the Minister of Health, who is also the Minister of Trade and Industry. It is interesting that he did not once mention health matters, nor did he say what he would do to improve New Zealand's trade. In that same Minister went back to his electorate and said: ``I am unprepared to support a policy that raises seriously the risk that one day we may have to tell our children that, yes, there is a job for you, but it will be in Sydney.'' The House has been debating the Budget for the past few days, but several Government members have not been prepared to stand up and defend the Budget. Opposition members believe that the Appropriation Bill (No.) should not be read a second time. The Government has failed to provide a coherent policy for the recovery of the economy. It has failed to maintain the living standards of New Zealand families; it has failed to reverse the serious and increasing level of unemployment; it has failed to respond to the plight of people in the regions; it has failed to promote growth in the export industry; and it has failed to check the widening rifts within society that have created unnecessary and unavoidable tensions, especially between the races. New Zealanders should realise what the circumstances were when the Budget was being written and discussed in Cabinet. Never before in New Zealand's political history has there been such anger and division between a Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance. Never before in our political history has there been such division and anger between the Cabinet and the Government back bench as there is at present. Never before in our political history has a psychologist had to be invited to a Cabinet meeting to try to straighten out Ministers. Never before has a Cabinet Minister invited Mr Lester Thurow to this country because he wants to promote himself within Cabinet, and because he is so against what the Minister of Finance is doing. Never before has there been so much division between the left wing and the right wing of the Labour Party. The member for Sydenham has said that he is not prepared to vote with the Government. Other Government members have said that they are prepared to follow the member for Sydenham. It is interesting to look at the list of Government members who have not taken the opportunity of speaking in the Budget debate. The member for Avon has not spoken in the debate. The member for Lyttelton, who is a supporter of the member for Sydenham, has not spoken in the debate. The member for Tongariro---another left-wing member---has not spoken in the debate. Even the Minister of Employment has not spoken in the debate. The Minister of Internal Affairs has not been prepared to speak in the debate. The Minister of State, and the member for Hamilton West, have not been prepared to defend the Budget in the House. Why have those members been so disgruntled and disappointed? On Tuesday night a week ago they watched their leader try to defend the Budget. It was obvious that the Prime Minister was not up to it---in respect of his health, his leadership, or anything else---and the country is beginning to realise that he is not. New Zealanders are beginning to realise that the Opposition has a leader who is strong, careful, and prepared to care for people. He is an understanding man. The country knows that he has a united team behind him---something that the Prime Minister does not have. The divisions within the Government are so deep and so wide that it was not capable of presenting a reasonable Budget. Government members are not prepared to go out and talk to the people. Never before has there been such a division between the haves and have-nots. Never before have so many people been unemployed. Before the election the Government said that if it was re-elected, and carried on with its policies, the number of unemployed people would reach . Government members are now saying that people will be unemployed by next March. The Minister of Employment has not been prepared to debate those policies in the Budget debate. Never before has there been so much division amongst local authorities, yet the Minister of Local Government has not been prepared to defend the Government's policies in the debate. The Minister of Health preceded me in the debate, but not once did he mention the subject of health, and that is because of the division within Cabinet. Cabinet is not united. Problems exist between the Minister of Health and the Minister of Finance over the Gibbs report, which has created division in the House. The Minister of Social Welfare has not told the House what will happen to the thousands of people who are being driven on to social welfare benefits. In , families were receiving some part of their income from the State. Three years later, families were dependent on the State for some part of their income. Now the Government is driving people on to the unemployment benefit. What track is the Government going down? Does it really want to make average, decent New Zealanders dependent on the State for part of their income? Opposition members firmly believe that that is what the Government wants. I received from a constituent a letter that states: ``The department is the Government's hospital for those whose economic health collapses in the reform process. The fact that the number admitted to this hospital is growing every day surely points to the fact that something is wrong with the economic medicine being administered by the Government.'' The Government knows the path that it is following. So many New Zealanders will be dependent on the State for their income by the time of the next election that they will wonder whether they can afford to get rid of a Labour Government. That is the kind of Government that is running the country. It has divided the people and made them dependent on the State, and it has deprived them of their jobs and driven them from their homes and farms. That is the Government that, months ago, went to the country and said: ``The pain is necessary. Give us one more term. There is hope. We want to finish the job.'' The Government went to the country without a policy or a manifesto, but Simon Walker was truthful about what would happen. He said that the Opposition was particularly aggrieved at the manner in which the Government was using Government expenditure and public funds to publish its policies. One of the saddest aspects of politics today is the abuse of taxpayers' money by the Government to put forward its policies through the news media. People do not pay taxes to promote the Government's policies. Opposition members are perturbed that the Government is suggesting that taxpayers should fund election campaigns, but that is what we are up against. If one considers the Simon Walker policy---the only policy that the Government presented to the country---one finds that the Government knew what would happen to the Government Printing Office, to the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation, and to the hundreds of railway workers who were put off work this week. Before the election the Government knew exactly what it intended to do. Government members knew before the election that they would be driving thousands of people out of their jobs. At that time they did not have the strength to go on to the public platforms and tell the people what would happen. They realised that the Government was getting into really deep and serious problems. What they did was a real con job. They had the December show in the Beehive. They made three or four announcements. They said that the Government could create the conditions that would contribute to, first, more investment; second, job creation; third, enhanced economic confidence; and, fourth, the provision of effective and efficient services by the Government. I want to consider each one of those points. I shall begin by quoting Mr Rex Jones, the President of the Labour Party, who said, when talking about the Budget: ``This Budget has been a Budget for the finance sector, not a Budget to encourage efficient expansion in the manufacturing and export sectors.'' He also said: ``The party now runs the risk of being badly compromised by the asset-sale programme.'' Mr Rex Jones represents average working people in this country. He represents the old Labour Party. But what we have at present is a Government that does not care. Government members are not worried about whether people have jobs. They are not worried about whether people are losing their farms, or whether houses have become more expensive so that people have to leave their homes. Government members are not worried at all. The Minister of Social Welfare represents one of the Dunedin electorates. He does not care one wrap that hundreds of jobs are being lost in Dunedin right now. He is one of the three Government members of Parliament representing the Dunedin region who do not care that a good firm such as Arthur Ellis and Co. Ltd. has left Dunedin and moved to Christchurch. He is the Minister who did not bother to turn up when freezing-workers lost their jobs at the Burnside freezing-works. The member for Dunedin West turned up late in the morning---after the people had gathered. The Minister of Labour, who is the member for Dunedin North, and the Minister of Social Welfare, who is the member for St. Kilda, did not turn up, because they did not care. They only just represent the Government at present. A well-known businessman, Hugh Fletcher, when talking about the Government's business policies, said: ``Many company executives, who initially whole-heartedly supported the Labour Government, are now hurt and are bleating.'' He understands that feeling. Those people thought they could have faith in a Labour Government, but now they understand that the Government does not care a rap about them. Hugh Fletcher also said: ``I favour a low exchange rate and other policies, and some element of protection for exporting policies to keep sheep numbers up.'' He said that because he knows perfectly well that there is only one way in which this country can survive---and that is by exports. That is a point that the Government does not fully understand. It also does not understand what investment is all about, and what investment is needed to get New Zealand going again. In recent times---in the Budget---it has made great play of its policy to reduce the various tax rates. If Government members consider the policy they will see that working people will not gain anything from it. Low-income people will pay more tax than they do now. If they read the many economists' reports on the Budget they will know that those people are saying that the Government has borrowed against the future to achieve the projected financial deficit of $. billion. It has borrowed against future generations just to try to achieve a reasonable deficit in this Budget. It has revamped the provisional taxes by many millions of dollars this year instead of next year. Government members know perfectly well that the Budget they have presented to the country is false. That is what the House is debating---a Budget that has been misrepresented to the people. The Government has even said to elderly people and to those on benefits that no longer will they get a -monthly adjustment. Instead it will make an adjustment every months, because it wants to shift that figure from one financial year to another. It is a specific move once again to con the people. When the Government made the promise on December that it would have a job creation exercise for the country within months, it conned the people. Unemployment figures show that nearly people are out of work. There is unemployment in various regions---in the South Island it is at record levels and has increased by more than percent in the past two years. In the South Island there is not one centre that has a rate of unemployment of less than percent. What does the Minister have to say about that matter? When will he tell the people what he intends to do? He was one of the dwarfs who stood up in the Beehive on December---he was part of the con job.

The Opposition is entitled to send South Island members to those meetings, and the Minister knows that. South Island members are as capable as any other member of discussing local body matters, yet the Minister is saying that there is no reason for them to be sent to Auckland. The principle is that the Government is moving motions of this kind more and more. This is the second motion within a fortnight suggesting that members should sit on select committees when they have more important duties to carry out. The Government knows that that is because it has misrepresented the position relating to legislation, select committees, and the sittings of the House. The Government is in a shambles. Why should the Opposition come to its aid every time it puts a motion before the House suggesting that members be sent somewhere else in the country?

The former Prime Minister is responsible for much of the mess that the country is in at present. He knows that more families are struggling today than ever before. Many families in the community are struggling to find money to pay their grocery bills and to clothe their children. The former Prime Minister and the former Minister of Revenue are responsible for much of the mess. The Minister of Employment sits over there. What has she done about the , unemployed? All that the Government has suggested is that people should gamble as a way of living. The Opposition believes that that is not right. That matter comes back to the heart of the Bill.
