In rising to speak to the Bill I must say that to understand any Bill that deals with the Treaty of Waitangi one must have a sound knowledge of what the treaty is all about. That is a very important precursor to any discussion of legislation that touches on the Treaty of Waitangi. Secondly, in relation to the previous member, it would be fair comment to say that with his legal turn of mind he needs to make some adjustments in the way he relates to the Bill. The Bill is probably a corner-stone of New Zealand's judicial system, and I use that word advisedly, because to me the term now encompasses, on the basis of the Act, another form of legal expertise that I refer to as the Maori one; and it is in relation to that matter that the member has to make major adjustments to his thinking. Maori did have a system of law that was obviously part of the culture in which it existed. The member referred to the tikanga, or kawa, o te marae in relation to women speaking on that institution. Generally speaking, women do have a right to speak within the confines of a marae. The matter in which one would need to pay particular attention to the so-called tikanga or kawa would be the mihi, the ritual that precedes such discussions. It is in relation to that matter that some marae are stringent about the roles that male and female play. I recognise no difficulty with the Bill in that respect. It makes specific reference to the issue of sex and the right to speak, subject to the understanding of what is known as the kawa of a marae. I bring that matter to the attention of the member and of the House because it is a matter that is subject to great misunderstanding, and one that is fraught with unjust attitudes to the procedure of the Waitangi Tribunal. I reinforce what the Minister in charge of the Bill said. The Bill has arisen out of legislation dating back to the Labour Government of , at which time the Waitangi Tribunal was established with a small membership of with power to act only in relation to grievances dating from forwards. Of course, it was an absurdity, in the sense that the vast majority of issues in relation to the treaty pre-date , and the tribunal was almost a hung jury in terms of what it could do. In its wisdom the Government has seen fit to modify the Act. Treaty of Waitangi issues dating from February until the present day will be able to be considered. Of course, as Opposition members would say, that has opened a can of worms. However, that is not what the Government is on about, and it is not what most Maori or pakeha believe---right-thinking people of the land, who are concerned about the issues of justice, equality, and equity, and all of the issues that are the corner-stones of a sound, harmonious society. When listening to Opposition members, one cannot help thinking that, by trying to convey a sense of doom and gloom to the people at large, they are not being honest with themselves. The Opposition is spreading a lot of unease amongst people; in essence, it is inciting the sources of racial tension---something that many Opposition members rarely do unwittingly. I suppose they were being political when they spoke about the Bill, but they took the opportunity to create dissent and to gain support in an unfair way. The Bill, of course, is not intended to create racial tension. When Opposition members stoop to talk about rabbits, and the number that will be produced at the end of the year, I wonder about their mentality in even suggesting the idea. If the member for Clevedon is interested in rabbits I might be able to provide him with some pocket-money so that he can establish a rabbit farm somewhere. He will then be able to examine all of the mathematical calculations to help him in that exercise. The issue of rabbits has no relevance to the Bill, and perhaps I have dwelt on that issue too long. The Bill has resulted not from a Court of Appeal directive but rather from issues emanating from a case that was put before the Court of Appeal by the New Zealand Maori Council. During the course of the discussions and decisions it was patently clear that the Waitangi Tribunal as currently constituted would not be able to cope with the large number of cases put before it---about cases to date. Significant modifications should be made to the membership of the Waitangi Tribunal and its mechanics to enable it to continue with its work and to overcome the work-load. I turn to the mathematics mentioned by the previous speaker, as about two cases a year have been actioned by the tribunal. That is a very small number. I think the member said that if the number of cases increased to it would take to years to deal with them. The tribunal's membership will increase from the present to , including the chairman, who would be the Chief Judge of the Maori Land Court. The Bill provides for the tribunal to divide into divisions with a minimum of three members in each division, and a maximum of seven in each division. Clearly, with that kind of formulation the tribunal would have the opportunity to act simultaneously on a maximum of five cases. If one takes the minimum number of divisions, and the total membership of the tribunal of , one would have divisions with members each able to pursue the various cases before them. On that basis it should be possible to deal with most of the cases in about years. Any rational person would realise that although initially there would be a large backlog of tribunal work-load the number of cases would diminish as the years went by. The number of submissions before the tribunal would reach a plateau, and at that stage the tribunal could no doubt cease to exist---that is a possibility. That is the important aspect of the Waitangi Tribunal, and I am sure that members cannot disagree with the need to alter its composition and the way in which the tribunal acts if it is to process the large number of cases before it. It was suggested to the select committee that if the tribunal is to be divided into divisions of three or seven members each division would act independently and somehow come down with decisions that might not be consistent. I do not buy that argument. The Bill allows the chairperson of the tribunal to select the appropriate chairperson for each division, and I am sure that in making those decisions he or she will have in mind the need to ensure consistency in the decision-making process. In the light of the mana that the tribunal has recently established for itself in our society that fear will be of little consequence. The Bill is important. I want to deal now with the racial issue. Both the news media and the member who preceded me have noted that in the past the tribunal has been considered to be racially biased. The member referred, in particular, to the increase in the tribunal membership from four to seven, with four of the members having to be Maori. I suppose that to some extent, because of the reality of our society, there is still a degree of suspicion between Maori and pakeha. I should like to think that that relationship is improving. It would be consistent with the nature of the submissions before the tribunal that its members need to be conversant not only with one of the major issues that the member raised---tikanga of the marae---but also with the whole spectrum of Maori culture. The people who would be most conversant with such matters would, in the first instance, be Maori, although I am not saying that there are not some pakeha people who have a considerable degree of understanding. However, mostly they would be Maori. Because the mana of the tribunal is very much at stake it behoves the tribunal to act wisely and justly in its deliberations, regardless of whether its members are Maori or pakeha. I am sure that with the present tribunal there is not one instance of anything else happening. The Leader of the Opposition spoke about the racial bias of the Waitangi Tribunal. He was asked to provide one instance of the tribunal's actions that would show such a bias, and it was noted that he did not answer that question. While the Bill does not make a distinction, contrary to what the member who preceded me said, it still does not prevent the tribunal from having a majority of Maori members. I am sure that, when selecting the tribunal's membership, the Minister of Maori Affairs will select individuals that he thinks are best suited to carry out the role. It may well be that he selects Europeans or pakeha, or Maori, or maybe some of each. Whatever his selection, it will be on the basis of the expertise and the sound judgment that the people involved can bring to the tribunal. I have no doubt that that will continue to be the attitude of the Minister. The Bill is important when one considers what is purported to be happening out there by some well-meaning, and in some instances not well-meaning, people who want to raise the matter of racial tensions in society. It is only when those problems are tackled in a rational manner that we will get a society in which I would be quite content to sit and have a tte--tte with the member for Otago without feeling that those tensions exist. Until those issues are dealt with on the basis of a just and equitable society the tensions will continue to exist. The Bill has the formula to achieve much good in society. I have no doubt that the future course of events will prove the worthiness of the Treaty of Waitangi.

The Leader of the Opposition would do well to contemplate what I have just said. For too long there has been conflict in Opposition ranks about the racial issues that beset us. Opposition members continue to stir and to aggravate the problem, rather than producing solutions, and that is a tragedy for the House. It would be a tragedy for the nation if they were to continue down that line. There are matters that should be dealt with in future submissions. The select committee's thinking has been constantly influenced by the need for a mechanism of delivery to Maoridom. The committee heard arguments about having a pan-Maori organisation of delivery to the people, in contrast with a tribe by tribe system. The treaty is specific on the issue. It refers to the confederation of chiefs of the united tribes and those chiefs who did not sign the treaty as being a collective body. In a sense, the matter of a pan-organisation is taken aboard in that section. The committee has considered the mechanism for delivery, and began with the establishment of a commission. It re-evaluated that suggestion, and went further and decided that another significant component to the delivery mechanism should be the setting up of a company. At that point I believe that we went wrong. I say that with all due respect to members of the committee, because if we examine the two sections in the draft Bill before the House we have to test what we mean by the Treaty of Waitangi, and the powers or conditions that in some instances were guaranteed in article of the treaty, and the relationship that has to the way te tino rangatiratanga will be actioned by the Maori people in the future. We have to revisit those two important principles. If we do not we will have transgressed the treaty.
Right, I will come to that point. Perhaps I could address that issue---

I listened to the previous speaker wax eloquent on the question of property rights, and I want to ask him a question: if, in fact, article of the Treaty of Waitangi refers to fisheries, who should be proving the issue of property rights? Is it for Maori people to say what their fishing rights are, or is it for the Crown to say what its property rights are? That is the argument that is constantly made against our people. I certainly agree with the Minister of Fisheries when he refers to sustainability and the conservation of the fishing resource of this land. New Zealand leads the world, to some extent, in this exercise, which was initiated by a Labour Government and is being pursued by the current Government. I do not think that the Opposition has any argument with that view, but I believe that, as a result of decisions in two recent court cases on fisheries matters, the Government is beginning to panic. I think that it almost is in a state of chaos, because not only is it not listening to what people in the fishing industry---and all those who are involved in fishing---have to say, but also it has virtually the whole of the industry against it. It is my view that this situation cannot continue. I believe that the Government will have to reach the stage at which it recognises the injustices---the wrongs---that are felt by the fishing industry. I am sure that it will then come to its senses and, I surmise, make some adjustments to the Bill. Because of the way in which the Government is attempting to push the Bill through the House, I believe that the Government's attempts with the Bill have been most machiavellian. Under the Bill the Government's responsibility to pay for ongoing conservation of fisheries has been virtually shifted on to those people who are the prime movers in that industry.

That was the only reference that the Government made to the issues facing our people and it indicates its attitude to the position in which it has placed not only the Minister of Maori Affairs but also Maoridom as a whole, in terms of philosophical and economic directions.

As Opposition members have said in their respective speeches, the Opposition will not oppose the introduction of the Bill. Perhaps I would not go so far as to say that I will wholeheartedly support the Government's endeavours. I think that it needs to be kept on its toes. I shall begin my dissertation on the Bill by referring to Maori land, because I say bluntly that this Bill must almost be the last Maori land-grab in the sense that basically it relates to Maori land throughout the country that has not been subject to the ravages---I am talking in general---of exploitation by various types of businesses. There are a number of reasons that that land has not been exploited. One reason, which already has been mentioned, has been the inability at times to provide capital to mill the timber on the land. But, equally, there has been the very strong desire of many Maori people to have their land remain in the virgin state in which they have known it. There are still significant numbers of Maori people who think that way today. Unfortunately, it is the mighty dollar that must determine the future development and direction of many things in this country, and that is consistent with the thinking of this Government. It is a tragedy that Government members are so blind to the need to cope adequately that they do not see that in places New Zealand should be kept in the pristine state that was known by their ancestors. I am referring to the early settlers in this country, as well as to my own predecessors of many years ago. That is the unfortunate thing about this Bill. Why has it made a stipulation about Maori land in Southland, which is a significant area of Maori land and one that has significant areas of virgin forest? Why has the Government seen fit to exclude that land from the Forests Amendment Bill? Again, the Government has shown insensitivity, and it is the power of the mighty dollar that has led it to make those decisions. I certainly am concerned about the fate of Maori land, and I am concerned about the virgin forests that still exist on those tracts of land. Those who look down the passage of history will see that generally what happened was that initially all the good pieces of land with the nice big trees were acquired; they were then clear-felled, ploughed, sown in grass, and converted to the lovely dairy land that we see in parts of the country today. In those times, these tracts of land would have been considered to be poorer areas without significance for the types of industry that our early settlers brought to the land, and these forests were left alone. But now---and this is the unfortunate part---those forests have become very valuable and, of course, the chain-saws and the axes have moved in. Instead of what I believe to be those significant tracts of land being preserved, they now fall to the power of the big companies and the like. To conclude this part of my speech, I wonder from my perusal of the Bill whether sufficient compensation is being made in those circumstances in which Maori land is involved. I know that the Southland beech forests were also a topic of considerable debate and interest during the time of the Labour Government. At that time the Maori owners were very much debating that issue and were attempting to draw it to the attention of the powers that be. That issue is still very much a part of their ongoing struggle to seek adequate compensation for the rape of their lands. In fairness, I have to say that some Maori landowners are in favour of having some of those trees cleared. Again, in large part that attitude is dictated by the fact that the need to survive in today's environment is putting pressure on them, and they need to have some form of income. It is a pity that our society and our mode of government---regardless of the form of that government---have developed in such a way that I am sure that those people who went to the environmental conference in Rio de Janeiro, for example, would have very red ears if they were listening to some of the things that we are saying in the House tonight. None the less, I am sure that this issue is not peculiar to New Zealand. It is an ongoing debate in many lands, and we know that countries not very far away from New Zealand---the Philippines and the like---are also having pressure brought to bear on their rain forests. Therefore, from an environmental and conservation viewpoint, I am not convinced that the Bill will do us much good.

I have listened with great interest to the member for Eden, and I make the following comments. It is important to realise that there are cultural differences in respect of certain attitudes and certain developments within a group---and I refer to the question of silence. I know that in European society silence indicates acquiescence to whatever the issue is at the time. When silence occurs in a Maori environment the reverse is true. One can take that matter on the basis of, perhaps, the two elements that are involved in this debate---probably more than two, but specifically two: namely, the Maori and the pakeha. In the Maori environment silence is definitely not a sign of acquiescence but of the total reverse. I was also interested in the member's comment about the need for the Representation Commission to proceed with some haste, and the reason for the Bill was that it was the method by which that could be achieved. I believe that that comment also clearly underpins the seriousness with which the Maori members, in particular, view not so much the timing of the legislation as the fact that it should even be a consideration in an issue that we have been grappling with---certainly as Maori members---probably for a generation or two; not just in recent times. As yet, no progress has been made. Progress is not being made---and I take the point that the member made, and on which the Speaker attempted to rule---because the issue of Maori representation is more of a holistic problem in terms of the electoral system. Not only do we have to consider the question of boundaries but we also have to consider the questions of the Maori population and the way in which the Maori rolls and the general rolls are formulated. In my opinion, the whole system needs to be taken apart and rebuilt on that basis, because that is the problem. At present all that we are doing is tinkering with a small process that has been with us since . We need not so much the tinkering and the manipulation that is within the narrow confines of the electoral legislation as literally to tear apart the system and rebuild it on a true democratic process for New Zealanders based on the essence of the Treaty of Waitangi. I know that that issue appears ad nauseam. None the less that is the way that most Maoris would begin their discussion on any issue that relates to our nationhood and particularly to safeguarding the interests of the Maori people. The Bill is just another effort at tinkering with the system---just shifting from point A to point B within a small alphabetic confine, without any due consideration to addressing the problems of Maori representation. That is a big challenge for the House, and I should like to think that it still has the ability to cope with that. Having said that, I must say that things are certainly wearing a bit thin for most Maori people, who have been attempting for a long time to redress the position and who have been achieving very little---in fact, almost nil in my opinion---in relation to the issue of Maori representation. The reality is that the Royal Commission on the Electoral System received only one Maori submission that opposed the abolition of Maori seats, and here we have that mighty tome of expertise that is able to come down on the deliberation and say that that is what it believes is the correct method of redressing that matter. The final comment that I want to make with respect to the commission was that it was never given a mandate by the Maori people. I put to the House that an issue that affects Maori people should surely be an issue that ought to have given the Maori people the right to deliberate on it without the royal commission taking the responsibility of that matter onto its own shoulders. On that basis, because of its failure to do that, I have little regard for the substance of the commission in that respect. If one cared to examine the records it would be found that most Maori groups have been arguing for a system that will give Maori proper representation on the basis of our democratic process. Also, most of them have argued that on that basis there should be more Maori seats in this establishment. Of course, if one reads the news media and takes what I perceive is their perspective on the issue invariably the answer is: ``Yes, we'll maintain the status quo until such time as it may be desirable to do away with it.''. The position never occurs in which we could say: ``We should maintain the system until such time as it either increases or diminishes.''; it is never put in that way. As I have said in the House many times, it is a reflection on the attitudes of many New Zealanders---partly from ignorance, but not always---that they are not able to see issues in a totally neutral way. That is the point that I want to share with the House. The other aspect is that of the representation of Maori women, and I appreciate the sincerity of members in the House who would argue that cause also. I should just like to add the point that it might be in that debate, as well, that one will have to address the issue of how many Maori women and how many pakeha women will be part of that process, but I shall leave that matter for that group to argue. I have always been desirous of being on the Electoral Law Committee. I think that it is one that many Maori members have always aspired to and probably others in the House have equally attempted to do be on it, because they see that as a means whereby they can address the system to their advantage, and I accept that reality. However, my interest---like that of my colleague the member for Southern Maori---is an attempt to see that Maori people get their fair share of the development in electoral law. I know that I have rambled on on a wide issue, but it is important to the debate in general, which I shall now address. Clause relates to the question of the breakdown of children into the categories that determine whether they are recognised as Maori children or non-Maori children. It is an attitude that I have great difficulty relating to, because the question of one's ethnicity is a matter of birth and not of legislation. Somehow that position is wheedled so that the poor child, the tamaiti or kotiro, who has a background of Maori ancestry suddenly finds that one day that child can no longer be placed in that category because it is legislated that for certain reasons he or she cannot be defined as a Maori child. That is a terrible indictment---a terrible position in which to place children who have no opportunity to argue their case until they reach the age of years. By which time they are so confused---like many people on rolls at present---that the outcome just compounds their position. That measure does not clarify the issue relating to the Maori population, but further confuses it. I should like to take that thinking a little further and have us look at the question of adoption. What if a Maori child is adopted by a non-Maori family? Where does that child fit in? That child may still be a Maori, but the laws on adoption have changed again with respect to the Maori way of looking at adoptions. I am talking about the whanau concept and the attitudes of youngsters within that concept. All those Maori issues are being overturned or influenced by the legislation, which confuses the matter. I am not sure that the Bill as it is drafted at present caters for Maori children who are adopted into pakeha families. Are such people lost? As someone said, it is difficult to gauge that sort of information or to define it. I draw the attention of the House to the Births and Deaths Registration Act. I understood, though I am not sure that this is still the case---but I fought it as a member of the Labour Government---that under that Act a person had to state the ancestry of the child being registered and whether the child had Maori blood. If that information is still available it is another method apart from the census of determining the correct ancestry of the child, no matter what environment it happened to be in on census night. Those avenues must be addressed. I know that the Government is concerned that time is running out for the next election and that something must be put in place to justify all the inequities that have not influenced it but have certainly influenced the Maori people. They have been at the bottom end of whatever interpretation has been made---whether it was made in ignorance or was contrived. I must admit that I have exposed a sense of cynicism about much of what has happened to our people especially in this House, because the very fact that more Maori are now on the general roll is taken purely from a statistical viewpoint, and that says to statisticians that Maori people do not want Maori seats because the majority of them are on the general roll. Some of the reasons given by my colleagues are certainly accurate in that regard. I take the view that the electoral system in this country is in a complete mess. It is a shemozzle and is tinkering to a major extent. One only has to think of the definition of a Maori. Anyone in this House could go on to the Maori roll by claiming Maori ancestry because that is all that is required. The whole system needs to be turned on its head and definitions need to be clarified so that future generations can say that we have acted towards the two major signatories to the treaty in a manner that is above reproach. I would challenge any Government member, and probably a few more, to say that that is the case in relation to the way that Maori people have been treated under our electoral system. It is a sad indictment in my opinion---and I say that in a sincere way and not in an attempt to denigrate anyone. I accept that people have the right to say what they want to say in our society but I would hope that, having been consistent with the principles of that famous philosopher Descartes, they would apply the same principles with regard to the Maori boundaries. I should have thought that the Government would be a lot more generous about redressing an issue to which Maori people have been subjected in at least three or four general elections. I think it required an attitude to be taken in the legislation to indicate to the Maori people what has happened in the past four or so elections and to indicate that there might have been five Maori members of Parliament three elections ago had the due process been carried through in the correct manner. In my opinion nothing in the Bill even indicates an attempt to be sympathetic towards what has actually happened. In Maoridom this would be considered an act of mana. In actual fact a wrong had been done in the past on the question of Maori representation, particularly to the Maori people but to a lesser degree to the general rolls, because as a result of the misinterpretation of a section of the Electoral Act the Maori people have been denied their rightful representation in Parliament. That misrepresentation or misinterpretation has led to the inaccurate definition of boundaries. Members who were in Parliament at the time may not have been here had the correct boundaries and the correct populations been registered and acted upon at that time. Where is the great-heartedness of the Government to accept the fact that it is predominantly the Maori people who were influenced in a negative way in relation to the rights of their people to have their say in the House by an Act that simply and purely states that four is the number and that is it? That is still the situation today. With the changes and the question of the Maori option one could argue that the electorates are not too different, although if one looks at the figures there is definitely an argument for saying that there should be another Maori representative in the House because the electoral populations are greater than those that would apply in a general election. I want to say that the attempt at tinkering with the Bill that has taken place is not justice, not only to the Maori people but also to others in terms of what it really means to be a democracy. We often go and travel abroad and paint a picture of our race relations. Again I notice the absence of the news media, and I should like to take them to task. They made some reference to the previous debate in the House---I do not know whether that was because of what I said to them---but I want to draw their attention to the question of apartheid. I know that the bogy has been raised in the past that what we are attempting to do in terms of Maori representation is an argument for apartheid but I have always argued the reverse and have said that the system that is in existence now, which limits the number of Maori seats in Parliament, is an example of apartheid in practice. If members think on that they will come to the conclusion---
For the information of the Minister of Justice, the direction in which Government members are moving has not, in essence, changed from that of the Labour Government.

The Crown did. The Treaty of Waitangi is a document in which the Crown stated that it guaranteed that it would give all the protections inherent in that particular document to those Maori people who signed it and to those who did not sign it. The Minister is applying that same argument to the Bill. The position is different. It is a situation that, in order to apply, needs to require the agreement of all those who sign it and to exclude those who do not. Therefore I believe that the Bill is a sham and that it is an insult to the Maori people of this country.

It is with some relish that I find myself following the address made by the member for St. Albans, because in the select committee I was often not able to be in agreement with that eminent member on several aspects of the Bill. But when I listened to what he had to say about what he claims is a tax treatment or a preference for certain items in the Bill, I found myself at complete variance---and that aids one in debating a matter. I regret a couple of matters about the introduction of the Bill. I shall mention them briefly. First, I regret that it has taken a little time to bring the Bill before the House, because it contains some worthy measures that the House will acknowledge; and, second, I regret the retrospectivity of the clause application. However, I am supportive of and am prepared to vote for the implementation of that clause because it recovers money that is due to the Crown, and it is a proper treatment of that money. Members will know from the previous debate on that clause that there was confusion about whether the amount added to the sums paid out as grants or under various wage schemes by the previous Government---and paid out with an amount added for goods and services tax---included the goods and services tax, because the matter was rather obscurely---that is probably a word that fits the case neatly---dealt with by the previous Government. However, the fact remains that it appears that more than half of the people who received that money saw fit to repay to the Crown the additional amount that they had received by way of the goods and services tax. They did that properly. The Bill regularises the position and it puts us where we should be. However, the main items that I want to deal with relate to farming---in particular, the livestock tax---and to particular items of expenditure. I shall also spend some time dealing with forestry, which has, I understand, engaged the attention of the member for St. Albans to a considerable extent. I should like to put some points of view that are directly contrary to his. The Bill makes various changes to the livestock tax. That tax system has been unduly onerous and quite non-productive in its effect. There were some good concepts in the livestock tax as introduced by the previous Government, but it followed from circumstances in which there had been quite significant fluctuations in the values of stock---in particular, the values of non-traditional livestock such as deer and goats. Those values had risen to a level that had never been anticipated. The tax arose also from circumstances in which the Government had let the system slip because the previous standard value system should have been reviewed each years but it had fallen into a period of lapse and was well behind actual market prices. The livestock tax, as introduced, was unduly complicated and was penal in its effect to the extent that farmers were, and until the passage of this Bill still are, required to bring into their accounts---and will be so required even by this legislation---animals that they have not reared on the farm at a value much more than the cost of those animals. I suggest to the House and to the Opposition that it is in the interests of the country to encourage an increase in the number of livestock on farms. One of the greatest tragedies that befell the country during the period of the previous Government was the serious decline in livestock numbers. During the past years there have been periods when New Zealand enjoyed record prices for its meat, wool, and dairy products, but, because of the decline in stock numbers, unfortunately the country did not gain the benefits it should have gained. This Government is committed to turning that position round. It wants to give confidence to farmers to increase their livestock and to expand. It wants the nation as a whole to enjoy the fruits of that expansion. The Bill is but one of the planks in that policy. The livestock tax will make changes because it will allow entry to the herd scheme, which has advantageous features for some farmers because they are now able to put all classes of stock into that scheme, and for tax purposes it enables them to spread the income that arises from entering it. I was interested to hear the member for St. Albans say that a cost of about $ million of tax apparently would be forgone as a result of these measures. I have difficulty with that figure as I have difficulty with some other figures that he quoted. The reality of the position---as you, Mr Speaker, being a farmer, will know---is that when a farmer elects the option of putting livestock into the herd scheme it means that they go in at a somewhat higher value than they might have done; that itself constitutes income for tax purposes. It is not tax forgone; it is actually opting to pay tax---albeit in the longer term it may be a more stable basis on which to carry that livestock---but tax results from that choice in the short term. Therefore it was nonsense for the member to suggest that there is a tax-forgone element because of items in the Bill. It also contains measures relating to high-priced livestock that regulate the position in that regard. The select committee heard in submissions that those prices were not pitched high enough. I believe that the measures are correct and that the position is well covered in the Bill. Significant measures are introduced in relation to the deduction of certain items of expenditure such as for the destruction of weeds, animal pests detrimental to the land, the clearing of the land, destruction and removal of scrub, repairs of flood or erosion damage, the planting or maintaining of trees for the purpose of preventing or combating erosion, the planting and maintaining of trees for the purpose of providing shelter, and the construction of fences for agricultural purposes. I found it incredible at the time as an accountant that the previous Government saw fit to deny expenditure of that kind to farmers at the time of the expenditure. It was nonsense that in reality was probably more honoured in the breach than in the observance. Therefore it is logical, and the member for St. Albans nods his head and recognises that. But there was little point in trying to make a definition about where a fence was to go before it was decided whether it was tax-deductible and whether the farmer had to count the number of battens and fence posts he had on the property and decide which were used for repairs and which went into the new fencing; or when he was cutting down scrub and bush it had to be decided whether that was maintenance, whether it had grown in the past few years, or whether he was making a clearance of land. Those matters were nonsense, and have been corrected in the Bill. I thoroughly support the intention and the actual result of the legislation. I want to turn now to questions about forestry. Members will know that the effect of the Bill is to grant deductibility to those persons carrying out this work on the costs of planting, of releasing, of pruning, and of thinning commercial trees for plantation purposes. The forest owner is now able to deduct those costs in the year of expenditure and against income from any other source. The member for St. Albans has advanced the view that this is a particular concession. I ask the House whether it is a concession, or whether it is a matter of consistency and a matter of equity. What other commercial operation denies an operator the opportunity of deducting the expenses incurred while earning his or her deductible income in the year of expenditure? I have difficulty in thinking of any, and perhaps Opposition members might be able to point something out to me later. However, I was not alone in having that difficulty, because the select committee received representations from the Society of Accountants and the Law Society, and the representatives making those submissions were prepared to say that they saw nothing improper or incorrect in accounting practices that allowed this expenditure to be deducted in the year of expenditure. The alternative, which was introduced by the previous Government in about , was that that expenditure needed to be held and capitalised in what was termed a cost-of-bush account for the whole period of the life of that plantation, and that could be years. It was totally illogical that anybody growing a commercial plantation for profit should be required to hold that expenditure for the whole life of that plantation before making a deduction. The effect of that position was obvious. Between and the present time, new forest plantings fell from , hectares to about hectares, and we will all live to rue the day that that happened. Those of us who are here now may not be here to see the day some to years hence when that shortfall in planting will tell against the country. The member for St. Albans asked what advantage accrues from planting trees. I shall tell him about the advantages, but, first, let me address the question of what is supposedly tax forgone in this respect. The figure that has been quoted to the House is $ million. If that figure is correct, what must have taken place for that amount of tax to have been forgone? I certainly contest the use of the word ``forgone''. For that to have happened there must have been an expenditure of at least $ million on forestry work. At a tax rate of c in the dollar on that amount, the most that would be charged represents $ million. I have done some calculations and the House may be interested to know that an average forestry operation such as pruning or thinning would be about $ a hectare, at the very outside. It would be more than the cost of planting and certainly more than the cost of releasing and thinning. If the Opposition's figures are correct, $ million means work must have been done on , hectares in a given year. Is that credible? The present forest estate in this country is ,, hectares, so we are talking about work being done in a given year on half of the total forest estate. That does not make sense. I cannot understand how this figure has been derived. The figure of $ million of tax allegedly forgone does not arise until . Who can say what the country's fiscal position might be in ? It is nonsense to talk now about the dangers and the worries of forgoing tax on a sum that may or may not arise in . The figures used are somewhat illogical when they require work to be done on at least half of the forestry estate, which grows for years and might be worked on times in that period. What would happen if we spent $ million on forestry work in a given year? I have some more figures in relation to what that would mean in terms of jobs. Forestry work is normally done on a seasonal basis with the men and women working for months each year. Let us say that they are paid $ a week and earn $ for that seasonal work. If they earn $, and if $ million were spent on that forestry work, there would be work for , people. Is it in the country's interests to provide work for , people? It is time that the Opposition recognised the significance of forestry. The present forest estate is about ,, hectares and produces about ,, cubic metres of wood a year, which will grow year by year. The export income received from forest products amounts to about $. billion a year, and it is the country's third-biggest earner, because wool slipped back a little. In the next to years that figure will double and it will double again in the following to years. If the forest owners and the forest developers are judicious in their choice of added value, the return could be even more. Within the period of years we should see, even from the present forestry estate, a trebling of the current export income in present-day dollar terms. However, that is only the tip of the iceberg. It is important to realise in relation to this Bill that the forest estate---whilst that seems large to us, we should relate it to our present forest exports---represents only . percent of world wood trade. New Zealand's potential in this regard is huge, and the potential in the land bank of New Zealand could result in the present forest estate of ,, hectares expanding threefold or fivefold. That will not take place unless there is investment. There need to be people bold enough to commit their money for the future. That commitment in the planting of trees, the clearing of land for that, and the tending of those trees, is virtually all labour-intensive. If we want to provide jobs now, if we do have a genuine concern for those people who want, are seeking, and cannot get jobs, we should have a commitment to the encouragement of investment in activities such as forestry and the farming that I mentioned previously. Forestry is just so obvious. A land bank exists---without interfering with our agricultural production that could bring about a trebling of our present forest estate, as I said, or even an increase of five times. The present export earnings of forestry are $. billion, and that is from a very good authority. I have had demonstrated to me that that could, under a very promising scenario, perhaps be expanded to $ billion. That is significant, surely. More than twice our present export earnings from all sources could---under a very best scenario perhaps, but under present-day dollar terms---come from forestry. That is a promising scenario. However, as I have said, it will come only if potential investors in forestry receive encouragement from the Government to the extent---I do not say that this is the only reason---that their investment is treated on the same terms for taxation purposes as investment in any other activity, and that would mean that it could be deducted from taxation in the year of expenditure. The cost-of-bush scenario that was brought in by the Labour Government is nonsense that I do not believe is replicated in any other country. I have some experience in forestry investment to the extent that I was involved previously in forestry promotional work. The difference I see is whether those private investors---many of whom are interested in forestry---leave their money to lie idly in the bank, spend their money on overseas trips, spend it at the races, or spend it on some other consumer item, or whether they make a commitment for their future and spend it on something that will create jobs for this country. To me, the choice is obvious.

I am directed to present the report of the Finance and Expenditure Committee on the petition of Heather Henare and others. I move, That the report do lie upon the table, and be referred to the Government for consideration. Motion agreed to.

I can hear someone on the Opposition benches calling out something about people. The emphasis in all of this is on people because, if the department heeds the encouragement given to it by the Government for the better expenditure of the health dollar, the ultimate beneficiary is the people, and that is the emphasis in the Government's drive towards efficiency in health services. The emphasis is on producing health services where they matter most---at the very coal-face of the health service where the patient is treated---by nurses and doctors---if in a hospital bed---or by the general practitioner, and where remedial services are offered. It is not on the overall administration---not the top tier of administration---but, rather, at the very coal-face of the administration of health services. That is what lies at the heart of the drive to separate the funders and the providers in the health service, and that is at the core of the health service changes that are being brought about now. As I said, the committee spent some time with the departmental officers and they noted that the department had to operate for a period under temporary leadership---under deputy administration---and I am pleased that that situation has now been resolved and the new director-general appointed. Bearing in mind that the Department of Health administers probably the most significant item of expenditure in the country's budget and one of the most difficult to control, the general tenor of the report on the department's activities commended the department on its activities---particularly while running with a deputy director-general---and the efforts were appreciated by the Government.

Thank you, Mr Speaker, for the opportunity to address an issue that has undoubtedly caused a lot of anxiety on both sides of the House. Judging by the amount of heat and excitement that have been generated from time to time, it is quite clear that members are deeply concerned about this issue. I, myself, have exercised some thought about the degree of significance that should be attached to this matter; after all, this is still only Tuesday, March, and the House has taken urgency for three consecutive days in order to deal with this most impelling, urgent, and dire matter. Coincidentally, along with the two previous issues that have been debated in this period of urgency---the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Bill (No. ) and the Postal Services Bill---this Bill seems to impact upon another event that is not too many thousands of kilometres away from here: the Taranaki - King Country by-election. Being a lawyer and having a legal background, I do not like to draw the obvious conclusion, because I am of the view that we should always give a measure of credence to the concept of the benefit of doubt in these kinds of circumstances. However, I have to say that almost beyond reasonable doubt there has to be a connection between the events of the last days in the House and the event that will occur in the Taranaki province at the beginning of May. I would not like to cast a slur upon the Government's motives in bringing these issues forward under urgency at this time, but it does seem to be very strange indeed that we should be targeting these particular areas, under urgency, at this stage. Considering the merits of the matter---and I do have a concern, as all members do, about the dangers to the public in crossing rural land while hunting, fishing, tramping, hiking, biking, or enjoying other pleasant social activities---it seems extraordinary that the Government has taken such a colossal sledgehammer to smash a very small nut. We are not here just to consider the question of recreational access to rural land, we are now effectively amending the law to cover all areas of activity in New Zealand---workplace related and otherwise. If that is the case, why do we not have to consider the option of dealing with these in compartments and sections? If we are going to talk about access to rural land, let us do so as a separate matter. If we want to consider access to other places---workplaces, factories, schools, and any other places of common interest or concern---let us do so. We have here a great feast, a movable feast almost. We are talking about the rectification of grievances from the past that go back to the last century. As a former magistrate and lawyer in previous days, I know what it is to have to deal with people who feel aggrieved with their circumstances in life. We have only to consider the notorious case of Arthur Allan Thomas, who was himself a victim of injustice and spent not less than years in prison. For that he was compensated to the extent of $ million after he was pardoned for the offence for which he was tried and subsequently convicted. Here we are dealing with claims that affect scores of families and thousands of individuals going back generations in time. I have a letter dated September addressed to all members of Parliament and sent by the Ngati Apa Ki Te Waipounamu Trust. I would like to speak about that letter and a number of the issues that were raised in that letter by the chairperson Kath Hemi, who is a recipient of the Queen's Service Medal. Her letter states as follows: ``We have, over the past years, endeavoured unsuccessfully to have the Minister of Justice allow tribunal hearings for the remaining South Island iwi before settling with Ngai Tahu. Ngati Apa in June filed a claim WAI to the Waitangi Tribunal at the same time writing and offering dialogue with Ngai Tahu. So far no reply. I refer to a couple of amendments that I have proposed regarding the Infrastructure Auckland deed. I must say that it is good to see the former Minister of Energy John Luxton in the Chamber because he would be pretty familiar with bodgie pseudo-corporate and unaccountable deeds signed off by the Minister of Local Government in place of democratic accountability in Auckland---a la Mercury Energy. I have proposed two amendments. The first amendment is to subsection () in section ZZW. It simply removes the consultation process between the Minister and the electoral college regarding the deed and makes it clear that there must be agreement from the electoral college before the deed is signed off by the Minister. We heard a whole lot of pseudo-constitutional arguments on why the Minister should not have to have agreement. None of those arguments was supported by evidence before the select committee. There is absolutely no reason constitutionally, or any other reason, that the Minister should not obtain the agreement of the electoral college, which, after all, theoretically represents the owners of these assets, before signing off on the deed. The second amendment that I propose relates to the regional growth strategy. When we discussed the previous clause, I referred to the fact that I would be proposing an amendment that, having completed a lengthy and complex process of drafting and consulting on a regional growth strategy, the strategy should have some teeth. The amendments to section ZZX would have the effect of requiring Infrastructure Auckland to give effect to the regional growth strategy. As it is currently worded, Infrastructure Auckland need only make decisions that are not inconsistent with the growth strategy, which means that any issue on which the growth strategy is silent could be taken as an area in which Infrastructure Auckland had carte blanche for its funding decisions. That seems to be an unnecessarily ad hoc approach to planning issues. It would be far better to assume that if the regional growth strategy has not proposed a particular type of development, that it has considered that development and ruled it out. Where there are gaps, they should not be filled de facto by a bunch of unelected and unaccountable board members. The decisions of Infrastructure Auckland should be driven principally by the regional growth strategy, and the amendment that I am proposing would require Infrastructure Auckland to give effect to that regional growth strategy. Those are two amendments that I would ask the Minister to respond to. The first amendment requires the agreement of the electoral college to the deed. Why is the Minister so anxious to preserve absolute power over the details of the structures of Infrastructure Auckland?

I rise to support the amendments in the name of Jim Anderton to the short title and to the commencement date. Firstly I rise to support the amendment that the legislation should come into force years from the date on which it receives the royal assent. That amendment is an important amendment because clearly it indicates a need to delay the implementation of this tariff reduction policy. The reason a delay is needed is that the issue of tariffs is a far more complex issue than the debate in this Chamber today has indicated to New Zealanders, in particular the New Zealanders who will be affected by the removal of those tariffs. There is some truth in the point that tariffs might appear to be a clumsy way of protecting New Zealand jobs, but until now they have been the only way that we have had of protecting the absolute outflow of New Zealand jobs in manufacturing, particularly in the exporting sector and in the import-substitution sector. Tariffs play two roles. First of all, the role of tariffs is to hold our own against other people's tariffs. As has been pointed out time and time again in this debate, to remove our tariffs below the level of our trading partners, and in effect to overprice our exports and to underprice their imports into the New Zealand market is economic lunacy and a socially disruptive policy. So the first role of tariffs is to protect us against other people's tariffs. That might look kind of absurd in an overall international economic sense, and it is, but the reality is that our trading partners maintain tariffs. While they do that, we owe a service to New Zealanders to allow our industries to compete on a fair footing with imports from and exports to other markets. The second role of tariffs---and it is the one that has not been referred to in previous debate on this issue in Parliament---is to reflect costs that New Zealand manufacturers and producers bear that are not borne by some of the countries we compete with. Two of these costs are a reasonable level of income for the workers producing in New Zealand, and a reasonable level of environmental protection. One of the functions of tariffs is to enable New Zealand companies that bear additional costs as a result of our labour and environmental protections not to be undercut by industries producing in countries where those costs are not borne. One of the key reasons for this amendment to take a rain check for a couple of years on the implementation of this policy is at the very least to look at other ways---or to fall back to tariffs as one of those ways---of acknowledging the added costs to New Zealand business. Should New Zealand continue to oppose, for instance, child labour, slavery---although a form of it came into effect today, with the introduction of workfare---and environmental degradation, then there is a need for New Zealand industry to retain some form of tariff or other protection against that kind of unfair competition in the international market place. So I commend the -year rain check to the Committee, in particular to those who think they have achieved a victory with this legislation. That brings me to the second amendment, which is to put into the short title the words ``by July '' after the words ``Zero Duty''. In reality the short title as it is currently worded is absolutely accurate. It is the Tariff (Zero Duty) Amendment Act and there is no protection against the Minister and Cabinet removing all duties the moment the royal assent is given to this legislation. But let us make an honest piece of legislation of this and insert the words ``by July '' in the short title of the Bill. This makes it clear that the principle is that is the end point but the reality is that this Government can do it any time it likes.

Oh dear, it is because of the delicate sensibilities of the member opposite. She cannot dirty her hands with the nasty things that go on in Parliament. It is all too hard. I am pleased to address the third reading of this Bill dealing with the abolition of the public broadcasting fee. I am not really sure why the Labour Party is not voting against it. It has said nothing in its favour, but it is voting for it. Perhaps the next speaker can explain it to me as it is beyond my ken. This move to abolish the public broadcasting fee means a saving to every household of $ a year. The legislation that the Government is introducing will abolish the public broadcasting fee from July next year. In future public broadcasting will be funded from general taxation. This move makes a lot of good sense. It means that the fee is no longer tied up with cumbersome bureaucratic red tape. In the past too much time and money have been wasted collecting this fee. Over $ million has been wasted in this way. Why should people with television sets pay for a fee that supports a wide range of activities? The public broadcasting fee funds locally made programmes for both television and radio. It is used to promote New Zealand music, for the archiving of historical programmes, and for Maori broadcasting. I hope that by now we all know what the fund does fund. These activities will now be funded from general taxation. Fears have been expressed that scrapping the broadcasting fee threatens the independence of public broadcasting. There is no basis for this fear and there is no proof of it. Only the source of funding has been changed. Funding will now be more widely and more evenly spread. For that reason it will be more equitable. Nothing other than the fee has been scrapped. The structure governing the operation and oversight of Radio New Zealand remains the same. The structure of all other institutions receiving the benefit of the broadcasting fee also remains the same. This funding change---and that is all it is---creates a more efficient and fairer system for all New Zealanders, and at the same time it reduces compliance and financial pressures on families. It is just one of a comprehensive range of measures in this year's Budget that will provide, I think, a far better future for families and all New Zealanders. The abolition of the fee also reduces the burden on sellers and hirers of television sets, who at the moment, for collection purposes, have to provide returns on television ownership and hire. I am particularly pleased that funding for New Zealand On Air is no longer tied to the level of the broadcasting fee. That is excellent news for the New Zealand broadcasting industry as it puts New Zealand On Air in a position to get more funding in the future. I have committed myself to enabling it to do this. The Government is still firmly committed to funding public broadcasting, and there is absolutely no evidence that it is not. In fact, it has been said several times tonight that $ million over years is being injected into Radio New Zealand for this very reason. Through public broadcasting New Zealand's special identity is reflected on film, television, and radio. These programmes reflect New Zealand's unique identity and culture, and we see that every day. I absolutely agree with Warren Kyd, who said that radio and broadcasting have never been healthier or more dynamic, and the ratings have never been as good. People are turning to radio more and more. New Zealand is, of course, a culturally diverse and rich country, and through public broadcasting I think we can appreciate that. Again, much has been said tonight about people's passion for culture and identity. Members on this side of the House share that passion, but we do not always bleed all over the floor about it. I have often talked about our identity. I am very committed to it. I have mentioned the flag a few times, because that is associated with it. But I want a dynamic and modern identity for New Zealand. I feel that a healthy broadcasting and television scene will bring this about. I reiterate what my fellow colleagues have already told the House: the abolition of the public broadcasting fee does not imply any change in the roles of New Zealand On Air and Te Mangai Paho, or the services they support. Both these organisations have achieved a great deal, and have made an outstanding contribution to giving all New Zealanders radio and television programmes and services of a highly professional nature, for the benefit of everyone in New Zealand. This service will continue. Only the method of how these organisations receive funding has changed. We will still have high-quality, locally made programmes on radio and television. New Zealand On Air currently provides about $ million to fund locally produced television programmes. This is about percent of all locally made programming on the three main networks, with the balance funded by the broadcasters themselves. Radio New Zealand currently receives $. million each year from the public broadcasting fee, and that has gone up by $ million for each year. This level of funding will continue to apply. So I reiterate that there is absolutely no evidence that this Government is not committed to funding Radio New Zealand and broadcasting in general. Te Mangai Paho will continue to receive $. million. New Zealand On Air is an independent statutory body established under the Broadcasting Act. Nothing changes. I am pleased to acknowledge that this Act expressly prevents any ministerial direction being given to New Zealand On Air about any and all programmes, including news and current affairs programmes. That is one of the requirements of the Broadcasting Act; it has nothing to do with the public broadcasting fee. This Act also prevents New Zealand On Air from having any direct say about the editorial content of any of these programmes, and that is how it should be. In supporting this Bill I say again that replacing the public broadcasting fee with funding from general taxation will be fairer, more efficient, less cumbersome, and an easier way of getting money through to the broadcasting end. The fee has been levied on owners of television sets, but it is used to support many other services and programmes. It has been a highly misunderstood fee, unfortunately. Perhaps many of us have not made a good enough job of explaining it to the public. Removing the fee also means the end of a great deal of confusion. In spite of detailed information campaigns by New Zealand On Air, the fee has been widely misunderstood. Abolishing the fee is common sense. It means that New Zealand On Air can get on with its main job of funding broadcasting services and programmes without having to spend time and money on fee collection. I say again that there will be no change in the role of New Zealand On Air or in the level of funding available to it for allocation to broadcasting programmes and services. The Government will make sure that New Zealand On Air receives from general taxation the same amount of funding as it always has. This amounts to $ million a year. During the period when the fee is being phased out the Government will top up New Zealand On Air's declining fee revenue to make sure its total income remains at the same level. I have pleasure in endorsing the passage of this Bill through the House.

The real rate of interest has not been as high as that, and I would have thought that the member for Tongariro would be able to count on his fingers up to percent, anyway---with a little help, perhaps, from his colleague sitting next to him. I want to go back in history a wee way on the matter. In the Masterton County and the Masterton Borough joined together through an agreed amalgamation---it was not forced---some period of time before the local government reorganisation law that took effect from November . As a part of the agreement the two councils decided in good faith that they would stick with the same differential rating system. The councils made that pledge and agreed that that was the way it would happen. However, on November , a new Masterton District Council came into being---it was a new body. The select committee was told that the boundaries were almost the same as those of the previous district council---there were just slight alterations. But it was, indeed, a new body. That new body did not think that it was bound by the previous agreement on rates. The Bill has come about because of the result of a decision of the High Court on a judicial review brought by a group of ratepayers in an area that has been described as the AB area. The court found that the Masterton District Council should have stuck to the agreement made by the former body. This has caused several problems. The judicial review was sought on the grounds that the present Masterton District Council should have preserved the differential rating system agreed to by the former Masterton County Council and the Masterton Borough Council of the time. The agreement was given official effect by a union order uniting those two councils in . At that time it was agreed that the county differential rating system for the rural area would continue for years until . That is the history of which the committee was informed. However, when the present Masterton District Council was constituted in the provision preserving the differential rating system was not re-enacted. The council did that because it thought that it was a completely new body. The legal advice it received was that that was OK. Having decided that, the council went ahead with a new differential rating system. That was contested by ratepayers. As a result of the court decision, the Masterton District Council has had a number of problems. It has had a shortfall in its rating base, and has not been able to collect the rates it expected to collect. It is now the ratepayers of the area who are being penalised. The Masterton District Council may not have acted wisely, but it acted in good faith. This has been an unfortunate chapter of errors. The council acted on the legal advice it sought. I rise to make a contribution as a member of the select committee that heard the submissions on this Bill, which was part of a suite of Bills that will supersede the Harbours Act. This Bill is commonly referred to as the ``America's Cup Bill''. The Minister has confirmed that the clauses that refer specifically to the running of special regattas, such as the America's Cup, will be split off and handled separately. However, those clauses are but one part of this Bill, which has four broad parts. One part has a major implication for my home town of Queenstown. The Bill amends the Maritime Transport Act to ensure that national level navigation safety controls can be implemented throughout the Act. It provides expressly for maritime rules to be struck by the Maritime Safety Authority in respect of maritime pilotage, navigational aids, and navigational safety issues. At face value this looks OK, but in reality it presents problems, and I wish to share those with members. It presents problems to Queenstown, which is the adventure tourism capital of New Zealand and where commercial jet boating and rafting all started. Queenstown administrators have the institutional knowledge of these two major contributors to adventure tourism in Queenstown. In recent years Queenstown has moved, by the introduction of local by-laws, to protect the reputation of Queenstown as the tourist Mecca. These by-laws enable safety and operational decisions to be made that protect the integrity of this very, very important tourism operation. Queenstown has established the position of a harbourmaster, who is employed by the council and is responsible to the council. That person knows the local conditions and sets the local rules. The Bill as presented to the committee has three major implications. The first one is that the Queenstown Lakes District Council currently operates the by-laws, not the regional council as proposed in the Bill. So that relationship of a regional council---in this case domiciled in Dunedin and which, obviously, will make safety navigation rules for the port of Otago---is obviously applicable not just to the Queenstown Lakes District Council area, which is some kilometres away from that particular port. The second problem is that the maritime rules that would become operative under this legislation would supersede the by-laws. So we have a case of by-laws containing local knowledge that could be overridden by the maritime rules that would come from a Wellington directive. The third concern that was expressed from the Queenstown Lakes District Council perspective is that under the Bill the Maritime Safety Authority would be responsible for administering the maritime rules. But the Queenstown Lakes District Council has by-laws relating not only to safety of the operation of jet boats and rafting but also to who operates them and where those operators can carry out their due processes. Currently, the council provides a one-stop shop. What Queenstown does not want is dual administration where the council's appointed officer would be doing some parts of the administration and the maritime safety officer doing other parts. Queenstown therefore sought total exclusion.

The Bill promoted by Mr Quigley does nothing to assist the final settlement of treaty claims. In my view it has the capacity to frustrate the treaty process. This would not be in the best interests of New Zealand or New Zealanders. The Bill imposes time-limits that would require all claims to be lodged with the Waitangi Tribunal by December , to be heard by the tribunal by , and to be settled with the Crown by . The promoter of the Bill said that this was simple and straightforward, but I believe that in his saying that he gives an incorrect impression to New Zealanders. This process is neither simple nor straightforward. If it was, we would have zipped through it long ago. Those of us who have been involved in this process for a long number of years now, know just how complex the process is. A complex process does not do well if arbitrary time-limits are imposed. Such time limits would serve only to damage the relationship between Maori and Crown, and would also place an unrealistic and impractical burden on claimants, on the Waitangi Tribunal, and on the Crown itself. I would like to speak for a moment on those two matters. The Crown-Maori relationship is one of the key aspects of our constitutional arrangements. In recent years a major focus of this relationship has been the Government commitment to the fair and equitable settlement of treaty claims. While the claims settlement process is but one facet of that relationship, it is extremely significant, and that is why it takes a significant proportion of the Government's time. If the Government on behalf of the Crown can resolve claims honourably, then past injustices can be put behind us, and Crown-Maori relationships can move towards a more positive future. It is therefore important to allow historical grievances to be heard, to be brought to their natural conclusion, and not to have any imposed time-limits set on them. On the issue of time-limits, it is interesting that the previous speaker made reference to the tribunal and what it was trying to do. Even if we were to pour more financial resources into the process, that would not help the situation. The reality is that there are human constraints as well on ensuring that this process is done in a timely and appropriate manner. Such a large part of the underpinning of settlements is about the efficacy of the historical research that underpins the tribunal's findings. In this country we are short of first-class historical researchers. They are all used up, and anything that suggests that suddenly we can address that constraint and make quicker progress is not being fair. Quite simply, it is in the interests of all New Zealanders that the process be allowed to run its course, rather than impositions being put on it. Maori want an end to the process as much as anyone else does. New Zealanders have demonstrated by the patience they have shown that they want these matters resolved in a fair, just, and honourable way. That is the commitment that this Government makes. That is the only way we will ensure that durable and lasting settlements are achieved. In my view, any activity that is conducted under a feeling of duress sets up the potential in the future for a finding that settlements have not been full or final. That would be a disaster. The National-led Government understands this, and that is why we have moved the process in a way that ensures that Maori, the Waitangi Tribunal, and New Zealanders by and large will come with us. It is important for the future of our country that the process runs its course. To push to deadlines is unlikely to be constructive, and a constructive process is what this Government has been about for the last years. We know a lot more about the process than we did years ago. Statements about when we would like to finish are helpful, but time-limits are not. We vote the Bill down.
