I move, That the Intellectual Disability (Compulsory Care) Bill be now read a second time. This Bill defines the circumstances under which certain individuals with an intellectual disability may be subject to assessment and compulsory care. There are four main reasons for the introduction of this Bill. Firstly, when the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act was passed, the provisions of the Act specifically excluded people with an intellectual disability unless they had a psychiatric illness. This was a deliberate exclusion because an intellectual disability is a learning disability, not a psychiatric illness. Secondly, there is concern about the appropriate care for a small number of people with an intellectual disability who either have been charged with or convicted of an imprisonable offence. People in this group are often inappropriately placed in prisons or in forensic units. Thirdly, there is concern about the appropriate care for a small number of people with an intellectual disability whose behaviour poses a serious risk of danger to themselves or others in the community if such a person with an intellectual disability refuses to access services that provide support to manage or contain these behaviours. Fourthly, everyone in the community has rights to protection and safety. This Bill may apply to approximately people, of whom about may be under the age of years, who meet the criteria for intellectual disability and who have been charged with and/or convicted of an imprisonable offence, and/or whose behaviour poses a serious risk to themselves or others, and who cannot be cared for on the basis of a voluntary agreement between that person and his or her caregivers. People who have offended may be detained under the Bill as either a special care recipient or a civil care recipient. People who have not offended can only be given compulsory care orders as civil care recipients. Status as a special care recipient applies to people who would otherwise have been imprisoned, and for whom a court wishes to apply the most restrictive powers available under this Bill, including detention in a secure facility. Status as a civil care recipient allows a wider range of care and support options, with the emphasis on placing the person in the least restrictive environment commensurate with keeping that person and others safe. The Bill also applies to people under years who meet the criteria for intellectual disability and whose behaviour poses a serious risk of danger to themselves or others, and who cannot be cared for in any other way. Currently the Department of Child, Youth and Family Services is caring for around five young people with an intellectual disability whose behaviour poses a serious risk of danger to themselves or others. It is inappropriate to place these young people with other young people subject to the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act and who do not have an intellectual disability. There are limitations to the secure care provisions of the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act, and I would add that the Bill in terms of these provisions is to be used as a last resort. I wish to repeat that this Bill affects a very small number of young people---about five a year---and the provisions in the Bill are a way of addressing some of the limitations in the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act. I do understand that there is concern about this portion of the Bill. The principles in the Bill underlying the provision of compulsory care apply to civil care recipients and also apply to special care recipients to the extent that they are compatible with the provisions of any court order. These principles provide that a compulsory care order is used as the option of last resort. Every care recipient should receive care that protects that individual's health and safety and that of others, and every care recipient should receive care that protects the rights of that care recipient. Additional principles in the Bill in relation to young people under recognise their special vulnerability. These include ensuring that the welfare and interests of the child and young person remain paramount, ensuring wherever possible that the family and wider family group participate in decisions affecting the child or young person, maintaining and strengthening the child or young person's links with the family group, and considering the impact of any decision on the stability of the family group. There is a detailed framework for administering compulsory care under the Bill. While it contains a number of statutory powers of compulsion that require care recipients to comply with a compulsory care order, these powers are balanced by specific safeguards against the abuse of these powers. That is always a paramount and overriding principle. These safeguards include -monthly clinical reviews of the need for the care order, a court review of the terms and conditions of a compulsory care order months after commencement, the role of the district inspectors, and the ability of a High Court judge to inquire into any matter relating to a person under this Bill, as that judge sees fit. In addition to the safeguards outlined, the Bill also provides for the protection of care recipients' rights including a careful assessment process to ensure that the legislation is used only for those people who meet the criteria set out in the Bill, information about the assessment, any care order and specific individual rights in a form able to be understood, and consumer rights under the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers Rights. In summary this Bill sets out the limits that can be imposed by the courts on people with an intellectual disability who meet the criteria for compulsory care, and in addition it ensures that the legal sanctions within the Bill are options of last resort only. It requires the courts to focus on the least restrictive intervention, and requires regular independent assessments and reports to the court. It sets out the legal and administrative responsibilities of personnel involved in assessment, care management, and review, and it ensures that the affected people have access to legal advice. It is a very important measure, and great care has been taken to ensure the proper balance between proper care for the people who are affected and the rights and safety of the community.

But here is the problem. What happens if they are fishing on an Australian boat? What happens if they are fishing on a Chilean boat? What happens if they are fishing on a Croatian boat? If they do not come back to the chief executive of the New Zealand Ministry of Fisheries and get a permit---and Mr Damien O'Connor knows that this is right---because they are fishing out of Croatia or Chile, they are criminals. They are crooks. They are breaking the law, and they are liable to a fine of up to $,. If they return to New Zealand, they could be for ever denied a permit to fish. This is not required by any international obligation that we have signed up to. It is not required by common sense. It is not required to protect the fishery resources. But this Government is doing it and Labour is supporting it against the interests of New Zealand fishermen. We have some of the greatest fishermen in the world. New Zealand fishermen are fishing on Icelandic boats for orange roughy, on French boats for orange roughy, on South African boats for orange roughy, and on Australian boats for orange roughy. Why? Because these New Zealand fishermen are very good. What is the response of the bureaucracy? What is the response of the Labour Party? What is the response of the National Party that supposedly supports industry, supposedly supports enterprise, and supposedly supports initiative? Its response is: ``Oh! You're being naughty. You're doing wrong things. You've got to come back to MAF in Wellington to get a permit.'' Why? Let the Minister explain why. How does coming back to Wellington to get a permit help in the protection of New Zealand fisheries? Not at all. We would like some explanation for that. What is it saying to the New Zealand fishing industry? It is saying: ``Don't be a New Zealander. We don't want you. Don't fish out of New Zealand. If you want to fish the high seas, go to Chile.'' We are telling them to take their business interests, go to Chile, and fish out of Chile, because that Government will not attack them. That Government will not put unnecessary red tape in front of them. All we have done is not to protect the fish. All we have done is to hobble New Zealanders. We have hobbled New Zealand fishing interests and driven them off shore. Where is the logic? Where is the sense? When we look at this legislation we get the sense that New Zealand politicians have gone overseas, signed up to a treaty, and felt great. They have hobnobbed with the politicians of the world. They have signed an agreement, and they have said to the officials and the politicians overseas: ``Don't worry. We will look good. We will lead the world. We will hobble our fishing industry more than you can hobble yours.'' In doing that, we have sold New Zealand's fishing interests down the Swanee. I repeat that everyone accepts that we need to regulate on the high seas. Everyone accepts that the fish need protection on the high seas. But why do we go as far as this? Why do we require a New Zealand national to carry a permit from Wellington to control him as though he is some paedophile going to Thailand? What he is in fact is a hard-working individual valued around the world---valued in Australia, valued in Chile, valued in Iceland, valued in Croatia---but not valued here in New Zealand by his own Government, by the National Party, or by the Labour Party. What we are doing is wrong.

I want to go through how to evaluate this Budget. The only way I can do it is to go back to what the previous Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, laid out as his programme in his famous ``springtime'' speech. He described what work was under way within Cabinet and what we would expect to see in this Budget if Ministers were doing their job. I remind the House that when Prime Minister Shipley took over from Mr Bolger she said that we would have more policy focus and more policy direction. One would expect to see everything that Mr Bolger said was under way, plus something more. In his ``springtime'' speech Mr Bolger promised increased private-sector involvement in health, in education, and in welfare. Did this Budget deliver anything on former Prime Minister Bolger's promise? No, it did not. What happened to that work? It has disappeared. Mr Bolger said that the work was under way. We have seen nothing. In his ``springtime'' speech Mr Bolger promised an increased commitment to the bulk funding of schools. On that promise we can give this Budget a tick. The Government is to be congratulated on its moves there. I predict that by the end of this year---contrary to what Mark Gosche believes--- percent of schools will have opted for bulk funding. They know that it is better for children's education. Mr Bolger promised a major rethink of the Resource Management Act and a review of the role and function of local government. None of those promises have been delivered on in this Budget. He also promised a decision that would provide for clear ownership of the Auckland Regional Services Trust. The coalition Government has failed to deliver on that promise. He promised privatisation of Government Property Services, airports, TVNZ Television, and Coalcorp---Coalcorp is now known as Solid Energy. The only thing that is definite to be privatised---and we think it is still definite---is the airports. In those terms we have a partial success. The other promise was to open up accident compensation to more competition. In that regard, the Budget has been a success. If we count up the promises, we have had four successes and failures. They are not on our terms, but on Prime Minister Bolger's own work programme. Using what Prime Minister Bolger said should be the benchmark, this Budget does not go far enough. We have heard much talk about what a centre-right Budget would do. We have heard questions from the Labour Party about what an ACT Government would do. I would like to explain to the Labour Party what it is to be in Opposition and what it is to be a parliamentarian. When the Government puts up its Budget, I suggest that a successful Opposition party should put up an alternative. We have heard nothing from Labour---not one idea or one policy. I will tell the House what members of an ACT Government would do---in coalition, of course, with our brothers and sisters in the National Party. The first thing we would do is halt the $ billion spend-up. That is a joke and a mistake. It is costing us investment and jobs. We would follow what the Minister of Finance and Minister of Revenue want to do. We would make a firm commitment to ongoing tax cuts---not just next year, as promised at the time of the last election, but in each year after that in order to give this country a boost and in order to put more money into the pockets of working New Zealanders. I know that Labour opposes that, but the ACT party favours more money in the pockets of working New Zealanders. The other thing we would do is open up the health and school sector to private competition. We would allow the money that we currently spend on behalf of parents and families to be fully portable to the private sector. That would allow the security, the choice, and the competition that New Zealanders are calling out for. We have to accept that politicians have failed our children in schools too often. They have failed us in terms of health care for our elderly, our children, and our families. If we cannot deliver on secure health-care we should allow each and every family to take their money, opt out of the system, and see whether they can get a better deal for themselves in the private sector. Just as with the post office and the railways, they would get a better deal. I know that the National Party wants to do it. It knows that it would work with accident compensation, and, so too, it would work in schools and in health care. If ACT was in Government it would undertake major tax benefit reform. It is not enough just to say that people should get back to work. We also need the incentive to get back to work. We need to follow the example of Tony Blair of the British Labour Party in terms of encouraging people into work rather than just waving the stick around. We have not seen any regulatory reforms to cut red tape. A centre-right Budget would do that. We have not seen any liberalisation of the labour market. That is a major barrier to people getting jobs. A centre-right Budget would undertake that reform in order to deliver the jobs.

When the House broke for tea, I was explaining about how the Minister of Defence and the Minister for State Owned Enterprises, the same man, Mark Burton, will appear only briefly in front of select committees. He was there for only minutes. That Minister runs from select committees. Earlier, I was making an observation about the LAVIII purchase deal of $ or $ million, and my prediction is that when the Auditor-General reports on this, heads will roll---within the military and, I believe, the Minister of Defence himself. That Minister does not just duck select committees, he refuses to answer written questions in this House, he refuses to answer requests under the Official Information Act, and he refuses to reply to letters. But last night, at . p.m.---and Mr Ron Mark will confirm this---the defence chiefs appeared before the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee, and members of Parliament could talk directly to them. We found out some amazing things. Let me go through those. Firstly, the Chief of Air Staff, Don Hamilton, agreed with me that in returning a Hercules C to Samoa, the chain of command was overridden, and the law was breached. When I asked him: ``Do you know, sir, who breached the Act; who overrode the chain of command?'', he said: ``I don't know.'' By that comment, it could have been the Minister Mark Burton, it could have been his senior adviser, Jennie Darby, it could have been his private secretary, Duncan Ferner, but someone ordered a Hercules C back to Samoa. The Chief of Air Staff and the Chief of Defence Force explained to members that unacceptable political pressure had been applied to the pilot of that Hercules C. That is against the law; that is a breach of the rules set out in the Defence Act. The Chief of Air Staff explained that this Hercules C was carrying , pounds of bombs. It would have made the Oklahoma bombing look like a small puff if the plane had gone up, and the Chief of Air Staff explained that to us last night, along with the Chief of Defence Force. He told us that the plane landed . tonnes over normal landing weight. He told us that the plane had flown . hours over the limit of time given for a critical rescue mission. He agreed that the mission was not a critical rescue mission. He agreed that it was highly dangerous---and Ron Mark is nodding his head---for this plane to be landed at Whenuapai at a.m. after flying for . hours. I will just say this again for the members: , pounds of bombs. I remember Chris Carter, who knows all about defence, laughing at one point, but once the answers started coming, he was amazingly silent, because the Chief of Defence Force and the Chief of Air Staff viewed it as being very serious. They told the committee that political pressure had been applied to a young pilot, and that as a result of that political pressure, a Hercules C had returned to Samoa and landed. They told us that that had placed ``unacceptable risks'' on the air crew, and that the Minister had ignored the advice of the military. When I said to them: ``Who do you think actually overrode the chain of command?'', the Chief of Air Staff replied: ``I don't know, I just wrote my memo for the chief of defence.'' I then said: ``In your memo you say that the plane was flying under ministerial direction. Have you ever heard of a Hercules C, with bombs, flying under ministerial direction?'', and he said ``Never.'' I continued: ``In the chain of command, is there such a thing as a C flying under ministerial direction?'', to which he replied: ``No.'' I said: ``Under the Defence Act, is there such a thing as flying under ministerial direction?'', and he replied: ``No.'' The chain of command is clear, and there is no such thing as a Minister beating up on a pilot to risk lives, and, indeed, to risk the airport in Samoa. When the Minister was prepared to answer questions on this in this House---he is not any more---he said that he could not contact the Chief of Defence Force, because ``He was in transit at the time, and uncontactable.'' Members know what that means: he was on a plane somewhere. The Chief of Defence Force told us last night that at the time, he was driving to Lower Hutt on the highway, with his cellphone switched on and beside him in the car, and no one rang. I asked the Chief of Defence Force whether he raised the matter with the Minister, and he said he did. I said: ``Did you manage to explain to the Minister that what he did was highly dangerous, illegal, and broke the chain of command?'', and he said he did. I asked whether he thought that this Minister would do that again, and then---and Ron Mark will confirm this---the Chief of Defence Force said, three times, emphatically: ``I can assure this committee that this Minister will never do it again.'' But the Minister has stood up in this House and defended the decision. He has said that under the same circumstances, he would make the same decision. I will not rest until we find out who broke the chain of command.

There has been only one election when that was put in place---in ---and the reason that it was put in place was that a royal commission looked at it and said: ``There is now no reason it should not be.'' It is true that in the th century the rolls were closed a month before time, because then what happened was that diligent public servants got out their quills, took the enrolment cards, and drew up something resembling a roll, which they then crossed off on election day. That happened through into the th century, and they needed a month to do so. What has happened since is simply this---computers have been invented and we do not need to close the roll a month early. That is why in some parts of the world they do not close the roll a month early, nor even a day early. In some states in America they close it as people vote. They enrol and then they vote. It is because we have the technology. There is no particular reason that New Zealand should not close its roll on the day of voting, and there is no particular reason that a voter cannot enrol and then vote---none whatever. There is no impediment to closing the roll late---to closing the roll the day before an election. There is no impediment, said the royal commission. There is no impediment, said New Zealand Post. There is no impediment, said the justice system. There is no impediment, said the enrolment control centre.

I want to turn straight to clause ---others will talk on the earlier clauses---because I want to pick up the debate about ``inherent'' versus ``intrinsic''. We have already heard in this House from Denis Marshall that the farming fraternity is concerned about the use of the word ``inherent''. We have heard from others that people who have a concern for environmental matters are also concerned about the use of ``inherent'', because it is not intrinsic. We have heard from the deputy leader of the Labour Party Michael Cullen, that if we use words that are similar but different there will be a lot of confusion. Michael Cullen asked whether the word ``inherent'' had the same meaning as it does in other legislation, or whether there were different ways of describing things. The word ``inherent'' does not appear in the Resource Management Act---probably the best Act of its nature---but the word ``intrinsic'' does. It is defined, and the definition is related strictly to ecosystems, or aspects of ecosystems. So it is a flora and fauna, air, water and soil type definition, and that is all, whereas inherent values include values of history, recreation, culture, and Uncle Tom Cobbleigh. So it is a much broader definition, yet it includes the flora and fauna type definitions. The scene is now set for a debate of mammoth proportions, because those from an environmental perspective will say: ``Inherent values are being applied to the flora and fauna of the land.'' No Parliament in its right mind would, in the same decade, pass one set of protections for one lot of flora and fauna defined by ``intrinsic'' values, and then later apply another set of protections that are defined as ``inherent'' values. The environmental lobby would argue, therefore, that there would need to be some similarity between the current use of the intrinsic values clause in the Resource Management Act and it being pushed across and used in the Crown pastoral lease legislation. The runholders would say: ``That'll be the day. That means you are going to accord some member of our flora and fauna that might be endangered, or similar, the same level of protection that is accorded a gold mine. That is bizarre.'' And so it is. The way around it is to distinguish between inherent and intrinsic. The place to do it is in clause . The way to do it is to change the word ``inherent'' where it appears for the second time in paragraph (a) of clause () to the word ``intrinsic''. That would get us around the problem, from both sides. We would have a cascade, admittedly of only two levels, of protection. We would protect the intrinsic values of the flora and fauna and the inherent values of other things, such as the land itself other than its recreational value. I remind the Minister what the definition of ``inherent values'' includes. It is all the cultural, ecological, historical, recreational, and scientific attributes or characteristics. I am simply saying that the word ``ecological'' be taken out and the word ``intrinsic'' ascribed so that it is consistent with the Resource Management Act. It will give the landholders the view that something that is part of the natural flora and fauna will be accorded a higher level of protection but, equally, something that is not part of that will be accorded a lower level of protection. It would be inferred, I think, that intrinsic values would have a higher test placed on them than inherent values. If that differentiation is not made, then there will be a running debate. I think that is serious, indeed. The other point I want to make about clause is this: if clause proves anything, it is that we must get on with high-country tenure review. If members do not mind me being blunt, a large part of this is to do with burning tussock, which has been a discretionary activity for some time the scientific debate on which has raged for about years. We are now writing into our law that the commissioner must, on the one hand, take into account the desirability of protecting inherent values and, on the other hand, the desirability of ``making it easier to use the land for farming''. What is a commissioner to do with that? What is the commissioner to do when being told on the one hand to allow it so the land can be farmed, and on the other hand disallow it so that inherent values can be protected? It really is a muddle. It really is a dollar each way. It is the opposite of the Resource Management Act, in which a series of things were set out as being matters of national importance, then other matters of importance were listed, and so on. Instead of having a hierarchy, we have a balancing act that no reasonable person can meet. So we must get on and do the sorting out of what can be burnt and what cannot, by changing the ownership on the one hand from leasehold to Crown ownership in the Department of Conservation, and on the other hand from leasehold to private ownership. The nonsense in clause can then be done away with, with the passage of history. There is one other matter. Nothing in this Bill, now or in the future, renders tenure review compulsory. If the runholder cannot strike a deal, the runholder has nothing with which he or she may trade and no trade will take place. That means we are likely to end up with this muddle in the middle for many decades to come. I am sorry that the select committee has seen fit not to put an end date on this, maybe years hence, so that between now and then everyone had to go through that review process, and, if they did not, they would be compulsorily reviewed. I am sorry that has not happened. It seems to me that we will need to revisit it.

I move, That the Resource Management (Aquaculture Moratorium) Amendment Bill be now read a third time. The bill imposes a moratorium on new aquaculture activities in the coastal marine area of New Zealand from November , the date the moratorium was announced, and ending years from the date this bill becomes law. This bill is a response to problems caused by unrestricted access to coastal space. Recently we have seen increased demand for coastal space for aquaculture. Applicants can apply for space in almost any part of the coastal marine area subject to the provisions of regional coastal plans, and the refusal of one application does not prevent the same, or another, applicant from seeking a consent for the same space. As a result, there is no certainty for the community or the industry about where aquaculture may occur, and much effort is expended inefficiently. Successful applicants must also apply for a marine farming permit under the Fisheries Act , which may be granted or declined. At no stage of the process is it certain that an application for a coastal permit, or a marine farming permit, will be granted. The main reforms will provide clearer certainty for applicants and submitters, making it clear where aquaculture can occur, and where it is prohibited. They will also enable councils to look at the sustainability issues relating to aquaculture, and therefore they will be better able to deal with all its effects on the environment, and assist the aquaculture industry to develop in a sustainable way. Aquaculture management areas are now provided for in this bill. This is to signal to regional councils that they can start the work now, identifying suitable areas for aquaculture. They should consider the effects of aquaculture on fishing, in doing so. This will mean that councils will be able to make some progress in developing aquaculture marine management areas before the main reform bill is enacted. The moratorium means that applications under the Resource Management Act for coastal permits for aquaculture activities lodged before November , and which had not been notified at that date, cannot proceed until the moratorium has expired. Those applications that do not require notification will be able to proceed, if the council had made its decision not to notify them before November . The bill, as introduced, provided for the moratorium to capture all applications in respect of which the hearing had not commenced as at November . However, after listening to a large number of submissions the Primary Production Committee recommended moving the cut-off date to notification. If, at the end of the moratorium, those applications that are put on hold relate to areas in which aquaculture is to be allowed, with a coastal permit, they will be processed and decided on the basis of the new rules developed by councils. Any that relate to areas where aquaculture is to be prohibited will be deemed to have been cancelled. Where, by the end of the moratorium, a council has notified a proposed plan, the rules in that proposed plan, including rules prohibiting aquaculture in any area, will have immediate effect, unless the relevant council decides that the effect of any of the rules should be delayed. The provision relating to lifting the moratorium, by Order in Council, in specific areas, now includes criteria to guide the Minister of Conservation in making a recommendation to the Governor-General. The lifting of the moratorium would be initiated by regional councils, and they would provide the Minister with information and explanations in support of its request. The bill now requires the Minister to make a recommendation within working-days of receiving a request, subject to the request fulfilling the criteria. The bill contains a transitional provision to deal with any consents that may result from applications covered by the moratorium but which are granted before this bill is enforced. Any such consents will be ineffective until the moratorium expires or is lifted. Then any that relate to areas where aquaculture has become prohibited will be deemed to have been cancelled. The remainder will be subject to review by the regional council, which may change the condition of such consents to reflect the new rules applicable to the relevant areas. The bill also affects Fisheries Act marine farming and spat-catching permits that relate to coastal permits caught by the moratorium. The bill provides that no Fisheries Act permits can be granted, or, if already granted, exercised, where the corresponding coastal permit has been put on hold by the moratorium. In conclusion, the enactment of this bill will provide time for the Government to develop legislation implementing the main aquaculture reforms. These will simplify the process for marine farmers wanting to commence aquaculture activities, and provide additional tools for councils in allocating space in the coastal marine area. The main reforms will improve the process for obtaining coastal permits under the Resource Management Act, and remove the requirement for applicants to obtain a marine farming permit from the Ministry of Fisheries, as well.

I agree with the previous speaker on only one point--that this short title poorly reflects what is in the Bill. I would like to suggest to the Committee that it considers making some changes. The Bill would be more accurately entitled: ``The Apple and Pear Industry Minimal Restructuring Bill'', because that is what this Bill is; it is a minimal restructuring Bill. We heard in the Chamber today that banks are reporting that percent of their customers who are growers will face going to the wall. When we consider the litany of poor decision-making and poor management we have seen from the current Apple and Pear Marketing Board for the last few years, and when we consider all the issues that were raised at the select committee--the rapidly changing circumstances in the international market place, the demands of international committees, changing buying patterns, changing relationships, ownership issues, consumer demands, and logistical requirements--then this Bill does not achieve restructuring, it achieves minimal restructuring. I suggest that would be a better title. When we also consider what the industry requires in order to meet those demands--flexibility, consolidation, the minimising of costs, the ability to pursue every market opportunity, and the ability to react quickly to changing demands--then I believe that the title I am suggesting is far more appropriate than what is there at the moment. Another equally valid title for this Bill could be the ``Apple and Pear Industry Monopoly Bill'', because indeed that is what it is. It maintains the single-desk structure. It makes it very difficult for owners to go about the pursuit of their own business. It curtails their freedom to follow their business and to rely on their own skills and entrepreneurial abilities. It forces them to go through an expensive, time-consuming, and biased process before they can go about their business freely. I suggest that perhaps another title might be the ``Apple and Pear Industry Freedom Curtailment Bill''. That seems to me to be hugely appropriate. We have heard in Parliament today from a number of speakers that there are more growers who do not want deregulation than there are growers who do want deregulation. I put it to the Committee that this issue can be decided in only one way--that is, if the growers are asked. What is missing from this Bill is the opportunity for the growers to be asked. There are two ways that the growers can demonstrate their wishes. The first way is that they will reply with their feet--those growers who do not want to be part of a regulated regime will simply take themselves and their cartons off and find their own markets and do their own thing. They should have the freedom to do that, and those freedoms are being curtailed under this Bill. That is why I am suggesting the title the ``Freedom Curtailment Bill'' instead. Let those growers of whom we have heard much in this Chamber today, who wish to remain in a regulated regime, stay with what was the Apple and Pear Marketing Board--that is, under the new ENZA company--if they so wish. This Bill is a curtailment of people's freedom. It maintains, in essence, a monopoly. It is a minimal Bill, and for those reasons I do not support the short title and commencement.

It has been a lengthy debate, beginning last Wednesday, and I have yet to hear from the Government a sensible defence of the implementation of this bill in regard to M~aori. I have been waiting here through parts, including Part A, and we have not yet heard at the very least the Minister of M~aori Affairs get up and defend how this bill will impact on the greatest production sector for M~aori, and that is M~aori land. I am referring here not only to those land trusts that are our wealth generators. If we scan through this country, there are , M~aori land trusts in Arawa alone. There are , M~aori land trusts over Te Puke way. These are small employers employing between to people. They are the kinds of trusts and small businesses that will be severely impacted upon by this bill. We come to part , which is yet another disincentive for those trusts that are not at the stage of those small businesses that are doing well, but are languishing undeveloped. I am referring to percent of M~aori land. Forty percent of M~aori land is not even developed---it is growing gorse. What incentive will there be for those trustees to get off their backsides, to develop a business plan, to go to a bank and get a loan, and to do something with their land, when they are confronted with a bill such as this, which provides a disincentive every step of the way for them? I am reminded of the situation of King Country land. If members recall, that collapsed years ago. Here were a group of M~aori land trusts trying to do the best they could. They found their way into a processing company, and then they went to the wall because of union interference. And what happened? All of those land trusts around Te Awamutu and Te Kuiti lost their money---all of it, not just some of it. I am reminded again of other businesses. I take members' minds back to the time of the M~aori Arts and Crafts Institute, which got into a litigious dispute with its own M~aori members. What happened there? It was a question of redundancy. Personal grievances were taken, and what happened? The redundancy payment demanded for each of those workers was $,. The union believed that the M~aori Arts and Crafts Institute was making too great a profit. In fact, the entire profit for that year was less than $,---less than the sum claimed for only one personal grievance claim. It was an acrimonious dispute that lasted for days. I also recall to the House the situation of Kaiangaroa Forest when it was privatised, when M~aori, especially those in the Rotorua area, fought to get themselves established as contractors. I have a letter here from one of those who helped establish M~aori as contractors---the biggest contracting group around there---to say that should this Part go through, those contractors will be in danger of losing their businesses. This simply is not good enough---it really is not. Clauses and will tie up small businesses in the Employment Tribunal, and through the jurisdiction of the court. It is simply intolerable for small businesses that are at risk, that are struggling to get going, to have to go through this time-consuming, time-wasting process, that will add tremendously to their costs. It is a complete disincentive to getting their land developed. It is a complete disincentive for M~aori to do anything other than collect the welfare benefit. I call on the Minister of M~aori Affairs to take the next call and tell us what he will say to these trusts about this bill.

I want to support the motion moved by the Leader of the House. I do so because the idea of having the sitting days for the year down on paper for everybody to see was introduced by the fourth Labour Government. In fact, I like to think that this was one of the things I called for for many years, and I was very pleased when the idea was finally promulgated. I hope that from now on we will always have the year's sitting days mapped out in advance. There are obvious good points in favour of that measure for planning and for helping members of Parliament to organise things with their families. There are a couple of things that I think should be said. First, the programme should indicate to all New Zealanders that being a member of Parliament is now very much a full-time job. I think that most members of Parliament and Ministers have found---certainly since I have been Senior Opposition Whip I have found this---that they are required every week to come to Wellington for at least days, and sometimes days. In the sitting weeks it would be on a Monday that I come down and a Friday that I return. I think that most members come down on a Tuesday morning; Mondays are for electorate work, and on Fridays I visit places in my constituency. We can reflect on the number of weeks in which Parliament has select committees or the House meeting. It is now more than weeks in a year; it used to be about weeks. In the years that I have been in the House I have seen that number increase. Parliament would start on the last sitting day in June and end at the end of November. We now have select committees sitting in January and we adjourn Parliament just before Christmas. I think it is right and proper that we do work through the year, but I think that it is essential to note that this is a very full year's work that is put forward. The second point I wanted to comment on was that of urgency. The Leader of the House said ``a reasonable amount of urgency''. Of course, there will be times when the House has to take urgency. I have been disturbed only about two or three times in the past year, but I was particularly disturbed a couple of weeks ago when we had the example of a Bill being reported back and amendments being proposed in an additional supplementary order paper. I would bet any sum of money that that Bill will be back in the House for amendment within a year, because it is not possible to get legislation right when it is being worked on so quickly. There has to be a better way of ensuring that we have provision for getting those mistakes in legislation ironed out and not needing to rush quite as much as we have done previously. Of course, sometimes there is a need for urgent legislation---as with the Marine Farming Amendment Bill that will be introduced later today---when there is a particular circumstance that requires the co-operation of the House. I am sure all members will co-operate because we are dealing with the livelihood of to mussel farmers who need to be given that assistance. I say to the Leader of the House that I think the arrangements this year are better than they were last year, because I think they coincide better with the particular breaks that are required. My only comment would be that I still wonder why a break of weeks is needed at the end of October and the beginning of November, rather than having a -week break then and setting the sitting days down until December. That would then give the Government the opportunity, if there is a rush of legislation at the end of the year, to use that extra week instead of taking urgency throughout the second to last and last week of the year. I will be supporting the motion.

The Labour Opposition welcomes the introduction of this Bill. We will certainly be supporting the motion, and we will be keen to have the Bill referred to the select committee. This Bill paves the way for future legislation to be worded with more account taken of everyday use of language and to be less tied by archaic legalese that may have its origins in language forms that have not been used for years or more. This is a good Bill. It serves democratic principles. Parliament enacts legislation on behalf of the people; it is fitting that the people should be able to understand fully and debate that legislation, and using language that people can more easily understand facilitates that democratic participation without compromising the ability of the legislation to convey its legal intent. I was very pleased to be able to have some sessions with the Law Commission on this and other matters. I was strongly of the opinion that the old Acts Interpretation Act should have been replaced, and I am pleased that we have got to the stage that this legislation is at now. The use of more easily understandable language will also assist Parliament in enacting the legislation it intends to enact. Few members of Parliament have formal legal training, and are often in the hands of drafters of Bills in trusting that their intent has been accurately translated into legalese. The use of language in Bills that members can more easily relate to will assist members in their assessment of Bills before the House. Similarly this Bill will ultimately help the judiciary in interpreting legislation, not only through its purpose as an interpretation Act, but also through the enhanced ability of the House to convey accurately its intent in passing legislation. There will be less ambiguity and greater authority in members' comments, therefore identification of the intent of Parliament will be easier. I am interested in this whole area, so I was able to get some help from the New Zealand Parliamentary Library Bills Digest. I discovered that the first interpretation ordinance in New Zealand was enacted in . This echoed the famous United Kingdom statute that emerged from the th century European legislative reforms. Lord Brougham's Act of was ``for shortening the language used in Acts of Parliament because standard terms should not have to be repeated in each statute.'' The Brougham Act introduced, for example, the provision that references to the male gender were to include females unless the context provided otherwise, and thereafter legislation all over the common-law world was drafted using male terms only. I am certain that this particular Bill will not have that provision in it. In New Zealand the ordinance was replaced, as the Minister pointed out, by the Interpretation Act , which also mentioned the possible value of the Act in shaping the form and language of legislation. That unnecessary Act, brought in by the Labour Government, has completely distracted the Government from the things it should have been doing, like taking the lead from Dr Lynda Scott who has had a member's bill on retirement villages in the ballot for the last months. It is only through the lead of Dr Lynda Scott that this bill is here today. In other words, the Government has been shamed into bringing in this bill. It is very good to see Government members blink suddenly. They have sat there motionless for the last half hour, and now, when they are criticised, they are finally brought to their senses and realise the hard fact that they have been shamed into introducing this bill into the House. This bill does deal with the care of elderly people. Indeed, the sentiments behind it are incredibly important. My colleague Dr Lynda Scott took the initiative and put a member's bill in the ballot some months ago. So, certainly, the National Party has done a lot towards the introduction of this bill into the House. We are hearing a fairly tawdry set of interjections from Government members. Naturally, they feel embarrassed that they took so long to introduce this bill into the House. The purposes of the bill are to protect the interests of residents, and intending residents, of retirement villages, and to enable the development of retirement villages under a legal framework that is readily understandable to residents, intending residents, and operators. Undoubtedly, this has been very necessary in the New Zealand scheme, because the framework of retirement villages that have existed in New Zealand has been quite confusing. One of the features of Dr Lynda Scott's bill was that it tried to keep regulation as minimal as possible, but absolutely maximised the care and concern for the elderly. I am quite concerned that this Government bill does tend to make unnecessary regulation and complicate what could, in certain circumstances, be much more simple. However, the National Party does support the major thrust of this long overdue bill. The legal structures in retirement villages are certainly complex and not always well understood by residents or intending residents. Many involve a licence to occupy a unit and a management contract under which the operator provides facilities and services. The licence is a personal contract and does not create any interest in the land, and that is one of the problems. The resident pays to acquire the licence to occupy and pays ongoing fees for the management contract. I note that there was an article in the New Zealand Herald of February entitled ``The caring business''. One of the points made was the problem that elderly people have with financial arrangements, which can be so confusing. The New Zealand Herald article pointed out that many senior citizens still do not realise there are no capital gains to be made in buying a home in a retirement village. On entering a retirement village, a person or couple must outlay a purchase price that is generally between $, to $,, depending on the location and style. They then have to pay, over and above that, a village facilities contribution, which is around one quarter of that price again, as well as weekly shared fees. In exchange, they have the right to use the shared facilities and are able to access other services the retirement village may provide, as well as having the security of knowing their neighbours will not interfere in the lifestyle they want to enjoy. One of the difficulties has been that some of the contracts are incredibly vague. They stipulate the fees for which services are promised, but only in a vague manner, and those services may not be provided. The other difficulty is that often the elderly cannot make money even if their property increases in price. So certainly this bill before the House has amongst it the elements to try to address that sort of problem. I must say that various features of the bill are important, for example, a disclosure statement, which is a written document containing information required by the applicable code of residents' rights and code of practice in regulation. That is contained in clause and is a fundamental and necessary element of the bill. A code of residents' rights is a code of rights for residents of a particular retirement village, prepared by the operator of the retirement village. Once again, it is to be done in a conscientious manner, and in many retirement villages around the country---probably a large proportion---that is the case, but unfortunately there have been some notable exceptions and therefore it is absolutely appropriate to make it into regulation. Again, as stated in clauses and , the code of practice is to be approved or prepared by the Minister and apply to all retirement villages. So there is a degree of standardisation throughout the country that retirement village operators are expected to comply with, and that, indeed, is right and proper. Once again I go back to one of the concerns about this bill, which is that regulations can become awfully complicated. It is a sad tendency of this Labour-Alliance Government to befuddle legislation with unnecessary and complicated regulations. Finally, I will comment on two other aspects of the bill. Clause deals with suspension of registration. The bill does allow the registrar to suspend registration of a retirement village if any of the registered documents are misleading or confusing in a material way, or if the operator fails to comply with the Act or pay any prescribed fees. In those circumstances the registrar must notify the operator, and set out the steps the operator must take to have the suspension lifted. In conclusion, I say that the National Party has agreed to support this bill to the Justice and Electoral Committee. But I must also say that the Government was shamed into bringing this bill into the House, after far too long a time delay. I would like to congratulate Lynda Scott on initiating the introduction of this necessary bill to the House. Bill read a first time, and referred to the Justice and Electoral Committee.

It is somewhat sobering to follow on in the speaking order from two acknowledged technical legal experts. Might I say that I think it absolutely fundamental that members of the minority Labour-Alliance socialist Government consider taking note of what those experts say, and abandon the bill. Nevertheless, Part is indeed a massive undertaking, both to read and to understand, and I believe that is very relevant. The Employment Relations Authority may well be composed entirely of lay members. Under Part the Employment Relations Authority will replace the well-regarded Employment Tribunal. The tribunal is well regarded by practitioners throughout the country. Some of the headlines that I read about the Employment Relations Authority state that the authority is an investigative body that allows the authority to make a determination without regard to technicalities. How can one authority make a proper decision when it has not got the full facts before it, particularly the technical facts? The authority members do not need legal training or experience, or to hold practising certificates. Yet they have certain powers available only in the High Court. How is it that the Employment Relations Authority can apply entirely different standards of legal burden of proof than other judicial bodies? The bill is an extensive and highly complicated -page monolith. Again, how is it that people without legal training, without authority, can wisely and knowledgably interpret this huge and extensive bill? In recording its determinations on any matter before it, the Employment Relations Authority need not keep notes! What sort of an authority is this? When I consider years of clinical practice, when I have kept meticulous notes for all that time, as a matter of course, I wonder how the Employment Relations Authority, in its determination, need not even keep records. What sort of a justice system is this? The Employment Relations Authority is to have an inquisitorial role with very wide powers of investigation and determination. Those powers will be far wider than those of any other institution in the country. What is happening to justice in this country of New Zealand when an authority with such wide powers of investigation and determination could well be made up solely of lay people who may not have a full grasp of the profound implications of this part? The opposition to the proposals in this part of the bill were virtually universal. The Law Society, industrial relations practitioners, and academic commentators all agreed that the authority would not improve the handling of personal grievances or disputations in the workplace. As I note the role of the Employment Relations Authority in clause , immediately there arises in me some deep concerns of conflict. The bill states that ``The Authority is an investigative body that has the role of resolving employment relationship problems by establishing the facts and making a determination according to the substantial merits of the case, without regard to technicalities.'' Yet when I turn back to clause (a), I see that the first object of this part, as stated in this clause, is to establish procedures and institutions that ``support successful employment relationships...''.

Under clause (), an enforcement officer may require a driver to remain stopped on a road for up to minutes. That seems to me to be an undue imposition on a driver who may be wanting to get to some particular destination in a hurry. Fifteen minutes is a long time for a person to be detained just to be identified---for it to be established who a person is. I think that is a draconian piece of this particular law, which, in itself, has too many draconian aspects to it. I think that minutes is way beyond what New Zealand drivers, who are clearly on the road to get to some particular place at a particular time, should be required to stay for. I would like to know from the Minister why minutes is required. With the kind of electronic gadgetry that the police have available to them, why does the law give them the ability to keep a driver there for minutes? Surely minutes---even minutes---is quite adequate to establish the identity of a driver. I can foresee a situation where, on occasion, people going about their legitimate business quite harmlessly, and quite safely, will be held up for minutes against their will, perhaps because they are in a hurry and under pressure, and an enforcement officer may take the full minutes just to slow them down deliberately. Why does the Minister think that minutes is necessary? A quarter of an hour is a long time if one is trying to get to a destination safely but in a hurry. I think the Committee should consider a lesser period of time. I have had several submissions from people on this particular aspect. They believe that it goes way beyond what is either necessary or fair. I would really like to see that particular issue reconsidered and restricted to no more than minutes---and preferably something even less than that. Fifteen minutes should be quite long enough---and some---for any particular identity to be established. Drivers should be allowed to get on their way unhindered by this action. I would like to hear the Minister's comments on why minutes was chosen, and what the rationale for it is. And I would like to know whether it could be brought back to something that is more considerate and would still allow the identity of a driver to be established, because I feel that it could be done in a lot less time than that. It is an aspect of considerable discomfort and annoyance to people travelling on the road going about their legitimate business, and it could be removed from the Bill.

We have on record, undisputed, the fact that the removal of Telecom, for example, from the realms of the first schedule and putting it in the hands of the private sector, has brought overwhelming benefits every year for New Zealand. Indeed, an independent scientific study showed that putting Telecom into the hands of the private sector has brought over half a billion dollars worth of benefits for New Zealand. That is important, but when it comes to electricity generation, why is ECNZ not in this Bill alongside Contact Energy? Can members give me one sound reason that ECNZ should not be sitting here alongside Contact Energy? Why should we not be getting on with it? Why should the Minister not be able to stand up in this Chamber and say that we are preparing ECNZ for sale and that we want it in this schedule for removal along with Contact Energy? Every New Zealand consumer of power, whether a domestic user or a business user, should have the opportunity that will come from the benefits that flow from privatisation. We know that there would be benefits from selling Contact Energy. Why not sell all of the State-owned electricity generators? Why can we not have the benefit from the privatisation of all the generators? We are being told that up to c is to be gained from this process. Why is the Government hanging out on the majority generator owner, ECNZ? Why does it not put it in this Bill? Why does it not amend the Bill and have it in there and give all New Zealanders an opportunity to benefit from that process? We hear from the Opposition that this asset is somehow strategic. Let me say to this Committee that the food industry is a whole lot more strategic to the well-being of New Zealanders than the supply of electricity is. But I do not hear anybody from that side of the Chamber standing up and saying that we ought to nationalise every supermarket and every restaurant around this country.

ACT supports the passage of this legislation. I just want to make one or two remarks. It is obvious that this legislation is aimed at establishing a clearer division between those activities undertaken by local authority trading enterprises to make a profit, for commercial purposes, and those activities that are non-commercial and non-profitmaking. It appears that, notwithstanding the fact that changes were made to the Local Government Act in and last year via the Taxation (Remedial Provisions) Act, there still was a lack of clarity with regard to the precise definition of a local authority trading enterprise, and changes were required to achieve that. Hopefully, the passage of this legislation will remove that uncertainty, and any misunderstanding---real or potential---will have been dealt with. Local authority trading enterprises, like State-owned enterprises, are unsatisfactory vehicles for ownership of assets. They ought to be deemed to be transitional and they ought to be deemed to be temporary. They lack the kinds of commercial drivers that we see in the market place that effect the levels of efficiency and accountability that we ought to have from ownership vehicles undertaking commercial activity. It is important that commercial structures have something like a publicly listed share price, for example, which is by far and away the best indicator of performance and accountability. The sooner we can move these kinds of commercial activities out into that arena, the better we all will be, and the better those activities will be in terms of their delivery of cost-efficiency and accountability. However, some activities are best undertaken---at least temporarily---through that ownership vehicle, and in the meantime it is important that, particularly, where some of those activities are in competition with their own ratepayers, they are treated the same. Their not being taxed, their sheltering behind some sort of structure that precludes tax from being paid, ought to be dealt with by Parliament, and, hopefully, it has been. If councils do need to control activities in their local area, they can do so through regulation. They do not necessarily have to do so through ownership. There are more effective ways, through light-handed regulation, of managing those things that the community wishes to control. ACT supports the passage of this legislation and we would like to see it pass. Bills read a third time.

Or put out another report! The second issue that the House should hear an answer on is why the bee mite was not discovered earlier. Where are the surveillance systems that are supposed to uncover such pests as the varroa bee mite? Why was the bee mite not discovered by Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry officials much earlier, considering the number of potential opportunities there were for such a discovery? The exporting of queen bees from hives that supposedly were infected for some time should have brought about a much earlier discovery of the varroa bee mite. Why did this not happen? Who is being held accountable? Are the complaints of bee-keepers correct when they claim that the ministry did not carry out its surveillance responsibilities because of lack of funding? It is now over months since the varroa bee mite was detected. Why was an emergency not called? Was penny-pinching the real reason? Here we have one of the worst possible threats to our entire agricultural and horticultural industries, and the Government failed to put emergency powers in place because it was worried about a few extra dollars that might have been put at risk. There should have been an all-out assault on this problem right at the very beginning. It is a sad commentary on the coalition Government's understanding of business needs and its commitment to exports that it allowed the problem to drift on for so long. It has taken this Minister over months to make up her mind on what to do, and she ends up making the wrong decision. Where was the urgency? Why were more resources not applied to this problem? It is no good the Minister hiding behind the ministry; it should have been on the ball much earlier, too. But the buck stops with the Minister. She should have insisted on an early decision, and on a decision in favour of eradication. It is now not too late. It was almost too late when it was announced, but it is a disgrace that it has taken so long for the Minister to make up her mind. If resources were a problem she should have obtained them. This is an issue of critical national importance. This Minister is obviously a failure. She is ultimately responsible for the whole of this debacle. She is responsible for the delays and the tentative and stupid decision to manage the problem instead of having the courage and determination to get on with an eradication programme early in the piece. Under this Government debt is decreasing, interest rates are decreasing, inflation is decreasing, and the balance of trade is better than it has been since . The Government has been successful on four counts. The path has been difficult; the Government faced a very large debt at the beginning of its term, and that debt increased because of devaluation. The Government knew that that would happen, and it told the people. That debt is now being reduced. The same progress is being made with interest rates. The Government knew that interest rates would rise at first, and that it had to take off the stupid wage and price freeze the National Government had imposed. The Government removed the freeze, and told the people that interest rates would rise and then decrease. The country faced the problem of the regulations that the National Government had imposed and the funny wage and price freeze imposed by that regulatory regime. The Government had to come to grips with inflation after it removed the regulations. It is succeeding, and inflation is decreasing. The balance of trade is improving. There is still the problem of unemployment, and the Government is not shirking that responsibility. It is a grave problem, but it is not as bad as it was under the National Government. The number of people unemployed had risen to more than , if those on special work were counted. The National Government did nothing about unemployment, and it did not tackle the root of the problem. I rise to support Mr Mallard's amendment to the long title to omit the words: ``An Act to reform the electricity industry'' and to substitute the following words: ``An Act to ensure that the electricity industry is not dominated by a single State owned supplier''. We have heard a lot during the debate on this Bill about the importance of competition and the importance of keeping power prices down. Members will have noticed that in the minority report the Labour and Alliance members stated that electricity should be reliably and affordably available to all consumers, and that that goal should be reached by a mixture of competition and regulation. That was the position that the Labour and Alliance members took in the Commerce Committee. But what did we finally end up with? We ended up with a Bill that concentrated on separating out the lines and energy businesses. The coalition Government was convinced that was the only way that it would reach the goal of having lower electricity prices and more competition. During the debate we asked why it could not be done another way. If the objective is transparency, to have no cross-subsidisation between the lines and energy businesses, why cannot there be a corporate split rather than splitting the ownership? Why does it have to be this way? Can the Minister of Energy tell us how the Bill actually stops monopolies? When we looked at all the parts of this Bill, we found that there was freedom to have vertical integration. Having separated out the lines and energy businesses, there was nothing to stop vertical integration, with the energy businesses being gobbled up by the new baby ECNZs, and with the lines businesses amalgamating. So we could still face a monopoly situation. I come back to the amendment. I support the words: ``An Act to ensure that the electricity industry is not dominated by a single State owned supplier''.

As I said last night, I am speaking in this debate as a member who voted for the original casino legislation, because I believed at the time that it was wrong to discriminate against one type of gambling when we already have a whole lot of other legitimate types of gambling in New Zealand. It was against my conscience to say that casinos should be outlawed when all these other forms of gambling are available. But since casinos have come in, a great deal of public concern has arisen as a result of the way that they operate and the social effects that they have, and a lot of public opposition to the proliferation of casinos has occurred. I now think it might be time to vote for a moratorium, because we need to get it right. I draw the attention of all members to the report from the select committee. If members have not yet looked at it and are still wondering how they should vote, I think it is very important that they get the information that was given to the select committee. When I finished last night I was talking about the problem of retrospectivity, because it was raised as a concern. I draw attention to the submission from the New Zealand Law Society on page of the committee's report. The society made the following points: ``Retrospectivity is not a fatal flaw in legislation and, indeed, is not uncommon. The issue of real importance is whether the retrospectivity is justified.'' I must say that in this case, given the public concern, given the concern about the way that the Casino Control Authority operates as an approval authority rather than as a control authority, and given the need to review all our gambling legislation, I am inclined to vote for a moratorium, and for including all the casino applications---that is, making it go back to January. As I said last night, I will need to hear some very convincing speeches to the contrary to influence me to do anything other than that. The report also states: `` percent of Hamilton residents do not want a casino''---that is from a Hamilton City Council poll---`` percent of Wellington residents do not support a casino in Wellington''---that is from an Evening Post poll, and---`` percent of Queenstown residents do not want casinos''---and that is from a Colmar Brunton poll. I think we need to think very carefully about this issue. We have two casinos already. If we look at how many casinos there are in Australia---I think there are ---then make a calculation from that figure as to how many there should be in New Zealand, two is enough. I think we should support this moratorium in the meantime, until we have a proper review of our gambling legislation.

The Green Party supports the overall bill, and in particular clause , because it ostensibly requires the Broadcasting Commission to ensure that a range of broadcasts are available to provide for the interests of youth. In fact, the bill will not really ensure that broadcasts are available to provide for the interests of youth, because section of the principal Act does not impose any obligation on New Zealand On Air to provide a specific number of services for youth. All that it does is provide New Zealand On Air with a mandate to allocate funding, if it wishes, for programmes aimed at youth. So we support this bill, but we want to make very clear that we see this provision as just a very tiny step in the right direction. There is much, much more that we need to do in the entire area of children's and young persons' television. New Zealand children, on average, watch more than hours of television every day. Indeed, studies show that many children spend more time sitting in front of a television set than they do in the classroom. What do they see on State-owned television? They see endless amounts of violence, and thousands of images of Los Angeles and other American cities, but they tend not to see their own suburbs or communities. Only percent of the content of TV, which is the channel aimed at youth, and which youth and children tend to watch, is local content. That means that percent of the programmes screened on TV are non - New Zealand, foreign programmes. If the Government does proceed with its plans to turn TV into a cash cow, I worry that that figure of percent may decline to percent or even further. It seems to me that if we do not do something to rectify this situation, our children will end up with American accents as well as American values and the sort of mindset of compulsive consumerism that many of these programmes project. The number of hours of children's television has been declining steadily over the years. In there were , hours of children's programming. That had been halved by down to hours, and the statistics are no better this year. So what is the solution? The solution is to look across the Tasman where all the commercial channels have local content quota for children's television. All the channels must show a number of specially classified children's programmes. All children's pre-school programmes must have percent Australian content. There are very specific guidelines for children's documentary programmes, and for the number of hours of children's drama programmes. I think it is essential that we introduce children's content quotas for New Zealand television. We should not simply impose television quotas on Television One but, at the very least, should impose children's television quotas on TV and TV; otherwise, I fear that our children who are at a crucial age will grow up without really understanding and absorbing our culture, but simply hearing and speaking the voices of Los Angeles and other American cities.
