The Bill will have New Zealanders paying more for, and receiving less, accident compensation coverage than since the scheme was introduced in . Far from bringing in fairness, as the member for Tarawera has just mentioned, the opposite will happen for tens of thousands of New Zealanders. The scheme will not be fairer. Some people will receive no compensation or will pay much more for the privilege of insuring themselves or their families. The coverage for accident victims has been slashed under the Bill and the eligibility of many people for earnings-related compensation simply will cease. Is that fair? Does the member for Tarawera think that that is fair? The Bill is the first step in a move to privatisation of the Accident Compensation Corporation. I do not accept the submission to the House by the member for Tarawera that that will not happen, and I shall explore a bit of that in a few minutes. The underlying philosophy that is in the Bill is to abandon the approach that the Accident Compensation Corporation has taken for more than years of having a scheme for social insurance reasons. That is what we have had, and it is being abandoned. Who suffers when that is abandoned? Many people will suffer who cannot take, or have not taken precautions to deal with a problem that may come up in the future. Instead, what has occurred is that the changes that have been made will gradually introduce a commercial insurance scheme. The other key feature that is motivated by the Government is that of cost cutting. Members heard the Minister of Labour talk in the lead-up to the Bill, during debate in the House, and again in his comments in his third reading speech, about the need to cut costs. I do not want to go into the details of that, but Opposition members argued that that was not a valid reason to slash and burn in the way that he has done. It has been shown quite clearly during the debate that the Bill is a result of lobbying by the Employers Federation---it could almost be called an employers' charter in the way that it has been tailor-made for them---and the absolute tragedy is that most employers in New Zealand do not know what they are in for. The Employers Federation has said that the changes would cut costs for employers. At present we have -hour, -day-a-week coverage for everyone in New Zealand---visitors included---and that is cheap by any standards in the world. A no-fault scheme exists. If people are injured they are fixed up. However, employers will be faced, as they are in Australia, with spending four times as much---I would bet that the Employers Federation and the member for Tarawera have not told them that. At the select committee, when Opposition members questioned employers about that issue, they said they did not believe that it would happen. The facts are that in every other country that has happened and it will not be any different here. In my view, moves will be made in the very near future, as a result of employers waking up to the fact that it will cost them more for less for everyone, to have changes made to protect employers. Families will pay more as well. They will pay more as taxpayers because of the petrol taxes that they will be paying.

This Bill is a result of the Government's lifting the age of qualification for national superannuation from years of age to years of age, and, in particular, in the short term raising the age of qualification from years to years immediately on April this year. People who had planned to retire now find that a very mean-spirited Government has treated them in a mean-spirited and unfair way. The Bill allegedly aims to ban compulsory retirement at any age between the school-leaving age and the qualifying age for national superannuation. The Government has broken another election promise. During the election campaign it promised to raise the age of qualification for national superannuation over a -year period, not the -year period that it has now brought in. The effect of that on April Fool's Day---next Wednesday---is that for many people the plans that they had made about retiring will in many cases have to be dramatically changed. The consequence of the legislation is that people may end up with no money at all---being forced out of work or forced to stay in work, which they otherwise would not have done. The Bill provides that the employment contract that is in force on April will force that employee either to retire or to resign because he or she has reached the magical age of years. Of course, the Bill provides that there can be some agreement in writing between the employee and the employer either to confirm that retirement or to alter the age of retirement to a later date. If people do not agree in writing to confirm the retirement or if there is no agreement in writing to vary the age, they can retire and receive the second-class dole pension of $ a week if they are married---less than they would have received under the guaranteed retirement income. So, their expectations have been changed enormously. People who want to retire before they are at the age of eligibility for national superannuation will not be able to do so without paying a high penalty. That high penalty is that half a year from the date on which they retire they will receive nothing. They will not receive the guaranteed retirement income, as expected. Under the Labour Party's policy the guaranteed retirement income would have applied at years of age for those people from April. They will not get the dole at $ a week---less if they are married---they simply will get nothing for their trouble---nothing after a lifetime of work and planning. Most New Zealanders would accept---even somewhat reluctantly---a change to the qualification age of national superannuation if the Government and the country could not afford it. What they do not accept is that this has been sprung on them without notice---and I do not accept that and the Opposition does not accept it. Another election promise has been broken. Those people have not got the opportunity at the eleventh hour, with days to run before April, to make any suitable alternative arrangements. To suggest that renegotiating employment contracts will all be milk, roses, and honey on April is naive in the extreme. Both parties up until now would have made arrangements in most cases---that is, if they were near retirement. In many cases employers will find other ways to get rid of those staff. They simply will not agree, and therefore they will have a reduced retirement income than they would otherwise have expected. Many people plan for retirement. They make savings and some people have investments to supplement their income. Those plans have been put aside and badly skewed because of the rushed legislation and the changes that were made overnight without warning. Apart from the few exceptions that we have heard in the debate, there will be a range of people in jobs---and we understand more are about to be announced before the debate concludes---that will be exempt from the age requirement. The exemptions may include airline pilots, because allegedly they may be at risk, or models. There may be some valid reasons for someone wanting a -year-old model rather than a -year-old model, or for wanting a person able to climb heights if he or she is to be a window cleaner. I do not know, but we wait with bated breath while the Government rushes the drafting procedure through to get a change made before the debate is concluded. The Government has appeared to be concerned about the issue only since December last year, when the Leader of the Opposition announced that I was to introduce a private member's Bill to protect those people who would fall through the cracks after the rushed change to increase the age of qualification.

I support the balance that the select committee has achieved in its amendments to the Bill. It provides a fine balance between those who are engaged in research---and who spend $ million of taxpayers' money---and those who one could describe as representing the public interest and who will help to determine the priorities for spending the money. I guess that it is like the balance that I hope we will see in the final of the World Cup, with the New Zealand A and B teams playing off. However, the changes to the Bill reflect a consensus view of committee members from both sides of the House. There were submissions in support of the Bill and against. The committee met in Wellington and in Auckland, and, speaking as a member of that committee, I was struck by the fact that we were dealing largely with a group of people who have a vested interest---because they were engaged in biomedical research as well as other research---and who are very articulate and literate. They are people who, compared with the rest of the community, stood a good chance of getting what they wanted because they were able to use their natural ability, skills, and expertise in those two fields. The final composition of the council is fair, given the amount of money that is being spent. The larger membership that was proposed originally would not have added one iota of difference to the result now achieved. In fact, a little bit of money may have been saved. The composition and the balance between biomedical and public health backgrounds that several people wanted as part of the council was not taken on board by the select committee. It did not think that it should get down to that finite detail; the Minister of Health can deal with the interests of each of those groups as he appoints new council members in the future. It did not think that the Minister should be constrained in the choice of members of the council, and, from what we understand so far, the council seems to be working reasonably well. The committee wanted to remove one aspect from the influence of the council. It related to political influence---that is, whether the Director-General of Health should be a member of the council. A large number of submissions suggested that if the director-general were a member that could be seen as having the potential for making political input into the decisions of the council---in particular, since the change in the employment status of chief executives of Government departments. That conflict of interest and functions was cited by those making submissions, and they asked that the director-general be removed. There was nothing personal against the director-general, but the committee believed that the submissions bore some weight. It felt that it was inappropriate for the director-general to be involved---given the nature of the budget and its size---because he or she would be writing the cheques, if one likes, for that council. The committee also felt that the body should shape policy, and that as the director-general held the purse-strings that could be done in such a way that political interference could never be alleged. It was also suggested that there may be an opportunity for the department to manipulate the activities of the council, and the committee did not want that to happen, either. In the amended Bill the Minister has the power to appoint the chairperson, and the Opposition is pleased to support that proposition. Motion agreed to.

The Bill that is now in its concluding stages in the House is essentially about destroying a public housing system that we have had in New Zealand for nearly years. The Bill is anti-family, because it removes the State's social obligations and social responsibility to provide housing for those in need. It removes the State from the lives of many New Zealanders, and it allows a company that was set up for reasons of profit to give a return to the State. The fact that the company is housing someone is secondary to the fundamental reasons for its new existence. The member for Waitaki said that he was concerned about the low-income people in his electorate who required housing, that there was now a major housing shortage, and that New Zealanders could consider living in Twizel or Waimate. When the Labour Government came into power in the number of State rental houses was ,. Many had been sold off and only about houses were being built each year. In years the Labour Government extended that stock to , by building about each year. Housing has been a commitment of the Labour Party since the first Labour Government in the s. In the intervening period Tory Governments in New Zealand have at given times either stopped or reduced their expenditure on housing. We are now seeing, as part of the destruction of the welfare State, the beginning of the end of the provision by the State of housing to meet a social need and a social good in this country. The member for Waitaki said that he was not suggesting that those people who needed housing should be marched to some far-off plot as if in some sort of Nazi programme. All that I can say is: ``He said it, not I.''. During the debate in the Committee stage the Opposition questioned the Minister extensively about the legislation and how it would work. The Opposition was treated in large measure to a wall of silence.

This Bill is historic, because it is the first occasion that a fishery such as the scallop fishery, which is an enhanced fishery, has been placed under the quota management system. I compliment the Minister for introducing the Bill. As the computer program for the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has still not been written, the second part of the Bill attempts to simplify a method of balancing the amount of fish caught with the amount of quota held. We are now into the third year, and this running sore has had to be dealt with. Therefore, there are further amendments in the Bill to deal with the situation until the stage at which that program is created. I want to deal with that matter a little later on. There also are provisions in the Bill that tidy up the method of invoicing overcatches that have occurred each month since October and for which quota was not obtained. There is one unfortunate matter to which I want to refer, and that is the Bill's having been rushed through the select committee because it has to be passed by September . While the Bill may seem rather innocuous, that rush has caused some considerable anguish to the commercial industry and to Maori, who, in one case, have disputed the allocation of their percent. There was not terribly much that the select committee could do about that, but I have to say that passing legislation at this pace does not do justice to those people who are involved. The Opposition will support the passage of the Bill, but will move a number of amendments during the Committee stage to reflect the concerns that were expressed to the select committee about the new concept of an annual allowable catch that is being introduced in relation to the scallop industry. That concept deviates from the system that has operated since the major amendment to the Fisheries Act was made in to introduce the quota management system, whereby the concept of a total allowable catch was introduced and has prevailed since. The final amendment that the Opposition wants to make during the Committee stage derives from the successful outcome of the negotiations between the Crown and Maori over the fisheries claim. The Opposition believes that there is no reason that that agreement cannot be incorporated in the Bill. I want to talk about the southern scallop fishery. A submission was made to the select committee by Simunovich Fisheries Ltd--an Auckland company that deals substantially in a different species of fish called scampi--about the implications of introducing the new, two-tier, separate quota management system, and the detrimental effect that that system would have on it and many other companies. The company's $ million investment to develop the scampi industry may be put at risk if the new second-tier system of an annual allowable catch is allowed to continue. On the surface, the new concept of an annual allowable catch seems reasonable for an enhanced fishery, but one has to weigh up that argument against the concern of this company, which was supported by all of the industry organisations that appeared before the select committee. When those organisations were asked their views on the new system, they said that the allocation should be based on catch history--since , catch history has been taken into account when considering the allocation of quota for any new species--and that an appeal process, which is not provided for in the Bill, should be part of that system. There was a difference of opinion between the ministry's policy advisers to the select committee and Opposition members regarding the submissions mentioned. Essentially, Opposition members were told by the advisers that an enhanced fishery was substantially different, that therefore the concepts were different, and that a different system of an annual allowable catch was justified. On the other hand, rightly or wrongly, Simunovich Fisheries Ltd said that the Bill altered the principles of the Fisheries Act, that it was worried about the precedent that that would set, and that its business would be put at risk if Part IIA of the Act was fundamentally altered. That deeply concerned the select committee. The issue then was raised with the industry organisations that appeared before the select committee, and they also agreed that the new concept made them nervous. They said that the implications of a fundamental statutory change that did not recognise catch history were significant not only for the scampi fishery but also for other fisheries, as banks and other financial institutions might not invest in their companies as their investment might be at risk. The introduction of the quota management system in encouraged companies to exploit fisheries that were previously underdeveloped or underutilised. That policy decision was made by the Labour Government of the day, and I am pleased to say that it has since been endorsed by this Government and this Minister. The uncertainty that is now being created was the reason for considerable discussion by the submissioners. At the beginning of , Simunovich Fisheries Ltd embarked on a very substantial investment initiative to develop the scampi industry. The company said that it was an investment risk. The sum of $ million was lent to it by financial institutions to be put into that industry on the basis that when scampi finally were brought under the quota management system following the settlement of the Maori fisheries claim, the investment would give a return. Now the company says that that financial return is at risk. I do not believe that the Minister or the Government should have proceeded with the new concept without the support of the industry. The fundamental principle of basing the allocation on catch history was the only incentive that led that company, and many others, to invest in that industry in the first place. Now a second-tier system is to be put in place, and those companies say that it will increase the risk for themselves and for others. If the industry does not have faith in the system under which it is operating, neither will investors or financial institutions when making investment decisions. The question is whether, after that change, it will be prudent for anyone else to risk any form of investment in the business of fishing. The Minister will say--and I understand his reasoning--that this fishery is an enhanced fishery and that therefore it is different. The view of the industry is that there was a way round that, and the Opposition will introduce amendments during the Committee stage that will deal with that matter in more detail. The next issue that I want to raise is that of deemed value. In my view the ministry has not accounted to the Government as well as it should, and that is due to the delays that have occurred because of the ministry's seeming inability to put in place a computer system that will record catches and will deal with the deemed-value provisions. Deemed values were introduced in April in an amendment to the Fisheries Bill, and were to serve as a civil penalty for overfishing. It then became extremely important to achieve precision in the accounting of catch against quota held. That precision was not achieved for the reasons that I have mentioned. Because the ministry has failed to deliver the monthly quota balances that were promised to each quota holder at the start of the - fishing year, when the deemed-value regulations first took effect, we now are forced to make further amendments to that piece of legislation without having any guarantee that the system will be up and running after another months or year. It is simply not good enough that that has occurred. There was not the will, or the management was not determined to ensure that that would happen, or--the worst possible scenario--the person doing it had no reason to ensure that the matter was carried through in a short time. I do not know what the answer is, but the industry is fed up to the back teeth. I am sure that the Minister is fed up; I am fed up because of the complaints that I have received. The legitimate business of the management of fishing has been inconvenienced and made totally uncertain for the past couple of years, and will continue to be so until the ministry gets its act together. The other factor is that the enforcement provisions in relation to the fisheries have been restricted because the ministry has not been confident enough to prosecute overcatches of more than percent. There is a large volume of suspected quota fraud. Several very large fraud cases involving millions and millions of dollars are pending, and they will put some companies out of business. That position is an open invitation to villains to rort the system. That is not in anyone's interests. The Minister has already boasted that people who are caught, no matter how ``big'' they are, will be destroyed through the use of the provisions of the enforcement and prosecution proceedings. But that cannot be done, so the Minister's hands are tied, the ministry's hands are tied, the hands of those people out on the high seas looking through binoculars are tied, and the hands of accountants poring over records are tied. If this situation goes on much longer, it will be an open invitation for more ``quota-busting''. The Fisheries Act does allow overcatching or undercatching of percent in a year, and there is a balancing-up in the next year. If one overcatches by percent in a year, the subsequent year one has to undercatch by percent. That is a good system that appears to be working, but I think that it is working because of the good faith on the part of most people involved, because there is no policeman or policewoman on the beat, as the case may be. I will ask the Minister further questions about that issue at the Committee stage, and will follow it up in the period ahead. We did have some difficulty with the regulations. I am pleased to say that the Regulations Review Committee is now satisfied with the answers that it has received about the annual allowable catch and the variations that are required. I should like to deal with an issue relating to Maori fishing. Opposition members have proposed an amendment to reflect the recent percent settlement, compared to the percent of the fishery that has been allocated under this Bill. As a matter of good faith, I believe that the Government can allocate percent irrespective of whether or not the Sealord Products deal is confirmed. There is no reason that the Government cannot do that. In relation to the second issue that I want to deal with, I am pleased that the Minister, as recently as an hour before the sitting of the House this afternoon, did meet representatives of Ngati Toa from Porirua to discuss the dispute between the runanga in Porirua and the Ngati Toa iwi from the top of the South Island. I had proposed to move an amendment to deal with that matter. The Minister has indicated to the House that both parties are satisfied with the outcome, and I am happy to accept that statement. This issue raises a fundamental question that we should be concerned about. Once the Maori fishery allocation has been dealt out to iwi, the dispute that has occurred on this occasion is likely to be multiplied a hundredfold. There is no way that any Minister or any Government can cope with such disputing parties. There needs to be a mechanism to handle that matter that does not hold up legislation or delay the development of the industry. I hope that a simple mechanism is established so that the subsequent legislation is not held up, and the Minister is not held up, but also so that justice is seen to be done when disputes between iwi, or disputes within iwi, occur. Another comment that I want to make relates to the amateur fishers who appeared before the select committee. They argued that not enough space had been set aside for recreational purposes. I am satisfied that their fears are groundless; that, in fact, substantial areas have been set aside; and that that will continue in the future. Any increase in the tonnes of scallop meat that has been allocated--and an increase will occur with a fishery such as this--will also be distributed to all parties. So if the allocation goes up, everyone will gain, and if the fishery appears to be overfished and the allocation drops, everyone will take his or her share of the cut-back. In conclusion, if this model is to be used in the future--that is, if attempts are to be made to get the parties involved together to agree on allocation, as has occurred with iwi--it is absolutely vital that ample time is set aside so that if a dispute does arise it does not hold up the allocation process. I suggest to the Minister that a formula be established as part of the mechanism so that disputes can be resolved early on, rather than at the last minute, to avoid such hold-ups occurring. I am sure that the allocation of quota to the companies operating this fishery will be of benefit to the country. It is a very valuable export earner for New Zealand. Growth of about another percent is envisaged. Our income and our standard of living depend on developments such as this, and I wish the industry well.

Government members are attempting to put into place their arrogant view---including that of the Associate Minister of Health, the Minister of Communications---about what they think New Zealanders need and what is best for them in health. We have only or months at the most until the election and then things will change. I am reminded of the defence that the Minister of Health used recently when he said that our system is not an Americanised model. That Minister went to the United States only last October. He talked to experts about health funding. When he came back he said: ``I think the United States system stinks.''. He also said that he would not touch it with a bargepole. That was in October last year. Regardless of all of that, we are now confronted with the introduction by the Minister of Health of the same sort of system that applies in the United States. The inspiration for the reforms came from Professor Patricia Danzon. She came from a Chicago school. She is a right-wing economist who believes in the free market and pay-as-you-go. She works for CS First Boston and she has made reports to the National Interim Provider Board about our new health reforms. If we look at the United States system, with its vouchers and so on, we know that that is not the structure we want in New Zealand. People certainly do not want it. In March this year an American consultant called Banks Warden, whom the Associate Minister of Health, the Minister of Communications, knows, was employed under specific instructions: ``The principle purpose of any seminars would be to provide us with an appreciation of the benefits and costs of the American system and their application to our particular reforms.''. I suggest, and I know, that those reforms are built around a commercially competitive profit-driven health system with more openings for the private sector. The Government has already introduced the commercialisation of our hospitals, which now have to pay a dividend; they have to make a profit. They have already been required to pay taxes. Therefore that is more money that could have been spent on health but will not be. Finally, we should look at the comparison between New Zealand and what it is about to get into. Before this mess started New Zealand spent percent of its gross domestic product on health---one of the lowest percentages in the world. America, which New Zealand is aping and using as a model for these experiments, spends . percent of its gross domestic product on health. We can expect many more dollars to be paid for receiving much less in return---duplication of services and under using equipment in the competitive model. Look at the disasters announced in the past week: a large number of smaller hospitals were told they were unsafe---significantly unsafe in some areas! We know that this model breeds that type of result. We cannot take money out of the health system and not expect the system to fall apart. We have had the embarrassment of Dr Peter Troughton, director of the Crown health enterprise establishment unit, having his legs cut from under him by the Associate Minister of Health, the Minister of Communications, who said on television last night that there was no list of unsafe hospitals. Yet we know today that the Opposition spokesperson on health, the Deputy Leader of the Opposition, produced that list. That is a disgrace for this Government---and for a long time.

If this Government is re-elected I do not hold much hope that there will be any statutory bodies dealing with labour law. Workers who want their employment cases to be dealt with will appear with people who owe parking fines, murderers, and rapists---if they are lucky enough to be able to afford to take a case. The report does not accept that any further restrictions need to be placed on the behaviour of rogue employers. The free market, according to this lot, reigns supreme. Well, there is a place for law and order, there is a place for establishing a way of dealing with disputes, because they do occur---human beings are human beings---and there is a place for establishing within employment law minimum standards of behaviour. The majority report ignores the obvious connection between workers' having a choice of bargaining agent and the restrictions that the Act has placed on them. The majority report wants as little involvement of unions as is possible. The Government members think that that is positive. Unions do have a right to exist in the civilised world, they do have a right to bargain for workers who do not have the confidence or economic clout to bargain for themselves, and they should be able to bargain with employers in good faith. The report has no recommendations that insist that employers do that. The report encourages further discrimination in the workplace. I want to deal with youth rates. The report---written by those two Government members, who picked up the Employers' Federation proposals---quite positively states that there is no need to have a minimum code of wages and conditions for young people. The committee heard a lot of evidence---sure, a lot of it was anecdotal, but it was there, nevertheless---that young people were being exploited and that they were being paid less. That was admitted by the Government members. If there is a doubt they should, in all conscience, deal with that injustice, but they have suggested otherwise. They have suggested that people ring an telephone number, as if that would deal with the problem when the Department of Labour has only labour inspectors at the moment. We do know the effect on wages and conditions of the Employment Contracts Act, and the report claims that pay rates have been raised to compensate for changes in overtime and penal rates. That does not square up with the facts presented by the Service Workers Union, which conducted a survey of , of its members. It showed that percent of them---mainly low-paid, part-time women workers---had had their overtime, penal rates, and conditions cut, and that the other percent had had no pay increases at all since the Act had come into force. We are dealing with a climate that is unreal. The report does not face up to the realities of what is happening in the market-place. The Government has abandoned its attempt to reduce unemployment, because it has risen by percent since the election. According to the Government's last Budget projections, unemployment will stay at the same level for the next years. It was said that the Act would make sure that more people could be employed. That has not been the case, and we know from the evidence presented to the committee that a substantial number of people have had their hours reduced. There is more flexibility, and the report suggests that as a result of the Act there is more productivity. Oh yes, there is more productivity, but at what price? There are fewer workers, fewer hours of work, and less overtime. True productivity is the same number of workers producing more goods. That is the test of productivity. The Act has failed on that score, and so has the report. I oppose this report, and I believe that the people of New Zealand will do so at the general election. Motion agreed to.

I tell the Minister that a quarter of the population of my electorate are immigrants from the Pacific Islands. Most of them are immigrants who were not born in New Zealand; some of them are second generation; percent of people have come here after being born in other countries. For a large proportion, and I cannot exactly quantify it, English is a second language and they have difficulty in communicating. They certainly do not read English, but they may read their own languages. Therefore the information coming out is not being read by them. They have difficulty knowing what is going on. They do not read the daily newspapers and they do not read the weekly newspapers that come free of charge to their letterboxes. In fact, in a large suburb in my electorate only percent of households get a daily newspaper that is written in English.

I believe that this Bill is an example of ill-conceived tinkering with the Sale of Liquor Act, and it was this type of ad hockery that gave us the pre- legislation jungle before the Laking report was written, and before the review, overhaul, and changes that Parliament made to the Sale of Liquor Act in that year. At that time members of this House said: ``Let's not again fall into the trap of passing amendments to the Sale of Liquor Act in a piecemeal and ad hoc manner without a proper review, and that review should take place about every years.'' What have we found since then? We saw the previous member for Hastings introduce an amendment to allow the sale of wine from winemakers' premises days a week. Now, only a few years later, we find another series of amendments without the overall review. I have no objection to an overall review, and I think the Minister of Justice has failed in his duty not to have seen and organised a complete review so that this House could deal with the issue in a proper overall manner, instead of doing this tinkering. The member for Tarawera, in introducing this Bill, said there was a lack of space on the Government's legislative programme and that we would have to wait until before we could do anything, and then he went on to say that no one knows what will happen in an MMP environment. If members took that attitude in every sphere of legislation we would have a mad rush in every subject imaginable as if the world were going to end when MMP commenced. That is just a nonsense. The member for Bradford has advanced the argument---
Is Radio New Zealand considering an alternative to New Zealand Public Radio as a news supplier for its commercial stations; if so, have discussions commenced with any potential suppliers?
Well, it is nice to hear the member say it, but what the Government is doing in selling Works, is giving oil companies more dominant power, and we will have less competition as a consequence.

I raise a point of order, Madam Chairman. I appreciate that this is a robust debate, but this is the second time in a matter of minutes that the Minister has suggested that Opposition members have said things that clearly they have not said. I suggest he will cause disruption in the House if he continues on that path. He has plenty of material to deal with without making up stories that are clearly designed to be unruly.

Part XIII deals with offences and penalties, and contains clauses down to . I shall refer to clause , ``Penalties'', and make some comment. The penalties under this legislation are minor, medium, and serious. The fines imposed range from $, up to $,. In the past, people who breached the Act for illegal fishing lost their quota. They also could lose their vessel. They could lose their factory, if they processed in New Zealand, unless the Minister at his discretion decided to give some or all of that back to them. The banks that loaned money for development to fishing companies have been reluctant to do so since because they wanted some security in lending. The Bill has been changed so that only in the most serious cases is forfeiture of the vessel going to apply. The fines are anything from $, up to half a million dollars. I would hope that the courts in judging cases that come before them will take account of the intention of the select committee, that in relaxing the total forfeiture of quota vessels and other assets they will not be lenient, given the fact that the fines that were provided do not come anywhere near the cost of the forfeiture. Losing a vessel is going to be a lot more costly than having to pay out $, in a fine. In a sense one could argue that we have all gone soft on the job. However, there are provisions that I think the commercial fishing industry will take seriously. I would like the Minister to comment on an issue that has been raised, and it relates to clause , ``Penalties''. It has been suggested that every person convicted of offending under this provision is liable to a term of imprisonment not exceeding year, or to a fine not exceeding $,, and every person convicted of a list of offences can be fined up to $,. The forfeiture provisions can apply for those fines up to $,. If a court, which is now the body that will deal with any fines and possible forfeitures for the most serious offences, deals with an issue under clause (), it can seize a vessel, or any other asset, and has no option but to retain percent of that asset, but it can give percent back to the fishing company. If a case involving a $ million vessel comes before the court there is no option; the judge has to keep percent of that.

The Minister cannot remain silent on this. He has to answer these questions. I want to know why the Minister has not made some reference about restricting the numbers. The estimates this year totally reinforce the Government's sort of slash-and-burn approach to the core public services that we have. If the Government were really serious about that issue then we would not have the sorts of minimal increases that we have had in this area with ---or is it six now---Labour Department inspectors throughout the whole country. The estimates for vote: Labour also show the continuation of the erosion of workers' rights in the workplace. Joy McLauchlan talked about strikes---work stoppages is the polite way she described them. She talked about the hours of work being roughly the same, and a . percent increase in the average wage. That simply disguises what the big picture is and what, in fact, is happening in the workplace. First of all I want to deal with the proposed announcement, probably this week, by the Minister about his changes to the Holidays Act. We have heard in this debate that he got a beating from the trade unions and the Employers Federation about not selling one week's annual leave. He had to back off from that, or maybe the Minister would confirm that he has backed off. I will ask him that question. Will he confirm that he has backed away from that?

In the commentary on the Bill from the select committee, the analysis of clause talks about the application of employment contracts. It states: ``Clause is intended to smooth the staff transfer process from the Department of Social Welfare to the new department.'' It goes on to state that where employees are transferred to the new department, their conditions of employment must be no less favourable than those of their existing jobs. That is what the Minister of Social Services, Work and Income said in the report-back speech. What I am not satisfied about, and what I would like the Minister to answer, is that if circumstances change in the new organisation within months---I am not talking about a case where a job disappears and a person gets redundancy---there is no redundancy provision, as I understand it. That would be a normal provision. I think that a couple of years ago it was written into a Bill that amalgamated some departments; I remember that we debated it in this Chamber. For up to months, people would qualify for redundancy if, because of the amalgamation, there were job changes that they did not agree with. The management does not know exactly how the new jobs will fall, or the amount of work that will be involved, and maybe there will be some other changes of jobs. I want to know whether that has been taken into account. It may be in an agreement with the Public Service Association, but there has been no mention of it. It was a factor months ago when we dealt with an earlier case like this. I want to know whether there is any provision that, within months of the change-over, if jobs change people will qualify for redundancy. I ask that simply because at the time of the change-over all the job changes may not be known by the management or the staff concerned, and that may have consequences for the new jobs. The second issue I want to raise is whether there might be an occasion where those employment contracts that are currently collective become individual. In other words, the conditions may remain the same, but the nature of the contract changes from a collective to an individual contract. Would that qualify an employee as having been disadvantaged by the change-over? I would like to know from the Minister whether that situation qualifies for redundancy. Indeed, the Public Service Association in its submission said that under this Bill people should not be disadvantaged in the transition to the new structure, should the collective nature of the contract of that person change to an individual contract. The fact that the Public Service Association raised the issue, in my mind, means that it must have had some concerns that it could occur. I want to know whether there is a guarantee that people will not be changed from a collective to an individual contract, and that if they are, that is not an excuse to say they are not disadvantaged. Clearly, their bargaining power would be disadvantaged in most cases, although it may not be in all cases, by doing that. Will the Minister give an answer to that question? The Public Service Association also raised another question. It said that it was made clear to the Public Service Association that one of the Government's aims was to protect conditions of employment, while ensuring that the new department was not locked into contracts of employment that were not suited to the needs of the new department. Can the Minister tell the House whether there will be any changes in terms of needs of the new department that did not exist under the two old separate departments? Debate interrupted. This Bill accepts the proposition that the market rent policy that the Government has for State houses is working, and it accepts the proposition that the accommodation supplement, as a contribution to low-income households towards the cost of that housing, is also working. I say that it is not working. On the one hand, the Government is increasing by percent the accommodation supplement for those in rental housing; on the other hand it is decreasing the accommodation supplement for those in boarding houses. The Government is effectively taking from the poor to give to the poor. I hardly think that is some form of social justice or fairness. In this last weeks, State house tenants---, of them---have been told that they are to have a rent increase from July. Worse than that, some of those , tenants are to get another notice saying that they will have a second increase on the anniversary of the date they came in to that house. The only reason they have not had it up till now is that there has been a freeze on State house rental increases, and I will deal with that a little later. The Minister assumes, and has told the country, that the increase will help lower-income New Zealanders. Well, on the one hand, some money is going into their pockets, at least one pocket. What he did not say was that, on the other hand, more than that amount is going out with the increase in the market rents that is applying around New Zealand. In Auckland the maximum increase---not the level of rent per week---in week is $ in Mount Albert. Now this pittance---these few pieces of silver---will not help that family, who will pay an extra $ more than it was paying before. Does the Minister think that is fair? Most people who live in Auckland will pay about $ extra, with very little offset. That is hardly fair. I think the Minister should be ashamed of himself if he is parading this policy to the country as fixing the problem. The problem is getting worse while he is throwing a few pieces of silver to those people at the bottom of the economic heap. Under the current abatement rules, as soon as people earn any extra money their accommodation supplement is then reduced. They are trapped in a cycle of, in many cases, poverty by not being able to afford to go to work. I want to say what the Ministry of Housing told this Government only weeks ago in a report tabled in this House. The Ministry of Housing found that market rents are above what people are prepared to pay, and that the system is not working. In spite of that, the Minister and his colleagues in Cabinet have simply ignored the problem. This is what the ministry said in the report that the select committee tabled in this House: ``If the market was working, the high number of vacant houses would be substantially lower.'', and: ``Housing New Zealand is failing to fill the stock by charging a level of rent above that which the market is prepared to pay.'' That comes from the Government's own bureaucracy. It is an admission of the failure of the whole policy. How many empty State houses are there? As at the end of January there were ,.
``Oh, rubbish!'', says Roger Sowry. What we have seen in the health sector has been a disaster.

The Bill is yet another measure in a long tradition of muddled legislation affecting agriculture. Some archaic statutes affect agriculture; some have been the subject of adverse comment in the House and in select committees, including ones that I have chaired from time to time. Who in the office put together the Bill? It seems to repeal the functions of the ministry. It repeals section of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries Act , which sets out the ministry's principal functions. They have been added to over the years, and they are all being repealed. No other section sets out lesser, minor, or incidental functions, and so on. Clause () adds a new paragraph to section () about the powers of the Minister that states: ``For the purpose of enabling the Department to carry out its functions, the Minister may''---and new paragraph (j) sets out additional matters. We have just heard that the ministry is to have no functions, so the Minister does not need powers if there are no functions to be carried out. The Bill could benefit from a more professional approach to its construction. Clause () repeals a long list of sections in many statutes. The explanatory note dismisses all those repeals with a few words: ``consequential amendments and consequential repeals''. One of the more important ones might be section of the Meat Export Prices Act . I checked the statutes to find that---bless my soul---that whole Act was repealed on December . So I wonder about that matter. As the repeal of the schedule takes away the ministry's responsibility to administer Acts, I checked to find out what the repeal of section of the Wine Makers Levy Act might mean---after all, the wine industry is important to Marlborough. It states that the Wine Makers Levy Act is to be administered by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. So I take the repeal to be a kind of belt and braces one. So I presume that, if that measure is representative, those Acts dealing with everything from hive levies, to pesticides, to the Phosphate Commission, and so on are now cast off into space unloved, unwanted, and unadministered. If the Bill is to be pushed through we are entitled at least to the courtesy of a systematic statement of the reason those things are being done, because by the time one hunted one's way round the shelves a great deal of time would be involved. Clause () substitutes a new section () of the Finance Act, which states: ``The Minister of Agriculture may from time to time---(a) On behalf of Her Majesty the Queen, subscribe for or otherwise acquire shares or interests in any body corporate that may lawfully do things similar to things the performance of which is for the time being a function of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries''. But the House is about to repeal all of its functions.

I know that the Government is keen to get its hands on money, but I think the Commissioner of Inland Revenue actually wants to get his hands on it. Do the normal laws about articles deemed to have been received if posted apply? If not, my argument is reinforced. The Minister drew attention to the provision in clause to remove the commissioner's power to waive additional tax. On the face of it that seems to apply to initial assessments only, but when the commissioner makes a subsequent assessment---and I am not talking about when he catches up with a ratbag who has deliberately been acting criminally in relation to non-compliance, but about the result of a routine audit in which there has been a difference of interpretation and the commissioner rules that tax must be paid on a certain item---does the penalty automatically apply from the time when the normal return would have been made or does it start from the date on which the subsequent assessment required payment? That important matter needs clarification. Clause does not seem to attempt to identify or define ``hobby''. I suppose one person's hobby is another person's livelihood. However, somewhere along the line there is a taxable activity---either totally recreational, at the one extreme---

What about the Defamation Bill that is before the House? Most of that should be struck down. Everybody should be able to have a go, because the test under clause is that those rights can be subject only to reasonable limits prescribed by law that can demonstrably be justified in a free and democratic society. No one can curtail my right of freedom of expression except for my having a chance to make an equal and prompt reply, and that is all that we should need. Clause deals with electoral rights, and states that everyone of or over the age of years is qualified for membership of the House of Representatives. That includes those imprisoned for life, including those confined legally against their will in a mental institution because of serious mental disease, and the criminally insane confined at the pleasure of the Minister of Justice. It is nonsense to suggest that those people are qualified to be members of Parliament. Every New Zealand citizen over the age of years has the right to vote. What about those people who at present have the right to vote and who are legal, and often long-term, residents of this country? The Bill seeks to disfranchise about voters, and it is called a Bill of Rights! It is a tyranny that seeks to take away the rights of people. Those people will not be able to vote at the next election because the Bill comes into force on December . That cabal babbling away on the Government benches proposes that legal long-term residents will not have the right to vote. The Bill is a monstrosity. It is an absolute denial of rights that exist at present. The pompous professor giggles and laughs. He is the author of this Bill that takes away the existing right to vote that is contained in the Electoral Act. I prefer the Electoral Act of New Zealand to anything that is in this Bill, and so should many other New Zealand citizens. I turn to the arrest, search, and seizure provisions. The Bill states that everyone has the right to be secure against unreasonable search or seizure. I will be damned if I will accept that. I want protection against unlawful search and seizure. I will not have the time of day debated about whether I could have my head half bent in, and so on. I should like the law to prevail---not the Prime Minister's concept of an application of the law, so that he can interminably argue and nitpick about it. I want the right to be free of unlawful arrest. It is a well-established tort, amongst other things. I want some more absolute rights. I want this to be a country that is subject to the rule of law as inherited and developed here---habeas corpus---that great Bill of Rights of which this is not even a shadow.

I have read the Bill, and it will cancel the freehold title held by the Marlborough Harbour Board. I used to be the board's solicitor, so I know what was in its title. The Bill would cancel the title, and the land would revert to the Crown. I presume that the Port of Marlborough would then have to go cap in hand to the Department of Conservation to get a lease of the seabed, would it not? The Minister will have a chance to explain how that title will be exempt from the provision. He says that for all seabeds, with the exception of harbour boards, title will be cancelled and come to the Crown. There is no provision for an exception for the seabed of the inner Picton harbour, which is in a freehold certificate of title now. The Minister could check that out during the recess. In fact, I will send him a photocopy of the title if he wants to see it. While the Government made announcements in and in ---everything was announced on December and then the people who were responsible for that were sacked; but I am not sure whether this Bill was another of those measures---the origins of many of those land-vesting endowments go back to the early days of settlement, to provincial government. In fact, they have been community assets, administered locally, and used by local communities. In this day of local government reorganisation they should properly at the very least be put in the care of the regions, with the Government's interests being accommodated through the setting of standards with resource management law reform legislation, whenever that comes in. Such assets properly belong where people live with them, use them, and benefit from them. Central government has no reason to haul them back into the centre except to build the empire of the Department of Conservation. Why not trust the local government and regional government structures set up by the Government itself? Why bring in the Bill now? The Bill is a vote of no confidence in the communities that the Government established by Executive fiat, and that is an important issue to consider. There is no reason for central government to be involved except to set quality standards, and that is acknowledged freely. Why is central government hauling back the assets? It can only be because it does not trust the regions. The Minister of Conservation may not trust the people in his Nelson area---and he will have to explain to them why he does not, because that area, as with some others, was settled quite early on. I do not realise how central government will do one whit better than the communities, but I will say, with certainty, that whatever is done will be done at a greater cost in the hands of central government. How will anyone benefit from that? Debate interrupted.

It was --- August. He said that the great advantage of the State Fire Insurance Department was that it would apply the mutual principle. That is hardly the framework of a State department. The canard---or maybe it is the catfish---has been introduced into the debate tonight, asking about the difference between the State Insurance Office and the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. The ministry was a department of State set up to administer an inherent Crown right and responsibility---the fisheries. There has been some argument about that recently, too: the tangata whenua thought the fish were theirs, but the Crown flogged them off, too. That is why we had so much trouble with the fisheries. A mutual organisation was set up in , and it is interesting to know what has happened since, because at about that time, and subsequently, two other great New Zealand insurance institutions were set up. Do members remember the South British Insurance Co. and the New Zealand Insurance Co.? Both of them have gone. They were messed up and their assets were stripped by the fast-money men. Into whose ownership have they gone now? Bless my soul, it is Scottish, is it not? Now the State Insurance Office is going all the way to Norwich Union, somewhere in England. We are now, in our sesqui centennial year---the year we celebrate our nationhood, independence, and progress---back where we were before Dick Seddon tried in Parliament to do something about the foreign domination of the insurance industry in New Zealand. Some progress! Some Labour Government! What I find offensive in the Bill is that Parliament is being treated with contempt by the Executive---the Crown, the Government---and therefore so are the people, in that the Government presumed to enter into a contract to diminish the sovereignty of Parliament and the people by saying to a foreign corporate body: ``We undertake to change the law of New Zealand.''. To whom is the Government answerable? It clearly does not consider the people first. It enters into treaties with foreigners to set out the law of New Zealand. In our sesqui centennial year, celebrating our independence and nationhood, we are again worse off than a colonial Parliament under the orders of Westminster. That is all a sign of a terrible regression in this beautiful land. I do not stand for the Government's obligating itself to someone who is not a citizen or with whom it has lawful business and ought to represent in the nation. We have entered into the very doors of the pawnbrokers of the world. The Bill contains yet another offence. I suppose that if one is going to insult people one might as well insult all institutions. Parliament may not count for much in the eyes of many people, but what about the courts? In clause (a) the Bill contains a provision that is effectively an ouster of the jurisdiction of the superior courts. When the two lady policyholders from Tarawera went to the High Court in their proceedings to request something that most people understand to be an injunction, the Crown counsel lamely tried to tell the court---to put the most charitable view or construction on the provision---that it was not intended to have the effect of preventing anybody from taking to the court any issues arising out of the sale. But the plain words of the clause can be nothing else. They certainly were not for the benefit of policyholders at all. They certainly were not for the benefit of the public. They certainly were not expressly stated to be for the benefit even of the buyer. They were for the benefit of the Crown, so that it could cock its nose at the High Court and say: ``We do not give a damn what you think. We will not let you rule on the law. We will make it so that we can meet our obligation to that bunch of foreigners for whom we have agreed to change the law of New Zealand.''. So the courts are held in contempt by the Government. Over the weekend I chanced upon a longstanding supporter of the Government. I greatly respect people who have been involved in political parties, even if they are not mine. They are the very substance of the democratic process. He said to me that Labour is going out like a light---in relation to the election, of course. It is that kind of action that turns the clock in New Zealand back to the first years of the century, and puts us in thrall to foreigners to make laws and to hand over industries in which New Zealand institutions had a major role. We are going back into colonial status under the Government, which made such a cry when it first came to office about a more independent, self-reliant New Zealand. Remember the rhetoric? We now hear the merest echoes. The Government sought advice about what it might do with the State Insurance Office---having, of course, decided to sell it. It was tut-tutted to about that. It was told---and this is about the best version I can get from the Government's side of the argument---that there was no clear legal right to the assets in the Crown or the policyholders. Well, the Government shopped around a little more, because that was not really enough information on which to flog it off. The Government obtained some more advice, which came in a highly distilled form from Treasury---and members know how much principle underlies that outfit. Treasury said that, while the ownership was unclear, the Crown's claims were stronger. Of course they are. Government members can use their muscle and numbers to walk in here and make the law whatever they want it to be. The Minister said in his opening remarks that the overwhelming evidence was for Crown ownership. Yes, it is---by to . That is the overwhelming evidence for ownership---the Government's majority in the House. I advise people who have anything of value to lock it up, if possible. If they cannot find somewhere to lock it up they should hide it, because the overwhelming power of the Crown---the Government---could mean they will be parted from it tomorrow. That is another reason that Labour will go out like a light. We are told that the sale is to be made to repay debt. I have some news for the people. After a succession of sales the debt is higher than it was before the Government started. I am not quite sure how that can be called progress, when all that seems to happen is that the money goes up in smoke, and the debt is not even reduced. New Zealand will end up with no insurance companies---my apologies to AA/SIMU Mutual; put them to one side as the sole survivor for the time being---and will exit from an industry in which it had a major involvement. We end up with more debt. I come to the House to try to do an honest day's work, but I cannot for the life of me see how the industry is progressing. Maybe the Government should explain. The sale shows what has become a consistent pattern of incompetence and muddle in business. The sale is announced, and the terms are disclosed. In court this week we find that, even in relation to this simple and straightforward sale, the terms have been changed since the sale was announced. That is so consistent. Copies of documents on the sale of Telecom---the so-called articles of association of the company---have been tabled by the Minister for State-owned Enterprises. We find out---and newspaper readers will read about it in the morning---that after the bids closed the articles of association of Telecom were changed. Some of the buyers are starting to complain, even to the extent of going to the news media. Every sale is being conducted with an unsavoury or unsatisfactory element, and people are entitled to say that the Government is not capable of organising a Christmas party in a brewery, even when the issue is one that the people do not want the Government to deal with. The Government is not even learning by experience---and, my word, it has had a great deal of experience in the flogging-off department. That is another reason for the Government to go. It is interesting to look back to November when the Associate Minister for State-owned Enterprises---who ought to be packing, because he will be a goner in less than weeks---said that the State Insurance Office was created as a department in but had never returned a dividend to the taxpayers since. His argument for selling the office was that taxpayers were not getting anything out of it except taxes. Such dividends would have been illegal, because the State Insurance Office Act did not allow for them. It dealt specifically with what had to happen to the profits, and it did not list the Government as being entitled to receive any of them---until recently. That raises an interesting point. When the Public Finance Bill was introduced in clause stated that the Minister of Finance could direct any other Minister to hand over the profits of any of a long list of bodies---Government departments and Crown agencies. The State Insurance Office was slipped into that schedule. I do not think it occurred to anybody in Parliament that by implication the schedule repealed section of the State Insurance Office Act, which laid out what was to happen to profits---to go into reserve, then to be rebated to policyholders by way of reductions in premiums. The matter apparently was not argued, and Mr Justice Ellis did not rule whether the Public Finance Act repeals section of the State Insurance Office Act. It was said by Mr Justice Ellis, apropos another argument before the court, that people ought not to be deprived of their right by an ambiguity in statute, and, when there is a difference between one being quite specific and one being quite general, I doubt whether the provision of the State Insurance Office Act determining what happens to its profits has in fact been done away with by the stealth of the Public Finance Act. It has occurred to me, after going over the judgment again tonight, that that is something that could well be argued. Even so, in the judgment issued today it is important to note that the court did not say that the State Insurance Office belonged to the Crown; it stated that those two ladies from the Bay of Plenty were not able to advance a cause of action. That is a quite different matter. In other words, the court did not, as an essential element of its judgment, have to give a final determination of the status of the State Insurance Office. Therefore the Crown has not got far in the matter, and it seems that Parliament should properly decide about a longstanding community institution that has been, to all appearances, operating in its day to day work separately from the political action of the Government. It should be for the people, through their elected representatives, freely to determine what should happen to the office---in other words, whether there is to be fundamental change. The Opposition does not consent to the State Insurance Office being considered now, after the event, to belong to the Government, and to the Government's keeping the money. The Opposition says, as it did with the Government Life Insurance Office, that any privatisation should be into the hands of policyholders. The Government agreed to that course in relation to the Government Life Insurance Office, and the Opposition concurred in the passage of that Bill---it being just one of many times when the Government has taken up the National Party's policy, being bankrupt of any of its own. It might well be asked who owns other community institutions---for example, the trustee banks---set up by statute. In Britain it was held that the Government could own them, but in New Zealand the Government recognised that there was a customer community involvement, so it established their capital into community trusts for the benefit of communities. Districts have already shared in some of the profits of those banks and will continue to do so. The same matter has arisen in the past week or two in relation to power boards; nobody is quite sure who owns them. The Government flirted with sequestering them to the Crown, but finally thought better of it. The State Insurance Office is in that stream, and ought to be handled similarly. It is the ultimate sadness that when the office is sold and the Government takes the money the country ends up with more debt, not less. Nothing has been achieved; there is a loss to the nation and to the community. For all of those reasons I oppose the Bill. I say that, if Seddon does not tonight turn round on his bronze statue in front of Parliament Buildings, he will be spinning around on the hill behind Bowen Street.

This bad Bill has been badly handled by the Government from start to finish. For the first time in many years a major policy issue that was not a fiscal matter was introduced and debated under urgency to prevent the people of New Zealand from having any input into what happens to the forests---in particular, in the regions in which they live. On behalf of my constituents I protest, even at this late stage, that they have been denied any say---they have had no opportunity to inquire about what is to happen to the Wairau forest, for instance. That is a very important resource for economic development and employment in our district, and is very important in people's day to day lives in terms of recreation, hunting, and other amenity uses. Opposition members sought assurances and details of what is to become of such resources that are priceless not just in dollar terms for cubic metres of wood sold but as a part of our heritage. However, a response has not been forthcoming. The Government does not know the answer. It is a matter of ``get the money''; it is another fire sale. During the Committee stage the Opposition sought clarification of what would happen to those amenity forests, to amenity areas in them, and to other sensitive parts that ought not to be leased. It said that there should be a specific definition to protect them for their present purposes---which are largely non-economic purposes---but the Government has made only the vaguest of statements. The clear impression that came out of that once-only, limited consideration in the Committee stage is that people have no idea yet of the extent of the loss they will suffer so that the Government can raise some money. The Government argued that it was being done because it needed money to reduce the national debt. It appears that that may not be the result. The reason for that statement became apparent when we were considering Parts III and IV, relating to Maori issues and the amendment to the Treaty of Waitangi Act, which are part of the Bill. The Government, in its headlong rush to cash up New Zealand, was ambushed by Maoridom, which was charging off to fulfil the expectations that had been raised to high levels by this same Government. On the courthouse steps the Government was forced into an agreement with Maoridom so that it could carry on with the sale process. Most New Zealanders would not know the result of that deal---it is in the Bill. The Waitangi Tribunal has been given the power to transfer up to hectares of New Zealand land from public ownership on behalf of all New Zealanders to Maori ownership in satisfaction of claims for past grievances. Past grievances ought to be settled between those responsible---the Crown and the claimants---and not handed over by the Crown to some administrative and quasi-judicial tribunal as a way of passing the buck. The Waitangi Tribunal is in possession of a great pile of signed but blank memorandum of transfer forms. It has become apparent that it is in possession of something else, too. It is in possession of a cheque-book giving it entre to the largest kitty in recent times---the proceeds from the sale of the logs in those forests, or the value of the standing timber remaining, and, in some cases, interest to inflation-proof the proceeds. It has not been widely recognised that the implications of the Bill are not just that the standing forest resources will be sold, but that New Zealanders will receive precious little benefit by the time the process has wound its way through all of the various claims. That state of affairs is unsatisfactory, and the Opposition opposes it. The forests will become a slush fund, and will not benefit New Zealanders as a whole. The Opposition vigorously opposed the conditions of sale of the trees, and forced Parliament to vote. I put before the House evidence that this is the only, and probably the last, great sale of standing timber in the world. Material was put before the House, stating that every other country---from all of South-east Asia to all the countries in the Americas---has brought in restrictions on the cutting and taking away in log form of their forests. Those nations are major timber producers. The Government has rushed out and said for New Zealand: ``Here are our forests, they're available to be taken away.'' How could the Government do that, when for year after year every other nation, in the interests of its economy and its citizens, has imposed bans and reductions on exporting unprocessed logs? On a grand scale, New Zealand has become the new participant in the field, and soon it will be the only one. The actions that the Bill seeks to authorise are a betrayal of present New Zealanders, and, most disgracefully, of the young and of those New Zealanders yet to come, who do not have a say in the matter and cannot bring the process to a halt if it is incomplete at the next election, months from now. New Zealand's heritage has been flogged off for precious little gain. Opposition members insisted that there ought to be a commitment to replant. The Government said: ``Buyers can replant only if it suits.'' I suggest that the Government, instead of talking about saving the planet, should adopt the enlightened policy that the Opposition commended, and that has been adopted in Europe---that the forest acreage should not be allowed to be reduced, and that if some has to be converted other areas have to be established. The Government contemplates the possibility of a drastic reduction in the forest estate---the greenhouse control---and is happy about that. The Prime Minister takes the platform at the United Nations, and the Minister of Conservation parades here and there yet, while they tell other people what to do, they are prepared to allow a policy that is completely at odds with the interests of the nation and the planet. The Government's direction is not sound. Those key issues have come out of the Bill. Opposition members are concerned that the Bill gives unconstrained powers to lease that are such that the Government can effectively dispose of the land under the forests---which it said it would not do---by giving leases of such long duration that they are, to all intents and purposes, equivalent to a freehold title. That device in the Bill defeats even the Government's policy, and Opposition members attacked that and voted against it as we exposed all of the failings of the Bill. However, none was worse than the way the Bill was introduced, because it denied the public a say in the disposal of its heritage.
