The questions were simple and fair. Mr Elwood described the questions as fair. I can show them to the member. I want to move on to the comments of the people of Kaikoura---and the member for Rangiora will speak on the matter---who have a different view. They did not want to be in with Nelson, and not really with Marlborough either. They were therefore surveyed, and as a region it was their clear wish to join Canterbury. I freely support that action, on the basis of the same argument I used about the reason for Marlbrough being free of Nelson. Indeed, it is even more ridiculous that the people of Kaikoura should be linked with Nelson and Golden Bay. They simply do not have anything to do with Nelson or Golden Bay, and they do not go there in their lives except perhaps for one or two holidays. It is an essential ingredient. The Minister of Conservation, who is the member for Nelson, can speak later. He does not consult his people, but he can speak through a hole in his neck. One of the important aspects of local government is that central government confers on communities the right to manage their own affairs in relation to certain responsibilities. It goes without saying that those who are not affected and who do not have to live with the consequences of their decisions surely do not have the right to impose their decisions on others; and that is a principle that is grossly offended in the case of the imposed joint Nelson/Marlborough region. Let us consider what it would mean. Even in circumstances in which Marlborough-elected representatives out of were of one mind about a proposal that affected solely Marlborough, if the others are not persuaded, perhaps because they have other priorities---and in relation to spending money that is usually the answer---the will of our district can be denied. One only has to state that that is technically possible in order for the unsoundness of the system imposed on us to be revealed. So what is always important in local government is the person who must pay and the place where the money is spent. The people of Marlborough take the view that they should be responsible for their own affairs and that they should pay. They do not want to bludge off anyone else. However, money raised from them should be spent by them. The people in the region do not expect to have imposed on them costs for services that have no impact on them. For example, it is unfair and unreasonable that the people of Nelson City should have to contribute to work such as rabbit control, which is a problem in Marlborough---and the member for Nelson must thank me for that objectivity. It is silly and inefficient for Nelson's affairs to be determined in Blenheim, or vice versa, as there are mountain ranges and gulfs of misunderstanding between us. When I see what has happened already my earlier views have been confirmed. We have now appointed a chief executive on a salary that makes no saving on the amount the previous incumbents earned. People will have to travel distances at great expense, for purposes that did not exist before. They will be put up overnight because of the length of the business they will do. It will cost us all more, and will be for no purpose. The people of Marlborough have no interest in the problems on the Takaka River, nor do the people of Takaka have any interest in the streams that vitally affect the town of Kaikoura, and they should not be wasting time on it. There are no real links that require us to be joined. The mountain barriers mean that soil and water functions are utterly separate. In civil defence our links that break down most often are those with Nelson, and we are least likely to be able to help each other; in maritime planning we have totally separate spheres; and so it goes on. There is no logical basis, and the key issues cannot be overcome. First, the Local Government Commission said that what we seek in the Bill is what should be done; and, second, most people seek it.

I shall support the Bill's referral to a select committee. There are matters in the text of the Bill that will need the careful attention of the select committee and that will almost certainly be changed, but that is not a reason to oppose its introduction. I know that on occasion private members' Bills are ridiculed in the House because of a phrase here and a sentence there. I am not one to indulge in such ridicule, so it is the Bill's concept to which I shall address myself. The proposed commission of inquiry is a concept that the House would do well to take up. It is no easy task that the House is proposing to entrust to a commission of inquiry---to inquire into the effects of dioxin and phenoxy herbicides and any other chemicals to which New Zealand servicemen who fought in the Vietnam War were exposed. I have had some contact with Vietnam veterans, a very small number of whom live in my district. One fine young citizen of Marlborough---a young man from Renwick---lost his life in that conflict. If the House does refer the Bill to a select committee it ought to know that very considerable resources will be required if the commission is finally to resolve the issue or at least to find a basis for resolution of the issue. It has been inquired upon at length elsewhere amongst nations that had servicemen involved in the Vietnam War. Nowhere has there been a satisfactory outcome. I am glad that I am speaking tonight rather than on the evening that debate on the Bill's introduction started, because I have the benefit---and I refer members to it---of this week's Time magazine of July. I do not regard Time magazine as being by any means the last word on everything, but it has shown through the years a willingness to be very critical of the Administration and Government of its own country, and it is therefore entitled to some respect. On page of that issue an article is headlined: ``A Cover-Up on Agent Orange?''. It seems that in a congressional committee authorised an organisation based in Atlanta called the Centers for Disease Control---an apparently prestigious institution---to inquire into the causal linkages between chemicals sprayed in Vietnam and the state of health of American veterans and the condition of some of their children, who appeared to be born with more than a normal number of birth defects. The article indicates---I can put it in no more than those terms---that it appears there may have been a cover-up. There was a religious sticking to apparently scientific principles to deny that it could have been ascertained properly from United States Army records that the Army, to its credit, was willing to make available information about soldiers who were, with a high degree of certainty, in areas that were directly sprayed with the defoliants. The matter has come up again because a former Chief of Naval Operations, Elmo R. Zumwalt, had a son who died of sundry cancers and other disabilities many years after returning from the Vietnam War. The position of Chief of Naval Operations carries a four-star rank---the highest rank in the United States armed forces. By way of an anecdotal reference, Elmo Zumwalt was famous for his ``Z-grams'' when he commanded the United States fleet---everyone jumped to when they turned up. He was not prepared to accept the responses in the way of duck-shoving and buck-passing, and in only the past month the matter has again come before the House of Representatives in the United States. It has been asserted that the person in charge of the investigations that were begun in has been accused in the United States House of Representatives---and that is no mean place to make accusations from, as some of us would know---``made it his mission to manipulate and prevent the true facts from being determined''. That is serious. A New York congressman, the chairman of the panel, charged that the Centers for Disease Control appeared to have ``rigged'' its investigation to support its view that a large study on exposed veterans was not feasible. It was not that evidence about the causal link, which was freely available, was covered up. The inquiry did not even get to deal with that material during a period covering much of a decade. That indicates that the matter has not by any means ended in the United States, despite the creation of a large fund by payment from a chemical company and the subsequent dispersal of that fund, some of which came to New Zealand. Organisations as prestigious as the National Academy of Sciences in the United States have joined the fray and stated that they believe that justice has not been done. The chief representative from the Institute of Medicine---an arm of the National Academy of Sciences, said in Congress: ``My feeling now is that this whole thing deserves another look.''. Without continuing to speak any further about what is happening in the United States Congress---not that we should in any way be influenced by what is happening there---I must say that if there is still that degree of concern, uncertainty, and non-resolution of the matter amongst the servicemen of the nation most affected surely we cannot presume to consider the matter closed in New Zealand, either. Out of fairness to our Vietnam veterans, I think that is owed to them. In setting up a commission of inquiry on Agent Orange we need to be mindful that the people who are appointed to run it will have to travel abroad. It will not be a quick process, and it will not be a cheap one, but those are not reasons for not doing it at all. I strongly identify with that, because New Zealand has had a good record---amongst the best in the world---in ensuring that those who serve in the armed forces are properly taken care of when they return home. However, I fear that for want of proper inquiry we have not served our Vietnam veterans well.

In the years since the tail-width measure was implemented there has been frequent consultation with rock lobster fishers from the southern fishery. The steering committee, which I appointed in to prepare a management plan for the whole fishery, included two industry members representing fishers from all areas. The southern fishery was one of the few fisheries visited by the steering committee. A number of southern fishers availed themselves of the opportunity to make submissions on minimum legal sizes. Staff of my ministry have also been kept informed of their views through liaison committee meetings, and since I have been Minister they have also attended on me personally at length, and I could recite their views by heart if I were allowed the time to do so.

No, many, many times more than that. I have been at some of the meetings, so I know how these groups have worked. There is a huge intimacy to their relationship, because there are not large numbers of them. But--and this is important--these people are fishing. Maori own commercial fishing-boats at work in our area, and those boats have Maori crews on them--just as the member for Eastern Maori would wish, and so would I. But, as part of their agreement that this Bill be allowed to proceed and that there be an enhanced fishery with transferable rights, all their meetings--well-attended meetings, I might add--around the district unanimously came up with an approach that they passed on to me. This approach was: ``Our mandate says, `Bring home the quota so that we can manage it, so that we can see that our people fish it, and so that we directly get all the benefits from it.' ''. That very local concern with their own welfare and their own employment is an approach that, frankly, I commend. I have been able to facilitate the development of this one fishery, without even knowing that there would be some form of Maori settlement.

One does not make an issue out of something just by shouting and winding up members. The Minister of Health cares mightily about these issues. I am well satisfied with what the select committee has brought back to the House in respect of Part II. It is important to understand that fisheries legislation is by nature a statute of use. The standard we are imposing is that anybody---and I am talking about all users---who takes a fish from the sea is required to do so in a way that ensures sustainability of the fisheries. In short, one hopes that by the proper application of these standards our grandchildren will have fisheries that are at least as good as, if not better than, those we have. Our law will stand in stark contrast to that, so I think we have got it right. The recreationists' concerns about utilisation of resources were not well founded. The Bill covers all takers from the sea, so we have to have regard to overall extraction. I move, That the Health and Safety in Employment Amendment Bill be now read a second time. In due course I will move that it be referred to the Labour Committee for consideration. It is a short Bill that has two objects. Firstly, it will ensure that people in control of workplaces, including landowners, will have no duty towards people visiting the workplace for purposes unrelated to the normal work activity, and, secondly, in an unrelated matter, it will allow codes of practices to be used more effectively. One of the principles guiding the development of the Health and Safety in Employment Act was that the Act should provide comprehensive coverage for all work situations. It was decided that legislation should focus on health and safety performance within employment relationships, including contracts for services, and that employers, principals, and contractors would have responsibility to prevent harm to people at work. In turn, people at work would have a duty to work in a way that would not endanger themselves or others. General experience with the Act in the years since it came into force has confirmed that this principle has worked out well in practice. As members will know from their electorate work---if they come from rural and provincial areas---and from news media reports, attention has focused recently on situations where farmers have publicly closed their properties to recreational visitors in order not to incur what they perceive to be liability under the Act. The fear of liability for the possible cost of legal representation and the sheer worry of that has led to more and more landowners reluctantly closing their properties to everyone, despite, in many cases, long-term arrangements allowing people access for all sorts of things---some of those arrangements going back through a number of generations of landowners. Their fear and concern in response is understandable. I can say that as one who comes from a rural background himself. Over the past year a number of recreational groups and Federated Farmers have approached Government about this issue. Following these approaches I convened a consultation process involving farming and a wide range of recreational interests, which in turn fed out to and provided feedback from others. It is from this consultation process that the proposed amendment has developed. The Berryman case---as it has come to be known---also involved publicity about the application of the Act in situations concerning visitors to farms. The case involved a prosecution of a farmer after a beekeeper keeping hives on the farmer's property was killed when a bridge on the farm collapsed. The effect of this amendment would be that, given the absence of employment or a contractual relationship relating to the work of the farm, Mr Berryman could not be prosecuted. In brief, this amendment will ensure that landowners have no duty towards people using the landowners' land for purposes unrelated to the work purpose of the landowner. This will leave the Act to focus on employment relationships and contractual relationships. In other words, requirements of the Act continue to apply to any person in a place of work, including land or buildings, for purposes relating to the work activity of that place. On the other hand, people who enter those places of work for other purposes not relating to the work operation are not covered and the occupier does not have duties under the Act to those people. A second part of this amendment---unrelated to the first---removes an unintended restriction on the use of codes of practice. Section of the principal Act provides for approved codes of practice. Codes of practice may be taken into account by a court in determining whether a person has complied with the Act or regulations made under it. The Act provides for regulations to place duties on designers, manufacturers, and suppliers of plant and clothing used in workplaces. This is where the problem arises, because at present those duties cannot be backed by approved codes of practice. At present the empowering provision in section () of the Act is too restrictive and covers only preferred work practices or arrangements. This excludes preferred practices for the design and manufacture of workplace equipment. This small amendment will allow codes of practice to inform designers, manufacturers, sellers, and suppliers of ways in which they can comply at low cost with their obligations under the Act and regulations. The codes provide an enhanced level of certainty for employers in achieving compliance in differing work situations without resort to prescriptive regulations. This is essentially a technical amendment as the policy intent of codes of practice remains unchanged. Taken together, these two changes will, on the one hand, help clarify the coverage of the Health and Safety in Employment Act and will reduce uncertainty, particularly in relation to non-work activities. On the other hand, it will provide lower-cost approaches to compliance through the wider use of approved codes of practice. With the House's encouragement, I will refer the matter to the Labour Committee.

That was an amazing demonstration of shadow-boxing and slippery-footed nonsense about a Bill that the member obviously has not read or does not understand. The Associate Minister of Health has set out the purpose of this Bill. The Bill has four main purposes. I am more interested in the reasons that we have this Bill at a time when the Ministry of Health is undergoing yet another restructuring. It is being changed from the ministry it is now, with the functions it has, into a policy unit. So it is in the process of shedding functions and roles. The Minister did not reply to an interjection from my colleague who asked why did we not need to have ministry representatives on registration boards anymore. I think that is quite significant. He said there was no need for ministry representation on boards. I would have liked to hear the reason that ministry representation is not needed. What we are really seeing is the Government's commitment to the coalition agreement to change yet again the structure of our health system. We have seen a series of changes in the health system in New Zealand since . If we think back to we will recall that was the time of Sir Alan Danks' report on changing from our old hospital boards to area health boards. It was from his report that we got the legislation of that set up area health boards. It took from to for the old hospital boards finally to become part of an area health board network. It was at a snail-like pace that finally we achieved area health boards in . When we went into the election, both major political parties represented in this House were committed to the structures that were in place, and they were the area health boards. We were committed to giving them the opportunity to bed in, be able to work, and provide adequate, efficient public health services. Unfortunately, in the National Government undertook another round of health restructuring. Between and we saw some of the greatest restructuring in the health system in the history of this country. The previous Minister Mr Upton proudly said that we were doing something that no other country had ever done before. Obviously, we did not know what the results would be either. That has meant that we have gone through some great upheavals in New Zealand. What was it all about? What was the reason for the restructuring that has taken place continuously since to today? We have yet another restructuring on our books. What is it about? According to Mr Upton, it was to provide us with efficient, effective health services and to remove the bureaucracy that had been growing within the health sector. He said that the bloated bureaucracy would go, it would be streamlined, and we would see a health service that would deliver services to New Zealanders. Has that happened? No, it has not. Since we have seen the establishment of a whole new layer of bureaucracy: the four regional health authorities that were established with employees. As of today there are people working within the Transitional Health Authority. There are new staff members at the head office of the new Transitional Health Authority. The Ministry of Health, which had around people working for it then, still has people working for it today. We see the cost of the layers of bureaucracy as a cost to the taxpayers and the patients of New Zealand. The cost of the bureaucracy in health has quadrupled over that same time of reform. We know that the ministry is undergoing restructuring again. This is the first part of yet another restructuring for the ministry. Two hundred and fifty people are to be taken out of the ministry. It is to be made lean and mean, and made into a policy unit. We were told at the select committee that of the who will go from the ministry will end up on other Government boards and bodies somewhere else. The ministry does not expect any redundancies at all. So this Bill is part of the restructuring that is taking place. What has the reaction been from the public and the medical and nursing organisations to this continual change within the health sector? It has generally been hostile, mainly because of the ambiguity of the Government's blueprint. What is, and what was, the long-term plan in health? Was it to make a largely publicly funded heath sector operate more efficiently and effectively, or was it a step-by-step privatisation of health-care funding and provision? The public has decided that it is the latter and not the former. The public judge it on the results, because they see a lack of elective surgery for them over the last few years. They see waiting-lists that numbered , in now number ,. They see changes in funding in which more funding has gone into the private health sector than into the public health sector, particularly our public hospitals. In fact, in the last years there has been a percent reduction in funding going into our public hospitals. This has concerned the people of New Zealand. We have seen that the Government's direction has not really changed, although there have been some cosmetic changes. The Government did abandon its proposal for alternative purchasers---the private health-care plan. But, of course, the ability to do that still remains in the legislation. It has removed the need to make a profit. But the people of New Zealand believe that the direction the Government undertook in health when it started the reforms continues unabated today. There is great concern that the proposed change in this Bill is part of a continuation to take away the responsibility that the Government has had in the past. I will say why that is. This Bill takes away the appointment of Government officials to boards and replaces them with ministerial appointments. So when the Government says that the boards will have greater control and be in charge of their own shops, they will also be required to have a ministerial appointment to their boards. I have to say that we have great doubts about the Minister's ability to provide people to those boards who will be free of political patronage and persuasion. The history of the National Party has been to provide opportunities for its friends and cronies to be appointed to most boards and bodies in New Zealand. As some of my colleagues said, that is something that we did not do when we were in Government. In fact, we were inclined to appoint some of the Opposition's colleagues and cronies. We have seen this Government appoint political cronies. In fact, only last year the Deputy Prime Minister said that Bob Simcock was nothing more than a political hack who was appointed to the board of a Crown health enterprise. He said that before the election. He said that he was concerned about these half-baked political appointees who knew less about health than Johan Le Roux knew about table manners. That was a quotation from Winston Peters. Labour has great concerns that this Government will use the opportunity to give positions to its old, clapped-out politicians who will be without a job in a few more months. I am sure that Paul East is already lining up for a job on the Dental Technicians Board. I am sure he can see an opportunity to get stuck in and bore away on that board. Labour members on the select committee will ask some very important questions about occupational regulations and the accountability that will be provided for the public to ensure that its representation is heard on these boards. We want to see that consistency is provided by this change and that it will maintain quality of service. We want to ensure that the safety issues continue to be addressed in order to protect the quality of the service. These are important issues. Those three criteria will be raised by the Labour members on that select committee. We will be putting it through the hoops to ensure that the public is protected with this change.

I believe that my colleague is right. This is an election ploy. This is a glossy, shiny political manifesto. Every household in New Zealand is to receive a little pamphlet next week---at the taxpayers' expense---outlining the National Party's health policy. That is what this is all about. It is a little political agenda. It has nothing to do with giving certainty and security to New Zealanders. The word ``plan'' is a misnomer. At best, this plan is just an idea. The Minister has not really worked out the detail of his idea. It is a lot of flannel and a lot of fluff. There are some threats in it and there are some vague promises of things that might happen in the future. I have to say to that Minister that I am bitterly disappointed, because I believed that he was better than that. After all, it was the Minister who started the debate. Now he is telling New Zealanders that Opposition politicians go around scaremongering about our hospitals. But I want to remind the House today of just where this debate started. This debate was started by the Minister, who in a statement on March on Morning Report told the people of New Zealand that he envisaged two ``super hospitals'' in New Zealand and that Wellington Hospital was not one of them. He then went on to outline what the layers of hospitals would be. That was in his own words. He started the debate and then he tried to blame everybody else, because they listened to what he said, and said: ``Well, he is the Minister of Health. Perhaps he knows what he is talking about.'' It was backed up by the report on acute services, dated March , which was put out by the Ministry of Health. That report set out the levels of service that we would have in New Zealand, and it identified by area and population where services would not be provided. It was to be part of the hospital plan. The Minister made it clear that it was part of the hospital plan. In April this year, the Health Funding Authority was responsible for a memo that stated that elective surgery ought not to be provided in places like Kaitaia, Whakatane, Blenheim, and Ashburton. That was the genesis of the debate on the hospital plan, which was started by the Minister and is responsible to the Minister. Then he whinges and moans around New Zealand that politicians have picked up his lead and are debating it. I say to the Minister that he cannot do that, because he started the debate and he is responsible for it. No wonder there has been speculation. I predict there will be three more years of speculation. No doubt, at the end of years, if this party is still in Government, its plan will be very much what it was at the beginning of this year. The Minister has given himself a breathing space. He has given himself the opportunity to be able to put in place some of the key elements of that plan. The Minister said in the House today that neither the booking system or the acute services were not part of the plan. I wonder why his own report states that they are part of the plan, and then sets out why that part of the plan is needed to make the hospital plan work. I believe what is written in that plan. The Minister does have to work out where the acute services will be offered. He does have to know where elective surgery will be delivered. Those parts of the plan have not been fully implemented, or even decided. The booking system, a crucial part of a hospital plan, which gives people certainty and security about the provision of elective surgery, has not yet been fully implemented. The Minister said that it would take two more years at least before it is implemented. In the meantime we have to listen constantly to clinicians and health professionals argue and fight over whether the system will even work, whether it is credible, and whether it has the right criteria, and it has not yet been agreed to. The second element of this report is the acute services. Those acute services were really at the heart of the fright that small hospitals around New Zealand got. The ministry said that the small hospitals like Kaitaia, Whakatane, and so on, ought not to be providing -hour-a-day acute services, which was something those hospitals wanted to provided. Unfortunately, the Minister has failed to prepare that part of the plan. It is not in this hospital plan---the grand blueprint for the future. The reason is that it has not yet been finished being presented or developed. The Minister said in a speech a couple of weeks ago that it would take two more years. I have to tell him that there is bad news on the way for him, because the Ministry of Health has just sent an e-mail to me saying: ``No, sorry, it's not going to take years to implement the acute services; it's going to take years.'' It will be years before it can implement a major part of this plan. That is what is wrong with a plan that purports to be a blueprint for the future and that leaves out large elements of what a plan should be all about. In the meantime we have health services in New Zealand that are in chaos. We have health services in New Zealand that are not being adequately funded. Even as the Minister's own plan comes out, we have health services that are disappearing. Today I could not get two answers from him to questions that I asked. I will repeat them, and maybe when he does speak, he would like to answer these questions. Will he guarantee that the Health Funding Authority will retain funding in real terms at the level it is today so that those hospitals that receive funding from the Health Funding Authority can retain their services? Good Health Wanganui, the place he went to announce the hospital plan, went on Midday on television and said that unless the Minister could guarantee that funding is available from the Health Funding Authority at the level it is today, then it does not have certainty and security. When I asked the Minister that question for all hospitals in New Zealand, he could not answer it, or would not answer it, because he cannot answer it. He cannot give that assurance. That means that the people of New Zealand will see some of their services go over the next years. His promise will be shown to be very, very hollow, indeed. The second question I asked the Minister was whether he would guarantee that Darfield Hospital and Rangiora Hospital, the two hospitals that are identified in this report as being part of the hospital plan, and are now under threat of closure, would remain open. He could not give an assurance that that was the case. Where is their certainty? Where is the guarantee that they will retain services? The Minister could not give that assurance. On his own measure the Minister has failed today. On his measure of certainty and security he has failed at least two hospitals, and probably every other hospital in New Zealand, because he could not guarantee that funding will be retained in real terms. In the meantime we have health services that are in chaos. I conclude with one of the most crazy things I have heard in this health system that has been set up by this Government, during my time as a politician. In the last week three mental health patients turned up at ward at Capital Coast Health seeking mental health services, because they were in an acute state. Those patients were issued with trespass orders for years. They are not allowed to go back to the mental health services at Capital Coast Health for years, because they have been issued with trespass orders. The very people who went to the door of a mental health unit wanting services, obviously causing some mayhem and uproar, were given trespass orders to be enforced by the police, not allowing them back into the mental health service for years. Has anyone ever heard anything so heartless? Has anyone ever heard anything so ridiculous? It is an indication that there is something wrong in our health system. This plan will not fix those problems. This plan will not give certainty and security. This plan is nothing more than a political document. It is a piece of flimflam a few months out from an election. I resent, and the people of New Zealand will resent the fact that we are all paying for this political exercise.

Roger Sowry in his contribution asked a question about the definition of rest home care. If frail people are receiving care or support, they are covered by the bill. If they are receiving residential care to promote their independence, they are covered. They are not covered if they are fully independent. Many residents in retirement villages have total independence within that village. They live in their own flats, for example. People who receive care or support, or receive care that promotes their independence, are covered by the bill. They are not covered if they live independently in a village, and do not need any care. That makes sense. We do not want to cover people who do not receive care, but who are living in a village situation because they want to be close to other people. I come now to a couple of issues. Ken Shirley in his previous contribution said that somehow this Government had changed the intent of the bill since we had taken it over. That is absolutely incorrect. Right from the start the bill was outcome based. We have not changed that. It covered public and private situations right from the beginning. We have not changed that, at all. I want to set the member straight, because sometimes words like ``private'' set him off into a frenzy. I do not want him to get it wrong. Part provides definitions to aid the interpretation of the bill. It includes some new definitions---for example, ``Cessation order'', ``Mental health services'', and ``Service standards''. But the most important measure in this part is the new definition of ``health or disability services'', on Supplementary Order Paper . It provides a broader definition, and indicates the type of service that can be covered by the bill. That means it can cover other services in the future that do not at this stage have safety standards. That is a major change. It was not in the original bill. The ability to apply the bill to other services was not part of the bill as reported back under the previous Government. That is one of the changes we have made. That change came from the submissions we received, and I think I am the only person in the Chamber who heard those submissions. There were strong submissions that we should be able to set safety standards for other health sectors, and I am sure Dr Scott would agree. This part enables, by consultation, the setting of other standards. I am sure Dr Hutchison would be interested in that, because it means that in the future standards could be developed for fertility clinics, laboratories, and gynaecological services, for example. We would not set those standards unilaterally or arbitrarily; they would be set by consultation and by working with the sector to get workable standards. That is a very important addition to the bill. I can see that members agree with me that it is a good improvement to the bill since it was brought back to the House. We could argue about how long it has taken. Dr Hutchison said that the bill was going to be implemented in July . I think perhaps he got a little confused, because it was not even reported back to the House until September , under his own Government.

I can hear Government members jeering. They think it is a joke to have all the rubbish of Auckland tipped into south Auckland. It is not good enough. The other problem that south Auckland has is that of a private sewerage scheme in Beachlands. The sewage was to be put into a sewage tank. The problem is that it will now probably have to be put on to a forest at Beachlands. It would cost several million dollars more for people to get their private sewerage scheme. The Manukau City says that the reason for that is that the Maori people will not let the sewage be put into the ponds. At local meetings on the matter people rightly asked why they should have to pay the extra cost of $ million. Why should private ratepayers pay perhaps $ to $ a year more to have their sewage put on to forest because the Maori people will not let it go on to land? If the Treaty of Waitangi is having that effect the scheme should be paid for by the Government, not by private ratepayers. It is bad that such problems should be caused by the treaty. The problem is being opposed strongly by the residents and it should be opposed by New Zealanders. If we are to pay for the treaty the charge should be a Government charge, not a local government one. Parts of south Auckland are becoming wasteland. Do members know that there are vast, empty factories in Takanini, and in Neilson Street? Do they know that last year south Auckland's major employer---the freezing-works---was closed, and that two horse saleyards and one stud farm closed recently because of the unfavourable industrial climate? Those are the results the Government has caused in south Auckland. It is not good enough. I have received many representations about the tariff regime. Every factory in south Auckland has complained that its future would be endangered by the cuts. Thousands of business people have told me that if the cuts come they will close and will import goods rather than manufacture them. That problem applies to the whole of south Auckland. It is wrong of the Government in to make cuts that will take effect in . The Government will not be in office in . It is much too soon to legislate for cuts. No one knows what the climate will be like in . More important things need to be done first. We should be studying the tax regime---the land tax, the capital gains tax, and the unjustified burden of accident compensation on manufacturers. We should also be studying the industrial system, compulsory unionism, and the unjustified changes in site agreements. We should be freeing-up the industrial environment before introducing tariff regimes that will apply in . That is a grave mistake, and already people in south Auckland are worried that they will lose their jobs. I spoke to people in Te Atatu the other day who were equally concerned that their jobs would be in jeopardy. The Government should leave the matter until later. It should be left until the election has been decided. If the Government does have the job of deciding tariffs it should first listen to industry properly. The Government has not consulted properly or listened to the industrial sector. It has not taken note of the wider industrial climate, or listened to consumers. The Government should be listening much more before it reaches a decision. The results of this measure could be catastrophic. Many thousands of people could lose their jobs if it were thought that the cuts would be made. The Customs Department is not suited to carrying out those changes. It has lost of its top people, and it has not consulted on the matter long enough. It should be going into the matter much more thoroughly than it is at present. I see that the Minister of External Relations and Trade is in the House. He knows what the effect will be and that morale in the industry will be lowered. The matter has to be dealt with more thoroughly and with more consultation before those changes take place.

The behaviour of the member for Tauranga was never disgraceful. It was perceptive, diligent, and searching. He was right to question the technical committee, because clearly it was made up of Crown and Treasury officials, with inadequate representation from the Department of Maori Affairs. The committee was advising on policy matters not technical matters. In relation to the visit to Owai marae, day's notice was given to the Maori people in the area. Very few of those who wanted to turn up had the opportunity to do so. They were incensed and angry. It is no wonder that there was dissent at that meeting. The Auckland meeting was supposed to be a marae meeting, but it was held in a gilt room in the Hyatt Kingsgate Hotel, and there was grossly insufficient room. Not everyone could get in or find a seat. The Maori people present were extremely angry, and made that clear. Poor management by the chairman caused that meeting to go wrong. The Bill is important and remarkable. It gives a tribunal the power to review years of history, and to overturn it if it seems right to do so. It has the power to rewrite history. It was important that the Bill should be percent correct. It was important that the rights of the individual should be protected; that there should be equity between Maori, pakeha, the State-owned enterprises, and the Crown. The Bill has not achieved that goal. The State-Owned Enterprises Act was passed without adequate consultation with the Maori people. Maori rights were not given protection, yet in the House the Minister of Justice said that the Maori people were adequately protected. Because the Minister did not protect the Maori people they were compelled to go to the Maori Council and bring proceedings in the High Court and the Court of Appeal. The people of New Zealand should know that the Minister of Justice and the Government opposed the Maori Council in the High Court and the Court of Appeal. The Bill is shot-gun legislation into which the Government has been forced, and it has created an adversarial element in the Act that will cause great harm and great difficulty. The Bill has the capacity to deal with assets worth billions of dollars---for example, assets of the Electricity Corporation worth $ billion. When assets and property of such dimensions are affected there should be a right of appeal, but there is none. That position is inconsistent with the Treaty of Waitangi, which guarantees the Maori people full protection as British subjects. The fact that they have not been given right of appeal is of supreme importance and indicates a lack of concern for their rights. There will be disputes between Maori people. Already there have been disputes between hapu and iwi and between iwi and iwi. The State-owned enterprises could have assets worth billions of dollars confiscated from them, yet have no right of representation before the Waitangi Tribunal. One would have thought that the principle of no confiscation without representation would apply, but it does not. Many other groups could be affected. For instance, Tasman Pulp and Paper Co. has an interest in some of the Forestry Corporation lands, which could revert back to the Maori people without there being a right of representation. Farm lands could be affected. Federated Farmers do not have right of representation. Individuals could be affected, and could have special knowledge. They do not have right of representation. Furthermore, the words of the Treaty of Waitangi Act are vague. The tribunal has to decide whether something is inconsistent with the treaty.

The member for Dunedin West will go west in , because Opposition members have heard the anger in Dunedin. Did she know that DDB Needham New Zealand Ltd was involved in advertising tobacco and liquor before the contract was awarded to Needham Consulting Group? Is it also correct that Carolyn Rennie, a former executive research assistant, was also involved? However, the same firm has been awarded the Department of Health contract. The Government has some explaining to do, and the Opposition invites Government members to explain the matter in the House, if they have not done so already. The Government has a habit of condoning corruption. The Electoral Expenses Bill was introduced to condone Reg Boorman, who spent more than $, too much during the election campaign.

The Minister of Regional Development said that the objective of the Bill was to let the Crown import medicines and to achieve fiscal goals. It is clear that the Government has cheated on the international conventions to which New Zealand was a signatory in order to achieve its goals. It has acted dishonourably. The Minister of Health was the person responsible for the legislation. This legislation introduced by the Minister of Commerce, not the Minister of Health, is an attempt to save face. The Minister of Health has been embarrassed internationally and throughout New Zealand because of the dishonourable way the Government has proceeded with the legislation. The Minister of Regional Development claimed that the Government was big enough to correct the Bill. What he means is that the Government made a monumental boob in the Importation of Medicines Bill and now it is trying to retreat. The Government claimed in the Budget that it would save $ million or $ million in the Health vote. Where is that $ million or $ million coming from? Is it through the reduction of patient services, and increases in the operating-lists? The Bill is a dishonourable measure. At the select committee it was opposed unanimously by the patent attorneys, the research medicines industry, the Importers Institute, the Pharmaceutical Society of New Zealand and the Pharmacy Guild of New Zealand, Glaxo New Zealand Ltd, and Professor Parker. They said that the Bill was bad for New Zealand, that it was making New Zealand despised internationally, and that it would not save the country much money. They also said that the Bill would allow the Government an unfair advantage over private industry because the Government did not have to submit itself to the checks and balances that private industry has to undergo when it imports medicine. That is what the select committee was told. Professor Parker said that the new legislation does not comply with international conventions such as the Berne convention, or with the GATT requirements, and that it is defective. In those circumstances the Government, in order to save the face of the Minister of Health, is still ramming the legislation ahead. Professor Parker has also said that that could have damaging effects on New Zealand. He said that he could not imagine a more damaging signal to the rest of the world, and that the Government could suffer internationally. Members were told that it could prejudice the current round of GATT talks---perhaps not openly, but by the unwritten acknowledgment that New Zealand has behaved badly in connection with the Importation of Medicines Bill and should not be given full credibility in the GATT talks. Therefore the Bill could have harmful effects in the wider context. New Zealand is acting in the same way as East Germany, Russia, and other similar countries that are willing to take advantage of the life-saving drugs provided by companies but are not willing to pay the price or to carry out the correct tests. That is not good for New Zealand. New Zealand is regarded as the cowboy of the GATT round in relation to the importation and distribution of medicines, and is getting a bad name. Many of the defects that were pointed out in the select committee remain. The Bill continues to exempt the Department of Health from most requirements to ensure the safety of medicines. The safety of New Zealanders and the confidence of doctors in prescribed drugs are not ensured. There is no requirement that imported medicines have to be registered in New Zealand under a system of registration with consent procedures. There is no requirement that imported medicines should be the equivalent of medicines overseas. In other words, the standards may not be as high. No mechanism exists to show that medicines imported by the Government are the equivalent of registered medicines in either the country of origin or New Zealand. The legislation enables New Zealand to set lower standards, and that means lower standards for the public. I believe that the Bill is not correctly drawn up. It still has holes in it, and the Opposition is worried that it will have a bad effect on health. Opposition members are concerned that New Zealand's reputation will suffer internationally if it does not abide by international conventions.

I welcome the third reading of this Bill. I commend the Ministers concerned and Cabinet for bringing this Bill, which separates the commercial arm of Radio New Zealand and eventually will lead to its sale, but also preserves a strong position for National Radio---that is, the Concert FM programme and the National Radio programme---for the future. These are two very important moves, and I am sure we all welcome these. It was a very necessary thing for commercial radio, which has a fragile balance sheet, to be separated off and to be sold. We should not be funding radio stations that are in a dangerous financial position in a very competitive market. It was mentioned that this Bill was all the result of the actions of the member for Palmerston North. I have to say that there is an element of truth in that, because he did prepare the charter that was adopted. But, of course, when the Bill was introduced into the House the then Minister who represented the Government, the member for North Shore, said that he invited the select committee to look at ways of protecting public radio. The select committee did what the Minister invited, because all members in this House want to see independent and quality National Radio programmes. The legislation ensures that that is what they will get. I commend the Government for some of the clauses and for some of the matters contained in this Bill to protect public radio. First of all is the minimal level of funding of $. million, which is guaranteed to June . This has been guaranteed by a direction of the Minister, and National Radio is now assured as it has never been before of funding. That will give it an assured base on which it can be confident in its production of quality programmes. There is the charter that has, of course, been put into statute and which gives great autonomy to National Radio to provide for intellectual, scientific, and cultural development, a range of New Zealand programmes, and varied interests---all those good things that we would want to hear. I made a criticism that perhaps it is a little bit too elitist and perhaps it is not populist enough, appealing to a small percentage of the population. But, nevertheless, I would not disagree with the select committee. It has given its consideration and the Government will certainly go along with the charter as reported back from the select committee. But the charter adds great independence to this programme. It means that the people who run it can be confident that they have got independence and integrity and that they will not be interfered with by any future Government that might possibly want to do so. The environment is now stable and secure. The promise not to sell shares except to another Minister gives us some assurance that National Radio will stay in Government hands. Clause A, which requires that the constitution be laid before the House, is again protection, because the public can see it is a patently open process. The appointment of the governors by the Governor-General and the description of the people who have to be appointed is also a protection that we will get quality people with skills and integrity. The words ``skills, knowledge, diverse range of views, and not representing particular interest groups'' are what the Bill refers to in the appointment of the governors. Clause entrenches the editorial independence that is already enjoyed. Again that is important, I believe, if we are going to have integrity in our radio and fair, equitable, and reasonable views coming across. Also, the Audit Office is given the important position of being the auditor. That, too, will protect the public in the programming, the value for money, the way the station is run, and in seeing that it follows the terms of the charter. I think that all the important matters are covered in this Bill, which is remarkably comprehensive. I think the assurance of capital in particular will be welcomed. There is also protection for the Maori language with Te Reo o Aotearoa. The Pacific Island unit will also be protected. I am sure the public will welcome those particular provisions. As to commercial radio, it is indeed an important step that it should be sold. For the first two month-periods in operation it was making a profit. Then we had three very serious loss years. Commercial radio could not compete with the other, at that time, fewer than stations. The Government strongly believes that it should not be running a station that is competing with private radio. It is the wrong culture that the public service should run commercial radio. After all, it purchased X, a station that lost $. million in little over year. It lost a lot of money. That is why commercial radio should not be run by a Government station. We welcome this separation of commercial radio and public radio. We think that commercial radio is now being run in the right environment. We believe it will compete well. We think it will be bought by people with the capital and the ability to run it, but it will not be a liability on the public. There is no reason that the public should run it.

I would like to commend the executive and staff of Radio New Zealand for improving a very adverse financial situation and making some sense of what was an awful mess. I want to congratulate them and the directors on the work they have done. They certainly pulled around a total loss-making company. They were given an awful legacy. I believe they are starting to do something about it, and I commend them for that. I would also agree with the member for New Lynn about the quality of National Radio and Concert FM. I sometimes do not like some of the news programmes---at times commentary takes over from objective news reporting---but I believe that on the whole National Radio does a good job. I commend them for that. I think Sharon Crosbie has improved things since she has taken over. I would like to mention the problems that Radio New Zealand has overcome in the past couple of years. Over years it had accumulated losses of $ million--- years of loss making under a Labour Government. The station has turned round and coped with these problems. It had losses year after year after year for years running, and for the past half year, in , it finally made a profit of $. million---a first. I believe that we should commend Radio New Zealand for that excellent result. It shows that the appointments made by this Government have worked out very well in making an efficient radio station out of something that, commercially, had not been particularly efficient. I have some sympathy, and I think I agree, with the belief of the chief executive that at some stage the commercial side of this network---Radio New Zealand---should be sold. It is doing a job that private enterprise can do. It is competing with over other stations in an area that totally depends on ratings and popularity. It is rather like President Bush---one year one can be the most popular President ever, and the next year, the most unpopular. In this area one is dealing with ratings, and I believe that at some stage it may make good commercial sense to sell the commercial section of Radio New Zealand. It is hard to see the objective of a Government keeping that station. When one is selling words and selling images, one is in a dicey situation, and risk minimisation principles of government should recognise that. I would like to commend Radio New Zealand for the moves it has taken to get rid of a great many surplus properties, the problem of overstaffing when it was taken over, and lots of redundant equipment. I think it has coped with these matters very well. Some decisions in the past were not good, but this seems to have been tidied up. Its FM radio station was a disaster. It should never have been in it; I am glad it is out of it. Perhaps, to a lesser degree, the same applies to the other commercial parts of Radio New Zealand. I do disagree with the statements made by the two members who asked for increases in the public broadcasting fee. I think Radio New Zealand gets $ million a year from the public broadcasting fee---

First of all, I want to reply to a comment made by a member of the Opposition. The comment related to a letter dated May, , written by Mr McDonald to the Minister, which stated: ``Myself and the other board members held the personal view that it was in the best interests of the shareholders that the company be sold at this time.'' I want to assure the House that the directors and the chairman have always been in favour of this particular sale. It is a non-issue to suggest that there was no agreement or that there was unwillingness on the part of the directors. They were at all times willing, and it is wrong to suggest that they were ever unwilling. Secondly, although GCS is a competitive company now---it had a strong balance sheet in ----it is in one of the most unpredictable, most competitive industries of all; one in which it could either gain business or lose business. It is the function of a Government to minimise the risk to the Crown. If a Government keeps a business that is in a very competitive world, that business could lose or it could win. If it loses the taxpayer loses at the end of the day, because it is a State-owned company. Therefore the Government should not be in this highly competitive industry.

I thought that was a most fascinating speech. I was really interested to learn about Negroponte switches, and I was wondering where I might be able to get one of them. In the time left this evening, I would like to express my extreme regret that the select committee has removed the mandatory reporting provisions from this Bill, and I will certainly be supporting an amendment to bring those provisions back. Failing that, I will be supporting the amendment from the member for Onehunga. My only objection to that is that the age limit is . I would like to see it an older age, because I believe there are people between years of age and years of age who do need protection, who are vulnerable. I want to signal that in the short time available. I welcome some aspects of this Bill, such as the welfare of the child being paramount. I welcome other matters such as recognition of the need for more education. I welcome those provisions but I cannot agree with the deletion of the mandatory reporting provisions, which I believe are important. I think that if one is going to make the welfare of the child paramount it is important that children should be protected, and I believe that the mandatory reporting procedures are necessary for that. After all, we live in a country that has family-inflicted homicides of children a year, and, I think, , cases of physical abuse a year. Our record is not good. Such desperate matters require desperate remedies. I think it is important that cases of abuse should be reported so that something can be done. If abuse is not known about it cannot be dealt with. If responsible agencies are not made responsible nothing may happen. It is by mandatory reporting that something must be done. Without it there will be many cases that fall between the cracks. One sees child abuse cases escalating, perhaps starting with a small slap, then a hit, then perhaps a broken limb, then perhaps brain damage, and finally perhaps death. Intervention at an early stage may be able to stop that. If a young girl is being raped it will leave scars for the rest of her life, but if one intervenes early the damage will be less. I believe that it is abhorrent to most New Zealanders that professional people know of these abuses and are not taking responsible steps to report it and see that something is done. It will be an indictment on this Parliament if we do not bring in mandatory reporting. If, because of this, cases of abuse occur---as they will---it will be an indictment on this House. We should bring in some form of mandatory reporting. In saying this I know I will probably disagree with many of my colleagues, but I feel the matter is important enough to disagree on this particular point. I think it is the duty of this Parliament to protect our young children between the age of day and years. Much concern was expressed that this could in some way be interfering with the iwi or the whanau. That is not so. If mandatory reporting occurs, the iwi and the whanau can deal with these cases before they get too serious. Failure to report might lead to a death or someone being hospitalised and perhaps the child being removed from the family. The original Bill enables early intervention, and that is why I favour mandatory reporting and those provisions that were removed. I am concerned that the Mason report---the ministerial inquiry---was rejected in respect of reporting. This was a responsible and objective report, and I think it is a very serious matter that the House has rejected the Mason report. I also believe perhaps most of the main organisations dealing with abuse---such as the Plunket Society, the New Zealand Educational Institute, and the Commissioner for Children---have come out in favour of mandatory reporting, and I am concerned that this Parliament is not going to support mandatory reporting. So I will be supporting the original provisions, and, failing that, I will be supporting what the member for Onehunga brings in as an amendment. I want to say that these are not red-necked provisions at all. They are very conservative. They apply only to professionals in serious professions---psychologists, doctors, people in education. Only the most serious of professionals---people who should be able to make objective judgments---are involved. That is unlike most other countries that have brought in this mandatory reporting law. Secondly, it requires a report to a social worker or a member of the police. It can be dealt with in a sensitive way and might not involve legal intervention by the police or the courts at all. I think the legislation is extremely responsible in that way. It applies only to the most serious cases of abuse---minor cases are not dealt with. I do not believe that we can leave this matter as an option. We have to give a clear message to professionals. We should not leave it to their discretion. Debate interrupted.

The member opposite said it all when he said that the Labour Party was in favour of competition, and that all we needed was laws against cross-subsidies. Successive Governments in New Zealand have been trying to delete cross-subsidisation for years. The fact is that we cannot do it. It requires lengthy court trials, regulation, and boards to control it. At the end of the day, when we try to have laws like that we end up with more controls than we have at the moment. The reason that we do not have laws like that is they are not very enforceable, at all. He also said that the analysis was incomplete. Mr Hodgson might have judged that, but the select committee has not heard the evidence yet, so I do not know how he can judge that sort of thing when he knows very little about the Bill yet. The select committee will report the Bill back by June, and it will do a thorough job. It will get submissions in the usual way. It will listen to the submissions and consider them. It would be naive for the Opposition to ignore the fact that it is a confidence matter. Whenever confidence legislation comes in, it is the duty of Government members to pass that sort of legislation--as well the Opposition knows. When Labour was in power it did it too, so Labour members should not express this sort of mock surprise at that. This is parallel with other Budget legislation--lower prices through the removal of prohibition on parallel importing, and because tariffs are off. This lowers prices for consumers. The idea behind this legislation is to lower the cost of electricity for people, for workers, for widows, for children, and for businesses. They will be able to get cheaper electricity because of this Bill. We might now have cheap electricity for businesses, but if we have true competition the cost of energy for businesses will be lower and they will become more internationally competitive. That is the compulsion for this legislation. That is the need for the urgency. This legislation will allow domestic consumers and our businesses to get cheaper power so that we can be more competitive internationally. Debate interrupted. Sitting suspended from p.m. to p.m.

Although I have not had the opportunity to discuss this with Muriel Newman, it appears to me that there is much good sense in what she says. We all subscribe to various things, such as telephones and electoral rolls. Our names are always included unless we opt out. The very reason for people going on the register is so they can communicate with other people. They are there because they want other people to get in touch with them and because they want to get in touch with other people. It seems to me that there is merit in the view that unless someone wants to opt out, then they should be included. I believe that there would be less than percent of people who would want to opt out from having themselves made available in this way. We may well find, as always happens with these forms, that many people will not bother to fill in the forms, and the registrar will have enormous problems chasing up people. It would be much simpler, much more streamlined, much more logical, and much cheaper to have an opt-out position. It makes good sense. I do not think we should be making legislation just to suit the rare exception of people who want to opt out. If they do want to opt out, then all they have to do is do so, just as they do with the telephone book and the electoral roll.

As I have said about every part of this bill, I am looking for something that will help us in this current crisis. This is a bill to help the industry. There is nothing for families, nothing for M~aori, nothing for Pacific Islanders, nothing for businesses---there is nothing here that will help. It enables mirror trusts to be set up, and allows renewable renewables, but these are relatively small issues in the magnitude of things. It is amusing to hear the Minister of Energy. We know that whenever he gets up he is going to say how bad Max Bradford was. He never stops saying that. Now he is getting into Doug Kidd and saying what a lousy Minister Doug Kidd was. I remind that Minister that Doug Kidd separated Transpower, separated Contact Energy, and set up the wholesale market. Before that Minister starts criticising other Ministers he should look in the mirror first, because we have this crisis now, and as reported in the Evening Post tonight people are blaming the Minister, because he, perhaps with Helen Clark, stopped the legislation from coming in. It would have made all of this unnecessary. It would have sorted the lines companies out from the industry, and perhaps allowed it to get on with tackling this crisis, which revolves round the generating companies. That is the problem we have today. This bill perhaps does something to help generation in that we can set up renewable renewables. Then again, that is due to our friend Jeanette Fitzsimons, who no doubt did more than anyone else to reduce the fixed charges and harm families. Now it is Jeanette Fitzsimons with the renewable renewables. It seems that the only ideas really come from Jeanette Fitzsimons. But I have to say that will not do anything to increase greatly the generating capacity of this country. There is nothing here to help that at present. The Minister shows his bias against other sorts of fuels, when perhaps he needs to think about how this country can gain more generating capacity. This bill is really just Green legislation that does not help very much. I do not think the mirror trusts will do any great harm; perhaps they will not do any good. That provision is a damp squib because the power companies have shown in the past how little they think of mirror trusts. In a way it is a distortion, because allowing businesses to build renewable energy sources and not fossil fuel generation distorts the need, and discriminates against certain sorts of energy. I would suggest that the Minister would do better to address himself to gaining increased capacity for generators generally. I would like the Minister---and we have been asking him this all day---to tell us what he will do to cope with the present problems. He is having a conference. He should have dealt with the matters beforehand. We have seen no leadership from him as to how he will deal with the current crisis. Will he bring in some sort of rationing, or is he looking at alternative means of generation? What is he going to do? Once more, we are disappointed that there is nothing here to help the energy industry in the present crisis.

Dr Cullen says that he is High Church. I very much doubt it. Perhaps he is Low Church like myself; I do not know. Perhaps he is ``No Church''. But that is pretty irrelevant. I believe that this industry can add value to New Zealand. It is an honourable manufacturing industry that is carried out in some of the most environmentally conscious countries in the world, like Sweden and Britain. In Germany, mining is carried on today under some ancient villages visited by tourists. That would not be allowed in New Zealand, because there is a particular mindset here that is carried to extremes. This is a negative bill that will stop encouraging future mining, will stop encouraging exploration, and is likely to end the industry. We will have a very close look at it at the Commerce Committee. I am afraid that the Government does not appreciate the ability of this industry to help develop New Zealand. I oppose this new form of Calvinism. I do not know who the Government is trying to help. Obviously, the Greens have run away from the Labour Party, and I do not think New Zealand First will support the Government on this bill. We will find out if a New Zealand First member takes a speech. I will be very interested to find out, if any New Zealand First member does take a speech. The Government should examine the industry closely, because it does have potential. The Government is quite happy to sell oil rights, to sell coal overseas, and to use coal in power stations, but this bill will stop exploration and stop mining. It is totally negative legislation. The Government should not have brought it in under urgency. That was not necessary. The Government has had years to bring in this bill; presumably, it will have another year in office. One wonders about the agenda. I would say that the Government brought it in under urgency because it is a grab at private property rights that the Government does not want to be exposed to the public---just like the other shonky legislation we have had in the last years. Many mining rights and much mining land are owned by M~aori people. The M~aori members should look at their own estates, at M~aori land, and see whether this legislation will enhance M~aori development. I say it will be totally negative to M~aori development. This Government professes to close the gaps; this legislation will increase the gaps. This is pretty bad legislation. We will try to improve it in the select committee. I hope that when Government members look at the legislation fully they will decide not to be so Calvinistic, not to have a mindset against mining, and that they will look at mining with an open mind, and look at the contribution it can make.

I have not had the benefit of being on either of the select committees that considered the bill, so perhaps I am able to stand apart and look at this a bit more objectively. Maybe it was good not to be on either of the committees. I understand that the bill was sent to the wrong committee initially---the Government Administration Committee. It coped with difficulty, and found it had days to call for submissions, and was expected to report back very urgently. Happily, it has a : membership, so in the end the Government members were rolled. The Government had to extend the time for hearing submissions. As a result, we have a bill that the Opposition can almost, but not quite, live with. In respect of legal aid, there appears to be different outcomes, depending on whether legal aid is granted. Mr Prebble has just decried the fact that people granted legal aid seem to be dealt with differently from people who are not granted legal aid. I would like the Minister to say whether it is true that those getting legal aid achieve a better outcome. Our law is based on the rule of law, and the contributions of Montesquieu---one law for all people, applied equally. If those who are getting legal aid are treated differently, that would seem to be contrary to our democratic principles. It would be unfair and unreasonable. If we treat people unequally before the law, we end up with apartheid of sorts. We would not want that. This bill seems to treat people differently if they are from the poorest and most deprived sections of our community, and I wonder why the Minister did that. I would like an explanation. Does he believe he is breaching the principles of democracy? It is a convention of our constitution that all people should be treated equally. I am also concerned to hear that, because of cultural differences, matters are being heard differently. It would seem that all people are entitled to the same hearing, regardless of cultural, religious, ethnic, or any other differences. To do otherwise would seem to be a bit of an outcry, and the Minister should explain why that is the case. Why are people who are granted legal aid treated differently in a hearing? Why are people from different cultures and different backgrounds treated differently? That sort of practice will be the cause of great concern and discord. I know some Court of Appeal judges, and I know they are inundated with appeals. Often a prisoner, who has had a High Court decision go against him---and does not have much to do in prison---will appeal, regardless of whether he has the right to appeal, and regardless of counsel. That can involve hours of work by the Court of Appeal on a matter that really has no legal issue, or substantial issue at hearing. Instead of the highest judges in the land being devoted to the most important aspects of these hearings, they are having to waste their time looking at papers that have no merit. The judges are grossly overworked, and we do need some sort of filtering system. So I am pleased to see this provision. The bill as introduced was a disappointment. It was ill-thought-out. I am pleased with the contribution made by the parliamentary select committees, because now all the relevant material from the trial has to be put before the judges. I understand that that was not so before. There have to be safeguards so that an appellant is advised of the mode of hearing, and given time to make a submission. Members may not be aware that that provision was not in the bill as introduced. The bill now confirms the rights of individuals to apply for exercise of the royal prerogative of mercy. It establishes a specific judicial process whereby people are able to seek redress. Those provisions add somewhat to the bill. I believe it is fortunate that in the end we had an alert select committee dealing with the matter. It is not often that I pay tribute to Government members on a committee, but I believe that one of those members made a good contribution, and I commend the member. Really, this shows that Parliament has been fixing the botch-ups made by the Government and the Minister responsible. I believe we should be grateful for that work.
