I do not share the confidence of the member for East Coast Bays. First, I want to deal with the issue of the democratic or antidemocratic aspects of the Bill. For a long time there has been a peculiar partnership between central government and local people in respect of the provision of hospital services. That partnership was characterised by a very peculiar generosity on the part of central government. It allowed local people the power to determine the nature of services in the area consistent with the funding allocations they received. Essentially the Government, from its central budget, paid for the administration of hospital services in a particular region, and the hospital board, as it was known then, determined how that money was to be applied. That, in a time of growing prosperity, seemed to be an appropriate way to deal with matters. It was also accompanied by the fact that in those days there was not the hugely voracious capital demand for high technology medical and surgical treatment, so that there was an easy balance in the relationship. Central government did not feel oppressed, local communities felt as though they were getting their money's worth, and the presence of medical services in their area was seen as very reassuring. Then, with the pressures of capital expenditure and high-quality provisions of medical care, increasing longevity, and the much more complex procedures within the hospital structure, there came to be the extraordinary tensions we saw. Both parties saw the challenge and both parties tried to meet it. There was a remarkable coincidence of conviction on the part of both parties that this could best be served by having a more integrated system of delivery of health care with a better focus on prevention and primary health care, and trying to move the first line of defence against illness into the community itself. That was the challenge that the health boards took up. There was then the development that central government felt that a better relationship with those involved in health expenditure would occur if the Government were not the exclusive paymaster, but it had some say in the deliberations about the way in which the services would be delivered. So a procedure existed whereby central government reserved the right to make appointments to area health boards, but there was a continuing local democratically elected representation on the health boards. When that came face to face with the exigencies of Government expenditure and cut-backs, and a rationalisation process was begun to try to match the needs against the available expenditure, those tensions proved to be too much in the case of some boards. It is correct that the former Minister of Health moved in respect of the Auckland Area Health Board to see that the management of those funds was taken over for an interim period, and we were able to see, and were pleased to see, the restoration of the normally constituted area health board in Auckland within the time of the previous Government. The other night there was a move by the Government to take over health administration completely by the structure set out in the Bill. It reserved unto itself, by the power of appointing commissioners to area health boards, the right to determine who would be responsible for the administration, and, indeed, the formulation of policy in respect of health services in the particular area health board district. It set up a system of regional supply contract people that removed it even further from the small hospital, the remote provincial area, or wherever the health services were to be delivered. Clearly that is a taking up by the State of the right of total determination of health/hospital provision, which is apparently to be justified on the grounds that the Government pays the lot, and therefore if one pays one is entitled to determine how it will be expended. That is alien to the way in which the health services have operated. The effect of it, apart from being antidemocratic, is to render the small community in the provincial town totally at the mercy of those who ration the funds. If that argument is extended there is no doubt at all that members of Parliament need not be here. If a couple of people have the right to determine the allocation of funds and the policy we need not be here beating our gums against the reality of the fait accompli of the Government's strategy. That is the argument we have just heard from the member for East Coast Bays. It is better, he said, that the local people do not have an input because someone else, somewhere else, knows better. It is better, he said, that we do not have an area health board because some have mucked it up. It is better to have it all in the hands of central government so that it can be mucked up totally! That is the most extraordinary logic to emerge from the member for East Coast Bays for some time. If we couple that with extraordinary statements made by people such as the member for Timaru, the Minister of Employment, who was very much in the forefront against the amalgamation of the hospital boards of Timaru, South Canterbury, and Canterbury; and when we think about the member for Fendalton---now the Minister of Commerce---who said that it would be Hitlerite to appoint Government representatives on hospital boards; and when one considers the member for Albany---now the Deputy Prime Minister---who said in Opposition that there would not be any alterations to area health boards if he were in Government; and when in the middle of the night people hear that they have just been sacked and that other people have been appointed, it seems that the rarified atmosphere of the Government benches concentrates the mind so wonderfully that Government members are able not only to forget every promise that they made but they are also able to embark upon a completely manic, lustful grab so that they can dictate what will happen about the provision of health services. I want to look at another example up north: the member for Bay of Islands represents an electorate that has within it the Rawene hospital and the Hokianga special medical scheme. My father was the acting medical superintendent there in . He relieved G. M. Smith, who took months off to establish the Social Credit Political League, and, notwithstanding those peculiar antecedents in the management of that hospital, it is a good hospital. It is a cosy hospital. It is not really a totally sterilised atmosphere; that adds to some of its charm. It has a kind of ``barefoot doctor'' approach to some parts of its provision of health care but it has one undeniable virtue---that is, one can go along there, as Winston McCarthy used to do when he retired from rugby commentating---present oneself at the hospital, or get the doctor to come, and not pay a cent. One could be rich, one could be poor, but one would be treated the same---the bill would be the same---nothing. That hospital is also the major employer in the whole of the old Hokianga County area. The people there had some mad ideas a few years ago: they decided that people in the Hokianga area could not wash sheets. A Bedford truck used to come up every day from Whangarei, take the sheets away, and bring them back the next day, washed. That is the kind of absurdity that seemed to plague the hospital administrations of those days. But the truth was, and is, that that hospital is pivotal to the community in Rawene. Rawene has lost its court; it is going to lose its PostBank facility. It is a community that exists on the fringes of New Zealand society. Under the provisions---the totally rational provisions---of this kind of planned, technocratic, remote, bureaucratic control, that hospital is absolutely doomed. Those who work there will flick their customers through to Whangarei. Will they flick them through to Bay hospital in Kawakawa? I am certain that they will not. On strictly rational grounds one cannot justify a hospital in Kawakawa. It could be knocked off for a street kids' shop. Will the hospital in Kaeo continue? Why would it continue when there is a policy established of flicking people through to a centralised institution? The hospital in Dargaville must be an absolute goner. It takes people a shorter time to get to Whangarei hospital from Dargaville than it does to get from Papatoetoe to Auckland hospital. If we look at the provision of health care from a purely technocratic, bureaucratic approach, that hospital is dog-tucker, but the point is that those hospitals are there because the people in those communities value them. They were extraordinarily cheap; they actually are still cheap. Some of them, I have to confess, are like non-stop project employment programme schemes of the kind that the member for Hawke's Bay is in favour of, but they did have an employing function. There is no doubt about that. But why should the people of Rawene or Tokoroa--- I ask the member for Tongariro whether he thinks that some remote bureaucrat, through the regional funding structure, will keep his hospital in clover. The Bill is a totally undemocratic approach to health care. I say to the member for Bay of Islands that if this scheme goes ahead his hospital at Rawene will not be there.

This is not the first notice of a general election to which I have been privy. There was an occasion previously when one was announced like this one---before the due date---with rather disastrous consequences for the National Government that called it. There is, however, a fortunate break from precedent---it has been called during daylight hours, and with a Prime Minister in reasonably well scrubbed up shape. But it is, I think, notable that not all the members of the National Party are given great confidence with that announcement. I see my friend John Falloon coming back into the Chamber. He will not wait for the result. He, like me, knows what will happen to us after the election is called, and I cannot wait for it---I cannot get there soon enough. If they were great people of principle as they say they are, they would have the election before June when they have their superannuation birthday. But no, no turkeys will be voting for an early Christmas; they will wait for a Passover festival. The fact is that this election will take place at a time when the Government has run its course. I want, from my personal perspective, to tell the House what it is like when a Government knows that it has run its course. It is a terminal condition---like pernicious anaemia. It gets a hold and nothing comes right, after a while. It can be seen in this Government. Bits and pieces happen, wheels fall off, defections happen---members going to some outfit called ``Untied New Zealand'' over there. Then they decide that they are going to go---Bruce Cliffe is jumping off it; Margaret Austin is reviving various acquaintances and relatives in a vigorous campaign to get out. She will go. I hope she does---and I hope her husband campaigns too. It cannot do opponents anything but good. Then we have Peter Dunne, who says that United New Zealand is a party for ordinary New Zealanders. Well, I say that Clive Matthewson made sure an ordinary New Zealander got a job there---in Cabinet. That is the third party he has been in, in the course of year. ``Cosmic Clive'' says that United New Zealand stands for stability. Peter Dunne has been in three parties in years, and professes stability and principle all the way through. They are done. The National Party is, of course, now reaching that accident-prone phase. When Ministers start sending out memoranda with their letters, disclaiming they have got them, that is time to realise that they have come to the end of the line. When I was Prime Minister the foreign affairs people would send me off around the world and would tell me what questions to ask and would also give me presents to give out. We used to give out greenstone clubs and little maps of New Zealand, and badges and things. This Prime Minister went off to Japan to lecture Japan about how to run its economy when it had a record surplus, at a time when he had a record deficit. Then he went off to Korea to present the Koreans with a gift-wrapped diplomat. It is absolutely extraordinary. While he is doing that, it shows that the whole thing just simply comes adrift. The public of New Zealand is getting that feeling quite simply. The Deputy Prime Minister referred to an article I wrote for the New Statesman---he actually said I wrote it for the Dominion. I wrote for the Dominion for money; I wrote for the New Statesman for nothing, and I think that sometimes that is about the merit of its payment. However, the truth is that that article said that if one looks at New Zealand First, the Alliance, and Labour, we will not get a coherent Government from that lot. I say that we will not. That was not a slip, that was not a revelation, that was a fact. A Government cannot be forged out of three completely disparate groupings, each with a different philosophy. In that sense I join that other distinguished columnist from the Dominion who has made a speech---that some people may have even understood---that said the same thing. I say to this party, to this House, and to the public, that we will not get out of that grouping of people---according to what they articulate now---a coherent Government. That leaves the Labour Party to win the election, which on present odds is not readily achievable---but give us weeks, and we would then be the major party within the Opposition. It is then perfectly feasible to form a minority Government. I can tell the House that a minority Government formation would work under the MMP system. It would work because a lot of people would have just scraped in, and they would be terrified at the thought of another election.

I move, That leave be given to introduce the Broadcasting (Complaints) Bill. Whilst a complaints procedure has been in place for many years in respect of both radio and television broadcasting, there is general agreement that members of the public do not understand the current procedures, and, if they do, they desist from furthering their complaints because of the very lengthy time factor. I first encountered this situation some time ago when two constituents informed me that they did their best to lodge complaints about a television programme, but finally gave up---beaten, they say, by the lengthy time factor and probably by their personal lack of understanding of what to do. The Bill before the House, therefore, seeks to make the following changes. It reduces the time for the complainant to lodge a complaint from the present working-days to working-days. It limits the television or radio broadcaster to respond in working-days instead of the present working-days provided for in the Act. It calls upon the Broadcasting Standards Authority, which can receive complaints if the complainant is not satisfied with the response of the radio or television broadcaster. It restricts the Broadcasting Standards Authority to a limit of working-days---no limit exists at all at the moment. The Internal Affairs and Local Government Committee is still addressing the matter of violence on television. Groups such as the Mental Health Foundation, the National Council of Women, Play for Life New Zealand, and MediaAware say that the complaints procedure is too complex. The complaints procedure should be better publicised and explained. It is also too long and drawn out. All these organisations felt that the Broadcasting Standards Authority was not taking an active enough part in dealing with and monitoring complaints. They stated that the authority should be required to inform the public about its specific role, to inform the public about codes of broadcasting practice, and to inform the public about the broadcasting complaints procedure. Particular concern was expressed regarding the procedure that applies to the so-called classification of complaints. Most people have an expectation that when they telephone a radio or television broadcaster their complaint will be handled, so to speak, as a formal complaint. However, there is a definition. People are not aware that there is a formal and informal complaints system---in other words, a telephone call does not constitute a formal complaint. Therefore the broadcaster may elect, essentially, how to respond to that call. In most cases broadcasters respond satisfactorily, but essentially the complaint remains classified as informal. However, people who have made a complaint, and obviously have had some concern and have gone to some length of action to do so, immediately feel they have not been listened to or responded to correctly or properly. I repeat that the Bill has two principal purposes. The first is that a complainant now has only half the time that he or she had in the past to lodge a complaint---namely, working-days. I believe that is satisfactory because if the issue is of concern it should be quite appropriate to put pen to paper within working-days to make sure that submission is made. Secondly, I believe that broadcasters, who have had this enormous working-days to respond to matters, can certainly deal with almost any type of complaint within working-days. The argument has been raised that the working-days could put a broadcaster under some pressure on some very complex issues when legal involvement may require research. However, again the select committee may wish to address that matter. If the complainant is not satisfied with the response of the broadcaster, the time in which the Broadcasting Standards Authority can receive complaints is limited to working-days. Now, the Broadcasting Standards Authority will, no doubt, be concerned about this compression of time because it is a quasi-judicial body. It does have to make responses, and I will accept that there are certain occasions on which the issues could be, again, very complex. However, because of the present situation of no constraint, I believe it has given rise to an interminable amount of toing and froing of the Broadcasting Standards Authority with the broadcasters, the result being that people just simply do not get answers---sometimes for months. That is covered in clauses , , and of the Bill. Importantly, clause of the Bill seeks to overcome the relative information education vacuum that exists at present in terms of how to exercise a complaint. At the present time, the Broadcasting Standards Authority issues a limited number of pamphlets and I would say that it does its best with what resources it has. The Bill envisages that this would be greatly expanded with the broadcasters, and perhaps the emphasis being on the broadcasters, and the Broadcasting Standards Authority probably using television as the best medium and the most powerful medium for educating people as to their rights, backed up, perhaps, by an phone line or maybe a box number---something that would facilitate the opportunity for the average person to be able to respond in the way people want to respond at present. Again, I have not attempted to take that any further but would be interested to know the Government's views on this matter and to know what the select committee, in turn, may wish to do. The present Act, I remind the House, has a requirement upon the Broadcasting Standards Authority to make known the process---essentially basic education---but this Bill takes it a long way further. That, again, is in clause , and requires a proactive stance on the part of the Broadcasting Standards Authority. It also implies by so doing that an increase in funding for the Broadcasting Standards Authority would be needed. I am unaware of just how that might be identified or assessed. Whether it is a cost to the industry or a cost to the Government, again, is a matter for the Minister or the select committee. However, I visited the Television New Zealand studios late last year and I was impressed with the amount of concern about its way of handling complaints, considering that thousands of calls are received by the television studio---or television groups. Television New Zealand started a campaign that embodied the TV Guide and the Listener, and television commercials through the months of November and December . I believe that that campaign has not been continued this year, but today the complaints manager intimated that it is Television New Zealand's wish to recommence that education programme. I understand, but I am not sure, that TV and Sky did undertake a limited campaign of a similar manner to improve the education factor. So this proactive stance on the part of the broadcasters is encouraging, but the Bill seeks to require that as an ongoing part of the broadcasting operation in this country. Finally, the Bill was an initiative to start a review of the complaints process and thereby bring about a new confidence for the public in terms of its input. There is deep concern felt by much of the public about many factors regarding programmes---violence being a very dominant one. This is particularly relevant, of course, to the types of programmes we are now seeing that are coming through all channels at this time. The relevance is also, I believe, marked because television is about to expand in terms of cable and specifically in terms of regional television. The last item alone, I believe, warrants this Bill being considered fully by this House. I commend the Bill.

I want to talk about jury trials. The number of hung juries is clearly a concern in our society right at this very moment. Our research has found that, for criminal trials in district courts, there has been an increase over recent years from . percent to percent. In the case of High Court trials there has been an increase from . percent to percent since . The Dominion today has an editorial titled ``Jury system is not working''. That editorial, and indeed most other comment on this matter, addresses the question of the majority verdict. We have at the present time, as members know, a requirement for a unanimous decision. The debate is on whether we can safely and appropriately move to a majority verdict. The Christian Democrats have an open mind about majority verdicts, but I do not think we have to address that matter at this point in time. There is one fundamental issue that is being overlooked, and it is a question of the fact that evidence should be available to the jury from the accused. The jury should have the right to hear first hand the accused person's explanation of the events, and to assess the credibility of that evidence when tested under cross-examination. If the truth is all-important, and it certainly should be in the context of jury procedures, all available evidence should be presented to the jury. I put it to the House that if the opportunity for all that evidence to be put to the jury was given, then there would be a much greater chance, surely, for a jury to come to a unanimous decision, and, most important, it would be more likely to come to a right decision. It should be noted that victims of crime have no right to refuse to give evidence. The right lies with only, I think quite incredibly, the accused, the so-called offender. An imbalance of rights is implied in that. Maybe it could be said it is somewhat typical of some of the imbalances of rights that now exist in our judicial procedure, notwithstanding how good that procedure is. I put it to the House again that the right of an accused person to refuse to give evidence is not a fundamental principle of our legal system. Originally---it goes back a long way---an accused person was barred from giving evidence on the basis that he or she could not be trusted to tell the truth. I talk about early English history. In the accused person was allowed, finally, to give evidence, but could not be compelled to do so. That actually remains the basis of the law today---an edict that stated a person may give evidence but may not be compelled to do so. I put it to members that this has left the accused with all the advantages. I believe that a balanced position at least would require all persons to give evidence and to tell the truth. Our courts should never be deterred from a scrupulous search for truth. But how can they effect that scrupulous search for truth when a very important segment of evidence---indeed, that from the accused---is not always available to them? I guess an illustration of this comment would be the O J Simpson case in the United States, even though it is under another jurisdiction. In that context many, many people believe that if evidence had been given by O J Simpson, there might well have been a different outcome to that particular trial. If this change was made, the need for a debate on whether to allow majority verdicts would probably dissipate. With all the evidence being made available, verdicts could be more easily reached. Why do we not have a revision of the law? I do not know. Why have the judiciary and all the eminent legal minds in our country not revisited this particular matter, which has existed for many, many decades? The civil liberties people would probably answer that they do not believe that in today's society it is incumbent upon anybody to do that---to be forced to do it. I say to those people that that is now not appropriate. I suggest that New Zealand---which has a very enviable record now of innovative considerations in most other fields of endeavour---should readdress the question of why we are not asking the accused to be compelled to give evidence if it is sought by the court. I just cannot see a logical argument that denies that outcome. Surely, I repeat, if we were prepared to agree to that, then we would be doing something about the hung juries. With all the evidence being available, there would be a lot fewer hung juries than we have at the moment. It would not eliminate all hung jury outcomes, but certainly there would be a sense, I believe, of satisfaction within the public at large. Let us be always conscious that our judicial system always should be seen to be fair, and its procedures to be above question. I would suggest that if people in New Zealand had the satisfaction of all evidence being brought before a court of law, then the public would always be satisfied with the final decisions. I want to take my final moments to pick up yet another story. I relate this to the question of victims' rights. We heard yesterday the harrowing story of a young woman in Porirua who had been terrorised by a man who was holding her -year-old son at knife-point. She and her children were so terrified by this dreadful ordeal that she had to move house in case, as she put it, the offender came back. The offender has at least been arrested. The fact remains that the woman and the kids were put through a most unfortunate ordeal. Apparently the kids continue to scream at night because of the nightmare of that confrontation. The news today is that people have been arrested in Masterton, after what police described as a reign of intimidation that had made the victims of their crimes too afraid to approach the police. Most were bailed straight away at the court. The police spokesman said that people who are worried about serious criminal offending should not suffer in silence, but should ``contact us with any concerns, and let us investigate them.'' The Christian Democrats totally support that action of, and the support given by, the police. They are to be commended for their prompt action in making arrests. But our justice system does little to support, again, the victims of crime. Many speakers have risen in recent weeks, if not months, to say exactly the same thing. There are few rights under the law for the victims. Criminals are well protected, it seems, with legal rights. Legal aid, psychological services, and the whole custodial system pander to their needs without ever holding them fully accountable for their behaviour, certainly in terms of restitution of the victims' rights. It is time that we switched our emphasis to fully protecting the rights of victims and ordinary citizens. They should not be required to shift houses in terror of an offender returning. They should not have to bear the emotional scars of a terrible experience simply because someone who in fact has scarred their lives has---and this is most important---got away, it seems, without having to do anything in terms of reparation or helping them out. Where intimidation is involved, bail should not be granted. Substantial custodial sentences are required where the offender is violent and dangerous. We want to go further than that. We say that we believe that the offender should have to make full restitution; not just nominal restitution as ordered by the court, but full restitution. The offender has to pay up, to pay for the crime, and should not get off with just nominal restitution.

I say again that this is another important Bill not only to the Wellington region but to New Zealand as a whole. The committee worked very hard to deal with this issue and to facilitate the report back to the House today. The Bill was first submitted to the committee on May . The supplementary order paper just spoken about by Pauline Gardiner was submitted on May . We received submissions on the Bill and oral evidence was heard from submissioners. These included the Wellington Regional Council, which promoted the Bill, the Department of Internal Affairs, the Wellington stadium development trust, the Hutt City Council, the Kapiti Coast District Council, and, of course, a number of lobby groups from regional city ratepayers. Two-thirds of the submissions were in favour of the Bill and the supplementary order paper. Those opposing the Bill were concerned about the cost to individual ratepayers, fiscal risk in the project, and that an undesirable precedent would be established that would allow investment of ratepayer funds in future development projects. Two councils supported the construction of the stadium but were concerned about ratepayer funding. The committee processed this Bill and it now provides for the authorisation of the Wellington Regional Council to lend a sum not exceeding $ million to the stadium trust to facilitate the planning, development, and construction of the stadium in Aotea Quay for the benefit of the public of the Wellington region. The Bill authorises the Wellington Regional Council to borrow money for the purposes of making such a loan, or loans. It authorises the Wellington Regional Council to levy a stadium purposes rate to fund such a loan to the Wellington Regional Stadium Trust or to repay money borrowed by the Wellington Regional Council to make such a loan. Finally, it requires the Wellington Regional Council, before exercising any of the powers conferred on it by the Bill, to establish jointly with the Wellington City Council a trust to be known as the Wellington Regional Stadium Trust to undertake the planning, development, construction, ownership, operation, and maintenance of the stadium as a multipurpose sporting and cultural venue. The committee decided to facilitate the passing of this Bill and to have this House look favourably upon the completion of the Bill today, because we believe it is in the interests of this region and, indeed, of the wider country, to do so. As I have mentioned, we noted again the concerns expressed by the submissions in respect of ratepayer funding. However, in deliberation we felt that it was not the responsibility of our committee to direct the Wellington Regional Council on matters that fall within its own discretion. The Wellington Regional Council is subject to extensive consultation requirements, which, of course, are laid down in local government legislation. We expect that the council will fulfil all the conditions associated with ratepayer funding and will have noted the points made by the committee in its hearings, and we certainly emphasise the public consultation procedures. So we wish all parties in this matter well in proceeding to agreed outcome and hope that one day we will see the stadium built with everyone's support.

I would like to speak to Supplementary Order Paper , which stands in my name and relates to clause . I think it is worth noting that when the Auckland water crisis struck home, many, many politicians in this House, and Auckland politicians as well, made much of the fact that there had not been adequate conservation strategies, adequate planning, to prevent the crisis situation that we found ourselves in---namely conservation water management. It is perhaps ironic that so few seem to be here now to look at the legislation that has come out of the work of the select committee. The select committee was well served by the officials throughout. I hold the view, and so does the Alliance, that one fundamental area is not adequately provided for. I put it to the Minister that he would not lose if my supplementary order paper were included in the Bill. It does not go against the intent of, or the work being done by, the Auckland Regional Services Trust and Watercare Services. It actually enhances conservation strategies by suggesting that they be specifically noted and included in clause . What would be the problem in including the supplementary order paper that stands in my name? I put it to the Minister that he may want to reconsider his position and to look at its inclusion. The amendments are small. They do not counteract any of the other provisions in clause , but, rather, enhance many of the things enshrined not just in resource management law but, in fact, in the conservation strategy being developed by Watercare Services itself. In a nutshell, the supplementary order paper does the following three things. It simply requires that Watercare Services conduct its financial affairs while having regard to the sustainable management of natural resources, including water. I well remember the call from politicians in this House to Aucklanders to conserve water, and how well we managed our water usage during the crisis. This reminder could be included in the Bill, to carry through that strategy and that call. The supplementary order paper requires that Watercare Services develop water demand management plans. What is wrong with that? That is a good thing. The intention is to increase the efficiency with which we use water. The member who has just spoken made the point that when the crisis struck, water conservation management plans, ad hoc although they were, were immediately implemented in Auckland. The amount of water that was able to be saved by having some sort of commitment to water conservation---given the fact that if we did not conserve water Auckland would run dry---does not go against that amendment.

I, too, would like to note the way that the select committee chaired this particular matter, which was complex, and the way it was supported by the officials, and I thank them for the way in which the business was conducted. It was a very difficult process for members of the select committee, because we were confronted with having to determine whether the allegations in this emergency private member's Bill were justifiable and proved. The judgment in relation to that required us to determine on the evidence what was an acceptable level of risk based on a prolonged period of low rainfall in Auckland and likely future weather patterns. Weather patterns and meteorology being known to be an imperfect science, it certainly poses a number of problems for anybody in that position. However, on balance, having heard the evidence---complex evidence, which was scientific, engineering, environmental, and cultural---in my view the allegations of the preamble seemed to be proved. The committee heard evidence from Watercare Services Ltd that the rainfall in the Hunua catchment had been the lowest in its years of keeping records. That contention is actually supported in the evidence supplied by the independent review panel commissioned by the territorial local authorities. It is true that in the past weeks the lake levels have risen to percent, and that is after the percent savings that Aucklanders have managed to achieve over quite a long period of time, and augmentation from within the Auckland region. However, the evidence that we received from Watercare Services was comprehensive and indicated to us that on August last year the dams in the area were . percent full, but even then it was recognised by Watercare that it was facing difficulties and had problems. Now with the dams standing at levels of percent full, with augmentation and conservation savings being achieved, the likelihood of getting through the summer period without putting Aucklanders at unreasonable risk and having to face significant water rationing is the issue that we had to determine. On that matter we heard evidence from Dr Jim Salinger, who was a witness for Watercare, and is the scientific expert for the National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research Ltd. He advised the committee that the El Nino effect is likely to continue but he also predicts continual low rainfalls, which may be alleviated by heavy downfalls---rainfall for August being slightly above average; changes of below average rainfall in September being percent likely; more dry weather likely during August to October, and the signal for El Nino, which has caused this unnatural drought, is strong for the period from November to January. The member for Dunedin North asked comprehensive questions about the standard of water quality in the Waikato River. Good on him, but charity begins at home, and the committee heard that Dunedin has very poor water quality and is renowned for that, and he should address that issue. He should set to work to clean up the water for his local constituents. It is all very well for the member for Dunedin North to play loose and fast with the people of the Auckland region, but I happen to live in the middle of the Auckland region---Auckland Central, the area I represent. I have watched the people of my electorate and throughout the region try to come to grips with this issue and it has not been easy. They are working very hard, but when the risks are taken it is all very well to take them from the safe distance of Dunedin. It is a different issue altogether when one is faced with the very serious warnings that we have had from the Ministry of Health in its evidence on this Bill. On the issue of Tainui, the Alliance will support any amendment through the Committee stage that will address the concerns of the Tainui people. Their evidence was compelling and sincere, and I believe is yet to be adequately addressed in terms of this legislation. So we will be supporting Tainui's interests.

The question that is begged in this debate is what the Government's definition of employment actually is. In this House over the last year, members of the Opposition, including the Alliance Opposition, have raised a number of concerns relating to specific matters that in no small part are directly affected by the reality of the lack of employment opportunities in this country today. For example, there was a long, heartfelt debate on the issue of youth suicide, and from the Government benches we heard again and again that there is no one simple reason for young people choosing to take their lives in such horrific numbers in this country nowadays. It is the view of the Alliance that undeniably a contributing factor in many of these cases where young people choose to take their lives, rather than to continue, is a lack of opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to society in all areas, including the area of work. The cruellest punishment we can impose on fellow citizens is to put them in solitary confinement without work. To deny them the right to work is one of the worst punishments that a society can dream up. Yet that is the situation for far too many of our young people at risk. Again, if one asks any police officer on the beat whether there is a causal relationship between crime and unemployment, without exception that police officer will say that in his or her opinion that is most definitely the case. In the report we see figures and pie graphs that suggest that things are on the up-and-up in terms of employment opportunities available to New Zealanders today, but the quality of the work and employment available needs to be called into question, as well. The casualisation of work, and the conditions of employment for New Zealanders, and for young New Zealanders in particular, are cause for concern. No real new opportunities are being created by the Government. I had the opportunity over the weekend to drive through Moerewa, in the far north. The images I saw in that town of closed shops that were boarded up, and places---including the freezing works, which has now been shut down---where once there had been meaningful employment for the local community, were very reminiscent of that television series, Boys from the Black Stuff, which portrayed the effects of Thatcher's England. Everything had closed down. There was social disintegration everywhere, a loss of opportunity, and a failure to recognise people's contribution and potential contribution to society. The provisions contained within vote: Employment---in terms of output classes, the linkages, the related outcomes, the policy advice that is being sought, and so on---do not recognise the fact, in my view, that the problem of unemployment is an ideological one. It is an ideological philosophy imposed by the Government that is creating the unemployment that we see in New Zealand society today. It is not an accident. It has not come about as a fluke of history. It is an ideological position that has been taken by the Government, and that is continuing to be taken by the Government as a matter of policy---despite the recommendations of the employment task force, and other matters---in all areas where the Government, through select committees, reports, departments, and ministerial advice, advocates restructuring. In real terms that means the destructuring of society and the removal of employment opportunities. The Government, as a matter of ideological policy, is creating unemployment rather than providing employment opportunities. A very good example the House has been dealing with in the last couple of months is the review of the Fire Service. Here we have people who make a meaningful contribution to New Zealand society, who are employed, who do have skills, and who are respected by the public for the work and the contribution they make to society. By way of policy from this Government, we see a situation whereby those employment opportunities are being destructured. The Government wants to replace paid, skilled staff, who are respected by the rest of New Zealand society, with volunteers. That is par for the course. Of course, the issue of the National Archives is another example.

When I was last speaking on this part I was saying that it is probably the most controversial part in the Bill and that we received a large number of submissions on the impact of it. One of the reasons is that under clause A, ``Meaning of Ngai Tahu and Ngai Tahu Whanui'', there is an intention to sweep in iwi such as Waitaha against their specific wishes. The argument goes that Waitaha are part of the three strands of whakapapa lines that go to make up Ngai Tahu, and that is true; but what is not recognised is that at the same time Waitaha as an iwi stand in their own right and do not want to be jackbooted as a result of this legislation into being represented ``for all purposes'' under the Te Runanga o Ngai Tahu Act by a corporate body that is not part of their iwi organisation. Also, there will be an amendment in my name in relation to clause ()(d) that refers to the matter to do with claims currently before the Waitangi Tribunal. There are matters of natural justice and ordinary New Zealand citizenship rights at law that are to be extinguished in this part of the Bill if clause ()(d) is allowed to proceed in its current form. I would like to point out to the Committee that those claims represent for many of the claimant groups many years of work. Considerable amounts of research and commitment have been undertaken on the part of the iwi whose claims will be extinguished, even though they are in train before the Waitangi Tribunal. These have involved considerable cost, such as getting other people to take these claims. They have to engage lawyers and other advisers and pay to have evidence gathered, and so on. Yet this Bill---this particular clause in this part of it---is to extinguish all that work midstream for claimant groups such as Waitaha, but not only Waitaha. If one looks at the list one will see that the Waitangi claims affected are Wai , , , , , , , , , and . Those simple numbers in this very large Bill represent a tremendous amount of work, effort, issues, grief, grievances, historical record, and financial commitment. This Bill simply intends to completely wipe the lot out. Also, the issue of the specific reference to the Te Runanga o Ngai Tahu Act is contained in this part. It is intended to consequentially amend that Act by omitting the words ``Ngai Tahu and Ngati Mamoe'' and substituting the words ``Waitaha, Ngati Mamoe, and Ngai Tahu''. The purpose of that again is to jackboot the Waitaha people retrospectively into Te Runanga o Ngai Tahu legislation that they were omitted from originally. Section of that states they will then be represented for all purposes by a corporate body from another iwi.

Tonight, in supporting the Minister's amendments, a number of things have happened and a precedent has been set in this House. The first thing that has happened is that the laborious work of the Maori Affairs Committee in hearing evidence---not just from those who support the Bill but from a large number of submitters who also wanted to be recognised but not as part of Te Aho Matua as described in section ---has been undermined. The select committee heard all the submissions, and one of the things that some kura who wanted to sit outside the more prescriptive form desired, was a place for themselves that was not lumped in with just any other alternative school and was also not constrained by the more prescriptive constitutional provisions that are contained within the Bill. That has now been undermined, and I want to endorse the words of Nanaia Mahuta when she said that one of the primary concerns Maori members on the select committee in particular had, was the resourcing issue---not just for the kura that are being recognised by the Minister, but for those who wanted to stay outside that prescription for a number of different reasons and who will now be lumped in with any other old alternative that comes along, and will be forced to compete for resources and recognition. Perhaps more importantly, what has happened is a very important issue in relation to Maori intellectual property rights. The select committee considered long and hard the proposition that the words ``kura kaupapa Maori'' should be a term used exclusively for those kura that will be recognised in the legislation and that fall within the ambit of the runanganui. On balance, we decided that the term was too generic as part of the language to be recognised in an exclusive way. Yet, in the explanatory note to the Minister's supplementary order paper, he described providing the exclusive use of that title as protecting the use of the term. In fact, rather than protecting it, the amendment has the effect of selecting that term for the use of one discrete body and class of people, as recognised in the Act, to the exclusion of all others. If the Crown and a Government can take a generic term, such as ``kura'', and make that so, then other parts of our language---likewise, through legislation promoted by the Crown---can be copyrighted, for want of a better description, at the expense of many people. So like it or not, it does have the effect of setting a very important precedent. The Alliance's position was to test the integrity of the Government in terms of this legislation and whether it is going to do that which it sets out to do by putting up the amendments that were moved previously, and I accept that they were voted down. But those amendments absolutely locked in the contentions that sit behind the Bill. They sought to ensure, for example, that the principles of the treaty would be fundamental in the interpretation. They sought to ensure that Te Runanganui o nga Kura Kaupapa Maori as the national governing body would be just that in law: recognised as a national governing body. It sought to ensure that the constitution itself would be protected by that governing body as a right, rather than by any ministerial appointee. All those amendments were voted down. I am quite surprised that that happened, because a number of members of the select committee supported the arguments I was mooting along those lines in the select committee, but they did an about-face here in this Chamber when it came to the voting, even though, when they spoke in the Committee stage, they spoke in support of the principles that sat behind those arguments. So now we have a situation where, having tested the integrity of the intent of the Bill, we have to recognise the fact that it gives no real protection, and that the interpretation of its intent will be subject to the whim of the Crown, ministers, and politicians who may come and go at any time in this Parliament---and, indeed, it will be subject to the whim of electoral systems that may one day see no Maori in this House. If we have a return to a first-past-the-post system, this Bill would leave Maori and Maori educational initiatives too open for us to vote in support of it at this time. I will say one more thing to the Minister: on the Minister's head be it, because although the Minister may promise in the name of his forebears that as long as he is here this Bill will be interpreted, when it is enacted, in an appropriate way, there is no one parliamentarian in this Chamber, unfortunately---with the best will in the world---who will be here for ever to protect the intent. That is why the words have to be very clear and specific. The Minister should remember that the National Government, in particular, has never been any great friend of our people, and for many years has made unjust laws that have affected Maori. Every time National members have done it they have thought they could get away with it. Yet again, although the theory is one thing in this Bill, the reality, which is subject to interpretation by Ministers who have sat on these benches for a long time, may prove to be something else entirely different. I would be delighted to be proven wrong, but the risks are too great.

This settlement has a familiar feel to it. It is similar to others, including the Ngai Tahu settlement, where families have been pitted against each other, not because they do not care about each other, but simply because the processes that have been imposed on them do not sit well with them. If the private property of Pakeha New Zealanders had been confiscated in this form in , I am quite sure that the settlements being arranged now would be very, very different indeed from what we see in the House today. Take, for example, the position of Pakeha lessees on our Maori reserved lands in Taranaki; I remember well when they arrived at Parliament on their tractors. In conclusion, I say that all politicians in this House had better understand during the election season that the treaty is an infinite document not a finite document. It is a compact between the Crown and Maori in this country, and as long as the Crown continues to breach the principles of the treaty that were agreed to by our people, then we will be back again and again to resolve these issues. Any political party that thinks it can sign off the treaty for the sake of political electioneering had better think again.

I rise on behalf of the Green Party to support this bill, but I have concern that too much has been attributed to it in terms of its potential for good. It is very difficult to whistle-blow. The examples that have been raised so far in this Parliament and in the report from the select committee show that. The case of Neil Pugmire has just been referred to. He protested against the treatment of patients in the health system. The case of Karen Silkwood was referred to in the report back from the select committee. She was killed on her way to expose grave deficiencies in the nuclear industry in the United States. Last night the case was referred to---that is, in the major film The Insider---that tells us about the case of Jeffrey Wigands, who had huge difficulties in exposing the harm done by the tobacco industry in the United States. A common factor in all those three cases is the thing that the authorities were really scared of was the media exposure. Karen Silkwood was actually killed to prevent that exposure. Those members who have seen the film The Insider will remember the threats to Jeffrey Wigands on the question of whether his case was to be shown on television and elsewhere in the print media. The thing that really inhibits authorities from committing a grave offence to the environment, to health, and to safety is the fact that the public can get to know about it through the media, and can discuss it. This embarrasses those in authority who act in an unethical and dangerous way. That is what really protects the whistle-blowers---that is, on all questions of major importance to health, the environment, and so on. In order to advance that, it is important to have more legal protections in the area of the media, which has been referred to by one of the previous speakers. But I do not see a counter position of protections in the media to protections under this bill. The two would complement each other. We need to extend this bill into the area of the media to give some legal protection for whistle-blowers to prevent them from being jumped on with big libel suits. That was the case in the film The Insider. The threat of libel suits and the threat of being sued for damages affects whistle-blowers. It is good that this bill has protections in that regard for people who try to do it within the system. The other thing that we have to do beyond what is projected in this bill is to have a very open atmosphere of debate in agencies in this country, particularly public agencies and State organisations that should set the example. Within public agencies, particularly where it is not self-interest that is at stake so much, there should be so more public debate. For instance, what is the situation in the Crown research agencies for scientists who argue against genetic engineering contracts in a Crown enterprise that is based financially around getting a lot of contracts for genetic engineering research? There should be a right, for example, that scientists should be able to give their views even if they are counter to those of the authorities, and in some ways are counter to the financial interests, at that particular moment, of the Crown research institutes. This bill is good, but within limitations. It is good that it has channels for people to go through if they have major cause for concern and that there is some protection for them when they do. But the reality is that organisations often close ranks. It is intimidating to have to go through that first hurdle of bringing the matter up within one's organisation. Even when people go over that hurdle to a higher level and up to the Minister, they might find, as Neil Pugmire found, that at the end of the day the Minister is on the side of the Government department, or whatever. There is a tendency for people to work together to protect each other in certain circumstances, as Neil Pugmire found. The protection against sanctions for dismissal, for example, is all good and well, but, as we all know from the workplaces that we have been in, there are all kinds of ways that pressure can be put on employees other than saying: ``You've blown the whistle. You are sacked.'' There are all sorts of ways that subtle penalties can be used against them, such as non-promotion and various ways of easing them out of the workforce. That is a major problem that inhibits people from whistle-blowing on very important issues. The Greens support the extension in this bill to private organisations because huge problems of pollution and safety are involved with them. Many of them are former State organisations that have unfortunately been privatised by Labour Governments and National Governments---the petroleum industry and electricity industry, to name two. The petroleum industry is obviously one where there is a huge potential for environmental pollution through leakages, and so on. Whistle-blowing should be encouraged if there is a big danger of pollution. In the electricity industry, obviously if a hydro dam is threatened with some safety situation where the dam might burst, whistle-blowing should be encouraged in that situation. In sum, the Green Party supports this bill but it has severe limitations. I do not see it as being counterpoised to exposure in the public domain but the protections need to be extended into the public domain so that we can have a society that is free in terms of public debate, media exposure, and protections for whistle-blowing in that sense.

The Bill received submissions, and the Government is still determined to push through the messy, piecemeal legislation. The original Bill contained pages and there are pages of amendments---that really is making policy on the hoof. One important role of Opposition members in Parliament is to bring the Government to account. Accordingly, in the reporting-back debate I should like to cover just briefly the promises made by the Labour Government for the tertiary funding of education when it went to the polls in . What did the Government promise the people of New Zealand at that election less than years ago? The Labour Party manifesto---admittedly, it was put out after the election---talks of financial assistance for tertiary students, and page states: ``Labour believes that access to universities, community colleges, technical institutes, teachers' colleges, and other forms of continuing education should not be governed by the ability of students to pay.'' The Labour Party was not going to make entry to tertiary institutions conditional on the ability of students to pay. What was the Government going to do? First, it was going to ensure ``that tertiary students are not required to pay a higher contribution to their own education than they do at present''. The Labour Party promised not to increase the fees of tertiary education, but what is the Government doing? With the Bill it is increasing the fees from $ to $,. If that is not a broken promise I will eat my hat. All of the way through education, that is exactly what the Government has been doing. One promise was the : teacher ratio, but now there are fewer primary teachers than in . Next, in a huge hand-out, it handed all of the assets of the education boards to a few privileged friends. Now there is the pain for those broken promises; tertiary students are to pay a higher contribution. That is what the Bill is all about. Not only that, the Labour Government was going to enable all people who wished to study at a tertiary level to do so, regardless of their socio-economic background. The Bill stops that, because it raises the fees for some of those tertiary students. When that announcement was made the principal of Manukau Polytechnic said: ``The new fee structure will make it even more difficult for disadvantaged students to get into higher classes.'' Those are two out of two promises broken. The next promise was to continue to expand the opportunities for overseas students to come to New Zealand to study. The other half of the Bill is all about closing the doors to foreign students coming to New Zealand.

The amendment seems fairly innocuous, in that New Zealand Liquid Fuels Investment Ltd has just been written out of two or three Acts, but it is important. First, I ask why such an amendment is being introduced now, under urgency; why it was not included in the original Bill as introduced; why it was not in the Bill when it was before the select committee so that the public could have some input on whether it approved of what was happening; why it was not in the Bill when it received its second reading so that the House could discuss it; and why it came sneakily into the House tonight while we were in the Committee stage. The issue is that New Zealand Liquid Fuels Investment Ltd---previously the Liquid Fuels Trust Board---was set up earlier this year, and the articles of association were signed on February . There are two major shareholders: David Francis Caygill and Richard William Prebble. Alarm bells should sound when one sees those names at the bottom of the paper. It indicates that Liquid Fuels Investment Ltd is a State-owned asset. When the Government amends legislation so that New Zealand Liquid Fuels Investment Ltd is written out of the Official Information Act, the Income Tax Act, and the State-Owned Enterprises Act, it is being made ready for the Government to hock it off. Liquid Fuels Investment Ltd happens to be the owner of the Synfuel plant at Motunui in Taranaki, and it is also associated with the Government's interests in the Maui contract, because the Government announced in December that it had decided to complete a memorandum of understanding with Petrocorp for the sale of the Government's contractual obligations under the Maui take-or-pay agreement, the on-sale contracts, and the Synfuel venture. The announcement on December stated: ``The memorandum is conditional on the consent of the other parties to these agreements where this is a condition of the contract.''. One would have thought that that sale would occur fairly quickly. The Government said that, in return, Petrocorp would pay $ million for the whole agreement. At the time the Minister said: ``This sale ends the uncertainty. The sale of the Crown's gas contract and the Synfuel venture ends concern and uncertainty arising from the Government's ongoing losses from the Synfuel plant.''. He rejected claims that it was a fire sale. The fire has been simmering away and smouldering during that time. The Government has made no further announcement about when it will conclude the sale, except to say through the news media that Synfuel will be sold by the end of the financial year. The end of the financial year is just days away, and that is the reason the Bill has come into the House quietly and secretly at the last possible stage that the Government can amend legislation with a minimum amount of flack. Last week in the House I asked a question of the Minister of Energy. The Minister of Finance answered, and said that the Government was still negotiating the sale of its interest in the Maui gas contract and its shareholding in Synfuel and Petrocorp, a subsidiary of Fletcher Challenge. When the negotiations were complete the terms and conditions of the deal would be announced. I asked during the Committee stage when that announcement would be made. Is the Government determined that it will complete the sale by the end of this week? The Government has ignored those questions. It refused to answer the Opposition's questions during the Committee stage, and, once again, the Government's arrogance is shown. It is not prepared to front up to the Opposition; it is not prepared to front up to the people of New Zealand, to make the decisions, and to be held accountable for them. That is also happening with the election. Many New Zealanders would like an election tomorrow, but the Government will not front up.

I start my discussion with a quotation from Thomas Jefferson about education: ``By far the most important bill in our whole code, is that for the diffusion of knowledge among people. No other sure foundation can be devised for the preservation of freedom and happiness.'' That quotation signifies the importance that I attach to this Bill. This important debate should not be rushed, and I am disappointed that only two Government members have been prepared to speak on the issue, particularly as a large proportion of Government members come from the education profession. Education is one of the most important investments in the future of New Zealand. At present New Zealand spends a little more than $. billion on education. Major concern is felt in society about the bureaucracy that has built up around education, and about the level of accountability. Fear has been expressed about the concept of social engineering and so on. There is a need, which the Bill addresses, to refer back to the consumers of education funds---the students and their parents. Under the present Government, New Zealand has not had real accountability in education. This Government promised a : teaching ratio, and today, years later, it is further away from that ratio than when it started, despite the massive drop in the school rolls, particularly in our primary schools. This Government has launched above-market rental rates on school houses in rural areas, and it is selling off school houses in small towns. The onslaught on rural education---already the poor relation---has continued. I fear that some of that onslaught will continue under the Bill. For example, the reading-recovery programme is available to most city schools, but to less than half of our rural schools. The policy outlined in Tomorrow's Schools was an offspring of the Picot report and its submissions. It will bring large changes in education, not only in administration; and one must record that it was a theme of the National Party's policy at the election, not of the Labour Party's policy. In one foul swoop the Government will introduce the Opposition's policy of the election, although it was not even mentioned in the Labour Party's manifesto, which it published after the election. The policy of Tomorrow's Schools is up and running. Nineteen new quangos have been launched to start organising the real policy to implement the changes that we are beginning to introduce this morning. The new quangos and the new appointments will take away some of the responsibility---and I dare say blame, if things do not go right---from the ministerial portfolio, and from the House. It is policy on the run. The result will be decided as the committees start to make decisions. The Bill appears to have been hastily drafted, and it contains several contradictions. I am pleased that it will have some time before a select committee, because those contradictions will need to be ironed out. Under clause the definition of an adult student is a student who has attained years, but other parts of the Bill refer to a student aged years. Why specify years of age? It would make no difference to have the age of years included right through the Bill, instead of having two ages. Clause highlights some of the confusion and some of the poor drafing that has gone into the Bill. The definition states that parent trustees must be parents of students who are enrolled at school in the year of the election of the board. At an intermediate school the new board would be elected in May of the year that the children started school. The Bill also states that those parents have to serve for years. However, in the case of an intermediate school the parents may no longer have a child at the school unless a second child is coming on. Therefore there is no way that the boards of trustees at intermediate schools can comply with clause . Clause plainly states that the parent trustees must be the parents of students at the school. Parents of students coming to the school, or who have left the school, may be elected, and parents of a child at an intermediate school in the previous year can take part in elections, but they cannot be on the boards of trustees. That clause contains an anomaly. It may be slack drafting, which I hope can be tidied up; if it is not, no boards of trustees at intermediate schools will be able to serve a -year term. That is the way I read clause , and I hope the Minister can clear that matter up. There is no other definition of parents of students except those parents whose children are at the school. The boards of trustees cannot start until May, and that means that there will be only an -month term, despite the suggestion that there should be a -year term. It is also a matter of concern for intermediate schools that there will not be a continuity of parent membership on the boards of trustees. At a -teacher or -teacher school all of the teachers will be on the board of trustees, but at a -teacher school only teachers can be on the board. The same rules do not seem to apply to the same position. The belief that the parents and the community cannot make the decisions as adequately as teachers can may be an onslaught on small rural schools. I do not want to discredit the role of teachers. I believe that New Zealand teachers are dedicated in the performance of their duties, despite some of the problems they have had with the Minister and his department. In relation to clauses and , in the light of the performance of teachers, why was the Minister not prepared to write into the legislation that teacher representatives and student representatives should be on the boards of trustees of the Correspondence School, newly established schools, and newly integrated schools? I am concerned that parents will not be involved with the Correspondence School. It is New Zealand's biggest school, and parents should be involved in the board of trustees by election, not by ministerial appointment. Clause enables the Minister to dissolve a board for mismanagement and incompetence, but the schedules do not include any liability for boards of trustees. How can there be responsibility without liability? Under the schedules the powers of boards are not affected by any error or defect in election. In other words, there can be a rigged election under clause of the second schedule. I have strong reservations about some of the drafting in the Bill. The Bill is contradictory, and it has not really dealt with the issue of the community being fully involved in the decision-making of boards of trustees. There is not the continuity in the boards of trustees that there should be, particularly at intermediate schools. Student representatives may be involved in disciplinary proceedings of boards of trustees against a principal or teachers. A clause should be included stating that a student may not be involved in any board meetings dealing with disciplinary proceedings. There is also the small problem of the commissioner and his or her remuneration.

When we finished last time I had acknowledged the very good work done by the chairman and members of the select committee, and by my staff of Te Puni Kokiri. I would also like to acknowledge the extra effort undertaken by my personal secretary on Maori issues, Mr Lewis Moeau, who does an outstanding job and is well respected right throughout Maoridom. I think it is increasingly being acknowledged that the Government has really made some quite remarkable progress in the whole area of Maori policy. We have quite clearly identified three areas. The first is to try to settle outstanding grievances, most but not all of them stemming back to the last century. My colleague the Hon. Doug Graham has done an outstanding job there. Secondly, this Government has put a great effort into revitalising the Maori language and supporting Maori culture. We currently have under way the process for a Maori language strategic plan. That, again, is a response to the calls within Maoridom for a more concerted and more considered effort to try to retain the language long term and, with it, to keep the culture vital. There is no doubt that we have used a mainstreaming approach in the rest of the policy, which is focused now on Maori development. We have mainstreamed much more than the $ million that used to be spent under the approach of the old Department of Maori Affairs. Why, for example, do we now have a record number of Maori graduates coming out of our tertiary institutions year after year? I move, That the Land Transfer (Automation) Amendment Bill be now read a third time. I am delighted to see the progress being made on the Bill. This is legislation that is important to allow us to automate the land titles system. I am confident that the automatic system will enhance the integrity and security of the land titles system, and, as noted in Committee, there will be full security, and the best practices will be followed in respect of security of the systems involved and the automation of our land titles system. I pay special thanks to the officials who have been involved in the whole process, particularly my officials at Land Information New Zealand, also to members of the select committee for the way in which they have worked their way through the Bill, and to members of the House for their attention to this particular Bill. We have often spoken in the House---even this morning---about the costs of compliance that the Government places on business in our society. This particular legislation and the follow-up of the automation of our land titles system is one of those cases in which the House is moving quite dramatically to lower costs of compliance and lower costs for business in our society. As we move away from a manual system of handling land titles, which has sometimes, with the checks and suchlike that are involved, seen delays of up to months in registering new titles, and delays of more than a month in transactions or the transfer of one title to another---that is likely to change as we move down the track of automation---it could be that access could be granted hours of the day to those people who do have access. Transactions could ultimately be registered at any time and be attended to instantly rather than there being those delays. It has enormous implications for the wider community in lowering the cost of doing business in the sector.

This is particularly important legislation amending an Act that is already partially in force. Although the title of this Act will be the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Amendment Act (No ) , there are quite significant issues behind this legislation in that it amends the principal Act, and tries to make some of the legislation that this House passed last year a little bit more practical and actually able to be implemented out there in the real, commercial world. One of the difficulties we have with the legislation that is being amended is that it will not work unless this bill is passed. As a result, the Opposition is supportive of the principles behind this legislation. In fact, it probably does not go far enough. I am very interested during the Committee stage to hear comment from the Minister of Energy as to whether there are some other areas on which perhaps we should be moving a little bit further than the current legislation does. It has become quite apparent that the costs involved---the compliance costs in particular---are quite high. I come back to the title. I think it is fairly obvious that this bill is an amendment to the principal Act, the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act, which was passed in . That Act is being amended in a number of ways. Although the Opposition could have introduced a number of amendments, that is not our intention. We are happy with the title, but I think there are quite a number of issues that we will want to raise during the Committee stage about whether the bill goes far enough, and whether the compliance costs are still far too high for progress to be made in the introduction of new organisms and hazardous substances to New Zealand---in particular, those that are in common usage in other countries. I think we have set up a bureaucracy that in essence is not necessarily going to help the aims and objectives outlined in this legislation. Members on the Opposition benches think the title is probably appropriate. The bill is a very, very important amendment, and we would like to spend quite some time on it as we work with the Minister on clarifying what the Government's long-term intentions are for the principal legislation. It was originally introduced by the previous Government in . I think in some areas it was possibly overkill. This amendment was introduced by the previous Government initially to make the Act a little more practical, a little bit more user-friendly, and to lower compliance costs. It is up to the Committee to decide whether it does that adequately, but we would certainly like to hear from the Minister in the chair whether he thinks it will do it adequately, and whether it will meet the intention of the title of amending the original legislation, even though the parts of the Act that are covered in this bill have not been implemented because they have been impractical to date. That is one of the key reasons why this legislation has to be passed by the House. The current legislation will not work in its current form. It is one of those cases where the House spent a lot of time, and it did not get it right. That is why it is important we spend a bit more time to ensure that the Minister and his advisers have got it right this time. We need to have legislation that is both practical and will not increase compliance costs unnecessarily for the many, many New Zealand businesses that have to use new chemicals, new hazardous substances, and new organisms. Given the Government's very, very cautious approach to genetic engineering in particular, we need to ensure that we do not stifle initiative out there in the wider community. In fact, there are some very real risks that the current legislation and the current approach of this Government are already preventing New Zealand from keeping up with some of the major changes occurring in biotechnology and other areas.
