I have not had the opportunity to sit on the Finance and Expenditure Committee in respect of this particular bill, but Part raises a lot of questions in my mind. I understand the general direction of self-assessment, and the nuances of the changed direction of this tax legislation whereby more of the onus goes on to the taxpayer, but, likewise, so do some of the compliance costs. I note that a number of definitions are withdrawn from the Tax Administration Act. I would like to ask the Minister in the chair the reasons for those definitions being withdrawn---such as ``foreign tax'' and ``New Zealand tax''. I assume it is because the amendments that are included in Part do away with any reference to those particular things. Given that self-assessment is a major part of this bill, I would have thought that ``assessment'' would have a definition. Maybe it is in the body of the amendment, and I have not been able to find it. I would like the Minister to take a call to answer that particular question. I also note the simplification of section of the Tax Administration Act. It concerns the furnishing of annual returns of income by taxpayers to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue in the prescribed form for the preceding year. The provision in the bill is much simpler than the current definition in the Tax Administration Act. Section () in clause states: ``... in the prescribed form for the preceding income year, together with such other particulars as may be prescribed.'' I presume that that prescribing is done by regulation. Again, I would like the Minister to take a call to tell me whether that is how the prescribing will be done. Will it be done by regulation, or will there be the usual communications from the Inland Revenue Department? One seems to get screeds and screeds of newsletters, and one does not take any notice of them unless something catches one's eye. Often, people who have to fill out these forms do not understand them. Without a doubt, the increased complexity of tax legislation is partly driven by the Government's crazy idea of increasing the number of bands of tax. These sorts of things give plenty of opportunity for the accountancy profession to increase its returns. I also note in clause that there are some changes with regard to people claiming housekeeping or charitable rebates. I would like the full implications of that to be discussed by the Minister. There is certainly a lot of concern about changes being made in the charitable status of many religious organisations. I know that is not covered here, but I would like the Government to comment on whether this provision is just a forerunner for those changes being suggested. The housekeeping area is a quite difficult area. On one side people can claim for housekeeping, and on the other side many housekeepers do not have to declare the income they receive, and many housekeepers do not actually pay PAYE because they are the sole part-time employee. It is the same for babysitters. I wonder why babysitters are not included here, as well. Obviously, there are some changes here, but I would like the Minister to take a call to explain them in greater detail. They are very important changes. I note that some of the submissions from the professionals in respect of this clause did complain about the complexity. The accountants society or the Law Society focused on the complexity that is raised with these amendments to the Tax Administration Act. From a preliminary reading, as a lay person, I can certainly understand its position, but when I hear the professionals say that they struggle to understand it, I have some very real concerns. Although the commissioner in many cases is no longer making the assessments, or may make some assessments, there is no doubt he will certainly follow up any mistakes that are made, even if they are made by the professionals in the industry. Clause is about taxpayer assessment. Again, some of the changes concern me, particularly given the powers that the department has. In terms of changes in the time bar in respect of income tax liability, assessable income, and tax payable, I note that assessment does come into this part of the Act, even though the definition of ``assessment'' has been taken out of the Act.

It was immoral, but now it is not immoral and the surtax has been removed, but what has been put in its place? A means test has been put in its place surreptitiously. If the surtax was immoral, I do not have a word to describe that means test---the income test. What about the cost of implementing it? I have heard Government members say that this Budget is fair. There is nothing fair about that income test. An example of what could be called ``poli-speak'' is taken from the Budget. Before I read it I should like to point out to the House that year ago the Minister of Health, who was the former Opposition spokesperson on welfare, wrote the superannuation policy. That Minister and the National Party campaigned on the fact that superannuation was to be universal. Listen to what was written in the Budget---only a few months after the election: ``A universal retirement income that pushes people out of the workforce at age would cause the loss of knowledge, skills and experience these people can contribute to growth and job creation. Furthermore, the continuing improvement in health status, and the progressive shift away from manual jobs, provide people with the capacity to work productively beyond age .''. That is a double flip and a backwards somersault, as well. Talk about changing within the space of a few short months! This Budget is a dishonourable Budget in many ways, particularly the income test. The Government should have resigned. The Minister of Finance said: ``We knew right from the start that there were difficult decisions to be made.''. Her words were: ``Right from the start''. So there is no question about knowing from the word ``go'' that in the view of Cabinet and the Minister of Finance there were difficult decisions to be made. The Government should have made the difficult decision to resign. It should have said to the country that it could not keep its promises and that it would go back to the people and let them decide. Many people want to retain the public health service. They do not want to see the private sector coming into health services. We now have a user-pays system. The Cabinet's favourite word is ``targeting''. It is moving away from public health. However, I have to say that not everything to do with health in the Budget is bad. The increased access for low-income people is to be applauded, but the erosion of the public health system by putting in, for instance, levels of income at which people have to pay to go to hospital, is something never before seen in New Zealand. It has all been because a few people in Cabinet, and probably many more in Treasury, have said that to increase taxes is the wrong way to go. The whole country welcomes the fact that interest rates have come down, but we have had months in which they could have come down much sooner. Would the Minister of Finance deny that interest rates have been held up by Treasury's intervention and that they could have come down much further? Even this morning the Minister of Finance said that she is removed from the Reserve Bank. She said: ``What gives our monetary policy framework its credibility is the independence of the Reserve Bank, and that's going to be jealously guarded.''. She says that she read the news on her computer screen this morning about the reduction in interest rates at the same time as everyone else. I wonder whether everyone believes that. I wonder whether that is credible. I wonder whether there was an occasion a few weeks or a few months ago when the Prime Minister suggested that the Reserve Bank was acting incorrectly. The member for Birkenhead thinks that that is a little far-fetched but he should think it through. The Minister of Finance went on to say this morning that the policies had to be sustainable both economically and politically. ``Politically'' is an interesting word. A little of the pressure is now coming off and, therefore, interest rates are coming down, which means that the Budget is, supposedly, becoming politically acceptable. In the meantime many businesses are finding it difficult to survive. In the meantime unemployment is continuing to climb in an unprecedented way. An interesting aspect of the Budget is that it has a sibling that was born on December---the benefit cuts. When one couples the Budget with, for instance, the housing changes, and with the housing supplement that, in fact, amounts to a cut--- I can tell the member for East Cape, who is trying to interject, that when the Budget is coupled with the December benefit cuts one finds that poor families have been made poorer. The Minister of Social Welfare admits that those families were taken to the bone and screwed down to their limit. The member for Awarua, who is the Senior Government Whip, shakes his head and smiles. If that were the case, would one have expected the Minister of Social Welfare and the Government to make matters even more difficult for such families? I certainly would not have expected that. It is a dishonourable and nonsensical Budget. The Budget is obviously one on which the Government's back-bench members have not been consulted in any way.

Take it easy, honourable Minister; I would not do that. I do not think that the restriction on ammunition is the way to go, and I think likewise with the photographs. What we really need to do is to register all arms. We register every holder of a licence for firearms but we do not register the actual arms, and I think that that is the missing link. If people had to register every firearm that they owned, that would not necessarily immediately create a huge burden for the police. The police then could check up to ensure that people had registered. If a person was found not to have registered a firearm, or if someone had broken any of several parts of the Arms Act itself, that person's licence should be removed. The relevant sections are sections and , and sections through to . For instance, section refers to unlawful carriage or possession of a firearm; section refers to use of a firearm to prevent arrest; section refers to carrying a firearm with criminal intent; and section refers to obstruction of the police. I think that, if there is an infringement of any of those sections of the Arms Act, that person's licence should be revoked and the firearm should be removed. In fact, section of the principal Act already contains a lot of powers. If someone is in breach of the Arms Act the police may search that person, the vehicle, the package, or anything in that person's possession. The police may detain that person and may seize any firearm. Also, if the police have reasonable grounds to suspect that a person has a physical or mental condition that will render that person incapable of proper control of a firearm, they may without warrant enter a place, search that person and that place, detain that person, and seize any firearm. What we really need to do is to enforce that law, instead of bringing in restrictions on ammunition sales that will not make much change, and instead of bringing in photographs that will cost people a lot and that will not really improve the way in which the law is being handled. Of course, the problem with David Gray was that he was not picked up on soon enough. I understand that he actually presented a firearm at a bookseller. In my opinion, the way in which to deal with that kind of person is to make the law more strict, or to encourage the police to be more inclined to deal with such people and to remove their firearms licences and their firearms. I also think that the Bill should address the problem of how one should reinstate a firearms licence. It is a bit like a judge sending an errant driver to a defensive driving course. There could be a standard psychological test and a standard practical test to determine whether people were safe psychologically and practically in terms of using their firearms. Of course, there would also need to be a provision enabling a firearms licence to be revoked for a specific period; after that time a person could be considered for reinstatement. People who are concerned that MMP will not work, today have seen a very good example of how it will work. We have seen something go through this House today---supported by United New Zealand and promoted by the National Government---that has been thrown out of two select committees. Select committees of this Parliament are the committees that examine and hear the submissions, that discuss and deliberate, and that make decisions and recommendations. Two select committees threw this out. This Government brought it back today. The Government's coalition partner got in behind as usual and supported the Government. It is a very sad day for the democratic process in New Zealand when there is absolutely no regard for the parliamentary process, and no regard for the many people who made submissions on this aspect of the legislation in particular, in relation to advances for major home repairs. The Minister has simply forced this through the House, supported by United New Zealand. I think it is an absolute disgrace. I think that New Zealanders have a right to be very concerned about it. I also want to mention today the abolition of the special rate of training benefit for married couples. This is a very small sum of money---$ a week is the amount that a married person can get through a training benefit. The Labour members of the select committee reserved their position on this. We do understand there is a strong case to do away with this benefit when it is not required because people are not on low incomes. However, we did not support this clause in the end, because of the inequity that exists within the whole system and because of the poor access to education that many people, especially women, have. Women often do not enter into training until after they have married and raised a family. This is still a generational issue. Many women would now like to access training. They were married at a time when they did not work and their husband expected them to stay home and mind the children. That was the way our society functioned. Those rules are changing now. A number of women would like to get back into training after they have had a family. This is one way of offering them the support to do that, without their being reliant on the support of their husband to enable them to go back into education and training. Labour's education policy is for lifelong access to education. A number of the very high fees and costs that are incurred in education at the present time will go under the next Labour Government. But at the present time the cost of education is prohibitive. I believe there are still women out there who are affected by the fact that they do not have any income. Their husband's income is still deemed to be just that---the husband's income. I am also aware that some weeks ago in this House we passed legislation that stated that somebody who applied for the widows benefit, even if that person was years old, would have to be available for employment, which meant that person would also have to be available for training. What we would like to do is to say to older women in their late s or early s: ``You can get out there now and get the qualifications and skills you need so that if you do become reliant on your eligibility for a widows benefit, you will be able to go out there and offer yourself for employment because you have had a chance to get those skills.'' I believe that we are still dealing with people in this country---as I said, it is a generational thing---who will need that training at a later stage of their lives if they are going to be able to take up the cudgels when they are and widowed but do not have access to the widows benefit until they have been available for employment. I do have concerns about that. It is a contextual concern about what is happening in the rest of society at the present time. I believe that that $ a week, although it seems trivial, is still very, very important in making available to many women those opportunities that they will need, thanks to the changes to benefits such as the widows benefit. I would also like to take the opportunity to point out that superannuitants are not beneficiaries. I get sick of hearing in this House superannuitants being called beneficiaries. Most of them have worked all their lives and paid their taxes. They have never been dependent. This issue is quite important to a number of superannuitants. They have paid their taxes and do not believe that they are receiving a benefit.

Unfortunately, Mr Brownlee did not have the benefit of attending the select committee for the past years, and I am disappointed in the Minister, because he did. He knows that there were very strong arguments against taking people with disabilities, calling them sick, and transferring them to the health service---especially transferring them to a regional health authority, which is one of the most nameless, faceless bodies we have in this country. Nobody has access to the regional health authorities---they are impossible to get to---and to a regional health authority in which there was no appeal process. So when the regional health authority says: ``No, and that's all you're going to get, so like it or lump it.'', the person with a disability, thanks to Labour members on that committee, now has an appeal authority he or she can go to. But that does not account for the fact that all the social services they are provided with are not funded through the regional health authority. If the Minister talks to the providers in his own electorate he will find out that they are scraping the bottom of the barrel. The regional health authority has cut them right down to the bone. They cannot afford to meet the basic needs of these people on the level of funding that the Minister's Government is giving to these people, through this peculiar regional health authority structure. Labour members were totally opposed to these people having different rights from other members of the community; to be told that: ``From now on you will access all your services through regional health authorities, and you will not be entitled to the same entitlements through the Income Support Service that other New Zealanders are entitled to.'' We now have a knack of looking at the accommodation supplement as though it is a benefit, for heaven's sake! Remember when the rents went up? Mr McCully, the then Minister of Housing, and Jenny Shipley told us that there would be a top-up paid through the Income Support Service and that it was to be called the accommodation supplement. That supplement would assure New Zealanders that there would be no more that $ difference between what people are paying for their State house now and what they were paying under a National Government. Now that supplement is a benefit. Now we are in the business of removing it from people with disabilities. This is exactly why the Labour Party opposed the accommodation supplement and why it opposed the transferring of residential services and disabilities services across to the regional health authorities. It is all about the Government removing access and entitlement, and removing eligibility from a group of people who are perhaps the most vulnerable and who rely most on these services. The fact is that in many instances that accommodation supplement would meet the shortfall between what the regional health authorities are actually funding and what it costs to provide services for those with disabilities. There is very little flexibility in the way the regional health authorities meet these costs. It is done on a fairly flat rate. People who have different disabilities often have a different range of needs. The one issue that comes up all the time with providers is the very high cost of continence aids for some people and the fact that regional health authorities do not include that in their funding. That is one example when the accommodation supplement could have been used to meet that shortfall through vote: Health. That cannot be done now because that entitlement has been removed from people who have disabilities and who have their residential services provided by the regional health authorities. If the Minister could assure people that the health funding to the regional health authorities and, in turn, its funding to the providers will be sufficient to meet those needs, then he could stand up and take the high moral ground about those who need support services and New Zealanders who want benefits, and everything else. The reality out there is that these people are not having their needs met and their families are in a position of continually lobbying for the family member who is receiving residential services. The need is no longer met under this Government.

I am glad the Minister of Justice is aware of that. Why have National Party members not taken a call to substantiate their position on this matter? None of them has. The Hon. Katherine O'Regan is fully aware of the discussion that went on in the select committee and the submissions that were received. This matter was the focus of the people who came before the committee. There is absolutely no reassurance. What we have heard is the deafening silence of the Government. This clause is wrong because it removes discretion. We have become used to that with this Government. It has removed discretion from the director-general, it has removed all the flexibility from our legislation, and it has made rigid rules that have to be applied in all circumstances. But this clause actually removes from individuals their discretion to make choices about the way in which they are cared for and the way in which their care is undertaken. For a start, the clause states that people with disabilities have to go to a registered medical professional. A number of people with disabilities rely on a variety of health experts for their treatment. Again, they will not have a choice. The Government has said that they will receive their services through the regional health authorities, and that they will be funded to see only a registered medical professional. Those people will lose yet another choice. I have yet to see a regional health authority that is prepared to fund things like the cost of a training course for someone who is intellectually handicapped. That was one of the concerns that the New Zealand Society for the Intellectually Handicapped brought to us. It is not a health issue. The regional health authorities will not get involved in the funding of those things. We brought to the attention of the Minister in the chair the concern of providers and constituents in my electorate that the regional health authority perceives things such as continence aids to be optional extras. It concerns me that either the provider has to carry the cost, or the family has to dig deep in its pockets to find that money. So many of the services that we have taken for granted in this country are no longer provided for free. Every time I use an ambulance for my daughter now, I have to pay for it. The regional health authority does not take these factors into account when the funding for a client is being drawn up. The funding has been pretty standard across the board. As I have said, at least now with the Transitional Health Authority we can expect some consistency throughout the country. But the fact is these costs are not being met. Nobody in the Government has been able to tell us how these costs will be met or what will happen. The Minister has been unable to explain to Labour members why these decisions have been made. There is only one reason that these decisions have been made---that is, to cut the amount that the Government has to spend. It is as simple as that. It is consistent with all the other areas of social policy that this Government has addressed. The focus is to cut the amount we spend and to reduce the level of services. It was easy to remove the training benefit for and -year-olds, because people can turn round and say: ``Well, their parents should be looking after them. We don't want to give these people a message that the State will support them.'' I do not have any problem with our giving that message, but I think there are far more constructive ways in which we could do it without putting people at risk. But the Government cannot give that message when it comes to people with permanent disabilities, so it has off-loaded the cost to the regional health authorities. It has reduced the range of services that will be catered for through those providers. The result is a drop in the level and range of services available to those people. The Government is simply trying to renege on its responsibility in this area. It cannot do it in any other way, so it is transferring the cost to vote: Health. The Government is taking no responsibility.

I am talking about the cuts that have been described throughout the debate---the drop in staff from to during the period that the debate covers. The member for East Cape pointed out, as did the Minister, that that drop was good and that it was a desirable shift in the staffing levels of the Department of Social Welfare. Let us go through it to find out whether the Minister actually does understand what it has meant for the department. This department is the Department of Social Welfare, but the member for East Cape made great play of the notion that cutting staff was a good idea because all that the department is about is paying out some money---a bit of income support---to people and providing, as he said, ``some services''. The Minister backed that up. Opposition members believe that the Department of Social Welfare needs to do some social work as well. It needs to work alongside people who have problems to get them back into harness again so that they can go out and live independent lives. It is not just about money; it is about having highly trained staff who can do the job. Did the Minister monitor what was happening in the department during the period in which the management tool that the Minister described as ``attrition'' was being used? For example, does the Minister know that, as a part of that management tool of attrition, people who work in outdoor skills programmes are now working in child protection teams? Would it be worth the Minister looking at what happens to people who are not given redundancy but who are kept in the organisation to do things for which they are not trained? Are we saying that it is a very good idea for the Department of Social Welfare to be run in such a way that people are held in the organisation but used to do things for which they are not trained? Is that a good way of doing things, Minister? I should really like to know the Minister's response. I should like to know what the Minister believes she has achieved by taking out of the trained people in the organisation--- supervisory staff---when she is on record as saying that she believes very deeply in the idea of highly trained staff. How do we train graduates in the Department of Social Welfare these days, Minister? People who gain degrees need supervision on the job, but there is no one to do that now. There are no student unit supervisors in the Department of Social Welfare any more, because they were part of the people who were taken out of the supervisory level. I believe that the Minister is saying that that is a good idea, but how do we get the highly trained graduates that we all know are needed in the department? Let me give an example of what happens if we do not have them. In my electorate of Palmerston North there were child protection orders in . How many front-line staff in Palmerston North are capable of dealing with that work? Does the Minister know how many front-line staff are in Palmerston North? There are four. There are four people in Palmerston North who can deal with child protection orders. It takes about hours to deal with a child protection order. They can be extremely complicated. Is the Minister saying that cuts that give results of that kind are a good idea? I do not believe that they are. A -year-old child was raped last night in Palmerston North. There are four child protection people in Palmerston North who deal with such matters and who work extraordinarily long hours to try to hold down issues of this kind in the city that I come from. Is that a good idea, Minister? It is the result of what the Minister said was a very useful cut by attrition in the number of staff from to . Those people were highly trained and dedicated to social welfare in the broadest sense, but that is not what the Minister means by social welfare; she thinks social welfare is about putting a bit of money in, taking a bit of money out, and making sure that people are behaving themselves. That is not what Opposition members believe. We believe that we must have a Department of Social Welfare with highly trained, qualified staff capable of dealing with the complex issues that they are presented with day by day. The question that I therefore have for the Minister is very simple. Can the Minister get up again and tell us what genuine benefits there have been for the welfare of people who come to the Department of Social Welfare with complex problems such as child rape, abuse, and all of the other problems that staff have to deal with when the department is in disarray of this kind? It is in disarray. If the Minister will not go down to Christchurch to take up the previous member's discussion---

The Minister is introducing legislation that will allow repayments on loans that are for living costs as well as for fees. That is a very clear difference. Students understand that this Bill means that they will be forced to borrow money so that they can have money in their pockets for living costs because the Minister has cut their allowances. That is a very clear difference, and students understand that. They have gone from having independent basic living allowances, which this Government introduced and paid to them, and a loan scheme that was going to be on fees only, to legislation that says that they will have to borrow money for living costs, for fees, and for everything else that comes along. I remind the Minister that other fees that have come up that he has forgotten about, which the Aotearoa Polytechnic Students Union had to tell him about, are examination fees this year. Students have no money for that, either, but I guess they will be asked to pay that out of this loans facility once again. Every cost is slowly being loaded into this loan scheme of the Minister's, which he used to call a financing facility, when the Labour Government's scheme was for fees only. The contrast could not be more sharp. The Labour Government's loan scheme had a nil real rate of interest. Repayments were over years, not potentially over . The Minister might like to do some sums relating to some common types of students who will be in this loan scheme, such as medical students. The figures that the Labour Party has been producing, and the figures that independent economists such as Brian Easton have been producing, show that it could take up to years to pay back a loan under the Minister's loan scheme. This legislation is a millstone around the neck of students in this country. And the legislation will make sure that students will have a millstone around their necks not only in this country, but that it will be a millstone also if they try to get out for months or longer. This is a real change in the legislation. This is a real change in the circumstances of students, and they did not know that it was coming. I think that is what is most offensive about the shape of the legislation. We are confronted with legislation that really does not fit the policy that was articulated before the election. No one knew about this. No one knew the details of what would happen about a loan scheme, and then how the repayments were to be made. This was not at all part of the bargain that the present Minister of Education tried to convince students would be on offer by a National Government. Now he comes into the House telling us that it is a fair deal to have this rate of interest, that it is a fair deal for a student to pay back the loan while he or she is still on a benefit, that it is a fair deal to have it paid back regardless of whether the student is in the country or out of the country. All of this is to be taken as a completely fair deal that will make students better off than they ever were before! No one believes that, and no one will believe it. Students want an independent living allowance. That is what they want. The Minister has not delivered, and he will pay.

They may well do. But it is no wonder---with the Minister being such a weak Minister when confronted by such dominant characters as the member for East Cape---that he is unable, in this situation, to make up his mind about where to go with this issue. That is the problem. It has been demonstrated time and time again this evening that Government members cannot agree on issues such as costs for rural boxholders. There are different scenarios of where this company ought to go. The Minister has no proposal before this House, or before his own party. I ask the Minister to take the opportunity this evening to talk about New Zealand Post in terms of what it has achieved during the past year, and to sort out for the public and for this House where that company is going. We have some proposals. We have some leadership. Let us look at a couple of proposals. The member for East Cape told the Minister that, on the basis of this performance, this company is ready to be privatised over a period of years. He said that the company should be given a monopoly so that it can generate a profit, can protect itself against the problems it will face once it is deregulated and privatised, and can pay for its social obligations. That is the kind of scenario we heard about from the member for East Cape. Of all of the scenarios that have come out of the Government, that is probably the one that makes the most sense. Suggestions from other Government members go down rapidly from there. The member for Tarawera has a proposal on the table. Would the Minister care to comment on whether that proposal is suitable, given the kind of performance of New Zealand Post this year? That member accuses Opposition members of having a social conscience and tells us that this company is made up of a set of ratbags and that its total arrogance makes it deserve to be sold off immediately---with all of the consequent problems that would go with that in relation to the social issues that we have talked about. This company, which has performed reasonably well in some respects during the past months in terms of its social obligations, has caused massive controversy in other areas, but has the Minister thought through those regulation issues that he is reported as saying have to be resolved before any kind of scenario such as the member for Tarawera suggested can be allowed to happen? I doubt it. I shall turn to the third scenario that I think needs to be explored, because it has been discussed extensively by the Minister of Communications, who suggested one of the most crazy schemes that anybody could possibly have dreamt up. I wonder what the Minister thinks of this one: the Minister of Communications does not just want a sale; he wants an asset levy on business to cover all the problems that we will have to worry about in relation to rural boxholders and social obligations. The way that this will be paid for, according to the Minister of Communications---who, this year, has entered this debate about New Zealand Post and its profit and its future---is that there will be an asset levy on the postal services that are provided by this company to business. This year, New Zealand Post did a great deal of its business through supplying the postal needs of businesses in this country. If the Government provides this levy on that business, as the Minister of Communications has suggested, I suggest that in very quick order most of those companies will find alternative ways of transferring their information around this country or across a city such as Wellington. Would the Minister comment on that alternative plan, and that which goes with it---the series of plans that the Minister of Communications has put forward---in terms of the way in which deregulation may be handled? The Minister of Communications suggested that perhaps there could be regulation across all competitors, which would be an interesting scenario. They would all be regulated, despite their competitive nature, so that they would provide some kind of social service in the future. Perhaps we will deregulate, but we will leave the obligation with New Zealand Post, anyway, by tying one arm up behind its back as it tries to compete with all of the other companies. Which scenario is the Minister favouring in terms of his thinking in relation to this company? New Zealand Post has done well. It has turned in a profit; it has returned a dividend. But we now have a series of competing plans from the Government. The crisis in leadership in this company's future is the Minister of Communications, who has no plan of his own and cannot decide what to do.

It is a pleasure to support the Transport Amendment Bill. The Bill tightens a series of loopholes that clearly should not have existed in the first place, and it will certainly make a difference over the Christmas period. I am sure that Opposition members will be happy to support its passage because of its obvious importance. I also pay a brief tribute to the previous Minister of Transport, the former member for Heretaunga, who had a deep interest in road safety. He should be remembered this evening for the work he undertook. The Bill's passage will be applauded by all New Zealanders. In the past few years New Zealanders have become aware that drinking and driving is a cause of deep misery in this country and that people who drive with alcohol in their blood are a threat to us all. Each time we go on to the roads and pass a car we are dicing with death, and it is important that we know that the person driving the other car is sober and able to be in charge of it. The Ministry of Transport and the police have reported to the committee their continued frustration with technicalities that prevent them from undertaking proper prosecutions. They can now take those forward, and the Bill will help them in that. Members know how important that matter is, and I take this time to say that much more has to be done. We live in a culture in which drinking is heavily endorsed, where driving quickly, and, often, dangerously is heavily endorsed, and the House needs to provide a great deal of leadership to ensure that the drinking/driving culture continues to disappear and that different norms begin to arise so that people ensure that they do not drink and drive. We should not build our society in a way that encourages that. For example, in the next few years we will have the challenge of encouraging people to drink in different ways in different places so that they are no longer encouraged to drive home because they feel the need to get home, which may be miles away from the place where they were drinking. This Christmas we can applaud the fact that the Bill has gone through quickly. It will make our roads safer, and the Opposition supports that. I shall close by expressing my appreciation to the member for Kaimai for his chairing of the committee. As a new member, I appreciated the manner in which he chaired the committee. He did so in a way that allowed new members to understand fully what was happening, and I thank him for that. Motion agreed to.

The reason I am pleased to speak at this time in the debate is, of course, that / years ago I introduced into this House a private member's Bill, the New Zealand Public Radio Charter Bill. What we have here tonight is an absolute, pale travesty of what that Bill tried to achieve. I am extremely disappointed that, after helping introduce that Bill, after approving of that Bill, after offering a bipartisan approach to public radio, the Minister brings this load of twaddle into the House tonight. The Bill shows an utter misunderstanding of what public radio is about. In fact it will not set up public radio; we will be one of the first democracies in the world to have ``The Voice of the Government'' radio, because that is what this Bill will do. It has nothing to do with the public and everything to do with the Government setting up a radio channel that essentially will be under the control of two Ministers. That is what it does, and members on the other side who wax on about choice, about freedom, about all the things that are coming because of new technology ought to think about that. What they will vote for essentially will put public radio in the hands of two shareholding Ministers. They will have control of it, and that is something no other democracy does. Let us go through this Bill. My Bill when it was introduced set out to do three clear things for public radio. It set out first of all to have a stand-alone, independent entity. The Minister will undoubtedly say: ``Well, I've done that. I've made it into a stand-alone, business-type unit. It's going to be trading away in the market-place.'' But what he has not done is to make it independent at all. What he has done, which is quite different to what happens in all other democracies, is to say that two Ministers---the Minister of Finance and the Minister responsible for Radio New Zealand---will be shareholding Ministers. If anybody on the other side, including the member sleeping, can tell me of any other operating democracy---let us leave aside all the fascists, the dictators, and all the banana republics---that we compare ourselves with that has public radio under the direct control of two Ministers, Labour members will vote for this Bill. That does not happen. What my Bill demanded in order to give independence was that the structure have its own board of governors and its own managers. That has to be the guarantee. If the people on the other side tell us tonight that what they have done is to set up an independent network that can stand aside from the opinions of the Government of the day, they should just think about the Crown health enterprises. We were told they were independent organisations. We were told they were set up to be autonomous organisations in the market-place, free from interference from any Minister. And what happens? Every time one of those organisations crosses over and causes political embarrassment, the Ministers intervene. Well, I remember a place called Balclutha. I can remember that. I know what happened then. I know that every time this Government is embarrassed it intervenes. Can anybody tell me that any Government---particularly this Government---will sit and listen to Morning Report one day and say: ``Well, I didn't like that, but I guaranteed them independence, so I am not going to interfere.''? This Government will interfere. It is setting up a structure that means it can fire the board. It can change the shareholding structure. It can demand more money or less money. It can say: ``Live on a smaller budget.'' or not, because it has control. This is wrong. People on the other side who are standing there saying this is not an issue have to sit and think. How does this read overseas? We set up a so-called independent public radio network with two shareholding Ministers who will, in essence, have control of the network. It is an absolute mockery of independent public radio. I think members on the other side need to go back and think about what the Minister said when I introduced my Bill. He said it would provide a clear charter that would lock in place some quality. There would be a board of governors that would be at arm's length from politicians. He said: ``I will fully accept that. I believe totally that if an entity is to be set up, it should be at arm's length from politicians.'' He welcomed the Bill. Now the Minister has gone back on those words. The organisation is not at arm's length; two Ministers will be round the scruff of the neck of it. This is not distance from politicians. Even in this country we know from looking back at what politicians have always tried to do to the media that they cannot resist interfering. My predecessor in the broadcasting portfolio did an outstanding job of getting distance between himself and State-owned media. This Government will bring back a direct relationship between the two. In fact, it will make sure that the relationship is so direct that only two Ministers will have control. The second element that I wanted in my Bill was a proper charter for public radio. This load of drivel does not add up to anything of consequence. It does not set a charter for public radio. There is some bare-bones discussion about what the station will do, but it is not a charter. If we compare this with the BBC, or the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, or public broadcasting in the United States, it is rubbish. I have to say to the Government: ``Go away, think again, and give us a proper charter for public radio in the s that actually means something.'' This is rubbish. It is really insulting to come into the House and say: ``Here we have a charter, for however long it might last, that's going to guide public radio.'' It will not do that. It is not broad enough. It does not reflect New Zealand in the s. It needs to be seriously reconsidered. The third thing I asked for was clear funding over a block of time. Public radio cannot be run unless the organisation is given guaranteed funding for, I think, in this day and age, at least a decade. That guarantee of funding is what will give broadcasters the ability to challenge new ideas, to be experimental, and to say ``No'' to politicians when they feel like it, because they know their funding will not be changed. Without it the organisation will be constantly worried about whether it can say things, whether it is independent, and whether it should be ratings-driven rather than public radio. All of that comes into it. In this Bill we see nothing about clearly identifying stable income for this organisation over a block of time. The BBC set the standard with funding for years, and out of that clear block of funding grew one of the most independent and respected broadcasting organisations in the world. If we reduce the funding for public broadcasting in this country to something that is given at the whim of the Minister and is changed each year, we might as well give it away. That is not public radio. Public broadcasters need clear independence, and that does come from a block of funding guaranteed over a period of time. The Government is playing with this issue. It is a serious issue. We do now have a market-place dominated by commercial broadcasters. They exist for one thing---and I do not blame them---they exist to make a profit. In that mix there must be a group of broadcasters who get up each morning with only one thing in mind, and that is to make quality, independent programmes---whether drama, news, comment, or whatever. That is what they must get up to do. In a free and open democracy, taxpayers' money is properly applied to giving an independent broadcaster the room to do that. The Government has not done that. It has not understood what public broadcasting is about. This Bill has to be understood as a shame on the national character of a free and open democracy. That is what we call ourselves. That is what we should live up to. One of the key ways we can express that is to make sure we do have the kind of public broadcaster that can represent this country not only in terms of its internal broadcasting but around the world as a flagship for the free and open exchange of ideas in this country. This Bill is wrong. I will make absolutely no effort in voting against it.

I stand in the spirit of goodwill. I also thank the Minister. This Bill has the support of the Opposition. I thank other people who are on committee, as well. We worked pretty smoothly on this. I also thank the officials, who have worked on what is a very difficult process and come up with a result that, hopefully, will be good for children on both sides of the Tasman. However, in the spirit of the Government claiming to have lots of similarities with Labour in the social policy area, while we may well agree on practical pieces of legislation like this, we do not agree on things like codes of social responsibility, community wages, and benefit-attack advertisements. We do not agree on cutting benefits, on shrinking invalids benefits, on worthless wastes of time on work testing people who are not currently looking for a job, and on and on it goes. There are vast differences between the Labour Party and the National Party in the area of social welfare policy. This just happens not to be one of them. I come back to the point that the Minister finished on, which is to say that this is an important piece of legislation. I go back to something that began the debate on this issue and a brace of social welfare policies that have come through over the last little while on which there has been agreement but also worthwhile debate. At the beginning of this debate I said that there is something very significant in this Bill---that is, its international nature. We are beginning to go down what will undoubtedly be a long and difficult road with legislation such as this. This legislation sets up the process of providing care and protection for children and young people who move between New Zealand and Australia. But, as the select committee heard, we are now going to face efforts from other countries asking whether we can have the same kind of legislation in place to protect children who move from this country to theirs, and vice versa. So we are getting into a very important discussion in terms of legislation---that is, the inevitable move to increasingly internationalise the kind of legislation we have in this country.

We learnt that that member is dead in the water---that is for sure. The community wage is the National Government's big-ticket item for jobs. Last weekend I think that the country was riveted by one event, and one event only---the meeting of the leading party of the coalition Government, the National Party. As New Zealanders watched that great party meet, their eyes turned to the man who is the person of the hour, Mr Jim Bolger, otherwise known, quite often, as James Bolger---by himself, usually James Bolger. He is the man who has come to be known in this country as the ``Great Helmsman''---the ``world leader'', as he has called himself at times. He rose in front of that once-great party, the National Party, to bring together its members with a vision for the next century---not just for the next century; this man wants to go on for ever. I want to pick up from where Joy McLauchlan left off. She argues that we are talking about legislation that grew out of the employment task force. To a degree it did. It is right that it grew out of the employment task force debate. It certainly has not got the stamp of the employment task force on it, and I want to explain why it cannot have the stamp of the employment task force on it; it is because we are dealing with the Government's response to that task force. Two other parties were involved---the Labour Party and the Alliance. We had different responses. Had Labour been in Government it would have been running a different programme because it would have read and understood that document in a different way. We need to be clear, therefore, that the legislation does not have the stamp of approval of the employment task force---it is exempt from this legislation; neither does it have the backing of the Labour Party. I assume that when Alliance members have a chance to talk they will say the same. Throughout this debate the Government has attempted to put on the record some words that may be read---if people did not understand where this debate had come from---as though there were that kind of support from the employment task force, and perhaps from other parties that were involved. That is not the case, and people need to understand that this is all the Government's doing. This legislation, apart from apparently being the Government's response to the employment task force, is also about two things. We have been told repeatedly by the Government---which is besotted with the very problems it has been creating over the last years of the breakdown of communities and families and the need to try to do something about that---that it is now going down the warpath of saying: ``Parental responsibility is what it's all about.'' But read for that: ``We want parents to pay for young people. We particularly want young people to be paid for by low-income families.'' That is what this is about. We are not talking about parental responsibility in the sense that all parents want to be responsible for their children. They do, after all. I do not know too many parents who get up each morning and say: ``I don't want to be responsible for these young people.'' Maybe, now and again, they might say that when they come home late at night but on the whole that is said with love from parents who, underneath it all, want to bring up young people and give them a good start in life. The Government is saying that parents ``will'' be responsible. What they really mean is they will be more financially responsible, particularly the ones who are most deprived, if we want to put it that way. The ones who have the least money are the ones most hit by this legislation. Let us not beat around the bush with that, either. Let us say that this is the Government that is off down the warpath of being against beneficiaries again and is cutting the benefits to low-income families, in the name of parental responsibility. Do not be fooled. Anyone listening to this debate needs to know that this is a Government that is cutting money to low-income households. That is what it is doing. The Government then says that the issue is all about staying in education---not getting jobs but staying in education. The Government says it is about young people getting the message. Young people are getting the message through the oblique business of their entitlements to a benefit being cut. They are supposed to get the message that says: ``Your money has gone.'' And then a series of words are arriving at the same time that say: ``Stay in education and get a higher qualification.'' I do not know how they will get that message from the cutting of their entitlements, but apparently they will. I have to say that the logic of Joy McLauchlan and the Government have escaped me. I was a bit bemused by the announcement yesterday, which has been debated a bit today, that the Government is backing off from raising the school-leaving age. The whole of this legislation, which began about years ago, was premised on the idea that the school-leaving age would rise to , along with all of these entitlements being cut, so as to lock young people into school where they would stay and supposedly do wonderful programmes. All of these young people would suddenly be undertaking wonderful programmes in schools, which would mean their education would be extended, and that by staying in school they would perhaps get the beginning of an educational career. The first thing is that the Government did not lift the leaving age to ; it left it at . There was a bit of a mismatch. The Government was undertaking all of this kind of legislation, but there was a year's gap. Today, there is a -year gap. I can see Mr Brownlee turning this over in his mind. He has been in schools. He understands that that was what the logic was about. It was about staying in school until the age of . The Government will lift the school-leaving age. It will cut out all of these entitlements that young people used to get that may have been useful to them to do a Training Opportunities Programme, or to go to a polytech, or whatever, and they will stay in school. The logic has gone. It escapes me what Mrs McLauchlan means when she says that we should all be happy, now that the Government has made this legislation even more stupid than it ever was before. It was stupid before because the programmes were not in the schools and young people were locked into school programmes when they must have been better off making choices to be an apprentice, or maybe going to a polytech or a university, or maybe doing something else educational with their lives. It was silly when that sort of choice was denied. But now the silliness has been compounded beyond all reason, by the Government saying: ``We can't lift the age to or as we promised because we can't provide the programmes in the schools.'' There is nothing for these kids to do. There is nothing in the schools that is providing proper education for young people who are not going on to academic training. The Government basically put up its hands and said: ``We can't do it.'' But the legislation will go on. This legislation will grind right on remorselessly. It will lock those young people into the schools. They will be locked in there at the same time as the Government says: ``We've got nothing for you to do.'' If the Deputy Speaker has been reading his newspaper clippings today he will have noticed that all around the country, schoolteachers and principals have been saying: ``Good on the Government for realising that it's not a good idea to lift the leaving age to .'' I want to put it on the record---and I see the Deputy Speaker nodding---that I have always argued for that. That is Labour's policy. Labour has always said that years was the right idea. Labour wants young people in education and training, but not necessarily in their high schools. Everyone is saying: ``Good on the Government for finally seeing what Labour has been saying for a long time. Common sense has prevailed. Labour's policy has been adopted by the Government. That's good.'' When Mr Brownlee gets up to speak he will undoubtedly endorse that policy, too. So we are all seeing common sense about the leaving age, but we have this legislation. Is the Minister not saying to himself---as he sits there remembering that it has taken years to put this together from the response of the employment task force---``There's a bit of the jigsaw puzzle missing now?. Why we are doing this? Why are we cutting out the training benefit? Why are we cutting out the entitlements? Why are we lowering the income to young people and their families, when the whole logic of this measure rested on lifting the school-leaving age to ?''. I hope that the next speaker---somebody, hopefully, on the other side---will explain this measure to us. Why are we carrying on with this measure when the Government has realised that it does not have the programmes in schools, that schools are not able to provide for these young people, that the money is not there, that these young people would have been put in situations in which they would not have the educational opportunities that we all believe they need? Why are we carrying on with this measure, now that the whole base of this policy is clear to the Government to the point that it has backed off from lifting the school-leaving age at all? That is what I want to know. I want the next speaker to come up with an explanation of why we should carry on debating this Bill at all tonight. Just before I close, I simply invite the Government to realise that this policy no longer has any basis to it, and the best thing to do now is to admit that and withdraw the legislation at this late stage because there is no reason to pass it. If the Government does intend to do something about getting proper programmes running in schools, proper resourcing, getting the teachers in place, giving young people a reason to stay in school for longer, let us do that first of all. The Labour Opposition will support the Government every step of the way to increase teaching, to give teachers more resources, to get those programmes running. Labour members will be right behind the Government. There is no argument about that kind of approach to the policy. That is the way things should go. If that is what happens, that will be great. But, right now, I ask the next speaker on the National - New Zealand First side to admit that this is wrong, withdraw the measure, and let us go back to the drawing board.

Mr Williamson at least should post it on the Internet, so that people could be in a virtual select committee, talking about this Bill. Last night people at home were unaware of these changes. The to -year-olds saw their incomes cut last night. The incomes of young people who stay at home with their parents were cut last night. Sickness benefits were slashed last night. The sickness benefit for people already on it was frozen, and it will sink to the level of the community wage. People with disabilities will now find themselves work tested. We do not know what the regulations are in relation to that work test, so people who are now on an invalids benefit will have to wait to find out what it actually means. One thing that is a warning to them is that the process does not require a doctor to be involved. The appeal process that they may go through if they do not like that process does not require a doctor, either. We are going to see such innovations as the word ``permanent'' being redefined to mean up to years. A person who loses an arm and goes along to be work tested will be told: ``That's a permanent disability, so you've got the invalids benefit for years. Come back and see us then. We will see whether it has grown again, so that you can go and do some gorse cutting with Mr McCardle on the Lower Hutt hills.'' Widows and solo parents will see their incomes sink into line with the community wage. They will have the chance to go out and do a part-time job, and they will lose more money than they do now in terms of their marginal tax rate. They currently lose c in the dollar in the $-$ band. They will now have the privilege of losing c in the dollar, as a result of this Bill. We have found that the priority of widows and solo parents will no longer be their children, their families. They are being told to go out to work, either part-time or full-time work. The kids and the family will come second. If some community work can be found for those people, taking somebody else's kids down to the sports field, that will be much better than their looking after their own kids. That is what we learnt from the Government last night. We learnt that , students will no longer be eligible for the unemployment benefit, but over Christmas they will have the privilege of joining the community wage queue, so that they too can go out and cut gorse with Mr McCardle on the hills of Lower Hutt. Last night we learnt that literally hundreds of thousands of people will have to shift from looking after kids, from rehabilitating themselves, from getting well, from being on a waiting-list for an operation, from being a student; all of those people will join the brave new world of the community wage. Last night we discovered that the community wage is the secret of life. It is not after all, as the Hitch-hikers Guide to the Galaxy tells us; it is the community wage. It seems that everybody in this country will be on the community wage. Under Mr Sowry, the whole drift of welfare is workfare. Under Mr McCardle, the whole drift of getting a job is workfare. The whole edifice that they are building with the one-stop shops is all about getting people into workfare. That is what we will spend all our energy on. All our public servants are going to be gunned up, trained up, and focused on getting people into workfare. That is it: no job, just work for the dole; no welfare, just work for the dole. That is what it is all about now. It is incredible. We have changed our whole welfare system, to push people into working for the money they receive as income support, and we have changed our whole employment system into the same process. It is remarkable. What a transformation we went through last night! We learnt about Tuku Morgan's vision. An emancipatory vision, he said. A brave new vision of people coming off the dole, he said. Huge numbers of people in Northland will be working for the community wage on the marae. Tau Henare will be swept back into Parliament on the backs of grateful unemployed Maori in Northland, because they no longer get the unemployment benefit---they now get the community wage. They know that Maori unemployment has gone up by percent already under Tau Henare, but their dole has been renamed. They will say: ``Thank you, Tau. That's great. What a wonderful thing! We used to be dole bludgers; now we are community wage bludgers. What a revolution!''.

One of the problems is the question of supplementary order papers, and whether in fact the supplementary order paper method means that Bill of Rights questions in relation to particular parts of legislation are not taken into account. It is quite clear that there is a debate about this issue. Chapman Tripp Sheffield Young made a very good case that there is a breach of the Bill of Rights as far as part of the supplementary order paper on the fisheries area is concerned. We discovered that the Attorney-General and the Solicitor-General had never been asked to rule on whether the Bill of Rights was being breached. We asked for a report. It was given to the committee through the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, and was dated last Friday. It states: ``Although there is insufficient time to examine the issue to the extent necessary''. It is quite clear that the Crown counsel, Mr Pike, who was dealing with this matter was absolutely unable to come to a final decision as to whether there was a breach of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. Many parts of this particular legislation are objectionable, and my colleagues will, today, tomorrow, the next day, and next week in parliamentary terms, no doubt, be opposing part of this Bill, clause by clause and line by line. I want to deal in particular with two questions. The first is the question of the fisheries legislation. I have been quite amazed by the Government's cavalier attitude to what, in my opinion, is nothing but retrospective taxation of fishers. What is clear is that a Mr Robinson has taken a case to the High Court. It is clear that Crown counsel are of the opinion that he is likely to win. What that case will establish is that the method of collecting fees for the deemed value of fish taken in excess of quota has been unlawful, that Mr Robinson has been overcharged, and that other people have been overcharged. What the Government is now moving to do, even before a final decision comes from the court on that matter, is to charge everyone on that basis, anyway. It is absolutely classic retrospective taxation, sneaked through with the support of one representative of the Fishing Industry Association. If I were a member of the Fishing Industry Association, and I read or heard that submission and thought: ``That's my union. They're the people I pay fees to represent me.'', I would get very, very unhappy. The association's members were sold down the river by their representative. It is quite clear that the fishers have been charged. They have been receiving invoices for a lot more money than some of them are liable to pay. In some cases it might be a bit less than they are liable to pay, but in most cases it is a lot more. What we saw was the Fishing Industry Association representing a small number of big companies that also have processing ability and that would otherwise have to pay a little more in the future. What the association did was leave its other members---the smaller members, the members who fish the fish and put it on the wharves, the ones who are being overcharged---alone and choose not to represent them. I think that is wrong. I think the members were not well represented and it is my view that charging retrospectively, as this Bill does, is absolutely wrong. Later on, the Opposition will be moving amendments to the section that deals with the Human Rights Commission. It is a complicated area of law that comes from the Coburn decision. It is something we will speak to more extensively in the second reading, but the essence of the question is whether the de facto widows and widowers of persons in superannuation schemes that currently breach the Human Rights Act should be left the right to pursue legal action. It is quite a complicated question. What we are doing here is legislating away a large number of the rights of many, many people---dependants, children, and people who do not have spouses---to take legal action as established in the Coburn case. What the Opposition is suggesting is that one small group---that is, the group of de facto spouses---should be left out of that, and that the ability to take individual legal action or to negotiate with schemes should be left to them.

This clause deals with disclosure of interest. Contrary to the comments that have been made before, this is a tightening of a clause but a loosening of the law in this particular area. What we are saying in this clause is that company directors who have business with the company, if it is on the normal terms and conditions for that company and for that business, are allowed to proceed without a disclosure of interest. What it does is stop what might be a nonsense whereby someone is working in a particular field and might have two or three companies working in that field, one supplying to another, and having a number of cross-relationships---in fact, someone might have an employment relationship or a contractual relationship with a company, as many people who would be referred to as executive directors would have. The effect of clause , disclosure of interest, is that it amends section of the principal Act. It effectively reduces the compliance costs for such companies. I think it is unlikely that some companies were actually complying with this provision. I think that the provision as it was drafted was probably drafted more tightly than it needed to be and it could well have been ignored by some companies. The current Minister might not have been particularly influential, or he might not have made a lot of progress on compliance costs, although he has said a lot about it. I congratulate him on this clause because it is a clause that will, for companies of all sizes---from some of the largest companies to some of the smallest---help make things clear. Some judgment calls will be involved in this because a judgment has to be made as to whether particular deals and contracts are in the ordinary course of the company's business and on usual terms and conditions. As we know, in the competitive world today in areas of financing, marketing, and purchase, there is quite often a range of terms of business. Things are competitive. I am not certain---and I would be interested in the Minister's opinion on this particular point---whether the term ``usual terms and conditions'' is appropriate in today's competitive environment. I thought everything was up for negotiation under these free-market days, and there is almost an implication in this that it is a fixed-price arrangement, and that things are not negotiable. If things are negotiable, then presumably the term ``usual terms and conditions'' might not apply. If a negotiation goes on and someone beats an extra / percent discount on a particular purchase---if it is a big contract it might be worth a quarter of a million dollars or something like that---how can we tell who is the person who makes the judgment as to whether it is within the usual terms and conditions? Is it the director in that role as a director? Is it the person who is the managing director or the chief executive of the company? Does that person make the judgment? Or does the person, as an individual, as part of their other business who is dealing with the company, make that judgment? I want to say also, and I have not checked the detail of it, that the comments I made about the previous clause could well apply to this, drafting wise.

The last few months have seen significant changes to our criminal law and justice system. I must congratulate the coalition Government on its activity in modernising our criminal law. This year, for instance, we have passed the harassment and criminal associations legislation, which is fundamentally important legislation that will provide security for New Zealanders up and down this country. We have also dealt with the issue of drug testing in prisons. Today we are dealing with the issue of juries. In the next few months we will be dealing with the issues of witness anonymity, community magistrates, and the Acts Interpretation Act. There is a wide range of legislation from this busy Government, which is getting on with the business of modernising our law. This short Bill gives judges the power to make orders to enable trials to proceed with jurors. It is, of course, a centuries-old tradition that we have jurors on our jury trials. The number, however, does not have any magic significance; it is simply one of tradition rather than, perhaps, planned and deliberate effort. We need to modernise our criminal law to bring ourselves into the modern world. There is no doubt that our justice system is undergoing change. We have to deal with far more complex cases, particularly commercial fraud cases, than ever in the past. Jurors take an increasingly sceptical view of evidence, because they are far better educated and far more able to absorb complex information, and, therefore, trials are increasingly longer. Next year alone we expect to have a very serious trial, as the previous speaker Ms Dalziel has referred to, that will take weeks or more. It will involve hundreds of witnesses and many, many charges of a very serious nature indeed. We can ill afford to have trials of that nature terminated because of the risk that the jury may slip down to members. This Bill is timely. It enables a number of specific features, such as new grounds to discharge jurors, and enables the court to proceed with juries of in exceptional circumstances---and I emphasise that point---relating to the length of the trial, and in the interests of justice. A judge will have the power to make that order. In other circumstances the jury could drop to below members, but that would require the consent of both the prosecutor and the accused. The previous speaker Ms Dalziel gave a wide-ranging address and raised a number of interesting issues that are, perhaps, quite beyond the scope of this Bill, but are matters that we need to consider. The Law Commission, of course, is charged with dealing with these kinds of issues, and I am sure that now it is taking a much more active stance, it will deal with these and other matters. I believe it is important to pass this Bill. It has not been rushed. We heard ample submissions through the select committee process. It is a timely Bill and goes a long way to modernising our criminal law in this particular area.
