The central recommendation of the Thorp report is the registration of individual firearms. I will reply to some of the points made by the previous speaker. The major concern in terms of public safety, and as particularly well-stated by the chairman of the Justice and Law Reform Committee, is the registration of the firearms. It is not the issue of buy-backs or of authorities, it is the registration of firearms. I remind the House of the cardinal points made by Mr Waitai. If a serious violent offence is committed and a gun is found, the police need to be able to know the ownership history of that weapon. That is why registration is fundamental. This whole area has had a lengthy history. Since we had a practice in New Zealand of licensing the owner and registering the firearm itself. There was a major change in because there were concerns about just how effective the registration system had been, relative to its cost, relative to its effectiveness, and relative to the protection of public safety. So in a new system of lifetime licences was put in place. The licences were highly and seriously vetted. A person actually had to undertake examinations and be very carefully vetted as to whether he or she was a fit and proper person to own a firearm. Certain categories of weapons---pistols and certain other weapons---were in fact registered. The reality is that there have been real concerns in the community about the effectiveness of the law. In particular, there was an increase in firearms-related homicides, and questions were asked as to just what good the law was. So in new steps were introduced. Photos were put on licences and there was more stringent checking. Military-style semi-automatic weapons were to be---and indeed are---specifically registered. The Government even at that point thought: ``Have we actually gone far enough? Has the legislation fully implemented its ideals?''. Accordingly, the Government commissioned Justice Thorp in to examine this whole area carefully. He heard extensive evidence. His report was produced just years ago. It has been a matter of substantial dialogue and discussion. It is only after a very careful consideration of all its points that the Government has decided that the core recommendation---that of registration of firearms---should be adopted. Many of the other recommendations are, frankly, in the opinion of the Government, not necessary and indeed not actually even helpful. For instance, should there be an independent authority? The police have made it very clear to the Government that they are in fact the best agency to register firearms. When the police, the very people who are charged with knowing the record of a particular firearm, say to the Government: ``We are the best agency to do this.'', then the Government has to take that very seriously indeed. We have adopted the expertise of the police, as has been well exemplified by Mr Rana Waitai today. The key principle, the fundamental principle, of registration of firearms is being reintroduced. The other system has been tried. It has been considered, and it has been found to be wanting in some respects. The Government has been very concerned. It is simply not correct for the Opposition to say that the Government is not taking this issue on board. It has. The Government has commissioned reports. They were lengthy. They deserve full and lengthy consideration. The Government has acted. I just want to talk about the issue of registration from the point of view of those who would say it is ineffective. Often the case of Canada is raised. In Canada, one of the reasons it is ineffective is that Canada has a federal system. It has numerous police forces around the country, and it does not have the efficiency of a central register. New Zealand is uniquely different. It has a national police force. It has central registries, and therefore this will be an effective piece of law. Also, New Zealand is an island. It is difficult to smuggle firearms in. I wish to conclude on this point of the importance of the centrality and central organisation of the police because it is a key point. What is Labour suggesting? Its president talked about local control of the police force. What was the response of the president of the Police Association? He said that was ill-informed, naive, and would lead to a lower quality of policing in New Zealand. That in itself should indicate the quality of the thinking on the other side of the House. I conclude by saying that the Government has looked at this issue very carefully. It has considered all the issues, and it has concluded that the key point is registration of firearms to back up the much more effective licensing of owners that has been introduced since . I look forward to the full consideration of this Bill by the select committee. I am sure that within a very short period of time New Zealand will have a far superior licensing and registration system for firearms. The net result will be a safer community.

The member might learn something about tax law if he listened. That is a sensible, rational part of this Bill to ensure that inadvertent approach to taxation does not occur and we do not attempt to tax the world, which self-evidently would be ludicrous in the first instance. Other features to this Bill will benefit ordinary New Zealanders. The first of those relates to provisional taxes. Currently in the system is a terminal tax date of February. Then provisional taxpayers have their third provisional payment on March. If members think about it, the ordinary hard-working New Zealander probably has a bit of a lean time after Christmas. Bills are a bit slow to be paid, yet they are being taxed twice in the space of months. Terminal tax is due on February, and third provisional tax is due on March. Anyone who knows anything at all about small business will know what a tough time that period is because of the way in which we ramp our tax time payments. So the reality is that if we smooth out that flow to a later date, then we give more people time to derive the revenue to pay their tax liability. So this Bill now shifts that terminal tax date to April where they are represented by a tax agent, and that would be in the normal course of events for most small businesses. That very sensible, sound feature eases the burden on small businesses. The other corollary---if one likes---is for PAYE tax payments. In those situations we have a situation in which taxpayers may earn extra emoluments, bonuses, and secondary income and are typically taxed percent. But if they earn more than $,, their actual tax rate is percent. So when they file their tax return they often get an unexpected tax bill and that often causes difficulty. We are making a sensible adjustment that enables that rate to be percent, so the tax is taken out---if one likes---painlessly so they do not meet this unexpected bill. This technical Bill that tidies up our tax system is a very sensible reform. I am sure that members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee will carefully consider its provisions, listen to the submissions, and make the appropriate adjustments. I look forward to this Bill coming into law as soon as possible.

I am going by what Mr Carter said in this Chamber last November. He was ignoring the fact of the differential contributions of the two parties to the relationship, and, more importantly, the different expectations that they had. He was oblivious to the fact that he was taking sides. If Mr Carter had looked at that relationship fairly, he would have asked what the expectations of the parties had been, because that is what the outcome should be measured against. When people go into a relationship with the expectation that if they break up each person will get specific amounts of property, then that is what this Committee should provide for them. It should provide fairness, and fairness is measured by people's expectations. Mr Carter says that this bill does that, but he is ignoring what actually happened in his own friend's situation. Based on what Mr Carter said in this Chamber, he was simply taking sides. That is the iniquity of this bill. There are , couples in New Zealand, many of whom have deliberately chosen not to get married precisely so as to avoid the effects of the Matrimonial Property Act. This Government is saying that it does not care what those people actually thought and does not care about their choices, but is just going to ram a treatment down their throats, whether they like it or not. That is the unfairness of this legislation. One has only to look back to see a principled approach to the issue. A principled approach would have been to look at what people consider to be joint property---typically the house, and some shared chattels---but not to include everything as relationship property, because that is not the expectation of the parties to a de facto relationship. That is the fundamental ideological flaw of the Government's approach, as Mr Worth has so ably pointed out. The flaw is that it is simply ignoring people's legitimate expectations, based on the choices that they made. But no, the Government thinks it knows better than them. It is saying that it will ignore the choices that people have made and their legitimate expectations, and will force some sort of model of ideological purity on them by treating them equally; everyone will be treated the same. That is of course how this Government treats issues of equity and of equality: it treats people in the same way. It does not look at their circumstances or at the choices that they have made, but simply treats people in the same way.

Kia ora. Thank you very much, and I thank the House for that. I will take only a few moments. I would like to share with the House something from my own experiences in respect of te reo Maori and tikanga, to give the House an indication of what it is like to be one of those New Zealanders who are proud of being of both Maori and European ancestry---maybe not so much proud of my European ancestry, but of the New Zealanders of European decent who played a large part in my upbringing. But for circumstances earlier in my life, I would be standing here as a member of Parliament---or maybe not---with the name of Rongowhitiao Maaka. But I guess in the s---in the late s, in particular---a lot was happening within Government departments when it came to paying attention to detail. There was also a lot happening socially out there amongst Maori people. It seemed that it was more appropriate for Maori kids to be known by their English names. I now know from my own searching that I was to be named originally after my grandfather, whose name was Rongowhitiao Maaka. He became widely known as Ron Mark and, hence, I was named Ron Mark. My father was still going by the name of Maaka up until the time he died. I grew up as a foster kid being looked after by Pakeha New Zealanders. In all cases I do not remember a time when my Pakeha foster families ever made me feel anything other than that I should be proud of my Maori heritage, my culture, and my race. I had a foster father by the name of Albie Field who had been a desert rat and had fought in the eighth army, in the nd New Zealand Expeditionary Force. He was extremely proud of, and often used to talk to me about, the exploits of the Maori Battalion, and would tell me what fine soldiers Maori people were. He always took it for granted that that came from their warrior background. My other foster father was Gordon Thorburn. Likewise, my uncles, Uncle Lou and Uncle Derek Thorburn, had been in the Army---one was in the third division and one was in the second division. Unfortunately, it was never possible for them to teach me or enable me to learn te reo, or to give me an understanding of tikanga in the way that that happens for young people today. I guess that is why it is important to me now that my daughter, who is at Canterbury University, is doing Maori studies alongside law and political science. It is the old story: we do not know what we have until we lose it. Years later, as a soldier and as an officer in the Middle East, I was working alongside Egyptians and Israelis. If there had been a violation, and we were liaising with them, it would annoy the heck out of me if they kicked back into their native tongue. I would not know what was being said. It was a point of huge frustration for many of the Kiwis working there, and we often talked about how great it would be if we could speak Maori---that it would be fantastic. One effect would have been that they would clearly know that we were not Australian and not British. We would have been able to talk to each other in discussions with privacy. I ask the House to reflect. I think there is goodwill in the House in that everyone wants to see more attention paid to te reo Maori, but it will take tolerance and forbearance from both sides. Sometimes one side will upset the other without meaning to. I do not believe that is the intent here at all. I think there is a very strong determination by members of Parliament right across the House to see te reo Maori recognised in deed as well as in word. Since I have to hand over to my colleague Brian Donnelly, I will close by saying that we are New Zealanders, and Maori is the only native tongue we have. Those who think we do not need it should travel abroad and live abroad, and they will soon see why we need it.

I want to bring the Committee's attention to new clause A put forward by the esteemed deputy leader of my party, Peter Brown. It relates to the disentitlement to accident compensation for personal injury suffered during the commission of a criminal offence. I draw the Committee's attention to something that I do not believe we have given proper consideration to, and that Cabinet and the Ministers involved with this bill have not given any real in-depth consideration to. I listened to Harry Duynhoven speak on an earlier clause, when he explained why the Government would not support measures such as new clause A. He quoted the example of a driver who was one milligram over the alcohol limit being held accountable and not getting accident compensation for an injury to his or her own foot when that occurred in the process of smashing into someone else's car and killing the person in that car. Although I can understand the member's concerns as to how a disentitlement to accident compensation would work, I do not believe that those concerns override the need to do something. I will help members to crystallise their thoughts on the issue, by giving this example. I ask members to close their eyes and to ponder the situation of a police officer on the beat who hears a yell for help, and, on turning round, sees a young lad---having snatched a purse from a little old lady---running across the street. The Minister of Survey and Land Information seems to be unfamiliar with the concerns the select committee had about the Bill. He talked about some minor amendments having been made. There was considerable debate at the select committee about the Bill and the amendments made to it. In plain and simple terms, it is another one of those Bills that extends executive power and removes yet another Government department from parliamentary accountability. The Bill transfers power from Parliament into the hands of the Director-General of the Department of Survey and Land Information---generally known as DoSLI. That provision caused considerable debate at the select committee. Submissions were received from the Institute of Surveyors---I am sure that my colleague the member for Maramarua will know of that body; submissions were also received from the Regulations Review Committee---which is a select committee; and from the Legislation Advisory Committee. I draw to the attention of the House the concerns raised by the Regulations Review Committee, chaired by the member for Remuera. The committee was concerned that the delegation of power would allow the setting of fees by the department to escape the controls that generally apply to regulations. It was concerned that the decisions of the director-general would not be automatically subject to the scrutiny of Parliament through the Regulations Review Committee, which was established under the Standing Orders. The committee was concerned that the publication of those fees would not be required, as it is at present. Concern was expressed that the decisions of the director-general would not be subject to the pre-promulgation process of scrutiny required of regulations---that is, consideration by Cabinet, parliamentary counsel, affected parties, and so on. Therefore the Regulations Review Committee recommended to the select committee that clauses and should be deleted, but they were not. They were left, with only a minor amendment, which states simply that all fees and charges so determined shall be reasonable. What on earth could the definition of ``reasonable'' be? One could drive a bus through it; in legal terms it means nothing. The amendment not only states that the fees and charges shall be reasonable, but it also suggests that in determining any fee or charge the director-general shall have regard to the costs and expenses incurred and borne by the department in undertaking or providing the service. However, it is a monopoly service. No one scrutinises its effectiveness. The director-general is in sole command of the fees that the department sets and charges. There are real concerns about a continuation of the removal of the powers of Parliament to scrutinise the operations of those Government departments. The Institute of Surveyors raised those very issues in its submission. Its main concern was that the proposed new section A in clause delegates to the director-general the power to determine fees and charges. The institute was concerned about his accountability; it was concerned about the absence of any basis for the determination of fees and charges---for mapping, for surveys, and for all services---applied by the Department of Survey and Land Information; and it was concerned about the possible inequities of fees and charges for the maintenance of the survey system. The committee heard evidence that it may lead to an escalation of costs for the survey of subdivisions. The institute is the main body that represents the surveyors. It believes that in the past there was a certain integrity in the system because of its direct accountability to Parliament. It would have preferred that position to remain. Sadly, that is no longer so. Now the director-general is all-powerful, and he has the opportunity to buy and sell land on behalf of the department and to acquire and dispose of assets. He has almost unlimited power in that respect. Those are my concerns about the Bill. It may well be that the Minister in charge of the Bill thinks that it is a minor one; that the amendments are of little consequence. I see the Bill as a major Bill. It is important in terms of public understanding of the direction in which the Government is taking departments of State. In that respect, it is an important measure. The Legislation Advisory Committee was also concerned about certain aspects of the Bill.

The debate is the second stage of basically the same debate. It is probably the only opportunity that members will have to express views on the issue. It is a pity that Opposition members, including the mover of the Bill, have fallen into the temptation of using the issue as a means of beating the Government about the head. The issue stands in its own right. I shall express a few views of my own on the issue, which was canvassed in this Bill and in the Bill that preceded it. I sit in this part of the House partly because I am one of the members who is leaving at the end of the term, of my own volition. One reason that I am happy to go was outlined to some extent in an earlier debate by the member for Eden. One does become tired of adversarial politics. The confrontational nature of our politics diminishes politics itself and Parliament. That has been a particular feature in the House recently. Many people long for a time in politics when we will not be in the business of saying that what we do is all right and what the others do and say is all wrong. The truth is---and most ordinary people know it---that politics is much more grey than black and white. Politics would be enhanced in the House if members were able from time to time to acknowledge the validity of statements made on the other side of the House and to say rather more frankly what they thought of what was being done on their own side. A few references have been made to the problems that people foresee if New Zealand decides to move to a proportional representation system, and it is valid to use West Germany as an illustration. In my first term I went to Germany as part of a Speaker's delegation. I was rather surprised at what one must call an undemocratic system, whereby the party that always comes third wins no seat directly, but basically decides who will be in office. That is fundamentally undemocratic. Some years later, in , I was in Scandinavia and I watched the Parliaments in Norway and Sweden at work. I noticed that in Norway if a Government is brought down there is no election. There is an election only every fourth year. If elected representatives bring down a Government they must find some way to make matters work during the ensuing period. There is something commendable about the Norwegian system. It has produced a degree of political stability. In both countries, and particularly in Sweden, I saw people working together constructively, having a constructive, useful engagement from the Opposition---something, in my experience, that does not happen much in this place. In the Swedish system there was active participation in the complete Budget formulation process, and that gave some meaning to being a member of Parliament. I am not advocating that we go as far as that---even the Government back-benchers have some difficulty in taking part in the Budget process---but a degree of co-operation and a diminution of the confrontational style that is very much a part of Westminster politics of necessity comes out of a system such as that. From Norway I went to Britain where Mrs Thatcher secured fewer votes in the election, but, because of the first-past-the-post system, she still ended with a larger majority than before although more people voted against her. Although I was no great supporter or believer in what the Alliance was trying to do, something was fundamentally undemocratic and unfair about a system that produced that British result. We must also bear in mind questions about the cultural appropriateness of our system. As part of a team touring the South Pacific for the Prime Minister, I have just been listening to politicians in the South Pacific reflecting on the inherited system that they have---largely a Westminster system---and asking themselves whether it is the most culturally appropriate system in the Pacific. One could ask the same question in this country. I make one comment about the timing of the issue. I do not believe that it is wise to put the issue to the test at the same time as another issue. I know that it was proposed that we hold a referendum at the same time as the election. Another notion abroad was that it be done coincident with the local body elections. I make my point with an illustration. In the country had two referenda on the same day. The country was so determined that it would move away from the mindlessness of the o'clock swill to o'clock closing that, in my view, the more important issue of lengthening the term of Parliament to years did not get a fair go. The voters ought to be required to focus on an issue in its own right and in its own time. As I voted on the first Bill, I shall vote on this Bill. I am in favour of its being advanced to the point at which there is at least an opportunity for the wider community to have an input. I hope the time will come in the not too distant future when New Zealand will move to a fairer, more democratic, and, therefore, eventually less adversarial style of politics with the advent of proportional representation.

The Opposition will support the referral of this supplementary order paper to the select committee, but we should note immediately that this does not imply support for everything in it. I think it is an absolute certainty that some amendments will come back---if not from the select committee as a whole, then certainly from the Labour Party---on the matters included. It is worth going quickly through the history that got us to where we are today, because it is an incredible saga of a Government unable to manage itself. I think it is probably incompetence more than malicious intent that casts a light on this history. But there might be some of the latter, at least in previous years. In the Government proposed some changes to the law that increased its powers of investigation. The Government said they would be useful in tracking down fraud and abuse in the benefit system. What the Government proposed at the time was changed substantially by the select committee, which recognised how bad those proposals were. But it did not catch all the nasties proposed at that time, and a little bit slipped through. Prior to the election, there was an outcry by doctors. The Minister at that time issued a press statement stating that the new powers the department had would be put on hold. The Minister issued a press statement that turned out to be misleading. The select committee had this to say about the press statement released by the Minister. It said that it purported to prevent the department from making requests to doctors for information pursuant to section . Actually it purported more than that because the headlines stated that the powers would be put on hold and the contents stated it was only for doctors. When the Government changed, the new Minister gave some directions to the department that actually reinstated the department's ability to make requests of people, including doctors. The department had those Draconian powers reinserted by the current Minister. Let me just say what those powers allowed the department to do by giving an example. Here is a letter that was written by the department to the manager of a hospital in Auckland. It states: ``I am currently investigating entitlement to benefits of the above person.'' Amongst other things, it states: ``Please advise if the father of the child was present during the birth and his name. It is inappropriate to seek permission from `Ms X' for the release of these details in this instance.'' Then ``The information is requested pursuant to section of the Social Security Act. Any person who refuses to comply with this request will be subject to a fine not exceeding $, and, if the offence is a continuing one, a further fine not exceeding $ for each day that the offence continues. Please treat this matter in confidence and address your reply for the writer's personal attention.'' So a letter was sent out to a hospital. It asked whether the father of a child was present at the birth and what the name of that father was. It said not to tell the person about whom the department was asking that the department was asking about that person. That is the sort of thing that was going on earlier this year. I think most New Zealanders would recognise that is a quite intolerable intrusion on a person. It is not just that questions were being asked but also that that person was specifically not to be told that questions were being asked. The select committee decided to do an inquiry into the powers that the Government was using in this respect. It was invited to do so by the Minister. The committee found out that the departmental officials who told the committee ``Give us lots of powers because we won't use them.'' were using them. They were going full steam ahead and using powers to inquire into the lives of New Zealand citizens. The select committee made some recommendations. It had meetings, it received submissions, and it produced some unanimous recommendations to the Government about the way in which it should revise the law. The Government has now produced some amendments as a result of that select committee inquiry. But here is the interesting point. The Government has not accepted all the recommendations made unanimously by a select committee that had both National and Labour members of Parliament on it. The select committee made some recommendations that were unanimous and they have not all been accepted by the Government. There are a couple of ways in which they have not been accepted that I would like to point out. The first point is that the committee recommended the Department of Social Welfare not be able to ask banks or financial institutions about whether people were married and not be able to ask for current addresses from banks. Furthermore, the committee recommended that employers not be able to answer those sorts of questions. The department could ask employers whether a person was employed there but it could not ask whether they were married or where they lived. The Government has not gone along with that. The Government says it does not support the recommendation that the Department of Social Welfare should be prevented from requesting details such as marital status or current addresses from financial institutions. So the Government still wants the department to be able to ask banks and financial institutions the addresses of people and whether they are married, without letting them know first. Secondly, although the Government did accept that information on marital status should not be collected from employers, I am not sure the Bill carries that out. The select committee also wanted the protection of privilege to be extended beyond such relationships as doctor and patient. One cannot ask a doctor about a patient but at the moment one could ask a hospital administrator such things as who was the father of the child or who was present at the birth. The committee---which was bipartisan with both Labour and National members of Parliament---said that sort of question should not be able to be asked of other people as well as of doctors. What the Government has put in the Bill is that a code of conduct may include restrictions from obtaining information or documents from specified classes of persons or from persons in specified relationships. That is not saying that those questions will not be able to be asked; it is saying that a code of conduct may restrict such questions from being able to be asked, and that is not good enough. The next thing that I notice from the Bill is that the Governor-General may, by Order in Council, make regulations authorising the director-general to obtain any specified class of information or document, or information or documents from any specified class of persons, or information or documents in any specified manner, notwithstanding that the making of this requirement would otherwise be in breach of any code of practice issued by the Privacy Commissioner. So this Bill has lots of fancy words in it but what it says is that the Governor-General---in other words Cabinet---can make regulations authorising the director-general to obtain anything she likes from anybody she likes and in any specified manner she likes. The Government can still, at the end of the day, just do what it likes in terms of finding out information about New Zealand citizens. This Bill actually contains some improvements on the current law, but the current law has been recognised by everybody as not being right. No one, apart from perhaps Department of Social Welfare officials, says that the current law is right. No one at all says that, because everyone thinks that the powers are wrong, they are Draconian, and they are excessive. A committee of this Parliament, comprising members of both the Labour Party and the National Party, said that that was so. The Government has responded to some of the recommendations of that committee but it has not responded to all of them and it may in this supplementary order paper before us have given itself the protection to backtrack on anything that the committee recommended. We welcome the introduction of this. I think that the intent of the Government is probably right and what has happened is that departmental officials have gone around the back way. They could not convince the select committee to give them the powers they want but they have convinced the Minister. Whether they have actually told him that that is what is in the supplementary order paper I do not know. They have either convinced him---which they could not achieve with the select committee---or they have snuck something in without his knowing. That is what I think has happened. We will let the supplementary order paper come in. The select committee can have another look at it. The committee is tougher than the Minister and harder to fool. It can have a look at it and that will be good but I expect some amendments will be coming back. Debate interrupted.

The member for St Kilda already is quite clearly supportive of the National Government's remaining in power until the end of , because of its tremendous economic policies, which he is coming in behind more and more every day. Finishing off on my personal views of some of the ramifications of the move to MMP, I also believe that the days of campaigning negatively have probably gone. The Labour Party will obviously have to rethink completely what it will campaign on. Its campaign was totally negative, and now it will have to turn round and come up with positive policies, and that is what people will be able to vote for under MMP. I would give one other piece of advice while talking about the major Opposition party. On most days during the past three years back-bench members have been taunted and goaded and called upon to stand up and cross the floor of the House. For the Opposition to have any credibility on that call it must relax the Whip system. It must learn to allow the consciences of its own members to engage and it must allow them to think for themselves. That will happen, I believe, because the differences within its ranks will soon become evident to the public. I will move quickly on to the economy. The turn-round in New Zealand's economic fortunes has really been quite remarkable over the past three years. The debate has moved from being about whether we have got economic growth to being about the degree of that growth. The latest annual figures seem to vary between and percent. That puts us ahead of European nations, of Great Britain, of pretty well all the OECD nations, and behind just a few of the Asian ``tigers''. I believe that most members of the public do not particularly understand what we mean when we say ``GDP''. Effectively our gross domestic product (GDP) is the product of all our work and therefore it is the clear measurement by which we grow our businesses and create jobs. That is why politicians talk about GDP all the time and why it is so fundamentally important. However, within that growth there is regional variation around the country. My electorate is part of a region that is at the end of that economic recovery. Wellington, in its retail statistics, still has to make up some of the ground that is evident in the Auckland area and the Christchurch area. I suspect that because we have had a large public service in the past---and I do not think we will see a great growth in the public service in the foreseeable future---we have to turn our minds to developing new industry and new manufacturing in particular. We need to do better and it is my hope that members from the Wellington region can work together across the parties for the benefit of the Wellington region. I will now move on to social services very briefly, and then on to employment and some of the policy areas that I believe we need to look to in the future. People talk of poverty in this country. It is not a term I use but I do recognise that some people in our community are in real need. A good percentage of people are on benefits, and they are the people who are on the lowest incomes in our country. Many of them can get by on those benefits but there are some for whom those benefits are not fully meeting their needs. It is my view---and I have had a background in this area---that we do need to review some of the matters surrounding special benefit and emergency benefit payments. There has been a good deal of discussion on some of these matters as to the technical way in which they are worked. For example, with special benefits a person has to have a $ deficiency before additional assistance is given, and I believe that such a policy needs the serious consideration of this Government. So I say that we need to look at some of those real needs of some of those people most suffering on benefits. I have real confidence that the Minister of Social Welfare, who has made a good start to his portfolio, will look at those areas and I am looking forward to working closely with him. I want to make a brief comment on the topics of the domestic purposes benefit and liable-parent payments. Most New Zealanders are not aware of the remarkable history New Zealand has in this area. Since the creation of the domestic purposes benefit in or the number of solo parents supported by the State has risen from , or , to approximately ,. My most serious concern is that so many of our liable mums and dads are not making the contribution that they should make to the families they have created. With the change to the Child Support Act we were given figures that showed that about , of the more than , liable parents in New Zealand were paying regularly, and that percent of those who were paying regularly were receiving a benefit and were only able to pay $ or $ a week. Nationwide figures show that the State pays out about $ billion a year to support solo parents and it gets in just over $ million---about percent. I say that that simply is not good enough. We have to send much clearer messages in the way we tell people to face up to their responsibilities. I have some concerns about the formula-based approach. Some people are doing their best and are struggling to pay for their responsibilities, but there are still too many who are not paying anything or who are paying intermittently and they in particular are the people we need to focus on. I want to move on to employment. Of all the issues that New Zealanders are concerned about, this is the greatest. There are two real areas of concern regarding unemployment. First is the number of unemployed. Twenty years ago, the Department of Labour could almost name the unemployed personally. Today, the figure ranges from around the , mark, depending on which figure one wants to use. That is bad enough. It sits at about percent officially. The unofficial household labour force survey figure for the jobless is much higher. That figure is a serious enough worry and a big challenge for the Government, but what I consider even more serious is the enormous growth over the past years in long-term unemployment. The figures are quite worrying. The figures---and I believe that the Department of Social Welfare unemployment benefit figures are amongst the most accurate for measuring duration---show that the number of those on the unemployment benefit for a period of more than six months has jumped from something like percent in to about percent currently. Just as worrying is that the number on the unemployment benefit for more than months is about half of the total number of people on that unemployment benefit---that is, about percent. Those are very serious concerns. I have my own views, which I intend to work hard on this parliamentary term, about the changes we need to make to the way in which we work to improve the lot of people looking for work. Fundamentally, we have several departments working with the unemployed. The Department of Social Welfare pays their income support, the Employment Service tries to find jobs for them, and the Ministry of Education and the Education and Training Support Agency deal with training schemes. My view is that we need to integrate the services that we provide to the unemployed. I am a great believer in a one-stop shop. Income payments, assistance to job seekers in terms of helping them back into work, and the training schemes need to be delivered by a single agency. I intend to push for that. That would be quite a dramatic change from what we have, and I know that a number of officials will not be wildly excited about the idea, but that is my personal view. It is also my personal view that it is fundamentally wrong to pay people an unemployment benefit and to ask nothing from them. It is wrong to pay them to do nothing. It is bad for their own personal development to pay them to stay at home, to lose their motivation, to lose their contact with the community, and to lose their skills. It is my view that some time in the future we will return to what we had when the unemployment benefit was first created; people needed to be involved in some form of part-time community work or training to get payment from the State. That was done in the s when the benefit was paid out. I am not talking about paying people $ to do a full week's work. I am saying that people need to be involved in constructive work, and in work that requires a fair number of hours for the dollars that they are paid. At the end of the day, paying people the dole to do nothing is a negative policy. We must, for the benefit predominantly of the unemployed people, begin to focus on making unemployed people accept part-time community work or training while we are paying them an unemployment benefit. It is also my view that the attack on unemployment needs to be driven from a regional level. The economies of Gisborne and Auckland are very different. How one attacks unemployment and spends taxpayers' dollars is best decided at a regional level. What one does to attack long-term unemployment in Gisborne is very different from what one would do in Wellington or what one would do on the West Coast, particularly in the development of industry. To pull those things together: we need to integrate the different departmental services that we use to provide services to the unemployed; we need to regionalise those services; and we need to ask the unemployed people to do something for the benefit that we pay them. There will be benefits to the community as well as to the unemployed when we do that. I want to reflect on a couple of achievements that we have seen in Upper Hutt in the past few years as a result of taking a regional approach. We have developed the Upper Hutt Employment Trust. We are using people on the unemployment benefit, who would otherwise be doing nothing, to patrol our school properties from at night until in the morning. Another remarkable initiative that we have is a low-income household van team of five workers who are available to help people do essential work around the house that they cannot afford to get done. The work that is applied for is approved by a private sector contractor and another, who make sure that work is not taken from the private sector. People on a widow's benefit or on a pension can apply to the trust and say that they cannot afford to get the hole in their roof fixed or their backyard tidied up, then the trust is able to use Taskforce Green and other city council subsidies to get the work done. Yet another initiative that is working very well in Upper Hutt is our on-the-job training scheme, whereby we have simply decided that it is more constructive to pay people an extra $ a day on top of the dole to train with businesses than to pay them to do nothing. Those are examples of the type of constructive uses of the dole that can be developed if a regional approach is taken rather than everything being left to the officials who sit in Wellington. That is not a personal criticism of them, because I have been there, but it simply is not possible to design in Wellington head office the best way to spend taxpayer dollars in the different regions when the regions are so different, when the economies are so different, and when the needs of the job seekers are so different. We will continue to build on the regional employment initiatives that we have seen in Upper Hutt. Those initiatives currently involve about people working for the trust, and we hope to do much better in the future. Debate interrupted

I have a good deal of respect for the member for Southern Maori. I am sorry that she was told to sit down by the Whip, and did so. I guess it is her job as a Government member to find what she can that is good and happy in New Zealand, but does she not know that her constituents---particularly the ones I know who live in Nuhaka and Mahia---have been devastated by the Government, and that the Budget she salutes tonight has done nothing to help them? They have told me that that is so. Why will she and her colleagues not face the reality of what the Government's four Budgets have done to ordinary New Zealanders who just want a fair go? She is an honourable and honest person, but her caucus will not listen to her. I hope that she does not give up fighting for the causes of the people she represents. I know that she believes in them. I want to help her if I can, particularly with those of her constituents whom I also serve in my Waikaremoana electorate. Many of the people who have concerns are well known to her. When we have a look at ourselves, as we tend to do in Budget debates, it is often good to have a look at the way in which other people see us. I was recently sent an article that appeared in the Sydney newspaper The Courier Mail on July---before the Budget. All kinds of amazing things are stated in that article. The writer was not seeking any political gain; there are no votes at stake; it was not a Budget debate. The article reported that the Prime Minister had ``called a hasty press conference. It was an attempt to paper over the gaping cracks opening up between himself and Finance Minister...But as one observer noted: `Cracks? Hell, it's a bloody chasm.' The two men who held sway over the nation have fallen out badly. Personalities aside, the split is a critical indication of the tensions and strains which are throwing a cloud over New Zealand's future.'' What is happening in New Zealand is happening in that Cabinet and in that caucus. It is a mirror image: old people fighting young people, race against race, and now Labour Party caucus member against Labour Party caucus member. Some Labour members are braver than others. Some will give notice that they cannot support the policies of the governing party, and that they prefer to support the policies of the Labour Party. Others say that they will do likewise. One in particular, the member for Avon, was very brave, but he was told by Ken Douglas, ``No, don't do that. Stick with the Government party's lines. To hell with the Labour Party's policies.'' The article went on to state: ``Nothing is clear in New Zealand any more.'' Since the Budget nothing is clear any more. ``Backbenchers, who still tend to learn of major government decisions through newspapers, began dark murmurings, and the party's Left published an alternative economic policy. A gulf yawned between Lange-Douglas and the Labor Party and trade unions, as traditional totems were hauled down. Meanwhile, the dole queues lengthened.'' The article goes on to make similar, very well-explained observations. The member for New Plymouth, who sits there looking as though he is going to get a headache any minute, should reflect on what other people, such as the Australian observers, say. He met some of them last year when he and I were there. That is what they think is happening, and they are not far wrong. The Minister of Finance has made many mistakes, but has learnt from few of them. By he will have been in Parliament for years. In his book There's Got to Be a Better Way he stated that MPs should be fired from office after years. It is time he had a golden handshake in the backside, which is what he said members who have been in the House for years should have. The years between to will be remembered as the worst years of financial management in New Zealand. That is not the sentiment of the principals of Registered Securities Ltd, or the friends of Burbery Mortgage Finance and Savings Ltd, which was in the news today, or the friends of Landbased Securities Ltd, or even the Fletchers, the Brierleys, or the Jones's. It is the sentiment of the Labour Party---the party that elected the Minister of Finance, and selected him to represent it and to carry out its policies. It is the sentiment of the member for Sydenham, the little people of New Zealand, the workers, the unemployed, the people who are concerned, the parents, the teachers, the carers in society, farmers, the purchasers, and the exporters. They will remember to as the most disastrous financial years the country has experienced. In February the New Zealand Herald reported the head of the Catholic Church, Cardinal Williams, as saying that the Government's policies were heartless and inhuman, and would produce years of divisiveness and alienation.

I congratulate the Leader of the Opposition on the magnificent speech he gave to Parliament on Tuesday evening. Government members too, know that it was a good speech. I cannot say that he is the next Prime Minister, because Opposition members do not think that the present incumbent will stay the course. That is sad for New Zealand, because, if one reads the Prime Minister's maiden speech, one can see that deep in his heart he probably has more feeling for New Zealanders than the rest of the Government put together---it is just that he cannot get Government members to follow him, or to implement the policies that he promised to implement last year and years ago. I am pleased that the Leader of the Opposition will be the Prime Minister. I like him. He is honest. He does not tell lies. Unfortunately, he is relying on his head. In his remaining time as Prime Minister he must, for the sake of ordinary New Zealanders, re-establish himself and implement his own social goals. It also means that the Government's annual expenditure has grown down to . percent of gross domestic product. Meanwhile, in Australia, where people have their own views about how well we are doing, annual expenditure has declined to percent of gross domestic product. The Budget does not offer anything to my constituents in Taupo, or to people in Wairoa or Hawke's Bay. It does not offer economic growth or jobs; it offers only the prospects of more unemployment. Less than months later, on June, the Minister of Justice said in relation to Registered Securities Ltd: ``The investing public is clearly not at risk.'' That is an important statement. On July, month later, the Minister of Justice told Parliament that the restructuring of Registered Securities Ltd had been accomplished with the assistance of the corporate fraud unit. I shall make a few remarks to qualify some of the issues about the Bill as it came out of the Committee stage. I shall respond briefly to the member for Porirua. He seems to have overlooked the fact that it is parents who administer schools now. I should have thought that he, of all the Opposition members---and I recall some of his first remarks about Tomorrow's Schools in earlier legislation---would remember that. He said that it is parents who should be on the boards of trustees, and that only parents should choose those boards of trustees; if there were to be other than parents on the boards of trustees, they should be seconded. However, it is not legitimate for him to speak about schools that, in his opinion, will now implement a policy that shows that they do not want Maori children in their schools. I do not know of one school that does not want Maori pupils---not one. I should imagine that most schools, if they had no Maori students, would do all they could to encourage them. It so happens, particularly in many parts of the South Island, that no Maori families live in various localities. All of the schools in which I have worked, and all the schools that I know about---particularly those that I have contact with these days---would appreciate having more Maori students in their schools. He may well be a contender. I intend to ensure that it is not this Chamber that he is able to occupy after the election. A second Chamber, modelled on the lines of the Australian Senate, would be able in a moderate, sensible, and responsible way to provide some checks and balances, having the opportunity to provide a second House of review and, in extraordinary circumstances, the opportunity to ensure that legislation was stalled and public pressure was able to mount so that unwise legislative initiatives were deterred. A recent example of that in Australia might be cited as the ``Australian card'' proposal, when civil liberties matters, which were deeply felt in the community, were able to be turned into a considerable political force as a result of actions in the Senate holding up legislative proposals. There have been several other examples of the Australian Senate playing a useful role in moderating the actions of the House of Representatives. Those actions in our system are unchecked and untramelled. A second Chamber would be a worthy development in relation to that problem. I have read extensively the public opinion poll research that has been carried out in recent years on the question of parliamentary reform. I accept that at this point there is no overwhelming constituency for a second Chamber. I am disappointed that the royal commission did not have it on its list of terms of reference---that would have given it some focus in the course of the debate. That may have had something to do with the views of the Prime Minister who, at that stage, as the Deputy Prime Minister at the time, was responsible for establishing the terms of the royal commission. His views are well known and he is on record as saying that he is opposed to a second Chamber. However, it would have been useful to put a second Chamber on the list of the terms of reference because, regardless of the personal prejudices of the Prime Minister, it would have provided a useful and much fuller debate on the real opportunities for parliamentary reform. I believe that the royal commission and the New Zealand people were done a disservice because of that serious omission from the terms of reference. I also want to comment briefly on the actions of the royal commission. It is a shame that this Parliament has gone through the process of establishing a royal commission, inviting very extensive submissions to be made, and establishing a special select committee to review the findings of the royal commission---the committee worked for the thick end of years reviewing those findings and reporting back in detail to the House---but has nothing to show for it in terms of an improvement to the way that the country elects its Government. The Prime Minister should ask himself some very serious questions about that. The royal commission approached its work with some diligence. While I found its conclusions and method of work well-intentioned and worthy, it lacked a certain quality of realism. It was my inescapable conclusion that the royal commission lacked a practical understanding of the operation of Parliament and of political parties. As a result, it failed to put forward solutions that Parliament could accept. However, within the discussion in that report there are some ideas that Parliament should be prepared to consider further. The fall-back position in that report---which was the supplementary member system, not the mixed-member proportional system---has some benefits in addition to the other methods that were discussed in the report. The mixed-member proportional system, which was the primary recommendation, has one serious drawback. It means that there will not be majority Governments in this country; it means that government will be by coalition, and elections will be determined on the basis of deals behind closed doors amongst party leaders rather than by electors and the ballot box. I am opposed to an outcome of that kind to democratically held elections. The supplementary member system does provide the considerable likelihood of a majority Government on almost all occasions. It provides a greater element of fairness in our electoral system and a greater scope for third parties to take part, and a weighting to ensure that parties that achieve a higher proportion of the overall vote receive a slightly fairer representation in the Chamber. For that reason I should like to think that receive a slightly fairer representation in the Chamber. For that reason I should like to think that that particular option will receive further public discussion and debate as a practical means of achieving parliamentary reform for this Chamber. I hope that the proponents of proportional representation are prepared to consider that option as one that provides, in large measure, the result that was looked for, without carrying the serious downside difficulties of the mixed-member proportional system---gross instability, and elections being determined by leaders in smoke-filled rooms rather than by electors at the ballot box. During the past few years Parliament has become more and more of a legislation factory. I make that comment not just in relation to the present Government. That accusation can properly be made against all Governments of recent years. The public has become increasingly cynical about the way Parliament conducts its business and it is prepared to register that cynicism in public opinion polls that have recently ascribed a credibility factor of percent to members of Parliament. Members of Parliament who blame the news media for that result are misjudging the position. Whilst it should be expected that the news media will not always be helpful in portraying Parliament in the most flattering light, I believe that we have to look to ourselves, we have to look to our own conduct, and look to our own procedures. We also have to look to our own methods of election under the Electoral Act to ensure that we do try during the s to achieve a much higher level of public credibility in relation to Parliament. The Leader of the Opposition, who has a personal commitment to Parliamentary reform, has given me responsibility to try to advance those issues within the Opposition caucus. I shall try to ensure that that occurs.

I do not want to delay the proceedings of the House. However, as a member of the committee that considered the Bill, I want to make a few comments in support of the report. Clause is significant, not only in relation to future local authority elections, but also in relation to the future conduct of general elections. It foreshadows the introduction of computer technology for use in elections, removes the requirement contained in the previous legislation for a counterfoil to exist, and opens the door for a greater use of computer technology for the production of ballot papers, and so on. I think that that is a healthy development, because I am one who believes that computer technology could be used to a much greater extent for the purpose of conducting local authority elections and general elections. I know that matter will be discussed in other select committees, and I simply recognise the significance of the development in respect of the Bill before the House. Secondly, clause changes the timetable in respect of the compilation of rolls. It ensures that voters will have days to check the rolls and improve the accuracy of such rolls therefore providing a greater opportunity to protect people's electoral rights. I support the provision contained in clause , and I think that it will have a worthwhile impact on the participation of people in local authority elections. Clause deals with a position that will no doubt occur when local authorities are created---pursuant to the Government's plans---outside the normal period of triennial elections. It clarifies the existing legislation to ensure that the provisions apply when a new authority comes into being, and when the first election for the membership of that local authority is necessary outside the normal triennial period. The clause has been made necessary by the haphazard approach adopted by the Minister of Local Government in relation to local government reform. I share the view expressed by my colleague the member for Coromandel, that clause has been made necessary because the Minister has seen writing on the wall. He knows that some of the bold plans he made and the timetables he set will not be achieved. The plans he made in relation to local government reform will not be achieved in the manner in which they were originally set out, and he is looking for a back-door exit in the form of clause , which will ensure that there will not be the confusion that might have existed. Those three clauses are the three to which I want to refer in particular. Finally, I want to refer to a matter that was contained in the submission made by the Manukau City Council. Its representatives argued strongly and cogently for establishing the order of candidates on the ballot paper by lot rather than by alphabetical listings. They produced compelling evidence to prove that those whose names commenced with letters high on the alphabetical list received an advantage in electoral terms, and that those whose names started with letters that were lower down the alphabetical scale were disadvantaged. That was a helpful analysis, because it explained the obvious reason for the marginal nature of my majority in the East Coast Bays electorate, and I also discovered the reason for the otherwise unfathomable electoral survival of the Minister of Local Government. The chairman of the select committee said that that matter would no doubt touch the minds of select committee members again in relation to the reform of the electoral law for general elections, and that it would be a matter for discussion between committee members. I flag the matter as an issue about which some compelling evidence was provided, and about which serious consideration must be given in relation to further reform. In conclusion, I thank the members of the select committee for the manner in which the discussions were held. I also thank those who presented submissions, and the officials who gave the committee their views. Motion agreed to.

What I am suggesting to the member is that there must be a streamlining of the procedures of the House to lend greater dignity to the Chamber. On the other hand, we must ensure that Parliament and the select committees have more teeth, and that members have a greater sense of accountability for the role they play. That can happen through two different processes. First, we must have greater independence for the member of Parliament, who is, after all, the key cog in this institution. Second, we must have greater power for the select committees, because there we can see those checks and balances exhibited in a satisfactory and constructive way. First of all, how do we achieve a greater degree of independence for individual members? I believe that a little knowledge would be a good starting-point. I suggest that a process of tabling Bills hours before they are introduced into the House, so that members can actually read them and know what they are debating in the introduction, would be a very useful starting-point. However, more important, I suggest that the reform of the whipping system on both sides is imperative, and I welcome the comments of all members in that respect. There can be no true accountability when members return to their electorates and say: ``Look, I fought that battle hard in the caucus and I was defeated.''. Finally, the restoration of credibility to this place depends on members being more accountable to their electorates. The whipping systems that operate in manifesto, supply, and confidence matters will be tolerated by the public. However, anything that extends beyond that on a day to day basis will bring the House into disrepute, as indeed I believe that it has done. The select committee process also must play an important part in reform. It is an important part of the trade-off that needs to be made. First of all, we must ensure greater resources, and I welcome the comments of members who have recommended that. There is a certain futility about the process that states that in a select committee those who come to make their submissions must persuade the officials who advise the select committee---who happen to be the officials who wrote the Bill for the Minister in the first place. That must change by way of the appointment of independent advisers to select committees. More important again is the need for select committee members not to be bound by their caucuses. It is absolutely insane that we say to members of select committees that they should go through the process of listening carefully to submissions and then go back to the caucus and receive their advice and direction from people who have not heard the advice from the submissioners, or from the officials. I believe that if we are to say to Opposition members that we want them to streamline the procedures of the House to ensure that less time is spent in the Committee of the whole House and less time is spent in the second reading debate we must make the select committee process meaningful. We must say to them that Government members of the select committee will not be subject to the direction of the Minister, or to the direction of their caucuses. We have a brief opportunity to debate these matters tonight. I believe that in the next few months we must make meaningful progress. Individual members must consider the matters raised today and look forward over the next few weeks to tabling notices of motion or receiving advice from the Standing Orders Committee, and make meaningful progress on this matter.

I am pleased to hear that contribution from the member who has just resumed his seat. I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. I welcome the Bill into the House finally after a long time, because it will resolve some of the financial problems that have plagued the Chatham Islands County Council. At the moment the county council has an overdraft in excess of $, because there are $, of rates unpaid for -. I must explain the reason that the county council has the ability to rate through a county due, which no other local authority in New Zealand has. The county council has a small rating base and it is unable to rate from general rates alone. Many people on the Chatham Islands do not own land or residential properties. They might fly in for the fishing season to fish their quota for a short period, and fly out again. It is obvious that they should pay their share of the rates, which is done through a county due. That county due is estimated on the amount and the value of the imports and exports for the year. Obviously it is impossible to estimate those accurately, which is the reason for the long period of time from to . The rates must be validated by this process. For instance, in tar-seal has been taken down to tar-seal the runway, but when the rate was set some months ago there was no way that the county council could accurately estimate the value of that work or the price variations for the wool clip. We all know of the problems that the wool industry has had this year. At one moment we have a supplementation scheme; the next minute we do not; but now it is back again. There is no way that the county council could accurately estimate the value of the exports. The same applies with fishing. At the best of times it can be only the broadest of estimates and the county council is able to set a rate only once a year; it has no ability near the end of the financial year to set a supplementary rate, which is the reason that the Bill is needed. We must remember that the county council is faced with high expenses. There are no economies of scale on the Chatham Islands. The Chatham Islands have a population of people, including children; therefore it is a small rating base. At the select committee there was some concern that no annual plan had been presented in the past. The select committee now has one for -, which is probably not the best that could be produced, but at least it is an annual plan and is now able to be scrutinised by all ratepayers and the county council's activities are transparent to every ratepayer. The Bill also validates some of the meetings that were advertised in the past. A small number of those meetings had not been accurately advertised in advance during the past few years. The Bill also validates some of the printing errors that were made when advertising the rates that had been struck. Those are very small points, but they needed to be seen to. I now move on to what the Government will do for the future of the Chatham Islands. It has set up a trust that will take away some of the responsibilities previously handled by the county council that have led to some of its financial problems. The county council has been involved in areas that no other county council or city council in New Zealand has had to handle. The trust has been set up after an interim local authority trading enterprise has been running for months, and the responsibilities will be handed over to this trust. Initially the trustees will be appointed by the Minister for periods of between year and years, with elections at yearly intervals so that ultimately all trustees will be elected by the islanders, which is most important. The responsibilities that the trust will take over will be the meatworks, the airport, and the wharf. It is hoped that the county council will retain the activities that other city councils and county councils handle, which are the general maintenance of the roads, and so on. The Bill is the end of a saga in which previous Governments have been unable to help the county council to run its affairs in a more satisfactory manner. I welcome the Bill because it gives Chatham Islanders the stability that they have not had in the past. The Bill puts the affairs of the county council on to a more sound financial footing. The National Government is to be commended for the work that it has done to get the council back on to a sound financial footing, which is what the ratepayers and the inhabitants of the Chatham Islands have wanted for some time. I thank the members of the select committee for the excellent work that they have done in getting the Bill to this stage.

We must recognise that some percent of businesses in New Zealand are small businesses. That means that a lot of shareholder/employees and sole traders are doing taxation returns. That is shown up in the fact that the Government has had to pass clause , which involves goods and services tax on Government grants. In March , the Inland Revenue Department realised that a lot of companies were omitting to include the goods and services tax portion of Government grants.
