The member for Whangarei could have that seat, come October. I join with others in saying how pleased I was with the royal visit earlier this year because, without a doubt, it was a very high point for New Zealand. However, not only was the royal tour a high point, but the Commonwealth Games were, and the sesquicentennial events and the Whitbread round-the-world yacht race are, as well. Everyone felt great to be a New Zealander in January. There was a good mood throughout the country. People were enjoying themselves, the weather was great, and it was good to be alive. Well, as Government members will find out, all good things come to an end. Those members have been told in caucus, time and time again, to link the success of the Commonwealth Games to the success of the Labour Party when they speak in the address in reply debate. Government members were told to blame the deficit and the shattered economy on ``think big'', and to talk about jobs. However, most of all they were told to link the success of the Commonwealth Games to the Labour Government. It is harder and harder to do so. Government members are desperate to ensure their re-election. Never would I have believed that the Minister of External Relations and Trade and the member for Hamilton West would suddenly be calling for Springbok tours to start up again. Never would I have believed that that could happen so quickly---Nelson Mandela was not out of prison for hours when those two members called for Springbok tours. The poor Minister of Social Welfare could not be more embarrassed. He has produced more retirement schemes and more changes to social policy that have been shot out of the water within a few weeks. He said, ``Let people die with dignity.'' Those are desperate attempts for the Government, and those policies will not come to anything. The Minister of External Relations and Trade presumably will come back to the country walking across the Pacific. Much paper is coming from his office now, claiming that he has been the great peacemaker in the world. Similar paper is coming from the Prime Minister's office denying that that Minister has done anything at all. What do Government members do when their Government is in trouble? They convince a few members that they should retire, Cabinet is reshuffled, and a new order is made. That new order is presented---but what happens? The Government suddenly goes up in the polls for about minutes until people look at it, and it starts to go down again. What can the Prime Minister do? The answer is to go back to the retiring members and ask them to come back and help out Cabinet. Every member in the Cabinet was given a vote of no confidence by the Prime Minister when he asked the other five members to come back. He got short shrift from many of them. The member for Dunedin North, that eloquent back-bencher, said that the Prime Minister had fluffed it and that he could not just shift people around like that and expect the ship of State to continue. He said that one could not retread those old tyres and bring them back again. Surely there is a message in that for the Prime Minister that his leadership, that the whole Cabinet reshuffle in moving into the s, has been singularly inept. He passed a vote of no confidence in his own Cabinet---he could not have the reshuffle the way he thought he could and has ended up by alienating many of the Government's back bench. He has been criticised by the Attorney-General. I do enjoy watching the smile on the face of the Attorney-General whenever the Prime Minister is in trouble. It looks good; he is very happy back there, and I suggest that everyone who is sitting in front of that former Prime Minister will have difficulty. The Minister for State-owned Enterprises was to provide the new, positive thrust to the Government when he came back into the Cabinet. Members all know that he negotiated his position up to No. . He said that there was nothing wrong with the country and that it was like an old house that needed a paint job. That is about the intellectual strength of that Minister when he views what is required in the economic domain. Nothing has been achieved; more uncertainty exists now in the community about where the country is going. There is a fear about where people are going to be next year. The sooner a general election is held in this country, the better. Then the member for Papatoetoe could go right back to that trade union job he had before he came here---where I am sure he will feel more comfortable---because the National Party has a good candidate in Papatoetoe, Mr Brewster, who will fill the position in a more positive way. I heard the Minister of Health speaking earlier in the debate. One issue on which I agree with her is that we need healthier people in New Zealand. I do not think anyone would disagree with that. The Government is concentrating so much on sick people and it should be doing much more in a variety of other spheres. What has the Minister of Health done in the meantime? Fine, a health charter has been introduced. Great words were put together that reflected probably something that anyone could do, given minutes with a pen and paper. What happens when the health charter is provided? Everyone says that that is good, that they like the health charter. However, how will it be implemented? Is money not needed to implement a health charter? On that issue the Minister says that area health boards will have to use their own funds. She also said that she had not heard the Opposition policy. However, that Minister will not hear one more Opposition policy on health because over more than years I have profferred different initiatives to the Minister of Health, all of which have been taken on board. I shall not give her any more; I shall hold back until a time closer to the election. If the Minister for Social Welfare really wants to know, I proposed the cervical-screening programme before the Cartwright inquiry did so. Opposition members proposed a nationwide mammography service before the Government did so. Opposition members would not agree with the proposal made by the previous Minister of Health that general practitioners should be funded through area health boards, and the Minister finally said that she would go along with that position. Opposition members had a fear of the use of generic drugs by substitution because we were not satisfied with the full testing procedure, and Opposition members still await the gazetting of a promulgation by the Minister of Health on that subject. Opposition members suggested that there could be more fees for service provisions in public hospitals, and the Minister agreed with that. Opposition members said that there should be a greater availability of the Zocor drug; weeks later people in Christchurch who had been refused that drug by the Minister of Health were suddenly receiving it. Opposition members stated that the pharmacy ownership provisions should be on a basis of to percent---finally the Government brought in a Bill to achieve exactly that. It was the Opposition that said that the Minister should not put a land tax on hospitals. The Minister put the tax on and she took it off again. Those are the initiatives that the Opposition has offered the Minister of Health. I am annoyed that she has taken them all, including the suggestion--- months ahead of the time it was implemented---to put a commissioner into the Auckland Area Health Board. The affairs of that board worsened because the Minister delayed such an appointment---probably because the Opposition said she should do it. Many people know that Opposition members have moved around the country talking to every area health board. Between us, my colleague the member for Waipa and I have probably visited every hospital. We have talked to all health groups in all communities, and we know what people are saying, because we are not sitting in the ivory tower of the Beehive making pronouncements on high about what we believe is good for people. Only the other day the Minister of Health said that she thought that the British, Canadian, and Australian primary health-care systems were better than those in New Zealand. It is interesting that two of those countries fund their health-care systems on the basis of a nationwide insurance policy. But weeks later the Minister said she was not interested in any form of health insurance in New Zealand. She said that the private health sector was a leech on the public health system. That is the Minister's attitude towards the private health system. Given the public hospital waiting-lists of , can members imagine what those waiting-lists would be if the private sector were not operating surgical hospitals?

It is indeed a privilege to have taken part in the event last night, and I am very glad that Opposition members raised this issue as a question that should be discussed today. In fact, at one point I leaned back to the Senior Government Whip and said that, if they lost this request on a technicality, I was sure that Government members would request the leave of the House to have this debate, because it is most important. I want to pay my tribute to those people who have worked so long and so hard: Matiu Rata, an old friend of the Chamber; Sir Graham Latimer; Bob Mahuta--we hope that he will return and be well again--Tipene O'Regan; Maanu Paul; Professor Winiata; and Dick Dargaville. All those people have been negotiators on behalf of the Maori people. With tremendous fortitude and energy, and a tremendous sense of commitment, they stayed the distance, knowing all the time that they might not be taking all their people with them; knowing all the time that they were working in a very fragile area; and knowing all the time that, at the end of the day, they could be put down by their people saying: ``No, that is not good enough.''. But those people went the distance; they made the personal commitment; and their people followed them. That was a very, very good sign. I pay tribute to my two colleagues the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Justice. Tipene O'Regan referred to the Minister of Fisheries as ``Doug Fish'' most of the time. This morning I spoke to my caucus about the tremendous maturity and experience of those two Ministers, and their commitment to achieving something that will be very positive. Yesterday, we crashed through a cultural barrier. We have gone past the point at which governments would throw something on the table for the Maori people and say: ``Take it or leave it'', without having any desire to negotiate or to achieve a settlement that actually would be sustained through the ages. For years the attitude was ``Take it or leave it''. Is it any wonder that Maori have had those problems and that misery, and the social problems that have lasted a very long time? I used to get very annoyed with people who said: ``Oh yes, but if you give them something, they will come back for more.''. Maori probably were justified in doing that because they did not get a settlement in the first place. People should read Claudia Orange's book, or the book written by an Auckland High Court judge whose name I cannot remember--he has written so much on Maori treaty issues. Some members may remember the American book, Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee. The same thing occurs over and over again. That is the reason that I say that last night we crashed through a cultural barrier. We now are in a completely different environment, and we shall never want to go back to the old days when another group of people, a minority, was looked upon as being inferior, and there was not the commitment that was seen last night in the banquet room. So many of those people really were almost emotionally fulfilled. There were tears, there was laughter, there was the lot, because finally something had been achieved. I want to say to all the land claimants whom the Government is dealing with that the Government's commitment is to achieve similar types of objectives. We want to achieve acceptance, an understanding that we will not go over the issue again, and the feeling that honour has been restored. The two negotiators, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Fisheries, are two people who really did have a very strong commitment. After a a.m. finish one morning, we were all together. The three of us all have ancestors who arrived in New Zealand either just before or immediately after the treaty was signed. We felt that our commitment to this country was as good as anyone's. We wanted a resolution, and we wanted honour to be restored, and so it has been.

I move, That the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea Bill be now read a second time. At the end of this debate I will move that this Bill be referred to the Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, and obviously be open for public submission and comment. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is an important multilateral instrument by any country's measure, but this is particularly so from New Zealand's point of view, given the significance of the sea to our economic well-being and security, as well as to our national psyche. New Zealand was accordingly actively involved in negotiating the convention, and was among the countries who enthusiastically deposited their signatures on the convention when it was adopted in . Some States have now become signatories, and the convention came into force on November . As much of the legislation required to implement the provisions of the convention is already in place, only a small number of legislative changes are required to ensure New Zealand's law conforms with the convention. The Bill is divided into four parts. Part II is directed at implementing Part XI of the convention, and provides for the regulation of exploration and exploitation of resources in the seabed beyond the limitation of national jurisdiction. This will be done pursuant to an international licensing system. This is designed to ensure the orderly and environmentally safe exploitation of resources once technology and knowledge have developed to the stage where exploitation of deep sea bed mineral resources becomes possible. Needless to say, this is some years off, but it is important to ensure that a system for regulating any such activities is up and running before anyone attempts to embark on them. Accordingly, clause provides that no activities are to be carried on in this zone, which is defined in clause as the ``area'', without a licence. However, this requirement may be waived as far as New Zealand citizens are concerned where such a person is carrying out the activity on behalf of another entity or person who has been duly authorised by another State party in accordance with the convention. Clause provides for the Minister to grant licences. The Minister must be satisfied the granting of the licence is consistent with New Zealand's rights and obligations under Part XI of the convention. Clause makes it an offence, punishable by a fine of up to $,, for any person, being a person who requires a licence to carry out activities in the area, to carry out any activity otherwise than pursuant to a licence. The purpose of clause is to confer jurisdiction on the New Zealand courts to enforce this regulatory system. Clause provides that, for the purposes of both civil and criminal New Zealand law, every activity carried out in the area by a person required to have a licence shall be deemed to be carried out in New Zealand. Every court in New Zealand that would have jurisdiction if the activity were carried out in New Zealand will have jurisdiction accordingly, and every power that could be exercised in respect of any such activity if it were carried out in New Zealand may be exercised as if the activity had been carried out in New Zealand. However, the consent of the Attorney-General will be necessary before the commencement of proceedings for offences if the courts of New Zealand have jurisdiction by virtue only of the provisions of clause . Part III aims to ensure decisions of the various dispute resolution mechanisms created by the convention will have the force of law in New Zealand in cases to which New Zealand is a party. The mechanisms created by the convention include the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, which is established as one option for the settlement of disputes concerning the interpretation or application of the convention, as well as the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf and the International Seabed Authority. Clause provides that where one of the international courts or tribunals listed in the provision has decided a vessel or crew detained by authorities in New Zealand must be promptly released, then the vessel or crew shall be released on posting a bond or other financial security determined by the court or tribunal. Clauses and provide that every final decision rendered by one of the international courts or tribunals listed in those provisions shall be enforceable in New Zealand as if it were a decision of the High Court. Part IV provides for a number of amendments to existing pieces of legislation to bring them into line with provisions of the convention and with changes to New Zealand's law to be made by this Bill. Most significant is clause , which amends the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act by inserting a new Part IA, which defines the contiguous zone of New Zealand. The contiguous zone is a sea area adjacent to the territorial sea in which a State is able to exercise the control necessary to prevent and punish infringements of its customs, fiscal, immigration, or sanitary laws and regulations, committed within its sovereign territory. As a consequence of this amendment, the Bill makes several other amendments to a number of other Acts to extend the area in which certain powers may be exercised under those Acts to include the contiguous zone. In this regard, clauses to amend the Customs Act in relation to the exercise of powers to board and search ships, fire on a ship, secure goods on ships, and seize goods and ships. Clauses to amend the Immigration Act to extend the area in which the power to enter and search ships may be exercised. Clauses and amend the Biosecurity Act to extend the area in which the power to board sea-borne craft may be exercised.

I am pleased to rise as part of this Government to speak in support of this Budget. This is a very positive Budget. It is a positive Budget in that it sends good, positive messages to business and communities. When I speak on business this morning, I am speaking about small business---those people, like myself in particular, who have spent years out there investing our own capital, our own enterprise, and producing jobs for this nation. This Budget continues the Government's microeconomic reforms, and it continues on its path to reduce Government spending. To promote growth in this country we need investment, as only investment in growth will produce real jobs for real people. Jobs are imperative, and whilst we hear some members of the Opposition saying that we need more social spending, I think this Budget sends a clear message that continuing to spend percent of our total Government revenue on benefits is unsustainable. We have to invest. We have to get people into jobs, and that is the only way we can do it. There is no other way. This Budget is continuing to produce surpluses---next year $. billion, down from the $. this year, but still a magnificent feat in view of the Asian crisis. The $ million that has been put in reserve signals to business and community that we as a Government will not let spending run away. The feat of the Government bringing down our net public debt from $ billion in to $ billion now---and the aim of this Budget to reduce it to $ billion---is a great feat, and certainly none of us wants to go back to the times when we borrowed heavily and had huge inflation. Inflation is continuing to be under percent, and that is great, as I say, for the small businesses in this country. Many of us remember the times when inflation was running at to percent, the struggle it was, simply to exist---the amount that had to be invested in rising stocks, the cash flow problems where businesses could not survive because they were simply reinvesting, and the inability to provide employment because one simply could not afford it. Small businesses, collectively, are the largest employer in this country, and they need a stable environment in which to operate. They have suffered, and we as a Government have to signal to small business that we have a stable environment and offer a suitable environment for them to want to put their capital on the line and say: ``Hey, we are going to go out and do something.'' I look around this House and wonder how many understand what it is like actually to put one's capital on the line, risk one's savings, and put one's family house at risk so that one can create a business and create jobs. I do not think there are very many. Small businesses do not ask for much. They ask for a fair tax regime, a fair accident compensation system, fair health and safety requirements, and fair employment law. That is nothing more than what the employees ask, and it is something we all ask. I must speak about current tax regimes. Last year some new penalties were brought in in the tax regime, and I hear many, many people in small business cry of the draconian penalties in that new tax regime. It is inflexible, and does not allow the department any flexibility at all in deciding what is fair and what is equitable. Whilst they advertise: ``It's our job to be fair.'', some of the penalties are not fair at all. I have a constituent who simply because he put a wrong date on a GST return was fined $,. That is more than some people get for committing very, very heinous crimes. We must address some of that legislation and make it fairer. This Budget reinforces the tax cuts coming in on July---tax cuts that make a real wage increase of . percent for people on the average wage. This will have a tremendous effect on the economy, it will boost business because it will boost the amount of money in people's pockets, it will help spending, and it has to be good for all. The Budget does that without increasing costs and without increasing inflation. The Budget signalled that the investigation into compliance costs would be continued. I hope that payment regimes for Government taxes and levies will be modified. As one of my constituents said, returns to Government departments in a -month period is absolutely ridiculous. That compliance cost on business is unfair, it is unreasonable, and we cannot sustain it. We have to look at payment regimes. Last week a transport operator in my region was complaining that on May this year he had $, to pay on accident compensation levies---a huge hit on his cash flow that severely impacts his ability to do business in the next or months until he recovers. One of the biggest things signalled in this Budget was the introduction of competition into accident compensation. This will make the Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Corporation more accountable, and we all know that that is needed. The accident compensation system has been abused, costs are excessively high, and we have to approach that issue. We all know that genuine claims are out there, but we all know that there are a lot of false claims, and these claims need to be investigated. I am sure that the introduction of competition into accident compensation will certainly mean these claims are investigated more thoroughly and it will reduce the overall costs of the accident compensation system. The competition will give employers a greater choice and will certainly bring more efficiency into the industry---it will bring down costs. The Leader of the Opposition in her reply to the Budget statement made the comment that the bringing of competition into accident compensation would have no effect on small business. That simply will not be true. Small businesses are already combining in forms of trade organisations, brokerages, and all other forms of insurance, and I am sure that accident compensation will simply be another manifestation of this. Perhaps it shows the lack of understanding that some people have of small business and what makes small business tick. I can tell members that this move was certainly welcomed in my electorate. The Government has signalled that it will review the Commerce Act, the Securities Act, and the Resource Management Act to improve their quality. Last week we discussed in a select committee the insolvency laws and redundancy claims. The Ministry of Commerce signalled then that it was going to review the insolvency laws in this country. This has been asked for for a considerable time by business and it will certainly be one area in which improvement comes. The review of the Resource Management Act and the costs associated with that have to be done as soon as possible and I know that the Minister is working on this. Some of the costs associated with complying with the requirements of the Resource Management Act to do simple subdivisions and simple buildings are absolutely absurd. The Standing Order and the Speaker's ruling are correct, and in the normal course of debate they should be followed. However, I submit that there are some exceptional circumstances in which the House must take into account the role of the Governor-General. Those circumstances relate to matters that affect the constitution of New Zealand---whether a Bill is constitutionally proper, and whether it is proper for the Governor-General to sign the legislation. In those very rare circumstances, of which this is one, it is inevitable, proper within the Standing Orders, and constitutionally necessary for the House to invoke the role of the Governor-General---not the person, but the role---as the House debates the Bill. The issue is whether the Governor-General can, and should, sign the Bill, and that issue must be debated by the House.

I shall try once again to go over the case that has brought the Bill before the House. At the moment there are individuals in society who are not stopping when signalled to do so by the Ministry of Transport. There is no evidence to show what other offences those persons have committed, because in most cases the Ministry of Transport has been unable to apprehend or to prosecute them in any way. The Government is assuming that every one of those persons is guilty of a drinking/driving offence, but there is no evidence whatsoever to support that contention. I concede that some of them may be guilty of drinking/driving offences. The figure may be as much as percent, or it may be as little as percent. The Bill that members are being asked to enact today will empower traffic officers and constables specifically to enter private property to gather evidence on drinking/driving offences. I want every one of those persons to be apprehended and to be prosecuted. I do not want people to think they can drive dangerously on the streets while trying to escape from the Ministry of Transport, and can do it with any kind of immunity. The House should always view with the gravest concern the empowering of any enforcement officer to enter private property and private dwellings by force. That should be the only resolution left that is available to the House to grant in order to apprehend the offender. The evidence presented before the select committee and the evidence heard in the debate have not convinced me that all options have been explored. The learned people from the New Zealand Law Society, the people from the Council for Civil Liberties, and the people from the Legislation Advisory Committee all hung up major caution signs about the way the Bill was being dealt with. They said that it was bad to process legislation such as this quickly; that it should be carefully considered; and that all options should be considered before a final decision was made. Even the Prime Minister echoed those cautions recently, when he said in a statement to the Dominion that hasty legislation had to be viewed with great caution. The Opposition put to the Minister some options that would have dealt adequately with the problem as it exists, but the Minister and the Government were not prepared to accept those options. As a result of the select committee hearings and some proposals made by Opposition members on the committee---I acknowledge that the Minister was gracious enough to accept the recommendation, and to adopt it and put it in the Bill---the circumstances in which the ministry can exercise the power of entry have been substantially contained. It means that the traffic officer has to be in fresh pursuit of a person who has failed to stop, and that the person has to have been pursued by a Ministry of Transport vehicle or a police car that is displaying flashing blue or blue and red lights and is sounding a siren. That makes the circumstance very tight. I suggested that in those circumstances the officer already had the evidence of failing to stop, because he had pursued that vehicle to the private property on which the driver tried to escape. He clearly knows the kind of vehicle involved, he has the evidence of the pursuit, and he has the evidence for the case of failing to stop. If the House made the penalty for failing to stop the same as the penalty for drinking/driving there would be no advantage to the person in trying to escape the breath test. The only evidence the officer is left needing to gather at that point is the evidence of identity. From the weight of the body of law it is known that the difficulty has arisen because when an officer is presumed to be entering a private property for the purposes of making an arrest the implied consent cannot be assumed to exist. In the circumstances I have outlined the officer is not entering for the express purpose of making an arrest. The body of law has clearly said that the officer has the same rights as any other citizen to enter a private property for the purposes of making inquiries. Establishing the identity of the person is just making one of those inquiries. That provides the House with another option that would not necessitate granting Ministry of Transport officers the power of entry on to private property and the power of forcible entry into people's dwellings. I have no sympathy with the person who has committed the offence. The forcible entry by law enforcement officers into that house is a very traumatic event for the family that lives in that dwelling, and should be prevented by any means possible. I believe that the option has been given, but the Government has declined to take it. I moved several amendments that would provide some additional protections for citizens, because I realised that the Government might not be prepared to take that option. I assume that the Bill will receive the royal assent---probably tonight or within the next hours. When that royal assent is received the powers are available to be used. At the select committee hearing the Minister admitted that the Government did not have in place a code of practice for Ministry of Transport officers to use those powers properly. I suggested in an amendment that in the event of a forcible entry the code of practice available to the police should be used. To protect citizens, the complaints procedure that is already available through the Police Complaints Authority should be an avenue for aggrieved citizens to use to lodge complaints. Unfortunately, the Government turned down both of those options, and said that it would do something in the future. That is not good enough. The Opposition put another option before the House: that the legislation should be terminal, and the public should be given the opportunity of being consulted widely on the best options; and that the powers provided in the Bill could be considered as emergency powers. The Government failed to adopt that option also, and that left the Opposition with no option but to vote against the Bill.

It is attacking the fundamental consensus of the welfare State, public health, and public education. When the Prime Minister was previously in Government he had a wage freeze. When he had a previous chance at it there were twice as many disputes as there were under the member for Mount Albert. Light the light! Light the beacon! Show some vision! Heal the wounds! Raise the dead! The opposite will happen. He said: ``What will the Labour Party do?''. I tell him that there have been massive changes in industrial relations over the past few years. Heroic changes have been made. Look at the waterfront! There are percent fewer people there now. That happened in a negotiated way. People understood what was happening. They went through it. Look at the dairy workers! There was a year no-strike accord. That was something good in this country. Now the Government is saying: ``Let's have a free market. Let's have a punch-up.''. Unions enjoyed agreement. We were getting industrial peace. The agreement was working. There was a feeling of commitment. That is what the growth agreement was all about. The Kinleith mill was upgraded. Investment worth $ million went in to create new jobs.

How can they believe that there has been full consultation, if the senior Government back-bencher, who is in charge of the select committee, had not seen the Bill before it came to Parliament? I do not want to hear a speech made on a marae in or years by someone who says that Maori were not given their time. Last week I asked: ``Hey, what's this about regulations?''. Surely it would be wise for Government members to send their regulations, at least, to the select committee so that its members could read them? We are being put in a position of deciding whether we are for or against issues that we have not seen, and of explaining them to and educating the people. Earlier in the debate I raised a point of order several times---stretching the Speaker's tolerance each time, I suspect---saying that if there are any supplementary order papers and amendments then, please, let the Opposition see them. Opposition members have some amendments; Government members may have amendments that will mean that we do not need ours---that will be fine. Let us do our best; we have circulated the amendments to colleagues. But still the member who has just spoken demanded to know where we stood on amendments that we have not seen and on ideas that we have not canvassed. I have had to have telephone conferences with our people all over the country explaining and trying to hose down the matter, not to light it. There is a difference between demagoguery and democracy. I was pleased when I heard the Acting Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice speak in the adjournment debate when this deal was announced---as far as it went. I remember speeches and debates that I have been involved in, when the Prime Minister said: ``I will not take New Zealand down the road to apartheid'', and that there would be no special deals for anybody as we are all New Zealanders. I stood there looking like a fool and saying that there ought to be special deals, because everyone cannot be treated in the same way; the sick cannot be treated in the same way as the healthy. I knew where the votes were; he did, too. It was good to see him speak for the whole of New Zealand. Let us go through the detail of the Bill. I have gone back through Hansard. I should like to know of any promises that the Government has not broken. There might be one or two, but the Government has been in office for only a year. What will it do over the next years? This incompetent Government produced a Budget---the mother of all U-turns. Twenty major decisions have been reversed since the Budget. It is no wonder that the electorate is dizzy and that the markets are confused. The Government comprises an incompetent gang. Is it trusted by the schools? Is the incompetent gang trusted by the elderly, the sick, or the frail? Who amongst the growing army of unemployed---, more than a year ago---trusts the Government? The Government itself had no trust in the former Minister of Employment. He was sacked because he failed. The new Minister of Employment is known throughout the country as having promised , jobs. We shall see how he gets on. The Government is incompetent. It has no stars. All of its members are second-rate, and nobody in New Zealand feels proud of them. Who feels proud of our New Zealand Government? Does anyone in this country say that the Government speaks for him or her and that it is on his or her side? The Minister of Conservation, the Minister of Energy, and the Minister for the Environment are supposed to look after the ``Greens''. The Minister for the Environment says that he wants nuclear generation in this country. What an incompetent! The Minister for Disarmament and Arms Control wants nuclear arms brought to New Zealand. The Minister of Police promised: ``Watch my lips. If I don't get $ million I'll resign. I'll give you police people on the beat.''. Has that happened? No, it has not happened at all. Are we worse off or better off? We are worse off. What is happening? In this country a sexual offence is committed every hours, a violent robbery every hours, a homicide every days, someone is assaulted every minutes, and a burglary is committed every minutes. Those are all increases in every aspect of crime, and we heard the leader of the National Party of the time say that he would wage war on crime. Has he done that? Has he got his $ million? No, not at all. If inflation is taken into account, the Police vote has been cut by $ million. What is happening to our pleasant country? Everybody knows that the Government does not tell the truth. It cannot be trusted. The Government has invaded the central principles of New Zealand society---the things we all used to believe in. It has no mandate; it cannot be trusted. It is a Government by trial and error---trial, error, and terror. It is no longer trusted. No one knows what it will do because often it does not know itself. It is a mass of hesitating contradictions. Its words are no longer a guide to its deeds. I do not know how it can continue for two more years. Government members are the people who promised a decent society. Those words ring hollow now, do they not? Society was to be decent and inclusive. The Government is finished. The power in this country comes from the people. The Government is not accepted; it has no moral authority, because people just do not believe anything it says. From time to time Government members may stumble across a truth, but, if they say that truth, no one will believe them. More important, the Government's policies are not fair for all New Zealanders. The mini-Budget before Christmas cost the bottom percent $ and the top percent $. The New Zealand Herald stated that poor families and modest-income earners have had a cut of percent in their spending power while the top percent have lost percent. The bottom-income earners are paying percent more, the top-income earners are losing only percent. Is that fair? It is not fair. Is the Government doing it deliberately? I do not know that any more because it is clumsy and incompetent. The same research states that all those user-pay policies are anti-family and hammer the person who battles the most. As for those filthy rich on $, a year, they will be paying more. The Government is so out of touch. The Minister who is supposed to speak for the poor and the battlers got up and said: ``Some elderly people own their own homes.''. Is that not the Kiwi dream? The Government ought to go. Two years is too long. It will be living hell for the Ministers and for the back-benchers. None of them has confidence in the other, and over the next years they will be further under siege and thus further out of touch. Why can they not seek a mandate from the country? They have broken every promise they made a year ago. I have not mentioned the Prime Minister, such as he is. Why should I mention him when the country has given up on him? The country pays no attention; there is no authority; there is no direction; there is no leadership; there is no trust. One cannot run a Government when one half of the Ministers is leaking and the other half is running the other way.

I rise to support the Prime Minister in this resolution. It is entirely appropriate. Sir Thaddeus is an outstanding New Zealander. He was an outstanding citizen and civil servant in war time and in peace. As has been mentioned, he served on seven royal commissions on subjects as diverse as Maori courts, horse racing, and nuclear energy. He was appointed by many Governments, and saw many Prime Ministers and Attorneys-General come and go. I think that I could save Parliament at least minutes if I simply tabled his entry in Who's Who. He distinguished himself in the law and in everything he did. He was the first president of the New Zealand Press Council. He did a lot of work for the council, and we should be grateful for that. But perhaps the most important headline about him was in the Evening Post when he retired. It stated that he was an eminent judge who had the love of his country and his fellow men. Despite having serious and profound jobs, he stayed a Kiwi character. He did not pretend to be an Englishman, and he still has that twinkle in his eye that makes him such a character and such a unique New Zealander. Motion agreed to.

I acknowledge it all the time. I do not stop acknowledging it. The Minister of Education then stood up with the paper Path to . Frankly, if I had put out a paper like that, I would have been laughed out of the Chamber. What a weak paper; it was plagiarised from a Trade Development Board report of a few years ago. What a joke! Michael Wall said to the Prime Minister: ``Hey, you've got to show some vision.''. The Prime Minister asked what that meant, and Michael Wall said: ``Don't talk about what is happening this year; talk about the year .''. Give us a break! People know that that is stupid. People know that things in this country are wrong, and they want things changed. The most beautiful line from the Minister of Education was: ``We shouldn't spend people's money to make ourselves look good or look popular.''. Is that what he said? Did he say that? The most cynical operation that I have ever seen in politics is the funding by this Government of $ million worth of advertisements on television and in the newspapers about skilling New Zealanders. I agree that people should be more skilled. Who would not agree with that? That is a good idea. Of course we should be more skilled, but the opposite is happening. At the same time that the Government spends $ million to tell New Zealanders to become better skilled, it cuts payments to universities, it cuts payments to polytechnics, and it increases student fees. Everything is the opposite of what it appears to be. The Government has cut the amount of money provided to a student going to university, it has cut the amount of money provided to a student going to a polytechnic, it has increased student fees, and it has broadcast television advertisements telling young people to be more skilled. That is a corruption of everything that is honest in our system. The Government now has its health campaign. What a joke! I now believe that the health campaign is so wrong, and that people understand it so well, that every dollar that the Government spends may as well be a dollar donated to my political party. The whole campaign is based on the fact that people are stupid. People are not stupid. In Parliament today the Deputy Leader of the Opposition asked: ``How does one judge whether the campaign has been successful?''. Look at the eyes of Government members; they will judge it successful if they are re-elected. The Government is trying to steal this election with taxpayers' money. The first advertisement takes place in a hospital---people have to have seen it; it is shown five times a night. A woman stands in an empty hospital and says that that is bad. Where is this hospital? It is on the North Shore. Who built that hospital? A Minister of Health in a National Government built that hospital in his own electorate. Amanda Millar, the journalist in that advertisement, was the press secretary of the Minister of Social Welfare. Another person in one of the advertisements was a National Party nominee for a parliamentary seat in the Manawatu. Come on! It is a case of jobs for the boys. One campaign has not gone through the Controller and Auditor-General because it is being run not by the Government but by the Tourism Board. Who is running the Tourism Board campaign? It is David Beatson. Who is David Beatson? He is the one who wrote the speeches about ``Lift the light'' or some damned thing. Light the light, stand on the hills, see the vision! Right through these campaigns one sees the mates of the mates of the mates.

I join the Prime Minister in expressing my thanks and the thanks of the Opposition---our , their ---to the staff and all of those who have made this place work over the past months. I refer to the staff in our offices, in travel, in research, and the messengers---who always know more about what is going on in this place than anyone else. I thank the library staff, the researchers, and Bellamy's---those people on telephone extension , whose toasted sandwiches are too hard to give up; those diet-busters. I thank the gardeners and all those who work round this place. Their commitment and their integrity make the place work. We should also pay tribute to our electorate secretaries. Their appointment was one constitutional reform introduced by Geoffrey Palmer that I totally supported. I ought to pay tribute also to those who work away, frequently without success, never in the headlines, behind the scenes, never noticed, never understood, people whom the public has never heard of---but then again it is up to the Prime Minister to thank his Cabinet! I thank the Senior Opposition Whip, his deputy, and their offsider from Avon for the commitment that they have given over the past year. The member for New Lynn shows that back-seat driving does work. I thank you, Mr Speaker, and also your deputy for your decency and honesty over the past months. This is a time to record our thanks to those who work round the country---in particular, those who work over the Christmas period looking after our interests: the police, the service people, the armed servicemen and servicewomen, the volunteers on the beaches and on the streets; the churches and agencies that will be working to make Christmas a better time for so many of our people than it would otherwise have been. I am sure, too, that we ought to express in Parliament our thanks to the servicemen and servicewomen in the Sinai, in Kampuchea, and elsewhere who serve the nation at this time. They will have a lonely Christmas in the service of peace, far from their families, far from their friends, far from New Zealand. Our thoughts ought to go at this moment also to our cousins in Samoa---a nation of people who are devastated but not broken. The Opposition supports the Government's efforts in the reconstruction of those shattered islands. I think that it is a good thing to encourage unemployed tradespeople to help with that reconstruction, but sometimes I wonder whether anyone has ever thought about why we have to wait until there is a cyclone before we can unite the energies of our people. I think that colleagues on both sides of the House would like me to express their sadness at the tragic events that concern one of our members. Our love and our prayers go out to that member. Today is the last day in Parliament for one of our most distinguished, and, alas, most successful members. I refer to the member for Tamaki. Let there be no misunderstanding. Let us get it absolutely right. I have never voted for him. My support for him was the kind of support that the rope ought to give the condemned man. He, more than any other political personality in my lifetime, kept me and people like me from office. He also did more than most to drive a lot of people into politics. We had different ambitions: I only wanted to be the Prime Minister; he wanted to be the Government---and he was, for years. He is the most dynamic and dominating political figure in the lifetime of my generation. His power, alas, his success, his strengths, his talents, his temper, and his temperament, imposed themselves on this country for more than a decade. That must be respected, and must be recognised. He made his party the most powerful political force in the land for a decade. He managed to defeat a Labour Government that had fewer than , people out of work. Let not my respect and admiration for his political skills be misunderstood. For all of the Opposition's attacks on him, it did not ever claim that he was out of step with the average bloke. Frequently he was in step---we just wished that he had marched the country in a different direction. It is possible to oppose a person's principles and still to respect that person. I should like to relate an old story from Westminster about a Liberal member of Parliament and a Tory member of Parliament. For years these two members had been hunting and fighting each other. These two were known as the enemies in Parliament. At one election the Liberal member was defeated. The next day a young Tory member rushed up to his colleague, introduced himself, and waited to be congratulated. He said: ``I'm the one who defeated your opponent.''. The old Tory looked at him and said: ``Dammit, sir, you've shot my fox.''. To the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance I say: ``Damn you, you've shot our fox.''. I wish the member for Tamaki well in retirement. I pay tribute to him and to Lady Muldoon for all their work. It is not the time to recall our great differences---and the differences were great and substantial: the Springbok tour, ``think big'', and the Moyle affair; nor is it the time to expose the substance of opportunities that we believe were lost. It is the time simply to admire and to pay respect to his energy and his commitment. No one knows the Standing Orders better than the member for Tamaki does, because no one has studied their loopholes longer than he has. He has almost become a cartoon of himself. By moving just one muscle he mesmerises the camera during debate. I would watch those debates and my heart would sink because I knew that my votes were going down the toilet. One chuckle, ``Heh! Heh!'', and the camera would move. He would mesmerise the cameraman. That still happens. Most of us can remember the odd flick. I remember that he gave me one saying when I was years going on , and now I am years going on . I remember the marvellous statement he made at the time of the negotiations on closer economic relations with Australia. Migration was a problem, and we were losing all our people. He said: ``That doesn't matter. It raises the IQ on both sides of the Tasman.''. I could have read out some of the quotations he has made about his colleagues, but really I do not have time. I wish him well in retirement, but I know that he will not retire. No lily will be safe. He will probably write, as well. It grieves me as a person who tries to write to say that his first book The Rise and Fall of a Young Turk was a huge best seller. Those of us who write leaflets and deliver them at night should remember that home in has a copy of that book. That book, which was written in , was another reason that the Labour Government lost the election. I am sure that he will write, and that he will keep talking on talkback radio, particularly over the next couple of weeks. I also read the maiden speech he made in . I wish that the boundaries for Tamaki were the same today as they were in . In that speech he said: ``As a Liberal I find my only possible political home in the National Party.''. He gave us the warning that the ordinary citizen should be at the forefront of the mind of the Government because that is the person ultimately affected by every act of government. Moreover, he in his wisdom is the maker and the breaker of governments. The member for Tamaki maintained the great consensus from last century. We would argue. We could have gone further or not as far, and I think essentially that he was and is a liberal. He essentially believes in the great consensus about issues such as public health. Parliament moves on, Sir Robert. Politicians are like sportspeople and beauty queens. We tend to fade and to fail. No disrespect is meant when I say that it is appropriate for me to talk about the motion before the House, which is that Parliament do now adjourn. People will probably say, ``Thank God, they've done enough damage.''. I look back over the past months and see what has happened to the country, and I understand why some people are disgusted with the Government. The past months have been the worst since the great depression. There has been no lifting of morale. Nobody believes that the Government is on his or her side. The Government is something to be feared, not to be joined. Never in the history of the country have a Government, a Prime Minister, and a Minister of Finance had so much disrespect and hostility shown towards them. Nobody believes the Prime Minister any more. His words are not a guide to his actions, and his colleagues do not trust him. They do not respect him, either. The Government is out of control. I look back to the mother of all Budgets. We think of those who have said during the past months that they would redesign New Zealand. The new Government back-benchers ought to know that this is an adjournment debate, and there is no disrespect intended to the member for Tamaki.

We had an interruption from a person who lives in the Hawke's Bay and who ought to represent the people of the Hawke's Bay---not ACT, not private medicine, but the people. Why does the Government do this? It would have been so much easier, polite, democratic, the decent thing in the decent society, or the inclusive society we were promised, to allow the member for Napier, his mayor, and the Mayor of Hastings to come to this Parliament to make a case. Nobody says that the select committee had to hear submissions. In fact, the outrage that the people of Napier will feel about being denied their opportunity to speak will make this thing go on and go. The Government is incompetent in managing itself. It is incompetent in managing this Parliament. The member for Napier is a good local member of Parliament, and he is proud of that. I know when I walk around my electorate, everybody knows me, but anyone going to Napier can see that the huge difference is that he knows them. He can name them all; and the greatest honour we can ever have in our parliamentary system is for it to be said of us that we are good local members of Parliament. That is the rent one pays to be able to do other things for one's country. I say that the member for Napier would have been failing in his duty had he not brought a Bill into Parliament. Then I see that ACT member of Parliament, who lives in the area, but who will not speak up for the Bill. We have Mr Kirton, who has attended rallies. The Government talks about how we need more public involvement, how the community must get involved in health. We know that , people signed a petition, and how many thousands have gone to meeting after meeting to express their views? That is public involvement, and the member for Napier has shown real leadership as a local MP. I can just repeat this, because there might be one or two on the other side who do not have closed minds. This whole fuss has been made worse, it has been blown up, simply because the Government was not prepared to allow a couple of mayors to have an hour or so before a select committee. Would it really have mattered? But, no, they know best. I want to tell that young Treasury official that he is not on staff; he is an elected member of the Cabinet of this country and his job is to represent the people, not to turn them back. He is the people's person in Cabinet, not Treasury's person in Cabinet. If we want Treasury's advice we can ask for it. When we want its advice we will tell them when we want it. That is what is wrong with this Government. That is what is so sad about this coalition, which could be doing good things for our country.

The role of the Crown health enterprises is specifically to deliver quality health services to the people of this country. With the benefit of hindsight after comprehensive inquiries and questioning over the last few weeks in relation to Crown health enterprises and regional health authorities, there is some glimmer of hope. There is some glimmer of hope because, in terms of Maori health, the last years have produced more than Maori providers on the ground. That means that there are far more Maori-friendly services than ever before. That means that Maori health providers, along with Crown health enterprises, are working to get a comprehensive strategy to provide quality health services for Maori. Over the past years the Crown health enterprises have focused on making a profit and balancing the books. That is a fact. This focus has resulted in Crown health enterprises exiting from services that are not profitable, particularly in small rural communities. The coalition agreement has changed all that. That means that the coalition Government will discard that notion and begin to provide a far more comprehensive range of services. I shall give an example. Northland Health has for some months now been working alongside Maori both to help address the issues of alcohol and drug rehabilitation and to try to establish, not in a competitive way but in a friendly way, primary health services for Maori when there has never been the opportunity to do so in the past. The coalition Government is committed to providing publicly funded and publicly provided health services to keep New Zealanders healthy and to ensure that New Zealanders, including Maori, have confidence in their health services. In order to get to their gateways of opportunity, Maori have to be healthy. The overriding goal of the coalition Government's health policy is to ensure that principles of public service replace commercial, profit-driven objectives. At the end of the day, Crown health enterprises are now in the business of trying to integrate with Maori. I give the example of South Auckland Health. This Crown health enterprise has, for the first time, taken within its own facilities and premises a Maori provider of primary services, more specifically, Raukura Hauora o Tainui. There has been a historic problem whereby more than , Maori and Pacific Island people turn up to the accident and emergency services, refusing to go to some doctor down the road. Instead, they jam up hospital waiting-rooms. They go to places like Middlemore Hospital and bring to bear unnecessary pressure. As a result of that, Tainui's health provider, Raukura Hauora, has joint-ventured with South Auckland Health to provide a primary service in a secondary service facility. It is a sign of change in this country that for the first time Maori primary health providers can join with a major secondary service provider to address some rising problems. Those sorts of initiatives are absolutely crucial. It is perhaps the best strategy of cooperation whereby two peoples can work together, and that is absolutely fantastic. In just the past months the so-called ``Maori doctor'' has helped more than , patients.

Mr Speaker, parliamentary colleagues: kia ora tatou. Over the most recent weekend four young people tragically died in our capital city and highlighted the need for a strong voice for youth in this our first ever MMP Parliament. Because the lives of our young people become ever more complicated with each passing year, we as a Parliament must acknowledge the pressures, and work, constructively to address them while also recognising and celebrating the enormous potential of our young people. The fact is that the certainty of past social and economic structures is over. We expect and demand from our young people greater responsibility for their own lives at earlier and earlier ages. We expect them to be adult and independent, but very often we fail to equip them with the abilities to be so. The value systems of our modern society no longer provide the certainty and strong direction of previous generations. Previously respected institutions and professions, including this Parliament, are now regarded with cynical distaste. This is not to suggest that past practices were necessarily the best practices, but it does serve to highlight the need for this Parliament to be aware of its responsibility in providing a safe and secure environment for all our young people, including Maori and Pacific Island young people. We need an environment that provides them with supportive family, a decent education, a high standard of health care, and a range of personal options and information before they make their life-changing decisions. I take great pride in being one of the youngest MPs in this new Parliament, and the youngest ever Minister of the Crown. It has been a sudden and dramatic path from university student to parliamentary researcher, which led me to the unique opportunity of involvement in the coalition negotiations, and now to the Minister of Youth Affairs. But rather than make things easier, I believe that both my youth and recent progress bring me a closer and deeper understanding of my age group, and a sense of urgency about the need to get real and give all young New Zealanders a proper chance at life. Before I outline what I see as my personal principles and aims I want to acknowledge and thank those who have given me this, the rarest of opportunities. My family and friends, many of whom are with me tonight, have provided me with the love and support that have made this political dream come true. My parents, Margaret and Wayne, gave me a good education, the freedom and support to grow, the opportunity to savour new experiences, but the safety-net, should I ever fall. My childhood was spent fishing and playing on beaches. For much of my teenage life we lived beside the sea on the rugged and beautiful south coast of Wellington. Like many Kiwis, I have an affinity with the sea. It is for this reason that I feel concern about the quality of our system for managing marine resources. Recreational fishers have been marginalised from decision making, in spite of the fact that they contribute an estimated $ million to our economy each year as a result of fishing. Now, on to my personal catch, my fiance, Chris. He is a quintessentially good man, and he has shared the twists and turns of fate over the past / years. Chris, I thank you for giving me the love and encouragement to take on this challenge. Knowing that you will always be there has given me the strength to make this choice and to make a success of my chosen vocation. I love you. To the New Zealand First Party, to Winston, Doug, Tau, and the team: I thank you for recognising that age should never be a barrier to public service and for giving a young researcher the opportunity of a lifetime to be a member of Parliament at this unique time in the nation's political development. Working with New Zealand First in the past years has been rewarding, if not a little challenging. It has enabled me to gain a good understanding of the challenges faced by our nation, including Tau's wicked sense of humour. To my Hutt South electorate team, in particular, Graeme Houghton, Ellen Te Moni, Denise Komene, Gary Logan, and Sarah Porter: thank you for helping me in the campaign. Your loyalty to me and to New Zealand First was unfaltering. I also want to acknowledge and thank those people who have made the MMP electoral system a reality. They include the lonely lobbyists who crusaded outside Parliament, the Electoral Reform Coalition and their supporters. They also include those MPs who advanced the case of proportional representation in this House---again, another lonely minority. I pay particular respect to the Royal Commission on the Electoral System, which sifted the evidence, researched the international examples, listened to the people of New Zealand, and created a unique political system that recognises our own identity as New Zealanders. As a party list MP, I do not possess a particular responsibility for a defined set of constituents based on geographical location. Although I reside in the multicultural harbour city, and will open a constituency office here, my role is much broader than that. Both because of my position as Minister of Youth Affairs and because of my personal inclination, I believe that my direct constituents are the young people of this country, particularly those teenagers and young adults who do not feel a part of the political process, nor had a voice to represent them in the past in this House. Political apathy is the curse of the young. It has not always been that way, however. The youth of the s ushered in fundamental societal changes. The anti-war, environmental, and feminist lobbies of the s and the s sprang from our youth and produced far-ranging reforms within our society. However, in the mid to late s many young people are dissuaded from pursuing the same active interest in their community and in their society. In part, that is a reflection on the political process. Politics in New Zealand has been severely discredited, and not just amongst the young. In addition, young people must now negotiate a bewildering array of personal choices and societal pressures. The pressure to succeed, the societal emphasis on material wealth, the lack of respected institutions, the attractions of alternative lifestyles, the dangers of drug and alcohol abuse, and the deterioration of family life are wholly different stimuli to those faced by earlier generations. These are the new challenges to our nation's youth, to create a meaningful and fulfilled life in a world that exhibits often confused and contradictory messages. It is not surprising then that the young are over-represented in all the worst social statistics such as crime, suicide, teenage pregnancy, and welfare dependency. I see it as my responsibility to establish proper bridges between young people and our democratic institutions, to involve youth in our decision-making process, and to provide them with not only a voice but also the opportunity to make that voice heard. I thus intend that the Ministry of Youth Affairs takes an upfront, high profile, and active role in the affairs of this Parliament and in the wider community. In the past the ministry has been little more than a bureaucratic add-on as Parliament paid lip-service to the aspirations of young people, and nothing more than lip-service. I reject the age-old political advice that fresh MPs should be seen and not heard. To play those kinds of political games would be to deny both my constitutional and heartfelt duty to the youth of New Zealand. In the short term I foresee three positive roles that the ministry and this Parliament can play in youth issues. The first is in coordinating a multi-disciplinary approach to the prevention of youth suicide. We all know that New Zealand rates poorly on the issue of young-person suicide. But in my view, regardless of how we rate internationally, the death of any young person is a tragedy. Therefore, we must make a concerted effort at every level of society to ensure that young people have the support they require. Second, I want to provide a literal voice to young people by establishing a youth radio network that will create a sense of community and connection between young people that will address their issues and their concerns. The pioneering project of Crowded House's Neil Finn is exactly the kind of positive intervention that the State can make in the lives of young people. Third, I want to see a much more positive second-chance education and training system; one that encourages and supports young people from welfare dependence back into work and provides a training or living allowance to allow them to do that. The time has come for the vast numbers of young people who have been wholly neglected by past Governments to have the opportunities they need to participate fully in our society. Again, there exists a greater need for coordination and cooperation between competing departmental bureaucracies. These may suit the internal power games of the technocrats, but they do absolutely nothing for our youth. In the various departments of education, training, employment, social welfare, and health there exists the opportunity for integrated projects that focus on health needs, and are created together, not in isolation from one another. That sense of cooperation is sadly missing from our youth services. It is my intention to call a youth summit later this year that will invite central and local government agencies, community organisations, and voluntary groups to plan a more effective strategy for assisting this country's young people. We need a blueprint that will identify particular youth needs and requirements, and then plan the policies that give our young people the chance to develop themselves to the greatest possible extent of their potential. I am not a great fan of the Westminster style of parliamentary politics. It is a destructive and confrontational system, and the move to MMP has ameliorated its side effects only a little. I believe that there are MPs on both sides of this House with ideas and concepts that will greatly benefit the youth of New Zealand. Good ideas should never be rejected just because they come from the other side of the House, and because youth affairs and the future of our young people are so important I want to make youth issues non-partisan. I am sure that some more experienced MPs would brand this idea as naive, but I have to say that all the best ideas have started from a challenge of the existing order. I similarly challenge this Parliament, on behalf of the nation's young people, to work in a more cooperative fashion. The cooperation of the parties in planning this year's Youth Parliament is a great start. Finally, I want to say what an enormous privilege we are all granted in being elected to this Parliament. It is also a huge responsibility. There is considerable public scepticism as to our profession, but I am optimistic enough to believe that the shared intellect, compassion, and wisdom of this House can be harnessed for the greater good. That will be my challenge over the next years, and I look forward to working with all of you, each and every one of you, in making that dream a waking reality.

I rise to support the Bill and would simply like to reflect on a few personal observations in the mental health area. Firstly, my mother-in-law has been an Alzheimer's patient for the last years, and I have had the same battles as any member in this House in trying to get some common sense out of the bureaucracy in the way that we humanly and humanely deal with the very serious problem of Alzheimer's patients out there in the community. I think it has to be the worst type of a permanent disabling disease that I have ever seen in my life. It is absolutely shocking. My father-in-law is an absolute brick because for years he has managed to keep his wife, his partner, at home and look after her himself. He is the fittest -year-old I have ever seen because for hours a day---through every minute and every second of a -hour-day---he has to look after his dearly beloved like one would look after a brand spanking new new-born baby, and do absolutely everything for her. I think he is a hero and people like him are heroes. But when the bureaucracy out there deals with them in such a very stiff manner it really makes me mad. I have found over the years that not enough common sense is practised in the handling of some of these issues. It really makes me angry. In looking at mental health, I want to reflect very quickly on what has happened in the past. I remember seeing mental institutions in the old days, and as a kid we used to call them the madhouse---places where they locked up lunatics and threw away the key. I remember many years ago seeing the film One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. It depicted in a way that was very sad and funny, and also serious, the institutionalisation of those mentally sick human beings. It depicted how they were degraded and lost their sense of who they were, and how they were controlled, in many ways, in those places. I have to say that I am very pleased that we have gone beyond that. It has been traumatic. It is only in the last years, or even less, that people have been taken from institutions and brought out into the community. That transition has and probably still is traumatic for society. When I came into Parliament in some of the first calls I got were from people who found that a whole bunch of ``lunatics'' were about to be housed in their street. They were worried about the safety of their children and themselves, and about what stupid things would be happening in the street---such as mad people running around nude. I used to go out there and sit down with people and bring in the community advisers who were putting the mentally ill out into the community. We would sit down and talk about it, and within an hour, in most cases, all the neighbours would be wanting to move next door to help, to join in to make those people comfortable, once they understood exactly what was happening in the community. I think there has been a big, big change in the way we treat those people. We are treating them normally. I think we are showing a lot more compassion, along with an understanding, and we are beginning to understand the total concept and meaning of love. It means a lot of sacrifice, and it means much understanding of and patience with people. I am happy to see that happen. But one thing that I do wish we would wake up to as well very quickly is the fact that there are still people out there who need protection. They are being put out into the community. There is a low tolerance rate of many members of the community seeing those people totally abused, frustrated, and driven to do things that they would not do in a more protected situation where they could receive the care that they need. I think a protected village-type situation has been overlooked. I see a shake of the head from one of my colleagues who thinks that is not the way to go, but I do not know. I think there are such people out there. I am not talking simply about putting these people in a village on their own but in a situation so that families can have the ability to live in a situation where they can care, teach, and be patient with mentally ill people and help them to look after themselves much better in that cared-for environment. I am not talking about an institution but about a village situation that they can retreat to and be safe in and have the ability to come out of. I think that needs to be looked into a little bit more. I want to congratulate all the volunteers who work in this industry. Some of my colleagues have done that in their speeches. The volunteers who work patiently, lovingly, and carefully with mentally ill people, deserve huge medals. I think that the Government needs to take heed of that input a little bit more and needs to nurture it and help it, otherwise if it collapses there is no way that this country would ever have enough money to take care of all the problems of the mentally ill that we have around us. I would like to congratulate all those people in the profession---the psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, and all the professional people. In the last years they have had to put up with a lot of abuse whilst trying to do their jobs in the transition of change from institutions into the community. I have had many of those people ringing me, as a politician, and almost crying about some of the problems they were having in the transitions and the changeovers, problems such as the lack of understanding from the community, and also the problems from their own bureaucracy during that change. I want to congratulate them on the work that they are doing at the moment, and to congratulate them on handling that changeover very well. I hope we continue to get high-quality and high-calibre people interested in the mental health nursing and caring field, because it is most necessary in this country. I hope that in the future the Mental Health Commission will look very carefully at the situation and make dead sure that every dollar that is spent in the mental health area will bring back some value to the people who really need it---those are the people who suffer from the illness. In the past I have seen too much money wasted in all sorts of stupid ways. It seems to me that the problem is that when the Government is handling huge amounts of money an awful lot of it seems to be poured down the toilet somewhere and gets lost, and those who need it miss out on it. I hope this Mental Health Commission will be able to stop any waste and will make sure that money goes to providers who are providing the results, the care, and the love and attention that is necessary. I hope they will also expose those people out there---there probably are one or two out there---who are getting rich from this and not giving back to society or to the patients the true value of the dollar that they are receiving from the Government. I support the Mental Health Commission in the work that it does.
