It will not be long before that person is out on parole. That person got a life sentence, but within a very few years he will be out on parole. Already people are wondering what day and when this will all happen; what sort of support there will be for him and for them. At the moment, there is very little support for them, and once again, at a very early date, the public will be endangered again. Mr Prebble was dead right when he said that most murders are done by recidivists. Most are done by people who have been let out of jail very early; they have not been looked after properly once they have been released, and they offend again. The system itself provides that opportunity for people, because we do not mean what we say. We do not do what we mean. The average time a murderer spends in jail is years, after being handed down a life sentence. I have to commend Justice Nicholson for giving an -year minimum sentence in a recent case. That is truth in sentencing. He said that the person will be in jail for years, and that is that. That person is going to serve out that full amount of time. If a few more judges around the place got it together and decided they would make the punishment fit the crime; if they were going to, by degree, look at the severity of the situation and make those sorts of decisions, we would not have to be standing here arguing about this today. I have no doubt in my mind that without some form of guidance, we will not, unfortunately, see a repeat of Justice Nicholson's attempts to make sure that the real bad people are taken care of permanently. Norm Withers toured the country, and he brought back to this Parliament a reflection of what the public feel. The public have stated categorically that they are not in any way enamoured with the way the law is enacted, either in the courts, in the justice system, by the Parole Board, or in the treatment of victims. They are making their point known quite clearly, and they are not receiving an ear from the Government at all about their situation. I have absolutely no doubt that the sentencing review that is going on will be simply another whitewash. It will put forward an awful lot of blah-blah, which simply will not solve the situation. It will not act as a deterrent for anybody out there. We will wind up in the same position we are in today, whereby this House, this Government, will be too afraid to do something certain about it. The Government has to come to the conclusion that the public have a right, when they speak in such a high majority, to expect this House to act in their favour to bring forward legislation that will cover them and protect them. The legislation is not protecting them now, otherwise we would not have seen such an overwhelming show of force from all the public signing Norm Withers' petition---not at all. The cost factor put forward by the Minister is a red herring. It is a load of hooey. There is absolutely no doubt that if firmer deterrents are offered, savings will be made because people will not be committing those crimes. There is no doubt that we would see some form of percentage shift in favour of the safety of the public, and therefore wipe completely those stupid figures produced by the Minister and his cohorts in his office. The cost put forward is a nonsense. It is a total red herring. This bill is about giving some assurance to people that when the courts speak they mean what they say, and they act accordingly. I have no doubt in my mind whatsoever that if we send firmer signals to those who are committing most of the crimes we will see a certain shift. The Minister talked about the crime rates and how things went up and moved forward. In actual fact, the National Government increased police numbers to the highest they have ever been. Crime has come down over the last years as a percentage per head of population, and sentencing is moving up, as judges, like Justice Nicholson, decide they will act in favour of the public rather than in favour of some liberal philosophy that thinks about the prisoner rather than those who suffered at the hands of that guilty person. Here in Parliament we have to understand that the public will not continue to accept wishy-washy legislation. The public will not continue to accept it when we deliver to them stuff that does not work, and then pretend that we are so righteous and have done a great thing---particularly in law and order. I have been in the House for years, and year after year nothing substantial has been done. Nothing that has pushed firmly as a deterrent has been put in place. Nothing from this Government that I have seen so far will do that, either. There is no doubt that we have to turn round the situation and build into our system some deterrents and some safety margins in bills like this that will give the public some reassurance that this crime will not be tolerated, particularly by a small group of people. It is always the small group. It is always the percent who do percent of the offending. Yet we still seem not to take any notice of warning signs, and we take no notice of families. We allow the system itself to operate in such a way that it puts these people back on the streets after giving them a short term in a rest home! It is the public's perception that I am expressing here tonight. That is what they see, that is what they experience, and that is what they read in the newspaper. Recently a young girl got off a bus and was murdered by one of those people, who should have been in jail. He should have been there for a lot longer. I hope that judges today will take note of Justice Nicholson's move and will follow suit, and maybe we will not have to be standing here again talking about having to bring in this sort of legislation.

I will clarify my statement. Some people did not understand it. The National Government, and the review, were bringing about more police numbers in the streets---that cannot be denied by anyone---and they would have produced even more. We will be watching this Minister over the next years to see just exactly what will be delivered. We believe he has made a very grave mistake in what he has done. He has cancelled a very important review in what were its last few yards. We do not have these reviews every day of the week. It is once in - years that this sort of review is done. It has to be done properly, when it is done. No matter who will be upset, that has to be done. This Minister has sold out to the unions---I have no doubt about that. He has sold out to the officials and the police union. He has done the policemen and policewomen on the beat a huge disservice. They needed his support. They needed to know that he was supporting them out there in their jobs. This cancellation of the review does not support the police in their work. It will allow a situation to continue that needs vital change.

If we talked to any of our allies throughout the world---or those who used to be our allies---they would tell us that what New Zealand has done is absolutely flabbergasting. They cannot believe that in this day and age we would do such a thing, when in every corner of the world some form of calamity is occurring that requires a fully equipped, balanced force to go out and defend the values that this country and many other Western countries espouse. They believe that for us to do what we are doing in the face of all of that is tantamount to absolute stupidity. They cannot believe it. The road that this Government has taken in turning round and reshaping our forces will pull us further and further away from our allies, and set us completely adrift. After talking to many people in Australia in particular, there is absolutely no doubt in my mind that the arms-around-the-shoulders relationship that we once had with that country has now become an arm's-length relationship. Australia no longer trusts us. The closeness that our Defence Force shared with Australia and our allies was the glue in our relationship with our allies and friends. There is absolutely no doubt that with the grounding of our strike force we have absolutely excommunicated ourselves.

The only interest that most New Zealanders have in the Alliance Freezing Co. is whether it will still be killing lambs at the end of the year and whether the schedule will be over $. Most clear-thinking New Zealanders do not worry about that other Alliance organisation, because its members are in fairyland, cuckoo-land. They are miles away and still think that money grows on trees. They will provide free health and free education, but where is the money coming from? From increased taxes! I say to that member that increasing taxes is no answer to the problems that New Zealanders face at this time. In every family there comes a day when the eldest child leaves the nest---leaves home and makes his or her way in our country. We still have a wonderful, beautiful country. We still have a country that offers opportunities. This week I had that unfortunate experience of my daughter leaving home to take employment before going to the University of Otago. She is under no misapprehension about what is before her. She understands her financial responsibilities and she understands what the position will be when, or if, she graduates from the University of Otago. She also understands that in she believed that there would be no user-pays costs, as was stated in the Labour Party manifesto. The Labour Party manifesto stated: ``Labour will ensure that tertiary students are not required to pay a higher contribution to their education than they do at present.''. What did the Labour Government do? It introduced the tertiary student fee. It introduced a fee of $---an increase of percent---and that fee has even been increased since that time. That was the user-pays principle in education. This Government indicated that it would abolish the tertiary education fee. It has kept that promise. However, universities will charge a fee, but that fee is less than the tertiary education fee that was introduced during the term of the Labour Government. Education is one of the most important issues that comes before any Government, and it is important that adequate funding be provided. The Budget provided an increase in the Education vote, not a decrease. In tertiary education, which is important to me at this time, $. million more was invested in education training. Polytechnics have come of age. I recently had the opportunity to travel to Australia to study its education facilities. New Zealand's tertiary education facilities are substantially better than those provided to Australians. Next year in New Zealand , more students will have an opportunity to attend tertiary education and training facilities. That includes places in tertiary institutions and places for trainees in traineeship schemes. The $ tertiary tuition fee has been abolished and replaced with study right. Study right is available to all New Zealanders in their first years of university provided they are under the age of years. They will pay percent of the fee being charged by the university, and the Government will pick up the other percent. In most cases that fee will be about $. In Australia the fee is A$, or about NZ$. Australia, of course, has a higher education contribution scheme similar to New Zealand's study right scheme. It has a loans scheme available. For fees for accommodation, books, and so on, Australian students can get Austudy, but that is available only after means-testing of income and assets. In New Zealand the loans scheme is available to all young New Zealanders. It is not based on assets or income, and the repayment is for a period of time having regard to the fact that the students are able to obtain employment. That is very important, because repayment is not necessary if students are unable to obtain employment or do not want to enter employment. For many years New Zealand has provided a very generous student allowance scheme in comparison with other countries. Some other countries with which we compare ourselves---Britain, Scandinavia, West Germany, and Japan---have user-pays charges for education. We are no different in this country. Sometimes I am asked to explain why it is necessary. First, we must consider the financial position in which this country finds itself. Second, if anyone has ever attended a social function at which the beer is free they will know that one finds that at the end of the night there are many half-empty bottles lying around the tables. But if one is required to pay a few shillings towards the beverages, at the end of the night every bottle is empty. It is no different in education. When students are required to make a contribution towards their own studies they ensure that their work ethics are much better than those under the hand-out mentality that some people believe we should have. It is always interesting to listen to, read, and understand the work of the Post Primary Teachers Association. Probably right now its representatives are filling out report cards on some poor members of Parliament who have attended schools or institutions somewhere in this country. They intend to carry out reporting on members of Parliament about their views on education. The president of that organisation, Shona Hearn, acknowledged to me that, because of my interest in education, I am willing at all times to meet the Post Primary Teachers Association and members of the association. I am prepared to meet them and to discuss education matters so that at least we have dialogue, but the difficulty is that the Post Primary Teachers Association is a difficult and dangerous union. Is it there to provide better education for New Zealand children or is it there to protect and preserve incompetent members and to obtain inflated privileges for them? There are many excellent teachers, but there are also a number of incompetent teachers and they are protected by a strong union. It is very difficult to remove an incompetent teacher from a school. I am pleased to be able to say that most of the teachers in the Waitaki electorate are of the highest standard, but even they will admit that a number within their sect are not up to it. The education profession is a highly protected one, and it does not take kindly to change. The suggestion of public accountability is unacceptable to the Post Primary Teachers Association. That association is strong and outspoken whenever its members' job security appears to be under threat. Strikes by teachers have never been about the quality of education. Rather, they have been about job security and conditions of employment. The Post Primary Teachers Association probably has an income of $ million. It employs people. This year it spent $, on special television broadcasts to air its views on the Budget. It also spent $, on bringing principals to Wellington solely for the purpose of convincing them that they should oppose bulk funding. That organisation needs to be accountable.
In the circumstances, why has no inquiry been ordered?

I am delighted to participate in the Budget debate of . There is an old saying in the Hawke's Bay: ``If you put a human face on a donkey you still have an ass.'' The member for Hastings indicated that he has been putting a telescope to his deaf ear, and he actually does not want to hear. He does not want to hear the good news that is coming from this Budget and the financial management of this National Government. He does not want to hear because he wants to return to some of the old policies of an old and stale Labour Government. He said in his speech: ``They have stacks of money and they should spend it.'' I think it is important in that we look at the economic vision that was promoted by Ruth Richardson, the National Opposition spokesperson on finance prior to the election. In National's Economic Vision she said that it was the goal of the National Government to have economic growth at percent by the end of its first term in Government. That she achieved, and not only did she achieve it by but it is still the case. The reality is that we now have sustained economic growth in New Zealand. Another of her goals was that she wished to halve unemployment by the end of the first term of the National Government. She did not achieve that goal. We cannot deny that---in fact, unemployment increased not decreased in the early years of the National Government -. However, the good news is that in recent times unemployment is falling, and is now falling rapidly. In my own town of Oamaru, unemployment in June is the lowest it has been for over years at this time of year. Unemployment is falling---, new jobs were created in the past months. Ruth Richardson's economic vision also wanted a to percent inflation rate. There was much discussion about this issue when it was released by Ruth Richardson in National's Economic Vision in . The member for Tauranga was very clear as to his view on the economic vision of to percent. He said that that figure was not achievable and the Government should not endeavour to achieve it. He made public statements that we should allow inflation to go out to percent or percent. But he has been proved wrong, and we have an inflation rate of between and percent. Another goal that Miss Richardson wished to achieve was single-digit business and home mortgage interest rates. This has been achieved, and maintained, notwithstanding the difficulties that are being experience at this point in time with the overheating of the economy. The last goal that Ruth Richardson wished to achieve in her economic vision of was that there be a balanced Budget and a fall in the share of Government expenditure and taxation as a percentage of gross domestic product. In we have a balanced Budget. Not only that, we now have a surplus, yet there are demands from the Labour Opposition that we should spend that surplus rather than repay debt. As we look to the next election---whenever that might be held---a number of key issues will be the focal point of the next election programme. They are education, health, and race relations. Some would say that, notwithstanding our Budget surplus, there should be further spending in education. I think that people forget the additional funds that have been supplied to education in the Budget. Over the next years there will be a further $ million for early-childhood initiatives. Over the next years there will be $ million for improved school performance through initiatives like increased teacher numbers. There will be , extra teachers in the school system. That includes extra teachers in my electorate, and, in particular, in the electorates with lower socio-economic factors attaching thereto. There is a further $ million to build new classrooms and schools. One of the concerns I have is the closure, and possible closure, of schools in rural communities. There is a need for certain rationalisation, but we must be careful that we do not wreck the fabric of small rural communities by removing schools. If we are able to create a better learning environment---and it is beneficial to the children---then I consider that there should be rationalisation. But if it is rationalisation solely for the purpose of rationalisation, then it should not occur. In the Budget a further $ million is to be provided in special education. This, of course, has been well received by those involved in this area. Substantial extra funding is being provided in the area of education. The other issue that will be an issue at the next election is health. In the last year the Government announced an extra fund of $ million for the - financial year, $ million for the - financial year, and $ million for the - year. In this Budget the Minister of Finance announced an investment of a further $ million in the - year for maintaining and upgrading hospitals. This is very important, and it is very important for the security of people in rural communities. It is very important because people who live in places like Balclutha, Ashburton, and Oamaru must be assured that health facilities are maintained in their areas. It is very close to my heart that Oamaru Hospital continues to provide services in accordance with the June accord, and that those services be available to the community. Only last week I assisted in opening a teleradiology unit at Oamaru Hospital. It is this type of new technology that will assist rural hospital communities in having facilities that will provide the security that they need, to know that treatment is available to them within their local community. I have been impressed with a number of rural general practitioners who are taking up the challenge to provide additional assistance far beyond that which has been expected from the local general practitioners in years gone by---specialist clinics, x-rays within general practitioners' surgeries, out-patients, and even, in Waimate, the building of a small accident and emergency facility with ambulance ramps and access. The third issue that will be an election issue is no doubt that of race relations. It is a matter that people are nervous to speak about, but it is a matter that we should not hide from. In recent times it has been emphasised by certain occupations, particularly in Wanganui. It is clear that the Government's policy on this matter be stated once again---that is, there will not be sovereignty in relation to the Maori people. We should be encouraging multicultural relationships; New Zealand is not a bicultural society. Some might say that the economic recovery that has occurred since has not had a trickledown effect to the smaller rural communities---communities like Oamaru. When we look at the fact that unemployment has dropped considerably in Oamaru, then the trickledown effect is operating and working in small rural communities. Only a few weeks ago, in the town of Oamaru, a new superstore for the Warehouse was opened. We appreciate the fact that Mr Steven Tindall has chosen Oamaru as one the towns in which to build one of his new superstores. Smith City will open soon in that town, whilst the North Otago Motor Group has had record sales in the month of May for its Toyota product. The Alliance Freezing Co. has had one of its best years ever, and is still operating because of the late development of stock in our area due to drought conditions. On the other hand, a number of industries have been affected by the rising dollar. In particular, Frasers Bacon, Regina Confectionary, and Summit Wool Spinners Ltd, have had to reduce staff or negotiate with staff over redundancy requirements. Earlier the member for Papakura talked about the need for community involvement and a one-stop shop. At the end of the month in North Otago we will open the North Otago Community House---a house that has as its tenants different social service organisations operating out of one building. It is owned by the district council on long-term lease to the North Otago Community House Trust. The purpose of it is to ensure that Government funding that is made available to social service organisations is spent in a manner that they can get the best possible outcomes. A large number of organisations such as the North Otago budgetary advice service, marriage guidance, which is now called Relationship Services, and the schizophrenia society will operate out of one property able to utilise fax machines, photocopy machines, computers, and the like so that they can get the best possible outcomes in that area. The electorate of Waitaki is not only made up of Oamaru, it is also made up of a number of smaller towns. In places like Waimate there is growth, even if it is of a small nature. The Skeggs pea factory at Studholme is now in full operation and employing a substantial number of people. There is concern in Waimate, and I am sure the member for Invercargill is very aware of it, regarding Waimate Hospital, a geriatric hospital providing for outpatients. It is somewhat sad that only this week a private organisation with whom the mayors' working group on health was having discussions on the construction and building of a new geriatric hospital has decided to go it alone. I ask and hope that that private organisation will reconsider its position, because it would be beneficial to the community of Waimate that a new hospital facility be built on the existing premises and that that be occupied by both Lister House---the private organisation---and the hospital itself for a better health service for Waimate. Again, I pay tribute to Dr Hammond Williamson, who has seen an opportunity where services have been lost in the public system, to provide X-ray facilities to the community of Waimate hours a week as opposed to the hours a week that were being provided for in the public health system. In the north of the electorate of Waitaki the Opua Dam construction is one of the first constructions since the reorganisation of the energy sector, which will provide electricity to Alpine Energy. This dam will be constructed in the summer of - and, hopefully, will be operational by . During construction this will employ some extra persons in the area and will be beneficial to the Fairlie area, in particular. Alpine Dairy Products has been one of the jewels in the crown of the Waitaki electorate and the annual increase in production from that company has been substantial since I became member of Parliament in . I do not claim to have had anything to do with its increased production but there is no doubt that the economic environment and the conversion to dairy cattle in the area of Waitaki has greatly contributed to Alpine Dairy Products. The rural sector has had a difficult year, partly due to the dry summer conditions and the fact that lamb prices, in particular, have dropped considerably in the past months.

It is interesting that in Auckland there are suggestions, rumours, or, perhaps, statements that it is intended to form a new party called the Auckland Party. It causes me some concern because, to me, it suggests that there is a vote of no confidence in the current MPs from the Auckland area. Having had dealings with Mayor Mills over the water crisis in Auckland last year I can understand why he feels that only those involved in local politics would make better politicians in the arena in Wellington. Last week announcements were made about the splitting of ECNZ. Two years ago we had the energy sector reform when power authorities became companies. There is no doubt that as a result of that reform prices in power have been maintained. But it is most important that we be forward-thinking and now begin a programme in which we take into account the power shortages that may occur in the year and later as a result of a lack of generation available, having regard to the increased demand. Whether ECNZ should have been split into two or more is a matter that only time will tell. But if we are looking for true competition, it is important that the split be more than into two as two will not create a true wholesale market, which is important if we are to maintain power at a reasonable cost to the people of New Zealand. It is important, and this House should take cognisance of the importance of the need, to ensure that there is an ability for overseas companies to invest in New Zealand. In the Department of Corrections had just been created. It appeared before the Justice and Law Reform Committee---a very good committee. During the course of its examination the department was asked about concerns relating to telephones in prison. The answer in was that that was a concern. The department was questioned carefully by the chairman and the senior Opposition member. It was interesting to note that the worst offender at that point in time was David Bain. That was interesting because those phone calls were not used to organise a crime; they were used in the preparation of the writing of a book. But what a nonsense that we need legislation to ensure that people cannot make telephone calls from prisons! That is a nonsense. Prisoners should not have the right to make calls to up to organised numbers. They should be entitled to phone their wives and children on occasion. They should be entitled to telephone their solicitors. But for them to have the right to telephone the ombudsmen, the Police Complaints Authority, and the like is an absolute nonsense and should not be allowed. We as a Government that is tough on crime should ensure that those sorts of crazy telephone calls being made from prison institutions are not allowed. I hope there are numerous submissions to the select committee from organisations indicating that telephone communication by prisoners should be only in emergency situations. We have heard today from both sides of the House that perhaps prisoners who phone their solicitors are using them as conduits for telephone calls elsewhere. I say to those people who have raised that issue: ``What a nonsense!''. As a member of the New Zealand Law Society, I can assure this House that whilst there has been an occasion---Karen Soich being the person involved---where that sort of thing occurred, it is more likely that psychologists attending prisons, rather than solicitors, are used as conduits. Weak-handed, weak-fisted psychologists are more likely to fall in love with their prisons clients than solicitors are, and to be used as conduits for this purpose.

The National Opposition will oppose this bill. In order that the community understands why it is doing so, I say that we believe there are two bills of huge importance at the local government level. There is this bill, entitled the Local Government (Rating) Bill, and there is the Local Government Bill, a major amendment to matters relating to local government issues. We believe that both bills---and we have clearly stated our preference---should be considered in tandem, rather than this bill being promoted and developed through Parliament on a stand-alone basis. In fact, both bills should have been treated as complementary to each other and should have passed through together. The Local Government Bill, as the other bill is titled, provides for the powers of general competence, and yet this bill, the Local Government (Rating) Bill is very prescriptive. So at one moment we will have councils being entitled to take action that they think appropriate for their communities, and yet in this companion bill to the Local Government Bill we have a bill that is very prescriptive. I find it difficult to understand why we would open the doors in certain spheres of local government activity, but in another area, on the question of rating, be very precise in what must occur. This bill, titled the Local Government (Rating) Bill, supersedes the Rating Powers Act. The question I put to the Minister, given that that Act has been in force for a period of years, is why is it necessary to change the legislation that councils are very familiar with and have acted under for a period of years? If I were the Minister answering that question, I would probably indicate that local government bills should be appropriately titled, in order that the community of New Zealand, when looking on the Internet, can find what they are looking for. People look on the Internet for Local Government New Zealand and for the Local Government Bill or the Local Government Act. It is possibly appropriate, therefore, that this bill should be known as a ``Local Government (Something) Bill.'' The question is whether the word in brackets should be ``Rating''. Some might say that the bill might better be known as the ``Local Government (Land Tax) Bill. Rating is nothing more than another tax, but in this case a tax on a group of individuals who happen to be fortunate or unfortunate enough to own property. I say ``unfortunate'', because if one were to own property in Nightcaps, the ability to sell that property is quite limited, whereas if one were to own property in Auckland, the ability to sell it may very well be substantially greater. The value of a residential section in parts of Oamaru can be less than $,, but the rates in respect of that property are often more than percent of the actual market value of the property, per annum. So owning property, in itself, is not necessarily a benefit. Perhaps if we were to be a little facetious we could call this bill the ``Local Government (Land Grab) Bill'', but I would not support that title. What I might ask the Minister is whether there is an alternative to land tax, or to a rating system based on land. Might a more appropriate method of gathering taxation to allow local government to proceed be by way of a dedicated tax through GST? That would mean that all members of the community would therefore make a contribution towards the facilities that are provided in any town, hamlet, or local community. Swimming pools in towns are funded from land rates.

I have listened carefully to the Minister's speech to the House. She is the Minister for the Environment. I have no doubt that she did not write that speech, because if she had written it and if she had read the bill that was before the House tonight, then she would understand that her speech has little relevance to the matters that have been raised in this bill introduced by Owen Jennings. This bill is very tight; it is not an issue regarding environmental controls. It is about a group of people being appointed by regional or district councils as specialists to give advice, where controlled or discretionary activities are being applied for, that they can be determined to be permitted activities, thereby reducing the resource consent requirements. Has the Minister ever read form of the schedule of the Resource Management (Forms) Regulations? Does she understand it, and does she understand what is required under the Act? I say to the Minister that if she is going to be the Minister for the Environment, then she needs to understand the Act that she is controlling. She needs to understand the Resource Management Act and the issues that come within it. Can the Minister explain to us what a permitted activity is? I would be surprised if she could. If something is not a permitted activity but is a discretionary activity, can she explain to us the requirements that are upon the applicant in order to bring it into the definition of a permitted activity? Is she able to tell us, where a business is to be set up in a footprint area in Christchurch, the conditions that the council will put upon that applicant if, in fact, he or she is to personally occupy, reside, and use less than square metres? The fact is that that is deemed to be a permitted activity. If the Minister understood the Resource Management Act she would know that a council prepares its own environmental report, and at the same time an applicant, at huge cost to himself or herself, also prepares an environmental impact report. The requirements of that report are quite extensive and are clearly set out in form of the schedule. The Minister should know that certain requirements must be met. If, in fact, one meets all those requirements it is a nonsense and an imposition cost-wise on a council to impose that additional cost, which is totally unnecessary. I say that expertise in the matter of resource management in the City of Christchurch and throughout New Zealand is indeed extensive. Councils will appoint those specialists who are available to help individuals with their cases. The councils will appoint them, and to say that democracy has been set aside because councillors will not be able to make the decisions on those applications is a nonsense, because council officials make and write the existing reports. The fact is that democracy has no place in those reports whatsoever, nor can councillors influence those reports. They read the reports and they make their decisions based on them. Sometimes those reports are extremely biased. I have no doubt that there may be occasions when specialists' reports also have a certain bias in them, but we should remember that the councils have approved those particular persons. In places like the Waitaki District Council, specialists are not available to the council. At a cost to applicants, they can obtain their own reports and submit them to the council, where an application is for a discretionary or controlled activity that could properly be approved as a permitted activity. I say to the Minister, with the greatest of respect, that she should learn to understand the Resource Management Act.

The Bill is an example of exactly what is wrong with the Opposition. It picks up an issue, grabs the wrong end of it, and decides it cannot bring itself to a proper policy position. The issue is the closure of post offices, but Opposition members have confused the issue. Most of the concern that has been expressed about the closures has related to banking services. Opposition members, despite all the petitions and all the concern that has been expressed, have still not worked out that people are concerned about banking services, not postal services. Having decided to pick the wrong part of the issue, Opposition members then picked a couple of examples that could be handled within present legislation without the need for new legislation. There would be no difficulty in changing the statement of corporate intent if that were a good idea---I doubt that the amendment contained in this Bill is a good example. Clause imposes a restriction on postal surcharges. The only Government that has done that in my lifetime is a National Government. It used to do so frequently in the days when inflation was so prevalent. It would overprint stamps before they were issued for the first time, and that meant that many New Zealanders bought stamps that had surcharges on them. The National Government did that because it found it impossible to front up to policies that would control inflation. The other point Opposition members have forgotten about is the example that all New Zealanders know about---paying extra for health stamps. The member for North Shore, who is a former Minister of Health, has decided that health stamps should be outlawed, despite people voluntarily paying extra for them. He has decided to introduce a private member's Bill into the House to outlaw health stamps. In clause Opposition members deal with the subject of closures, but that is the wrong issue. I have been listening to most of this debate, and I have listened very carefully to what Opposition members have said. Every Opposition member has shed crocodile tears over the issue of post offices. When one gets to the point of asking them whether they will open one of the post offices that have been closed, there is an amazing silence. The Opposition has not promised that a National Government would open one of the post offices that it has joined in crying over and petitioning about up and down the country. The Opposition is not so stupid as to believe that there is a case for opening those post offices, and that approach merely reveals that when the National Party was in Government it did not have the gumption to make the hard decisions. This is one more area in which the Opposition is indicating why it will stay in Opposition for some time. It is not prepared to take a stance on any issue that is likely to concern some member of the public. A Government has to make decisions that are good for the country as a whole. It occasionally has to make decisions that mean that groups will not get what they want because the collective is more important than the individual or one small group. That is the type of decision that this Government has been prepared to take. Opposition members are hinting to members of the public that they share their concern about post office closures and are distraught at what is happening, but when the finger is pointed at them, and they are asked what they are prepared to do about it, they say that they will allow the matter to go to a select committee, and that they will think about it but will not reverse it. The Opposition is taking that approach because it knows that the State-owned enterprise policy makes sense. It knows that one of the reasons that there were post offices---about three or four times the largest network of any business in the country---and that decisions were not made, was the same petty political point that this Bill is based on. The Opposition was not prepared to front up to the public and tell it that there was a strong case for not having all of those post offices. The member for North Shore has picked the wrong issue. It is clear that despite the post office closures there are almost as many postal services outlets in the country now as there were before those closures. In many areas the hours of availability of that service have been extended, and the service provided to people in more remote communities is more convenient. That is the position of postal services.

This is one of the least controversial Bills to come before this House and it does have the support of all parties. The Bill has been passed without the normal acrimony and politicking that all too often punctuate the behaviour in this House, and I think that is a credit to every member who has examined this Bill and spoken on it in this debate. This legislation extends the special superannuation portability arrangements that already exist for the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau to all the other Pacific Island countries. The Bill increases the level of superannuation and veterans pensions paid to those superannuitants who choose to return to those countries, and it provides more generous provisions reducing the requirement for a -year residency before people are entitled to full New Zealand superannuation to years. There is a provision that if people have lived in New Zealand for years they will be entitled to percent of superannuation, and it will increase by percent a year. In this debate a number of contentious issues have been raised. One of them is the call by one of the political parties to lower the age of entitlement to superannuation to because the population data shows that not as many Pacific Island people live to be as the rest of the general population. I have to say that is a typical shallow political response to a problem. The ACT party is totally opposed to any legislation that brings two laws into this House. We believe there should be one law for all people, and the problem is that if we lowered the qualifying age for one group of New Zealanders or one group of people who live in New Zealand, we would have to lower it for all New Zealanders and that is something this country simple cannot afford. It is important to reflect on the original intention of superannuation policies. The debate on superannuation first occurred before the turn of the century. Bismarck in Germany was the first politician in the world to bring in a ``super'' policy. That debate started in , and superannuation was brought in later that decade. Germany brought in a contributory scheme. It was an insurance-based scheme that employees paid into, and employers and the Government paid into. The whole idea was that over time it would build into an investment fund in Germany, and would keep pace with inflation and with the growing number of people who would receive it over time, because of an ageing population. That scheme was brought in for people once they were . That is the equivalent of bringing it in now for -year-olds. Most people did not live that long, and that is the important thing about superannuation schemes. They are designed as a safety net. What Governments should do is require and encourage citizens to make provisions for their own retirement so that they can have a decent quality of life with a decent income. A Government can simply never provide that level of superannuation for people. If this National Government wants to see elderly people living on larger incomes than they do right now, it must encourage saving for retirement. To do otherwise would simply be to break the bank. We know only too well in this country that after the war we had nine working New Zealanders to every retired New Zealander. Presently, the ratio is four workers to one retired person, and by there will be two working New Zealanders to every retired person. It will be unsustainable, and more New Zealanders have to recognise that that is coming up. We are almost at the year . Many New Zealanders will be retiring in and they must know they have to save and invest now; otherwise the country will be in deep financial trouble and we will be facing a crisis. We actually did have that debate about superannuation in . The whole country engaged in it when we had the referendum, and it is a shame that the referendum was defeated. There is no doubt about it: pensions will have to become less generous as time goes by. The Government, whichever Government, will have to push out the age of retirement and reduce the value of the pension. It is inevitable. That is something we could have turned round. We could have gone down a different path in but, unfortunately, that referendum was more about the person who promoted it than the actual issue. The call for the lowering of the age of pensions for Pacific Island people was irresponsible and illogical. It was sound-good, feel-good election-year politicking, designed to benefit one group of New Zealanders over another, and it is not to be treated seriously by members of Parliament, who have a responsibility to pass good laws that build a strong New Zealand. We do not want laws that weaken or divide this country. Other members have spoken about a number of other concerns. They spoke about the lower life expectancy for Pacific Island people and for Maori. They said that the answer is to look at health care and at the health status of those people, and to introduce a sense of personal responsibility that we are in charge of our own health, as long as we have a health system that can be there when we need it. The goal for this Parliament, for every member of Parliament, and for every New Zealander should be to lift life expectancy not to lower pensions. This Bill has led to the call by many members for the extension of portability arrangements in reciprocal agreements, now available to a number of countries, to many other countries throughout the world. This Bill has made portability available now to many other Pacific Island countries. But when we look at the other countries that have a similar portability arrangement, where people can retire back home and take percent of their New Zealand superannuation, we see that the list comprises Australia, Greece, the Netherlands, Ireland, the UK, Canada, Denmark, Jersey, and Guernsey. That list is not comprehensive. There are a number of people living in this country, working here, who would like to be able to retire home to be with their family in their old age, and who are not covered under the current law. So I would urge this Government to continue down the path of looking to see whether arrangements can be made with those other countries. When we had the second reading of this Bill one country in particular came to our attention---the United States. That country, like all those others, has no special arrangements. So American citizens who come to New Zealand and spend their working-life here find when they go back home to the States to retire that they get only percent of their pension. There are about people who are affected in that way. On the other hand, those US citizens who come to New Zealand and spend their working life here have to have a special provision to be able to obtain their American superannuation. They get it only if they are able to return twice a year for a minimum of month each time to confirm their residency rights. There are many United States citizens who are now New Zealanders living here who simply cannot comply. They cannot afford the trips or they are too old, or there are a number of reasons. There are about people in that category. If they were able to pick up their American superannuation it would be worth about $ million, and they would bring it back home to this country to spend, invest, or whatever. When this issue was first raised I was approached by constituents who are in this situation whereby they have to go back to the United States twice a year, and they asked that this Government find a better way of dealing with that. It did cause us to reflect on the difference between levels of superannuation of New Zealand citizens and those of American citizens. A New Zealand citizen gets about $ a week from Work and Income New Zealand but a United States citizen gets about NZ$ a week after tax. That is a reflection on the fact that the United States has a contributory insurance-based scheme, like the sort that Bismarck put in, whereas we have just an ordinary ``pay as you go'' pension. When we look back at our history of superannuation we see that at the turn of the century, in , the Government at that time made the wrong decision by bringing in a ``pay as you go'' scheme. Then, in the mid-s, Muldoon made another mistake. One of the good things that the Labour Government had done was to bring in a contributory-based scheme, then Muldoon chucked it out. It means that in we will have a crisis. The ACT party is pleased to support this Bill. It is good legislation, and we are proud to be a part of this House that has done so.

It is with pleasure that I speak on the final stage of this Bill. I have sat here for a couple of days now listening to the left-wing members of this House with their tactics of personal attack. Mr Pete Hodgson was doing it just before. It is below-the-belt politics. It is the sort of politics that New Zealand does not want, does not like, and it is absolutely despicable. They question the integrity of honourable members, because they cannot hit their ideas so they go straight below the belt. I have to tell that member that when the people of New Zealand voted for MMP they voted to get rid of that sort of politics. The sooner the Labour Party understands that the people of New Zealand despise it, the better. This House deserves a better style and level of debate where ideas are questioned---not people's integrity. The debate on this Bill has been quite bizarre. While we are talking about a Bill that helps people to move into work, we are at a time in the history of this House where our Government is in a state of chaos. We have a situation where the Government is paralysed. We have a whole lot of sideshows going on that we all know about. We have our Treasurer who speaks so many inconsistencies that we cannot believe him. On the one hand he is applauding the sale of Auckland Airport to foreign investors, and on the other hand he is stopping the sale of Wellington Airport for the same reason. We understand that John Delamere is about to form his own Maori party to be launched by Te Puni Kokiri, the Government funding agency. We understand that Brian Donnelly approached the Prime Minister over the weekend to ask whether she would support him in his candidacy for Whangarei. We have all these bizarre happenings at a time when we need stability. That was on the National Radio today. The whole country is paralysed. Who in business would make any long-term decision to hire people, given all of what is happening right now? This country needs stability and certainty. This Bill is all about that. This Bill will work if we have employment growth going on. We need this Government to stop its spending. There is $ billion there that has not been spent. That should be given back in tax cuts. That should be given back to the families of New Zealand to help to create jobs in their local communities. This Bill will then have a chance of working as it was meant to. I want to reflect on the small-business sector. Its help is fundamental to the workings of this Bill. The small businesses of New Zealand hire four out of five New Zealanders. While the Government cannot do anything about the Asian crisis, it sure as heck can make a difference at home. It sure as heck can sort out the troubles that it has within its own coalition, and it sure as heck can help families to keep more of what they earn. The Government has to sort out all the burdens and costs on small businesses that make them stop hiring people. The No. issue is tax. Small businesses pay personal tax, provisional tax, and GST. A few weeks ago, late at night, there was a new move to bring the IRs to the responsibility of the employers. I understand that many employers of small businesses will now have to have computer systems that link into the new system at the Inland Revenue Department, and that the employer will take the rap if the employee makes a mistake with his or her form. It will be a nightmare for small businesses. The problem is that it is a huge additional burden on them, it drives down productivity, it drives down profitability, and it just stops them hiring people. This Government should make sure that it has policies in place that allow people to hire other people. That is what this Bill needs if it is to work. If this Bill is to help people to move from welfare into work, the fundamentals have to be in place. We have to have an economy that creates growth and jobs. Without a vibrant and flexible economy we will see the welfare lines grow. Already, in the term of this coalition Government, another , people have moved into welfare. Already, in the term of this coalition Government, another $ billion has been spent on welfare. It is now $, for every man, woman, and child in New Zealand, and it will get worse unless the Government is able to put policies in place to create growth and jobs. At the moment we have more and more sole parent families. We know that we have the highest percentage of sole parent families in the Western World. That is a social crisis. Already, in the term of this coalition Government another , children live in sole parent families. I was incredibly disappointed that when I put forward an amendment to this Bill that allowed sole parent families or sole parents to opt into the Bill to have the provisions and the help and support that the long-term unemployed will have, the Minister did not see fit to allow it. This Bill is all about connecting people with the work force. Our party has to agree with that. We just saw another Bill that came through a little while ago that was to put in place the one-stop shops. That means that people will have to go to one place to get help from the Income Support Service and the Employment Service. That is one of the best pieces of legislation that this Government has put forward. I was amazed to find out that the Labour Party will have the dissolution of those one-stop shops as one of its major policy platforms for the next election. As we know, the Labour Party does not have many policies. It was really sad to hear that one good piece of legislation will certainly be dismantled if Labour and the Alliance get to run this country. I would like to finish by just quoting a few of the comments made in the last couple of hours. I heard that this is the nastiest Bill to have been passed by this Parliament, it is all about punishing people, it is a Bill for the rednecks, and it is punitive and coercive! The Green Party made those comments. I have to ask Labour Party members: ``Do you really want the Green Party as a part of your new coalition?''. It seems to me that that is so absurd and ridiculous that it is simply off the planet. This Bill is a step in the right direction. The Minister knows that we believe he could have done more. I guess he has put forward a framework that will allow us to move forward in the future. This Bill is all about helping people to move from dependency into the work force, helping them to become work ready, and the ACT party supports it.

I can add up at least other taxes that have been imposed, and it is just not right for this tax to be imposed by a back-door method. Most people in the sector will not even know that it is being imposed. The education sector has already been battered by Government policy. The export education industry was hit last year by a retrospective tax law, which meant that GST that was owed to that industry, and to tourist operators, was not allowed to be refunded. We understand that about $ million worth of GST should have been refunded to those people in the export education industry; the Government kept the $ million. That was a big hit on that sector. But if we go on, we see that the universities and polytechs in that sector, which are heavily involved in export education, have been pushed and shoved by the Government to keep down fees. Private training providers have probably been the worst hit by Government policy. A moratorium basically has meant they could not expand their courses, or provide students with the new opportunities they had actually had in the planning process. Some private training providers lost millions of dollars because this Government, out of the blue, slammed a moratorium on new courses. While that moratorium has been in place polytechs have been encouraged by this Government to go out and start new courses in areas that have always been the domain of private training providers. Today I received the answer to a parliamentary question for written answer that shows that newly established polytechs had new courses last year, and this year have new courses. Most of those courses will be competing absolutely head-on with private training providers that are not allowed to do anything. Private training providers face a percent cost increase over last year. Again, a reply received today to a parliamentary question for written answer shows that the cost increases for that particular education sector in compulsory fees, levies, and all sorts of other costs have gone from $. million last year to $. million this year. This Government wants to put yet another levy on those providers, but it does not even have the decency to say how much the levy is. All of those people who are out there in the education sector running their businesses, and who are trying to help New Zealand and be part of this $ billion export education sector, do not even know how much to put aside for this levy. It is just appalling that the Government does not think enough of them at least to let them know, to let them have a say, and to warn them what sort of liability they will be responsible for. This is the other question I want to ask: where is the evidence from the Government and from the Minister---maybe he said it and I did not hear it---that this sector cannot work cooperatively and collaboratively on a voluntary levy scheme? Such a scheme would stop freeloaders, be industry-wide, and have a strong test to make sure the funding to be used for a particular project really should be used and that the project could not be funded in some other way. This Supplementary Order Paper does not tell us the answer. The explanatory note does not tell us anything about it. It does not tell us what lengths the Minister has gone to, to find out that he does not need to ram the levy through via legislation; he could go instead to sector representatives and ask whether they could combine and work through some sort of self-regulatory environment to achieve the same ends that he will achieve by compulsorily putting this legislation through Parliament and by not allowing any of those affected the benefit of having their say at a select committee. Embattled tertiary providers really have to understand that this Minister does not know about running a business, he does not understand what this imposition will do to them, he has not told them how much it will cost them, and he has not set any parameters or limits. It is appalling legislation from this Minister, who mismanages everything.

We are now debating clause of this bill, which defines all the terms that will be used in the new bill. Annabel Young, who, as she said, was a lawyer before she came into Parliament, put her finger on a really important point---that is, this legislation has many undefined terms. To my mind, that means it is bad legislation, because it does not give protection to people. For example, if we do not define exactly what ``force'' means, then we leave ourselves open to have either the young people at risk of having excess force used on them---then maybe they will try to go for compensation one day or bring about some form of action---or the staff members at risk, because they can be the focus of disciplinary action. It is a shame that some of those issues have not been more clearly defined in this new legislation. This clause talks about strip-searches and pat-down searches, where harmful items are found and seized. It talks about the use of dogs, basically to search for those items, as well. It is all about keeping our young people and the people who work with them safe. Although this is not the sort of legislation one gets really excited about, it is necessary legislation if we have residential care and difficult young people living in those residences. I would like to spend just a moment thinking about terms that have not been defined in this bill---terms that, in my opinion, should have been included; that should be enacted for young people who are in care. I know it is not appropriate in relation to this bill, and it is a shame really. But when we visited with those young people, it seemed to me that they were all bored. They were bored out of their brains. They had nothing to do. I thought to myself that they all came from really tough backgrounds. Virtually all of them had been abused as children. They have all suffered a whole lot of bad things during their growing-up period. This could have been a real catch-up time for them---not only a time when they were certainly safe but also when they could have been kept busy, had structured lives, been taught boundaries, and learnt some personal responsibility. It could have been a time to turn round their life's potential, because most of them---certainly the ones who were there because of the criminal and youth justice system---were heading for prison. It seemed to me that centres of this sort should put an enormous amount of effort into doing things that will help with rehabilitation, catching the young people up with all the things they had missed out on. One of the things the young people were very proud of and very good at was their art. They obviously spent a lot of time doing art. It was great, but I just wished they spent the same amount of time on reading, writing, maths, and some of the other basic skills they will need when they are eventually released into the community---in some cases to head for jail---at the age of . It is a real opportunity for their lives to be turned round. There was not a computer in the place, yet just today I spoke to somebody whose -year-old child went to school for the first time, and there were computers in the classroom. Many of the young people in the residences need the opportunity to learn the skills that will help them. If they end up moving away from the criminal justice system, they will need those skills to go on to become contributing members of our society. So it is a shame that this legislation is so negative. We need a Minister who will put in place policies that will help the residential centres to do better for the difficult young people they have in their care. I think that should be a major focus of this Government. It has an opportunity to make a real difference. We all know that the one issue that has raised more public ire than any other issue in the last year is child abuse. We saw at first hand a whole lot of very disturbed young people, all of whom had been very, very badly abused as children and who came from very dysfunctional families---families that were not coping, at all. I want to know what has happened to the mentoring programmes. The National Government put in place some great ones. Where are they?
What has been done to increase the opportunities for adults and women to obtain apprenticeships?

There are some important points of principle in the Bill that should be commented on. I was pleased that the member for Rotorua raised the point about the validity of companies taking up the time of Parliament to make changes in the law that will affect their operation. There may be a need for a more general change in the law to facilitate that process, or to determine whether it is appropriate to do that. The Bill is for the benefit of the company concerned, because it will enable it to wind up certain subsidiaries, and will enable the contractual obligations entered into by the subsidiaries to pass on to the major company, General Finance Limited. The Reserve Bank commented on the validity of the process, rather than seeking to transfer obligations through a series of changes with the creditors and clients in each case. The committee considered the matter seriously, and decided that it would mean that no harm would be done to the clients, but that the clients would benefit from it. It was clear that the obligation would be passing to a major finance company with substantial assets of the order of $ million in relation to insurance and financing. The committee considered that change to be of benefit to the clients as well as to the company. The next point related to amendments to existing contractual obligations without consulting the clients to find out if they agreed to that happening. Once again the committee recognised the difficulty that such a requirement could place the company in, and the time-consuming work involved. It agreed that there would be benefit to the clients, and that no loss would be incurred. A point was raised about whether there would be an increased or a decreased financial obligation to the State as a result of the change when such activities occur. When similar companies---such as the Westpac Banking Corporation in and the ANZ Banking Group in ---have come to Parliament to change the law, changes were made in relation to obligations to the Crown to ensure that an equivalent payment was made to the Commissioner of Inland Revenue. In this case there is no change in obligation in relation to stamp duty or any other form of taxation as a result of the change. The committee resolved that the action being taken by the company was appropriate. For the benefit of interested and concerned clients I point out that the companies that will effectively go out of existence, and whose obligations will be recognised by law as applying to this particular company, are the Autokred Corporation Ltd, which has been involved in motor vehicle financing for the Mitsubishi New Zealand Ltd franchise dealers; and General Finance Acceptance Ltd, which has been the principal lending arm of the group and provided finance to the financial and commercial sector up until April . Since that date the company has always been conducted under the name of General Finance Limited.

Goodness gracious! People need information about their entitlements. Opposition members have criticised the advertising of the additional living-alone entitlement for superannuitants. Opposition members have said that they are on the side of superannuitants, but they do not want superannuitants to be told that they are entitled to another $. a week. Superannuitants must receive that information. The Audit Office has suggested restraints, which have been adopted by the Government in its advertising. That is the way it should be dealt with---through the Audit Office and with appropriate rules. The mechanism in the Bill as amended by the select committee makes it absolutely clear that broadcasters must give identical terms to every party, whether major or minor. The Bill provides insurance that there will be no political interference. It ensures that the Broadcasting Standards Authority will issue the invitations. That must occur at least months before a general election. The replies from the parties go directly to the authority. All of the parties are informed within days about what is offered to each of them. There is also provision to ensure that the broadcasters offer the same terms to each of the political parties and to each of the candidates so that the terms are equitable. There is provision for an appropriation to ensure that in the event of a snap election the amount of money available is guaranteed to be at least the same as for the previous election. That aspect is important for the purpose of certainty so that parties can plan ahead. All of those factors remove political interference. Treasury was against the allocation of that money in advance, but the committee felt that the advance was necessary to ensure that there was a level playing-field; that everyone would know the amount of money that was available; and would know the rules that would apply. The allocations are to be made through the Secretary of Commerce on a reimbursement basis so that the funds can be used only for the production and development of the broadcast material. There is even provision for the repayment of funds if a party makes a false claim about the number of candidates who are standing. We have made it clear that representatives of the Leader of the Opposition and of the Government cannot be involved in the settlement of disputes by the authority in the application of those rules. That provision clearly removes the opportunity for political interference. There is additional flexibility in relation to the time that people can choose to broadcast their opening addresses. In response to the requests of broadcasters, we have made it clear that they, and not the political parties, are responsible for programme standards, so that if they are concerned that proposed advertising material is libellous or contrary to the principles of the Human Rights Commission they have editorial control over that material as they do over other advertisers. The broadcasters made a strong case for that responsibility at the select committee, and the committee agreed to that change. The new section in clause provides that under the criteria an offence is committed if broadcasters do not provide identical terms for each political party. The terms from the broadcasters make it clear that it may become public that the parties have dealt with it properly. Those measures build on the past understanding to ensure that political advertising is made available to all parties on a fair basis. Those provisions have to be adjusted to take account of the deregulation of broadcasting, and to ensure that public broadcasters and private broadcasters are on an equal footing. That requires a greater amount of State funding, not to the extent that was made available in in real terms to enable that to occur, but to ensure that none of the political parties---including those that are supported by the rich and by those with special interests---will be better off than the others. The public will not be faced with an amount of political broadcasting that is greater than the maximum. That was made absolutely clear in the Bill. It will not be possible to do so outside the campaign period. The Bill is a sensible and workable measure and all members should support it.

I also want to support the report back of the Bill. There are some crucial questions relating to both parliamentary sovereignty and national sovereignty that are part of this consideration. These tribunals are set up by resolution of the Security Council, in terms of the United Nations law. The question really arose as to whether they should also require legislation in New Zealand for us to give effect to them. I agree that they should. I think the public is concerned that there are important international obligations that New Zealand enters into on which Parliament ought to have a say and be formally involved in. For instance, there was some public concern, when our Government ratified the GATT agreement, that although there was some consequential legislation arising out of that, the agreement itself did not come before Parliament to be ratified. I think that as a matter of principle we should be moving in this direction. I think it is appropriate that New Zealand's accession to this and agreeing that we will be involved with these international war crimes tribunals is a decision to be made by this Parliament. We are doing that. We are specifically agreeing to the establishment of tribunals covering offences in former Yugoslavia, perpetrated since , and in Rwanda and surrounding countries, which include Burundi and Zaire, since . It is good that we are doing this. There is provision for further tribunals to be agreed to by regulation. The Regulations Review Committee, which I chair at the instigation of National members, said that Parliament should also be required to agree to New Zealand acceding to further tribunals. In the event, the Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee has compromised on this matter by saying that the regulations be ones that this Parliament could move to disallow, and thereby we would not be agreeing, eventually, to our accession to those further tribunals. The effect of the submission made by the Regulations Review Committee has been agreed to by the select committee, and I appreciate that agreement. There is the question of national sovereignty, to the extent it is subsumed by United Nations decisions. I think in general we should agree to them. The imposition of sanctions on the countries that make up the former Yugoslavia and on other countries such as Haiti, before the restoration of the legitimate Government there, were done by regulation. The question arose as to whether Parliament should be involved in that. I think it is part of our international obligations that we do apply those sanctions. It can be done by regulation, and there is at least the option for Parliament to disallow those regulations if, for some reason, it disagrees. I am pleased with the responses made by the committee. These are important tribunals. It is important that people do not escape the force of law and justice merely because conflict is still occurring and merely because they may have held office in a Government or in an armed force. There are some standards of justice that apply with respect to widespread rape, pillaging, and ethnic cleansing that we should stand up to. I note that New Zealanders are involved in the tribunal based in The Hague. Senior Sergeant Steve Upton has gone there as a researcher to build up these cases. I am pleased that New Zealand is involved. I hope that issues that still arise, such as where these people are to be incarcerated, can be resolved. I fully support this Bill.
