We will vote against this proposed clause, which artificially interferes in the borrowing of local authorities by restricting their ability to borrow on behalf of local authority trading enterprises. The Government has been working for ages to try to get this right. When the Bill came in, new section Q, which related to borrowing powers, provided a prohibition on borrowing on behalf of local authority trading enterprises. It stated: ``No local authority may borrow any money or enter into any incidental arrangement on behalf of a local authority trading enterprise or for the purpose of lending the money to or providing financial accommodation to a local authority trading enterprise.'' Subsection () states: ``Nothing in subsection () of this section shall prevent a local authority borrowing money for the purpose of subscribing for or otherwise acquiring equity capital in any local authority trading enterprise.'' So on the face of it, it was absurd. Firstly, it said local authorities will have the general power to borrow---that was new section Q. Then under new section N it had power to enter into incidental arrangements. Then under section P, no, no, one is not allowed to borrow in foreign currency. Then new section Q stated that one is not allowed to borrow on behalf of local authority trading enterprises, but one can raise equity capital. Now what is the message to local authorities from this? It is that they should not set up a local authority trading enterprise, because they will be limited in their ability to borrow. Do it in-house in a slightly old-fashioned organisational structure, because one can certainly raise money for the purpose of that by borrowing. Secondly, if one does have a local authority trading enterprise, one cannot borrow but one can put equity capital into it. So that was the original format. Virtually every local authority that came before the select committee said that this was unfair, unworkable, and silly. So eventually the Government members of the committee were not persuaded to go as far as we did and say ``Take it out.'' because otherwise they are just being encouraged to work with old-fashioned business units or raise equity capital instead. Instead, they took it out of the borrowing thing and put in a whole new clause A, ``Restriction on borrowing on behalf of local authority trading enterprises''. The principal Act is amended by inserting the following section ZPA---where they get these numbers from beats me---``no local authority may borrow or enter into any incidental arrangement on behalf of a local authority trading enterprise or lend to, or provide financial accommodation to, a local authority trading enterprise on terms and conditions that are more favourable to the local authority trading enterprise than those that would have applied if the local authority (without using rates or rates revenue as security) had itself been the borrower.'' I know that the intention was to try to provide a level playing-field but I read it, and local authorities and others, when they heard it, asked: ``What on earth does this mean? How is it going to work?''. So after we had reported it back, we got a supplementary order paper from the Minister, trying again to get some wording that is sensible. Now we are going to vote on an amendment that would state: ``No local authorities shall lend money to, or provide any other financial accommodation to, a local authority trading enterprise on terms and conditions that are more favourable to the local authority trading enterprise than those that would apply if the local authority were (without charging any rate or rate revenue as security) borrowing the money or obtaining the financial accommodation.'' It is a bit more likely that that will be able to be interpreted in terms of its applicability. As I said, I can understand that the Government has been struggling with something that provides that the local authority will be on all fours with other commercial enterprises in terms of borrowing. But it does not achieve that. The wording is still not really clear. Although the committee struggled with the issue, it has not come up with something that is really clear. It will be a playground for lawyers to interpret. Thirdly, let us look at the alternatives to this, which make it clear that it is not appropriate. First of all, as I have said, providing restrictions on a local authority raising money for one of its own trading enterprises simply encourages local authorities, which are already encouraged to do this for tax purposes and also for borrowing purposes, to keep the operation entirely in-house as one of the operations that they will carry out within their normal activities rather than setting up a local authority trading enterprise, which in most cases is probably the most businesslike and appropriate way to carry out these activities. Secondly, by putting these restrictions it does nothing about the issue that was raised before about raising equity capital for this purpose as an alternative. If people are worried that local authority trading enterprises will have a commercial advantage then there is nothing about the fact that a local authority that does have a light structure will simply raise equity capital instead so as to work through this. There is certainly no way one can prevent from that happening, in a legal sense. This is a measure that acts against the operation of local authority trading enterprises. It sends the wrong signals to local government in terms of doing things in-house or raising equity. It is not genuinely a level playing-field. If a private body wants to bid for local authority contract work then nothing in the company law of this country would prevent a major enterprise, like Fletcher's or Fulton Hogan or whomever, from simply putting money at an advantageous rate into one of its sections that wants to get into contracting for local authority work. So it is getting it on favourable terms to enable that company to take over local authority work on those advantageous terms and then, having cornered the market, to raise its prices to take into account the real cost of borrowing. They have no laws within them like local authorities have.

That may be great; the member for Tamaki may consider that that is great in normal circumstances. I have to ask whether that is enough to achieve our goals and objections in education for our country. One has to ask what we are trying to achieve when we spend a single dollar, and how far that goes. Are we currently providing educational opportunities for the children of our country, and does the additional . percent go any way to alleviate the problems that every one of us here knows exist in education? Education is an investment in the future, but . percent is not an investment---it is peanuts. It will not provide for the growing number of children, pupils, and students who urgently require the skills to lead us into the st century. The Minister of Education may spout on, as the member for Tamaki does, that an increase is an increase and we should be very thankful for that. The question I ask is whether it is enough. Is it what is required? How best can we provide the opportunities for our children? If the education system was providing those basics, I would say that we do not need an increase and that . percent is generous. But in fact the system is not. It is in desperate need of extra support. It is in desperate need of extra funding. It is in desperate need of a bit of guidance and direction from a Minister who cannot even distinguish a back door from a back window. Pre-school children and their parents need support. The member for Birkenhead spoke of ``parents as first teachers''. Traditionally families have had support from Plunket organisations, kindergartens, and child-care centres run by happy, willing, and competent people. Those were all the goals of previous Governments, but it does not seem to be the goal of this Government. Last year---as it happened, just before the election---the Minister announced ``parents as first teachers'' as a new programme that would solve all the problems of pre-school children. The programme had been trialed and run in the United States previously and has been found to have huge flaws in its implementation. However---to carry on---there was extra funding for ``parents as first teachers'' in this Budget. How much was that? A whole $. million was provided for ``parents as first teachers''. That still provides pilot programmes only in a limited number of regions. The West Coast---one of them, thankfully---is to pilot and to check out whether this system works. That does not go anywhere near providing enough assistance for the growing number of problems and pressures on pre-school children throughout our country. ``Parents as first teachers'' is not the answer, and I would ask the member for Birkenhead to go and check his facts and to check the effectiveness of this programme. We still have Plunket societies, child-care centres, and kindergartens running raffles and closing down in spite of this extra funding and effort going into ``parents as first teachers''. What is the logic of that? What is the logic of withdrawing support for existing networks and trying to prop up new trendy programmes that have not even been trialed and proved to be successful? Luckily, some of the children can get to attend their local schools and actually get through pre-school education. But they go along and find that they need extra assistance at school. They need the little bit of extra help that makes the difference between achievement and failure, that hour or two or three perhaps that the teacher can spend on individual reading assistance, on spelling, and on giving attention that is so often lacking in many home environments. The Special Education Service has provided that essential service. We will continue to have high unemployment as long as this Government takes the market approach to solving the problems. We will continue to have pressure from poverty, from the stress of extra hours because of the Employment Contracts Act, from worse conditions imposed in the working life, and from the stress of relocation through redundancy. These social pressures mount, and the first area of exposure is in schools where children cannot cope, where they do not have the social skills, where they have not received the right attention to allow them a chance to learn and carry on and contribute as good citizens. The Special Education Service provides assistance for these children---a chance to learn and carry on, and a chance to catch up. That is what we would consider an investment in the future. What did this Government, in this past Budget, consider was a fair investment in the future of special education? It was $. million at a time of a projected Budget surplus of $ million. What are the Government's priorities? Whom does it consider it should be helping? We need to help families and children in this Year of the Family. This is where the priority should lie. This Government has to get those priorities right. It has missed out. It has missed its chance in the Budget, and I urge it to go back, take a look, and provide the assistance that special education requires in our country. In my region we can provide assistance only for category pupils. Some members might not know that category pupils are pupils who are severely disabled. They have disabilities, are handicapped, and are in desperate need of assistance. We luckily can provide assistance for them on the West Coast. Unfortunately, there is no funding to provide special education for category , or pupils in my region. I think that is criminal. The Government bears the responsibility for that, and it should go out and make that extra expenditure to allow those children an opportunity in their lives. If we do not make that extra effort and provide the funding, those children will end up missing out, end up on the wrong side of our legal system, and become a burden to our society. They will become a cost rather than a contribution to this country. Not only are the pupils in need suffering through the lack of funding but so too are the rest of the pupils, who are in classrooms with mainstreamed pupils and who have to suffer from the extra pressure of having mainstreamed pupils in there. I thank the member for Glenfield for the remark she made at the beginning of the debate. The member for Coromandel and I were happy to work with the Government on the Bill. It is important to bring the purpose of the Bill to the attention of the House and the public. The Bill's prime purpose is to limit the transmission of the human immunodeficiency virus that, as far as is known, eventually becomes the acquired immune deficiency syndrome. The Bill has dealt with only one of the avenues of transmission---drug addiction---but that is the most potentially dangerous avenue, particularly to the heterosexual population. The committee received excellent submissions from many interested groups such as health workers, unions, the AIDS Foundation, the Pharmaceutical Society, and, most important, drug users. I learnt a great deal from the information received, as I am sure other members did. The major myth that was blown for me, and I am sure for other committee members, was that needle-sharing is part of the culture of drug addiction. Need forces drug users into sharing needles and syringes because not enough needles and syringes are in circulation. The sharing of needles and syringes is not a part of the culture. Another interesting point on which submissions were received was that homebake is of great concern not only to the Department of Health but to many others involved in drugs. I also found out that homebake resulted from New Zealand technology, and is now exported. One cannot be proud of that, but it resulted from New Zealand technology, however misguided. Another important submission from drug users and the AIDS Foundation was concern for the corporate users, who shoot up only once or twice a year and who are not considered addicts and would not usually call themselves users. The concern was that those people are not likely to consider owning needles and syringes. In the future the numbers would come out through corporate users, usually heterosexual, who would shoot up only once or twice a year and possibly pass the human immunodeficiency virus antibodies to other sexual partners, either homosexual or heterosexual. Those were the three matters of interest to me as a newcomer to this subject. The submission made by the Intravenous League was interesting. It is a new group of people, who are rehabilitated drug users recovering from the effects of drug abuse, working amongst the users in the community and trying to convince them that they should change their habits. That task will take a long time. It will take some persuasion and a certain amount of education. Mr Lindberg of the New Zealand AIDS Foundation said that it is hard to measure prevention, and that is a matter of concern. He said that there is a great fear of encouraging drug use and that that fear has inhibited the thinking on such changes, and that was the reason the Bill was necessary. In relation to the argument that the supply of syringes encourages drug addiction he drew the analogy that the provision of glasses and bottles does not increase alcoholism. That is a sensible approach. The Opposition is pleased to be involved with the Bill. The member for Coromandel has had considerable success in making amendments relating to the sale, supply, and exchange of needles. The report of the Department of Health refers to the exchange of needles, and the importance of ensuring that syringes are returned at the time when those requiring them enter the system, at whatever point, to claim the new and clean syringes. As the member for Glenfield said, the Minister has suggested tightening up the authorisation of particular outlets rather than having the system loose-ended. There should be more authorisation, guidance, and closer observation of the outlets. It is assumed that many chemist shops and pharmacies will voluntarily become part of the scheme. Perhaps drug clinics and doctors will also become involved. The scheme is voluntary, and it is important for the community to realise that point. Clause , which is a major clause, creates the regulations for the sale, supply, and exchange of needles. Several amendments and clauses considered matters such as making magic mushrooms illegal. In New Zealand only one kind of mushroom is illegal, and that has been included in the Bill. The term ``human consumption'' has been redefined in the amendments. Opposition members were able to persuade the committee on the matter. The problem of AIDS is of great concern to the community, but the public must realise the importance of trying to contain it as much as possible. Many people may consider that the sale, supply, or exchange of syringes and needles go against their natural grain of thinking, and that drug addicts should not be supplied with further tools of abuse. The matter of AIDS must be considered by the community. It was pointed out to the select committee that AIDS, not drug addiction, was the matter being considered. The committee was concerned about the human immunodeficiency virus, not about drug addiction. The consequences of the spread of the human immunodeficiency virus to intravenous drug users includes the rapid spread to others---intravenous drug users, predominantly, by the sharing of needles and syringes, and also by sexual contact. Those concerns were expressed in some of the submissions received by the select committee. Although the fertility of female intravenous drug users is somewhat reduced by drug abuse, it is unaltered by human immunodeficiency virus infection, and consequently vertical transmission may result in the birth of children infected by the virus. That is the reason the Bill must proceed. Our natural instinct not to encourage drug addiction must be set aside, and the matter of AIDS must be considered. The Opposition has been pleased to be involved with the Bill. The select committee has approached it in a sensible fashion, and all members have learnt from the submissions. Only one submission, received from the New Zealand Medical Association, did not agree with the provisions. It doubted the value of implementing such a scheme, and quoted the survey and experience in Edinburgh and Australia. The committee had experience of Edinburgh and Australia referred to it, and the position in both regions has improved quite considerably.

As I have been involved with local authorities myself, I have worked with some very good health inspectors. They have the interests of the community at heart. The time for writing is surely when a Bill is before the select committee when people make submissions. In fact, two groups of people made submissions to the select committee. Those groups represent many people. The first was the Service Workers Federation of Aotearoa, which represents more than members of affiliated cleaners' unions, caretakers' unions, hotel workers' unions, and hospital workers' unions round New Zealand. The other was a much larger body of people---the National Council of Women. Both groups expressed some concern. During the Committee stage it was reported that the National Council of Women had expressed concern in its submission that the demise of the Board of Health had been rumoured for some time. When the board and its standing committees were reconstituted the National Council of Women, together with many other organisations, went to great lengths to nominate to the board appropriate people who had independent voices. It was also said during the Committee stage that perhaps the Minister did not like some of the advice. It was pointed out that several Board of Health subcommittees had recently reported, particularly on community health and primary health. There was a massive shindig in the Beehive for the launching. If the matter was not important, why was it given such prominence in the promotion of health? The Board of Health has certainly served the country well. The National Council of Women expressed its concern. The Opposition wanted to make sure that that concern was expressed. This Bill does deal with the establishment of other advisory committees and subcommittees. I hope that he takes an interest in children's health---as I suggested in the Committee stage---because the nation has an abominable record of natal deaths. The Opposition is very concerned about children's health. Once upon a time New Zealand was proud to have one of the highest standards of health for our children, but we now find ourselves well down the ladder of world results. That position concerns me, and I am sure that members of the House are concerned that the issue of child health is not being addressed. The Government abolished the children's board, which was actually an advocate for children. Now there is no organisation to stand up for children, let alone children's health. Therefore I hope that the Minister will take some note and establish an ad hoc board, subcommittee, or advisory committee on children's health. I move, That the Summary Offences Amendment Bill, the Criminal Justice Amendment Bill (No. ), the Summary Proceedings Amendment Bill, and the Crimes Amendment Bill (No. ) be now read a third time. The Bills were all introduced as part of the Disorderly Assemblies and Restrictions on Association Bill, and the measures have two major features. First, the Summary Offences Amendment Bill creates a new summary offence of participating in a disorderly assembly. The new offence deals with a specific public order concern that was debated substantially in the Committee stage---that is, that the presence of persons who congregate in public places in a manner that causes other members of the public to feel intimidated should attract the attention of criminal law. The new offence does not apply to any group of persons engaging in bona fide protest. In the Committee stage Opposition members criticised the efficacy of the exemption. However, I put it to the House that it has never been part of the purpose of the Bills to alter the law about public protest. That is a fundamental right. In any event, I do not consider that there will be any difficulty in practical terms for the police operating with the exemption. I do not think that the police will be fooled by any bogus attempt to hide behind that exemption. As in all other offences, the police will make a judgment and, if there is doubt, the courts will decide. That is the way in which our system works. Another matter raised during the Committee stage relates to the issue of a warning. The disorderly offence is committed when the assembly continues after a warning from a constable to desist is ignored. The reason for the warning is that the offence is a public order offence. If the persons disperse, the public order concern is met, and if they do not disperse, or if they reassemble shortly after, they may be arrested. The requirement for a warning is also consistent with the approach used in another public order offence---namely, obstructing a public way. The effect of that provision is well understood by the police and has not caused any difficulty in practice. During the Committee stage concerns were also expressed by Opposition members about the evidence required to prove the offence. I do not consider that those concerns are well founded, either. A conviction will be able to be obtained on police evidence alone, depending on circumstances. The new offence sets out an objective test in relation to the fear engendered, and, to satisfy it, will not generally require members of the public involved to give evidence in court. The other major feature of the measures is the introduction of non-association orders as a distinct sentencing option for offences that are punishable by imprisonment. That option does not exist under the present law. Because of the nature of gangs and the manner in which they are organised, it is considered that the measure will be efficacious in preventing people who have committed offences from associating with gangs.

With the current economic policy, the balance of payments deficit is more than halved as a percentage of gross domestic product. It is markedly down in dollar terms. As the Chair has remarked, there have been speakers in the debate. I am the fifty-first speaker. The debate has taken hours. It can be said that the debate has been of considerable quality. It has also been a debate of considerable diversity of view. Perhaps the time has come to try to sum up some of those elements, and to determine where we can go from here. The first matter I want to deal with is the amendment proposed by the member for Tarawera. That amendment, which postpones the second reading, is unlikely to achieve any purpose. The select committee that examined the matter heard evidence for hours over days. It started its consideration in late November and reported back to the House in May. The saga that led to the legislation goes back further than that. The Laking report was distributed in October . That committee heard many public submissions. When the report was delivered to me I called for more submissions, and I received more than . Some modifications were made as a result of the submissions, which have been made available to anybody who wants them. When the Bill was introduced it attracted a further submissions to the select committee. There can be few questions about the matter that remain unconsidered. The motion moved by the member for Tarawera suggested that the select committee should give further study to the drinking age, the number of liquor outlets, and the sale of liquor at grocery stores. No doubt all those questions are controversial, and no doubt members have differing opinions on them. All the reports and submissions that I have outlined dealt with those questions. To send the Bill back to the select committee for further study will not produce any more enlightenment. All those matters can be dealt with by the House. The House needs to face up to its responsibility and decide what it thinks on those issues. However, it will not be able to do that at the select committee because, on a conscience issue, the select committee will not be able to determine anything. The amendment moved by the member for Tarawera, although well intentioned, will not achieve anything, cannot achieve anything, and ought to be opposed. I turn to the second reading itself. Some members have suggested that the Bill should not be given a second reading, on the grounds that there is nothing wrong with the existing law, and that, if it works, it does not need fixing. That view is not correct, either. The existing law is in a bad state. The parent Act was first passed by the House in . It has been amended on a piecemeal basis on many occasions since that time. As a result, it provides for varieties of licence, many of which overlap, and there is a degree of confusion about them. The Bill before the House reduces those licences to licences. That is a considerable advance. It will make matters simpler and better. Some members have suggested that the incremental approach to the sale of liquor is the way in which that subject ought to be dealt with. That approach has been tried since , and it has not been a success. Although the Bill involves a conscience vote, and the outcome of conscience votes is always unpredictable, it is appropriate to deal with all of the elements of the law relating to the sale of liquor at once, because each part relates to every other part. The matter needs to be considered as a whole, in perspective. The Bill does that.

It is probably the biggest Bill of a substantial character ever to be introduced into the House. Its introduction is certainly a milestone in resource management in New Zealand. It is the first comprehensive and integrated review of the laws governing the management of the country's natural and built resources---that is, land, air, water, and minerals---and is the largest law reform of its kind in the country's history. The Bill repeals statutes and more than regulations. New Zealand is the first country to approach resource management as a unified poll, writing into law the principle of sustainable management as the guiding principle of the Bill. The Bill demonstrates the Government's commitment to reforming New Zealand's domestic laws on environmental matters. The Bill's objective is to bring together the laws relating to resource management, but it does not simply amalgamate those laws; it sets up a new system. That new system will promote sustainable management of natural and physical resources, and with that will provide for considerably greater efficiency in the planning and consent processes. In one Bill, Parliament is reforming the management of land, water, soil, minerals, energy resources, the coast, air, pollution control, and noise control. It also sets up an agency for the control of hazardous substances. The Bill is a significant advance in the way we manage our natural and built environments, and the way we plan for the future. It has been the subject of lengthy and considerable consultation for more than years. More than public meetings have been held on it around the country, dozens of hui, many informal meetings, and two freephone sessions. More than submissions were received. In many ways the Bill is a product of the views of all the sectors of society that have an interest in resource management. It consolidates New Zealand's reputation as a nation looking clear-sightedly into the future. It will enable the growth and development we seek, while protecting the environment that nurtures us all. The Bill sets up a system of policy and plan preparation and administration that allows the balancing of a wide range of interests and values. While the Bill aims to achieve good environmental outcomes---certainly better environmental outcomes than are possible under the combined effect of present legislation---it is concerned with balance. The system it establishes will ensure that all relevant values are taken into account in reaching resource management decisions, and that that is done in a fair, consistent, and efficient manner. The Bill provides a new framework for resource management. That framework complements the reforms of local government, which, in turn, provide for greater efficiency, greater accountabiity, and more focus on resource management functions and decision-making. The Bill also sets out roles and responsibilities of central government, and of Ministers, in relation to resource management. Far from opting out of resource management---as some have suggested during the lead-up to the Bill---central government has clearly made itself part of the resource management process. The Bill provides for national policy statements to which local government must have regard; national call-in provisions affecting major projects; national water conservation orders and heritage orders; national coastal policy statements under which coastal management through regional councils will develop; minerals programmmes, which will set the ground rules for the Crown's allocation of its mineral, including energy, resources; and opportunities for central government to set technical standards for environmental quality. Preparation of those statements will be particularly important. They, along with related powers to set standards, will provide firm guidance under which regional and district plans can develop. The Bill also provides for the establishment of a Hazards Control Commission. That, of course, is the environmental protection agency promised in the earlier versions of the policy. The Government decided that the name ``Hazards Control Commission'' best represents what it will do. That agency will have responsibility for licensing and advising on national standards and controls for hazardous substances, and for new imported and genetically modified organisms. Regional government will have a pivotal role in the new administration. Each region will have to prepare a regional policy statement setting out the objectives for management of all the resources in the region as an environmental whole. Part II states and defines the purpose of sustainable management. In essence, sustainable management means that the needs of the present should be met without compromising the needs of people in the future. It means people living within the realities of the biological and physical resources that support our well-being. Part II sets out a list of principles that are important for thinking about sustainable management. The purposes and principles taken together form the corner-stone of the new resource management system. The Bill contains some provisions to ensure that Maori interests and values are carefully and appropriately included in resource management decisions. Part III sets out responsibilities for resource management. It enables people readily to find out their rights and obligations. That, in itself, is an innovation. Another important change is the reference to uses of land being permitted unless they contravene a plan. That not only gives greater certainty to landowners but it is intended to make planning authorities much more specific about the scope of controls they might impose, and the reasons for those controls. Part IV sets out the functions, powers, and duties of central and local government---and I have already mentioned those of central government. Regional government will have responsibility for managing water, soil, and geothermal resources, for pollution management, and for natural hazard identification and mitigation. Under the regional resource policy statement, separate regional management plans can be prepared on a range of matters important to that region. Regional rules should reflect not only the balance between the rights of individuals and the interests of the community, but also the responsibilities all individuals have to maintain environmental quality. Territorial government will be obliged to prepare district plans. Those will cover matters similar to present district planning schemes, but are expected to be different in two respects. They will be concerned first and foremost about the effects of activities. Any controls over activities will need to be justifiable in terms of environmental standards that a community wants to achieve. Second, the new law requires that all local authorities examine all available methods---including service delivery, provision of information, and the making of regulatory rules, or a mix of them all---to determine the best way of resolving a community's resource issues. By shifting the focus from the means to the environmental ends of resource management the Bill aims to minimise adverse environmental effects and to promote good environmental outcomes. To achieve that aim, resource management authorities must monitor the effectiveness of their plans. Part VI establishes a new system of integrated consents to cover land, water, subdivision, discharges, and activities on the coast. Those provisions are all major advances on all those in present legislation. The Bill classifies activities and their effects into several categories, including those that are permitted, those that are discretionary, and those that are non-conforming. The Bill specifies time restrictions for the consideration of consents, which will be a considerable advantage to developers who are held up by lengthy delays under many existing statutes. It incorporates many of the features of environmental assessment and enhancement procedures by integrating impact assessment with consent procedures. Significant streamlining is achieved by requiring all the consents needed under the Act to be heard together. That is why many other statutes are repealed under this legislation. The Bill will ensure that major projects can be dealt with speedily and effectively. A significant new feature of the Bill is the provision of greater encouragement for mediation in all of the processes. That means that parties will be encouraged to reach agreement amongst themselves and that informal pre-hearing meetings can be held, rather than the parties always saying, ``See you in court.'' Part VII deals with designations and public utilities. Current law permits public utilities such as power lines and water and gas pipes as of right in every district without a planning consent. The Bill provides for those utilities to be subject to the same scrutiny as other land uses, and to be dealt with, and provided for, in management plans. A new provision is that designations will be required to be reviewed more frequently. All designations will lapse after years, and that will remove many of the sources of blight by designation in our cities. A very important point is that the Bill makes it easier for affected landowners to obtain compensation. With those measures, the Bill will significantly reduce the abuse of private rights previously experienced, and it will force designating authorities to think more carefully about the nature of the designations they make. Part X deals with the Planning Tribunal, which plays a very important role in current planning legislation. The Bill provides for the continuation of its existing functions, and includes new enforcement functions and an adjudication role relating to landowner consents for mining activities. Mediation and pre-hearing meetings are encouraged. Part XI strengthens considerably the enforcement provisions in existing law. Three different enforcement mechanisms are provided: declarations, abatement notices, and enforcement orders. Any person will be able to seek a declaration from the Planning Tribunal on any matter relating to the operation of the Act, including interpreting plan provisions. Local authorities will be able to issue abatement notices requiring abatement of environment nuisances. Finally, any person will be able to apply to the tribunal seeking an order to restrain unlawful activity, to restore the environment, and/or to claim reimbursement. The Bill sets out clear offence provisions. An important new development is that the period of prosecution of offences--- months---will apply from the time it was reasonable to discover the offence rather than the time the offence was committed. Penalties have been strengthened considerably. The maximum fine will be $,, plus $, for each day that an offence continues. Imprisonment is provided as a sentencing option. The Bill provides for company officers to be personally liable for offences that they knew about, or should have known about. Water management will be carried out within the context of regional management plans. Existing use rights will be phased out, and rights granted in perpetuity will have their duration limited to years. The Bill provides for the transfer of water permits between users and sites in certain specified circumstances. Permits for damming or diversion of water cannot be transferred between sites. Geothermal resources will be managed by regional government as an element of water management, with provisions for central government interests to be reflected. The Bill continues and extends the provision for water conservation orders as a means of protecting water bodies of national significance---an important provision, as it extends that means of protection to geothermal resources, ground-water, and wetlands. Under the Bill there are three distinct elements in the assessment of mining proposals: first, the granting of mineral rights; second, the consideration of the impact on the community and the environment; and, third, the impact on affected landowners. All of those aspects are consolidated in the Resource Management Bill, with their distinctive features being recognised. Technical changes are made in the use of the terms ``prospecting'' and ``exploration'' to reflect international conventions. Central government will retain the responsibility for allocating mineral and energy resources. Minerals management programmes drawn up by the Minister of Energy will form the basis for those allocations. Sustainable management, together with recognition of the Crown's interests as owner of the resources, will be a focus of the minerals programmes. Those programmes will define the frameworks within which commercial allocation of minerals and energy resources will occur. The Bill changes the current provisions on landowner consent. Generally, landowners will have more rights and more say about developments. No landowner will lose rights that are held at present, and some will be given increased protection. The Bill rationalises the existing confused and inconsistent legislation, providing instead for coastal management to be shared between the Minister of Conservation and regional councils. Regional government will be required to prepare regional coastal management plans. There will be one coastal consent process for all resource management aspects of coastal development. Of course, that radically streamlines the present position. Indeed, in many respects, the Bill does streamline; it cuts down delays, cuts down cumbersome procedures, and makes the whole process more integrated. Fisheries management will remain the responsibility of the Minister of Fisheries. However, fisheries management plans will be required to have regard to coastal management plans. I come now to pollution and hazardous substances. The Bill provides for integrated pollution control. That very important provision will control in a consistent way all the processes of discharging to the environment or producing wastes. Discharge permits will be required, and discharges will be expected to conform to a best, practical option management system. The establishment of a Hazards Control Commission is provided for in Part XV. The commission will deal with hazardous substances as part of its responsibilities, and will be the subject of separate legislation to be introduced next year. The commission will advise on regulations that set national standards for the control of hazardous substances and potentially hazardous new imported and genetically modified organisms; it will licence new organisms or products containing hazardous substances; it will develop a manifest-based tracking system for every hazardous substance; and it will monitor and enforce controls on hazardous substances and new organisms. The Bill is a very large measure. The Government proposes to send it not to one of the existing select committees but to a specially constituted select committee comprising seven members, so that the range of topics dealt with in the Bill can receive scrutiny from members with different backgrounds---all of which need to be brought to bear on the legislation. The introduction of the Bill is the culmination of a set of changes that go back to the National Development Act and the Water and Soil Conservation Act. For many years there have been promises that the Water and Soil Conservation Act would be changed, but amending legislation has never managed to make its way into the House. Finally, the Bill brings together all of the statutes that deal with planning of natural resources, and integrates them into one set of procedures in one statute so that they can be dealt with comprehensively, expeditiously, and effectively. It is a massive change. The Bill will need to stay in front of the select committee for a considerable period, and to be worked through. I particularly thank the core group of officials from the Ministry for the Environment who worked on the legislation. It is obvious that many State departments played a big role in the measure, but the convenor of the core group, Ms Denise Church, has done a superb job in bringing the legislation together. I pay a public tribute to her and her team of officials for a job of mammoth proportions that has been well done. I commend the Bill to the House.

This occasion will be looked back on as a historic one, because the Employment Equity Bill rights a social wrong that has long been a problem. The member for Taranaki, did not really say what the Bill was about, nor did he advance any argument about the reason it should not be introduced. The Bill really has two primary features. First, it is about equal employment opportunities, but hardly anything in the Bill on that front has been debated. I wonder whether the Opposition opposes equal employment opportunities, because it is plain from Opposition members' speeches about pay equity that the Opposition is against pay equity. The Opposition has made that much clear. It is interesting that the Opposition has suggested in the debate that it is interested in women's rights, but not in helping women. On many occasions the Leader of the Opposition has said that the National Party should select some female candidates, but of course no notice is taken of his advice. Since the Leader of the Opposition exhorted the National Party to select women candidates not one woman candidate has been selected---its Leader's direction has not been followed. That should tell the House something about the attitude of the National Party to women. The member for Selwyn has sold the women of New Zealand down the river in her attitude to the legislation. She knows that since the equal pay legislation that was passed many years ago was implemented, females in the New Zealand work-force have remained quite substantially behind their male counterparts. They are still behind, and, years after the full implementation of the Equal Pay Act, they receive only . percent of the amount earned by their male counterparts. That is the position the National Opposition regards as appropriate; one that it seeks to advance. It says that women should not be treated equally with men. The argument the Opposition has been advancing in the House this afternoon amounts to that. All of the wind that the member for Tauranga, the Leader of the Opposition, the member for Maramarua, and the member for Selwyn have been advancing in the debate amounts to one thing, and one thing alone---the Opposition is opposed to women. It wants discrimination against women to continue: it does not want them to have equal pay, and, particularly, it does not want women to have pay equity. Therefore it opposes the Bill. The politics of the Business Roundtable are unlikely to advance the Opposition very far in relation to New Zealand women; they have been sold a line. The member for Selwyn, who has been going round sucking up to big money interests in order to try to satisfy some of their more extreme doctrinal demands, is finding that she has to abandon any commitment to New Zealand women to do that. The result is that the Opposition will oppose an important social measure that will advance the interests of women in New Zealand society. It is an appalling prospect for Parliament to see that the Opposition is against women. It wants discrimination against them to continue, and it will vote against a measure that will bring to an end discrimination against women in New Zealand . The New Zealand electorate has to contemplate that prospect carefully, because, in essence, that is what is involved. The party that cannot select women candidates and that will not advance women candidates to Parliament will continue its historic policy of discriminating against women by voting against the legislation. That is what its behaviour amounts to. The Opposition has a sexist policy of discrimination against women, and that is very sad.

I withdraw that reference. However, what I want to say---as bluntly and as clearly as I can---is that the Leader of the Opposition does not really know what he is trying to do with the material and the allegations that he is making. He started off with the ``gang of '' and took up the charges of Keith Peterson, which turned out to have no substance. He abandoned those charges, and he has now taken up with a Dominion journalist. He has engaged in the House in impugning the integrity and actions of a very fine public servant, who has acted honourably and properly throughout the matter and who has tried to do only one thing---to protect the interests of investors. The Leader of the Opposition has tried to damage the interests of those investors because he needs public prominence as a result of his political insecurities and the instabilities in his caucus. He has borrowed Luigi's ferret. Unfortunately, that ferret has lost its nose because the researchers for the Leader of the Opposition have been basically irresponsible about the matter. The Leader of the Opposition has already upset many people. I have read letters from his supporters in Hawke's Bay who have accused him of political opportunism. Those people are small investors who have lost money as a result of the member's actions. He has already had to apologise at least once publicly for what he has said. Therefore he does not make his allegations outside the House any more; he makes them under the cloak of absolute privilege in the House, where no one can get at him. Indeed, the fact of the matter is that he does not know how to conduct a responsible Opposition. He does not know how to act in the public interest, and that is why he will not stay in office. All of his actions show that he and the Opposition want a maximum number of companies to go broke. He wants a maximum number of small investors to lose their money and then to blame the Government, because he can see a political advantage for himself in that. That is the reason that he has conducted such a disreputable campaign that will do nothing but damage the commercial interests of New Zealand and the investors who take part in them. The Leader of the Opposition has been led by the nose in a speech that he could not even construct for himself. He had to read it out, and he probably did not write it. He does not even remotely understand the legality of the matters. He is pushing a cause that responsible elements of the news media have long since abandoned, and the result of his belittling and maligning campaign will simply prejudice investor confidence in companies. His attacks are baseless and irresponsible, and I shall answer those attacks now. I spoke to the Minister of Police earlier, and he told me that the police are not investigating Mr Ramsay. Indeed, Mr Ramsay co-operates frequently with the police---something he must do because they are engaged in similar activities. It is no use trying to make anything out of Mr Ramsay's tipping off of Registered Securities Ltd that articles were being published about the company. The company was told to batten down the hatches in case small investors wanted to get their money out immediately---and companies need to be prepared for that. It was nothing to do with Mr Ramsay that the company brought an action for an injunction, and it was nothing to do with Mr Ramsay that the action succeeded. The Leader of the Opposition has made several charges---all of which have changed in nature from time to time---over a period of weeks. He is unable to keep anything about them constant. When the National Government was in office it did absolutely nothing about corporate fraud. It changed the provisions in the Companies Act, but it did not provide resources to enforce those provisions. In years the National Government did nothing. The Labour Government set up the corporate fraud unit when it took office. The unit has six full-time investigators and one part-time investigator. Further, it has inquiries in the hands of specialist people who work under contract, and additional resources are made available when needed. The enforcement structures are one side of the equation. The other side of the equation is the development of appropriate investor protection legislation. On that front, the Government is developing very important legislation on insider trading, take-overs, company regulations, and futures trading, which will soon be introduced into the House. I announced that legislation in February. The corporate fraud unit has had a considerable effect on the maintenance of discipline and commercial probity in the corporate arena. The unit's principal objective in any inquiry is to protect the interests of the investing public, and, if possible, to retrieve or preserve intact those investments. Of course, if that protection is in doubt the unit has the power to make recommendations to the Government so that statutory receivers can be appointed, and that should be done so that the interests of the investors can be protected. However, if the objective is not immediately obvious the unit pursues breaches of the Companies Act and prosecutes for those breaches. The effectiveness of the policy is amply demonstrated in the unit's role in the closure of more than businesses in . The action taken by the unit prevented further investor loss in those companies. While the investing public should understand that, clearly the Leader of the Opposition does not want the unit to continue doing that. He does not want the unit to protect the interests of investors, and he has made no secret of the fact that he rejects the unit's initiatives on that matter. Indeed, I suggest that he read this morning's National Business Review, in which the head of the corporate fraud unit, Mr Ian Ramsay, pointed out why he was trying to do what he is trying to do. Unlike the Leader of the Opposition, I support what Mr Ramsay is trying to do. I want investors to keep their money rather than lose it---and, of course, the actions of the Leader of the Opposition will ensure that people do lose their money. The law will be enforced without fear or favour, and prosecutions have been launched when breaches of the law have been found. I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition should think that that is so surprising, except that he seems to want to try people in the House rather than in the courts. I do not know why he wants to do that. Throughout the whole matter, the Opposition has shown its cavalier disregard for the interests of the investing public. The Leader of the Opposition has said that the unit should abandon any hope of retrieving and protecting the funds of investors, and that its only mission should be to clobber people. The recovery of investors' funds is very important. The corporate fraud unit would have abandoned the policyholders in Capital Life Assurance Ltd if the Leader of the Opposition had had his way. It would have ignored the investors in the Commercial Advances Group, who shared the $. million that was recovered with the assistance of the unit. It would have ignored the investors in Mortgage Markets, for whom it recovered $,, if it had taken any notice of the approach to the matter on the part of the Leader of the Opposition. The Leader of the Opposition is looking round for a cause that he can hitch his star to. If only he can find that cause, and if only it takes off, he will be secure. His approach in this matter has been a manifest failure---the only evident fraud that has not been properly attended to is the fraudulent claim made by the Leader of the Opposition in this debate about the effectiveness of the corporate fraud unit. His attacks on the integrity of the leader of the corporate fraud unit, Iam Ramsay, are quite scurrilous. Mr Ramsay is a person of total integrity and trust, and I back him percent. He is a person of unimpeachable integrity. For the Leader of the Opposition to attack a very fine public servant who has done a great deal of good work to protect people from the difficulties of the corporation environment is disgraceful and political. Indeed, the Leader of the Opposition said that people have been arrested and tried for offences. He did not say in what respect those offences were committed or what the charges were. He said nothing of the date and the time. The Leader of the Opposition spreads innuendo, doubt, and uncertainty, but he gives no specificity. His is a disgraceful performance.

I was not going to take a call on this clause, but while the Minister is considering his reply maybe I could be a little bit helpful to him. One of the reasons we are so careful about changing legislation, and one of the reasons we are scrutinising this legislation so closely, is that over time a body of case law is built up that sets precedents as to how the law applies. I suggest to the Minister that it might be appropriate for him to take some advice from officials as to whether the changes being sought will change the precedents that have already been set as a result of the body of court law on this matter. The anomalies that we have talked about this morning are just a few anomalies that we have been able to think of off the tops of our heads. As I explained earlier, none of us taking part in this debate has had the benefit of being on the select committee, or has had the benefit of studying this Bill in any great depth. It is a serious matter. If we change the law, it has an adverse effect on the way in which the issue has worked in the courts in the past, and, particularly, on the understanding of those people who have to work with it. That, to me, is the most important thing. It is easy for us to make law in this place, but people out in the workforce who run companies, and their lawyers and accountants, have to administer these laws once we make them. I suggest to the Minister that, as he is considering his response to the comments made by my colleague Paul Swain, he take some advice from the officials---particularly any officials aware of the precedents relating to this clause---and reply along the lines of what damage will be done to those precedents if we make this change. Clause agreed to.

Maybe I can start where the previous speaker finished off. Firstly, I do want to say a few words about Peter Dunne. People in this House will know that Peter Dunne has campaigned for many, many years on taxation issues. He is a man who understands revenue and tax issues well and has taken a consistent line on this matter throughout the debate. I always like following his speeches because there is always something to learn. I want to talk about two points that he raised. One is the Scully report. It was fascinating in the select committee that we had a bit of a talk about the Scully report. Treasury indicated that it had engaged in a debate on the Scully report and that a lot of the propositions advanced in that report in fact could not be sustained. The ACT member got very agitated at that select committee because he has staked his policy almost entirely on the Scully report. Treasury made it clear that many of the ideas advanced in the Scully report could not be sustained. When they engaged in a debate with him on the issues he admitted that maybe the deadweight loss in taxation was a bit lower, in fact considerably lower, than his previous projections. So I think it is important that when we are talking about these issues we take account of the facts in the debate as well. I come to another point raised by Peter Dunne, and that is that we will have another debate on this issue in the future. He is right. People do not learn from history; he is dead correct about that. He is also right that the tax system into the future will need change. There is no doubt about that. There are plenty of international reports around at the moment for people to read, which show that the issues of taxation and the collection of revenue across nation States will occupy Governments for many years to come. They are controversial issues and emotional issues, because they are about how we raise the revenue to run the services in this particular country. It is fascinating to look at the other side of the House. Those in the gallery will see who is sitting here, who is in the House, and they are silent. National members are silent about this particular issue. They know exactly what they promised to the people of this country when they went up and down the country at election time, saying they would bring in tax cuts. They are not even trying to defend what is happening in this legislation today. In their heart of hearts they would rather they did not have to postpone these tax cuts at all. They are doing it only to satisfy the Treasury poodle, who has got his butt next to the Prime Minister. As we all know, that seating arrangement will not last terribly much longer. They are doing it only because that was the price of the Prime Minister sitting in that chair. People are not fooled at all. I agree with my colleague Michael Cullen when he says there will be no tax cuts. They will come back to this House next year. Mr Ryall from the East Coast will get up again and make a speech about needing to be fiscally prudent and all that sort of thing, to defend again the fact that they are not going to put their tax cuts through, and to defend the fact that they welshed on their promise. I am looking forward at that time to John Banks taking part in this debate. We know what John Banks thinks. John Banks thinks that lot cheated. If he did not have the whip on him he would be down here saying so. That is why we had that little scuffle in the House not so long ago.

My colleague does not agree with me. Maybe I have read the Bill wrong, or maybe the briefing was wrong---who knows? But it is good to see there is not a lot of retrospectivity. I think the Bill will work well.

I notice that Mr Hide is interjecting. I say to him that I understand that in a technical sense maybe the matter is not a confidence one. But that member works with the public, as we all do, and we know what the public thinks when the Government loses a vote of this magnitude. It is an important vote to lose. The Government could have managed it slightly better, but it chose not to. The Government has suffered a defeat in an important area. Now it is a matter of going back to the drawing board and looking at how we resolve these issues. Clearly, Parliament is not of a mind to deal with this taxation of life insurance and superannuation fund savings legislation in the way that the Government proposed. There is now a challenge to Parliament to do something that will provide the sort of relief that we have talked about for people who save for their retirement. I come back to a point I made earlier. It is important to start a culture of people saving. It is important to have that culture bred into people at a very young age while they are still on low incomes. The method of doing that that we looked at was never going to succeed. Now we have to go back to the drawing board and look at some way in which we can do it, because this country has some serious financial problems. We have a current account deficit that is in some difficulties, and one of the ways through it---not the entire way through it---is to increase our savings as a nation. It is now time for us to sit down and think about how we deal with that.

Sir William Birch was in a position to so something, and he took the extraordinary step of tabling a memorandum in this House that states that we now have an understanding of how we will deal with it. One of the things I have done in my lifetime is learn a little bit about negotiations. One of the things I have learnt about negotiations is that when one signs off on something, one makes sure that it means something. As I read through the memorandum that the Rt Hon. Sir William Birch tabled in this House, I see that they are fine-sounding words that mean nothing. It was as if a character in Yes, Minister had written those words. I also want to speak against the part by part motion. At the outset, I ask the Minister of Health to think again. I have had a quick flick through the supplementary order paper. There are substantial changes, on pages , , , , and , to the Bill that was presented to the select committee. The select committee was unable to make any amendments at all to the Bill. We were told the Bill had to be back in the House to implement the tax changes that need to come into effect on July. The Bill was rushed through without any reference at all to some serious submissions that people had made. We are talking about an almost totally rewritten Bill being presented to this House. The Minister has brought this in, simply because not to do so would probably mean that one of his coalition partners might leave. That is what it is about. It is about holding the Government together. The other problem we have with this is a very simple one. This supplementary order paper has now been introduced but most of the people who were on the select committee are not in the House. They are away in Australia on urgent public business. They are deemed to be within the precincts of the Chamber but they are unable to contribute to this debate and to scrutinise what this means. There are serious changes in this supplementary order paper and it should not be allowed to go through without proper scrutiny and full debate. In the very short time I have had it, I have flicked through and noticed a number of changes. I want to satisfy myself that the changes that are listed here do make some substantive changes to the way the health system operates and are not simply window dressing. My concern is that sometimes the words that are used in these Bills can also be used not to do anything. I want to make sure in this case that that is not so. We need the opportunity to go through it in some depth. The Bill is a difficult one in two respects. The first is that it does not, as the Rt. Hon Bill Birch said it would in an earlier debate, just adjust the name. It actually starts to change again from Crown health enterprises to hospitals and sets up the regime for public hospitals again. This supplementary order paper gives some teeth to that, and one can see that when one starts to work through it. We have to make sure that that bit of work is done properly, and that it will stand and provide the accountabilities that people in this House want to happen. But the second thing that is of concern is the change to the taxation legislation. The Minister used that as the grounds for the select committee not to hear submissions but to get the work done quickly and get the Bill back into the House. He said it had to come into effect on July. We need to know that what is being done in the taxation area is not going to disadvantage hospitals in respect of the way that other health providers will operate. There is still provision for private operators. There are some caveats around it and we want to make sure those caveats work, but it is still here. We do not want the public hospital system to be disadvantaged by a tax change that might advantage the private operators at the expense of the public system. I know the Minister quite well and I know what his agenda is. I know that he does not share Neil Kirton's views. That is why we have a schism here and why we have the supplementary order paper. I ask the Minister to take a point of order at the end of this speech to do this Bill clause by clause so that we can have the proper debate on it. Finally, I want to make a point that I think is important. It concerns the process. The communities in this country expect this Parliament to deal with their legislation in a proper way. That is what people expect us to do. They do not like to see us being presented with -page supplementary order papers that completely change what was written in the Bill in the first place, then for us to ram it through in maybe four debates, with members on the other side getting up to move closure motions because they do not want the debate to go on for any great length of time. That denies us the opportunity to go through the Bill and have a proper examination of it. The Minister of Health certainly should not support that. He should allow the Committee of the whole House to be able to get on and do it properly. The Opposition has very real concerns about the way the Bill was introduced in the first place. This motion is a further outrage in this respect, and if the Minister allows the Bill to be dealt with part by part he does this Parliament a disservice. Then he wonders why the public feels odium towards us. It is because of this sort of behaviour and it has to stop. It is about time that the Standing Orders Committee had a look at something like this because it is so wrong, and the people know it is wrong. If the Minister of Health has any---no I have to be careful what I say. If the Minister is listening to reason he will stand up now and allow this Bill to have a clause by clause debate. If he does not we will oppose the motion to have a part by part debate. I promise the Minister that we will give him a very vigorous debate on the issues in the Bill but if he wants to deal with it on the basis of actually trying to get the legislation sorted out, if that is what he really wants to do, then let him recant the part by part motion and let us get on with the work. I know that it will take some time. There are serious issues in the Bill, and in the supplementary order papers, and they deserve consideration. It is simply not good enough to railroad it through like this. It will be on his head if he allows it to go through in that way. He will get the opprobrium that he deserves if he does that. It is about time the Opposition parties were given an opportunity to deal with these properly. It is the first time I have seen this supplementary order paper. I had only time to flick through a few pages while my colleague Jonathan Hunt was speaking. I knew that something was going on behind the scenes; it has been obvious with the toing and froing and the way that the Government has been organising its business today. It is just not good enough to put it on us like this and expect us to have a truncated debate. It think it is wrong and the Minister should think again.

There is a second point--- percent of Maoridom lives in the cities but does not have any official overall recognised tribal authorities. The Minister wants to speak in Maori. Remember the last time he spoke in Maori? He said that time that within the lifetime of this Parliament he would produce legislation on Maori land leases. Where is it? There are days to go, and where is the legislation? It will not turn up; it will not appear. That is one more broken promise by a failed, incompetent Minister. That Minister should speak Maori to the people and tell them that little truth. He should tell them in Maori the way that they can be let down again. Did the Minister like it? Was it good? I know it was good. In the Hon. Matiu Rata brought a Bill into Parliament called the Treaty of Waitangi Bill, which did not have a Maori majority on a three-person tribunal.
