Ko Tongariro Te Maunga. Ko Taupo-nui-a-Tia te Moana. Ko Te HeuHeu te tangata. Nga mihi ki te whare e tu nei. Nga mihi ki te tangata whenua. E hora nei i te Whanganui-a-Tara. Nga mihi ki nga kai korero. Nga rohe o te motu i te Whare Paremata o Aotearoa. Ko te wehi ki te Atua te timatanga o te matauranga. Na reira tena koutou tena koutou tena koutou katoa. The mountain is Tongariro. Taupo of Tia is the lake. The chief of all this domain is Te HeuHeu. Greetings to this house. Greetings to the original inhabitants. Greetings to the spokesmen of the electorates in Parliament. To fear God is the beginning of knowledge. Therefore greetings and greetings to you all. I count it a privilege to stand in the debating chamber tonight as the National Party member for Tongariro. In taking my place in the House, I acknowledge the outstanding support of my wife, Joan, and my young adult family. I also salute my parents for their motivation and sacrifice to us in our youth and for the support of my brothers and sisters. I record my appreciation of and thanks to my electorate executive, the Waikato division, and my enthusiastic campaign team. All worked tirelessly for the prize. But there is one other group to whom I owe much gratitude. I refer to the voters of Tongariro who were prepared to make a change and support my candidacy and my party. To them I say publicly, thank you. I also offer my best wishes to Noel Scott in his future endeavours and thank him for his stewardship of the electorate. I am reminded of the words of Edmund Burke, who centuries ago said: ``Government is a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants. Men have a right that these wants should be provided by this wisdom.'' In essence that is why we are here; to be sensitive to and to legislate for legitimate need, whether it be the collective need of the group, the community, the region, the nation, or the specific need of an individual and his family. I cannot imagine any greater privilege than to have the opportunity to share in that process. In Tongariro became a new electorate with its northernmost town, Tokoroa, its largest vote base. At the time of the election, as reflected by the Labour Party's voting support, there was great hope that a new Labour Government would usher in more employment, greater rural security, better education, and a general upturn of the economy. Sadly for my electorate, as for every other rural electorate, that was not to be. Neither could the economy prosper under the Labour Government's hidden agenda of unproven theory and free-market garbage. The hope that many people had soon turned to despair. Businesses crumbled. The rural infrastructure was damaged, and unemployment continued to increase. The end result of the former Government's economic policies led to the closing of post offices, the closing of railway heads, the closing of some school-bus routes, and the further downturn of the services that rural people expected and thought were their rights as the biggest producers of the export wealth of the country. What had taken successive Governments many years to develop and nurture was smashed by the former Labour Government through its sheer inability to understand or its lack of knowledge about New Zealand's fragile rural and manufacturing economies. Questions that have always been asked about the economy are, first, how do we make it perform to its best advantage; second, how do we combat the pressures and blows that have been brought to bear upon it; and, third, how do we use the unique characteristics of a colonial people to bring the country into the kind of prosperous future that we all believed was possible, but that was made all that much harder by the incompetence of three Prime Ministers presiding and exercising executive power over the past years? Six years of hard labour have left a cruel mark on the towns and on the people that I represent. It is to be hoped that under a National Government things will begin to change. Last year was a momentous year in the history of the nation, because acknowledged the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi---a treaty of partnership between two peoples of such different and varying backgrounds. I am proud to say tonight that in a real way I stand here as part of that living and developing partnership. I am proud to say that as I recall my father's history I recall the great Maori migration---the Mataatua canoe that brought my father's tupunas to these shores. It is also with considerable pride that I mention the Breadalbane, the -ton ship captained by Captain John James from Big Bras D'Or, who left Nova Scotia on December and arrived in Auckland on May . My mother's people, the McInneses were fellow travellers on board who later travelled from Auckland to Waipu and became, along with other travellers, the early settlers of the Waipu Scottish settlement. We had the advantage of being brought up in a privileged position of partnership, and no one ought to be surprised when we speak in terms of racial harmony, of sharing of friendship, and of fair play. Whatever one's view, Maori migrated first. All others came after. But, whether one's ancestors came first or last, we are here as citizens of this great country. We are New Zealanders. We are in this together, and those were the earliest lessons taught in our household, for which I give my parents praise and thanks. We are required again tonight to call on all peoples of New Zealand to draw on their rich and varied cultures and traditions to advance the interests of our nation. To all new immigrants I say kia ora and welcome. The strength of an electorate is in the quality of its people. The Tongariro electorate profile is an interesting one. Based on the census of population we had Maori; Pacific Islanders---most living in Tokoroa; others, including combinations; and , Europeans. I should like to pay tribute at this time to the team of Pacifica who are working so hard with Government support for the benefit of the Island people in my community. Tongariro's population, in keeping with the failed economy over the past years, has decreased. Tokoroa was a town described by a previous member of Parliament, Mrs Rona Stevenson, some years ago as a ``throbbing vitality'' and it was then only people short of city status. Today it has also suffered severely. The Kinleith work-force of more than has decreased to about and it is still decreasing. Certainly, the change of ownership from Elders to Carter Holt Harvey Ltd has brought greater security and confidence to the south Waikato. As a company it has welcomed the Government's forestry policies, and greater work opportunities should follow in the near future. Tokoroa, the northernmost town in my electorate, and the largest, is the centre of New Zealand Forest Products Ltd. Apart from New Zealand Forest Products Ltd, Tokoroa has other large industries that not only service the needs of the Kinleith mill but are also exporters of its products. Kinleith forest occupies a land base of , hectares, of which , are under productive plantation forest. Radiata pine, with , hectares planted, accounts for percent of the productive area. The hectares of eucalypt plantation are a significant hardwood resource by New Zealand's standards, representing nearly half of the natural eucalypt resource and, unlike the balance which is scattered throughout the two islands, concentrated in a single block. The forest region is responsible for the supply of all the wood requirements for the large pulp and paper complex at Kinleith and for the supply of logs to sawmills belonging to Pinex Timber Products Ltd---a subsidiary of New Zealand Forest Products Ltd. New Zealand Forest Products Ltd exports , tonnes of logs to Japan and Korea through the Port of Tauranga, thus contributing significantly to the forest industry's generation of overseas funds for New Zealand. The annual harvest is ,, green tonnes of logs---,, tonnes from clearfell of hectares of mature forest, and , tonnes from production thinning of about hectares of immature stands. That yield contributes percent of the total demand of ,, tonnes. The balance is purchased as logs from other growers and as chips from sawmills in the region. The Kinleith forest is managed on a sustained-yield basis. The land is maintained for the current and subsequent crops, and the company conducts large plantings, pruning, and production-thinning operations. The growth rates of those trees are up to times greater than in most northern hemisphere countries. Efforts by New Zealand Forest Products forests have ensured that second crops are superior to the first rotation in height and markedly better in stem quality. In the Kinleith region nearly all the original forest plantings have been clearfelled. About percent of the region's clearfelled yield this year is scheduled from second rotation stands. Coupled with increasing knowledge of the response of the species to various forms of management those factors promise that productivity and flexibility of the forest resources can be maintained. A comprehensive $ million modernisation of the Kinleith mill operation commenced in mid- and is due to be completed in mid-. The modernisation programme will bring about a major rationalisation of Kinleith's manufacturing activities, with the future focus being on quality packaging papers and pulp for the New Zealand market, and for major Australian and Asian export markets. Key elements of the modernisation include the closure of three small-capacity paper-machines. The expansion and modernisation of pulp bleaching and drying capacity include a unique chlorine tree-bleaching process and a rationalisation of product lines. The modernisation and its consequent quality and productivity improvements will provide the international competitiveness necessary for the company to maintain a competitive force in its domestic and export markets, and will provide a sound base for future growth and development. I turn now from New Zealand Forest Products forests to another large operator in the Tongariro electorate---Pinex Timber Products Ltd. Pinex Timber Products Ltd is New Zealand's largest sawmilling company, producing , cubic metres annually. That company, which employs people, currently exports percent of its production to different countries. Its aim is to place percent of production in export markets. In my electorate its sawmilling and the processing of sawn timber PLVC-treated roundwood products amount to , cubic metres annually. The company has people working in Tokoroa, but it is running into very basic problems. While it is expensive for it to develop export markets it is finding that the current domestic environment is the worst the industry can remember. Also, at this time we are going through a low in building activity that I believe is due mainly to high interest rates. Companies such as that must see some improvement or they will be forced to rationalise, and, of course, we know that rationalisation means more unemployment. As I have already indicated, forestry plays a large part in the electorate of Tongariro. It would be fitting for me at this point in my speech to mention the Tuwharetoa trust at Turangi, the trout centre of the world. Lake Taupo forest, comprising , hectares of Maori land, is leased to the Crown for the production of exotic forestation. The lease is for years from April to March . Originally that land, lying to the east of Lake Taupo, from Taupo south to Turangi, was totally undeveloped Maori land. In and the Tuwharetoa tribal elders cast about for a way and means to develop that large area of land to make it productive and income-bearing---first, for the benefit of the owners of the land; second, for the benefit of the nation; and, third, to protect Lake Taupo and its tributary streams from man-created pollution. The answer to those three principles was in a properly developed and managed forestation concept. To that end, after a number of years of discussion amongst the Maori owners, and negotiation and discussion with several Government departments and agencies, agreement was reached on the philosophy, concept, and principle of a lease of land to the Crown for the production of forestation. That was signed in May with the Minister of Forests and Lands of the time, the Hon. Duncan MacIntyre, for the Crown, and elected trustees for the Maori owners, representing of the subtribes of the main Ngati Tuwharetoa tribe who own and live on their large land holdings in the central North Island plateau. Planting of the , hectares Lake Taupo forest in Pinus radiata under the control and direction of the new New Zealand Forest Service started in and was completed in . The capital for the development and management of the forest was provided by the Crown, and its investment will be replaced from the sales of forest wood. Clearfelling of Lake Taupo forest is planned to start in , and as the yield from the forest is at a ,-tonne annual sustainable basis its employment possibilities to the central North Island area of Turangi and its district will be of tremendous benefit to all. The Taupo District Council has plans before it at present to zone land in Lake Taupo forest as a sawmilling zone to attract the sawmilling industry to the local Lake Taupo area in order to process the wood from Lake Taupo forest rather than have it transported out of the district for processing elsewhere, especially through log sales to Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and other Pacific rim countries. The Tuwharetoa trustees are all in favour of local processing of their forest logs. Standing alongside the first-mentioned forests is the smaller Roto Aira forest of , hectares. The forest planting, again mainly in Pinus radiata, started in and was completed in . The land is owned by the subtribes of the subtribes of the main Tuwharetoa tribe. In every way it is a similar pattern to that of the big Lake Taupo forest. Clearfelling of this forest will start in with a sustainable annual yield of , tonnes of forest wood, sawlogs, and pulping components. It is the wish of the Tuwharetoa trust to purchase this forest from the Crown. They own the land and already have a part-share in the forest. It will be a pleasure for me to play a part in those negotiations with the Crown on their behalf. In addition to the , acres of forest close to tree-felling, and employment for a large part of the Tongariro electorate with a profit to the forest owners and industries, the Tuwharetoa tribe has also about , acres developed for domestic farming in traditional sheep, cattle, and deer. About percent of their farming enterprise is debt-free. The loan funding for development has been reimbursed to the Crown and the properties are freehold. They are all run as large station farm entities, and they not only provide income to their beneficiaries but also employment for beneficiaries and industry and commerce in Turangi, Taumarunui, Taupo, Tokoroa, and Rotorua. The Tuwharetoa tribe from Turangi is also blest with the possibility of geothermal development in the future. There are clearly defined areas with a geothermal resource located on Maori land: for instance, the Tokaanu geothermal field on Roto Aira forest trust land, the Wairakei field on Tauhara trust lands, the Mokai field on the Turoa Paki trust lands, and the Ohaaki field on Ngati Tohu trust lands---all those geothermal fields are looked on by the Tuwharetoa landowners as a resource for development to provide profit and employment for the landowners and the wider New Zealand public in general. In the past the New Zealand Electricity Department reserved to itself the sole and exclusive right to develop and sell this resource. However, with corporatisation and the pending privatisation of New Zealand Electricity Corporation Ltd, the geothermal resource is a fuel that can be developed by the private owner. The Tuwharetoa tribal trust will certainly in the future plan to develop this valuable resource with the aim of using the resource to process the very large volumes of exotic forest wood that will shortly come on stream to start from Lake Taupo forest in and in from Roto Aira forest. It is a fact beyond dispute that Turangi has the best trout-fishing and produces the biggest trout in the world. It is also well known for its magnificent recreational holidays, with an unlimited source of opportunity. New Zealanders who have erred can be found in either Rangipo or Tongariro prisons. Rangipo prison houses inmates under the watchful care of officers. At the Tongariro Prison Farm are a further adult inmates. Further up the road are younger offenders at the correction detention centre and all under the care of another officers. A pleasurable responsibility given to me since I have become Tongariro's member of Parliament has been the presentation of the merit star, a new ranking insignia, to selected officers of those two prisons. The award is made only to officers who have attained a senior grading and who have frequently been involved in performing higher duties. I was delighted to thank those men for their services and faithfulness to duty. I say to all prison officers tonight that they have a difficult and unenviable task, often made harder by the lack of Government policy or supervisory quality---present management exempt---and I salute them in their work. I reiterate to the prison officers in my electorate that the Labour Government's monument to prison policy, Waikune, will not be duplicated in Turangi. These are hard but interesting times. In the course of two vigorous election campaigns one became aware of problems as well as successes in the electorate. Farmers in the electorate have suffered much over the past few years at the hands of an uncaring Government. I am amazed at the lack of understanding among many New Zealanders about our reliance on the rural economy. I believe that sheep farmers who have not sold this year's wool clip have the right to equal support from the New Zealand Wool Board until all have sold one annual clip. There must be a fairer way than that which has happened. Many of the trusts and incorporations in our area are working exceptionally hard in a tough environment to better the resources that they have. An important economic enterprise for Maoridom is that carried out by the Ngati Kahungunu people from the Wairarapa on land in my electorate at Mangakino, adjoining the Maraetai power station on the Waikato River. This land at Mangakino was granted to the Wairarapa Maori in in part settlement of claims for loss of rights in and adjoining Lake Wairarapa because of Crown action during the late nineteenth century. At Mangakino the Maori incorporation, known as The Proprietors of Mangakino Township, has responsibility for the administration of the residential, commercial, and industrial land in the township, together with three forest blocks, the larger two of which are leased on a royalty basis to New Zealand Forest Products Ltd. Pouakani Trust was formed in to take over from the Board of Maori Affairs the land development scheme originally established after the Second World War. In there were sheep stations and leased dairy farms. Since then the owners have been involved in a very extensive farming scheme for those farming properties and have implemented a policy of taking over the leased dairy farms and running them under various sharemilking arrangements. The cost to the incorporation in loss of resources in the township land has been considerable in that it has been very difficult to administer economically some leases that are perpetually renewable and have a rental tagged at percent of Government valuation. The net return to the owners is minimal, with considerable administrative difficulties. In the case of the farm development scheme the condition of the leased farms at the time of hand-over was such that development to a satisfactory level was a considerable drain on the owners' resources. The wish of the owners through the incorporation and trust is to develop its resource to its full potential, to provide a sound economic base for the owners and their families. Although the incorporation and the trust endeavour to operate as a commercial enterprise and to use the assets to the best advantage they are severely constrained by both the expectation of the people that they will retain the land, and the inadequacies or unfairness of previous transactions during the time that they held the land. It is only with the sympathetic support of Crown agencies that this taonga can be preserved for future generations. Current economic forces are operating to restrict severely the manner in which the asset can be developed and used by the people, and the alternative of treating the land as being part of the trading stock of the enterprise is not acceptable. During the campaign, candidates and members of Parliament offered their parties' policies to the voters in the electorates. In good faith we reiterated our parties' policies, believing at that time that our party would deliver on its promises. We spoke to voters of the welfare State giving way to the enterprise State. Our policies reiterated the necessity for good fiscal management, a balanced budget, and a low inflation and interest rate regime. While all of that is true, we found to our dismay that the economy was worse than expected. That position was compounded by the Bank of New Zealand bail-out, an increasing internal deficit, and still-rising unemployment. I am disappointed that the National Party has failed to keep faith with its senior citizens and is no longer prepared to link pension payments to the consumer price index this year. I believe that pensioners and those on social welfare benefits would have readily accepted the policy cuts if we had had the courage to reduce the top-level salaries of State servants and State-owned enterprise executives. In my opinion that should be a future direction. Taumarunui was once a flourishing town of considerable worth. It has faced hardship in the past, but never directly as a result of a Government's philosophy that cared nothing for the rural dweller. Taumarunui is well served by good community-minded people, a responsible council, an outstanding hospital, Radio King Country, Taumarunui Development Inc., and its own Ruapehu Press. Government policy must never be a hindrance; it must be supportive of the aspirations of such people. The challenge to the National Party is to keep its promises laid down in the election manifesto that were reiterated further in the speech from the throne. When I stood for nomination as the National Party candidate for Tongariro I mentioned to the voting delegates that bureaucrats would not find me easy, and that I would not be walked over by such people. I am thankful for the arm of experience that has been gained through a long involvement at National Party branch and executive level. That I am now here as a member of Parliament is but an extension of those beginnings. My promise to the people of Tongariro is that I will listen and serve them well. My promise to the National Party was that I would be a faithful member of our great party. The task in my hands is to ensure that the people I represent, their families, and their problems will receive a fair hearing in the House.

On September last year I raised the matter of a $ million insurance scam, and I said that I would stake my career on that being proven to be the case. It has been proven to be the case; in fact, the Securities Commission found that there was no insurance at all. At that time Professor Trow of Victoria University defended the accounting practices of the BNZ (Bank of New Zealand), so did the board of the BNZ, and so did Lindsay Pyne. The then executive officer of the commission said that the commission was robustly of the view that there was nothing in it. That was all before October. On October the Prime Minister said that there would be no inquiry; he asked what an inquiry would be about. The commission began an investigation on October. On November I wrote a letter to the Securities Commission that I would like to table today, because it is the core of the complaint that I had. If that letter is put against the commission's findings one will see who was right and who was wrong. Then in March the commission released a draft report to interested parties that it said were likely to be affected, although I did not get one myself. On May the final report backed up every allegation it was in a position to investigate. There are three stages to this inquiry. The first stage occurred on September last year; the -month inquiry was the second stage; and the third stage is the full public inquiry I am still calling for. In two critical areas---evidence and legal status---the Securities Commission investigation was always going to come up short, as I always said last year that it would. The commission hit a wall of silence on the Cook Islands operation of European Pacific Investments, which is evidenced on pages and , and the commission had no power to bring in a conclusion of conspiracy. The Mahon report on the Erebus disaster, and all the precedents, the law, and the constitutional history of such inquiries prove that. Also, the commission did not investigate breaches of fiduciary duty. But let us look at what it was told and examine the truth. Michael Fay, in a brief, vague piece of evidence, as reported on page , talked about this insurance exercise. I want to examine that briefly. He said: ``. . . we had the capacity in my mind as a director to look at the insurance policy, the general provisioning and then specific provisioning.''. He goes on: ``. . . and I saw the insurance policy as part of the general provisioning exercise.'', and he kept on talking about an insurance policy. Another director, Robin Congreve, is reported on page as saying this---and he is a man who has a doctorate and a Masters in Law: ``. . . I saw this and I still see it in the context of the Bank's provisioning and it was, I saw it and I still see it as a mechanism that the Bank put in place quite proper purposes as part of its provisioning . . .''. What is at issue here is whether any of those statements has any merit whatsoever. Both are key men, and they are arguing that it was a legitimate insurance, about which they claimed that at the time of its implementation they knew nothing. They told the commission, which found in their favour, that there was a ``Chinese wall''. That is reported on page : ``We were told that FRL directors of BNZ were assisted by three members of the staff of FRL, John Laird, David Botting and Henry Tait, on a full time basis. These three staff members signed confidentiality agreements with the Bank and, according to Fay and Congreve, operated within the offices of FRL behind a permanent Chinese Wall.''. That is what they said. They claimed that they did not know about it; that they were just new directors after June . The issue here is whether their denial is true, whether it has any veracity whatsoever. Michael Fay's partner is David Richwhite, and he put together the European Pacific Investments operation about which I speak. Here is a document, a memorandum to shareholders, signed on October , signature David Richwhite. Now, this is the man who was a lifetime friend of Michael Fay in business. He set up the operation, they owned a shareholding in it. They would claim that they were minority shareholders who knew nothing; yet he, David Richwhite, was the chairman---Michael Fay's friend and business partner. Their denial expects us to believe that Michael Fay and David Richwhite never talked to each other and that they did not have any conversation on this matter. They had just put together a $ million scheme with all these fees flushing about the place. They had also tried it on with Waitaki NZR and then Brierleys; in those two cases they had received an outright rejection. Yet they told the commission and the country that Michael Fay knew nothing about it. They expect us to believe that they have never spoken about it. Richwhite was chairman of European Pacific Investments, and the memorandum of October proves it. Look at clause () in the report of the Securities Commission: ``We noted that the same partners of Budfin accepted instructions from both the Bank and EP interests in respect of the arrangements.''. The same partners! Well, who are these people? What are their names, were they operating in the Cook Islands or New Zealand? Who did they report to? Those are the questions that should be asked because they go to the core of whether or not we are hearing the truth. Clause () states: ``We consider that the directors should have been informed of the level of fees payable by the Bank and should have been required to approve them.''. One director did know. In fact, three did. Are they telling me that European Pacific Investments picks up those sorts of fees and David Richwhite did not tell Michael Fay? This ``Chinese wall'' has ladders and bridges all over it, and every business person in Auckland who knows those two gentlemen knows that what I am saying is true. There is a stinking, acrid silence here about what goes to the core of the matter. That is why a full, public inquiry is required. Did Michael Fay already know about these fees in the deal? Yes, he did. He claimed before the commission not to know, but who first used the phrase ``captive insurance'' last year? Sir Michael Fay did. When did he learn of that captive insurance? He did not first learn of it in June ; he and his partner had integral interests in European Pacific Investments and that is when he knew. European Pacific Investments has David Richwhite's fingerprints all over it and those marks go to Michael Fay. How could Congreve call it an insurance policy when he was the key man in BNZ Finance Ltd in Singapore, through which institution that money was washing $ million? If one believes that that key man, with a doctorate and an LL M in law, did not know what was going on in his own company, one will believe anything. But what is worse is this silence from the House. Why is the Opposition saying nothing? Why is the Government, like the Minister of Justice, not prepared to do something about it? Two billion dollars of losses and injections of finance were put into the Bank of New Zealand, and nary an answer. On September last year members did not want to know about it. They closed and shut down every tabling of documents and disclosure. Today they know volumes more than they did before, and they still do not want an answer. The inquiry and the issue have been like a dirty nappy put in Napisan; every time it was pulled out it stank more and the spots were blacker and dirtier. But, in the end, they had to report. Labour Opposition members would like it to go away. I will give them an assurance that the matter will not. It is not going away. I am just showing them the connection, which anybody in the know in Auckland knows. Why in this country is there non-accountability and a Parliament that will not respond to its fundamental duty to the people who owned the bank and who suffered those incredible losses? Every other Western democracy has answers from its Parliament, but, oh no, not in New Zealand. Who is in whose pocket? The reason that there is silence here is that somebody is in the pockets of those businesses.
What is the current membership of the Bank of New Zealand board of directors, and how does it reflect the shareholding in the Bank of New Zealand?

I ask the Minister to inform the House and the country how she thinks a percent shareholding on the part of Fay Richwhite is fair with respect to its having directors, as opposed to the Crown, with percent-plus shareholding, having only , and why has she not given some equity by replacement for the recently retired person?

This afternoon has been very interesting as the Ministry of Maori Development Bill has progressed through the House. Having seen the Bill introduced in the House some months ago and proceed through the select committee with total agreement, if I might say so, from both parties, we are now, on a Friday afternoon, sitting arguing about matters that are not necessarily related to the Bill, but are certainly related to Maoridom and to Maori development. If a judgment were to be made on what has happened it must be said that the Government and democracy demand answers to some questions. That is one of the reasons that the Maori Affairs Committee requested correspondence from Maoridom to say what it thought in relation to moneys lent to the Quality Inns chain of hotels deal. I say that in passing because it is necessary to know what Maoridom thinks about its own affairs and how those issues should be resolved. If we had taken notice of what Maori had said before, we may not have gone through some of the problems this afternoon. The Bill creates a new era because it brings to a conclusion the two ministries that develop from the closing of the Ministry of Maori Affairs. The Bill sets up one arm that it is hoped will develop Maoridom not only for the good of itself, but also for the good of the whole country. We heard in Committee today the four arms of the Bill---education, training and employment, health, and economic resource development. Many speakers have said, and I certainly say, that if Maori fail, we all fail. Whether we like it or not we are linked to the country and to the people. While Maori may be only percent of the population, it is imperative that the politicians---from both sides of the House---get it right once and for all. The history of New Zealand and the history of Maoridom have not been a pathway to success. In the past, it has been so easy for people to point their fingers at different groups. We are saying today that that finger-pointing must come to an end. The problems must be dealt with and resolved. The Bill will begin to improve the lot of those people who were here first and who are rightly referred to as the tangata whenua. This afternoon during the Committee stage both political parties made worthwhile contributions. If one were to try to draw a conclusion to what was said, it is simply that there has been a very strong wish that the Bill be successful. That certainly was the impression gained from the speeches today. I want to close by thanking again the select committee---the clerks, and the officials---for the outstanding work that they did in the production of the Bill. For my part, I sincerely hope and desire that while we are a mixed people, the Bill will create a climate for people to get on, because not only do others say that they are equal, but they are equal in ability, in education, and in resource management.

I support the reporting back of the Racing Amendment Bill because I support the racing industry; not only the industry, but its work and the employment base of the racing industry. The select committee, the officials, and the chairman of the select committee, the member for Horowhenua, have worked long hours trying to restore the racing industry, and, through the Bill, to add something to the industry. The Bill was widely supported and altogether submissions were made to the select committee. It is interesting that of the submissions made came directly from the racing industry. The racing industry is concerned about itself and officials were prepared to come along to the select committee and make submissions and to tell us how they thought the racing industry was failing, or beginning to fail, and how they thought that the select committee and the Minister for Racing could make improvements to the industry. I support the call already made for the imposition of a lower tax on the racing industry. I would love to see a -year trial during which . percent less tax was taken from the industry than is taken at present. I am sure that the racing industry would begin to recover if that were to be the case. Considerable criticism was made by some people at the select committee about what was stated in the original Bill. This afternoon I want to comment on some of the points made in those submissions. For instance, it has already been mentioned by the chairman and others that the membership of the industry board in clause was initially of concern to all who read the Bill. The primary contention of this clause was that merit will substantially govern the selection of members to the racing industry. By the time the committee had made some alterations to the industry board I am sure that people in the racing industry felt much happier. Clause particularly interests me, not so much as a racing person but as a person who is interested in the thoroughbred as a show horse. In the original Bill the general purposes account referred to money given to charity, which was a clumsy way of putting it. I believe that the select committee, in hearing the submissions against that direction, has come up with a much better idea and one that is needful for the racing industry. Clause now states that grants are to be made for the purpose of education training and the implementation of personnel programmes for all sectors of the racing industry. That is the first point made in the Bill about the changes to the general purposes account. The Bill also refers to expending money for the purpose of establishing a comprehensive racing industry drug-detection system. As I believe I said in the House when the Bill was introduced, New Zealand needs to fall into line with what Australia does---as we do with sporting people---and have a drug-detection system similar to that of Australia. If New Zealand does not do that it will find that in the world sporting arena, as with the racehorse industry, it will be denied opportunities because it has failed correctly to drug-detect horses on the race-track. The racing industry has been given the ability to take extra funding from the general purposes account to establish a comprehensive racing industry drug-detection system. The select committee was most impressed by a submission on equine research. The Bill, through the general purposes account, gives the ability to make grants for the purposes of equine research. That submission detailed how much money is lost to the racing industry because on the morning of a race a horse is withdrawn because of illness or lameness. The committee was told that if more research was done that would not happen as often, and the racing industry would be in a much more profitable position.

What I am really saying is that this legislation started a long way back. At the end of the day, the question that will settle the viability and validity of the Bill is whether we have done something for Maori economic resource development in the national interest--the benefit of Maori development will advance the nation as well, particularly because land is involved--and whether we have done something that is futuristic and is able to meet challenges that may be coming that we do not know about. If we fail, I am afraid that the same arguments that have continued to be part of the canvas of history in this country will go on. My view is that there still will be significant changes during the Committee stage. We cannot afford that sentiment, and during the Committee stage we can make the improvements, the considerations, and the changes that still have to be made.

I want to raise a matter that the Government of this country knows about but, despite its own international commitments, is refusing to act on. It is a sad situation in which not only is the Government of one of our neighbours allowing itself to be ripped off but also it is assisting people in this country who in many other jurisdictions would be branded for what they are, but who here are protected by legal devices and a conspiracy of silence of politicians and businessmen to rip off the revenue of New Zealand. What is worse is that the country I refer to receives substantial amounts of aid from the New Zealand taxpayer, courtesy of the same politicians here who do not want the public to know what is going on---aid in the financial year - to the tune of $ million. I speak of the Cook Islands. It is a small nation struggling, so we are told, to establish a stable economy. That is why we give it over $ million a year---money taken away from the elderly, the sick, and the poor here in New Zealand. We do it as an act of friendship. We do it because the Cook Islands people are our neighbours. But what has happened is that some people in that Government, assisted by our Government's blind eye, have become the agents of corruption. Contrary to an agreement between the Cook Islands and the New Zealand Government, the Government of that country---people such as Mr Robati, Norman George, and others, and certain persons in the Government of Mr Geoffrey Henry who have permitted this to continue---has allowed international criminals, including New Zealanders, to connive in the corruption of its tax-haven laws to allow the revenue of friends and benefactors such as New Zealand to be defrauded. That started in the late s. It was a concerted and planned effort on the part of high-powered tax lawyers and merchants of greed in this country, and crooked officials and politicians in the Cook Islands, to use the tax laws of both countries to enrich themselves with countless millions of dollars by raiding the tax revenues of both countries. It is done through the issue of millions of dollars of false tax certificates, secret accounts, and banking secrecy laws that enable such practices to escape normal scrutiny and, indeed, the scrutiny of Government auditors. The Cook Islands Government operates two sets of books to hide the truth from its own people and the world. One set shows huge tax revenues in accordance with the published laws, but conceals that it deliberately loses that revenue by pre-arranged, pre-determined shams. The other set, which is published to the people, is false. Put simply, the Government of the Cook Islands collects tax but gives it back to the favoured and malevolent few. Documents exist that show that, in just one example, a tax deal raided the New Zealand revenue for a sum in the order of $,,. Before the tax was paid a deal was entered into, to buy and sell promissory notes, incurring a loss of $ million. Who signed the deal? A Mr Norman George, of whom we will hear more shortly, and a Pomani Tangata, Secretary to the Cabinet. For a mere $, they gave away $ million in taxes due, on the face of the documents, to the Cook Islands revenue. They allowed people who should be labelled criminals in this country to steal from the revenue of New Zealand. All that appears in the legitimate, audited books of the Cook Islands Government is a small fee. The loss never sees the light of day. The Cook Islands Government Property Corporation is used to trade promissory notes that see tax revenue due to the Cook Islands Government given away while the New Zealand Government, through its aid programme, seemingly makes up the shortfall. The false tax certificates are then used in turn as receipts, which are shown to the tax authorities of New Zealand and other countries in order to provide illegitimate deductions from the amounts due in tax to our Government. The present leader of the Alliance in that country, Norman George, said: ``What kind of man would give away information so that the people of the Cook Islands would be deprived of millions of dollars of income from offshore banking? What sort of person would do that so that the people of the Cook Islands miss out? What kind of person would do this so the poor people of the country will miss out on millions of dollars of withholding tax?''. The records show that this man, Mr Norman George, was actually a signatory to a scheme to give those same millions of dollars away by taking them out of the pockets of those same poor people and giving them to the coven of conspirators. It is worth repeating: records available to us show that in Mr Norman George and some of his colleagues, and the Government of Geoffrey Henry since that time, have deliberately given away millions of dollars of that same withholding tax---money that belongs to the poor people of that country. They have allowed the sort of people in this country that in another great time a former President of the United States called ``malefactors of great wealth'' to raid foreign revenues under the protection of the tax and banking laws of the Cook Islands. That means that those corrupt and evil ``malefactors of great wealth'' here in New Zealand can hide behind a facade of legality created by the conspiracy of silence in this Parliament and outside it. They call them tax schemes but in this case they are operated on a grand scale and involve the direct complicity of one Government and the blind connivance of another---this one in this country. I call that a fraud and so does every other democracy. The body called the Cook Islands Government Property Corporation buys and sells promissory notes, incurring pre-arranged, pre-determined losses so that the tax that the Cook Islands Government is due under its public laws is swindled from the people and is given to those icons of society in New Zealand. The laws involved, instead of existing to protect the rights of ordinary people, are used both there and here in New Zealand to protect the malfeasance of the rich and powerful. Our Government, by its persistent refusal to honour its own pledge to hold a public inquiry, is helping them to get away with it. I wonder why. What could the reason be? What explanation could there be that is in any way adequate or acceptable to New Zealand people? The full story of what is happening here is going to be told. The international news media have published parts of the story. The New Zealand news media, due to those malevolent few who use our court procedures to prevent publication, cannot. But I promise this country that the truth will be told. I know the names, and the names will be known to every New Zealander. But in this brief speech I say to the Cook Islands Government that it has let its people down badly, and there will come a day when neither the banking laws of the Cook Islands nor the stranglehold that these ``malefactors of great wealth'' have through the court procedures of this country will protect it any longer, and that day is coming soon. The Cook Islands Government will suffer the public outrage due to its actions. The malevolent few will be dealt to, and will not be filling their private pockets any longer. The US Government is now investigating that country for money laundering and other serious crimes. The Government of Japan will soon be asking questions, as will that of Australia. I say to the people of the Cook Islands and to their Government and their politicians that they have allowed the good name of their people and their interests to be hijacked in the interests of a corrupt and crooked few in that country and in New Zealand. We know what their names are. I call on the politicians of the Cook Islands to hold a full public inquiry into the conduct of the Cook Islands Government Property Corporation so as to disclose openly and honestly to the world what the malevolent few have been doing---and in the name of the Cook Islands. I call on the New Zealand Government to withhold all future aid for and funding of the Cook Islands until such a full public inquiry is held. That is what this Parliament deserves, that is what the taxpayer of this country deserves, and that is what the National Party promised before ---a full public inquiry into the connection between politicians, business people, and political corruption. It is now time to turn up with the goods, to deliver, and to become true and honest with the people of New Zealand. If one has read the Independent and the National Business Review, and has followed the court cases, one knows that it has been going on for much too long. Why is this Government protecting those people? What is the explanation for some people having so much power in this country that they are beyond the law and can seek to tie up the courts, when this Parliament knows and this Government should know that they have the power to bring them before a full public inquiry and to have the truth come out? My explanation is this: they have a hold on some people in New Zealand politics; they have some New Zealand politicians in their pockets. That can be the only explanation. Meanwhile, out in New Zealand taxpayers are paying their hard-earned tax---

Some speeches inspire a certain awe, evoke a certain magic, gladden the heart and make it wander, and everyone who listens is pleased to have been there. That was not such a speech. This important debate is occurring against a backdrop of international uncertainty. An economic, sometimes political, crisis besets Asia, and has for the last months. We have now an emerging crisis in the Middle East. Domestically, back home in this country, we began the year with a very healthy surplus, and the certainty of further tax cuts on April for superannuitants and on July for every New Zealander who is earning. We begin this debate against a backdrop of regional recession and finding a way to manage New Zealand through it. Above all else it concerns a strategy to shield New Zealand against the potential effects of these very adverse developments. What we have just heard from the previous speaker is terribly sad. It is sad because it was totally irrelevant to the needs of the New Zealand people and of this country. It was putting petty policies and petty politics before people. It was about putting negatives before the national interest. It was putting personalities before progress. It was putting political interests before the interests of New Zealanders. Above all it was tired; it was boring; it was not inspirational. Only half the Labour Party members could move on their hind legs to give any applause. The other half were driven to it by instruction from the whips. It was putting the pursuit of political power above all else. Members opposite will rise in this House, terribly predictably, and they will agree on only one thing: that the Government is not doing it right. That is where the agreement ends. Some will say that we are not spending enough. Others will say we are spending too much. Some will argue that we should forgo the tax cuts of July. Others will argue that we should increase them. At a time when the country is calling for leadership from the members opposite, for statesmanship, and for some sort of alternative direction, what we had was an abysmal failure by the leader of the Labour Party. It is not good enough to say, every time one is interviewed: ``Oh, I'm making a speech next week.'' When asked on Morning Report: ``Mrs Clark, what will you do?'', the reply is: ``Well, next week I'm making a speech.'' ``Mrs Clark, what are you going to do about the farmers down there in Marlborough?'' ``Oh, I am concerned. I care.'' This is an age when people want real answers to real problems. Across the floor this House is seeing the inevitable. They do not have a policy. They do not have a vision. They do not really have an ambition ever to be back in Government. On this side of the House, as the Prime Minister articulated, we do have a plan, and we are putting it in place. It is called sound government with a human face. It is growth in a sea of regional turmoil. It is surpluses when every one of our neighbours is running deficits. It is repaying debt of former profligate Governments and generations, paying over $. billion a year just on servicing that debt. That is $ million a month, just on servicing the debt of former Governments; $ million each week, just on servicing the debt of former Governments like the last Labour Government. That is $. million each day. What is important is that that $, million of debt servicing---each dollar of which, annualised, is a drain on this country's national wealth; each dollar of which is a dollar that we cannot spend or cannot save---is what we are left with every day. This is about managing Government expenditure downwards in relation to gross domestic product (GDP) whilst reprioritising and making critical investments. Which other Government in any part of the world is doing all of these things at the same time? I would like Mr Cullen to answer that question. There is not a mutter, not a murmur. He cannot answer. Which other Government is repaying debt, building up growth, and reducing expenditure in relation to GDP all at the same time?

I think that New Zealanders have cause to have the greatest degree of cynicism about the debate that has taken place today as a result of the Prime Minister's announcement at the commencement of the year. This is the hoariest old political chestnut being wound out by the National Party---``Miss Law and Order'' with a blue sash---in . In truth, the National Party is soft on law and order. The most compelling evidence for that is that when proposals were put to it last year to take away one of the most severe elements that leads to lawlessness in this country---namely, unemployment---it had no sense of commitment or personal drive to see that all around this country the armies of unemployed become employed. The old adage of the devil finding work for idle hands is the most significant element in the rise in crime in New Zealand and every other First-World country. This is a ``Saatchi and Saatchi'' Bill. A person like Mr Ryall comes along---a bank teller from the Bank of New Zealand---and swings out arguments about us being soft on law and order. He might tell us about his own circumstances of departure from the Bank of New Zealand. He has that smart alec approach to what is one of New Zealand's most serious and disastrous problems, and claims that the Government has an answer and the rest of us are soft when it comes to law and order. For example, what is his answer to white-collar crime? How about the young people in our country who look to the standards set by our leading businessmen, in some cases, and think: ``Well if that's the law, there is no law. If that's the way it is, it's everybody for himself.''? What is National's answer to white-collar crime? It is cover-up after cover-up. It can dish out a knighthood and think that Joe Bloggs, the ordinary young man growing up in New Zealand, can see any standard or role model of behaviour to follow. The ACT party is no different. It talks tough, yet in every way, and the figures prove it, it has failed this country, it is failing the community, and it is failing the taxpayer in particular. Everyone knows how fearful New Zealanders are about lack of safety in the streets. By the same token, everyone remembers that last year, when a lady was assaulted, bashed up, she had to sell her assets to get care, because of an income and asset testing regime that the National Party and the ACT Party subscribe to. I went to Jenny Shipley, and told her that this was appalling. The Government's idea was to put up some discretionary fund. It is one thing to talk as if one cares for people's safety; it is another thing to have a record of doing anything about it. The current extreme penalty for murder is life imprisonment---members here know that, no doubt---and for burglary it is years. But the criminals are not getting years from the courts; they are getting years. Parliament is skirting around the most significant element in this problem: a simple failure on the part of the judiciary to follow the will of Parliament. Whatever our failings might be, Parliament still makes the laws of this country. What is the difference between being raped in one's home, raped in the street, raped at a campsite, raped in a car, and, for that matter, raped in a taxi? What is the difference between being murdered at a campsite, murdered at a hostel, and murdered at an old people's home? There is no difference. It is cynical manipulation of people's fear and misery. It was not the National Party that increased police numbers by ; it was New Zealand First that increased police numbers by . I can remember every Treasury argument put up on that very matter by my then National Party Cabinet colleagues. Home invasion is a media term, the use of which appears to give a form of approval for what is just plain, old-fashioned thuggery. Why on earth is the Government suddenly becoming passionate about home invasion? The Government has been here in one form or another for nigh on years. Why is it becoming passionate about this thing called home invasion, and about law and order? The answer is simple: it thinks there are votes in it. I do not believe that New Zealanders, when they see the record trotted out month after month from this day of introduction of the Bill onwards, will be fooled by those crocodile tears. To treat thuggery in the home more harshly than that on the streets implies that street violence is of lesser importance or that, in some way, because it is done on the street its impact is diminished. It matters not one iota to the victim---and this goes to the core of the sincerity of the argument being put up by the Minister and his colleagues---whether the crime is committed in the home or on the street, but it sure matters that the offence happened at all. Why not introduce mandatory minimum sentences, if we want to get really serious about crimes of violence? Why not, as Mr Robson rightly points out, look at some of the underlying causes of crime, which the forefathers of us as parliamentarians always knew about, and seek to eliminate them wherever we can? The solution is employment. The Government pays out billions for people to do nothing. It pays out conscience money, as some sort of sop to its social conscience, for people to go to a welfare agency every week. It then throws them on the scrap heap and forgets them, following some Treasury advice that it costs too much to put people, already paid now to work, back into the workforce. Many crimes against the person already carry lengthy terms of imprisonment. Everyone knows that. But we can count on the fingers of one hand the number of times the maximum possible sentence has been given. This Bill will change nothing. The message to our judges should be that if they cannot bear the thought of dealing to violent offenders meaningfully, with the law they currently have, then they should either step aside to let someone else in who will, or Parliament should remove any doubts in their minds by introducing minimum sentencing. That is something that would be real and tangible. Let me come back to the real point. This law change is not about crook catching; it is about vote catching. Mr Ryall went on television, trying to look as manly and as virile, and as strong and macho as possible. Down the barrel he said to all those crooks: ``Just watch out; we're coming for you.'' Can members imagine the fear and trembling in the dens of iniquity of this country when they saw Mr Ryall, and heard him say that he is coming for them? They know the police have not been provisioned properly.

Yes, I have too, so I do speak from personal experience. I am concerned about the increase in crime. I want to refer briefly to the increase in violent crime in my electorate of Wanganui. I do not intend to spend the rest of my speaking-time condemning the police of Wanganui---quite the opposite. I am fulsome in my praise of members of the police department in Wanganui. They do an excellent job, but they cannot do that job on their own. In no way do I lay any responsibility for the increase in violent crime in my electorate at the feet of the police, because they do not go out and cause it. The increase in crime has, unfortunately and quite predictably, come about from an increased number of male offences against females. It is up from last year to this year. That increase is too big, and I join the police in their concern about it. I also want to say how much I support the police family violence programme. Its Not Just a Domestic programme is commendable. Society cannot expect the police to pick up all the pieces. Society has a responsibility, too. Increased reporting of crime has not occurred only because women feel more confident about reporting. I believe that increased reporting has occurred because there is more crime to report. I believe that more incidents of crime are occurring. Unfortunately, and I do not like to say it, society is becoming more and more violent. People ask, and I ask, too, why we are experiencing such levels of violence. One of the things that I believe we can attribute this increase in violence to is the Budget cuts. I expect there to be groans from the Government benches about that but, as my colleague the member for Dunedin West said, the connection is direct: poverty, powerlessness, and crime. The connection is absolutely direct and there is no escape from it. Since the Budget, which saw benefits cut, we have seen a direct correlation between poverty and crime. Market rents increased, so there was a double whammy for low-income earners. Not only were their benefits cut but their housing costs went up. We saw an increase in homelessness. We saw an increase in parents who were not able to meet the education costs of their children, and that leads to a feeling of powerlessness. What happens when people feel absolutely powerless? They feel the Government does not care, and that society does not seem to care. Unfortunately, some of them know only one way to react and that is to strike out in a violent manner. We have to do something to address this. I do not want to spend the rest of my term in Parliament talking about the terrible incidents of crime that are occurring. It is a far more productive use of our time to talk about ways that we can address the issue. One of the first things that we need to do is to teach people coping skills. Not everybody is born with the ability to cope with all sorts of adversity. We can liken it, particularly this week, to the workers who have been laid off from the Weddel plants. Nobody has taught them the skills to cope with sudden redundancy. Many people were not given the skills to cope with benefit cuts, increased housing costs, and all the other downside effects that result from them. One of the things that I have been promoting, just quietly at present as I gather more information, is establishing community centres in the suburbs that are readily accessible to people who do not have access to transport. Since the increased housing costs, we have seen a marked increase in the number of empty Housing New Zealand properties in the suburbs. Why can we not put those empty houses to good use by establishing community centres that are just down the street from the very people who need them? I have seen community centres in action and they perform a wonderful job. They are low-key and are operated by the people who live in the community. They are an extension of the whanau, and visiting them is like going to a neighbour's home because they are right there in the same street. They would be extremely cost-effective because those houses are empty now and sit empty for a long period of time. In fact, not so long ago we read about empty Housing New Zealand properties being vandalised because they had been empty for such a lengthy period of time. It would not cost very much at all to have a community centre in every suburb in our city. Surely it is better to spend money preventing crime than to spend the huge amounts that we spend incarcerating people, only to let them out on the street again without ever attending to their rehabilitation. Absolutely; the member is quite right. Now years have elapsed and what has the Government done? It has done nothing. The high paperwork requirement actually reduces people's access to service; it does not increase it at all. One of the things I want to point out is that the recent stocktake of enterprise assistance schemes found that a reason many small businesses did not take advantage of the business development board grant schemes was the paperwork involved. Many people who go to business development boards, economic development agencies, and other organisations like that have never been in business for themselves. Many of the people who approach business development boards and suchlike are there as a result of being made redundant, and they are looking for self-employment opportunities because many have been told---the message is sent out---that self-employment may be a way of securing further employment. Well, when they are confronted with the absolute avalanche of paper that they have to fill out, many of them just throw up their hands in horror. They have had no experience of this kind of thing, and they are intimidated by it. They are intimidated by the huge amount of paper they have to contend with and all the form filling. Everything is in triplicate, and whatever happens to that third copy goodness knows---it probably goes away and gathers dust in a bottom drawer somewhere. People who want to make a contribution to their families and the nation are put off taking advantage of and utilising the skills that they feel in their hearts they have, because of all the paper they are confronted with. How many community groups never make an application for funding because the pile of forms is too daunting, and volunteers do not have the time to fill them all out? I draw attention to the use of that word ``volunteers''. The groups are called voluntary organisations of course because they are run by volunteers. Because those volunteers are spending so much time running around trying to put in funding applications, applying for this and applying for that, and filling out the necessary forms---unnecessary forms, quite frankly---that come across their desks, they are not able to deliver the services that are the reason they got involved in the organisation in the very first place. Each hour spent on paperwork is an hour not spent on helping the people whom they joined that organisation to help; organisations like women's and children's shelters, and the whole wide range of voluntary organisations right throughout our community. I know from personal experience, and from the contacts I have with people in my community, that our voluntary agencies are spending an absolutely disproportionate amount of their time filling in forms, and that is not why the volunteers joined that organisation. This Bill is a first step, and I congratulate my colleague again. It requires all Government organisations to conduct an audit of their forms and information collection methods, to determine how they actually use the information, what their actual information needs are, and how they can reduce the burden on the public. I spoke before about forms being required to be filled out in triplicate. I want to know, and the audit process will show, for example, what happens to that third copy, and to all the repetition that goes on. This audit will be conducted every years, and is an ongoing commitment to review paperwork and information collection issues, because needs change. The need for information changes, but nothing has changed in respect of the Government doing anything about assisting small businesses by reducing the amount of forms they have to fill out. It has had five long years. Think of all the forms. Just imagine, if we had the time to sit down and count the number---

I was very interested to hear the response of the Minister of Commerce, particularly when he referred to immediate need. I would like to draw his attention to the fact that senior citizens, in particular, in New Zealand do not take out loans or advances on their benefits unless there is an immediate need. Older New Zealanders have been particularly frugal over their lifetimes, out of pure economic necessity. They have lived through some of the harshest times in New Zealand, particularly those in their very senior years. They are not in the habit of borrowing money for anything other than immediate need. I cannot wait until I return to my electorate on Friday and visit my branch of the Returned Services Association. I will tell the members about what has gone through the House this week. I know that they will be particularly interested in this clause. I remind the Minister that people of his generation and mine have lived a life of relative ease compared with our forebears. Those people will not be delighted to hear that they are considered bludgers if, because of their tight financial situation, because they have struck difficult circumstances, they have to borrow money---their own money; an advance that they have to repay in full. I draw the Minister's attention to an aspect that can impact on people both young and old. I refer to an advance for the repair of a basic item like a hot-water cylinder. Most of us give no thought at all to our hot-water cylinder; we just turn on the tap and out comes hot water. I remind the Minister of the difficulties a young mother with children can have, of the difficulties an older person who is infirm and looking after an infirm partner can have. It may be that either the husband or the wife is in particularly bad health, and it is absolutely necessary for him or her sometimes to shower more than once a day. If there is no hot-water cylinder, then, for goodness' sake, what will happen? That senior citizen, that person who has paved the way for our generation to have a much easier life, will be told: ``No, you can't borrow a sufficient sum to repair your hot-water cylinder.'' I ask the Minister how, in all honesty, we can do that to our senior citizens. How can we say to them: ``No, you've contributed to New Zealand society all your life, but when you come upon hard times you're not eligible to borrow the money that you require so that you can have a decent standard of living and can have some quality of life in your retiring years.''? Sitting in the Chamber this evening and listening to the contributions of Dr Wayne Mapp, Richard Worth, and Stephen Franks has left me feeling somewhat lacking, on two levels. The first relates to the legal experience those three members bring to this bill, and the second concerns their detailed knowledge of the Government Administration Committee process with respect to this bill. I listened carefully to what Stephen Franks had to say. But what concerns me most about the title itself is that it could be replaced by a much better title that would reflect the lineage of the bill, in a way that would clarify some of the difficulties faced by those members of the public or other members in this Parliament who may not have a detailed working knowledge of the bill itself. That title would be the ``More of the Same Government Mismanagement Bill''. The reason that title would be appropriate is reflected in the history of the bill itself. In an attempt to explain my proposed alternative title, I wish to explore a little of that history. This legislation was introduced on November , quite some time after the Government had won the last election. The first reading took place very shortly thereafter, on November, and then the bill was referred to the Government Administration Committee. It was reported back some time later, but not without the Minister realising that the initial version of the bill would cause a great number of problems. On that basis, on May , the Minister was placed in the position of having to introduce a substantial amendment in Supplementary Order Paper .

The fact of the matter is that the select committee has amended in clause what it described as the rigid rule of a -month limit on the filing of an application for a review. What does this Committee know about -day or -month limits? Well, the Government had the opportunity to amend the same types of limits when it passed the Employment Relations Act and it declined to do so, deeming in those circumstances that, in fact, days or months was a perfectly appropriate period of time in which someone should be able to lodge a personal grievance or a complaint of unjustified dismissal. But in this instance---and this is extremely interesting---under clause (), instead of the corporation having the option of accepting a late appeal, ``the Corporation must accept a late application if satisfied that there are extenuating circumstances...''. Then, very helpfully, the clause goes on to list those extenuating circumstances. The Minister nods, but one of those circumstances, in particular, is not actually a very extenuating one. It is the circumstance ``where the claimant made reasonable arrangements to have the application made on his or her behalf by an agent of the claimant, and the agent unreasonably failed to ensure that the application was made...''. Why on earth should the corporation be required to accept a late application when an agent, acting on behalf of the principal under the law of agency, makes a late application for no good reason? We have a common law remedy to resolve that situation: the principal can sue the agent who was negligent and failed to perform and carry out the duties of the principal. But the situation gets worse. Under clause , the select committee has given reviewers the power to adopt an investigative approach. The Minister claims that this measure is a victory, that it will seek out the truth, and that there will be no opportunity for contrary views to be raised. Well, we have legislation that deals with those types of processes: the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act. That Act is all about ensuring that both parties have their day in court. An adversarial approach would allow evidence to emerge in a way that is consistent and fair. Both the claimant and the Accident Compensation Corporation, and their representatives, should be able to be put under cross-examination so that the facts of a case are determined in a fair and equitable way. There will be some things that the investigating officer will simply not know. If the person or the corporation are placed in a position where the facts cannot be revealed by cross-examination, the truth will not come out and justice will not be served, in the way that is intended by this legislation. It is a simple principle, and an investigative approach to this type of decision making will result in some very poor decisions being made, indeed. The worst change, in my view, is in clause . That is where the select committee has now recommended that costs have to be paid, even if the review is not held! Even if the review does not go ahead and the matter is settled, costs still have to be paid. This is an environment where the parties have not even had to front up to the review panel. They have not had to front up to the tribunal and put their cases, yet they are able to claim costs when the matter has been settled prior to even arriving at the hearing. If that type of decision making was extended to the justice system overall, can members imagine the carnage? Someone could say: ``I am going to take that party to court. We will settle before we get there, and he or she can pay me costs before I even incur the costs of going to court''. It is simply a backward way of looking at justice.

The member for Taranaki is really asking the House to return to the bad old days. Let us remember what the Post Office was like under the National Government. Post office buildings up and down the country opened at o'clock and closed at o'clock. People could not buy stamps in the evening from stamp retailers, as they can today. In my electorate, people can buy stamps hours a day, days a week. Under the National Government they could not do that. Even more significant is the way in which the National Government priced those services. We all know the answer. Electricity prices rose in the year after the election. They did not rise by percent or percent, but by percent. Of course, in election year everything was perfect and no prices rose. The year after the election prices were whacked up by another percent. The Post Office was exactly the same. The year after the election there was an increase in the cost of stamps and telephone calls. The year after the election was extraordinary in that for the first time that I know of in New Zealand's history the price of stamps did not increase. For the first time the price of telephone calls did not increase, but decreased. The member has said that that does not represent a sense of social responsibility, but it does. People can telephone Sydney for c a minute after p.m. on a Saturday. They could not do that under the National Government. After the election year electricity prices were reduced, yet the member for Taranaki wants to return to the old days when we had meddling, incompetent National Government Ministers---the member fits perfectly into that mould---who used to muddle and moan, promise anything in election year, and a year later whack up all the prices. The Bill is a large part of the reason for the Opposition seeing its lead in the public opinion polls vanish, and for its being discredited. The National Party is demonstrating to the House its incompetence to govern. The Opposition is hopeless and useless. In relation to the issues that have been raised, I point out that the price of stamps is being held, the price of telephone calls is coming down, and electricity charges have come down; yet the member for Taranaki has jumped on his horse, charged in, and said, ``Vote for me and I'll increase them again. I'll go back to the bad old days.'' The member for Taranaki will be lucky to hold his seat.

Unfortunately, the statement made by the Leader of the Opposition was predictable. The Leader of the Opposition asked several questions. He asked whether all New Zealanders would be able to fish both commercially and in the non-commercial fishing areas. The answer is yes. The law will apply equally to Maori and to non-Maori. He then asked whether the Maori would pay resource rentals. Yes, the law is to apply equally to Maori and to non-Maori. He asked whether the Crown was prepared to amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act to ensure that the -year ban that has been introduced will have full force and effect. The answer is yes, and the Government is also negotiating with Maori people in relation to the court injunctions, and is prepared to legislate on that matter if necessary. He asked how the Crown would allocate the quotas. The Leader of the Opposition asked whether the Government regarded the provision of extra jobs as being a help towards employment. Yes, it does. Every job that anyone can get is helpful.

I was told by the General Manager of the Railways Corporation that Christchurch will be the focus of a railway extravaganza when the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of the opening of New Zealand's first public railway is celebrated. Ferrymead will involve a week of railways activities from to October, organised to mark the opening of the line between Christchurch and the wharf at Ferrymead in , that could be described as a Save Rail project, I suppose. A subcommittee of the Canterbury branch of the New Zealand Railway and Locomotive Society is organising and co-ordinating the events with the Railways Corporation. It sounds like a good time.

I appreciate the situation that you find yourself in.
