The Stamp and Cheque Duties Amendment Bill (No. ) is the last part of the various finance measures that were introduced by the Government in the Budget last night. I agree with the Minister that we have certainly debated---
One could not describe it as open government; one would have to call it disgraceful government.

It is excellent for a Wellingtonian. I am sure that it will not earn the honourable member a single vote in the Hutt Valley, but I think that she is correct. That Bill covers the question of whether Landcorp should be able to charge for its services. In a sense, that matter is a user-pays provision. I looked at it, and I think that it is not unreasonable for Landcorp to be able to charge people who want to move from having leaseholds to being freehold. There is no reason that taxpayers should subsidise that activity. Having said that, I think that Landcorp is obliged to do it properly. Landcorp gave us an assurance that people who might want to transfer from leasehold to freehold would have a choice, and that they would not be trapped into using Landcorp. They would be able to go to their own lawyer if they wanted to. I am recording that comment because this measure might result in a row some time in the future. So it is important to repeat Landcorp's assurances that, first, their clients would have a choice about whether to use Landcorp; second, that it intended to charge only the real costs; and, third, I got the impression from Landcorp---and I think that I am correct in saying this---that it was of the view that its legal charges would be lower than the charges that one would normally expect from the Law Society. However, having said that, I want to tell the House that the Opposition supports the measures as a whole. Indeed, one could sum up these measures by saying that they are the sort of measure that the Government normally can expect the Opposition not to oppose. Frankly, the Government would have been wiser not to have introduced the legislation in the Budget debate. I do not think that it was part of a Budget debate. However, the Government did send it to a select committee, where it received proper scrutiny, and that certainly has not done the Bills any harm. I say to those Cabinet Ministers who might be thinking about objecting to legislation going to a select committee that sending it to a select committee takes the heat off. Am I the only Opposition speaker? Yes---the fact that there has been only one Opposition speaker is a signal to the Government that, if it behaves reasonably, the Opposition will be reasonable, and it will get a perfectly reasonable statesmanlike speech from me.

It comes as a surprise to the news media---they thought that they heard the Society of Accountants say that it thought it was an unnecessary tax.

I say to the member that he has a double standard. Saddam Hussein has used those weapons against Iran. He has fired missiles at Israel and at Saudi Arabia. He has not only done that; he has actually gassed his own citizens. The member asked what was the difference between that and East Timor. There is no one in the world who has done what Saddam Hussein has done, and, furthermore, I doubt whether even the leader of the Alliance doubts that if Saddam Hussein were allowed, he would rebuild his weapons of mass destruction and use them again. That is the difference. That is the situation that the United States is facing. I say also to the leader of the Labour Party and the leader of the Alliance, who are now saying that the United States should wait for the Security Council, that we all know that it would wait for ever. I say further that international law does empower the United States and the United Kingdom to carry out the actions they are taking. Yes, we do regret that they are necessary, and, yes, I have no doubt that innocent people will be killed, but I say to Labour and the Alliance that the person responsible for that is not our ally the United States, but Saddam Hussein. He is the person who is responsible. The West has done all that it can. We waited years, we tried sanctions, and Iraq has broken its word. It is worth drawing to the attention of members who have not been following the matter that the United Nations inspectorate has reported within the last hours that Iraq has completely defied all the United Nations resolutions on this matter. It has said that it is unable to make any progress on ensuring that Saddam Hussein and his bloody regime are disarmed. I say to members of this House that we are a small trading nation, and it is the Saddam Husseins of this world who are a threat to world peace and a threat to New Zealand. We ought to be grateful that the United States and the United Kingdom are prepared to take the actions they are taking. Members have asked what else will happen. Well, we realise that the reason the decision to attack has been made is that the Muslim holy month is starting this weekend. That is why the strikes are happening now. As the leader of the ACT party, I say that Parliament should indicate to the United States and the United Kingdom, and to the people of the United States and the United Kingdom, that we are percent behind the actions they are taking.

I rise to speak to the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Bill (No. ), and to make it quite clear that the ACT party intends to vote for the Bill.

The member says that it is years ago. The view is that because Maori have not received full compensation, this group of property owners---about , of them---should not receive full compensation. The dilemma for the House is this: either this change that is going through the House under urgency, on steroids, is cosmetic, or the ACT party is correct---and this is our view when we read this Bill---and this is a full change. I have received a number of phone calls from people saying: ``Listen, Prebb, we want you to get up in the House today and not explain what the Bill really means, because we want to get it through.'' As a parliamentarian I am offended by such a suggestion. It is the responsibility of every member of Parliament to tell other members exactly what they have in front of them so that when they vote they know what it means. I will meet my obligations by saying to the House that I have no doubt at all that this amendment is a profound amendment. The crucial part, relating to the valuation change, is in paragraph (a) of clause (), which states: ``First on the basis of what that market value would have been, as at January , if the Maori Reserved Land Amendment Act and this Act had not been proposed or enacted;''. Now that is a fundamental change, because the law that was passed prior to Christmas stated that the valuation had to be done as of January . Now what is the difference? Well, we now know what the valuations of January mean, because there have been two auctions of perpetual leases this year.

That is correct, but under the Land Act, before people can do that they need to have permission from the Commissioner of Crown Lands. Is the member suggesting that the landowners are lighting fires without getting permission? I think the member is pointing out that we already have environmental measures that cover this land. Indeed, I point out to members of the Alliance that in fact all the pastoral leases are covered by the Resource Management Act and the regional councils. Measures are already in place. I do not believe that any case has been established for introducing the legislation in the first place, but I must say I am speaking on behalf of Ken Shirley, who was on the Primary Production Committee and put forward a number of amendments. The particular clause that violates property rights the most would have to be clause , whereby before people can get permission to do a wide range of actions they have to get the commissioner's permission. It is a discretionary consent. I assure the House that a perpetual lease is recognised in the Land Transfer Act as being an estate in land. The lessees are property owners. A Crown pastoral lessee now has to go to the commissioner, who takes into account the desirability of protecting inherent values. I am a lawyer. I have an honours degree in law. I do not claim to be a great lawyer, but I do not have a clue what that means. I say to members of the committee that they do not have a clue, either. We should not be passing laws when the Minister and the MPs do not know what they mean. That is what is wrong with the Resource Management Act. We passed the Resource Management Act although no member of Parliament knew what sections of it meant, and now no local body knows what it means and no property owner knows what it means. We have a series of court cases and complete confusion. This is bad lawmaking. Why are we doing it? We are doing it because it sounds good. Members say ``inherent values'' means ``conservation values''. If that is so, why does the legislation not state it? It states ``inherent values''. What on earth does that mean? If a property owner writes to the commissioner to ask to do something, why should it be a lottery as to whether the commissioner will say ``Yes'' or ``No''? It will change depending on the commissioner. To call this measure communist is probably wrong, because at least communism has some purpose behind it; it is just statism. The House is assuming that a commissioner sitting in Wellington, presumably one of my constituents, somehow knows better than the owner of the land what he or she ought to be doing. There is no way that the commissioner can go down there to have a look. The commissioner does not have a set of incentives to make the right decisions. Indeed, a number of paid lobbyists here in Wellington for the various environmental groups will make his life hell if he does not say ``No''. That is what will happen. We all know that. The same group of people who have been making the lives of various members of the committee hell will be lobbying that commissioner not to make proper decisions. That is a violation of property rights. Our party says that the ability of citizens to own property without interference from the State is a basic freedom. The pastoral owners have done a good job in protecting conservation values. They are far more likely to do so than this particular measure. Therefore, I want to record that Ken Shirley put up alternatives to the Committee. They were voted down to . Once again, the ACT party was the only party prepared to stand up in Parliament for property rights. As such, we will continue to vote against this legislation. This Parliament is far too ready to violate basic property rights and to violate the rights of citizens. This legislation is misconceived. It is the result of lobbying groups. When we as parliamentarians are faced with issues like this, we should be prepared to stand up on behalf of the property rights of citizens. We should say that we are opposed to their being undermined. Therefore the ACT party is opposed to this legislation. It is a great shame that Mr Gavan Herlihy will not vote with his heart against it, because what he knows in his heart to be wrong he should also know in his mind to be wrong. This is bad, statism legislation, and it is a shame that the Government is putting it forward.

I rise to speak in response to the Prime Minister's statement. We are gathered here for the second session of this Parliament, and it is our role to scrutinise the programme of the minority Labour-Alliance Government. I think it is possible at this point---and I want to be positive---to say that this Government has the best spin of any administration that I have ever seen, and possibly the best spin of any Government that has ever been. I thought that Jenny Shipley's phrase, that the Prime Minister was the master ``spinster'' of New Zealand politics, was putting it exactly right. If Helen Clark had been the captain of the Titanic, she would have broadcast to the passengers that there was no need for alarm and that the ship had just stopped to take on ice! But the Labour-Alliance ``Titanic'' has stopped; we have not been given positive policy. But again I want to be positive in this address. The Prime Minister said in her address that if we can look ahead, we could be in the top half of the OECD, not falling towards the bottom; that was a goal that she had set. Unfortunately, in her speech there were no measures to do that. Let me just draw to the attention of the House what would be involved in being in the top half of the OECD, because the ACT party is most certainly in favour of New Zealand growing a bigger political cake rather than dividing up the country by carving up the present cake. If we look at the OECD economic ladder, we see that we are currently country out of , and that our relative position is falling. Last year, the country that was behind us was Spain, and it grew at . percent. Korea grew at . percent. Last year, we grew at just . percent. If we continue last year's growth rate out for years, we will fall below Spain, Portugal, and Korea in the OECD. If we take the Government's own projections, the Treasury projections of what it hopes the economic growth rate will be---it is hoping for a . percent growth rate---that will still see us falling behind Spain. To get into the top half of the OECD, one of three things has to happen: either every other country will have to stop growing, or, as Rodney Hide said, the OECD will have to invite every African country to join, or, alternatively, the Government will have to put forward a programme to this House for an economic growth rate of percent every year. That is not contained in the Prime Minister's statement. The Government wants to know what economic policies it needs in order to get to the top half of the OECD. The ACT party is quite prepared to share those policies with it. As we and other parties have indicated, it can be done. The prescription is lower tax and a massive cut to red tape. We do not want just one overseas yacht company to be given a fast track through the Resource Management Act procedures. I have heard of a New Zealand yacht-building company that has been waiting months to gain permission from its local body to make a small extension to its yard, but it does not have the Deputy Prime Minister going along to fix the local council for it. That is what we need: a commitment to private property and a commitment to the sanctity of contract. What we actually have, when we read the statement from the Prime Minister, is a Government that has run out of ideas and policy and initiative.

It is appropriate that this House debate this issue. Under our Westminster system the politicians make the law, then other organisations---the courts, the coroners' court, the police, and other enforcement agencies---enforce it. We have had a Westminster convention that it is very important that politicians do not make statements that make it difficult for citizens, including serving police officers, to be able to get justice. The last time that I can remember a Prime Minister making statements that could be interpreted as being designed to influence the outcome of judicial hearings would be some of the statements made by Sir Robert Muldoon. At that time, the then Attorney-General spoke out and stated that it was vitally important that Ministers did not interfere in the judicial process. The statements made by the Prime Minister need to be explained. I have read to her the statements that were in the Evening Post, which she told us today she did not make. I would be interested to know which of the statements she did not make, which statements she actually made, and why---given the importance of the statements and the fact that they were on the front page of the newspaper---she waited until today to tell us that the statements were not correct. Let me quote what was reported in the Evening Post of May in relation to the Prime Minister: ``Waitara is an outstanding case of where things have not been good.'' Did she make that statement? It might help the debate if we knew. There is no answer from the Prime Minister, so we do not know whether she still thinks that is an outstanding statement.

I was rather hoping that the mover of this bill would actually get up and explain again why we have gone back into Committee, after having been told by the Leader of the House that we would be on the third reading. We now find ourselves back in Committee. We are back in Committee on clause to omit from the definition of M~aori constituency the words ``the M~aori constituency established by section or''. Well, why? That is the question I am asking the member. I would like to know why he thinks we should be making this change. Did he get it wrong? Is it because of some other amendments that we have now made? Why has the member been telling this Committee every Wednesday for months that we should support this bill, only to come back and say to us that we should omit the words ``M~aori constituency means the M~aori constituency established by section ''? I would like to know whether the member made this amendment, or whether the law draftsman drew it to his attention. Or, has the Bay of Plenty Regional Council written to him saying: ``Whoops, we've been looking at the drafted bill.''? The bill we had went to a select committee, so the select committee has considered it. We have had a Committee stage on this bill lasting longer than on any other bill dealt with by this Government in this Parliament, and I think probably the longest ever session on a member's bill. I suspect that the member has established some sort of record. I have been here only years, and I have never seen a member's bill that has taken as long as this one has. Yet, despite all this scrutiny and this careful examining of the bill, the member then comes to us and asks us to change clause . But he is not prepared to tell us why, nor are any of his colleagues. Indeed, it is interesting to note that there was a great deal of support by the member's colleagues for this bill months ago. They wanted to debate it, but now they have lost all interest. Is that because, as Mr Winston Peters has told us---and he is the local member---that in fact in the Bay of Plenty the bill is not popular? Indeed, I heard a remark being made across the Chamber that this could be Mr Peters' ``Reviving of his Political Fortune Bill'', if he and the mover got together on this matter. Is that why Labour now wants the bill to go through without discussion? Well, the ACT party is not going to silently let the bill go through just because opposing it might be of assistance to Mr Peters. We are a party of principle. We do not actually like the whole idea of M~aori constituencies, amended or unamended. We say that we should have constituencies where people are elected on merit. The ACT party welcomes the thought of electing more M~aori to constituencies. We are even prepared to concede that first past the post has not worked well for M~aori, though we are not prepared to concede that it is not possible for M~aori to get elected on a first-past-the-post basis. We have had M~aori in this Parliament who have managed to do that without the hand-up of being in a special M~aori seat. Of course, as has been drawn to the attention of the Committee, we now have the option of having a form of proportional representation available in local body elections. So I ask the member in charge of the bill to explain to the Committee why he believes we need M~aori constituencies. Would he explain to us what is wrong with the amendment? Is it because we have struck out Part ? Is that his worry? Is that why we have done it? Is that why he is concerned? Is that why we are making this amendment? If so, is it not quite extraordinary that when he was striking out Part , he never got around to realising that he ought to have some associated amendments to the definitions? Why did no senior member of the Labour Party help him with the amendments? That is one of the interesting things about this new, modern Labour Party, and I know a little bit about the Labour Party. The Labour Party used to give assistance to new members. When I introduced my first member's bill I got great assistance. In fact, Judith Tizard might be surprised to hear that Bob Tizard was quite willing to give new members assistance, to point out the traps, and to say to members: ``Well, if you're going to make an amendment to Part , you'd better go back and have a look and see whether you're going to need amendments to the definitions clause.'' Well, of course Mr Ririnui would not have been able to get any help from the members who are in the Chamber at the moment because they do not know any more about members' bills than does the member in charge of this bill. But he might like to tell this Committee whether he has had any support from senior members, because if one looks across the Chamber that does not appear to be the case. Not a single front bencher is here ready to support him.

Maybe I have not looked at the right Standing Order. Perhaps you can help me. But when I look at the certificate it states that it is a certificate by the Government. It does not state how one obtains a certificate by the Government, or how one is supposed to know when receiving a piece of paper that it is from the Government. It is very hard to credit that Mr Burton can be the Government. That cannot be right. I suspect that this should probably connect up to one of the financial bills, and that maybe a certificate is not valid unless it is signed by a Minister of Finance. Indeed, tonight we have seen this muck-up because we have had the situation of the Minister of Finance coming down and saying that if anyone had asked him he would never have signed it. It would appear to me that a certificate signed by just any old Minister might not be what is meant in terms of a financial veto certificate. I cannot recall a Chair ever ruling on what a financial veto certificate actually is and who should sign it, but I do say that Mr Burton told us that he did it as Minister of Defence. It is appropriate that we pause the business of this House to mark the passing of two great New Zealanders. On behalf of the ACT New Zealand party I join the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and the other party leaders to pay my tribute to them. With the indulgence of the House, as it is the first day, and as I am one of only three MPs who served with the late Bill Fraser, might I also make a remark regarding that remarkable New Zealander. He was an MP of the sort whom we do not see in the House today. He was a humble man. He started his life as a carpenter, and he used to say in the Labour caucus, when various people were plotting about promotion, that he was the only registered cabinetmaker in caucus. He had a great sense of humour, he served the people of Dunedin very well, and I extend to his family my and the House's condolences. Might I have the further indulgence of the House to mark a personal loss that my party has suffered. My press secretary, Mike Lorigan, was killed tragically in an aeroplane crash, and, as can be seen, that still greatly upsets me. He was a young man of enormous talent, of the sort that many caucuses have working for them, working extraordinarily hard for us for very low wages. Not only my party has suffered a loss. He was a young man at the beginning of his career, and I think he could have gone all the way. The country has suffered a loss. I extend to his family our condolences. I wish to say a word about, first, Sir Robert Mahuta. I knew Sir Robert well. We spent hours and days together because I was the Minister designated to negotiate with him when he made the first Waitangi Tribunal claim under the present legal regime. I can report that he was a negotiator of great tenacity and great ability. It has been reported that I offered him $ million. Of course, I did nothing of the sort. I was acting on behalf of a Labour Cabinet, and the figure was $ million. I just say to those people who think that was a small sum of money that at the time it was a very large sum of money, and Sir Robert had the courage to turn it down. Not only that; he had the belief in the righteousness of his cause to think that he should turn it down. He also had faith in his fellow New Zealanders that he would get a better offer. I have acknowledged at his tangi that I said to him that he would not, he said that he would, and I was wrong and he was right. Those who now criticise him should remember his courage in personally standing out for what he thought was correct, and that is what I think we should remember him for. The other remarkable similarity between these great New Zealanders whom we are remembering is courage, because that is a quality that Sir David Beattie had, as well. One of the aspects that I remember about him---and I could talk about many---that I thought took courage was that as Governor-General he was the patron of the New Zealand Rugby Football Union. The rugby union is now very popular. At that time it became very unpopular, and it would have been very easy for him to resign from being the patron. I remember, as a Minister serving when he was Governor-General, discussing the matter with him and saying to him that I thought he should continue to be the patron of the rugby union, because he had to recognise that rugby was more than just our playing sport with one particular country; that it was, in fact, our national sport, and that, of course, thousands of volunteers supported the game every day. He stayed in that position, and that was typical of the man. He was courageous. I join all other members in extending to his family our sorrow at his passing.

The question is well put---where have we heard that before? Let us look at some of the places where we might have seen something like that before. Let me quote from page of a document titled Saving and NZ Super: A Brief Overview of the Retirement Income Report: ``Our current combination of New Zealand super paid from taxes and voluntary private savings is flexible enough to deal with the changes we'll face over the next years. If that was the perceived wisdom as recently as , why do we see these substantial changes---and they are substantial changes---before the House on this particular occasion? The Minister was suggesting that this Bill would be the end of the matter. It reduces the band that we can pay retirees in New Zealand pursuant to New Zealand superannuation. Instead of being between percent and . percent of the average take-home pay, the floor will be lower--- percent---in order to put superannuation on an affordable and sustainable level. Where did that figure come from? It came from the negotiations that took place between the Rt Hon. Bill Birch---the peacemaker within the National Party Government---and the dissidents who make up the remnants of New Zealand First. I ask Mr Sowry how that lines up with his comments made earlier this morning that this Bill will put superannuation on to an affordable and sustainable path. It does not make sense. Nor does it make sense in terms of another publication issued in June . . Shut up!

We at least got some facts from the member who has just resumed his seat. He read out an extract from a piece of correspondence from the chief executive of the Auckland Regional Services Trust. I have now heard that extract read out three times. It is part of the process that has gone on over the last hours: trying to line up ACT to side with the Government, which does not have enough people within its own two caucuses to carry this piece of legislation through the House. I remind Mr Birch again of what he read out to the House from the chief executive officer's letter. It says: ``it is, therefore, arguable''---that these assets are owned or belong to the people of Auckland and not to the ratepayers of Auckland. I repeat: ``it is, therefore, arguable''. I say to Mr Birch that if there was no doubt about it, the comment would have been far less equivocal than that, and he knows it. The real issue is the question of who has been carrying the risk since the Auckland Regional Services Trust was originally set up, since the losses were incurred by the Auckland Regional Council, and since these businesses have been in operation. Mr Birch knows, as I know, and the rest of the House knows, that the ultimate risk has been carried by the ratepayers of Auckland. ACT's position is that we will support the Government in a piece of legislation that does the job properly, if, in fact, the Government does not have the numbers to do what it should be doing in the first place---that is, governing in the interests of all New Zealanders. That is what the coalition Government came together to do, pursuant to a coalition agreement; it was to govern in the interests of New Zealand. But let us not get too carried away. Let me get to some of the facts. The leading fact is, and Aucklanders know it, that there are substantial infrastructural problems in the Auckland region. But what are they? First and foremost, they are congestion on the roads, and Aucklanders see that every day of the week. They also see pollution on their beaches. There are some places where people cannot swim or take the fish. They also know, as they saw a couple of years ago, that there are real uncertainties as far as water supply is concerned. But I have to ask the House what that has to do with, as the Prime Minister said in her speech, a honey pot that has a potential fund of $. billion, which she said belongs to the people of Auckland? If the honey pot of $. billion belongs to the people of Auckland, why not give it back to the people of Auckland? That is the real issue that this Government cannot face up to. We heard the Deputy Prime Minister talk about democracy and principles. I can see through him on that particular issue, and the New Zealand voters can see through Mr Peters on that issue. That is why New Zealand First is at or percent in the polls, and probably below that. If we face up to the real end point as far as New Zealand First is concerned, we see that it has nothing to do with democracy or with principles; it is all about differentiation. It is all about trying to be seen as a party that stands aside and does not follow the National Party line. As I said, that is something the people can see through. So what is the answer to Auckland's road problems? What is the answer to Auckland's sewerage problems? What is the answer to the stormwater problems? These are problems that local government has been attempting to solve in Auckland for generations. But have they solved the problems? The answer is no. What do they want to use this honey pot for, which the Prime Minister talks about? It is very interesting to see what they want to use it for. There is a municipal accord on what this surplus cash should be spent on. Let me quote from that accord: ``Transport, particularly passenger transport''. Will that help the private cars on the road? ``Environmental management, including stormwater''; ``Open-space requirements, including parks''; ``Community facilities, such as museums.'' The Minister who introduced the Bill shakes his head, and rightly so. These are all the things that the local authorities in Auckland and the Greater Auckland region have not been able to get the ratepayers to front up to and pay for. What the regional authorities in Auckland have not done is say: ``These are our priorities because we have real problems. These are our solutions, and we want you to pay the rate to fund all those activities.'' Suddenly we have this honey pot, which is a golden opportunity for them to try not to face up to their responsibility. So what is the Government's answer? Because it cannot put the heading dog around all its members within its two caucuses, and therefore at least a couple of them have wandered out into another paddock, its answer is to hold a referendum. I move, That the House take note of miscellaneous business. ACT members of Parliament were absolutely disgusted yesterday when the Government did not accept the opportunity to debate the issue of confidence, to test the issue in this House and to show the public of New Zealand that it has the votes to put through its legislative programme. I suspect that there were two possible reasons for hiding behind the Standing Orders. First and foremost, members opposite could not rely on some of the members of the coalition Government; or, secondly, they are too arrogant to bother having the issue tested by this House. I suspect that it is maybe a combination of both circumstances. I wonder how the new National members of Parliament feel about that decision, or how they feel about New Zealand First---or was it perhaps only the leader of New Zealand First---flirting with the Labour Party during the weekend. It must create tremendous confidence within the National Party, as a builder of that confidence, that New Zealand First is percent committed to the coalition agreement! I cannot help but think that Sir Robert Muldoon must have been laughing in his grave when he saw the events of the last few days unfold. The parliamentary National Party has adopted his ideology in toto. His ideology was that one had to be in Government to do anything. The result of that---and I note that the leader-elect is taking notice of this point---is that the National Party members of Parliament have prostituted themselves and their political party. Perhaps we should ask some of those National Party members, particularly the new ones who were first elected in , whether they have taken account of what their party says in this blue book---the rules and constitution of the New Zealand National Party. It seems to me that the party can do away with the reams and reams of comments on principles, and adopt only one objective, and that is to stay in office no matter what the cost is to New Zealand. There has already been a very, very high cost to New Zealanders because of this coalition Government. There have been delayed tax cuts and a dramatic reduction in the proposed fiscal surplus. It is down from the projection of some years ago of around $. billion to a figure now which, depending on whom one believes, is between $ million and $. billion. Look at some of the other areas the Government has been involved in. Health is in an absolute shambles. What upsets me more than anything else---and upsets, I suspect, a number of other members of Parliament---is that this coalition Government has debased the status of members of Parliament and reduced the standing of the parliamentary process in the eyes of the New Zealand public. If Government members do not believe me on that, they should take note of the latest opinion polls on the public's approval of this Government. It has a disapproval rating of percent, and an approval rating of a mere percent. The Government had a very narrow window of opportunity a little time ago. It was to call New Zealand First's bluff, to get rid of the rotten apples that are infecting the whole Government, and to put in place sensible policies in the interests of all New Zealanders, instead of policies that are designed for some particular interest groups. That opportunity has been lost. What we now have is a new chauffeur. She is behind the steering wheel, but she is not yet allowed to drive the vehicle of State. When she is allowed to drive the vehicle of State, the shots will still be called by the political puffball sitting in the back seat. I do not think that is good enough for New Zealanders. I put the National Party and the Government on notice that while we have a continuation of the process of the National Party cuddling up to New Zealand First, they should not take ACT's support for granted.

Before the dinner adjournment I was talking about the controls that are in place to monitor overseas ownership, and, very briefly, those four controls are the Commerce Act, the Overseas Investment Act, the Broadcasting Standards Authority, and the Broadcasting Commission. The Broadcasting Commission is an important body because it helps to boost the level of local content, as does competition for local production, and that is vital to audience retention. The public---the consumers of media outpourings---is the ultimate arbiter of the quality of programmes and the material that is delivered to the people through the media. If the product is below standard those particular media sources will not succeed in the market-place. It is important that investment is able to take place in the media industries---television, newspapers, radio, and so on---so that levels of competition are retained. A great fear in the present climate is that the economy is so bad that if fresh investment moneys are not made available to the industry the level of competition will diminish and, accordingly, standards will diminish with the lack of that competition. The Porter report mentions the value of internal competition in setting standards for our industries. The possibility of percent foreign ownership of the media---television, radio, and the newspapers---does not pose the threat that some people think.

The rest of New Zealand would say that the Government was responding and rising to that challenge. The member for Auckland Central used to come into the House like a bulldog on a chain. Because the chain used to be held by Roger Douglas---who has now gone---the member for Auckland Central comes in like a rampant bulldog running around the place unrestrained and dragging his chain behind him. I read with some amusement recently that those fantastic tablets of stone, on which had been engraved the promise that telephone calls from private homes would not be metered or charged for, had been thrown out with the rubbish. A former member of the Labour Government made a similar promise, but the difference between the Minister of Police and Russell Marshall is that the Minister of Police will keep the promise he made and will not back down or ``wish-wash'' out of them as Russell Marshall did. Government members are honourable men who keep their promises, and will deliver when they say they will deliver. Much comment has been made about the police and their resources. The result would be anarchy. That would be denied by nobody in this House. Nobody of maturity in this House would deny that the result would be anarchy. But the member for Tauranga continues to insist that either Government members are in the House to vote on every piece of legislation or the Government falls. Why does that member not grow up? Oppositions will always disagree with key points of Government legislation. Nevertheless, the Government, having been elected with a majority, has the right to govern. The member for Tauranga has to pause and reflect on that, and to realise that he has a part to play---albeit very minor, representing a small percentage of New Zealand voters---in co-operating to ensure that this Parliament can carry out its necessary work. I want to respond to the challenge from the member for Tauranga and to turn to the good news that this Government wishes to share with the House and the public of New Zealand today. The Budget of has been extremely positively received by New Zealanders. It confirms the Government's commitment to policies that have driven strong economic growth, low inflation, flexible labour markets, Budget surpluses, a broad-base, low-tax policy, and encouragement of an open, internationally competitive economy---exactly why this House voted today to send clause of the Maritime Transport Bill for its next reading; that is part of New Zealand being an open, internationally competitive economy. Gross domestic product statistics released last week for the March quarter show that this economy grew by . percent---that is, in the year ended March. That is the highest figure since the year ended March , which was itself out of kilter with growth patterns for the previous years. The latest Dun and Bradstreet survey of New Zealand business expectations was also released today, and I think the member for Tauranga might wish to hear some of these statistics. Three hundred and fifty manufacturing, wholesaling, and retailing businesses were surveyed. The result included information that percent of those businesses expect sales to increase, and percent expect sales to decrease; percent expect profits to rise, and only percent expect profits to fall; percent expect a rise in new orders, and percent expect a fall; and percent expect to hire new staff while percent do not. That reputable survey released today by Dun and Bradstreet states the results of Government policy for the last / years. The Budget is about sustaining that high growth. That will allow us to achieve Budget surpluses and to reduce debt. Let us have a look at the debt, which has got to unsustainable levels. I regard the debt as intergenerational theft. I regard Governments that borrow to pay for the groceries---not hardware, not dams, not roads and the bridges, but day-to-day groceries and day-to-day social spending---except in particular parts of an economic cycle, to be committing intergenerational theft. I applaud this Government's determination to repay debt while we are moving towards the top of that cycle, and to get debt down to more manageable levels and more responsible levels. At present, the Budget sets out percent as a more prudent level. I also applaud this Government for having a policy to continue to reduce debt beyond that, down to percent, and over a longer time scale---probably something like years. We could not go on borrowing money that we did not have. We could not go on indebting our children and grandchildren with debts they had no say in the raising of and had no receipt of the spending of. Those debts were raised by Governments that were borrowing for political support. Those Governments could not, and did not, face the hard decisions that need to be made for Governments to live within income. Now for the first time we have a surplus, and we find the Labour Opposition wants to spend it all, and more. We find the Alliance wants to spend it all, and more. Of course teachers need to have a pay rise. Of course shortages need to be addressed. I am hearing from my principals today that they do not have the ability to pay to keep the best teachers, and that the best teachers are moving on to better-paid positions in the private sector---as has always happened in times of economic recovery. Thanks to the National Government we are in a sustained period of economic recovery. So while we cling to collectivism and while we cling to paying the mediocre the same as we pay the best and the worst, teacher shortages will continue. It will not be helped by the member for Hamilton East claiming that police start on $, and teachers start on $,, because the reality is not so. I want to make a brief comment about the member for St Kilda before he leaves this House. That member excelled himself today in what was an awful rendition of vitriol and personal attacks---the worst kind of debate possible, which has tended to bring this House into great disrepute with the public, with news media commentators, and with everybody else who takes an interest in this House. I want to urge the member for St Kilda to read his Hansard as soon as it is produced and to consider coming back to this House to apologise to members for the invective and vitriol that he pours constantly upon members in this House. When the member for St Kilda cannot succeed in debate he resorts to personal attacks of absolutely the worst kind. That member---and his understudy the member for Dunedin West, who seems to be following in the same mould---ought to think seriously about what they do. I think that the Opposition has failed policies. It cannot put policies before the public that will excite people's interest. The Opposition is very concerned that the Government's agenda is not only working but working very well. Therefore the member for St Kilda and others resort to a personal attack on the Prime Minister, who, in my view, has in the last years led this Government through the most challenging social issues of our time. He is the preferred Prime Minister for voters in this country, and that also must grate heavily on Labour members, who in their caucus room have obviously decided to move to personal attacks as a means of trying to advance their failing fortunes before the public of this country. Let us turn now to positive outcomes in education. I want to spend the time that is allocated to me dealing with education and with the most positive initiatives, some of which are being announced today. Some of those initiatives were referred to by the member for Dunedin West when he spoke about the report on truancy that was produced by the select committee that I have the honour to chair. Perhaps I will deal with that subject first, because the member for Dunedin West raised it today. He talked about the disgrace of the Government in not dealing with dysfunctional families, solo parent families, and those most in need. Of course, that is entirely untrue. This Government has set up the Parents as First Teachers programme. It set up the first programmes within a year of taking office and currently has pilot programmes either running or in the final contractual stage. Those pilot programmes deal with families each. They deal with the exact group that the member for Dunedin West was complaining about was not being reached. I want to ask the member for Dunedin West, or another member who will take a call, how many dysfunctional families the Labour Government reached when it was in office. How many Parents as First Teachers programmes did the Labour Government set up when it was in office? How much funding did it put into reaching out to the very people whom the member for Dunedin West, in Opposition, can now carp about and say that not enough is being done for them? I say to him that this Government has done a great deal more than either he or his colleagues ever did when they were in office. Furthermore, we on this side of the House will not resort to personal attacks in the House when our arguments run dry, and I commend that approach to members of the Opposition. The report on truancy that was released yesterday is a multiparty report. It was agreed to by all members on the committee. It is a means of moving forward in education and of ensuring that young people get an education that will fit them for life and make them employable so that they can participate in society. It identifies particular areas in which there are blockages at present. It was a unique opportunity for a select committee to call together experts from right across the country to hear evidence from schools with best practice and from schools and organisations with not such good practice. At the end of the day it was able to come up with a set of recommendations that all schools will be able to follow. These are recommendations for Government to unlock some resources---that is true---but there is also an affirmation that early intervention is the key to success in education. If there is one message that comes through extremely strongly it is that the earlier we can intervene, the more success we will have in integrating children from even the most dysfunctional families into our education system and equipping them with the skills and education they need for life. Let us look at the initiative that was announced today by the Minister of Education. Eight hundred new teachers will be provided for schools, of whom go to primary schools and over to secondary schools. This initiative will permanently lower student-staff ratios in virtually all schools. Two-thirds of schools have a net increase in staff. The figure of new teachers is a net figure that is available across all schools. In my own area in Birkenhead / new full-time equivalent teachers will be available for the same number of students, and I know that will be welcomed not only by teachers but also by parents and everybody interested in the education community. I wonder if one person in the Opposition has the grace to rise to his or her feet and welcome that initiative and say that it was something that the Labour Government, despite its fine talk in this House, never, ever got around to doing. This Government has committed itself to education. There is an enormous amount of spending. Funds for specific items have been allocated for the present and promised for the future. That is welcome. It is something that all New Zealanders want. There has been a call from the Opposition to share in the recovery, and what happens? When the Government begins to allocate substantial extra funding---$ million into education over the next years alone---there is not one word of support from the Opposition; there is simply more carping about a different issue. Why does the Opposition not become a real Opposition and concentrate on the things that really are not working and give praise where it should be given? Opposition members cannot do that because they are locked into a time warp. They are locked into the invective of people like the member for St Kilda. They cannot think and look positively at any action, so that is where they are destined to remain---in Opposition. Let us look at the Ministerial Reference Group that brought this initiative into being, and also at the composition of that group. The Ministerial Reference Group, whose recommendations were adopted by Cabinet in their entirety, included the New Zealand School Trustees Association, the Secondary Principals Association of New Zealand, the New Zealand Intermediate Schools Principals Association, the New Zealand Principals Federation, the Post Primary Teachers Association (PPTA), the New Zealand Educational Institute, the Association of Proprietors of Integrated Schools, the Independent Schools Association, the Association of Bulk-funded Schools, and kura kaupapa Maori schools. The purpose of reading out that list is that all those groups, with the exception of the PPTA, agreed with the report of the Ministerial Reference Group. It is a sad day for that association that with those esteemed bodies sitting and working through a package and a document such as this one is, it had to stand aside. Having looked at and listened to the arguments of the PPTA I cannot understand where it is coming from. It appears to have its own philosophical argument and debate going on, and its own philosophical position. Perhaps it is may be useful to colleagues to quote from a prominent Auckland radio host who when asked about whether the PPTA was a conservative union replied: ``Yes, it is a conservative union. If you want a moaner on the radio, if you want somebody to say that some new education initiative is a dog, a backward step, and the beginning of the end, ring up the PPTA. You learn this in the news media. If you want somebody to negate any advance, ring up the PPTA.'' There is a lot of truth in that statement and it is something that the association ought to take on board. It ought to learn to work with fellow players in education to advance education. At the end of the day it is the children that count. It is the children and the outcomes that count, not any individual philosophy.

I feel as if I am doing my best jack-in-the-box impersonation, but finally I take a call! I rise in support of the words of my colleagues. The first comment I would like to make relates to discussion regarding the timing of this bill. We discussed earlier that this bill has been pushed through too fast, too soon, but it is worth while mentioning again that we believe that the timing of this bill, especially with regard to the impact of it, has not been taken into account. Part really is the heart of the bill. It takes away the competition within the market. It does so without providing businesses with compensation. It cancels their contracts. It basically kicks them out of the market. One of the things that I am interested in is what this says to the business world in New Zealand--not just our domestic businesses but also international investors who may be looking at New Zealand for investment. Basically, this legislation should make businesses very worried about investing in New Zealand, because it says that if the Government has an eye on a market, if it changes its mind, it can come in, it can legislate, and it can take one's business, cancel one's contracts, and kick one out. This legislation really is nationalisation. However one describes it, it is theft of a market. These businesses came into the market in good faith. They did so under the law of the time, and they made their investments wisely. But the Government is saying that when people enter into a business arrangement or any contract, the Government can come over the top and make that contract null and void. It can make the contract null and void not for good reasons but for reasons of pure ideology. It is simply not common-sense to make many of these changes. If some of the indications for the privatisation of the insurance market had been bad, many of these changes would be common-sense. But they are not. The Government is returning the provision of accident insurance to a monopoly, when the early indications are very good--fatalities have come down, premiums have come down, and companies are reporting improved service from insurance providers. The evidence so far shows that things are working, but, of course, we will not have enough time to conduct a trial and really know. The main part of this bill, which I think is quite frightening, is that it steals from companies the possibility of compensation. The Government is saying it is going to kick them out of this market, but it is not going to compensate them or give them any compensation for the market it is taking away. One particularly frightening aspect, as I said earlier, is the message that this gives to international investors. Businesses make decisions every day. They make the best decisions they can with the information they have, and enter into contracts. This sets a frightening precedent, which perhaps puts us into a category with the likes of Cuba, Albania, and other countries--

As a loyal New Zealander I convey my respects and those of my constituents in Selwyn to Her Majesty the Queen. As a family person, I say that it was just great to have the royal family in New Zealand during the summer. For my children, the memorable parts of the royal tour were the endless parades of diamonds and guns. However, for me, the memorable part was standing literally at arm's length from the Queen and singing ``God Save the Queen'' to her. It was certainly a new experience of that anthem. Mr Speaker, if you were a rugby referee you would be admired for your willingness not to interrupt the run of play. Can I tell you how much I enjoy your speakership. The member for Auckland Central has had the cheek to argue numbers and to try to claim some supremacy in sums. He would do well to consider Te Atatu, because there we saw the new mathematics of the Labour Party. By my reckoning, four beats three. However, under Labour Party new mathematics, three beats four, and that shows the credibility of the Labour Party with mathematics. The Government has tried to cost the commitments made by the National Party. Its opening bid was $ billion, then the next version was $. billion. The member for Auckland Central had a different version again, and quite frankly nobody trusts the Labour Party to do its sums. I want to address two important issues: the reason the Labour Party is bad for business; and the reason the National Party will be good for growth. The Minister of Finance is undoubtedly bad for business. The headlines say it all, and they are written for two reasons: because he has displayed bad judgment time and time again; and because he has initiated bad policy time and time again. Let me give a couple of recent examples. The Minister's bad commercial judgment was confirmed again during the weekend when he appointed the Mayor of Christchurch to the Reserve Bank. I find it disgraceful enough that the Minister should actually breach the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act---which is very specific, because the Act requires that the Minister shall have regard to two factors. The first factor relates to the person's knowledge, skill, and experience. Vicki Buck emerges with flying colours. However, there is a second requirement. It is not an ``either/or'' requirement; it is an ``and'' requirement. The second factor to which the Minister shall have regard is the likelihood of any conflict between the interests of the bank and any interests that that person has or represents. The Minister flew in the face of the acknowledged conflict and appointed the Mayor of Christchurch. Not only do I find it disgraceful that a Minister of Finance would breach his Act, I find it unforgivable that he should so compromise the integrity and the reputation of the Mayor of Christchurch. She is a person for whom I have the highest regard. We have some common causes in the combination of children and careers. Her integrity has been disgracefully compromised by the Minister of Finance, who gave the following insulting sexist comment in Saturday's Christchurch Press when he acknowledged that there was a conflict: ``Well, Vicki will be limited in some of the things she can say to her husband.'' It is a disgraceful state of affairs that the Minister of Finance should not know his Act, and that he should compromise the integrity and the reputation of a person who should be beyond such reproach. There is a stench about the Minister of Finance, and that stench was first seen in the handling of the Development Finance Corporation. I gave the Minister a couple of pieces of advice. First, he should have exercised some commercial savvy and looked at a creditor-management type of arrangement in the first place. Second, when he was ignorant and insulting in handling those creditors who would be out of pocket I told him that he should say he was sorry. Both of those comments have come to pass, in a way. The Minister has been forced to say that he is sorry, although he could not get even that right. The sorry explanation was then met with a flurry of further letters from him. He now recognises that the Government will be forced to participate in a settlement of the affairs of the Development Finance Corporation, and that will probably range all the way from legislation to allow tax deductions for Development Finance Corporation losses, to being at the wrong end of a legal claim. The Minister cannot wash his hands of the fiasco, and corporates have discovered up and down the country that New Zealanders are being forced to pay a considerable price for the Minister's appalling commercial judgment. Let me turn to the Minister's policy initiatives, because they are just as bad. The balance of payments figures were released last week. I do not think that I can better the assessment of one senior economist, who said: ``A rapid growth in imports and constraints on agricultural production have exposed New Zealand to an unsustainable position in its balance of payments.'' As we look down the barrel of a balance of payments deficit of $ billion---adding to the dangerous level of debt---we see that all New Zealanders will pay the price for the Government's allowing the balance of payments to reach an unsustainable figure. This week it is the growth figures. Today we find that New Zealand's growth record is times worse than that of the rest of the world. In typical economies such as ours grew about percent. What about New Zealand? New Zealand had a weakling economic child---it had . percent growth. Our economy remains stagnant, and we are piling up debt through our inability to pay our way in the world. The Minister of Finance has lost his nerve, and is incapable of tackling the four problems that cause a stagnant economy. New Zealand has a highly regulated labour market, but the Government does not have the will to tackle it. New Zealand has excessive Government spending and taxation, but the Government does not have a strategy to rein that in. We have poor skills, but the Government has said that it will not support students with tertiary opportunities. We have growing and alarming dependence among New Zealanders, but the Government has a middle-class guilt in throwing conscience money at those who are consigned to the scrap-heap. Not only has the Minister failed when it comes to important bottom lines such as the balance of payments and growth; he has failed in the bottom line he created for himself, which was interest rates. During the weekend, hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders received a note from their banks stating: ``Dear customer, your mortgage rate is going to increase.'' The economic statement made on March was designed to reduce the cost of money. There is revolt in the business sector, because it does not know where the Government is going, nor does the Government itself know. So we have been told that there will be another March statement, which will be designed to settle uncertainties. We do not know when the statement will be presented, or where, and we do not know what it will contain. Two days ago the Minister's office said it would probably contain a revamp of the Accident Compensation Corporation. However, that statement did not last for hours. Today we have been told that that is not ready; that the March package will not deal with a restructuring of the Accident Compensation Corporation. However, we do know---we think---that it will contain a change to the building code. If that is the stuff of the media hype and the fiddling we will be just as badly off with this March economic statement as we were with the March economic statement. Indeed, the Minister's office has had only one comment to make, and that is that the forthcoming March economic statement will have a bearing on economic growth. However, the question relates to the kind of bearing. Will the statement have the kind of bearing on economic growth that the December package had, which was to send us into a recession? Will it have the kind of bearing that the March economic statement had, which was to increase interest rates? We do not want March economic statements of that kind. From what we have learnt today it is clear in advance that whatever the Government can produce next month---originally it was billed as a statement of economic and social policy---the social policy has gone by the board. Government members cannot agree on that aspect. They are having a big cat-fight, a big dog-fight in Cabinet. They cannot agree on that matter. We know that whatever is in the statement it will be a combination of media hype and financial fiddle, and it will not deal with the critical issues. Difficult issues face the economy, and the Government has not had the courage to take the hard decisions. The best action for the Minister of Finance to take is to come to Auckland on Friday, because on that day the National Party will launch its economic framework. In fact, he would be much better advised to come to Auckland on Friday and hear about the National Party's economic vision than he would be to sign a piece of paper---that nobody believes in---with the Governor of the Reserve Bank. What will happen on Friday in Wellington will be a continuation of an unbalanced policy approach in which the Government looks wholly to monetary policy to do all of the job. We know that that is a formula for scorched earth, for high interest rates, and for an uncompetitive climate for New Zealand producers. The balance of payments would bear out that analysis. The Minister of Finance and his colleagues should come to Auckland. I issue an invitation to the Minister for State-owned Enterprises to do the same. They should come and hear about the formula for growth for this country, because the National Party has an economic vision and a commitment to the reforms that will drive growth. It has a commitment to a high-income, high employment New Zealand. That will take a combination of four policy initiatives. There will be policies to give skills to New Zealanders; policies that actually being about a work-place that is busy and productive; policies designed to ensure that we have a benefit system that gives New Zealanders---as the Leader of the Opposition put it so well---a hand up, not a hand-out; and policies that ensure that the taxation system is consistent with the National Party's growth objectives. I shall look first at the skills objective. The National Party knows---as every country in the world whose economy is growing knows---that growth finally is driven by knowledge and technology. The National Party is prepared to act on that understanding, because New Zealand is the dunce in class at the moment. It is not a position that any of us is comfortable with. The kiwi at the bottom of the class with that other flightless bird, the turkey, because only Turkey is worse than New Zealand when it comes to participation in education. That is why the National Party has already unveiled its policy of investing in educational opportunities. That is why the National Party is prepared to support students. It wants New Zealanders to have opportunities post-school, and it is prepared to put its money where its mouth is. That is to be a budgetary priority, because that is the most important investment we can make towards the country's future prosperity. New Zealand is an underperforming country. The National Party has already announced policies to lift New Zealanders' skills. A National Government would make the investment in research and development. It would not collapse the country's technology base. The National Party is offering a quite different approach to skills---that is, putting a premium on education, investing in skills, and ensuring that we maintain a research and development capability. Let us look at the work-place, because if one were to look for the maximum difference between the formula pursued by the Government and that being offered by the Opposition one should take a trip to the work-place. I cannot think of any reason that we should put up for more than one more day with a rigid industrial relations system that denies us jobs and denies us the productivity break-out that we must make. A National Government would not put up with such an archaic system. The National Party does not want New Zealanders to be denied the chance to earn higher wages through higher productivity. It does not want New Zealanders to be denied jobs, and it will take the policy initiatives that will be applauded by all New Zealanders who want a high-income and high-employment society. Such people say of the Government: ``If only it had been prepared to deal with the vested interest in its party ranks. If only it had been prepared to reform work-place practices.'' A National Government would answer those problems. It would reform the work-place. I turn to the issue of benefits. The Minister of Social Welfare has gone around the country saying that he is sick and tired of benefit bashers. I tell the Minister that the Opposition is sick and tired of a system that bashes people; a system that makes New Zealanders worse off in work; a system that traps people into dependence and strips them of any self-esteem. The benefits are not at fault and neither are the beneficiaries. It is the system that is at fault. It is a matter of poor public policy, and the casualties are New Zealanders in their hundreds of thousands who are trapped into dependence. The social effects of dependence are tragic, and the economic effects are crippling. All New Zealanders know that the system has failed. They understand that it is common sense to say: ``Give people a fish and you feed them for the day. Teach people to fish and you feed them for their lifetime.'' The National Party seeks to have a social welfare system that reassures those in genuine need---and we should be generous to a fault, to the extent and the capacity of the economy, to support those in genuine need---but we need to redesign the welfare State so that we reduce New Zealanders' dependence on the State. The Government spends c of every dollar on social welfare, or, put another way, percent of all the pay-as-you-earn tax collected is spent on social welfare. The Government has failed to grapple with that reality. It has been indifferent to the plight of beneficiaries. Social welfare spending is driving this nation and the economy into the ground, and it is driving our population into dependence. New Zealanders are not historically people who are pessimistic. We are not historically people who are mediocre, and we are not historically people who are dependent, but poor public policy has brought us to this pass. Better public policy---and that is the commitment of the National Party---aimed at encouraging enterprise and re-equipping people for independence, will make a difference. That brings us to the difference we intend to make to the taxation system. The National Party wants the taxation system to be driven by growth, not driven by more revenue raids, as has become the habit of the Government. That is why a National Government would say ``No'' to growth-denying taxes---that is, ``No'' to the land tax, ``No'' to the diesel tax, ``No'' to the superannuation surtax. The country is desperate for investment and savings, yet the superannuation surtax is a savage disincentive to save. A National Government would say ``No'' to estate and gift duties, and would say ``No'' to a capital gains tax. It would say ``No'' because it is serious about gearing the economy for growth. I suppose that members should be indebted to him for what has become---in the Labour Party---an unfashionable display of socialism. Perhaps he has caught the Anderton disease, because members were treated to a classic socialist view of human nature. The Minister said that there were many ways of saving. However, he ruled out the possibility of leaving dollars in the hands of individuals for them to make the savings decisions. What he effectively said was that the Government can do better, and that that is why it has proceeded to hang its argument on the subsidy peg. What is reprehensible about the Minister's argument is not only that he is wrong about individuals making arrangements about saving but also his implied contention that the Government can do better. If private individuals were to be stripped of their ability to make savings arrangements I suppose the second-best option would be if the Government were to make those savings arrangements for them. However, the Government will do none of that; it has no savings record; it governs a country that has for yonks preferred consumption over savings. Government members come into the House knowing that it is the lack of savings---among other things---that has bedevilled the economy and turned New Zealand into a welfare State along with its costly State dependence, yet Government members are prepared to remove what little incentive there is for saving. I come immediately to the design of that incentive. I have not heard any member defend the status quo ante; nor have I heard any member defend the existing directed nature---as imperfect as that direction is, because the deduction is achieved without necessarily having any stream of income on retirement. The royal commission made it clear that it was necessary to consider the private sector as a very important part of securing income for retirement. If the Government had been serious about the role of the private sector it would not have spent its energy on removing the existing incentives---imperfect though they be---but would have spent its energy on perfecting the existing arrangements. Government members adopt the arrogant, classic, socialist view that dollars should not be left in the hands of individuals. The Bill is nothing more than an unprincipled tax grab, and the debate is not a debate about superannuation and proper arrangements for a guaranteed stream of income on retirement. If the Government had wanted to have that debate it would not have moved in a retrospective manner. The Bill is premature, and the royal commission has confirmed that that is so. However, the Government is determined to proceed with half of the package that was announced on December. The Bill does not redesign savings records in New Zealand, because the onus is on the Government to show that, in the absence of any incentives in the taxation system, people will make their own savings arrangements. The evidence that was tabled by the Opposition, which has not been refuted by the Government---rhetoric will not do; evidence will---showed that more than percent of the people who participate in private superannuation schemes are receiving average incomes of $, a year, or less. The Bill will hit percent of average-income New Zealanders who have made contractual arrangements. I shall now turn to the real reasons that the Government introduced the Bill. The first reason is that, immediately the package was announced on December, such is the Executive's arrogance that it issued an instruction to the Government Printer to start printing tax packs on the basis that the deduction had been removed.
