That contribution is just typical of what we have come to expect from the Labour Opposition. First, it is the Deputy Leader of the Opposition who is leading the charge and leaving the rest of her leadership in the shade. Second, this is the first major debate after a general election has been called and is an ideal opportunity for the Labour Party to unveil its platform and to present the positive, but, no, what we have heard this afternoon has been bereft of policy---not one policy, not one contribution designed to generate growth and jobs in the economy. There has been just the hypocrisy of crocodile tears for the Public Health Commission, which that member opposes. To use her words it is ``a nasty little saga''. That is the typical, negative, nasty type of approach that we have come to expect from the Labour Opposition; there has been not one constructive contribution to good government in this country. If the people had sense they would clean out the Labour Party membership, clean out the Labour Party leadership, and install Vanessa Brown in Mount Albert---at least she wants to contribute to good government. If I could make the contrast---it has never been more clear than this afternoon---the Labour Opposition is negative, and concentrating on its nasty little sagas, and the National Government is seen as positive for New Zealand. I tell members that, as we campaign in our electorates and around the country, surprise, surprise, New Zealanders find the positive very attractive. They find that the positive appeals. There are three reasons that the National Party, the positive party, appeals to New Zealanders. When they are asked, they say that the National Party is the party that is favoured to improve their lives. New Zealanders now say that under a National Government they are looking more positive, they feel more confident about their future---so the positive party, the National Party, appeals when it comes to answering: ``Who best would you want to improve prospects in your lives?''. We are also favoured to run the economy by the order of :. When the people were asked which party they would like to run the economy, New Zealanders favoured by : the positive party, the National Party. Finally, the polls show that New Zealanders favour the positive party, the National Party, to run the country. So, on all three counts---to run New Zealanders' lives, to run the economy, and to run the country---it is the National Party that is favoured because the National Government is seen as the Government of recovery. It is seen as the Government that has taken the responsible decisions, and New Zealanders will not contemplate, will not back, and will not tolerate any Government that would put the recovery at risk. It is only under a National Government that New Zealanders know that the recovery is secure. The Government's record has been one of promoting growth and jobs. We see such a broad base now to the economic recovery. Take, for example, the Reserve Bank forecast that was released yesterday---the economy is expected to grow, consumer spending is expected to grow strongly, investment is expected to register further increases, imports are expected to grow, the current account deficit is expected to decrease, unemployment is expected to decline, and underlying inflation is expected to fall. That is a broad-based recovery. That is the one that New Zealanders love and that is the one they will back. That positive report on the economy was seen instantly as positive news for New Zealand. We saw wholesale interest rates tumble to historic lows. We saw retail rates fall, and the first of a round of cuts in retail interest rates. What does that mean for those who want the growth in jobs, those who want opportunity for their families and opportunity in their workplaces? If one were to take a family in receipt of the average wage with, say, a mortgage of $, and a repayment schedule of years, the drop in interest rates achieved under a Government that is being positive for interest rates is equivalent to a wage increase of more than $ a week. The National Government's policies have delivered a tangible $ a week into the hands of an average family with an ordinary mortgage, or, in terms of that family's purchasing power, it is equivalent to an extra $ a month. It is not just good for householders; it is even better for businesses. Businesses now know that they can make investment and employment decisions, and they are making them. Here we have a broad-based recovery with interest rates tumbling, but, more important, the recovery is with jobs. I invite members to look at the report of the Reserve Bank, particularly at what we were able to achieve in terms of bringing about a recovery with jobs. The Reserve Bank forecast shows that, from to , some , new jobs have been, and will be, created in the economy. So, one sees the graphs of growth, bringing with it the jobs that we have sought---, new jobs---and contrasts that with the years to under a Labour Government, when , jobs were lost. That is the difference. This has been a Government for recovery with jobs. That is , reasons that people should be backing the National Party at the general election; the alternative has no credibility at all. The Opposition spokesman on finance, in the wake of falling interest rates and a recovery with jobs, chose to issue a press statement saying ``not good enough''. That is absolutely typical of the sour approach of that member. He is sour and he is out of step because we have achieved the growth in the economy, we have achieved the jobs, and we have the policies that will continue to strengthen those trends. But that Labour Opposition member would do the same again, given the chance, as he did last time his party was in office---he would ruin the opportunity for growth. When the Labour Government left office we did not have growth; we had depression. We had minus . percent growth in the economy and a legacy of , jobs lost. Given the chance, a Labour Government would do the same again. The Labour Party's policy on tax is bizarre, unfair, and unsound.

The Government has many economic targets, including higher productivity, greater international competitiveness, an improved trade performance, stable prices, lower interest rates, a balanced Budget, more jobs, and sustainable economic growth. The Reserve Bank forecasts released today indicate that this Government is on target to achieve all of those outcomes.

In debating the reporting back of this measure to the House it is intriguing that the two contributions from the Opposition did not mention where it stands on the essential measures at stake. Members opposite have not been prepared to say whether or not they support the removal of the intercorporate dividend exemption. I want to thank two colleagues on that select committee who do know where they stand: the member for Waitotara and the member for Lyttelton, who preceded me in the reporting-back debate. They and two other colleagues on the Government side of the select committee have put in an enormous amount of time and energy in the scrutiny of a most difficult yet crucial piece of legislation. At the heart of the measures before the select committee was the greatly prized tax planning device---the intercorporate dividend exemption. It was that exemption, as the Government knew when it prepared the legislation, that enabled the money-go-round to cut the tax bills of companies in profit. It was that exemption that allowed the erosion of some $ million from the tax base. What would happen because of this great prize, which was the ability to transfer income tax-free, is that companies would tie themselves up with a loss-making company, they would invest in it, they would pick up some non-taxable income and a tax deduction, and the result would be less taxable revenue. If, indeed, the Opposition does have a position---and I do not believe that it does, apart from the posturing---does it stand for the erosion of some $ million from the corporate tax base in this country? In the time that the measure has been before the select committee, evidence has been published that showed that the effective tax rate for New Zealand corporations is but percent, and, indeed, the existence of the intercorporate dividend exemption is in large part responsible for that very low contribution by the corporate sector to the life of this country in terms of the tax base. Simply put, this measure asks those companies to pay their fair share of tax, and we ask that of them at a time when other New Zealanders are making a contribution to dealing with the deficit---including beneficiaries, who have had their benefits cut. No valid arguments were presented to the select committee as to the reason companies should not be taxed on dividends when individuals are taxed. Is that what the Opposition is saying---that when a dividend is paid to an individual then tax should be paid, but when it passes between companies it should not? Is that the position of the Opposition? It has no position apart from political posturing. These measures were always likely to provoke criticism; they were always likely to be controversial, because they struck right at the heart of tax planning, which is the ability to transfer income tax-free. I want to use the occasion of the reporting back to say a word about the beneficiaries of this legislation, who are not self-interested vocal minorities such as those we saw before the select committee. The beneficiaries of this legislation are thousands of New Zealanders who do pay their tax---the thousands of householders and businesses who now pay lower interest rates because of the Government's responsible fiscal policy. Simply put, the choice before the select committee was this: unless companies pay their fair share of tax, other New Zealanders will have to pay more tax or suffer higher interest rates. The Government, in the form of the Minister of Revenue and myself, issued a press statement just before Christmas last year in which we indicated that valid concerns were raised by businesses before the select committee, and that we did need to consider, because of the delays in introducing legislation on consolidation, making some modification to the Budget proposals. However, I stress that none of those modifications in the Bill now reported back detracts either from the essential tax design---which is to have a broad-based low rate---or from the fiscal position.
I cannot confirm that. However, the Government's decision to remove the intercorporate dividend exemption saved the tax base about $ million---a measure that that member opposed.

I do not share the view of the honourable member on the sale of the State Insurance Office, but that is politics, and I suppose that we can agree to disagree. It appears, however, that the honourable member has spent the whole of the dinner-break in the Miramar workingmen's club---a club that does not exist. The case that the member put up in the House tonight was of much the same quality; it does not exist. Members should be asking why the House is debating the sale of the State Insurance Office. It is doing so because of the horrendous debt problem the Government was left by a bankrupt Government in July . The State Insurance Office is being sold to meet the horrendous debt left by the National Government when it vacated the Treasury benches in July . It must be remembered that percent of the tax moneys now taken are being spent to pay the interest bill on that debt. I thank my colleagues on both sides of the House who sat on the select committee for the assistance given there. There were times when the experience of the more senior colleagues from both sides came in very handy. I shall briefly outline my position on the Bill. I was not persuaded during the select committee hearings that the Bill should be set aside pending the court case. Legislation is indeed silent on the whole issue of ownership, but the same could be said for the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, or any other Government department. I was persuaded by evidence given to the select committee that the Tower Corporation and the State Insurance Office are different cases. The State Insurance Office is not a mutual company owned by its policyholders, unlike the Tower Corporation. The select committee was also told, even before the issue went to the court of law, that the court would say that policyholders would not have a claim in law. The deficiencies in the ownership of historic buildings do not lie with the Bill; they lie with historic places legislation, and should be taken up in that quarter. The Bill itself provides for the State Insurance Office to be constituted as a company under the Companies Act and owned by the Crown. The Bill authorises the Minister to subscribe for and to hold shares. It provides that the property, the rights, and the liabilities of the General Manager of the State Insurance Office and of the State Insurance Office shall be vested in that company. As I went through the submissions, read them, studied them, and listened to the petitioners who presented the petitions, it became obvious to me that there were two dominant issues. The most dominant issue was the allegation that policyholders and not the Crown have the strongest claim to ownership. The second was about the future of the State community theatres after Norwich Union acquires the State Insurance Office. I shall deal with the issue of ownership first, because that is the issue raised most seriously in the debate this evening, and, indeed, in the reporting back. I am surprised that the House should be debating the matter. It was the honourable member for Tarawera who wrote the National Party manifesto that stated that the State Insurance Office would be sold. The National Party manifesto specifically promised total privatisation of the State Insurance Office. Are the arguments genuine that we have heard tonight from the member for Tarawera? I shall detail some background material in connection with the court action over the State Insurance Office ownership. On November last year Paulette Small and Selina Smith, beneficiaries, filed papers in the Wellington High Court seeking declaratory judgments against the Attorney-General and the State Insurance Office. They sought declarations that the only persons entitled to the profits of a State Insurance Office were the policyholders. No further action was taken by the plaintiffs until recently. They applied for legal aid in Tauranga, but it was was declined. They appealed that decision. The appeal found in favour of the plaintiffs on May, and a hearing date was set down for June. We all now know the result of that High Court decision, which came out yesterday. The decision confirmed that the State's policyholders had no stake in its ownership, and that the Government could sell the insurance giant to the British-based Norwich Union Life Insurance Society. I suggest to honourable members opposite that they should accept that decision for what it is: a categorical decision that ownership of the office belongs to the Government. The news media, in referring to the hearing date, seized on that point to the extent that the plaintiffs were awarded legal aid to fund the court action and the Government was perceived to be overriding action in the court. However, two points should be taken into account. The first is that the granting of legal aid was nothing more than a red herring. It had always been up to the plaintiffs to process the case, and it was not for the Crown to concern itself with the way in which the plaintiffs funded their action. The granting of legal aid does not stop Government legislation. The opinion of both the Clerk of the House and the Crown Law Office officers who came before the select committee at the request of the member for Tarawera was that Parliament should not be frustrated from legislating by the possibility of court action. If taxation legislation was before the House and someone was taking a case before the court, or a matter in dispute was to go before the court, we would not hold up that legislation but would process it. I support the idea of the House setting up this committee, and I do so for a number of reasons. First, better accountability from State-owned enterprises is needed. We need to challenge the management of those organisations to perform and to be responsible to this House. We need to be sure that the directors are acting in the best interests of the taxpayers. I want to ask the Minister a number of questions. Has the committee been set up as a sop to public outrage about the accountability of Electricorp and the fiasco with the rationing of electricity during the recent crisis? Since that has happened we have been told that the rationing on the part of normal consumers in New Zealand was not necessary, and a lot of people suffered as a result of that. Can the Minister tell me whether the committee is being set up as a result of the shambles in the Communications and Road Safety Committee, in which there is a report on an inquiry into civil aviation, and of which members are still awaiting the outcome? Or has the committee been set up as a result of the recommendation that came from the Commerce and Marketing Committee that there be an inquiry into the cost of finance for small sized and medium sized businesses? Is this committee a way of overcoming problems that the Government faces within its ranks? Or has the committee been set up as a result of the revelations about the expensive taste in entertainment of New Zealand Post Ltd? What degree of responsibility does the Minister accept for the actions of the taxpayers' State-owned enterprises? Does he accept responsibility for the overseas junkets and special privileges enjoyed by New Zealand Post Ltd, such as the hospitality box at Eden Park? Has the Minister ever been to Eden Park? Has he enjoyed the privileges of the hospitality box? Why do we, the taxpayers, need a hospitality box at Eden Park? How many other State-owned enterprises have similar luxurious hospitality boxes? I see that, in answer to a written question to the Minister, Television New Zealand has outlined a number of issues. I am most concerned about what Television New Zealand had to say. Have other State-owned enterprises got hospitality boxes, or is it only Television New Zealand and New Zealand Post that have them? Is it correct that a New Zealand Post executive said that the boxes were to entertain politicians? If they were to entertain politicians, I want to know whether anyone from our side of the House received an invitation to Eden Park.
It is the one that on a statistical basis is supposed to happen every years, but, who knows, it might be just round the corner. The question is, does the Government have sufficient funds?

It is a major debate and one that I am pleased to be taking part in. A colleague is throwing in a few comments about productivity, but this is not a debate about productivity; it is about the future of democracy in New Zealand. I believe also that it is right that constituents should know the views of their elected members of Parliament. I will support this legislation, basically as recommended by the royal commission. I do so because I believe that the people of this country voted for a change to the electoral system and for what has been recommended by the royal commission. However, I do not believe that everyone who voted fully understood the ramifications of what they voted for. Having said that, I say that it is important that the electorate continues to be informed about the aspects of mixed-member proportional representation (MMP) so that when the election is held in November or earlier people will fully understand what is likely to happen. I think we are in for one hell of a joy-ride because many of the people I have spoken to are not really aware of what MMP is. However, the awareness of MMP is much greater now than when the issue was first canvassed. There is a much greater awareness of what it stands for, but not to the extent that I should like. But if MMP is wanted by the people of New Zealand, so be it, and I will support the legislation. The worst thing that New Zealanders could do would be to vote for change because we do not understand it. New Zealanders must become aware. Many of us have seen the change that has occurred during the past decade. That change has been rampant but I do not believe that change, of itself, will become any slower. I think we are in for more change, given the advancement in technology that New Zealand is rapidly becoming aware of. I have heard a number of members mention different electoral systems. Many have spoken about the system in Germany, and others about the systems in Italy and Israel. Why is it that New Zealanders continually go overseas to search for better ways? Is it because we lack the intellectual capacity to be able to decide for ourselves? Are we not mature enough as a nation to decide on our own electoral system? Why do we tend to copy from overseas? Not only have we done it in electoral legislation, but also we have done it in health, in education, and in a number of other areas. I believe it is time we recognised that New Zealand is a mature nation and that we can and should do things for ourselves. The future of New Zealand is in the hands of its elected representatives inasmuch as most of us in Parliament will be re-elected come November. That is, those of us on this side of the House. The future of our country is dependent on the way in which people vote in October, November, or whenever the election is held. It is important that people really understand what they are voting for; I cannot emphasise that enough. It is important that the public is educated. I hope that many people will now take a great deal more interest in the whole issue of MMP. My colleague the member Ohariu intends to move an amendment about candidate selections. I will support that amendment. I believe that the requirement for registered parties to follow democratic procedures in the selection of their candidates is most important. That is not to say that it does not happen now, but we have to recognise that, come a change in the electoral system in November, or October, or whenever it might be, parties will have to look at the way in which candidates are selected under a different electoral system. So I support the amendment of my colleague the member for Ohariu when it comes to democratic procedures and candidate selection. I have also thought at great length about the whole idea of lists. We have heard about the national closed-list system---as has been recommended by the royal commission---and about open lists, regional lists, and open and closed regional lists. I shall support the system recommended by the royal commission---that is, the system of national closed lists. I have thought about that matter a great deal over the past couple of days, and last night I thought long and hard about whether we should have a system of regional closed lists or national closed lists. I shall support the system of national closed lists because I believe that the objectives of MMP will be much better served by that. I shall also support that Parliament should have members. It is important that we have sufficient constituency members of Parliament to serve the needs of constituents. I cannot support the ``Shirtcliffe'' amendment, because I believe that members of Parliament should reflect the views of their electorates in such matters, and I have spoken at length with a number of people in my electorate about the amendment. While I accept that that might not be representative, at least I have taken the opportunity to canvass the views of a number of influential people in my electorate and ask them about the matter. Last September voters were given the opportunity to vote for an electoral system. At that time I supported preferential voting but now I am prepared to support MMP, provided that we do not get too much variation from the views that were recommended by the royal commission. I believe that the royal commission did an exceptionally good job in bringing forward this legislation to the House. It is important to give consideration to all matters of electoral reform so that we are able to come to a considered and balanced viewpoint in this House. Change for the sake of change has never been the answer. I believe that the call today for a changed electoral system is based as much on frustration with New Zealand members of Parliament and Governments as on any real evidence that any other electoral system can serve our country better. Having said that, I say that I recognise the views of the electorate, which wants to see a change. It is obvious from the referendum that voters favoured a change. As I said previously, I do not believe that people favoured a change because they were sufficiently informed to make a judgment on the pros and cons of either system, but because they were fed up with the way that events have gone. They were fed up with change. New Zealanders have been basically a conservative people who have lived in a protected economy for many years and have never had to face the realities of the market-place. As a result of managements, trade unions, and Governments working together to protect the people of New Zealand from a harsh economic environment, we had never had to face change prior to those changes that occurred just before and since then. I believe that people are fed up with the way that things have gone. They voted against the present system because they saw that as a way of hitting back at politicians and Governments. I have met few people who really have a fair understanding of the ramifications of change. The electorate, in general, was very disappointed with politicians. That has been caused mainly by the fact that our economy has gone---and is still going---through a very rough period of change and adjustment. Now people have voted for change because they consider that the mob we have is no good, therefore ``out with them''. An article in last month's Metro canvassed a number of people in the seat of Eden. It was interesting to read why a number of people voted in the way that they did. Basically, they were fed up with all the changes that were going on.

Those issues cause members on this side of the House a great deal of concern. The Bill before the House does not provide for the distribution of shares to consumers, but provides for total control of the company in perpetuity to be vested in trustees. It also provides that the new trustees will be established by the board and the current trustees without reference to the Minister; exempts the company from following standard valuation procedures; and allows the same people to hold office as both trustee and director. It also sets no time-limit for the issue of shares to the public and may effectively exempt Auckland from the light-handed regulatory regime that is essential to the success of reforms. There is a need for competition within the industry so that the huge potential of the industry can flow on to the economy. Energy reforms have a huge potential to contribute significantly to New Zealand's performance over the next years. That will not happen under a protected and non-accountable ownership structure of the kind proposed in the Bill. I shall be waiting with a great deal of interest to see whether the Minister votes for this Bill. Electricity restructuring is important. Electricity plays a very large part in the costs of industry. Electricity prices could actually fall if the Government introduced the Energy Sector Reform Bill, which is still awaited. A conservative estimate of the potential increase in efficiency is at least percent, maybe more. We are told by the electricity distribution reform unit that the potential gains are about percent. Why does the Minister not bring reform? Why not do it properly? I suggest that, more than anything else, the Auckland Electric Power Board is trying to embarrass the Minister into taking action. It wants change, and it has signalled that it wants change. It hopes that the Bill will draw the matter to the Minister's attention, and that he will take action. The Opposition does not believe that the industry should be split into bits and pieces; it should be reconstructed properly.

As international citizens we have occasionally to make tough decisions. None are tougher than those involving the commitment of one's armed forces to a conflict under way on a distant continent, in an arena that to us is confusing, and on issues that we do not entirely understand. When that conflict is complex, when it has a religious, ethnic, and territorial mix of issues, when it has its roots in ages past and its solutions, perhaps, in a distant future, and when it involves exposing our soldiers to dangers, it is right that we pause in this Parliament to debate the rightful role for New Zealand. Others before me have outlined the puzzle that has developed following the breakup of the former Yugoslavia. I need not repeat it. We know of the human rights violations. We know of the entry of the United Nations. We know of the attempts to establish safe areas. We know of the recent taking of hostages, the United Nations peacekeepers. We know of the Serb blockade of Sarajevo and the other three enclaves. This Parliament supported the decision to send New Zealand troops to Bosnia-Herzegovina as peacekeepers under the United Nations mandate in September . It did so to support the United Nations efforts to develop a peace. It did so to save lives. That, I believe, was the right decision. But now, with the taking of the United Nations peacekeepers as hostages, with the blockade of cities like Sarajevo, and with the perpetuation of human rights abuses, the stakes have become higher. The question we face is whether our forces can use more forceful means to uphold international law---for instance, to escort food convoys, or to protect civilian enclaves. If they join the convoy needed to enter Sarajevo, they may need to use arms to protect themselves. Clearly, securing the release of United Nations hostages through diplomacy instead of force is preferred. Opening up access to Sarajevo for humanitarian aid by way of diplomacy is preferred. But, sadly, the Bosnian Serb leadership is showing the world that it is prepared to continue to abuse international law, to abuse human rights, to let thousands starve, to thumb its nose at the diplomats, and to abuse those who try to keep peace. We have to ask ourselves whether we now withdraw, or hold back, or join others to use a little more force to relieve a city, to feed civilians, and to make a peace---a fragile peace---knowing that as we do so we expose New Zealanders to higher levels of risk. I have listened to those debating this issue in terms of what our national interests are. I have heard those who suggest that this is a European conflict for the Europeans to solve. I have heard the argument that New Zealand lives should not be put at risk. All these lines of argument have merit, but none convinced me that we should or can afford to wash our hands of this conflict. For human rights are fundamental rights and know no boundaries, and when I hear of abuses of those rights being committed in the most atrocious way, as already noted by the member for Christchurch North---of starvation being used as a weapon of war, of rape and murder, and of torture and genocide on a grave and a huge scale---I cannot hesitate to join calls for an end to such abuses. When diplomacy has failed and when the peacekeepers are being abused, I must back those who support the use of force, limited to the rescue of those who are being abused and, in this case, starved. We cannot solve the differences between the political and religious factions by way of force. However, we can save lives. My parliamentary colleague the member for Roskill has noted that he and I were in Europe recently. We met a distinguished jurist from Norway who was one of the five experts set up under Resolution of the Security Council in to draw conclusions on the evidence of breaches of international humanitarian law committed in the former Yugoslavia. That commission reported in . As the member for Roskill has said, this jurist left us in no doubt that the abuses carried out in that theatre of war were crimes against humanity of the worst kind. She described to us some of the atrocities committed by some of the Bosnian Serbs. She described them, as has been noted, as possibly being more extreme than those committed by the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia. She left some pictures in my mind that I will never forget---brutal, brutal pictures. It is easy for us to sit here in this place and look the other way. It is easy for us to condemn those who conduct atrocities, while remaining on the sideline in terms of taking action that exposes us to risk. I support wholeheartedly a cautious and diplomatic approach to conflict resolution, but when systematic ethnic cleansing on a grand scale is taking place---genocide, horrendous torture, gang rape, and sexual assaults---when all these violations against humanity are being conducted on the other side of the fence, then it is my opinion we have a right and, in fact, a duty to intercede. On this I differ so much from the leader of the Alliance. I cannot support the arguments of those who say that our responsibilities are diminished because of our distance from the place of persecution. I cannot support the arguments of those who say that our responsibilities are lessened because the issue is too complex for us to understand. And I cannot support the arguments of those who claim we should not be prepared to risk our own lives to save the lives of others---the women, the children, the elderly, and the frightened of Sarajevo. For we are all human beings. We all have a right to life. We all have a right to dignity. And we all have a duty to protect those rights, as international citizens. I salute those in our armed forces who serve our country. I salute them for their service to humanity, for that is the mandate under which we are in Bosnia. They serve this Parliament well, and carry New Zealand's flag well. No parliamentarian would wish to increase their exposure to risk, for no good purpose.

I want to explore just one area, and that is the move taken by the Government recently to allow the Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Corporation to contract directly, as I understand it, with the Crown health enterprises. I think that will be seen as one of the most significant steps in terms of the reform of the accident compensation system that we have seen. We have had a crazy situation up until now whereby there has not been an ability for the corporation to relate the purchase price of an operation to the costs of earnings-related compensation that it has had to pay. I want to give an example to highlight that. We have people who have had an accident and injured a knee, and are waiting on earnings-related compensation for an orthopaedic operation. I had a constituent in Papakura who waited years. I believe she was on earnings-related compensation, which was paying her about $, per year. That amounted to about $, for that -year period, whereas if the corporation had been able to go out and purchase that operation from some provider, I understand the operation would have cost $, to $,. So I want assurance from the Minister that the steps taken recently by the Government will cater for that sort of anomaly and ensure that the corporation can go out and purchase operations like that from some sector. The question I have then with regard to the Crown health enterprises is another issue that it introduces. Along with my colleagues I have listened to the arguments put forward by Opposition members. I suspect that, like me, my colleagues have been unconvinced by those arguments. I shall answer some of the points that have been made and make a couple of points from my experience as a probation officer working with people in the rehabilitation sector. The member for Rotorua suggested that it should be up to the convicted person to apply to have his or her convictions sealed or made inaccessible, but that would place the onus on the offender to make such an application. Without placing any slight on former offenders, in my experience a number of them would not do that because they would be unaware of the matter or they would lack the initiative to take the steps required. Some of them would be scared of re-engaging the system in that particular battle. Most of them would not know that the provision existed; they would remain disadvantaged when applying for a job. Another point in relation to the member's suggestion is that all applications would have to be investigated before a pardon was granted. That investigation could well bring up information that the people consulted did not know about. They might not know that the person involved had a conviction. The member's suggestion is a watered-down way of dealing with the matter and does not achieve the aims. Another point that has been made is that offenders, particularly serious offenders, will get off the hook in the same manner as anyone else. However, the Bill states that people who commit sexual offences or murders involving a sexual element can have their rehabilitative period extended. In such cases the sentencing judge can make a decision starting from the -year base-line and extending it beyond that time. That decision would stand. Serious offenders would not be let off the hook as lightly as others if that was the decision of the court. The next matter involves news media publicity. Members talked about looking back at some of the more dramatic, serious, and important cases. I do not want to mention names, as some members have done tonight. There are times when news media publicity can be given to cases. For example, the rehabilitated person may consent to publication or broadcast, or publication or broadcast may occur at least year after the rehabilitated person's death. There is no blanket ban. Disclosure by officials is allowed in several circumstances when the information is necessary, particularly in relation to sentencing, proving a conviction, and treatment of a person with a mental illness. A range of provisions applies, and when the information is particularly important it will be able to be accessed. The most important point I wanted to make comes from my experience of working with people in the rehabilitation area during my years as a probation officer. The Bill stops young people from becoming locked into a path of crime simply because a mistake they made earlier in their lives continues to be brought up. People will not have anything held against them from the Children and Young Persons Court or the Youth Court, but if they have been convicted in the district court or High Court the -year period will apply. The average person who has received a conviction in the district court or the High Court often has no incentive to go straight. Getting a job is probably the key factor in the rehabilitation of most people. We all know that New Zealand has a long-term unemployment problem that was inherited from the National Government. People with a record are at the bottom of the heap when it comes to getting a job. If a dozen people apply for a job, and one of them has a conviction, that person would be at the bottom of the heap. That is a key factor in the rehabilitation of such persons.

The member for Wairarapa and other Opposition members described the Bill as being conceptually wrong, but they supported it in principle. I am not surprised to hear that kind of response from Opposition members. It is a classic bob-each-way approach for Opposition members to say that the Bill is conceptually wrong but that they support it in principle. The principle is important, but doing something about it, as the Bill seeks to do, is equally important. Some Opposition members indicated that the Government wants a ban on all forms of music on radio. That is absolute garbage. One Opposition member talked about an percent New Zealand music quota to be played on radio. That is the exact opposite of what the Bill is about. The Bill is concerned with moving gradually during a period of time to an easily attainable and reasonable figure of percent. That figure has massive support throughout the country, as was evidenced in the debate on the Bill during the past few months. I welcome the reporting back of the Bill to the House. It was a good Bill when it was introduced, and it is an even better Bill in the form in which it has been reported back from the select committee. The Bill is concerned with New Zealand's cultural identity in all its diversity, and with the protection and enhancement of that cultural identity. We are primarily talking about the broadcasting media, because that is where music obviously features. In this media age the media, whether public or private, has a responsibility to nurture the culture of the country by virtue of its occupation of the airwaves, and of its right to use the airwaves. The private and public sectors have a responsibility to nurture our culture on the airwaves. One of the many interesting facts that emerged from the select committee during its deliberations on the Bill was that many other countries---some of them smaller than our country in terms of population, and poorer---have quotas and play much more local music. As a result, they have much more active and successful music industries in their countries. Our closest example is Australia, which has a percent quota. Canada has a percent quota and is aiming for percent. Countries such as Jamaica, Israel, Ireland, Tanzania, Tahiti, and Sweden are examples of countries that have successfully applied a similar quota. Canada's quota is considerably higher in proportion than that proposed for New Zealand. The Bill is not just concerned with New Zealand culture but also with employment. The music industry is an employment-rich industry, as the Australian experience has shown. It is sad that many of the people employed in the music industry in Australia are New Zealanders. Over the years those employees have taken off to Australia and other places because of the conservative approach of our broadcasters, and they have been successful, showing that New Zealand had that talent here but opportunities had not been available for those people to develop that talent. I recognise that the Bill is unlikely to pass through all its stages before the election. I say to the House and to the thousands of supporters of the Bill that it is the Government's policy to give this private member's Bill further consideration during the next parliamentary term. Opposition members are urged to front up in the debate to state what support they will give to the Bill in the unlikely event that the National Party becomes the Government. It is not enough for Opposition members to stand up and have a bob each way and say that the Bill is not bad in principle but that it is conceptually wrong. What do they really mean? The supporters of the Bill want to know whether the National Party will support the Bill in the unlikely event that it will become the Government. The answer to that is obvious.

That is the Government's attainable goal. It has done the hard work; it has done the economic restructuring that was necessary because of the mess left by the previous Government. It has bitten the bullets and laid the foundations to make realistic the goal of full employment by . The position we had to deal with in restructuring the economy has a long history. I should like to go through the history briefly from the year when I was born, because in that year New Zealand had about the third-highest standard of living in the world. Between and ---in which year the present Government first came to office---that standard of living had dropped from about third to about thirty-third. High unemployment had also developed. When the National Government came to office in about people were unemployed. When that Government left office in the mess we had to inherit involved , people unemployed and another , on project employment programme schemes. I shall come back to those schemes later. They did nothing, and the Opposition wants to reintroduce them. The number of unemployed people we inherited in was , plus , on schemes, and that is a grand total of , people. That is what the National Government achieved between and . On top of that there was high inflation. During some years inflation was between percent and percent. A massive overseas debt was being developed. That was something that the member for Selwyn tried to deal with in her speech, completely ignoring the huge amounts of overseas debt that were hidden in the ``think big'' projects and the producer board debts. Those problems were so exacerbated by the shape that the economy was in when we came to office in that we had to devalue. That added to the overseas debt. That is the position the Government had to turn around. We have done it. The fundamentals are in place, and that is why we can realistically look forward to full employment. Several aspects are involved in the full-employment goal, and a major aspect is that of education, not just in the traditional sense, but also very much in relation to training. My electorate of Manawatu offers a fine example of the education and training resources available. The way in which those resources have been improved and added to by the Government over the past few years means that we are in a position to provide the education and training that people will need for the jobs available now and for the jobs that will be available in the future. My electorate has a very fine polytechnic. The polytechnic side of education has been the poor relation of education for years under former Governments. The present Government recognises that polytechnics are places where real work-place skills can be developed for today and for the future. The Government has put vast amounts of extra funding into polytechnics, and there are now many more polytechnic students, not just in the Manawatu but throughout the country. Those students will have jobs in the future---jobs that will add to the economy. The Palmerston North College of Education is turning out teachers. The Government has reduced class sizes and has put in extra teachers. The college was to be closed down by the National Government, and it had fairly nearly run down to that point when the present Government came to office, rescued it, and turned it around. It is now producing fine teachers for the various sectors of education such as primary and secondary. The college is contributing to education of the kind that produces school-leavers who can actually face the challenges of the s and beyond. Another fine institution is Massey University. Once again there have been massive increases in student numbers there, and the spending to go with them. One accepts that, because of the rapid increase in student numbers, per capita spending simply has not been able to keep pace. However, a massive amount of extra money has been put in, and the results are there, in a whole range of study sectors that speak for themselves. Equally important are pre-schools, and primary and secondary schools into which, once again, we have put massive amounts of extra money. If the foundation for education is not built at the pre-school, primary, and secondary levels not much can be done at the tertiary level. Another of the schemes the Government has introduced---and which it has added to significantly, as announced recently---is the Link programme. Secondary school students can spend part of the school week at polytechnics doing courses for which they are credited both at school and at polytechnic. As announced in the past few weeks, there has been a massive increase in apprenticeship training, not just in my electorate but also across the country, and that will help with the goal of full employment. That relates back to polytechnics. I know that the polytechnic in the Manawatu will play its part in that project. In the very short term the Government aims to increase apprenticeship numbers by at least . That is another sector that has been neglected over the years, and numbers have dropped. It plays a key part in training for employment. I completed an apprenticeship in refrigeration and air-conditioning many years ago before I moved on to other things. I did that in Australia where employers recognised the need to support apprenticeship training, the need to give people time off to study, and the need to look after their apprentices, because that was the way to develop their industries and the economy as a whole. New Zealand employers, and perhaps the system as a whole, have been a little slow to recognise that need in the past, but with the Government's extra injection of support there will be a rapid and necessary growth in apprenticeship numbers. I am talking about dealing with the problem of employment, giving it a goal, and giving the solution of full employment in by attending to the need for technology and retraining of people. Jobs change, and the needs for people's skills change, so we are giving training and retraining in order to deal with those problems. The Government is also dealing with the issue of productivity. People have talked about that issue here today. We are giving consideration to the international marketing of our products. The Dairy Research Institute in my electorate is one shining example of the way international needs for our goods have been dealt with, and as a result the dairy industry is thriving, both at the primary level on the farm and in processing. New Zealand is processing and producing goods that the world wants, and that we can sell. New Zealand's clean, green environment adds to the value and attractiveness of those goods on the world market. Hence we sell goods, we get back overseas funds, and we sustain the lifestyle that New Zealanders want. The whole focus of our development is sustainable development. It is not just development for development's sake; it is development based on a sustainable basis, because the environment is an essential part of the whole complex picture. If we want the New Zealand economy to continue to develop as it is developing now---and it will---if we want full employment---and we do---we have to have education, training, research and development, and a clean, green environment. All those things are happening under the Government. They are certainly happening in my electorate, and the goal of full employment by is completely realistic. I applaud it.

I am pleased to be speaking in the second reading debate on the Transport Amendment Bill (No. ), because it is a debate about law and order and the concept of the decent society. The Government believes that the State should exercise its powers responsibly to protect innocent citizens. The Opposition has talked about a gentleman's home being his castle. That is sexist for a start, and it is litist. The kind of people the Government represents do not normally live in castles. The citizens of New Zealand have nothing to fear from the forces of the law as long as they observe the law. Drinking drivers are criminals. In my view, they are potential murderers. The Opposition's decent society is one in which potential murderers would be assisted to evade their just deserts under the law of the land. I said that decent citizens have nothing to fear under the law in New Zealand; even offenders have nothing to fear, inasmuch as they will be treated fairly and justly. That will be assured by the excellent training and leadership in the Ministry of Transport, and by the very sound safeguards that have been added to the Bill. The offender---the potential murderer---will have failed to stop when pursued by a traffic officer's car with flashing lights and sirens. He---and usually it is male---would have been pursued by a uniformed officer who had received special training. The officer would have good cause to suspect that the driver, the potential murderer, was affected by alcohol; it would not just be a case of a faulty tail-light, or something of that nature. The pursuit would be fresh and hot. Other guidelines will be issued by the Ministry of Transport and will be tabled by the Minister in the House. There will probably be a complaints authority along the lines of the Police Complaints Authority in case any citizen feels that his or her rights have been trampled on. The officer who conducts the pursuit will have to report to the Secretary for Transport or the Commissioner of Police about the exercise of the powers. And the whole procedure will be reviewed early next year. As a result, the roads of New Zealand will be safer for all of the children, women and men of New Zealand over the Christmas period. That is the kind of decent society I believe in. When I am on the road, or my wife, children, relatives, friends, or neighbours are on the road, it is a fundamental human right to be safe; not to be murdered or permanently maimed by drunken hoons---the kind of hoon that the Opposition seems to be trying in this debate to defend---the cowardly hoon, the potential murderer, who thumbs his nose at the law and thinks he can evade the consequences of his actions by running away and hiding on his property or on the property of anyone else. That is the kind of person the National Party wants to protect in its so-called decent society. The legislation is to be enacted urgently to protect innocent New Zealanders from drunken hoons on the road this Christmas. It is a good law; it is a necessary law; it is a thorough law; and it is a balanced law. It protects the civil rights of law-abiding citizens, and ensures due process for those who break the law. I am fascinated to watch the Opposition oppose this law. Its stance sounds the death knell for its simplistic slogan of the decent society. With this legislation the Government will protect innocent New Zealanders from being killed or maimed by drunken hoons on the roads this Christmas and henceforth. I am proud to support the Bill.

As Minister of Corrections, Minister for Courts, Minister for Disarmament and Arms Control, and Associate Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade, I am extremely proud to support this bill today, and to find that a majority of parliamentarians support it coming into law. One year ago today I was hiding in a suburb of Dili while the militia---set up, armed, trained, and financed by the Indonesian Government---ran rampant throughout Dili, and continued to kill people in East Timor. I was not one of the brave ones who stayed in the United Nations compound; I was waiting for an aeroplane, to get out of there as quickly as possible. I had a place of refuge; the people of East Timor did not. This bill is not for the powerful countries of the world. It is not a matter where we should have great concern for privileged countries, including New Zealand, that have a strong rule of law. I have every confidence that if persons in New Zealand commit a war crime or are alleged to have committed a war crime, they will be dealt with under our judicial system with all its safeguards. The people of East Timor did not have that guarantee. Recently we had the leader of the people of East Timor here---Xanana Gusmao. He was feted by Parliament and received warmly by the people of New Zealand. We gave him a high honour. This bill is for the protection of people throughout the world like those he led. It is in that spirit that I say we should celebrate the passing of this bill. Ceding sovereignty has a pejorative sense to it, of course, if one passes out of one's control the ability to protect one's own interests. But what is the danger of joining with everybody throughout the world who supports the upholding of international law and the right of human beings to live without oppression? Some people want to wait until Judgment Day when tyrants and oppressors will meet their Maker, but I say that the best thing to do for people on Earth is to give them the weapons to be able to fight their oppressors. One of the key weapons is to have an international system that can act as a recourse for justice. In New Zealand we have not actually had a proud record of standing up for the poorest and the humblest people of this world when they are faced with oppression. It was not that long ago that President Suharto had up to a million of his own people killed, and we in this country said nothing. But, worse, the leaders of this country from onwards actually supported President Suharto and excused his war crimes. He now stands before his own people, and, hopefully, through the judicial process of the Indonesian people, he will be brought before the justice system of that country. Many of the leading generals of Indonesia will also suffer that same fate, and very soon, I hope. But we must address the world's problems as one of the countries that knows that issues in terms of the United Nations, issues in terms of universal human rights, have to be solved collectively. I would find the arguments of ACT persuasive if they had a shred of genuineness about them, and a shred of fact. But I know that their arguments are aimed at a very small percentage of people in this country who believe that by our involving ourselves with international organisations we are betraying New Zealand. What we are actually doing is affirming to the rest of the world that New Zealand is one of the countries that seeks to be treated without fear or favour. If we have acted wrongly---which I believe we will not do---we are prepared to have an international court say: ``You must be brought up on this matter, under international law and before a world tribunal.'' So many countries have signed this ratification that one would have to start a very strict process to go through them and say which ones measure up to the high standards of New Zealand. But if one looks, even cursorily, at the countries of the European Union, which have similar judicial processes to New Zealand, one sees that they have decided they will support the International Criminal Court. I believe that, in terms of a point of reference, that should assure the people of New Zealand who may have heard some of those spurious arguments. I do not believe it is necessary to speak at length on this bill and do not intend to do so, but for the public record I wish to say this. The process by which this matter has been before the countries of the world has been lengthy and arduous. It has not been done in haste. In fact, many compromises have been made to make sure that the ratification goes through. Those compromises have, in fact, weakened the force of the international court, not strengthened it. It relies upon the judicial processes of each country being carried out, in terms of human rights violations, but if those processes are not carried out, then countries like New Zealand will be there, through the International Criminal Court, to make sure that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and all the conventions upholding human rights that have flowed from that declaration, are upheld. I would like to pay tribute to the people in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade who have provided information to Parliament that has allowed us to make an informed judgment---particularly Felicity Wong, but also our own Professor Roger Clark, who is actually a legal adviser for Samoa in this key discussion, but played a very big role in making sure we have a document from which we can move on. The last issue I wish to put before the House is the signing by the Prime Minister of this document in New York. Surely it is a very important step that the Prime Minister of New Zealand, on behalf of all of Parliament and on behalf of all the country, ratifies such an important international document in front of the world, so that there is extra affirmation that New Zealand is one of the countries that will uphold international law. Lastly, to put it into the record, I will read a short statement from the New Zealand Herald of Saturday, May, which I think shows vividly why we need an international court that will take to trial those who violate international law. The article goes like this: ``In one corner might be a score or more of the Chilean secret policemen who did such a good job of silencing General Augusto Pinochet's critics, usually for ever. In another knot, former Argentine dictator, General Leopoldo Galtieri, and his aides, who disposed of troublemakers by pitching them from helicopters far out over the Atlantic. Panama's dope-dealing strongman, Manuel Noriega, would be there, perhaps trading sympathy with Guatemala's General Rios Montt.'' It is for that reason, because of those people and for the protection of the wretched of the world, that we need an international criminal court.''

Billboards are ACT's sole contribution to safety in New Zealand. I do not mind the billboards. What I do mind is the double message that they give. It opposes new prisons, despite the fact that it called for new prisons. In speaking on the financial review I would like to address my remarks to the Minister of Finance. I also wish to draw to the attention of members of the House a potentially crippling problem that is facing a sector that is well known as the backbone of New Zealand's economy. It is particularly important today, as the Reserve Bank has just brought out its March forecast. No one can argue that the farming industry has a tradition of producing and exporting and has formed the base of New Zealand's growth and prominence in international markets. Yet this very sector of our economy is currently experiencing hardship due to the mechanisms of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act, which are combined with constraints apparent in the domestic economy. Not only do farmers provide for the country's table, but they increasingly supply other farmers and exporters who provide for New Zealanders. New Zealanders have those farmers to thank for cheaper overseas holidays and cheaper imported products. The rising Kiwi dollar may be a sign of economic success, but one has to question at what expense that is to the rural and farming sectors. Those in the provinces do not applaud with the rest of the country when the trade-weighted index rises---as it has by percent since . For farmers and exporters, even a small rise in the trade-weighted index can mean the disappearance of hundreds of millions of dollars of basic income. That simple fact reverberates in the rural sector in those towns and regions that were founded on farming, and amongst those who rely on revenue from that farming for their very survival. Last week the Otago Daily Times released the alarming news that up to percent of Otago and Southland sheep and beef farmers are expected to make a financial loss in this current financial year. One can only wonder what effect those losses will have on satellite towns that really do rely on income from those farmers in order to exist. Is the Minister of Finance aware of the recent report on the economic position of New Zealand's meat and wool industries that shows that farm products and profits this year will drop to almost half their average since ? In the face of this hardship many cattle farmers and sheep farmers are attempting to diversify, or, frankly, to get out of farming altogether. In - a great number of sheep farms and beef farms were sold to forestry. This amounted to , hectares of farming land. This trend has been projected to continue, with the real expectation that forestry will gain about , hectares of cattle farms and sheep farms every year right up to the year . In real terms this translated in - to about million fewer sheep and approximately , fewer cattle potentially available for export. It is true that some farmers have diversified into dairy-farming, but as an industry it, too, is facing financially difficult times. The New Zealand dairy industry has missed out on about $ billion in earnings in the last years, which equates to about $, per dairy-farmer. The Dairy Board confirms that these losses are in direct relationship to the appreciating New Zealand dollar, and that the burden of keeping New Zealand's inflation low is falling on exporters who cannot sustain such rapid and massive erosion of their income. The Dairy Board has warned, and I agree, that this agricultural exporting sector will not be able to hold up indefinitely if profitability is not sustained. In February this year financial experts pointed out that to have producer price index figures that were lower than projected was evidence of the Reserve Bank high exchange rate policy hurting the agricultural industry. Could the Minister of Finance explain this? The current situation highlights the need to review mechanisms of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act, and to take account of the changes in the economic landscape since the Act's inception years ago. Although the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act is a valuable instrument and has been designed to stabilise wages and prices, and to keep inflation down, the current state of farming raises the question of what exactly the cost to the general economic well-being of this country is of having the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act functioning within its present constraints. The New Zealand Conservative Party believes that the point has now been reached where effective management of the economy must take into account all sectors of the economy, otherwise there will be a risk that the benefits of prosperity for some will become an albatross around the neck for others. Could the Minister of Finance advise on what steps have been, and are being, taken to resolve the negative effect for farmers, of low international prices and high exchange rates that have been exacerbated by high interest rates and an overheated property market---particularly in Auckland, but not just in Auckland---New Zealand - wide? The growth of the Auckland property market has been attributed to the influx of overseas immigrants purchasing properties in areas such as my electorate of Howick, but in fact this is incorrect. The availability of favourable interest rates to speculative builders, and the high frequency of property turnover---a New Zealand phenomenon of buying and selling houses that is a tradition with New Zealanders already living in New Zealand---has contributed to this growth far more than has the nominal number of new immigrants who purchase homes in the Auckland area. Do the Minister of Finance and Treasury realise that the effect of tightening money supply to keep inflation under the desired percent has meant that many farmers are also struggling to meet mortgage repayments? This has caused farm closures and an exodus by rural people into the cities, in particular into Auckland. This has further added to the demand in the property market and at the same time has denuded rural towns of their population. It does not take the brains of Einstein to show that where there is a downturn in the rural economy, small towns cannot provide jobs for young families and school-leavers in the rural sector, and such people will automatically gravitate to the major centres such as Auckland. That simply compounds the problem somewhat. The New Zealand Conservative Party is aware that many of the problems in the rural sector are exacerbated by the huge growth in Auckland, which is in effect creating two economies---one in Auckland and one for the rest of the country. It is also not practicable to consider ring-fencing Auckland as a separate economy. We believe that much has to be done to stimulate growth in the rural sectors and in small towns in New Zealand. There must be incentives to immigration to encourage immigrants---doctors, dentists, and other professionals---to spend time in rural New Zealand and our small towns. Would the Minister of Finance agree that there must also be a mechanism covering a range of ways---including marketing of small cities of New Zealand---in which to encourage repopulation of those areas? I believe that some possibilities could be explored, such as the opportunity to set up free-trade areas in port cities of New Zealand other than Auckland, which might encourage off-shore and domestic manufacturers in industry to set up and produce a product under favourable conditions, for export and domestic use. Very obviously, this would enable the local economy to prosper and at the same time would provide more employment in those towns, reversing the population drift to Auckland. There also needs to be a concentrated effort by local governments and regional councils to promote each province to business immigrants and interests. In other words, we need a sales job to be done by the various towns and cities in New Zealand to attract prospective residents, employees, and wealth into those areas. Further incentives could be created by giving new immigrants a points programme that would encourage them to take their skills and professions and settle for a period of up to years in areas of New Zealand other than Auckland. To enable our immigration policy to keep up with the development of New Zealand and the growth required in rural provincial areas, excluding Auckland, there needs to be an assessment of what effects immigration is having on Auckland and the rest of the country. We in the New Zealand Conservative Party believe there is a need for the rationalisation of New Zealand's meat industry to modernise methods of supply and delivery to overseas markets---perhaps restructuring along the lines of the New Zealand Dairy Board. At the same time there is a need to move away from our traditional frozen-meat markets and exports to a pre-prepared supermarket-cut chilled-meat delivery into markets around the world. This will require new technology, new marketing approaches, and, I believe, a single-seller mechanism if the meat industry is to have substantial growth into the future in New Zealand. I would like the Minister to comment in that regard.

I would like to thank the Minister for his kind words, and also Mr Barker for his comments a few minutes ago. It has still ended up being over an inch thick, or centimetres thick in modern terms. This Bill is a major Bill and an important Bill. The legislation has not changed much since , even with the minor modifications that took place in . I also thank the Minister for being available to the committee when we needed him. We took the unusual step of having the Minister available on a fairly regular basis, and that eliminated a lot of problems. It gave an opportunity for both Opposition members and Government members to ask the Minister exactly what he wanted and why he wanted it, so that we did not end up with a difference between what the ministry required, what the Minister was thinking, and what the members who had to deal with the Bill actually had to decide. It solved a lot of problems. It meant we were able to be very thorough and to spend a lot of time on this Bill, but to get it right first time. I would also like to pay tribute to the long-suffering customs officials, who went through a form of water torture in going through this long-drawn-out Bill and the submissions. Their humour and support during that time were very much appreciated by the committee, and we have developed good friendships. There was some humour and enjoyment during that period of time. I also note that Ministry of Commerce officials attended the committee from time to time, and saw its reasoning on matters that needed to be tidied up, and I thank them for their efforts in that regard. I would also like to pay tribute to Clare Sullivan, the hard-working clerk of the committee; to her assistant in the early stages of the committee, Ria Tomoana; and to her new assistant, Shelley Leeder. They were very helpful and valuable to the committee. In particular, I pay a major tribute to the parliamentary counsel, Jacqueline Derby. It is without question that the Bill would not be here today without her help. I have taken the unusual step of talking to the senior officials in her department to express the delight of the committee with her work, her efficiency, and her performance in getting this Bill through on time and so effectively. I express a big ``Thank you'' on behalf of the committee to Jacqueline in that regard. I think, finally, it is important to acknowledge that Opposition members have played a major part. Their support in getting through some of the more complex parts of the Bill, and the ability to talk on an even basis, without getting into political rhetoric, about the matters that had to be discussed in terms of finding a resolution for the excise tax, have been very helpful. I pay tribute to the Senior Opposition Whip, Mr Jonathan Hunt, and thank him. The Bill is a large and complex Bill and it involved hours of deliberation. There was a lot of work--months, in fact--but there is a degree of satisfaction in seeing something completed that has been well done and well prepared, and will stand the test of time. It will be something that we can be proud of in the future, for having brought transparency to the customs structure. That will enable members of the public to have confidence, in that they will be able to see what the structure is designed to do and where it stands on issues, without their feeling as perhaps they have done in the past that there was a huge machine--as the customs structure is seen sometimes--behind a bureaucratic battering ram. This is important from the point of view of the public, and to make sure this legislation is workable. One of the interesting things that the committee had to deal with was the excise indexation question. Clause deals with that, and the committee particularly felt the need to bring this into the modern environment. For many years the excise taxes on beer, spirits, wine have been dealt with all in one lump. It is fair to say that the wine industry and beer industry have been big overseas earners for New Zealand, big exporters, and they need our support. In the not too distant future they will be competing against some fairly hefty opposition--for instance, from South America and South Africa. We must make sure that those industries survive--particularly the wine industry. That industry has the potential to grow and develop. It needs to have enthusiasm to do that, and there needs to be stabilisation to encourage growth and development. To do that the committee decided to split up the indexation and to treat each issue separately--beer, wine, spirits, tobacco, and so on. It decided to take out the provision for a -monthly review of the indexation, and to make it annual but to make it permissive. That means in effect that the Government of the day will be able to decide whether it wishes to remove indexation, which it cannot opt out of at the moment; now it will actually be able to remove it for a separate industry, for tobacco or whatever. We dealt with this particularly in terms of beer and wine, because we believe that the export growth in those areas is important. There was less interest in dealing with spirits and tobacco--in fact, none at all for tobacco, and we have set a different indexation date for it. A couple of other things are important. First, with the willing support of the Minister of Finance we have also changed the payment date for excise from the th of the month to the last working-day of the month. It is a fairly minor issue, one might say, but a very major issue in terms of the industry--one that amounts to millions of dollars. For instance, a company that is struggling to pay excise tax in the middle of the month, and has an overdraft, in the past effectively was paying excise on its overdraft. That was totally unacceptable to the committee and totally unacceptable to our modern way of life in New Zealand. I thank the Minister of Finance for dealing with that issue. By allowing the permissiveness, I hope that in the long term--hopefully, not too long a term--we will see a reduction in excise and eventually its removal, but that is a different issue. One of the other things that we have changed is the ability for the wine industry and the beer industry to be able to take their product off site. Under the present legislation, if a company manufacturing a product wishes to move one of its products down the road into storage, the minute it leaves the premises it is excisable--which is a little ridiculous if it is to be stored for quite a few months. We have allowed the product to go to a controlled export warehouse off site without its incurring the penalty of excise. That is a big step in the right direction. Brew-on premises occupied quite a lot of the time of the committee, but committee members had the benefit of an expert in our midst. We had the benefits of Mr Rick Barker, who was able to go out and actually view and taste the various products. I can advise this House that he suffered largely, and actually had to test, as I understand, a chilli beer that he found character forming, to say the least. He was able to report back with a much higher level of accuracy than we would normally have expected--in fact, one could call it ``hot'' accuracy. He recommended that the Bill provide a limit of only litres for home brew provided on brew-on premises; that that would be satisfactory and there would not be a problem. We do thank him for that hard work and those specialist skills, and the suffering that took place accordingly. An area that I also want to touch on briefly is the title of Comptroller of Customs. In the past we have had collectors of customs all over New Zealand. Under the existing law some of those collectors could set a quite different requirement or charge in different ports, and could not be overruled by the existing comptroller. Some changes have taken place to that. The Bill recommended that the name of that position be changed to chief executive, but because of a historic situation the select committee believes that it should also be known as Comptroller of Customs. I commend this Bill. I thank again all the people who have taken part in its overview. I am sure that the public will see large benefits--certainly the industry will--from this Bill.
