The member would obviously know that by ``we'' we are talking about the collective Parliament. We were given this great diatribe about the fact that New Zealand First would make sure that everybody involved in it had a mandate. Now we have a change of verse---unbelievable. I want to talk about something quite different today---about an education problem with a difference. In particular I draw the attention of members to an immigrant issue that is coming up constantly. An Iraqi immigrant in my electorate is going through what I think is a gross amount of gobbledygook. A lot of people have the impression that professionals have come to New Zealand who do not meet our qualifications criteria, and that therefore they cannot work here. In fact that is not true. The reality is that people who come to this country are required to have their qualifications approved by the Qualifications Authority before they can come to New Zealand. The delays are mostly caused by the registration requirements of their own professional bodies---delays that these, for want of a better word, ``closed unions'' create. I draw members' attention to an interesting exercise. An Iraqi living in my electorate is a dentist. Not only is he a dentist but he is a professor of dentistry. He has to go through a registration process that is totally ridiculous. The requirements to be registered as a New Zealand dentist are contained in a booklet. People applying for registration have to go through a whole process, including reading required and recommended texts. One of the people whose work is required to be read is a Professor G L Howe, who by all accounts is an authority on the extraction of teeth who has worked at a British hospital. My constituent is somewhat bemused by this. He has a letter from that particular professor, who is now working for the Jordanian hospital authorities, requesting that the professor living in my electorate go and work in a Jordanian hospital as a specialist, yet he is supposed suddenly to read this required text! A further form sets out material suitable for professional dentists to read. Ironically, when I look down on page I find that he is required to read literature he wrote. I find that rather remarkable. In fact he is being asked to study his own work as a means to his gaining registration in New Zealand. It is ironic that this particular professor has an advanced diploma in special dentistry from the Baghdad college of dentistry. He has also been a highly qualified professor at the University of Alabama, in Birmingham in the United States, and he has a Master of Science in Dentistry from that university. He has licenses from Liechtenstein and many other places. It is very obvious that this gentleman would be an expert, in any sense of the imagination, in New Zealand, yet he is going through a process that is demeaning and ridiculous, and delayed throughout a period of over year. I think our professional standards are a little bit awry in some respects. This is but one example, and I think we should be looking at expediting the applications of some of the people who have to get registration when they come to our country, to have it done as reasonably and sensibly as possible. The qualifications that this man has are unquestionable---I have talked to some of the people involved---yet he has to go through the whole process as if he were from somewhere in the middle of Timbuctoo. I find that offensive. It is ridiculous, and it is time that we as members of Parliament did something about sorting out what I consider to be a total farce.

It is interesting that there is such anxiousness by various members of the House to speak on this legislation, which can hardly be called the most riveting legislation to come before the House this year. Indeed, the Internal Affairs and Local Government Committee has a wide variety of legislation to consider, and this Bill would be one of the more unobtrusive or less contentious issues that it has had to face. The community of Hastings has addressed several issues in its community, and one issue has been to create and upgrade a cultural facility in its municipal centre. This particular Municipal Theatre is jointly owned by the Hastings District Council and the Municipal Theatre Trust. I think that as a House we should applaud the endeavours to upgrade a recreational facility, a facility that will give an opportunity for more cultural activities in the town. Yet the good town of Hastings has said it would like the opportunity to provide alcohol for sale at this venue. In considering doing that at this particular venue, council members have looked at the Act and have seen the restrictions that it places upon them. The district council looked at other venues that it owns within its confines. It found other such venues, and has said that maybe in the future it will require or deem it necessary to have a sale of liquor provision for those particular venues. Whilst the Bill does seek permission for the sale of liquor by the council holding on-licences and special licences for different venues, it is my expectation that the Hastings District Council will not seek the opportunity to enter the liquor market at all of these venues. In fact, if one looks at some of these venues, one would have to say that it is indeed not likely that the provisions of this Bill will be called upon very often. We have such buildings as the Hastings Holiday Park, Windsor Avenue, Hastings; the Flaxmere Branch Library, Swansea Road, Hastings; Fantasyland, Grove Road, Hastings; and several others. But the key to this legislation is really the Municipal Theatre. It is a simply a matter of, instead of the council having to rush before this House on each occasion, tidying up the legislation on this particular occasion. The sale of liquor is controlled by the Sale of Liquor Act. Part I, section (f), and Part IV, section (f), state that only local authorities may hold on-licences, and that special licences are those expressly authorised by any other enactment. That is what we are asking for. This special enactment will allow the Hastings District Council to fulfil those particular duties. The Bill raises the issue that the legislation is out of date, and an empowering Bill has been sought in two other cases by local bodies in New Zealand---Dunedin being one, and the other just escapes my mind at this time. We cannot delay this case by saying that a review of the legislation is coming to hand, because that will penalise Hastings. I believe that this House should deal with the issue of upgrading the legislation but in the meantime we have this particular problem in Hastings. Only two submissions were received with regard to this Bill---one from the Hastings District Council itself, which was seeking the approval of this House, and one from the Department of Internal Affairs, which said it had no objections whatsoever to the intent of the Bill. This Bill gives maximum flexibility for the Hastings District Council to serve its community. As a House we should listen to the community and take something of a progressive stand on this issue. I support the Bill.

That is a very Draconian approach, but certainly it embodies something of the feeling that one side has. I am delighted to be able to respond in the House at the report-back stage of the Bill. We have had a large year on our committee, in terms of hours sat. I would be surprised if any other select committee has sat for percent of the time that our committee sat. This Bill, containing -odd clauses, which was tabled in June and reported back to the House within a -month deadline, is somewhat illustrative of the work output of our particular committee. So I want to place on record at this point my thanks to every member of the select committee and particularly to the deputy chairman, who filled the role of chairing the committee for some time in the early stages of this Bill. I also want to place on record my thanks to the clerks of the committee, Bob Bunch and Amy Chilton, who have had a rather tedious year dealing with the select committee business. It has been a big undertaking for them, and the quality of their work can be judged particularly as is evidenced in the commentary to this particular Bill. I also record my thanks to the officials, who have put in considerable effort to assist the committee in its deliberations. I know that on one occasion they worked through the night, went home, showered about a.m., and appeared at the select committee again. That kind of devotion to duty is to be commended and is certainly appreciated. The genesis of this Bill goes back to about when interested parties were called together to seek a way forward as to the best shape that the Meat Producers Board, the Wool Board, and the Pork Industry Board should be configured to deal with a changing market scene. Consideration was given to their powers and their structure, and legislation took some time to develop from those original meetings. There was a large degree of consensus between those particular boards and bodies in the early stages. I think it is fair to say that the whole debate about just what shape a producer board should take is a moving destination. There are seven different producer boards in New Zealand; this Bill relates only to three of them, but every single one of them is uniquely different. At the moment, every single one of them is under some kind of consideration as to what shape it should take. In this report back we have moved two or three steps beyond the original consensus that was agreed with those parties that began their work in . Some of the areas in which there was considerable agreement---and those are the matters that we have locked in---include removal of the powers of intervention in the market. It is now seen that the boards do not have a role in the commercial area, which they did have in terms of price stabilisation and price support. That has gone. The whole thrust of this legislation, if we can have a theme, has been to increase accountability and to focus more on the consumer, and that required an industry-shaped board. That is really the thrust of what has driven this legislation. We have to say that our committee has worked right through the year on all bits of legislation and has achieved consensus. It is interesting that on this particular Bill, the last one that we did for the year, the attitude of our committee was tested to divide on an issue that the previous speaker has mentioned, No doubt we will get into that debate in the Committee stage. I think in a way it says that there is no perfect solution to finding the best kind of representation. Value judgments can be made on the best approach. From our point of view, the Government has said that the most critical thing is accountability and a more inclusive way of dealing with the line of accountability. We have made some suggestions and accordingly, by a majority of the committee, have moved to suggest a weighted voting structured system. Before I get on to that, can I just say that there are some other areas out there in front of us that we never actually dealt with, and in a way that has ended. I think those areas are developing. We are concerned about the continuity of commodity trading in New Zealand. If there is a future for the New Zealand farmer, it is to develop the product---to target market niche products into a range of markets. Accordingly, I would have to say as an individual that if we really had some fortitude and wanted to shift wool, which is at an abysmal price at the moment, then maybe we as a committee should have recommended to the House that we abolish the auction system. It is a continuity in commodity trading. That is a big bite and a big step to a destination, which we were not prepared to make. But having said that, we also recognise that some initiatives are taking place out there. We heard submissions from Saxon Merino, Merino New Zealand, and from a range of other people who have said that we need to do some things that are outside the scope of the board; we need the flexibility to do it, and we need our levy stream back. This was not in the original Bill but we inserted the requirement that the boards must determine who is the best service provider for a function or element that has to be performed by the board. No doubt we will come to that in the Committee stage. The boards are actually required to do that. Can I say to the Wool Board that it is my view that the best way that it can deliver that is to go to a funder/provider split, that there is actually a separation---more than an arm's length separation---of the referee/player syndrome. The board actually needs to do that. I say to the board that if it is not prepared to do that, and we get into squabbles over the likes of Merino New Zealand or Saxon Merino, bulk Perendale wool or pre-lamb shear, or Shetland wool lambs, or whatever are the other initiatives out there, that will be the death warrant of the Wool Board. I say to the board that it consider very seriously the best course of action to pursue. The first speaker on our side, Maurice Williamson, listed a number of credible critics who have said it is a good Budget. Well, it will, and the member knows that. He spoke a lot about this particular issue being a problem of this particular Government. The House should note that it dates back to when the Hon. Colin Moyle was the Minister of Fisheries. Since that time five Ministers have succeeded Colin Moyle, and none of them picked up this issue. The member and the House should note why it is being picked up now. Fishers who felt that the monthly reconciliation of their own particular quota situation was inaccurate had days to register that they thought there had been a mistake. For years no one did that. For ten whole years not one soul out of , transactions actually did that. In March of last year one individual did understand it! The member who just spoke said it took months for something to be done. The House should note that it took months to scope the size of the problem and to stop it from occurring further. The time that lapsed subsequent to that was spent deciding whether individual alienation could be assessed, and whether it was appropriate to take that course and tie up the resources of the Ministry of Fisheries---whether that was the most appropriate way to redress the issue. So we have common sense. We have decided to validate the registry, which again has some integrity, and we have put in place a system of remunerating anybody who can prove his or her alienation. But those funds are not locked up; the Government has recognised that the funds should be able to be used in a productive and forward-looking way if they are not absorbed in remunerating those who have been alienated. This is common-sense legislation. I recommend it to the House. The select committee received only seven submissions. The four from the fishing industry were all supportive of the cause. I recommend this report back to the House, and look forward to the Committee stage and the third reading so that the final saga in what has been a sad and complex issue can be completed.

I move, That the Courts Security Bill be now read a second time. On behalf of the Minister for Courts, the Hon. Georgina Te Heuheu, it is our intention that at the conclusion of the second reading the Bill will be referred to the Government Administration Committee with an instruction to report back to the House by August . The purpose of the Bill is to provide for the establishment of court security officers who will exercise powers regulating the entry of people into the courts and the removal of people from the courts for the purpose of enhancing the security of the courts and the safety of those New Zealanders who use the courts. Access to courts in order to have impartial dispute resolution is a fundamental right of the people of New Zealand, and in exercising that right they are entitled to feel safe and secure. Over past years there has been an increase in the number of reported security incidents in courts. In , security incidents were recorded compared with in , one of which, sadly, resulted in the death of a woman. While the Department for Courts has instituted a series of measures to enhance court security, ensuring the safety of people in our courts remains an ongoing concern. The Bill seeks to address that concern by providing for the establishment of court security officers who will be authorised to exercise specific powers and duties in respect of courts and their associated buildings and grounds. Their powers and duties include: asking any persons to identify themselves and their reason for wanting to enter or for being in a court; asking the persons to submit to a search of their person or any property in their possession; examining any items detected in a search and taking any items considered to be a security threat into temporary custody; detaining until the arrival of the police any person who commits a specified offence in a court. These offences relate to offences involving the possession of unauthorised items and offences relating to acts of violence. The power to ask for identification and reason for entry and the power to search and take items into temporary custody cannot be exercised without the consent of the person concerned, unless otherwise ordered by a presiding judicial officer. Court security officers will not, except in exceptional circumstances, be able to exercise their powers in any courtroom where proceedings are being heard without the express consent of the presiding judicial officer. In addition to their powers, court security officers have particular duties. A person asked to submit to a search must be told that the search cannot take place without his or her consent. A person asked to hand over a dangerous but not offensive item must be told that the item cannot be taken without his or her consent. Other provisions make it an offence to obstruct a court security officer in exercising his or her powers or duties or to obstruct anyone helping a court security officer to do so. Similarly, there is a provision for immunities for court security officers who are exercising their powers and for anyone helping them to do so. The Bill takes a balanced approach to security, recognising that prudent rather than excessive security measures are appropriate in facilities owned by and serving the New Zealand public. Care has been taken to ensure that access to courts is not impeded but that security measures being implemented work effectively so that the estimated half a million New Zealanders who come through our nation's court buildings for various reasons each year can go about their business without fear of harm. Court security officers will be required to have reasonable grounds before asking any persons their reason for wanting to enter or for being in a court and reasonable grounds for asking persons to consent to a search of their outer garments and any property in their possession. This Bill safeguards the security of the courts as a cornerstone of the proper functioning of our community and contributes to safer communities by helping to prevent crime. Access to court in order to have impartial dispute resolution is a fundamental right for the people of New Zealand. All members of this House agree on that. In exercising that right to access our nation's courts New Zealanders are entitled to feel safe. Secure courts contribute to the credibility of the judicial system, to our New Zealand community feeling safe, and to the prosperity of our nation, social cohesion, and strengthening New Zealand families. I commend the Bill to the House and look forward to the debate and contribution of members.

We had violent crime coming down, and now it is going up. It is going up because this Minister of Police is completely hopeless. This guy has singlehandedly destroyed the morale of the New Zealand Police. I can recite a litany of stupid actions by this foolish Minister that have needlessly caused a lack of morale. Not only do we have fewer police today---that is, vacancies in front-line positions---but do members remember his speech that to make police recruits pay for training would make a lot of sense? I say at the beginning of this session that, while at the end of this debate there will be a free vote, National MPs have agreed to vote en bloc against the reporting back of this bill. We believe that the bill should go back to the select committee for improvement and further public submission. Only month was allowed for public submission. Also, a number of professional organisations made submissions. Their views have been totally ignored by the Government, and we think it is appropriate that the bill should be referred back to the select committee. However, having said that, I point out that next week National members will exercise a conscience vote, as is our party's usual practice, on the Minister's motions in respect of de facto and same-sex relationships. The report back on this bill and the Supplementary Order Paper present Parliament with the need to strike the balance between extending rights, and the burden and obligations that come from their extension. On the Opposition side of the House we say that irrespective of the merits of extending rights to different groups in the community, the burdens and the obligations of this bad law do not warrant such an extension, because they will be bad for anybody in either a matrimonial or a de facto relationship. The National Party, in Opposition, takes the position that, as in every other country in the world, there should be separate pieces of legislation to recognise the different levels of commitment to, and the different nature of, relationships. My colleague Dr Wayne Mapp will talk about that when he seeks a call. My colleague Mrs Anne Tolley will also seek a call to talk about how bad this legislation will be for women and children. She will quote from the extensive correspondence that the Minister has received. She will also talk about the advice that we have received from professional groups such as the family law section, warning the select committee about what is proposed in this legislation. The National Party, in Opposition, does not question any of the benefits that might arise from the extension of rights in this bill. But we do raise the issue that what the Government is proposing is bad for anybody in a relationship. The Minister, in her introductory speech, talked about its being wrong that people in de facto relationships had to take their cases to court to get any justice, but she is proposing a prescription that will massively increase the number of New Zealanders who will need to take their cases to court. The reason is that the Government is proposing to give judges wide and far-reaching judicial discretion in a number of areas where we have never had it in legislation before. Judges will be required to make an assessment of future earnings and future differences between the parties, and the Government cannot say what happens if the judge guesses wrongly or circumstances change. In the Opposition, we are concerned that it will lead to a massive increase in the number of relationship break-ups that come before the court. Some lawyers appeared before us, and suggested that up to to percent of relationship breakdowns will end up before a judge. Right now, only percent of cases make it to the clogged Family Court, and that is because the law is current and straightforward. The law makes it clear that matrimonial property is basically split :; that is the advice given by the lawyers on both sides. It encourages settlement, instead of litigation. The certainty of a : split allows matrimonial and relationship disputes to be settled quickly, so that people can start afresh and children are no longer involved in acrimonious legal battles. But that is going to change. The Government is proposing to give judges the power to compare the parties' respective likely future earning capacities and likely future living standards, and to make a judgment awarding a lump sum to the lower-earning partner. We heard unprecedented advice from the Principal Family Court Judge, Patrick Mahoney, that the new provisions in this legislation involved a broad discretionary element that will engender litigation. That is in contrast with the general thrust of the existing legislation, where the predominant feature is a considerable measure of certainty, with only limited discretion given to the courts. In picking up on this and going further, the New Zealand family law section---the association of all the family lawyers; the people one would think would be in favour of having lots more people appearing before judges---said that this bill and the Supplementary Order Paper, in particular, would lead to confusion and concern over what is meant. For example, how likely is ``likely''? What is meant by ``significance''? There is no guidance as to how the court will assess future income, over what period of time it will be assessed, or how the court is to assess the security of employment. As I said earlier, what will happen if a judge guesses wrongly? The Government is proposing that if there is a significant difference in the potential future earning capacity of the two partners, then judges can make an assessment. So it very much hinges on what is regarded as a significant difference. The Law Commission came before the select committee and said that hardly anyone will be affected by that measure. A prominent family lawyer in Auckland then told us that, in her opinion, a $, to $, difference would be significant. Yet the women's consultative committee of the New Zealand Law Society told the select committee that if there was a $ difference, people would be in for it. The point that the Opposition makes is that when we cannot get any of the professionals to agree on what this bill means, how are we providing the certainty that the Minister has talked about? Such a level of uncertainty will encourage lawyers to recommend to clients that they have a go. The lawyers told us that they would have to recommend that every person take his or her dispute to the courts. Judge Mahoney told us that an additional six Family Court judges would be the minimum number required to cope with what is proposed. As I said, this bill asks Family Court judges to predict the future. One of the submissioners highlighted the unpredictability of that, by asking the select committee to advise how the legislation would apply to a whole range of family scenarios that were given to us. The select committee could not reach a predictable conclusion on any of those cases. We put it to the House that this huge increase in judicial discretion, and the uncertainty that will be created, will be bad. I will give members an example that we have put in our minority report about the difficulties of making predictions. For example, a wife may own shares in a company that is doing very well at the time of separation, the settlement may give the husband percent of the property, but imports may flood the market years---or months---later, and her company may go bust. Would the husband give the extra percent back? No. What about the case where a couple in their s may separate, and he has a high-paying job and she has a low-paying one? When they separate he may be earning $, more than her, so she gets percent of the matrimonial property. But months after the settlement he may be made redundant. I do not have to tell members of this House how difficult it is for people in their s to get another high-paying job. Would the wife give back the extra percent of the value of the family home that she had received? No. So my point is that this large measure of judicial discretion will lead to different assessments, different results, and overall uncertainty. That uncertainty is something on which the Parliament should be providing greater guidance to judges. We, on the Opposition side of the House, also heard that there is evidence in Australia that three-quarters of de facto relationships break down after years. We say that if there is a legitimate concern, particularly regarding long-term de facto relationships that involve children, we have put forward our proposals to fix that. We say that there are a whole lot of New Zealanders out there who have entered into de facto relationships for companionship, with the express desire of not being caught by the matrimonial property legislation. On February this Minister will marry more New Zealanders that the Reverend Moon, because the , New Zealanders who are in de facto relationships will be caught by this legislation, whether or not they want to be. We are talking about the inspirations. When Tainui comes before its hearing, when its hearing is conducted in terms of establishing its tino rangatiratanga over the Waikato River, I know that the Minister will be the first to front up and give evidence in saying how inspired he is in terms of the relationship that Tainui had, not dissimilar to Ngai Tahu, with the lakes and the rivers. I want to pick up on that because I want to follow on with something that I think the Minister will find interesting. That is the statutory recognition provisions of this Bill that he has given to that tikanga, if one likes. There are a huge number of clauses that relate to statutory acknowledgment of that type of relationship. I believe that it is important he knows what that relationship is all about, and that is why I said I am inspired, because the basis of the statutory acknowledgment is on the relationship that Ngai Tahu have with these natural resources. Perhaps the Minister will take the next call. I want to ask him what he knows about spiritual and cultural values. I am not asking him to relate back to his Scottish whakapapa, but rather what he knows about tikanga Maori, in terms of spiritual and cultural values, because he has based these statutory acknowledgments on that issue. I ask him that question because there are a huge number of clauses that relate to that matter. The provision goes as far as saying that local and territorial authorities and other authorities---that are responsible for putting into place such district, coastal, and other plans that affect the whole community---must take cognisance of these statutory acknowledgments. Although it may be appropriate, in terms of this Bill, that those agencies that represent the wider community must take into consideration, or give effect to, or take cognisance of, these statutory acknowledgments, I ask the Minister whether the same relationship that Ngai Tahu have with those taonga is duplicated in the same way for those people in the far north---the iwi of Te Ika-a-Maui. There are no differences, but this Bill gives Ngai Tahu recognition by way of the statutory acknowledgment over and above the majority of Maori people and iwi who live in the North Island---Te Ika-a-Maui. They do not have the same privilege or the same consideration as Ngai Tahu, yet their relationship with the taonga that we are talking about here is exactly the same. Is the Minister suggesting that these are the criteria---and they can be the criteria---for further claims by Ngai Tahu and claims by Maori who are not Ngai Tahu, because I believe that the Minister has set a precedent? Not only must the local and regional authorities acknowledge it, in terms of this Bill, but also the Historic Places Trust and other quasi-Government agencies must acknowledge it. Does the Minister think it will set a precedent for other claims by other iwi asking for acknowledgment with regard to the settlements? That is the question I want the Minister to answer.

I would like to use my time this afternoon to speak in relation to vote: Justice and the appropriations therefor. I think that it is fairly common knowledge at this time that the Government is trying to save $ million in the present financial year, but so far it has been unable to convince any commentators---political or financial commentators---that anything like true savings of this figure will be achieved. The interesting thing---and the rumour that is fairly strong---is that no Minister wanted to volunteer where cuts could be made in their area. I find that quite incredible because it means that no Minister believes that his or her department can be run more efficiently or more effectively on less money. Unfortunately, this is an attitude that permeates government. It is an attitude that permeates the public sector. Whereas, conversely, it is an attitude that is rarely found in the private sector. The appropriations for vote: Justice total $. million. I suggest, in all seriousness, to the Government that it could probably save half that figure in the current year from vote: Justice alone. Seventy five million dollars could be cut from vote: Justice and I wonder whether there would be any real detriment to the country. I would like the Minister to consider that. Some might even suggest that the country would be better off if the Ministry of Justice spent less in receiving outside advice. The appropriations show that $. million will be spent on purchasing services relating to the management of the parliamentary electoral system. A huge amount of departmental policy advice is to be obtained with that vast sum of money, yet the Ministry of Justice never seems to get any better from one year to the next---cynics might even say that it gets worse. If the department wants to purchase only half of the policy planned for the next year, would the country be any worse off? I doubt that sincerely. Then the department will spend $. million on purchasing policy advice from the Law Commission. There is a widespread belief in many quarters that the Law Commission has been hijacked by the politically correct; that its reports on subjects such as women's access to justice are of very limited value to the wider community. The Minister of Commerce, in fact, is churning out far more credible commercial law reform proposals than the Law Commission can even begin to imagine. Canada abolished its Law Commission overnight and managed to survive. I am sure that if New Zealand did the same thing we would certainly survive and we would get a straight-off saving of $ million. Then $ million is being used to purchase equity promotion and protection services---whatever all that means---from the Chief Human Rights Commissioner, the Race Relations Conciliator, the Police Complaints Authority, and the Privacy Commissioner. Certainly, I would not want to see the Police Complaints Authority go---that should be retained---but do taxpayers really get $ million worth of valuable advice from those other bodies? I suggest that the majority of New Zealanders, sensible people who just want to get on with their lives, certainly do not think so. The amount of $ million being spent on legal aid is a vast subject and one that I will pass over for the purposes of this debate, but certainly there is room for reductions on a large scale in that area, also. Finally, there will be $ million spent on purchasing services from the Electoral Commission. We have just seen the Electoral Commission lose its case concerning party election expenses in the High Court. Not content with that, the commission is going to the Court of Appeal. Undoubtedly, we have an overly bureaucratic Electoral Commission and if it was forced to spend a little less money, I think the country would be better off. As soon as one puts any area of Government expenditure under the microscope, one realises how much money is wasted. One million dollars out of this Parliament is a very large sum of money. Inside Parliament, hundreds of millions of dollars are spent as if they have no meaning. It is time we put some tight controls on all areas of expenditure and asked whether we really get value for money---in the area of justice I am convinced that we do not.

I am pleased to speak on Part . We have heard from many of my learned colleagues---and David Carter---about the provisions of this part. They have talked about the major changes that are coming up, and it was correct for them to do that. It was correct for Bob Simcock to talk about the dissolution of the Health Funding Authority, because that is what clause states. For the members of this Committee to discuss what they think about this bill is very valuable. ``HFA'' refers to the Health Funding Authority. The terminology used in this health legislation is very confusing for the public. We have ``HHSs'', the ``HFA'', ``DHBs'', and various things. People in the community do not understand what we are talking about when we mention those sorts of things. The Health Funding Authority will be dissolved and we are going to have district health boards. District health boards will take over the role of delivery of all health services in the community---not just hospitals but also community services. That is a major change. It is not just a matter of our putting a few elected people on to a hospital and health service board; it is a major change. I do not believe that the New Zealand public knew what it was getting when it voted for this Labour Government. It did not know that there would be a radical restructuring of the health service. People did not know that it would be turned completely on its head once again and would go through another major restructuring. It really is ideology over common sense. I ask where the evidence is that the system we had was not working. I would like to know that, because it is about time that not just Parliament but all the health service had a look at the evidence. Let us have a look at what works and what does not. We keep coming up with new ideas. Part identifies precisely the new idea of totally rearranging our health service---dissolving the Health Funding Authority, dissolving our hospital and health services and turning them into district health boards---but where is the evidence that the Health Funding Authority was not working? Where is the evidence that our health service was not delivering in that respect? Where is the evidence that a major structural change will make any difference whatsoever? Most people in the health service say that all that this change will do is slow down any improvement in our health service for at least to years, because what happens when one markedly changes the whole way that health services are delivered? People spend their whole time concentrating on that. I was talking to somebody from the Arthritis Foundation in Christchurch, and this is an example of how changing things stops what has been happening. This person from the Arthritis Foundation has been working with the rheumatologists for years to develop a new system for Christchurch. But what has happened now? It has gone, finished, end of story. Two years of work by those people in the community has been suddenly scrapped. It is out the door. It is not going to happen. That is what happens all the time when we create a radical change, as this is. We are dissolving the Health Funding Authority and moving its functions to the ministry, which for at least the first couple of years will have total control over the budget. What people do not understand is that there was a major change whereby the funding of the health service was held by the Health Funding Authority. Originally there were four regional health authorities. We then moved to the Transitional Health Authority, and then to the Health Funding Authority. That authority was settling down and beginning to work.

They do not have inherited wealth and have not had the opportunities that come with wealth. If there is one matter we should celebrate today as we celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the Social Security Act in New Zealand it is the opportunities that that Act began to provide for women and men in New Zealand. It meant that at long last there was not only a safety net but also a springboard of opportunity for the people who needed it. There was an opportunity for them to enhance their life chances, and an opportunity for proper provision not only of education and health but also of social welfare and decent housing. Social policy should be dynamic and responsive to the changing nature of society and the economy, and if we consider the social welfare State as it was in and as it is now we will realise that it has undergone quite dramatic change---and so it should, because, after all, we are now living years later in a very different world. The first Labour Government initiated dramatic social policy reform measures to support New Zealanders in their recovery from the great depression. The fourth Labour Government has had to initiate similar dramatic, social, and economic policy reform to support present-day and future New Zealanders in their recovery from the economic and social mismanagement of three terms of a National Government. The fourth Labour Government is following in the footsteps of its predecessors in the first Labour Government in its commitment to comprehensive, innovative social policy reform; but it is taking on board the actual realities of New Zealand today, and in so doing it is continuing to carry out the original principles. The policies are developing to meet the realities of today. In the needs of women were taken into account. The widows' benefit was increased substantially and extended to include women without children. There was free maternity treatment, including, for the first time, the cost of care in the maternity home. That tradition started at the time of the first Labour Government and will be continued under this Government. Present provision is much more generous, and people tend to forget when they look back that at the time of the introduction of the welfare State, when Michael Joseph Savage and his Government proposed policies to deal with some of the awful deprivations at the end of the depression era, there was enormous objection from the Tories---huge objections and cries that somehow or other those policies would be the end of New Zealand and the end of society. Of course, when the Tories became the Government they dismantled only bits and pieces. They used the welfare State as a means to bribe the electorate from time to time. We should remember that today we are meeting the needs of the community in a much more profound and sophisticated fashion. When pensions were introduced they were equivalent to about percent of the average wage---that is, they were equivalent to about five-eighths of the present pension level. Universality was available only at years of age. Members opposite should remember that they used public money to bribe the rich to make universality available from the age of , and they have objected strenuously to the suggestion that there ought to be some kind of abatement. The Government makes no apology for always trying to equalise opportunity and to provide help for those who have the greatest need. We should also remember that the abatement procedures in the original provisions were very harsh. That position has been changed, and now there is a range and an understanding of welfare that is much broader. The matter that I am most proud of in the fourth Labour Government's approach to social welfare has been its concern not only with benefits but particularly with the provision of support for those activities that the National Government ignored or made inadequate provision for. For example, there has been an enormous emphasis within the social equity committee on the need for changes in income maintenance, early-childhood care, matrimonial property and family law, and equal pay and equal opportunity---matters that the Prime Minister referred to in his speech earlier in the debate. Those changes will empower people---they will enable women who have had unequal status in society to stand on their own feet, to make their own decisions, to carve out their own careers in the home and outside the home, and to be real people. Earlier displays of that commitment have been seen in the Government's economic reforms---particularly in the reform of the public sector. For the first time in this country equal employment programmes have ensured that women working in the public sector will have equal employment opportunities, and will have the chance to stand alongside their brothers and be considered as whole persons. The State Sector Act is another part of welfare for people, because welfare must be seen as empowering people---not just throwing a few crumbs to beggars. The Ministry of Women's Affairs has been extraordinarily active in drawing attention to the needs of women, and one of the hallmarks of the Government has been its willingness and its ability to seek reports---a matter that was criticised by the previous speaker---in order to face up to the facts and lay them out openly, and to pursue the principle of open Government and then make the right decisions. Opposition members seem to think that if one has a report one has to do exactly what it says. Sometimes there are a variety of opinions on a matter, and the job of Government is to govern. Opposition members seem to think that the job of Government is simply to follow, meekly and blindly like sheep, whatever the latest opinion may be. The Government has also been extraordinarily active and of particular help to women in the housing sector---another aspect that is essential and in which there has been gross inequality. Housing has been identified as a crucial economic issue, and, as a result of the Government's approach to welfare and empowerment, the -year rule has been abolished. The -year rule crippled some families headed by women for too many years in their search for decent housing, or just for shelter. The women's project fund that has been set up by my colleague the Minister of Housing provides $ million for sheltered accommodation and accommodation for groups of women. The Ministry of Women's Affairs has considered another aspect of the empowerment of women---the very belated recognition of the value of the work that all women do in the home. If the Ministry of Women's Affairs stands for anything it stands for those women who have carried the work of this community in voluntary agencies, in their own homes, and in caring for children, aged people, and disabled people. I am pleased to move, That this Bill be now read a third time. The Bill was introduced late in . It was important from the point of view of compliance and streamlining of the quota management system. It was referred to a select committee, which took many months to consider the matters before it. Essentially, the main items were the records and the returns that the fishers were required to return to the Government to provide for streamlining the quota management system. The individual transferable quota system and the total allowable catch system depend on the flow of information of good quality. A substantial part of the Bill relates to offences provisions. The Bill substantially increases the penalties for offences under the Fisheries Act. I am sure that the country as a whole is pleased with the recent progress made in clamping down on illegal fishing activity, because the livelihood of honest fisherpersons depends on the integrity of the quota management system. People who cheat and poach are thieving from the public estate. Not only the commercial industry but also the enhancement of the recreational fisheries are put in jeopardy if poachers feel that they can get away with illegal activity. Therefore the measures contained in the Bill go a long way to enhance the ability of officers of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries to apprehend people engaged in illegal activities. More particularly, substantial increases have been made to the penalties for offences under the Fisheries Act. Several adjustments to the Bill were made by the select committee and reported back to the House, and I shall go through them. In relation to the provisions for forfeiture of boats and quota, the Act provides that when people are convicted of an offence they must forfeit their boats and other equipment associated with the illegal activity. The point was made that a large commercial company could lose a large trawler worth many millions of dollars, and also its quota, which might be worth tens of millions of dollars. In theory, those assets could be forfeited on the basis of a very minor charge. Therefore the select committee made a sensible adjustment by providing for a gradation of offences. Instead of its being an all-or-nothing penalty there is a gradation so that the charge can be matched to the severity of the offence. That worthwhile change came through in the reporting back of the Bill. The problem of by-catch was also dealt with. It has been a longstanding problem with the fishing industry quota management system that a company or a large boat could be targeting a species, and, inevitably, other species of fish were also caught. That is the by-catch, and there can be difficulties in holding enough quota to cover it. Therefore the Bill introduces a greater flexibility for by-catch, and allows for a trade-off between different species. I know that the commercial fishing industry warmly welcomes that change. The Bill contains minor amendments to the conversion factors. For example, when fish are caught there is a conversion between the green weight and the processed weight. That aspect has been built into the Bill. The Bill also contains provisions that deal with people who fish on behalf of someone who holds a quota. People often lease their quotas. The Bill provides greater flexibility to allow people to fish on behalf of others who hold a quota. The commercial fishing industry also warmly welcomed the balancing of quota at the end of the year, which is given much greater flexibility. All of the increased flexibilities enhance the quota management system, and increase and improve its integrity. Members will know that a substantial supplementary order paper was introduced on March. That paper was really the consequence of two broad issues: first, several points in the Maori Fisheries Act, which was passed late last year, needed to be cross-referenced to the Fisheries Act. The sensible approach was to add an amendment to the Bill before the House. The second broad issue relates to the change to proportionate quotas. In essence, proportionate quotas provide that when scientists have done stock-assessment work and have shown that the stock either needs to be reduced for conservation purposes or to be increased because it is greater than was previously realised---the total allowable catch has to be varied and changes made. Under the old regime the Crown would have been required to pay compensation for a reduction of the total allowable catch, and, conversely, the commercial industry would have had to pay for the increased total allowable catch. Under the proposal we have moved to proportionate quotas: the total allowable catch is set and the individual holders of those transferable quotas have their quota varied according to the proportion they hold. No compensation is involved, and, equally, people do not have to purchase any increase. A transitional period has been provided. That matter was negotiated between personnel of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries and of the industry last October. It is loosely referred to as the ``accord''. The Government substantially adopted the accord, but not in its entirety. There were two qualifications. First, in meeting the conditions of the accord the Government would first make provision in the fish quota for the obligations it had under the Maori Fisheries Act. Second, it would make provision for the obligations it had under international law and under the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act. With the exception of those two qualifications, the agreed position between the ministry and the industry was adopted, picked up, and introduced into the legislation under the supplementary order paper. Biological sustainability is the bottom line in the management of fishing. That is the essence of managing our stocks, and it is the purpose of the quota management system. Many issues were debated during the Committee stage. Many concerns were brought before the House and also before the select committee, which, this week, sat for hours. I shall briefly explain some of those concerns, because they relate to the legislation. The fishing industry believes that when the Crown holds quota---in other words, when the fishing effort does not match the total allowable catch as the biological limit has been set higher than the amount the current industry can catch---that surplus stock, as it were, should be distributed to the existing participants in the industry. I am bound to say that the Government does not accept that belief. Commercial fishers may enjoy the full individual transferable quotas they hold---which were issued on the basis of their catch history---but when the fishing effort into a new stock has not developed, that new stock is owned by the Crown. In effect, the Government is really saying that the fish in New Zealand's oceans are part of the public estate. The Crown has responsibility to manage that public estate and to grant harvesting rights to the commercial industry. To do otherwise---to issue the total amount to the commercial industry---would be unacceptable. Conversely, Maori claimed that the percent provided for in the Maori Fisheries Act should be related to a fixed tonnage at the date of the passing of that Act, and that no proportionate cuts should be made during the transitional period of years. The Government also rejects that view on the basis that it would defeat the principle and object of the Maori Fisheries Act of providing that percent, because in many of our fisheries a proportion much greater than percent would be achieved if that policy were adopted. In other words, when a total allowable catch has to be reduced over the next to years, then, to the extent that Maori were guaranteed percent at the commencement before the proportionate reductions, at the end of that period they would obviously end up by owning an amount much greater than percent. The Government does not accept that proposition. The change urged by Opposition members has not been adopted.

I would like to pick up the point that Peter Brown made with regard to accident compensation coverage for criminal activity. Certainly, we all recognise that the no-fault philosophy has been a key part of accident compensation since it was first introduced in , but that does not make it right. The case put forward by Peter Brown was very persuasive. Accident compensation for criminal activity is wrong in principle. It is perhaps one of the worst aspects of social engineering. It actually removes any personal responsibility. When one removes personal responsibility from society, one actually debases society. There are no checks and balances for those who actually engage in illegal activities. There are no sanctions. Part of the sanctions are those checks and balances. If a person injures himself or herself performing a criminal act, then that person will suffer. But this bill says that if a burglar falls through the glass window, or damages himself when breaking through a door, the State will pick up all the costs, all the bills, from any disadvantage that he suffers. That is wrong in principle. I challenge any speaker on the other side to justify why hard-working, struggling, ordinary New Zealanders, who pay their taxes---in most cases far too much tax---who are struggling to keep their families together, living law-abiding lives, putting their kids through school and university, and fronting up to inadequate health services should have to pay taxes to condone perpetrators of crime who have all their hospital costs covered, though they themselves cannot get adequate service, because the criminals are there on accident compensation, with the Government paying the bill. That is sending the wrong signals to society. It is removing personal responsibility, and one thing that ACT is very keen on is promoting more personal responsibility in our society. The State is progressively invading all aspects of society, and it is not doing it well. I come to the medical misadventure aspects of Part , because they are an absolute shambles. It is a disgrace that a Minister of a Government that has been in office for almost years has come along and said: ``Oh, we know we've got a problem here, but we're working on it.'' Well, that is not good enough. This Government has brought a -page bill, which has been some years in gestation, to the Committee today with all its detail and prescriptive nonsense, but has not addressed a fundamental principle in terms of dealing with, and putting bounds on, medical misadventure. A lot of academics have done a lot of work on this issue. Peter Davis, in particular, has done a lot of work on medical misadventure, and I understand that he has actually spoken to various members of the Government. In fact, I believe that he has even spoken directly to the Prime Minister on this issue, and it was not just pillow talk but a serious discussion on the problems of medical misadventure. Yet with expert advice like that, the Government comes along today and admits to the Committee that the area is a shambles. The extraordinary thing is that it is not shamefaced about it. Why are Government members not shamefaced about it? Why are they not getting up and explaining why they have failed to address the very critical issue of medical misadventure? We also have an incredible situation with cover, and some of the nonsense associated with that. I refer to a landmark ruling in the Christchurch District Court that found that injuries caused by sneezing are not covered by accident compensation. We had a case last year where an Aaron Shane Lovelace, who suffered hay fever, lodged a compensation claim with the Accident Compensation Corporation, because a sneeze had sent him crashing to his bathroom floor. The doctor said that the sneeze, which had caused a disc to be ruptured in Mr Lovelace's spine, was the final insult in a series of back injuries. The Accident Compensation Corporation agreed to cover the cost of his injuries, but subsequently revoked the cover, claiming that the sneeze was not an accident.

I am talking about the early support for this Bill. Everything I say is the truth. Business and professional women's groups supported it. Judges, ambulance officers, chemists, many journalists, the National Council of Women of New Zealand, and victims galore supported it. In fact, members would not find a victim who did not support it. Retailers supported it, for good reason. Social workers and home helpers supported it. A passive resistance spray will give people the means to feel secure. It will give them confidence. If legally used, there will no longer be the invasive requirements of a court case and all the problems that go with that. It will decrease the use and the costs to the police, to hospitals, to social welfare organisations, to the courts, to doctors, and to the Accident Rehabilitation and Compensation Insurance Corporation. It will reduce all of that. It is clear that women in particular are not able to protect themselves from violent attack. A passive resistance spray gives them that ability. Opponents of the Bill are quite wrong to claim that it will be used for offensive purposes. It is not an offensive weapon, even in the wildest imagination of those against it---although it is defined as that in the Arms Act, where the Governor-General may from time to time by Order in Council make regulations declaring sprays such as these to be restricted weapons. The Governor-General can also change that definition. It is a simple matter to change the definition of a restricted weapon to exempt passive resistance sprays, because they are not weapons. There is no evidence to show that the sprays would be used as an offensive weapon. They would not be used in the case of rape or attempted rape, because if the offender is sprayed with the contents of a CS spray, firstly, he would not be very interested in rape, and in any case, if he turned it on the victim, or the prospective victim, he would be unable to get near that victim for some little time. There is no good reason not to proceed with this Bill. It simply calls for a redefinition of what is a restricted weapon and it calls for the exemption of passive resistance sprays---defensive sprays---from being categorised as restrictive weapons. One or two amendments would be needed to the Crimes Act, but the remedy in respect of passive resistance sprays lies in penalising heavily those who misuse them. It is as clear as day that members of the public should be allowed to have these sprays. The vast majority of law-abiding citizens, for whom this would be a great protection, should be allowed to have them for defensive purposes. Those who misuse such sprays should be hit as hard as possible. If there is no provision now in the legislation to do that, that can be attended to quite easily. Misuse of sprays should be attended to and the offenders can be dealt with.

There is no cost when inmates are granted a temporary release to attend a tangihanga, except some external transport costs. There is a cost in departmental terms when an inmate is considered unsuitable for a temporary release and is instead granted an escorted outing to attend. The fares and travelling expenses of the inmate and the escorting officer, including the officer's salary and overtime, are charged to the nearest hour. The family are advised of the estimated cost and have the option of whether to proceed with having their family member escorted. The Public Prisons Service has to roster staff back to work when an officer is acting as an escorting officer. This is a cost to the department and it is not considered an appropriate additional financial burden to New Zealand taxpayers that they should bear the cost of inmates attending ceremonies of compassionate significance.

I am glad that the member for Rangiora adopted a more constructive attitude to the Bill in the select committee than he did in his second reading debate speech, because his approach in that speech was extremely negative. The crocodile tears that he expressed about minor parties came as a great surprise to me, because he did not make any such claims at the select committee hearings---nor did the National Party do so in its submission to the Bill, if it comes to that. I shall answer a particular claim made by the member that the Bill was rushed through the select committee. That is not correct. A full month was available for parties to make submissions after the Bill was introduced. Only submissions were received, but all of the parties that wanted to appear before the select committee did so. The committee gave as much time to every witness as witnesses wanted to take in order to express their views. There was no question of the Bill's being rushed through, and I reject that suggestion. The Bill's substance is contained in Part II---Part I and Part III deal with minor matters not relating to election programmes---so I shall confine my remarks to Part II, which focuses on election programmes. I shall summarise the main aspects of the scheme set out in the Bill. The first feature that I should emphasise is that the scheme is entirely voluntary. Broadcasters are invited to offer time, either free or at discounted rates, and whether they choose to do so is voluntary. There is no compulsion upon them to participate. Any decision made to participate, as is happening this year with both radio and television, is made by the broadcaster alone. That is the first point; it is a voluntary scheme. The second point is that it is a scheme that depends upon public funding. I emphasise that the principle of public funding of broadcasting was advocated in a report by the Royal Commission on the Electoral System. The report was subtitled Towards a Better Democracy. I shall read a few sentences from that report in which the commission makes explicit its belief that public funding of broadcasting is appropriate. The commission stated: ``We are of the view that the allocation of free broadcasting time to political parties is highly desirable. The provision of such time has not only been of informative value to the electorate but it has also been an important factor in keeping the cost of elections within limits sustainable by New Zealand's political parties. In our view, and notwithstanding future changes in the administration and organisational structures of broadcasting, the corporation should be legally obliged to continue to provide free time to political parties.''. Fundamental changes to the broadcasting regime in New Zealand have been made since that report was written. The Broadcasting Corporation has changed its structure. It is now a stand-alone State-owned enterprise comprising both radio and television, and there is now a private television channel as well as private radio stations. Given the fundamental change to the structure of broadcasting in New Zealand, it is entirely appropriate that legislation should be introduced to set up a new regime that takes account of those changes. So public funding is the basis of the scheme, and there is already an indication of the extent of that funding for the election. It is funding on a modest scale in that $. million has been set aside for television programmes and $, for programmes on radio. An additional $, has been allocated for the cost of the productions of the opening and closing addresses. However, $. million is less than the amount that was spent on television and radio advertising for the general election. So the amount of public funding to be allocated for that process is relatively modest.

This will be the thinking person's election. People will think through slogans such as those about integrity. I remember thinking, after listening to speeches made by the Minister of Labour who is now the Leader of the Opposition---in , or at about that time, that he had been well coached because certain words were used again and again. At that time the National Government wanted to introduce a compulsory form of voluntary unionism, and the Minister of Labour---the present Leader of the Opposition---used the word ``freedom'' continuously in his speeches. I have noticed that habit beginning to creep back into his speeches. In his television debate with the Prime Minister people heard this choice little exchange: ``To me, integrity is the most important thing in politics---my personal integrity and the integrity of my party. I believe very firmly that we should tell the public the truth, take them into our confidence, have the integrity. Integrity is all-important.''. Within a couple of minutes the word ``integrity'' was used five or six times. When I hear a word overused with such monotonous regularity I become very suspicious. What lies behind the integrity and the credibility the Leader of the Opposition keeps talking about? I am not the only person who is suspicious about that kind of iteration. The editorial in the New Zealand Herald a few days ago stated: ``National's advertising aims at uncertain voters, particularly those who are for ever telling pollsters and radio programmes they are deeply disillusioned with politicians, and politics in general. In response, National seems to be embarking on a campaign of high-blown slogans about integrity and credibility. The strategy is not without its dangers. Integrity is a brave claim in politics.''. It is not without its dangers that the thinking person will see through it. When one considers the National Party from the point of view of its integrity and credibility the story is not a pretty one. Let us consider the Opposition's economic credibility and integrity. It has promised to balance the Budget, but at the same time it has promised at least $. billion in additional Government spending and many thousands of dollars in reduced taxation. I shall spell out some of the details. A National Government would abolish the surcharge on superannuation, which would cost $ million. It would give a tax rebate for the first $ in superannuation schemes. That would cost another $ million. A National Government would abolish land tax, which would cost $ million. It would abolish diesel tax at the cost of another $ million. A National Government would abolish estate and gift duties---at a cost of $ million. Those add up to almost $ billion of revenue promises. There are also the expenditure promises: additional police at a cost of about $ million; new programmes for long-term unemployed at a cost of $ million; and the list goes on. Those promises total about $. billion, but how do $. billion of extra spending and $ million of savings in taxation add up? How does one obtain credibility from that equation? It does not convince me. The National Party lacks credibility in other respects---not only economically. I saw an interesting headline in an Auckland paper---``Does National know where it's going?''. That question must devoutly be asked. Almost any area of that party's policy presents a picture of contradiction, confusion, and anything but credibility. I take, as a random example, the issue of monetary policy. The National Party's spokespersons are all over the place. The member for Selwyn said: ``Those who advocate direct intervention in the market to lower interest rates or exchange rates in reality invite boomerang solutions.''. On the other hand, the member for Tauranga said: ``That is conventional economic wisdom only contradicted by the Labour Government's false obsession to eradicate inflation.''. A similar confusion or flip-flop occurs with tariff and trade barriers. The member for Selwyn supports the Treasury and the Reserve Bank line of urging the Government to speed up its restructuring process, especially in terms of tariff removal. However, the member for Fendalton says that the Government's reduction of tariff protection on clothing is an extremely harsh, unsympathetic, and totally uncaring approach to New Zealand industry. How is one squared with the other? Where is the credibility of a party that is so contradictory in its policy statements among not only its leaders but also its spokespersons? Another classic example of an absence of credibility is in the crucial area of nuclear policy. In the election campaign the Leader of the Opposition said: ``The National Government will not seek short-term popular appeal by ignoring its responsibilities to generations of New Zealanders as yet unborn.''. He talked about the naivety of the Government as being beyond belief. The naivety of the New Zealand public would be beyond belief if it swallowed that idea of credibility and integrity. After the National Party's grand sounding rhetorical statements about its principled stand on nuclear policy it has returned to do a flip-flop and has announced a switch in policy, in that under a National Government no nuclear weapons would be brought into New Zealand.

The Bills deal with the repeal of sections of the Area Health Boards Amendment Act and the Hospitals Amendment Act . When the House rose last night the Deputy Leader of the Opposition was speaking, and his contribution to the debate was typical of the bombast and confusion that marked the Opposition's reaction to the Bill throughout the debate. We were presented with the comical and grotesque spectacle of Opposition members parading as the defenders of the State unions, when we know that a National Government actually tried to deregister the Public Service Association. Behind the surface rhetoric of their defence of the State unions the real agenda kept peeping through---their further intention that a National Government would deregulate the labour market in both the State sector and the private sector. It clearly sticks in the craw of Opposition members that State sector workers---for example, the Nurses Association and other workers' associations in the health sector at present covered by agreements---will come under the terms of the Labour Relations Act, and become unions covered by awards with the right to ballot their members on the matter of compulsory coverage. It is clear that the Opposition's agenda is that a National Government would slash Government spending by shrinking the size of the State sector. That has been explicit in the speeches made by Opposition members during the debate, particularly those made by the member for Selwyn and the member for Ashburton. They do not want to see the State as one of the big players in the game of the nation, but to see it simply as a referee that stands aside while private interests battle it out. Such an agenda is incompatible with the pretended support and sympathy for the State unions that Opposition members manifested in the debate. I speak of the apparent confusion in the approach to the legislation by Opposition members, because not only does their ``shrink the State'' agenda keep peeking through but there is another response, which could hardly be called an agenda, because it is derived from blind emotion and conservatism. It is the kind of reaction that lies behind the mindless repetition of the word ``evil'' that we heard from the member for Hobson and from the member for Whangarei. It is a reaction based not on reason and an analysis of the admittedly major changes proposed in the legislation but a reaction of hysteria and panic. The Government's philosophy, as embodied in the Bill, is predicated on a strong and vital State sector, especially the health sector. The Government believes that it is important that the State should not relinquish its central role in that sector. However, if the State is to remain a strong, vital,and vigorous institution in the health sector, it must change to meet the realities of a changing world. The State must not be allowed simply to lose itself in inertia, and throw its collective hands up at the thought of the sheer difficulty of modernising the institutions. We must get away from the idea that the only kind of change that is acceptable in the State sector is growth through accretion. It may be necessary for some parts of the State to grow, and if that is so, well and good, but we must get away from the idea that the only acceptable change in the State is a sheer increase in size. The quest for security has been a powerful impulse in New Zealand's history. Many members of Parliament have probably read Dr Sutch's book The Quest for Security, which is a phrase he used to attempt to characterise and summarise one of the strongest impulses in the Labour Party's history. However, there are circumstances in which the quest for security can become a self-defeating motivation, especially if security is interpreted in too narrow a framework. There is not much point in looking toward immediate security if the security of the nation is at stake because of the need to survive in a larger world that is subject to continuous change. That is the real motive behind the changes in the State sector that the Bills will promote. It may cause a sense of insecurity in people who are not used to seeing the role of the State change and who would prefer things to carry on in the familiar way, but if we allow ourselves to give in to a fear of change and a blind concern for security, and if we allow the forces of inertia to take over, we will not be able to protect the important aspects of our national security upon which our survival as a nation depends. The health and education services are so vital that New Zealand cannot afford not to change and to modernise and to ensure that those institutions are vigorous, vital, and responsive. We must avoid the circumstances whereby the health sector, for example, is crippled by inertia and caution, and is unable to renew itself. That is an example of the dual role of the Government that is embodied in the principles of the legislation---that is, to preserve the crucial and central role of the State and to protect that role; but to do so not with a conservative response but with an acceptance of the need to make the State change and become more flexible, more responsible, and more responsive to the realities of the world in which we live. Those principles are embodied in the Bills. The Government is attempting to steer a course between two opposite impulses---on the one hand the self-protection impulses of those people who want to keep the status quo because it is familiar, and on the other hand the ``deconstructive'' agenda of the Opposition that wants to expose the inert carcass of the State to the depredations of unfettered private enterprise. The Government's policy is based on the priority of maintaining a vital health sector that will be as responsive as possible. Getting that balance right was the main aspect of the select committee discussions and the Committee stage. It is important to get the balance right between preserving the State and the people who work in it and protecting their rights, but at the same time introducing changes that make the State more responsive and responsible. I can refer to particular aspects of the health sector in which that has been achieved. The appointment of general managers by the boards themselves was a change that was introduced in the select committee. That change gives area health boards and hospital boards the power to select their general managers, who will be the chief executives of each area health board and hospital board, and to review the performances of those boards. That position will give the local communities of each hospital board and of area health boards a say about the way in which the institutions are operated in their regions.
When are the details of any such scheme likely to be announced?
