I am pleased that the member opposite has such a charitable view of our endangered species. This is a serious Bill, and I firstly want to thank Mr Eric Roy for introducing it to the House and providing for a strengthening of the convention---for which, I think, there is strong consensus in the House---in this important legislation for New Zealand. Our ecological history means that we have more endangered species in this country---and I am not talking of the political variety---than any other country on the planet, and that gives us a special responsibility to make sure the convention is strong and robust. The original amendments provided by the member do patch up some acknowledged deficiencies that received some publicity last year, and I thank him for taking the initiative for correcting those. Subsequent to that, TRAFFIC Oceania has come forward with a report identifying that New Zealand is a shipping post for endangered birds from Australia. The great difficulty for New Zealand authorities is in trying to work out which of the Australian birds leaving our shores have been pre-smuggled in from Australia and which have been legitimately bred from stocks of birds in New Zealand. The current provisions of the legislation do not provide us with any mechanism to be able to clearly sort that out. When the member seeks to introduce a supplementary order paper---which I acknowledge that my department has assisted him with---I hope that the House will be sympathetic to allowing its introduction alongside the Bill so that the amendments to the legislation can be treated simultaneously. The principal provision in that supplementary order paper is to allow the Director-General of Conservation to be able to have DNA testing done of birds that are planned for export. The reason quite simply is to provide a verifiable method to ensure that the birds are not simply being on-smuggled. Despite there being maybe some friendly rivalry with Australia, it should give New Zealanders no pleasure at all that we are the single-largest staging post of smuggled birds from Australia, and Australia is obviously putting some pressure on New Zealand to deal with the deficiencies addressed in the Bill. Further to that, the deficiencies in the original Act do not make it easy to enforce because it has a very narrow definition of what is, indeed, meant by ``export''. In the same way as Parliament dealt with pornography laws and said that it became an impossibility for our enforcement agencies to just stop the importation of pornographic material, and that it should be an offence ``beyond imported'', this Bill proposes to extend the definition so that it is possible to pursue prosecutions of people who have smuggled in birds successfully but have not been able to show that they have the necessary permits, and the like, to maintain them in New Zealand. So again I thank Mr Roy for introducing this Bill, and I hope that Parliament will allow the introduction of the supplementary order paper. Together they will show that this Parliament and New Zealand are committed to the protection of those endangered species and to the prevention of the abhorrent trade in things that are valuable because they are rare, and that people will be prevented from making a quick buck out of those things that are special in nature.

Further work on the Transmission Gully route will require a change in Government policy. I believe that it is simply crazy and an unsustainable argument to say that a cost-benefit ratio should be worked out based on the total cost of any project rather than on the Government contribution to the project. For example, for a project like the Transmission Gully route that would cost $ million, if the State contributes only half of that---say, $ million or $ million---the cost-benefit ratio should be worked out based on just that part of the contribution. It should not be worked out based on the total cost of the project, which would include money that would come from local ratepayers, or money that would come from private entrepreneurs if the route were developed as a toll route. This year I will be pushing for a change in Government policy that will see cost-benefit ratios worked out based on the contribution of Government money, not on the total cost of the project. Governments should and must be interested in a return on the money that they spend. It is exactly right for them to be doing so. But Governments have no interest in seeking to have the same ratio applied to money that is put in by other parties. I hope that we can make some movement on that over the next months. Finally, it is time that we at the central government level took a much more strategic overview when looking at the infrastructure of this country. It is my belief that there is an urgent need for State Highway to be upgraded by the development of the Transmission Gully route right through to the Kapiti coast. If that is not done, and we sit around on our hands and wait for it to reach some national cost-benefit ratio level, by that stage the whole of the Wellington region will be suffering economically because the stranglehold in relation to movement in and out of the region will be costing us enormously. If we achieve the current economic growth of percent year on year, it will cause huge problems for this country as we try to move people and products around places that simply do not have the roading network to sustain that economic growth. So there is an argument that, in cases like the Transmission Gully project, the Government has to make a strategic, long-term decision that overrides some of the more traditional ways of looking at cost-benefit ratios. I hope that, in recognition of the strong and sustainable economic growth, we will certainly be able to do that in the near future. So I do not share the despondency of Porirua City councillors on this issue. I am disappointed that they feel despondent at the moment. All I can say to them is that they may feel that they were knocked back by some bureaucrats within Transit New Zealand last night, but they should not get downhearted; they should in fact live to fight another day, and that other day may be a lot closer than they think. We have some challenges before us as a nation. The challenge now is to make a decision about how we should spend the surpluses that this country will shortly start to have---and this country has not had to address this problem for about years. I hope that some of the new Labour back-benchers, who are very keen to come here and spend everything, look to the future with a bit more conservatism.

This Bill is identical to the Bill that the House rejected some months ago. It is fair to say that some members of the House have changed their minds since then. It is fair to say that the National caucus has not. The National caucus does not believe that the Commissioner for Children needs to be an officer of Parliament. The mover of this Bill has already scoped the fact that there are only two officers of Parliament at present. What the member did not go on to say was that in , under the Labour Government, the Finance and Expenditure Committee, in its report on an inquiry into the role of officers of Parliament, decided that officers of Parliament should be very, very rare, and that Parliament should consider creating such positions only very rarely, and it rejected any extension of the officer of Parliament principle. I do not have any problem, and neither does the National caucus, with the independence of the role of the Commissioner for Children. What I do have a problem with is the Commissioner for Children being made an officer of Parliament. I hope the select committee will look at this issue and determine that there should be, if one likes, a halfway house---a role whereby, rather than being an officer of Parliament, the Commissioner for Children stands aside from receiving his rations through vote: Social Welfare. This argument is all about whether the commissioner is seen to be independent. I say to members that I have never, in dealing with the current commissioner or the previous commissioner, had either one of them tell me that he believes that I as Minister have been acting in a way that has compromised his independence. I acknowledge that Mr Wright in his speech also backed up that point. I believe that both the current commissioner and the previous two commissioners have shown a considerable amount of independence. All three have expressed frustration at having to get access to pay and rations through the Department of Social Welfare, and we can certainly look at other ways of dealing with that---and perhaps the select committee will do so. But to make the commissioner an officer of Parliament, and to widen the commissioner's brief to bring it outside the examination of, in particular, cases under the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act, is a step that I think will ultimately weaken the office. One of the most important tasks, if not the most important, that the Commissioner for Children carries out is reviewing cases that have gone through the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Agency and have been acted on by social workers. I believe that the public and Parliament need a place where the casework of the Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Agency can be reviewed independently and can be reported on on that basis. Each and every case that the department gets involved with is a tragedy. Each and every one of those cases involves families and children who have been at risk. Those cases go through a process whereby social workers are required to make judgments and the court is asked to make decisions. I see the role of the Commissioner for Children of reviewing the casework and looking at it as being the prime role of that office. It was why the office was established.

I am very pleased to be able to continue to speak on this bill. This moratorium has become quite emotive and the whole issue of gambling has been canvassed. The bill is, in its totality, quite selective. It seems to target casinos and their applications, when really a lot of people are concerned about what is perceived to be quite clear evidence of problem gamblers within the country. I will come back to the Supplementary Order Paper in due course. I want to reiterate the comment that I will be supporting the extension of the moratorium, but I have some concerns about the Supplementary Order Paper as far as retrospective legislation is concerned. I will highlight again a couple of the comments that there are various forms of gambling available to New Zealanders. The protections and controls that are present in casinos are far greater, more effective, and more rigidly applied than any supervision of the pokies in various clubs, pubs, bars, and other parts of our towns. We have heard lots of examples of problem gamblers. I would say the biggest problem with the gambling situation in New Zealand is the Totalisator Agency Board (TAB) and its sports bet, where people can bet on who will get the first wicket in a test match or who will score the first try, and there is the possibility of making a bet on virtually every aspect of a game. The people who are doing that are, unfortunately, taking a huge gamble, and usually it is at great expense not only to themselves but to their families. I am in a position to see this for myself in Hamilton, in the sense that Work and Income New Zealand's office is just across the road from the TAB. I have seen a number of beneficiaries come out of Work and Income New Zealand, presumably with the support that they have just got, and go straight across the road into the TAB. There is a sort of open licence, shall we say, for them to do that. So I have a real concern about how selective this moratorium is. I can only hope that during the course of it there will be time for this country to have a good close look at gambling per se, and at the risks for those who become problem gamblers and develop an addiction. As I said earlier, casinos provide greater protection for problem gamblers, and have greater standards of supervision, than any other form of gambling that is available to tempt New Zealanders. I hope that, during the course of the moratorium, we will recognise the need for some balance on this whole issue and will get some consistency. I hope that we will not be selective in relation to any one particular form but rather that we will have surveillance over all aspects of gambling, with more stringent supervision and the like. New paragraph (a) of section A() in clause on Supplementary Order Paper states: ``the Authority may not consider or reconsider any application for a casino premises licence (whether received before or after the beginning of the moratorium period), or grant a licence in respect of any such application;''. That, to me, is the retrospective aspect of this Supplementary Order Paper. When we compare that with the explanatory note on the back of the Supplementary Order Paper, there seems to be a contradiction. The explanatory note states: ``If the Court of Appeal upholds the High Court decision, the grant of the licence remains set aside.''---that is, if the Court of Appeal agrees with the High Court decision. Then it states: ``The Authority will have to reconsider the application afresh, and make a new decision. The Bill as introduced does not affect this.'' Yet by my reading, under new paragraph (a) it would have to do that. Similarly, the last paragraph in the explanatory note states: ``However, if the Court of Appeal overturns the High Court decision, the grant of the licence is automatically reinstated, and the Hamilton casino would subsequently go ahead. This is so under the Bill as introduced, and the amendments proposed by this SOP will not change that.'' I still come back to new paragraph (a) and I believe there seems to be a contradiction there; I suppose it is the purpose of the Committee stage of a bill to deal with that. It seems to me that quite outside the explanatory note, the bill reads as retrospective legislation, with all the consequences that that will have.

Before the election, Labour went around saying it would be pragmatic, that it would be economically pragmatic, and that businesses had nothing to fear. It did not take it long. In the very short time that Labour has been leading the Government, it has raised the taxes, and it has increased business costs. The one increased cost that has been confirmed at this stage is that of insurance through the reintroduction of the monopoly of the Accident Compensation Corporation. The costs to the charitable trusts, the church fund-raisers, and the city councils, have increased by the best part of half a million dollars. That is in those sectors alone. I know that it is going to cost the Anglican charitable trust---in the fund-raising that it does for charities, and for the assistance it gives to those in need---over $, more just in insurance levies for its people. Churches do not have that sort of money. Previously they were able to channel that money and those resources to those in need. The increased business costs from accident compensation cannot yet be measured accurately, but they are millions and millions of dollars. Now we have the newly introduced Employment Relations Bill, which will cost businesses again dearly. It will cost jobs, and will reduce the opportunity of expansion and business growth. It will reduce employment. Already interest rates are starting to increase. Already inflation is on the move. It will check the economic growth that the country was experiencing. This has all happened in less than months. Remember, before the election, when Labour went around saying: ``We will be pragmatic---economically pragmatic. Businesses have nothing to fear.'' As a consequence of this months, already business confidence has fallen, as confirmed by a number of recent surveys. Employers and businesses are apprehensive and pessimistic about the new State-decreed economic direction that Labour has taken. I just look around the Chamber to see how many members here were here in . There are five; the rest are all new. The Labour Government inherited an economy that was experiencing a high level of growth. But, in contrast, when the National Government came into power in , the Labour Government had claimed that there was an $ million deficit in the Budget. When we got to the Treasury benches we found that there was a $. billion deficit. There was no Fiscal Responsibility Act in those days. The economy was on the brink of disaster. The country owed $ billion. The Bank of New Zealand was ready to fall over. Contrast that situation with the situation inherited by the Labour Government when it came to power. Already, the growth that was being experienced and the low interest rates that were present are changing. Inflation was very low, prospects were promising, the outlook was positive, and confidence was high. It is not so today. In the last Labour Budget, as I indicated, told nothing that was really true. As I said, the Minister of Finance, Mr Caygill, maintained that he had that $ million surplus. I remember that on the Sunday after the election, during a luncheon, Mr Bolger, as Prime Minister, was summoned to Wellington by Treasury. He was informed of the state of the economy. Members should be able to remember that interest rates during the last years of the Labour Government were in the mid-s, inflation was at or percent, and unemployment had been at its highest level since the Depression. Contrast that situation with what this Government has inherited. The Labour-led Government knew what it would inherit---that is, low inflation, low interest rates, strong economic growth, increasing employment opportunities, and a high level of business confidence. As I have said, already the growth is being choked, interest rates are rising, inflation is increasing, and taxes have gone up. The Labour Government does not appreciate that if taxes are increased, the overall tax take decreases. That was demonstrated when taxes were lowered in the last financial year of the last National-led Government. Taxes were dropped, growth was encouraged, the economy expanded, and the net result was that the overall tax take increased. Today, unemployment is increasing. Taxes have been increased. The tax take will fall. Inflation is increasing. The construction and building industries are experiencing a drop in demand in business. Companies are checking their expansion plans. Not only are they checking them, but they are revising them and looking at relocating. I am sure that members in this Chamber are all aware of a number of major corporates that are looking to move their headquarters to Australia and further overseas. At the moment , young people are in training in apprenticeships. The Labour Government implied to the electorate that it would bring back apprenticeships, because in the eye of the public the standard, base, trade-training regime that was in place was not in apprenticeships. By sowing that seed it was then committed to bringing back apprenticeships, as it promised to do. We now have an additional , to -year-old apprentices to be given apprenticeships at a cost of $ million. My question is whether, given the situation of the trends that have already been developing, there will be jobs for those trainees. I doubt whether there will be jobs for the , who are in training now, let alone the extra , that are planned under the modern apprenticeship programme.

The Opposition has indicated its support for the reform of the waterfront. Opposition members recognise the need for urgent reform now, not in year, years, years, or at some time in the future, as suggested by the Minister of Labour. The reform is needed now; that is why Opposition members have labelled the Bill a Claytons Bill. The Government has backed away from the commitment made by the Minister of Transport that there would be substantial reform on the waterfront. The Minister of Transport has lost the fight. He was gazumped by the Minister of Labour and by his own Parliamentary Under-Secretary. The member for Hamilton West understands the need for reform, and he has probably done his best to try to get that need through to his colleagues in spite of the antagonism that it would arouse in the waterside workers' union. Unfortunately he lost that fight, and the changes that have been made are the changes accepted by the Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Transport, who made an arrangement with the watersiders and said: ``We won't go too far. We won't damage your position. We'll change the words in the legislation, but effectively your position on the wharves will be firmly entrenched and you'll be able to resist all competition from that point.'' That is what is wrong with the Bill, and that is why the Opposition moved several amendments that would have substantially improved the Bill. The Government rejected those amendments. New Zealand has five major ports and six regional ports. Many people would say that one of the problems is that New Zealand has three times as many ports as can be justified by the volume of business that goes across the wharves. In that circumstance, if we are to indulge in the luxury of too many ports, we must make sure that the ports are extremely flexible in their work practices; that they accept that there will not be ships in those ports every day, and that there will not be the same amount of work when no ships are in port as when ships are being loaded. That has been one of the great difficulties. One of the reasons for the establishment of the Waterfront Industry Commission was to try to combat the indulgence that has been put up with over the years of having too many ports. The commission introduced a grandiose system that moved workers, at great cost, from one port to another to try to plug up the gaps. Along the way, the myth was created that those people should be employed permanently on the waterfront, and that they had to be guaranteed regular employment every day of the year. That myth is not perpetuated in most other countries---certainly not in those countries in which the costs on the wharves are substantially lower than those in New Zealand. The member for Maramarua made the point that the Government was dancing on a pin-head. The power of the Minister of Transport is certainly declining in Cabinet, and I think he recognised that his last chance to go down in history as anything other than a totally unsuccessful Minister was to obtain some change. As a consequence, some changes have been put forward that the member for Hamilton West---in a burst of uncharacteristic honesty---referred to as ``tinkering'' with the Labour Relations Act. There was tinkering, and the tinkering was agreed to by the waterside workers' union because it was told that the Government would tinker with the Act. The Government told that union that it would allow it to take out the pool system after April, after which date the union would, effectively, be in a strong negotiating position. The Government said to the union: ``You are the only union that will be negotiating with the employers, and if you can't call the shots in that position there's not much hope for you.'' The waterside workers' union will be extremely good at calling the shots after April, and after October as well, because one matter that is not generally recognised is that the watersiders do not sit only on the employees' side of the table---they sit on the employers' side, as well. The waterside workers' union owns at least one-third of the present stevedoring businesses, so the watersiders will sit on both sides of the negotiating table to present their views as both employers and employees. That is a pretty sweet deal.

The member for Ohariu is a person devoted to the cause of the environment, and I give him full credit for that. However, it does occur to me that he possibly wanted to introduce this Bill when he was the Associate Minister for the Environment but was unable to win that argument. There was ample opportunity at the time if the Labour Government had believed that the issue was important. I think that the balance between environmental matters and economic matters is an important issue, but I would deny that those matters are not debated by the Cabinet, because they are. In commenting on the Bill I want to say that the thought would have been a good one if it had not been happening, but it is happening and the proposal as I read it goes far beyond requiring that there be debate on matters that have environmental significance; it requires scrutiny of all Bills, and that scrutiny would severely stretch the resources of the existing ministry. I am satisfied that the existing provisions of the Environment Act are sufficient to ensure that I am fully and properly advised on all matters affecting environmental issues. The member for Ohariu talked about urban passenger transport. At the time he refers to I was Minister of Transport, not Minister for the Environment. I had a discussion with the Minister for the Environment about the effects of a reduction in a very unsatisfactory method of giving benefit to regional passenger transport---namely, the taxing of motorists around New Zealand whether or not they were within kilometres of a bus route, for the purpose of subsidising those people who used buses or trains in urban areas. That is a sensible thing to do from an environmental point of view. I understand that the Ministry for the Environment was not asked for a comment because the Minister for the Environment understood why the changes were being made and had talked about them with me. The changes were made not to reduce the flow of money into the three major metropolitan areas but because we had a very blunt instrument with no cause and effect relationship to the person sitting alone in a car in Lambton Quay in the rush hour when a perfectly good train or bus service is able to transport that person from home to a place of work and back again. The Government has challenged the city councils in Auckland, Wellington, and Christchurch to consider methods by which they can persuade one-person car users who drive their cars into the central city at peak hours that they should not continue with that practice. I have suggested that such people should be penalised if the city council considers that their actions cause problems. I certainly consider that their actions cause congestion problems and environmental problems. The one way in which the message can be put across to the person in the car is that there is a cost and that that person will bear the cost and that part of the cost will go towards providing a better alternative bus or train service. Enlightened cities in Norway, Sweden, and Singapore adopt that approach of providing a market-driven message to the person causing the problem that: ``Here is a problem and you will help pay for its solution.''. That is why for very good environmental reasons the Government has moved away from its broad brush, outmoded, blanket approach of taking money from every car user throughout New Zealand and has suggested that, if the problem is just in the metropolitan areas, that is where the solution lies. If the problem and the solution are tied together in the minds of the people causing the problem, progress will be made. It would not have helped one iota to have the Ministry for the Environment commenting on that matter. The Minister was well informed throughout the discussions that he had with the Minister of Transport of the time about the objectives, and he agreed with them. The member for Ohariu talked about two papers that had been released by the Ministry of Commerce and by Treasury that commented on the Government's target of a percent reduction in greenhouse gases. A meeting was held today to discuss climate change and the way that the Government would meet its targets. About people attended that meeting at which the papers released by the Ministry of Commerce and by Treasury were discussed. However, the base paper was provided by the Ministry for the Environment. This legislation would not have changed the position one iota. The Ministry for the Environment had already presented a paper on the issue. The meeting was chaired by myself, and the discussion was engendered by the Ministry of Commerce and by Treasury but other departments were able to comment on those issues, and they did. But at the end of the day I am pleased to say that the private sector groups, the ministry's representatives, and the Ministers present were able to say that there was common ground that would be used in formulating the Government's policy to help us to move towards a reduction in greenhouse gases and also to provide the platform from which we could talk to the rest of the world at the United Nations conference next year. The legislation would not have affected that situation one iota. The member for Ohariu talked about Lake Manapouri. If the Minister for the Environment and the ministry believe that we should comment on this issue, we will, but the effect of the proposal by the member for Ohariu is not that just issues and legislation that have an obvious environmental significance should be commented on---which either the Minister, the department, or both, decide should be commented on---but the proposal is that all Government legislation should be commented on. In other words the Minister for the Environment, the Minister in charge of the Bill of Rights, will have to approve all legislation. On the Order Paper under Government orders of the day are listed the Immigration Amendment Bill, the National Library Amendment Bill, the Dog Control and Hydatids Amendment Bill, the Land Transfer Amendment Bill, the Maori Education Foundation Amendment Bill, the Ombudsmen Amendment Bill (No. ), and the Civil Aviation Amendment Bill. Perhaps there should be an environmental comment on the last of those Bills, although that is probably marginal. One could go right through the pieces of legislation on the Order Paper, but it would be stretching one's imagination to say that there is a reason for the Ministry for the Environment to be cluttered up by having to comment to the Minister on every one of those Bills. The member for Ohariu, who was the Associate Minister for the Environment in the Labour Government, knows that the Ministry for the Environment is not large. It has a specialised work-load that is carefully scrutinised. It does not waste any time and it is under some pressure. The Government has not reduced the ministry's staffing, which is much the same as it was under the Labour Government. However, the member will know quite well that if the Government accepted his recommendation as he has propounded it the ministry staff would have to be doubled to consider the effects of all aspects of Government policy upon the sustainability of the environment---all those issues that are on the Order Paper. Any one of them---if one stretched one's imagination far enough or long enough---could have some impact on the environment. I suppose that changes in superannuation could have an impact because some environmental organisations say that they are not receiving the donations that they were receiving in the past. It is a small impact, but nevertheless the impact is there. However, I do not believe that it is the function of a specialised ministry to consider all legislation. That would be total nonsense and a waste of time. If that was the proposal that the member for Ohariu put to the Labour Government, I can understand why it did not go ahead. It is not a goer, for that reason. There could probably have been some merit in the proposal for matters that had obvious environmental connotations to be referred to the ministry if he could say that that was not happening. That is one part of the Bill in which a change of that kind could have been of some merit. It would be quite impractical to take on board the suggestions made by the member for Ohariu even though the point he made that there needs to be an environmental input into issues with environmental connotations is one that I agree with. I argue that devices are in place under this Government to ensure that that happens. There have been occasions when the Ministry for the Environment did not appear to have been involved in an issue. When I have noted that, I have asked whether it had been involved. If it had not been involved, I have asked for it to be involved. There may be some occasions when the member for Ohariu would like to ask me whether the ministry has been involved in a particular issue, and direct me to it. That is an eminently more sensible and practical way of ensuring that the ministry exercises its responsibility as guardian of environmental policy, than to put in a blanket provision that requires substantial amounts of staff time, which would have to be obtained from some other function, to look at a range of legislation that has very little relevance at all. The existing Act is capable of doing the job that it was intended to do. It advises the Minister on all aspects of environmental administration, including policies for influencing the management of natural and fiscal resources and ecosystems to achieve the objectives of the Act. That is a broad statement in the Act. It also seeks to solicit and obtain information from any source to conduct and supervise the research necessary for the formulation of advice to Government on environmental policies. Those are broad terms of reference. Finally, it generally provides advice on matters relating to the environment. The ministry is capable of doing that. I hope that its function can expand to meet some of the critical issues that were not dealt with under the Labour Government and that are now being dealt with under great pressure. I should not want the excellent work being done on key issues to be cluttered up by having to consider numerous pieces of legislation that have little relevance. There would perhaps be some merit in having the select committee scrutinise the legislation to ensure that the mechanisms that the member is concerned about are in place. It is particularly good because the Bill has been around for years. It just about made it during the term of the former National Government, and it had several false starts during the time of the previous Government, so I am very pleased to be able to introduce it. The Bill replaces the provisions relating to ship registration contained in Part XII of the Shipping and Seamen Act and thereby establishes for the first time a completely independent New Zealand ship register. It contains important and long-overdue changes that will ensure that true nationality is conferred on ships that are registered in New Zealand. The qualifications for owning a New Zealand ship under the existing legislation are quite deeply rooted in the past---so much so that being New Zealand - owned is not a requirement for current New Zealand registration. Instead, as long as the owner is a British subject or a company that has been established and is operating under Commonwealth law, an overseas-owned-and-operated ship may be registered in New Zealand. That reflects the concept of Commonwealth ships as provided for in the Commonwealth Merchant Shipping Agreement of . The effect of that agreement was that New Zealand's national ship register has been little more than an extension of the United Kingdom register, which was regulated under the provisions of the United Kingdom Merchant Shipping Act . Those provisions are still preserved in the Shipping and Seamen Act . There is a bit of catching up to do in terms of modernising our shipping legislation.

I move, That the Civil Aviation Amendment Bill be introduced. The central purpose of this Bill is to empower the making of percent refunds to persons in the aviation industry who have paid charges under the Civil Aviation Charges Regulations . Members will recall that, with effect from March , this Government reduced by percent the charges that the previous Government had imposed upon the industry. That was done because this Government, while supporting the general user-pays principle, was extremely critical of the way in which those charges had been imposed. I must say that the industry had been even more critical of the way in which they had been imposed. In particular, the Government believed that it had to move to meet industry concern about the level of the new charges and their impact on an industry that was already under very severe pressure. The percent reduction in fees and charges effected by the Civil Aviation Charges Regulations was an interim response---and I emphasise that it was an interim response---to that concern. The Government had wanted to make immediate refunds of percent of all charges that had been paid by the industry before the coming into force of the new charges. Unfortunately, legal advice was that such funds required empowering legislation. As I have mentioned, the percent reduction in aviation fees and charges was only an interim response to the concerns expressed by the industry. I am pleased to report to the House that Cabinet has approved a revised scale of aviation fees and charges. This new scale reflects the important contribution that the aviation industry has made through its representatives on the consultative group on cost recovery, and I must congratulate the industry on the way in which it has been prepared to work with the Government in trying to arrive at a solution to a very thorny problem. The consultative group reported to me earlier this year. As a result, regulations incorporating that new scale will be before Cabinet very shortly. I trust that they will further strengthen the relationship between the Government and the industry that this Government has established, after the destruction wrought on that relationship by the previous Administration mainly because of the precipitate way in which it acted in introducing a new charging regime. The Government has also signalled its intention to co-operate with the industry through the amendments it proposes in this Bill for section of the Civil Aviation Act. In its report to me earlier this year the consultative group on cost recovery also recommended that all necessary civil aviation regulations should be amended or revoked as soon as possible to reduce the costs that were being incurred by the aviation industry. However, the regulation-making power under the Civil Aviation Act is deliberately drawn very narrowly, because it was envisaged at the time that the Act was passed that no further amendments to the civil aviation regulations would be made until the new civil aviation rules came into force. Unfortunately it will be some time before a comprehensive set of civil aviation rules can be put into place. I think that it is imperative that the Government have the ability to make needed reforms to regulations without having to wait for the rules to come into force. Accordingly, the Bill provides for the repeal of section of the Act and for its replacement by a provision that will clarify the ability of the Government to amend civil aviation regulations. I think that that is a very important part of the Bill. In proposing this amendment the Government has been very conscious of the criticism by people, both within the industry and elsewhere, of the width of the regulation-making powers in the previous Civil Aviation Act. The new regulation-making powers contained in clause of the Bill are, in consequence, very tightly circumscribed. Regulations may be made only for those purposes for which an ordinary rule may be made under the new Civil Aviation Act. So there is a very strict limit on the way in which they can be used. The regulation-making power is further restricted by clause of the Bill, which provides that all civil aviation regulations will expire years after the Bill comes into force. This timetable reflects the expected coming into force of the new system of civil aviation rules. It underlines the Government's commitment to the principles embodied in the Civil Aviation Act. These principles were, of course, modelled on the recommendations of the widely respected Swedavia-McGregor report into the aviation industry. When mentioning that report it is timely to recall that one of its central recommendations was the establishment of a stand-alone civil aviation authority---a recommendation that inexplicably the previous Government rejected. This Government is truly committed to the establishment of a stand-alone civil aviation authority. There has already been widespread consultation with the industry on the form that a stand-alone authority might take, and I expect that the necessary legislation will be introduced into the House before the end of the year. Having noted the central features of the Bill before the House I should point out that the opportunity has also been taken in the Bill to clarify and correct minor various technical matters that arose out of our experience of some months' operation of the new Civil Aviation Act. Briefly, clause of the Bill amends section of the Act to make that section more consistent with the rest of the Act. Clause rectifies some incorrect cross-references in the Act. Clause clarifies the powers of the Secretary for Transport to delegate powers that arise under the Civil Aviation Regulations or the Civil Aviation (Security) Regulations to persons who are not employees of the Ministry of Transport. The practice of delegating certain aviation safety functions to persons and organisations outside the State is common throughout the world and has been a feature of our own system for many years. Therefore the Government is not proposing something new. The proposed provisions provide a means of increasing the resources and expertise available to the safety authority at a very much reduced cost. I think that at this point this is a very important consideration. As the delegations are of powers under regulations that will be eventually subsumed into the new civil aviation rules, they too expire within years. The Government is not considering anything that will be in place for a long period. All of the conditions that I have been talking about have a -year time-span. The other technical amendment contained in the Bill is to be found in clause . That amendment corrects a minor oversight in section of the Transport Accident Investigation Commission Act . The measures contained in this legislation are specifically designed to enhance the Government's improved relationship with the aviation industry. I am very pleased about the way in which that relationship is developing. I cannot say that it is totally harmonious, but at least we have worked through some of the rough spots that seemed to cloud the relationship in the past, and it has laid the groundwork for a less bureaucratic and more cost-efficient administration for aviation safety. The provisions in the Bill anticipate the Government's imminent creation of a stand-alone civil aviation authority and an equitable charging system for the industry. The important issue about this more equitable system is that it has been developed after some months of consultation with the industry representatives who considered the reason that we needed to carry out the particular function, who should be responsible for paying and, in the end, whether they were to be responsible for paying, and the way in which that cost should be allocated according to the service provided. There are very few countries in the world that depend on civil aviation to the extent that New Zealand does. The changes embodied in this legislation are in the interests of the aviation community and industry customers---hence they are in the interests of New Zealand as a whole. I commend the Civil Aviation Amendment Bill to the House.

It is time for this Government to think again. I say that because I have had a chance today to examine aspects of this legislation. It is stupid, inconsiderate, and heartless of the Government even to bring this Bill into the House, and it is even more stupid to allow it to go through its second reading. Jenny Shipley, in her speech, put up straw people and knocked them down by making accusations regarding speeches made by members of the Labour Opposition. She said that we are irresponsible and do not care. That is the sort of speech Jenny Shipley should be making to her own caucus and to her own Minister, not to Opposition members in this House. Opposition members are concerned about women in violent relationships, and are concerned about doing something effective about that. I want to tell the senior whip that the question is this: if Government members are saying that they are concerned about this, too, then why are they introducing retrospective legislation to go against a sensible decision of the Court of Appeal? Quite clearly, the Bill is being introduced to avoid additional costs. Government members contemplate that if the decision of the court is allowed to stand as a precedent, then we will have women lining up right, left, and centre saying: ``I've got bruises all over me. I am entitled to receive a domestic purposes payment because I am a battered partner.'' I think members on that side of the House should know that, apart from this issue being of major concern to women, it is also a major concern to men. I say that because in my own experience, as a young kid, I saw my own mother in that kind of relationship---being beaten up every day. That was at a time when things were worse than they are now in terms of what is provided. I would like to think that this can be effectively dealt with. I think that the court's decision gives us a way, in fact, effectively to do that. This Government might say that the criterion of a woman living in a violent relationship does not entitle her to a form of assistance in terms of the domestic purposes benefit. I say that most men who put women in that situation in those relationships are stand-over merchants. They beat up on them and quite often, as a result of that, part of their momentum is to prevent the woman from having any income of her own. They want women in a subservient relationship. They want women in a situation where they are dependent and do not have their own income. That situation is totally unacceptable. If this legislation introduces what is called an emergency benefit, a downgrading of the benefit entitlement to a situation in which a woman receives a benefit for a -month period, it is wrong. In many cases the abuse of women in relationships is ongoing. It is wrong to discriminate against women with this legislation. Annette King pointed out in her speech that if the staff of the Income Support Service are responsible and active in the area of counselling women, there will be a backlash from violent men such as Stewart Murray Wilson---the example she used---and staff will be intimidated. I do not think we should be putting the staff of the Income Support Service in that position. It is totally unfair and extremely dangerous. It does not in any way address the problem itself. I expect that when this legislation goes to the select committee it will generate a tremendous response from women's organisations---organisations like Women's Refuge that deal with women who are battered and mistreated. There will be a very widespread response to this. I am certain that, after reading this Bill and listening to the arguments that have poured forth today, the Government will meet with overwhelming opposition to this Bill. The arguments put forward by Government members do not make any sense. Both sides can accuse each other of not being concerned about women or of not caring about women in situations where they are being battered or beaten or treated violently. I say that is not the argument, because I do not believe that anybody in the House at present condones that at all. The question is how that should be best dealt with. The question is whether a person in those circumstances should be denied their right to receive State assistance in terms of a benefit. That is what it is really all about. I cannot see that any argument at all that the Government has used justifies the introduction of this Bill. It can be seen only as a move by the Government because it has this tremendous fear that women are suddenly going to misuse this provision, that women will get somebody to put a couple of oranges in a plastic bag or something, whirl it around, and beat them over the head with it, beat them about so that they have bruises on them, so they can then demonstrate that they have been mistreated and convince the staff of the Income Support Service that they should be receiving the domestic purposes benefit. I think that is stupid. I think that underrates the intelligence of women in this country. I think it panders to the redneck attitude of this country. We know that in many respects there are people out there who will feed off this kind of thing; they will feed off it because it suits them to do so. We know that there are strong prejudices against people who live in circumstances in which they are quite often treated violently, and in situations that those people with their prejudices do not understand. They think that those sorts of relationships are just made up and put on. I do not believe that anybody would actually orchestrate abuse under this particular legislation, or in any kind of situation that would allow them---in circumstances other than if they are genuinely being mistreated and abused---to try to convince the department that they have been beaten up when they have not. This House has to realise that people out there are getting sick and tired of this Government singling out people in our community, different groups in our community---such as women, in this situation---and being seen to beat up on them. If Gerry Brownlee---or any other male still present on the National Party side of the House---is going to make the next speech, I challenge him to join me in rejecting this legislation. Most men do not condone violence against women. Most men do not want to see women mistreated. I abhor men who mistreat women. Gerry Brownlee might think that that is some joke, but to me it is not. Having, in my life's experience, seen my mother treated in a way in which a lot of women in marriage and partnership relationships are treated, I do not wish that on any woman.

I want to quote a few figures. The Tasmanians started farming Atlantic salmon in sea-pens in . They produced tonnes last year, and will produce tonnes this year, and tonnes by . I want to talk about the science policy, which I addressed briefly in the estimates yesterday. I think the user-pays, cost-recovery approach that the Government is implementing is very good for the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, and for other science-related Government departments in New Zealand. It is something that is working well. For example, the Forest Research Institute has achieved its target for cost recovery over a -year period within year. That result indicates the potential for directing research and development efforts into areas in which people are willing to pay---although the policy is not sufficient in itself, as it does not address the question of funding basic and subjective research. It is a matter the member for Tamaki happened to mention yesterday---quite correctly---and those of my colleagues who said that he did not know anything about science were wrong; he knows a bit about lily-breeding. There needs to be a funding mechanism for basic research, and I believe that that matter should be separated out from the providers of research services. The way to do it is to have a Government-funding organisation for basic science to decide which areas should be funded. Funds should be allocated on application from research organisations---whether they be in Government departments, the universities, or the private sector. That is a mechanism that the Government should consider; it would be an improvement on the present system. I do not believe that the Beattie report suggestion for a science and technology research council goes nearly far enough. It is only playing with the basic problem. We need to have a funding mechanism that will allow the full play of the creative energies of the science community.

There is much new material in the legislation as it emerges from the Committee. I shall touch on a few matters that Opposition members have chosen to ignore. The changes introduced by the supplementary order paper exempt the first $, of redundancy payments from liability for fringe-benefit tax. The legislation as reported back from the select committee included a list of exemptions. It is important to study the list to see what it relates to. The provision has been included for the clear reason that the Government does not want to create a loophole by which retirement allowances can be used to replace superannuation allowances in order to avoid taxation. The Government realised that a grey area separates retirement allowances from redundancy payments. The list sets out items that are not exempt from fringe-benefit tax and several items are set out that are not true redundancies. The Bill provides that redundancy payments mean payments other than retiring allowances on the occasion of termination of employment, and that excludes seasonal workers from the immediate definition unless the position is contingent on the termination of the normal operation that gives them seasonal employment. It is interesting to note that the Opposition turned round in the Committee, opposed that approach, and voted against the clauses relating to separating redundancy payments from retirement allowances, and thereby voted for a fringe-benefit tax on all redundancy payments. That was an about-turn on the part of the Opposition and a sad reflection on its inability to arrive at a position on the legislation that is based on principle. Either the Opposition is in favour of taxing redundancy payments or it is against such taxation. From the way Opposition members voted---as distinct from the way they spoke at the select committee hearings---it appears that they are in favour of taxing all redundancy payments. The Government is not in favour of that, and it has included provisions that exempt genuine redundancy payments up to a level of $,, or one-third of income over a period of years, whichever is the lower, from fringe-benefit tax liability. Several important changes to the provisional tax provisions were made by a supplementary order paper, but we are still left with provisional tax provisions that will bring in an extra $ million in the coming financial year, and that is an important part of the whole package. If the Government does not get the money in, as the Minister of Revenue is so fond of telling the House, it cannot give it out, and it is giving it out wholesale in the legislation through the slashing of income tax rates for ordinary wage and salary earners to the lowest levels that have applied in New Zealand since World War II. The Opposition should support that provision. The Opposition should put its weight---small as it might be---behind the Government's efforts to reduce tax rates. Opposition members should show their support for that procedure by not putting the third readings of the Bills to a vote. The new provisional tax regime will make it possible for companies to estimate their tax liability near the end of the financial year.

I move, That the House take note of miscellaneous business. People throughout New Zealand feel absolutely betrayed by recent developments in health policy. It is especially true that people from smaller communities and provincial centres feel betrayed by the Government. They have every reason to feel betrayed in that way, given the enormous discrepancy between National's pre-election promises and its post-election performance and the really frightening news coming of planned closures of hospitals and cut-backs in services in rural areas in particular. In addition, the lack of consultation has revealed an absolutely breathtaking cheek on the part of the Minister of Health and her colleagues. The unfortunate prospect of having private patients jumping queues on public hospital waiting-lists haunts this country. It contributes to a feeling of insecurity that low-income and modest-income families have when they contemplate the chances of themselves or their children getting simple surgery or treatment in public hospitals and facilities---given that they cannot afford to pay to move up the queue, or to get into a private hospital, or to get the private consultation that is the key to getting on to the queue for an operation in a public hospital. Prior to the election, National Party members were telling people that Labour's prognostications and predictions that the so-called health reforms put in jeopardy the level of services that rural communities were entitled to expect---and to which they were accustomed---were just scaremongering. Now the truth is emerging. The truth is that, if anything, Labour understated the risks to public health services for the people of New Zealand, and in particular to people in rural communities and provincial centres. That certainly includes the people of Timaru, South Canterbury, and North Otago, in whom I have a particular interest. In Oamaru the hospital services are under threat, despite a particular piece of propaganda---a pamphlet put out by the member for Waitaki prior to the election. It is a very stirring thing, which I would like to quote from. I quote the member for Waitaki: ``I thank all those who marched in the great march,''---from time to time he confuses himself with Chairman Mao---``those who signed the petition I have presented in the House of Representatives,''---that is a making a virtue of necessity, as he had no option but to present the petition in the House. He could not get out of it, so he has tried to imply that he was its author, rather than the gofer who took it from one place to another. He continued, thanking ``those who attended public meetings,''---they roasted him, and he thanks them for it---``and those who helped negotiate an acceptable outcome for the benefit of the community.'' Those who negotiated an acceptable outcome for the benefit of that community have recently had some more to say on that matter, because that acceptable outcome was put in the trash can once the election was out of the way. Nevertheless I want to quote a few more things from the wonderful message put out by the member for Waitaki, who at that stage was starting to feel a bit worried about his majority---and events proved that he had every cause to be worried. If he had not put out this litany of misinformation it is very unlikely he would still be a member of this House. It was an orchestrated litany of misleading misinformation, and the member for Waitaki should cringe and blush in embarrassment. He cannot attribute the pamphlet's authorship to anybody else. He continued: ``North Otago, a community working together ensuring we all have a future''. It is just all too plain whose future it was that he was trying to ensure, and now that he has ensured it for a couple of years he has forgotten all those promises. I want to quote further from the report. This wonderful publication states: ``Agreement has been reached between the Otago CHE, the Southern Regional Health Authority''---all people appointed by the Government and not likely to forget the need to get the member for Waitaki re-elected if they ever want to get reappointed again---``and the North Otago community leaders, after negotiations over the past months on health services.'' I refer to those promises that were made, because they were pretty considerable. They involved the building of a new unit for surgery in Oamaru, a guarantee that percent of surgery would continue to be performed in Oamaru and that there would be two surgeons, and so on---all those new facilities. But now Healthcare Otago chairman, Peter Rae, cannot give any assurances as of the th of May, which is well after the election.

I will not speak long on this part at all, but I want to refer to clause (b) whereby this Bill has to be consistent with the Treaty of Waitangi (Fisheries Claims) Settlement Act . This is where we reconcile our ambitions for the fisheries management and this Bill, with our obligations to the Maori treaty partner. There were some complications. Not all New Zealanders, unfortunately even today, accept in the spirit intended, the Treaty of Waitangi fisheries claims settlement, or indeed the treaty itself. Various rather belligerent statements were made in the course of hearing evidence that this one or that one would not tolerate Maori being treated any differently from other New Zealanders in respect of fishing rights and so on. I would just like to say that, so far as this member of Parliament is concerned, there is a clear and complete distinction between the role of Maori in terms of the treaty settlement and the role of everyone else except the Crown. To me the settlement means that Maori own a proportion of the fisheries. Everyone else who has a quota or annual catch entitlement or whatever do not own the resource. They have a property right to exploit it for the time being, but they do not own it in the way that a sovereign nation owns it. To me the settlement means that Maori have in this case percent ownership. That is on all fours with the Crown's ownership of the resource. The Crown and Maori went to the treaty and negotiated as equal partners and got a deal that had them as equal partners. No one else involved in the fishery has that same status. To me, all those arguments about whether it was right about Maori aggregating quota, the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission aggregating quota, and so on, failed to understand that basic concept that Maori are the co-owners of the resource. Everybody else has a quota entitlement to exploit for the time being. It is like being the tenant or the owner of a property. I think that if New Zealanders can see it in that light then they will find it easier to accept the structure that we have here and, indeed, the treaty fisheries settlement itself. I hope that is so, but I would like the Minister to confirm that the Government's view is as I have given it myself.

The health services remain sick in the face of the failed health reforms. We know what went wrong with the health reforms. Government members read too many economic textbooks and said: ``The story is that we bring in competition. We separate the providers from the funders, and we bring in competition.'' Well, they have set up a very, very expensive system to enable them to call for tenders and to administer contracts, but unfortunately no competitors have come out of the woodwork. This is an urgent social matter that requires the attention of Government, and it is not getting it in this package. The Government is doing nothing to assist the ever-growing number of people who have to travel further to get treatment at a hospital in one of the major cities. Nothing has been done to restore accountability to the public health system. Schools and hospitals need more money and they are not getting it. Children need help and they are not getting it. We will not penalise them because the head of the household is sick, injured, or unemployed. The United New Zealand leader, I note, picked up the code words of the Tories today and used them. He talked about decent, hard-working New Zealanders. This is how he justifies supporting a package that discriminates against the children of sick, invalid, or unemployed parents. He talked about rewards for initiative. We are back to the s when we had the deserving and the undeserving poor, and the leader of the United New Zealand Party wants to pick the difference. My word, those principles did not last long when there was a Cabinet seat in the offing. Labour has other priorities too. We have as a priority our senior citizens, who made some of the greatest sacrifices to turn this economy round. When Labour was faced with a deficit of percent of gross domestic product---$ billion in today's terms---the senior citizens of New Zealand had to endure the imposition of the taxation surcharge. Then National came in and slashed benefits, and the senior citizens had to endure that. It is time they got a pay-back.

I have done that in the case of Landcorp Farming and the clincher for me is the conclusion that there are some things that a large corporate farm can readily do that the traditional family farm cannot easily do. We have only one large corporate farm in New Zealand and I believe it is very much in the public interest that it be retained as a large corporate farm. That cannot occur if it is broken up into small pieces and knocked off for some short-term capital gain. Only a property with large numbers of animals, closely co-ordinated, can indulge in the sort of large-scale breeding schemes in which Land Corporation has been a world leader. It is not practical to get that close co-ordination of large numbers of animals simply among co-operating small farms. It has often been tried and it is very difficult to sustain. No one in this country has ever sustained it with the sort of numbers that Landcorp has been able to put together. The Landcorp Romney flock, and its Angus herd, add value to the whole industry in this country, and that is a very good reason that Landcorp Farming should not be broken up for sale, as the National Party caucus had apparently decided it should be in . I want to dwell on some of the virtues of the product of Landcorp Farming's group breeding schemes, and consider, for instance, the Angus cattle, which have not been held in thrall by the fashions of the show ring. In fact, they have been unique in their unsusceptibility to those fashions. The Angus cattle of Landcorp Farming are objectively screened for the traits that have traditionally been important in the hill country of New Zealand---their maternal ability, their fertility, and their freedom from calving difficulty. Landcorp Farming is simply not following the fashion of the day, which, at the moment, is to try to breed Angus as if they were Charolais or Simmental---cattle perhaps too big to survive easily a hard winter on a hard hill without expensive supplementary feed and, certainly, with calves too big to be born without assistance that are totally inappropriate in a situation when assistance simply cannot be provided. All of this is done in a ludicrous attempt to compete with Simmental and Charolais---terminal sire breeds---in the meat and wool cup section at the Royal Show. It spells disaster, and it is not something that exists only in my imagination---it has all happened before. The stud breeders made the breed ridiculously short, small, and fat in a sort of ludicrous attempt to slavishly follow the lead of the Perth show---that is, Perth in Scotland. The breeders used imported Scottish bulls that were so small and short they had to be mated in the yards with little boxes in the race so they could stand up high enough to actually reproduce the species. That is absolutely true! That is the sort of nonsense the stud industry got up to. That stud industry needs some honest people like those in Landcorp Farming, which has some professional population geneticists in-house, to keep the breed honest, to keep the industry honest, and to provide somewhere for practical farmers to turn when the stud breeders go off the rails. The Romney is the same. I do not believe if Landcorp flocks had not been in existence with its massive group breeding schemes that the Romney would have survived or responded adequately to the challenge of the new synthetic breeds like Coopworth and Perendale, which did, after all, lead the way in the improvement of performance traits for some time until, first and foremost, Landcorp Farming demonstrated that it was possible by screening large population numbers, by objective measurement, and by rational selection procedures to match the performance gains available in the shorter term by crossbreeding. I think that that demonstration gave Romney breeders in New Zealand the confidence to go ahead and improve the breed and respond. That is the sort of competition one gets from a large viable corporate farm with an ethos, I may say, of public service---which is not something to be dismissed lightly. That is a real argument for having a bit of State ownership here and there. I am not suggesting the State own all the land---that would be ridiculous---but I do believe that there is room in New Zealand for one corporate farm with an ethos of public service. The only chance we have to maintain that is Landcorp Farming, and we should do so. I would like the Minister to respond to those comments by, perhaps, letting us know what his current thinking is. I do not imagine that much rational thought comes on this from the caucus as a whole.

The Minister of Agriculture, although I acknowledge that is not his official title any more, has backtracked and been defeated on that matter. The roading reforms have vanished. On Tuesday the Government said: ``No new frigate.'' Talk about decisive! Indecisive would be the only description. It is completely the tail wagging the dog. The sale of Solid Energy was another U-turn. The Resource Management Act reforms were another non-event---big talk and then nothing delivered. There it is. In September the Prime Minister said: ``You will know by Christmas whether we are able to deliver and whether we are characterised by progress or paralysis.'' Well, I think that question has been well and truly answered---it is paralysis. Government members are in election mode. Look at what is going out through the letter boxes of rural New Zealand: an -page National Party propaganda sheet, and it is paid for with taxpayers' dollars. It is paid for entirely by the taxpayer. This publication is a misappropriation of public money. It was paid for with taxpayers' money from start to finish. What is in this publication? Is there valuable information in this publication? Let me quote from it: ``National is working''; ``National working hard''; ``Priority for National''---this is very informative; ``National is committed'', the word ``committed'' is in there twice; ``National's values''; ``National's goal''; and ``National is publishing''. It goes on to state: ``National is putting the emphasis''; ``National is determined''; and ``National is the only party that can deliver''. Why does the taxpayer have to pay for this rubbish? How does the Government justify dunning the taxpayer to pay for this blatant, ignorant, party-political propaganda? Just in case anyone who gets the publication does not know who put it out, it has seven National Party logos in it. This is an election pamphlet. It is paid for entirely by taxpayers' dollars. There is not a shred of integrity in that Government. Government members do not know the difference between their own money and public money. The reason for the insufficient notice was that the Government fell over in its discussions, its promotion, of its previous tax Bill. The Government thought it had the numbers and it turned out that it did not. It had to collapse the Order Paper relating to the tax Bill, because it did not have the confidence of the House to proceed with it. The Government lost the confidence of the House on an important tax measure, so it rushed in the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (Restructuring) Bill without proper preparation, without a competent Minister sitting in the chair, and without giving the Minister who was sitting in the chair a reasonable briefing. He did not know what he was doing. He could not answer the questions and he had officials write out answers to the questions while he was in the chair, and then wondered why Labour was repeating the questions in the absence of any answers. The Minister should not complain about wasting taxpayers' money! When we finished consideration of the Bill, just after o'clock in the afternoon, the Government had no more business ready to proceed, so it sent us all home. We all went home an hour early because the Government had not prepared any more business. And the Minister complains about wasting taxpayers' money! Perhaps he would care to explain to the listening taxpayers how much money he thinks the Government saved by sending members home early because it had no work ready to proceed shortly after o'clock in the afternoon. Did we save a lot of money? Perhaps the -odd employees around this place said: ``Oh, well, we will chuck our hour's pay back into the pot for the poor old Government, because its members cannot even take a pay rise. The Government is so hard up that we will forgo an hour's pay when we have nothing to do, because the Government ran out of business in the House in the afternoon.'' If the Minister does not like the sound of that, he should not raise such spurious points of debate. This is a classic little Bill. There were no public submissions, but it was not because members of the public were not interested. Some of the , loyal public servants who cease to be public servants as a result of this measure, and who will have to take their chances in the private sector, will not have jobs at the end of it. While at the end of the day we believe that reasonable terms have been extracted from the Government for the support and care of these people, we know that that support was not given willingly and that it was necessary for the Opposition to make an issue about this as it went through its various stages in the House. Despite there having been no public submissions to the select committee, the Government nevertheless introduced a supplementary order paper with numerous amendments, which just goes to show once again that this Government does not know what it is trying to do. It amends its own legislation even when it receives no submissions from the public or interested parties. The supplementary order paper made a couple of interesting provisions. One provision was to change the commencement date of this Bill, from November to November. The actual change made legal by this legislation was carried out on November as originally planned, even though it had not been sanctioned by Parliament---in other words, the Government acted without legality in this matter, and is now retrospectively making it legal by the passage of this Bill. This is stuff that even the Rt Hon. Sir Robert Muldoon would not have tried. He got into enough trouble in the case of Fitzgerald v Muldoon when he was told in no uncertain terms by the Chief Justice of New Zealand that no matter how high and mighty members of the Government might be, they are still bound by the rule of law in this nation. That lesson has not sunk into the skulls of the Ministers in charge of this Bill. That is to say that the Minister for Food, Fibre, Biosecurity and Border Control and the Minister for State Owned Enterprises will, briefly at least, have charge of these new companies before the Government privatises them. If it was wrong for the late right honourable gentleman to act without the sanction of Parliament in a matter such as this, it is equally wrong for the present Ministers to have done so. Here we are, on November, rushing through at the very last minute a Bill to make legal on November something that actually occurred on November, when, by press release, it was announced that the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry ceased to provide the services it is required by law to provide, and the two new corporate entities picked up those tasks. The next matter that I will refer to is the naming of these new companies, which was changed by way of supplementary order paper in the Committee stage. That also is rather symptomatic of this Government, which is so preoccupied with its own image and so little concerned with plain English and common sense. In the one case the name of the company is AgriQuality New Zealand Ltd. There is a capital ``Q'' in the middle of that word, just to prove that the Government does not believe in plain English, plain spelling, and reasonable tradition. The Government wants to be trendy so it has put a capital letter in the middle of the word. The other company is to be called Asure New Zealand Ltd. Asure in this unique case is spelt with one ``s''. This is a Government that saves the taxpayers money by economising on the letter `s' when it spells the word ``asure''. Frankly, it could do better. There are members of the Government who are embarrassed by this. I have seen official correspondence that spells this company's name as Assurance New Zealand Ltd, with two ``s's'' where indeed there is but one ``s'' in this word. However, this is the company name that is to be in the legislation---Asure New Zealand, spelt with one ``s''. I think in a way that that sums up the whole performance of this sorry Government.

I have some pleasure in rising to speak to this Bill, because it is the penultimate move in the search for reconciliation and settlement of past wrongs done to the Ngai Tahu people. I am pleased that this Bill marks the return of the Tutaepatu Lagoon in North Canterbury, because in so doing, as I understand it, it revokes the classification of the lagoon as a wildlife management reserve---a rather odd designation. It vests the lagoon in the Ngai Tahu runanga, freehold. It will be free of any existing encumbrance, except there will still be a public walkway across the south-eastern corner. The area being returned will be free of any obligation to create a marginal strip---a Queen's Chain. That is because, obviously, to undo the Crown's wrongful retention of the lagoon it has to be returned without any new encumbrance or new condition such as the creation of a marginal strip. There is the revocation of certain existing reserves, and there is provision for the declaration, classification, and vesting of a new recreational reserve, subject to certain conditions. The lagoon is included in the management plan for the new reserve. The whole object of this exercise was to build a basis of goodwill, and I say to the House that that goodwill may well be necessary, because we have not reached the end of the process whereby the final deed of settlement with Ngai Tahu is signed. If the Minister in charge of that process persists in his adamant approach that there will be no changes in the deed as a result of select committee hearings, no matter what evidence is brought to the committee, no matter how compelling that evidence may be, then he makes a mockery of Parliament's processes, and it will take a bit of goodwill to get through that situation without damage being done. So I suggest Government members think again about the way that Parliament is being used in this matter, and remember that Parliament is sovereign in New Zealand. It is not up to anyone, including Ministers, to come to Parliament and say what a select committee must or must not find when it hears evidence on a Bill before the House. We note that the lagoon itself is not included in the Bill, and we note that there are significant changes.
