When it comes to the great apes, it was interesting because it was pointed out to us that in the particular case of chimpanzees and bonobos their DNA is . percent identical to that of humans. Great apes have the linguistic skills of a -year-old human and the general intelligence of a to -year-old human. Most non-human hominids are as intelligent and emotionally sensitive as young human children. There are many other attributes, behavioural and mental, that can be cited that demonstrate a close genetic relationship and similarity to human beings, including self-awareness, self-control, a sense of time, the capability of relating to others, and blaming others for one's own mistakes. I move, That the House take note of a definite matter of urgent public importance. The first thing to be said about the presumed illegal introduction of the rabbit calicivirus is that no one who believes in the rule of law can condone it. But to move on and to deal with the situation that now exists, we must start by facing facts, however unpalatable they may be. After the most thorough scientific investigation we could devise we know that the virus is relatively stable and safe to everything except rabbits. Its introduction does not add significantly to the background risk to human beings that we already accept and that already existed. We already accept that rabbit calicivirus is harmless to all species except rabbits, and there is only a very low chance of its mutating in New Zealand to affect anything else. The impact of predator prey-switching following the introduction of rabbit calicivirus disease is unlikely to be any greater than that following a large-scale poison programme---of which we have had many without arousing the vocal concern of the present Minister of Conservation. So the risks are very low, although, of course, they are not zero. Nevertheless, the application was refused mainly because we did not know enough about the epidemiology of rabbit calicivirus disease in New Zealand conditions to be able to calculate the likelihood of a benefit. Our decision-making process requires that risks---however low---be weighed against prospective benefits. The decision was a huge disappointment to many who love the land and understand the high-country environment. I believe that those people would all have accepted the situation, had the Government responded by saying: ``Well, public conservation and ecosystem values have been found by this study to be the main beneficiary of rabbit control in the high country, so the public will pick up the bulk of the cost while more research is done on the biocontrol.'' The member for Rakaia said that she was very angry at the declined decision. The Minister of Agriculture said that he would immediately take a case to Cabinet for assistance. But what actually happened? Cabinet meeting after Cabinet meeting passed with no such support forthcoming. Eventually, it became obvious that no such commitment would ever come from that quarter and that the early support of pronouncements by the Minister were nothing more than empty blather. It was also clear that the urgings of people like myself that runholders not break the law, because in the end the Government would come to the aid of the runholders, were unjustified by the facts. Also, despite the clear findings of the inquiry, self-styled high-profile environmentalists immediately resumed spreading public fears for human health and native species---fears that are not supported by the findings of Dr O'Hara and Dr O'Neil. This deliberate misinformation made it obvious to those locked in battle with the rabbits that there would be continued powerful political opposition to there ever being any biocontrol. So, in short, the high-country community was sent the message by this Government---and, it must be said, by urban New Zealand---that it was on its own, that even though powerful members of Cabinet publicly thought that the decision was wrong, the high-country farmers could get stuffed, they could go broke, and, as far as a lot of people were concerned, the sooner that happened, the better. It was probably at about this stage that someone fought back by taking the law into his or her own hands. We cannot condone that; those who break the law should pay the price. But members of this House should be aware that if ever anyone is prosecuted, public collections will certainly pay any fines levied, so the deterrent effect will not be great. There is a further lesson here: if people are to be expected to respect the law, the lawmakers must set the example, and they have not done that very much lately. And so must the judiciary set the example. Who can be expected to respect politicians who spend public money on themselves, or judges who do not know the difference between right and wrong---as determined by jury? We should ensure that the hunt for scapegoats in this affair---the hunt for someone to prosecute---is not pursued to the extent that it deters people from offering reliable information that is needed to help understand the epidemiology of rabbit calicivirus disease in New Zealand. People who supply that information should be able to do so without its potentially being used to put their friends in the dock. And the information needs to flow both ways. Apparently farmers are breaking down the virus with water. They probably do not know that this causes the virus to fragment and that by spreading such a mixture they are possibly causing rabbits to eat fragments of the virus that will not make them sick but that will induce immunity. That sort of information needs to flow in both directions, and the Government must take a lead. Even if rabbit calicivirus disease is not a self-sustaining biocontrol in the New Zealand environment it may still provide us with a biocide---a natural poison that kills only rabbits and enables us to dramatically reduce the use of broad spectrum poisons such as that have known environmental risks.

I am going to take a slightly different tack from that of my other four colleagues. I want to come back to the question that I have not yet heard the answer to. Why do this? It is a very important question. Under clause there are two ways in which a company can be returned to the register. According to this clause, basically those two ways are: firstly, in the case of a company that was removed from the register under paragraph (b) or (c) of section () of the principal Act, and I have gone back to have a look at the legislation, paragraph (b) states: ``The Registrar is satisfied that---(i) The company has ceased to carry on business; and (ii) There is no other reason for the company to continue in existence; or (c) The company has been put into liquidation,''. In that particular case the registrar restores a company to the register and it is up to the registrar to notify the various things that have already been described. In the case when paragraphs (b) and (c) are meant, it is the registrar's job to advertise or to notify. Clause goes on to state: ``In the case of a company that was removed from the register under paragraph (d) or paragraph (e) of section (),'' so I have had a look at that. Paragraph (d) of section () states: ``There is sent or delivered to the Registrar a request in the prescribed form made by---(i) A member authorised to make the request by a special resolution of members entitled to vote and voting on the question; or (ii) The board of directors or any other person, if the memorandum of the company so requires or permits, or the articles of the company so require or permit, as the case may be,---''. Paragraph (e) states: ``A liquidator sends or delivers to the Registrar the documents referred to in section ()(a) of this Act.'' The situation basically is that there are two ways of getting a company back on to the register. One is when it has satisfied the requirements of paragraphs (b) and (c); then the registrar is required to notify and to list the name of the company, the name and address of the applicant, and the section under, and the grounds on which, the application is made or the registrar proposes to act, etc., and the date by which an objection to restoring the company to the register must be delivered. We need only read some of the headlines in this morning's paper, the Dominion, to see some of the comments the media is making. I comment quickly on three: ``More gloom on mortgages, sinking dollar''; ``Overseas debt swells to record $b''; and ``Savings hit by health cuts, credit cards''. Those are the sorts of headlines that are now in our newspapers day by day. The Labour Party asks the National Party what it is doing about it; to give us a policy that will address this. Absolutely no new policy is in place. What we hear about are tax cuts. People are being told that they should save their tax cuts because that will help the current account. Then in the next breath they are being told to spend them, but that that will worsen the current account. The ultimate advice from the Government is for people to do both with the little bit of tax cut, if there is anything left. What is needed now is a new vision, a new way---a third way---of trying to deal with New Zealand's economic problems. But first a new vision needs to be painted for New Zealand, saying that this Parliament and this nation should have pride in itself again, that it should be concentrating on a smart economy, and that we should be competing effectively overseas, producing goods and services of a quality that people want to buy at prices they can afford. We want business growth, profitability, jobs, and people's incomes rising so that our public services can also be funded adequately. That is the sort of vision we want, not the dog-eat-dog, hands off, unequal society that is being promoted daily by New Zealand First, National, and ACT. How are we to achieve that? We will be promoting a number of policy issues. The first one is that there needs to be much more aggressive market development for New Zealand goods and services, the type of thing that Mike Moore did---get out there, bang a few heads together, start pushing and promoting New Zealand, and lead the way in terms of market development. It should be not be a matter of simply cutting tariffs and saying to people that they are on their own; some leadership should be given at the same time. In skills development and education we should be making sure that our schools are smart schools. We should not be allowing schools in poor areas to be without decent information technology. We should be making sure that they have access to information technology, the Internet, and the like. We should not be allowing polytechs to be competing openly with universities. We should say that we have skills holes in New Zealand. We need technologists. We need people to go to applied technology colleges and institutions, like polytechs. We should tell them to stick to their knitting and get on and try to fill in some of the skills holes that already exist. We do have an infrastructure deficit. We should look at the positive impact that the Museum of New Zealand has had on the Wellington economy. There are things that need to be done in New Zealand. One need only look at Auckland to see that those things need to be done. We cannot have cars and trucks sitting idle in traffic. That has a downward impact on New Zealand's competitive advantage. In monetary policy we simply cannot stand by and let the dollar appreciate, which it will do at some stage in the future at the expense of our exporters. Our whole policy thrust has to be to make sure that it promotes the tradable sector. Then there are things like industry policies where we are promoting heavily research and development and technology transfer, where we have decent workplace relations laws once again that allow people to compete on their effective business, not driving wage rates lower and lower, trying to compete with Asia and other countries. We should be competing at the high end of our goods and services. We should be competing at the technology end. We should be a smart economy. We need a new vision. We need new policies, and we are not hearing them from the National Government.

From the outset I want to say that during the financial year under consideration the commissioner and his policemen and policewomen carried out their duty ably and in keeping with the longstanding and very high standard of the police, and I commend them. I particularly commend them because during the latter part of that year they had to carry out their duty under an exceptional handicap. They had to carry out their duty under the handicap of having to carry a Minister who was known to make asinine statements and to be full of wild, boastful self-praise, and they did that without demur. I commend them for that. In October of that year there was an election. Prior to the election, during the term of the previous Labour Government, the police had every reason to believe that under a National Government they could expect extra police and that the new Minister of Police would find $ million to fund those extra police. In the latter part of that year it became very clear to the police that the Minister would not be able to make good his promise of finding $ million. They had to face the fact that the Minister of Police, who had promised that if he could not find the money he would resign, would backtrack on that promise, too, and they had to carry that Minister. As my colleagues have pointed out, during the earlier part of that year when the member for Auckland Central was Minister of Police---he was probably one of the best Ministers of Police that this country has ever had; well, he was the second-best Minister of Police---there was a period during which crime actually fell. Violence and serious crime actually decreased. Many good initiatives were begun in that period---community policing, and a whole range of technical advances. Yet during the latter part of that particular year the police became aware that, in budgeting for the extra police that the Minister had promised rather wildly, they would have to think of cutting back on capital works and on the technology that they needed in order to face the modern crime wave. In the latter part of that year---and since, although that time is not included in this debate---they had to put up with carrying on their police work while they were short of equipment, short of motorcars, and short of the technological advances that they really needed, and that was solely because the Minister of Police had made idle and asinine boasts prior to the election. My colleagues have set out very clearly---and it seems to me that this particular debate brings to light very clearly indeed---that during the first months of the financial year being discussed, under the previous Labour Government, the crime rate fell. During the term of the Labour Government the police were provided with a whole series of modern innovations to enable them to fight crime. Since then they have received nothing. Since then the police have had to sacrifice their budget---or a substantial part of their budget---to make good the idle and asinine promises of their Minister. They have had to carry him. Every policeman in this country is aware that the police are handicapped by a Minister given to wild statements and asinine self-praise. They are handicapped by a Minister who, as I remember, at one stage was going to bring out the commandos. The police have to put up with a Minister who has no confidence in them; he was going to bring out the commandos. During the latter part of that year, and since then, the crime rate has risen in every category. Where are the commandos? That Minister has been reduced to blustering---and just a moment ago we heard his idle blustering---and he has not been able to make good any of his promises. Many policemen are now saying to themselves: ``Our Minister said on television---and everyone saw him---that if he couldn't make good his promise of extra police and $ million he'd go.''. The police are now having to carry a Minister who could not make good what he said he would do, who could not stick by his word, and who is well known throughout the police force as being utterly idle, utterly asinine, and free with only his self-praise.

The Opposition supports the Bill. After all, it is an expected and relatively insignificant and non-controversial amendment to the parent Bill, which was promoted by the Labour Party when in Government and introduced by my colleague the member for Yaldhurst. The Bill clarifies certain matters about which some dubiety has arisen since it was introduced---for example, in future there will be clarity with regard to marine structures not being considered as buildings. The major impact of the Bill is to set out a process by which the Building Industry Authority will in future be funded, outside Government funding. As the Minister said, the provision states that there will be a levy on building consents that will amount to . percent of the cost of the building work, if that building work costs over $,. The levy will be collected by the territorial authority and paid on a monthly basis to the Building Industry Authority. As the Minister noted, the Building Industry Authority can receive in advance from the Minister an indication of the parameters with regard to policy that the Building Industry Authority has to address. The authority must provide an indication of its budget to the Minister of Internal Affairs. The Minister and his colleague the Minister of Finance will then have the power to accept or reject that particular budget. There was some concern felt by certain local authorities that the percent commission that they would receive was inadequate. Certainly we are convinced, and the select committee was convinced, that percent will adequately compensate the territorial authorities for collecting those funds on behalf of the Building Industry Authority. This is bearing in mind that they already do that for the Building Research Association of New Zealand. The important aspect of the general trend that is set out in this Bill and in other Bills is that we are moving towards what is considered to be a performance-oriented consideration in order to determine the desirability or otherwise of buildings. In future, the concerns that will be paramount are those of health and safety. It is hoped that in due course we will see a greater flexibility with regard to what is permitted in relation to buildings, but at the same time a uniform building code is needed for matters of health and safety. The other point is that, as a result of new communications in territorial authorities, and with the introduction of computerised storage of information, we are entering a new era. In future, local authorities will be able to provide anyone with a computer read-out which sets out the boundaries of a particular section, the utilities, and the water and electrical supplies. Virtually all the information with regard to any one section or area will be available to the person who seeks a building consent by way of what is to be called a project information memorandum. Those two features are important, and we are unlikely to see the full effect of them for some years to come. I want to comment on the point raised by the Minister that to date there has been some reluctance by private individuals to take up their role as compliance persons. To date, building consents have been issued in the main by building inspectors of the territorial authorities. I certainly hope, as does the Minister, that in due course private enterprise persons will set up in competition with local authority building inspectors in order to provide a more flexible and a cheaper service. I am confident that the Bill will lead to better building standards throughout the country. Bill read a second time.

I would be one of the first to accept that the time has come to examine the structure for the organisation to promote the arts in New Zealand. At the same time I must tell the House that I am very disappointed with both the direction in which the Minister has chosen to take the arts and the degree of commitment that the Bill demonstrates for the arts. My first concern is that the Minister has chosen to centralise and politicise the organisation for promoting the arts. The regional councils are to be abolished. The Arts Council of New Zealand is to be composed of no more than six persons, all appointed by the Minister. Where in the Bill is there any provision for the major arts groups or the local community groups to make suggestions about who should be on that board? It has been pointed out that there will be two separate boards---the Arts Board to provide for non-Maori arts, and Te Waka Toi. The power remains totally in the hands of the Arts Council of New Zealand. It has the money. It even has the staff. The two boards will have no greater role than simply passing on money that the New Zealand Arts Council will have handed to them to pass on. That is its sole role. In my view that is a retrograde step in the creation of new organisations for the promotion of arts in New Zealand. That role is centralised and politicised more than ever before, and that is a mistake. The second concern I have is that the Bill shows that the Government has no commitment whatsoever in relation to the provision of funding for arts and crafts in New Zealand. Not so very long ago the Government set out for the Hillary Commission a clear, definite, and major contribution from the Lottery Grants Board. The Hillary Commission, which provides funds for sport and recreation, was given a clear and major commitment of Government funding.

I have changed my mind. I had intended to stop earlier, but, goaded to carry on, I might do so. The Opposition takes the view that there was no need for this measure to be introduced and driven through in the middle of the night. The Government purported to introduce the increased tax on tobacco products as a health measure. The effect of the Bill is to increase the cost of a packet of cigarettes by c. If it is intended to discourage the use of tobacco---and I think that we ought to do that---it is essential to bring in such a charge that will clearly discourage tobacco use. This charge is just sufficiently large enough to reduce people's ability to buy other goods, such as shoes for their children and items of food. They will not stop buying cigarettes.

The Opposition member in front of me says, ``Dead right!'', but the Government has deliberately not promoted open slather in labour relations because it knows that to do so would strip protection from working people on low incomes---particularly women and people working in provincial areas such as the Bay of Plenty. In effect, the stripping of that protection would mean that in time their wages and conditions would become worse. Particularly affected would be women employees, workers on low incomes, and young workers, who are the most vulnerable workers in the work-place. They tend to be part-time workers and people who are working in scattered work-places. Therefore the awards are a basic and very important protection. The select committee heard from the unions, quite naturally, expressions of concern about the changes, although minor, that are to some extent promoted by the Bill. All change is threatening, and it is understandable that concern would be felt about that. However, the protective provision introduced in the Bill to provide final-offer arbitration as a back-stop in negotiations has been very important. The provision recognises the different bargaining strengths that parties can have in award negotiations, particularly in the large work-place occupational awards that cover large groups of employees. I refer, for example, to the clerical workers' award that covers , to , clerical workers around New Zealand. The settlement of that award has been difficult. Protection of that award is given by introducing in the Bill the ability to go to final-offer arbitration if the parties have not bargained in good faith. The Bill ensures that the protection does exist, that it continues to exist, that negotiations will continue, and that the provision of protection to the workers concerned will continue. When one hears the scoffing of Opposition members one understands how little they realise the importance of the protective provisions to those workers. Often the awards provide only minimal conditions---for example, days' paid sick leave a year---and any domestic leave taken by a worker comes out of that entitlement. Those are minimal provisions, yet Opposition members wish the protections to be stripped away from the employees and they want the awards providing the protections to disappear. That is not the Government's position, and I am very pleased that it is not. The Government recognises the protection provided by the awards. In summary, the Bill does promote changes for industry. It promotes the ability for enterprise and industry bargaining to take place when the parties want it. It provides for democratic decision-making by employers and employees in determining whether they should enter a work-place agreement. It limits the provision to apply to large work-places, which protects both the workers and the employers. Many employers, particularly small employers, do not want to enter strong negotiations with unions. The Bill provides for such negotiation in large work-places; it allows for enterprise agreements; and it allows for particular work-place increments to be determined in negotiations. That is a good thing. At the same time, however, the Bill provides for the basis of protection for those who are most vulnerable, and that is very important.

During the lunch-hour I canvassed the views of Maori community leaders, Pacific Island and Polynesian leaders, and also medical researchers whom I represent. They are concerned with the section on health status, which provides that people with body organisms that might cause disease may not be discriminated against. That section was requested by the New Zealand AIDS Foundation in a letter of June to the Minister of Health. That foundation suggested that that section was imperative because the foundation objected to the discrimination against people with AIDS. It is the view of some senior medical researchers and learned medicos whom I represent that unless they are permitted to take cognisance of circumstances in which their staff and they are working with people with AIDS, the discrimination is against their own protection. They are strongly opposed to the removal of the discrimination because of the protection needed for those who work with people who have AIDS. They are concerned that that condition and other communicable illnesses and diseases that are contagious should be handled with greater care. They feel that it is not provided for in the Bill. After all, AIDS represents the single greatest risk to health in New Zealand. That statement was made in Parliament. The director-general of the World Health Organization has pointed out that: ``We stand nakedly in front of a pandemic as mortal as any pandemic that has ever been, with the threat of AIDS.''. I therefore take great cognisance of the view of medical researchers who suggest that the clause, which would consider it discriminatory to regard anyone with AIDS in that way, will not be helpful in attempting to combat the spread of that condition. We know that the rate of AIDS in Wellington is now approaching the rate in Auckland. How will the clause relating to health affect the health regulations, which require notification of communicable, contagious illness? It will be contrary to the Bill to take the measures that are at present being taken. We have had at least AIDS cases since the disease became notifiable in ---and I am sure the number will now be higher. Under the clause, what happens about the notification of contagious diseases? That point has been raised by doctors. What about the guidelines endorsing automatic testing for the virus of donors of blood, organs, and other tissues? We heard on the news during the lunch-hour today that there had been a second needle attack, not in New Zealand but in Long Bay, which resulted in a warder---Geoffrey Pearce---developing AIDS. How do we protect people who work in prisons from such incidents? If such people discriminate against prisoners in that way they will violate the new law. Should we proscribe concern for the security of staff, doctors, and nurses that takes the form of adopting measures against those with AIDS who come under their care? That is the principal concern. Where does the argument that makes it a violation of the law to discriminate against anyone who has organisms in the body that may cause disease---to use the exact words in the Act---leave those people? How does it affect the need to notify those illnesses, and the care to be taken in relation to them, if that behaviour amounts to discrimination under the Bill? Concern has been expressed by the Maori and Polynesian leaders whom I was able to contact in the lunch-hour. They are most unhappy about the clause relating to health status, and they were concerned about the clause on sexual orientation. I am sure those two communities, or single Polynesian communities, will be concerned. They were at least gratified that pedophilic orientation is not to be included in the proposed new law. They could not suffer its being an offence to discriminate against a person who is a pedophile. They could not accept that and they did express a certain concern. Very few would object to the Bill in other respects, but those two matters are controversial. I agree with the member for Napier that the Bill is a Trojan Horse. Perhaps those issues could have been separated, and then I think most in the House would have approved the rest of the Bill; but they have not been separated, for obvious political reasons that we all understand. It is therefore important to enable New Zealand citizens and community groups to come before the committee and to express their views. I am sure there will be some amendments. However, my final statement relates to employment. When a person has the qualification for a job, that qualification should be the prior determinant of whether that person gets the job.

I want to ask the Minister what he considers to be the best way of assessing the urgency of need of an applicant to the corporation for a loan or for a State rental house. The Government has shown through its housing policies that it neither cares much about the less well-off New Zealanders nor understands the reality of people's needs. Affordable housing ought not cost more than one-quarter of a family's net income. That is a reasonable way of assessing how much a New Zealand family should pay for housing, particularly when they have not otherwise owned a house before. In relation to home ownership---let me be more specific---I want to ask the Minister to give to the House the gauge, the measure, the principle, by which the corporation under his ministerial stewardship assesses and evaluates its contribution to the New Zealand community. It seems to me that there is a totally inadequate understanding of the needs of our families, and this has been done under the Government in the year under review. The Government is also contributing to the problems of the building industry. The building industry has collapsed, which in itself is a measure of the fact that it was industriously engaged before in building houses, and the inability of New Zealanders to finance home ownership has caused the collapse of the industry. That has been the end of the domino effect of the Government's decreasing the ability of New Zealanders to be able to afford to borrow. In relation to State rental tenancies, how do the Minister and the corporation rationalise the fact that former State rental house tenants have withdrawn from their tenancies and are living with other members of their families, and that families are having to double up in State rental tenancies or other accommodation? What does the Minister have to say about that?

I want to take up two observations made by two Ministers during the debate this afternoon. The Minister of Transport made the observation that the Government has a policy of increasing forest planting, and I therefore want to ask what second-chance training programmes for the training of young school dropouts have been considered by the Government. There are places on the East Coast where most young people are unemployed. Training schemes of the type that the Minister has talked about as being Government policy could be established in those areas. Why are there no training schemes for those unemployed Maori? I want to concentrate on the need for second-chance training and education for those who have missed out, as well as speaking on the general theme of education. The Minister of Education conceded early this afternoon that this country is not providing the training that New Zealand industries need. Why is it not providing such training? Literally hundreds of thousands of young unemployed people are on the dole with no hope and nothing to look forward to. Those people are seeking a worthwhile future. Why will the Government not provide the training whereby they would learn the skills needed in industry, and therefore gain a chance of future employment? Two Ministers have referred to areas in which there are vacuums. There is a crying need. My suggestion is to take those people up, start training courses, and, instead of having so many thousands unemployed, let there be second-chance education in those areas in which industry has an immediate and future need. The cost-cutting in education generally has meant that many hundreds of young Maori with capability have missed out on any future formal training. I speak from a personal knowledge of dozens and dozens---indeed, scores---of such young people. Why has there been cost-cutting in this area, which is the very area that ought to have priority for investing in the future of young New Zealanders and the future of New Zealand industry? Well-informed and well-educated parents pass on those attributes. Less well-informed or uneducated parents who have not had a chance also pass on to the next generation a cycle of underattainment. Government intervention in education in a more global and holistic sense is required. Why has that not been included in the Government's education policy? There seems to be an inability to hear the cry of so many parents who are unable to take their children through to higher levels of formal schooling. The Ngarimu V.C. and th (Maori) Battalion Memorial Scholarship Fund Board had many applicants appear before it a week or so ago, but it was unable to satisfy them. Certainly some will go on and be financially assisted by the Ministry of Education, but many will miss out. Many will not be able to find jobs. There is no doubt that the Government's actions on the educational attainment of Maori have disadvantaged Maori who before were not disadvantaged for those specific reasons. I have known of the disadvantages for many years but there are those who are now disadvantaged who were not disadvantaged just a matter of a couple of years ago. I want to talk now about the abolition of the right of children to attend their neighbourhood school. Better schools will be able to choose, and, in fact, some schools are enforcing zoning as a means of exclusion. It is a semantic means of creating a barrier to exclude certain children. Maori are more likely to be excluded in the present and in the future than they have ever been. We have seen instances of ``white flight'' before, but not to this degree. Maori parents used the Parent Advocacy Council to a considerable degree to enable them to advise their children, and parents certainly sought advice from the council because of the unprecedented growth in the number of suspensions of Maori children during the term of this Government. The council does not now exist, and parents will not be able to get help. I want to mention other areas of disadvantage besides the abolition of zoning and legislation that allows schools to draw up their own allowance schemes, which, as I have said, encourages elitism and racism. I want to turn to the abolition of balloting and the creation of criteria for enrolment. Allowing schools to set criteria for choosing pupils is a form of social engineering. The Minister says that he opposes that, but that policy is a form of social control. Allowing schools to pick and choose the pupils they accept is a negative form of social apartheid. Balloting was a fairer system. I also want to talk about the result of allowing schools to restrict their rolls. That has been done in an arbitrary manner, and some privileged schools virtually have different requirements. They have been able to hand-pick their pupils by using the new provisions introduced by the Government.

The Chairman of the Maori Affairs Committee pointed out that Standing Orders prevented us from giving a favourable consideration to this since the Act to which it referred, the Ngati Rarua - Atiawa Iwi Trust Empowering Act, was a private Act. Therefore, because of that technicality, we were not able to give a favourable consideration to Bishop Sutton's petition. However, the committee was persuaded to enter a rider to our recommendation because of the importance of Maori education. That is the principal reason Bishop Sutton sought a change. In fact he wanted to emphasise that the original purpose of the trust from which the money is derived was for the benefit of Maori and Pakeha youth education, and bi-cultural sharing with the whakapapa preference for young Maori. It was not exclusively to promote Maori education; it was for young Pakeha as well. But because the trust arose as a Maori initiative, it was Bishop Sutton's aim to emphasise that education of young Maori still be the main purpose of the trust's activity. I could not agree more on the importance of Maori education. Bishop Sutton echoed the thought that, in dispensing money and funds in reparation to groups, if there is no direction that an emphasis be given to health and education of Maori then we are acting irresponsibly as parliamentarians. That was the main purpose of Bishop Sutton's petition, and I do not think that anyone in this Parliament would disagree with his aim. We know that poverty and deprivation are affecting Maori of all ages, and that there is no validity to any suggestion of Maori sovereignty until individual Maori have their economic sovereignty and the education to enable them to get jobs. Otherwise, young Maori are primarily a jobless group. Young Maori who have left secondary education are in the majority jobless, because they did not have the education to prepare them to qualify for the available jobs. Although more jobs may be being created this year than there might have been last year, those jobs are for highly skilled people. Those on the low socio-economic scale are simply not finding their lot improved or bettered. So that was the Bishop's point, and I want to pay him a tribute for his concern about that. The question arises of whether this House has the right to say to any group receiving funds from the taxpayers of this country that those funds should be directed to given purposes. I believe it is irresponsible of us if we do not direct them. I may be in the minority. It is much safer to say: ``Oh, no, we do not direct how the funds are to be spent. We give them a lump sum. We give them compensation. We give them reparation. But we must not tell them what to do with it.'' I belong to a different school. I have seen funds given for overseas aid when the greatest need was for health, and especially the health of mothers and women. But no, we felt unable to direct, and the money has been in large measure wasted. It is the responsibility of this House to indicate a direction. I am sure the trust itself will accept that Bishop Sutton's aim was simply to improve the education of young Maori, and that they will take note, as the rider says. The matters referred to in the petition were dealt with by the House in the context of the Ngati Rarua - Atiawa Trust Empowering Act. As this is a private Act the committee considers that the matter of whether to amend or repeal it to restore the original purpose---namely, Maori education---was not for us to do. None the less, we sympathised with the Bishop's aim.

In speaking to this period, I want to say that it was inevitable when this Government diverted the budget for Maori affairs to mainstream departments that its intention was to bring about the demise of the Ministry of Maori Development/Te Puni Kokiri. I ask the Minister whether that is the case. Was Sir Graham Latimer correct when he predicted the demise of the ministry? He is a senior member of the National Party with very close connections to the Prime Minister and Cabinet. I ask the Minister whether this Government requires Te Puni Kokiri to monitor the outcomes of Maori budget expenditure by mainstream departments when those departments do not, in fact, provide the data. One or two do, but many of them do not. How can Te Puni Kokiri monitor a Government department or an agency of Government in the expenditure of their Maori vote when that agency or Government department does not provide the data that is required to enable an assessment to be made? It is imposing an unfair burden on Te Puni Kokiri. The auditor-general's office pointed to this dilemma for Te Puni Kokiri, and made it very, very clear to the Maori Affairs Committee when it considered and examined this period that it was extremely difficult for Te Puni Kokiri to carry out its requirement---especially in the period under review---when Government mainstream departments do not provide the data. The auditor-general's office made that so clear, and pointed us in the direction of Government departments that offend in this manner. Why has the Minister not amended this contradiction? Why has the Minister not demanded of his ministerial colleagues who have the direct responsibility for the mainstream departments to provide the facts and figures on how they expend their Maori budget? It is his responsibility to do this. Will the Minister not ask his Cabinet colleagues to assure this to Te Puni Kokiri? Of course, it is a classical way of getting rid of any Government ministry or department to require the fulfilment of tasks when the facts and figures required are unavailable. Why has the Government proceeded with regard to this anomalous situation? I ask the Minister whether it is because it gives the Government a reason to terminate Te Puni Kokiri. Furthermore, if the role of Te Puni Kokiri is primarily advisory, as, for instance---and I quote for the moment---the area of health and education of Maori, what priority does Government give to Te Puni Kokiri when compared with the Maori advisers in these ministries? Because these ministries already have their own Maori advisory units there appears to be a duplication, but it is the result of Government policy. It does, however, provide yet another reason to say there is a duplication of services here and therefore we do not need Te Puni Kokiri. I challenge the Government and the Minister to say why this anomalous situation has continued. I am speaking of Government policy. Clearly, the Government has stripped the budget from Te Puni Kokiri as the beginning of a process of terminating the ministry. I want the Minister to give a clear and unequivocal answer to this House and to me---and therefore to Maoridom---that he has no such intentions. There are the natural reasons: first, there is a duplication of services; and secondly, the budget has been consistently decreased. As I say, it was an inevitable result of Government policy. I am addressing myself to the year under review and to the Government's policy in administering it. Te Puni Kokiri has excellent officers and excellent analysts. In some areas they are better than those in the mainstream departments. Whose advice does the Minister take? Is it the advice from the experts in his department, or is it the advice from the Maori units in the mainstream departments? The Minister is accountable to Maori people for their progress at a time when they are in a state of crisis. Maori youth has the highest rate of unemployment in the OECD countries. Whose advice does the Minister take on that? Te Puni Kokiri has many experts in the field. Does the Minister take their advice, or does he go to the mainstream advice? Does the Prime Minister take the advice of Te Puni Kokiri? It has often proffered it but has been totally ignored. I want the Minister to tell me whether the Cabinet committee on social matters takes the advice of Te Puni Kokiri. What was the advice of Te Puni Kokiri in respect of Maori unemployment and, for instance, the training opportunities programme? If we have this as a result of the Maori unit in the Department of Labour---the mainstream department---I want to say that there is concern about the way the training opportunities programme is handled, in particular the access to training for mature students. Many mature students are unable to take advantage of the training opportunities programme. In particular, they are then faced with finding student loans to pay fees for such courses, and they are unable to do so without unduly burdening their families. I bring this as a matter of concern from the Maori people of Murihiku, Southland. Whose advice did the Minister take on Maori employment strategy? The matter of Maori being overrepresented in the unemployment statistics was raised at Murihiku, Southland, where I will be tomorrow night. That is right. I am sure the Minister has been given excellent analyses from his own department, but how has he influenced Government policy? This is a matter of concern to the Maori people. I refer to housing as another area where clearly the move by Housing New Zealand to market rentals is causing great strain on a number of Maori families, many of whom are on a benefit or low incomes and cannot afford market rentals. The effect of this policy is forcing people into substandard low-cost housing. This, again, is a matter brought up by the people of Murihiku, Southland, and I have their statement before me. They are concerned about many things. But whose advice does the Minister take? I ask the Minister to make very clear the extent to which he values, or otherwise, the expertise and advice he gets from his own highly expert officers compared with units in other departments. I come to the area of health. In Te Puni Kokiri there is an excellent health programme, as there is also an excellent education programme. But there is the Maori unit in the Public Health Commission and the Maori unit in the Ministry of Health. Is there any conflict? To whom do the Minister, Cabinet, and the Prime Minister give priority? Why does this situation exist? What will be done to remedy it? Which one has priority? We need to know when the advice of Te Puni Kokiri has had priority---the ear of the Prime Minister, of Cabinet colleagues, and of mainstream departments. I, personally, have greatly admired the calibre of officers in Te Puni Kokiri, but the role they are given by this Government's mainstreaming policy is a role that is sidelining them absolutely perfectly to be shot down and for Te Puni Kokiri to be closed down for the reasons that the Government can validly argue: first, that there is a duplication of services; and secondly, that Te Puni Kokiri is there to monitor departments, and that has not been done---as the Controller and Auditor-General's office observed. But, as I have pointed out, it has not been possible to do because Government departments who get the budget often cannot account for it in detail. I will not list in detail those mainstream departments, but some of them are not doing a good job. I ask the Minister to answer.

Thirdly---and perhaps harder to quantify---the proposal emphasises the civilian and research aspects of the Antarctic programme by removing operations from the base, with its direct contact with the United States Navy and with military transport, to a zone of commercial development.

As I was saying, the Bill is a bad Bill but a typical Government action. The Bill is clumsy, incomplete, incompetent, and inconsistent. It also represents a major departure from past policy. The Bill introduces ``cheque-book'' immigration. Wealthy people will be able to buy New Zealand residence. The Government will allow people to come in on the basis of their money, not on the basis of their commitment to New Zealand. During the past years, since the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi when the Maori confederation of tribes agreed to allow Europeans into the country, waves of people have come to New Zealand to make better lives for themselves, their children, and their grandchildren. In some cases those people were fleeing from poverty, oppression, or a class-ridden society, but all of the migrants had in common a commitment to make a better life for themselves as well as a commitment to New Zealand. Those people brought their skills and their energies for their country's good. People will now be able to buy their way into New Zealand, and I believe that that is a very bad policy. Some of the measures in the Bill will improve administration and processing, but most of the measures are a vast over-reaction, like so many of the Government's actions. New Zealand has a proud history of helping refugees and of providing access to people who may not be able to find a home in other countries. During the debate we heard a pathetic attempt from a Government member to smear the asylum-seeking process. A person who was seeking refugee status was named in the House---a practice that is totally against the ethics and practice in the House and is a disgusting use of the important privilege that members of Parliament enjoy, which should be used very carefully and never to jeopardise people's lives. It was an appalling example, but one that is very much in keeping with the tone of the Bill. Concern has been expressed internationally about the way in which New Zealand handled asylum-seekers during the Gulf war. The chairman of Amnesty International in London is quoted as saying that he found it odd that a country as far away from the Gulf war conflict as any should have had the strongest reaction to supposed security risks. We have also heard of the problem in defining security risks. The police officers who assessed whether the man named by the member for Birkenhead on the basis that he was a Muslim and that Saddam Hussein had called on Muslims around the world to commit acts of terrorism was a security risk to New Zealand were presumably the same officers who had rejected another. What an appalling reaction theirs was, and a sad racist response to somebody's plea for help from New Zealand---a country that has in the past been able to stand up for the rights of quota refugees and spontaneous refugees. That is a very small group that is badly affected by the provisions of the legislation, but many other people are as well. The people who will be affected by the policy that the Government is introducing and refusing to discuss in Parliament are those who will have to deal with the , net increase in migration. The Minister has said that this is an important economic tool. What evidence does the Government have that increasing migration by , people a year net will bring benefits to New Zealand? Social services in many Auckland schools are already badly stretched. We have already seen the housing crises created by past migration. What will the Government do to ensure that adequate housing is available for these quality migrants who will come rushing to New Zealand as a result of this policy? What about the jobs that these people will find? While many ``cheque-book'' migrants may well be wealthy and will have the money to provide some employment for themselves, many business migrants have not. They have families, and those families will need jobs. What will the Government say to the , New Zealanders whom they have betrayed by not providing training or work for them in the months since the election? How will the Government face those people with the additional , New Zealanders each year? The Government has over-reacted to a very small problem by providing for the issue of transit visas. This will be a huge administrative burden because , or more people are likely to need transit visas. Genuine tourists and genuine business people coming to or just passing through New Zealand will now need transit visas because the Government is so wobbly that it cannot cope with the administrative burden caused by about people a year seeking asylum. Countries such as Canada are dealing with hundreds of thousands of refugees.

No, not when I have been drinking; I do not drink and drive. Many people are legally entitled to be on the road, and they should not have to be apprehensive about being stopped at any stage. It is perfectly reasonable for New Zealanders who have not broken the law to expect to be able to start and end a journey without their being stopped arbitrarily. I think that that is an infringement of one's freedom, and I am sure that there are other steps that could be taken that would have more effect on drinking/driving. For example, in Massachusetts in the United States---where I have family---if somebody is caught drinking and driving, not only that person is charged but also the person who served the driver alcohol. That means that if a driver has been at a dinner party or a luncheon party, or in a bar or a restaurant, as well as the driver being charged, the person who is in charge of the establishment can be charged with causing the driver to consume alcohol. That means that one has very responsible hosts, and that the whole community becomes responsible for preventing people from drinking and driving. I would prefer the whole community to be involved in legislation of that sort, rather than innocent people who have every right to be on the road being stopped in an arbitrary fashion. We have to think about alternatives and not just about punishing the offender.

Yes, because if someone is driving a vehicle on which the warrant of fitness has expired that is a relatively minor offence---or as an unlicensed driver, in some cases, but then compared with some of the enormity of some offences the court looks at it is a minor offence. Then when one looks at the problems that are caused by the lack of public transport, in areas such as the one I represent, one sees that if those people want to get to work---if they have jobs---they are often forced to use private transport. It was interesting to read in the annual report of Transit New Zealand Ltd in relation to the transportation of disabled that they were described as those who did not have access to private vehicles. So we are talking about a large group of people. They get into a conviction cycle and often end up in prison---when a lack of a driver's licence is the first offence---because obviously, as they go on offending, those penalties mount. The Ministry of Transport in my area has begun public education classes to help young people---in particular, poorer young people---to get driving licences so that they can understand the rules of the road. Often education is a better method of dealing with serious offending, or what eventually becomes serious offending, rather than using a large stick. I argue that there are some matters---such as the one signalled by the Attorney-General---that may well go too far. I do not know that, because I have looked at the Bill only in a cursory way, but it is a waste of the time of the House that a Bill of this kind should be brought forward in this manner.

I am sad to follow the member for Onehunga, who has had an opportunity that is given rarely to Government back-bench members to talk about issues that face New Zealand today. It seems that we have had an advertisement for Auckland Grammar School and for flags. I do not think that either of those matters will solve the problems that New Zealand is facing today. Opposition members want to talk about the absolutely basic building block of all New Zealanders' lives---housing. The Minister of Housing was warned in an unusual move about the content of this debate. He was warned that the Opposition intended to talk about housing, but he has not bothered to speak, and that reflects the attitude of Government members. During the Budget debate, a statement was made that the Government believed that as many as , State-house tenants did not have serious housing needs and it wanted them to consider moving into housing accommodation. That is much along the lines of the kind of statement made by the previous Opposition's spokesperson on housing before the election, who told Estate magazine: ``It's true that some people are living in shacks, sheds, and sometimes cars, but not all want to change. Some are quite happy as they are.''. That is the kind of attitude that the Government has about housing. I want to talk briefly about the percent of New Zealanders who cannot afford to own their own homes. They are people who have often suffered the worst from the problems that society faces people with. They are poor; they are disabled; and they are often women whose marriages have broken down and who have been forced out of matrimonial homes because they cannot afford the mortgage rates, and who are trying to bring up children. They are often ex-psychiatric patients or older people, who, because of working in low-paid jobs, or, for some, because of the injuries they sustained in wars on behalf of the country, were not able to have high-paying jobs. They are often young and are often people who are disadvantaged. They are people who have not been able to take advantage of the opportunities available to those who are well housed. It is outrageous that that percent is being penalised by the Government's action, with the claim that some others supposedly will be better off. We are being told that those people in sheltered accommodation---the people who are really at the bottom of the housing market---and those who are in emergency housing will have to pay market rents for the houses that they occupy. It is often women who are escaping violence and families that have had catastrophes of all kinds. Those people are expected to pay full market rents. It is interesting that this vindictive Government refuses to pay community grants allowances to organisations such as the Monte Cecilia emergency house that stand up for the rights of those people. I understand that they have had their community grants allowances stopped by this vindictive Minister. People such as Sister Mary Foy at the Monte Cecilia emergency house and Campbell Roberts of the Salvation Army are saying that the position for people who deal with emergency housing is impossible because people in emergency housing can no longer afford to go into Housing Corporation houses. They cannot find the deposit; they cannot find the bond; and they cannot afford the rent. It makes me see red when the Minister says that empty houses are a sign of the success of the Government's housing policy. Presumably, Government members have no inkling of, no interest in, and no sympathy for the generations of New Zealanders who, through State housing, have risen out of their parents' social problems and have been able to take advantage of good housing, good education, good health care, and have made lives for themselves. The Government has no interest in the percent of New Zealanders who do manage to look after themselves in housing. When I went back as a member of Parliament to Glen Innes, the suburb in which I was raised, I was most impressed that in that suburb, which is percent State-rental housing, the parents of the people I went to school with are still in Glen Innes, but most of the people I went to school with were able to leave. It is sad that, because of the Government's policies and its refusal to spread State housing throughout communities to provide a range of housing in communities, those people cannot live in Glen Innes near their families. If people want to buy a house they have to go somewhere else. They have to go to St. Heliers, to Meadowbank, or to Pakuranga; they cannot live near their parents. What I ask is, with the Government forcing out of their bigger houses those people who brought up their children in Glen Innes, where will they go? The one-bedroom and two-bedroom houses are not there. The Government has slashed the building programme. It does not care what happens to those older people. The Government is saying that it will make no guarantees that it will rehouse people who cannot pay Housing Corporation rents. During the past years National and Labour Governments have both agreed that housing was essential to the mental, physical, and economic well-being of the country. They said that housing was provided by a mix of policies---a mix of market forces and Government actions. They have provided not only good quality State houses for people to live in, but also subsidised mortgage finance. What does the Government plan to do? We are told that the mortgage role of the new State-owned enterprise, which the Housing Corporation will transform itself into on July, is uncertain. We are told that we do not know who will be designated as the ``new rich'' who will have to pay market rates. Will they be people who are on an income of $,, like the ``new rich'' who have group and group community services cards? That is pathetic. Those people who are struggling to bring up families and to exist will not manage on the market. The member for Tasman, who was brought up with a silver spoon---perhaps a platinum spoon---in his mouth was whingeing earlier about having to pay market rates for mortgages. Does he or does he not believe in the market? These new Government members believe in the new religion of the market---the market that has kept people in poverty and poor housing for century after century. Does the member believe in market rates? He whinged that he had to pay percent. I tell that member that under a Labour Government people who really needed help were able to go to the Housing Corporation and either refinance or get a mortgage at a decent rate. I want to tell Government members the reason that the Housing Corporation was set up in its present form. The Kirk Government decided that the policies for developing good housing in New Zealand were interdependent. Mortgages work with the building of houses. The old Department of Housing was amalgamated with the State Advances Corporation to create the Housing Corporation. That is what works. That is why New Zealand has the best housing policy in the world, but the Government is destroying it. The Government has said that it will introduce a system of housing vouchers. The Minister said that they will be cashed in for either State housing or private housing. Private landlords have written a series of letters to the Minister of Housing complaining that they cannot let their substandard rental accommodation because of the competition of good quality housing offered by the public sector at decent rents. The British Government provides housing vouchers to keep people in temporary bed and breakfast accommodation, but evidence shows that the system does not work. Evidence from the United States shows that under a voucher system a cap is immediately put on the total cost of the vouchers; the few who are lucky enough to get vouchers are OK but the rest live in poor and inadequate housing. Not only do people who pay rents suffer and those who pay mortgages suffer, but their children suffer, too. When one looks at any group of successful New Zealanders one finds that a reasonable proportion of them grew up in State houses. If not, they were like me and their parents had a loan from the State Advances Corporation because they were returned servicemen or low-income earners. I did not grow up in a State house but my parents had the same subsidy that the rest of New Zealand has had the benefit of.

I only want to speak once in the Committee stage of this Bill, so I will address my comments to the short title. I am delighted to be able to speak tonight in support of my colleagues who oppose this bill. Part is a rather technical part of the bill. When we look through all the technicalities and read the meaning of this part, we see that this is part of the sham. As my colleague said earlier, this is part of assuring the bankers of Housing New Zealand that all is well. What we have actually done is created this new entity. Part then goes through and puts everything out of the old and into the new. It renames it. It shuffles it around. It basically massages the concerns of the lenders to Housing New Zealand who took fright at some of the policy announcements and put their investment in Housing New Zealand at risk. The Government has had to do some serious massaging, and this part of the bill reflects that. In other words, it is putting up the sign that all is well, all will continue as far as the investors are concerned, and it is business as usual. I just happened to get in my mail today a magazine called the Hawke's Bay Property Investor from the property investors association. The editorial talks about the new policy that we see reflected in this bill here tonight. I would just like to take a few minutes to read out a little bit of this. It is written by a Mr Harry Lawson who has been a national president of the New Zealand Property Investors Association. He says that ``now that the new Labour-Alliance Government has well and truly settled down, one has to seriously wonder who has been giving the policy makers advice on housing. Under the previous Government policy, housing resources were generally targeted at those with a housing need, and it was generally noted that it was not a housing shortage but an affordability issue. Hence the accommodation allowance given not only to the lucky State house tenants, but those who were being housed in the private sector---an important part of the policy and the result was that tenants had a choice.'' Well, that has gone completely by the board and now tenants do not have a choice. He also talked about the headlong rush, which we see here tonight, to dismantle the previous policy, bring back income-related rents, and some ludicrous situations that have developed without any consultation with the industry. He named a number of the harebrained schemes that have had prominence in the press, including things like physically turning round State houses so that they face the sun, which brought great joy to all the house removal people throughout the country. He talked about the warrants of fitness for rented houses, suggesting that those in the know would understand that percent of substandard housing in New Zealand is owner occupied. But to get back to the bill, he talked about the lack of consultation with representatives of people who have invested their life-savings in property and consulting people---not just the anti-landlord groups, but people like those in the property industry and in church groups and, in particular, people who are involved in community housing. He said earlier in the debate that homes throughout New Zealand provide community housing for a wide range of people with a wide range of disabilities. I, too, have had representations from groups concerned at what will happen in this part of the bill---whether all the accommodations that they have currently will be transferred across into this new corporation. There is uncertainty and there is fear and I would certainly be grateful if the Minister could reassure those people that their fears are groundless. In reading through this part of the bill, as I said at the beginning, it is rather technical and it is about transferring parts---

We have heard a lot today about the topic of democratic process. I have to say I am outraged at the gerrymandering of the democratic process embodied in the passage of this bill to date. I would say that this Government is gambling with democracy. This Minister's last-ditch attempt to put legislation in place before the moratorium ends next week is unacceptable, is an abuse of the democratic process, and is another example of this Government's inability to get its own house in order. It is yet again ramming legislation through the select committee process---such as we saw with the Employment Relations Bill, health restructuring, and matrimonial property legislation, to name a few. Despite the deadline looming, this was left until the last minute, and, as a result, the select committee was unable to invite public submissions or even request written submissions from particular people. This bill was introduced on September. The select committee considered it on September, with a report-back date of October--- days later. That is outrageous. I found the rapidity of that process intensely frustrating, but as responsible Opposition members we realise the Minister's difficulty and we took a responsible attitude and cooperated. Now we find ourselves debating a Supplementary Order Paper. It is a Supplementary Order Paper introduced by the Hamilton member that changes the nature of the extension bill quite significantly, and introduces an element of retrospectivity and a specific removal of a specific casino from the intention of that moratorium. In addition to that we have another Supplementary Order Paper introduced by Donna Awatere Huata that is trying to allow for specific considerations of casinos in Rotorua. What an absolute mess! I would have to say that if this bill had been able to go through a normal select committee process we would have been able to hear submissions from the public of Hamilton and those concerned with Rotorua, and we would be sitting here going through a committee process with a considered report from a select committee. That is the process that is the norm, and this Government's sheer mismanagement has brought us to this debacle that we face today, with several members pushing their own particular special interests, and without a considered response from a select committee made up of members of the House. I have serious concerns that the process cannot ever be seen to have been democratic or to have upheld parliamentary process. If we go back to May earlier this year, the Waikato Times carries an article about Martin Gallagher's member's bill staying in the ballot, despite the High Court decision to quash the planned Hamilton casino. There is a comment from the chairperson of the select committee, who was at that time considering casino control and gaming law reform, that she would use her position as chairperson of that select committee to call for an extension of the moratorium, in order to address a local issue. In addition, in that article, the Minister is also quoted as saying that he would support that call for an extension if the select committee strongly called for it. Well, of course, the select committee did not strongly call for it. It made no comment on that whatsoever until the actual legislation was referred to it with days in which to report it back to the House. We have before us legislation that extends the moratorium, that has had no public consultation, that is not tied in any way to the Minister's review on gaming, and we are still waiting for terms of reference and a time line for that review. Now we are faced with a Supplementary Order Paper introduced by a member of the select committee, albeit temporary, that substantially alters the intention of the moratorium extension bill, which was to extend the original moratorium until , dependent on a review.

Yes, there is research and development in here. It says: ``Labour will: undertake a national conference...;'' Labour will ``require that the Ministry of Social Policy actively consider the impact of legislative proposals and policy programmes on children;'' Labour will ``review key legislation...;'' Labour will ``ensure a transparent independent system of review...;'' Labour will ``ensure research and data collection that reestablishes the state of children...;'' and Labour will ``make the Commissioner for Children an Officer of Parliament to ensure complete independence;''. I will read that again, let us be very clear: Labour will ``make the Commissioner for Children an Officer of Parliament to ensure complete independence;''. Is this not a promise? I would have thought that if a party went around the country in an election campaign saying: ``Labour will make the Commissioner for Children an Officer of Parliament.'', when a bill is presented to Parliament to do just that, its members would vote for it---I would have thought that. If a party came before me and promised that it would do something, as a voter I would expect that when that party is elected it would carry out that promise.

I am a new member of Parliament. I came to these hallowed halls---the seat of Government, the home of democracy---expecting and confident of finding respect and reverence for the democratic process, the core values of which are freedom of speech, freedom of thought, and freedom of the media. What have I found? Welcome to ``Helengrad''.

I want to finish very briefly what I was talking about earlier, when I referred to the follow-up study years on from the initial research and the results of the analysis of the effects of casinos on groups resident in areas where they had been introduced. The conclusion of the follow-up study was that the introduction of casinos had not been associated with significant changes in gambling behaviour or with current probable pathological problem-gambling within the study groups in the Auckland and Christchurch areas where, of course, casinos had been introduced. Here we have a reasonably definitive study, done by our own Department of Internal Affairs, that does not support some of the emotive talk that we have heard in this Committee today. In fact, one of the rather disturbing conclusions from this study is that we have heard a lot about the damage done by casinos, and gambling machines are said to be out of control in this country. But we have not heard anything about track betting, which according to this survey did not show any significant reduction between and . If we are really concerned about problem gambling and the social effects that gambling brings upon our communities, then I am concerned that we must focus, first of all, on the facts. We must focus on those areas where gambling is shown to be doing the damage. At this stage there is no definitive evidence to show that casinos are, in fact, causing huge social problems. I will finish not by reiterating the ground that I have already covered, but by responding to Phillida Bunkle and saying that the judge's decision in the case of the Waikato casino was not the fault of the applicant. The authority was at fault, not the applicant. Why, then, should the applicant be punished because the authority did not do its job correctly? The applicant has the right to have its application heard again in a proper manner by an authority, just as the opponents of that application have the right to make their cases and to be heard in a proper manner. Justice must be done in Hamilton, but it must be seen to be done for both parties.

I have to say that this is a mess. The legislation around shop trading has become an absolute shambles.
