People around the country will be pleased to know that finally there may be within Treasury corridors one politican who does not accept every word spoken by Treasury on research and development. The Heavy Engineering Research Association was the last research association to be set up. It is a very efficient, modern organisation. It has not got a large bricks-and-mortar investment in research, but acts rather like a research committee, in many instances, and simply allocates the funds collected by those levies to particular projects. They might take place within the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, in the universities, and elsewhere. The Heavy Engineering Research Association grew out of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. Those were the days when the Government took a role in public sector research that it did not expect would be immediately market-related, but then tried to spawn it off. People should have some doubts about research conducted in the public sector. It does not stand a chance of being commercialised unless it is admitted immediately that it is long-term pure research, which I personally believe is best carried out in the universities. In terms of the ordering of priorities it seems a sensible suggestion for sections of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research---when they attain sufficient critical mass as an identifiable industry group---to go on to become research associations. The Goverment does not believe in research associations. The Heavy Engineering Research Association is lucky that the Minister has been prepared to sponsor the Bill. If Treasury's line is followed to its extreme, there are reasons why there should be no compulsion to pay levies; if those people really want to get together they will do so; they will find it useful enough to them to put the money in themselves. But the Bill will allow for the use of a levying technique. I applaud the Government for sticking with the Heavy Engineering Research Association and other research associations, but I make the point that that kind of initiative is destined never to recur as long as present orthodoxy holds, because the Government has not got much time for that kind of mechanism. I do not regard the second reading debate as being a time when Ministers simply parrot their introduction speeches. I am interested in some of the policy reasons behind persisting with the Heavy Engineering Research Association. That is a matter of considerable interest when there is no enthusiasm for that kind of mechanism. For the record, the official Treasury line is that the research associations should slowly have Government input reduced to the point at which they stand on their own two feet. Because of the paranoia about producer boards and industry groups---issues that need legislative backing, as this organisation does---I suspect that Treasury would be very happy to have them go out of existence. The Government is taking the right action. The Heavy Engineering Research Association is a valuable association. The House should approve the Bill in time for its implementation by January . Members should be aware that they are taking part tonight---and next week---in a legislative exercise that is unlikely to occur in any other industry groups. I am afraid that the Minister of Science and Technology, on whose behalf the Associate Minister of Finance is speaking tonight, has been an abysmal failure when it comes to making a case for research and development. Nobody in New Zealand is asking for massive interventionist policies.

The Brash committee's consultative document---which is from Treasury and is not independent---stated that there were strong incentives to provide an acceptable standard of living during one's retirement. Treasury says that there are strong incentives. I want to see the evidence. Where is the evidence that people will save if they have the funds? With the way in which the tax incentives operate at present, the Government tells the taxpayers that they will be taxed at a certain level according to their income, but if they defer income of $, the Government will defer its claim. The Government is getting savings from people to reduce its liabilities at a later stage. In other words, the State is saying that if taxpayers' consumption is deferred today the State will defer its claim. The $ million revenue grab unleashes the money that is being received in extra revenue straight back into consumption, because it has all been spent. It is not a Budget reduction. Government spending will not be cut by that amount. Savings for the future are being diverted into current consumption. How many New Zealanders believe that in the present straitened economic circumstances it is sensible for the Government to raid tomorrow's savings for present consumption? That is precisely what the Government is doing. The third argument was dreamt up ex post facto, because the Government had to have a reason. The Government decided to come up with a socialist reason that might keep the member for Sydenham quiet. It decided to argue the point on the basis of fairness; that it is fair that people should not be able to save and be forced into depending on the Government. Bizarre claims have been made about who benefits from those deductions or incentives. The evidence from the industry that looks after those people showed that percent of people contributing to such schemes were on salaries less than times the average weekly wage. Most citizens---this is a truism of any debate about tax---are in the middle-income group. They earn a little less, a little more, or the same as the average income. Most citizens pay taxes, and the Government is effectively increasing the rate of tax for middle-income people. Is that fair? Wonderful benefits are available to people who earn $, to $,. The socialist Minister of Overseas Trade and Marketing and the member for Sydenham will troop into the lobby to vote for people on those incomes to obtain massive cuts. However, those are the people for whom that reduction is scarcely relevant. Those people have a disposable income that allows them to enter into commercial property dealings. They can buy their own buildings. The people who rely on that deduction---for whom it makes the difference between their being able to save and not being able to save, the people for whom $, is a lot of money---are not rich, but are middle-income earners. They are people who at the margin will save with the incentive and will not save without it. This Government in the name of fairness wants to remove the incentive that means that more rather than fewer New Zealanders save for their retirement. Saving for retirement will be for the rich, and the Government will squash everyone else into becoming beneficiaries. The fourth interesting argument that has been raised, which is totally spurious---and it will be raised also in the committee, and Dr Brash will receive submissions on it---is the wonderful statement that nothing is special about savings, and that there is no difference between savings and consumption. The document states: ``Subject to the Government's redistributive goals this saving can best be achieved by creating an environment in which resources are efficiently allocated.'' The problem is that there is no neutral playing-field. About percent of income is confiscated by the Government in taxation. That tends to affect people's ability to save. The incidence of tax is directly loaded against savings. The document states: ``There are at least two areas where Government action can distort decisions which determine the economy's overall level of savings''---I will bet---``the first one is, by running Budget deficits which it does not finance from domestic sources it may significantly reduce the net overall level of savings.'' That is what the Government is doing. It is financing its deficit and pulling in resources that could be available to the private sector, and therefore it is reducing the opportunity for private savings. Private savings are being confiscated to provide the Government with its ``dissaving''. Secondly, the document states that the income tax system inherently imposes a tax penalty on savings. That is it. That is why incentives were there---savings were considered to be important. The Government admits that that is the problem, and so it has removed the problem. Then the document contains a spot of propaganda: ``The announced tax rate reductions and other tax reforms, combined with the Government's monetary policy, are far more likely to produce some more appropriate savings response.'' The only problem is that the Government is not giving the tax rate that was promised on December, but is giving a tax rate that is c higher. That is an invitation to State provision, with all that that implies. Finally, I shall comment on the tax treatment of superannuation funds. It was announced on December that not only will deductions vanish but also funds that have been paid into superannuation funds will be taxed. However, that is not in the Bill.

Yes, it was a Sesqui Budget. The promises in it make interesting reading. I go to the beginning of the Budget, because it sets out to reaffirm the Government's economic goals as well as its social goals, and it comments on their interrelationship. It did much of that, but, in fact, much evidence suggests what the interrelationship is between economic policies and social policies. The equation works in this way: Labour Government overspending plus monetarism equals high unemployment. That is the prescription---it is a simple relationship between the two. The Government puts its hands on monetarism and , people are out of work. That is the social vision---it is great stuff. A Government member has told us that the Government is only half-way towards its target---it is heading towards a figure of , people out of work. Most New Zealanders are saying that they have had enough. Whatever the Christ's College old boy who spouts socialism says, he sat at the Cabinet table that imposed undiluted monetarism, which has been the envy of the right wing of the Tory Party in England. But whereas in England inflation has run out of control because the economy is growing so fast, here the inflation has run out of control, followed by a complete bust, followed by inflation still running at nearly percent when the June quarter comes out, and the economy going nowhere and unemployment mounting. That is a real feat. I think that Sir Geoffrey Howe, John Major, and Margaret Thatcher could not have managed that. That was not part of the prescription, but it happened here because in the first years the Government had a party. There was a boom, credit ran out of control, and central business district property prices doubled in a couple of years. That does not tell members anything about the productive capacity of the nation. It tells a hell of a lot about the fact that there was loose money and that things ran out of control. What about the stock market? I can recall door-knocking in Churchill, in the north of Hamilton, and speaking to people. People said that they were normally National Party voters, but that things were going OK for them and the stock market had been doing fairly well. I could see the dollar signs flashing in their eyes. Many people were carried away and the Government and the Minister were re-elected for a second term principally on a stock market bubble that had nothing to do with reaffirming the relationship between economic and social goals. That had nothing to do with the conscience of the Labour Party.

Yes, as I understand it, but I am not an expert. I am told it is less partial to cucumbers, zucchinis, pumpkins, and grapes. However, only the latter is likely to be inadvertently brought in. Unfortunately, it is something that is found on a large amount of fruit that people find very attractive. A female lays up to , eggs in batches of one to six. The adult lives for about days, and in the height of the Auckland summer the whole life cycle can be completed within days. If allowed to get loose, it could go through five to six generations in a year. That is why this is so extraordinarily serious. The multiplicative value of that---, eggs per adult, five or six generations in a year---if it got out of control, is extremely serious. The eggs are laid under the skin of fruit, the maggots feed on the pulp---of course that is what does the damage---the larvae come to the surface of the fruit, drop from the fruit, tunnel into the soil, and pupate. In that condition the species can withstand some frost, so this is not something that would even be confined to the non-frost regions of New Zealand. If it were to get loose it really would be a threat to the entire North Island. The good news in this particular case is that ceratitis capitata is not a great disperser. Provided there is adequate fruit it will stick within the vicinity of its emergence. That means that with the sort of occurrence that we had in Mt Roskill, where there is still fruit around in the area, it is likely to stay within to metres of the release site, in the presence of fruit. With that in mind, and in view of the fact that no fruit fly have been found more than metres away from the initial discovery, and the bulk were much closer to the actual point of discovery---the larvae were found in a feijoa fruit only metres from the point of discovery---one would have to say that the Australian decision to impose an -kilometre-radius ban is somewhat extreme. One can only hope that the Australians reconsider that position. My understanding is that given the particular facts of this occurrence---the fact that there has been nothing outside a -metre area, which is no larger than Parliament grounds, just to give that some dimension for people listening---a prudent buffer might be kilometres. One would hope that the Australians would reconsider their position. The other point is that there is real confidence that given the massive level of response by officials on the ground, and the fact that the discoveries are all within such a contained area, we can get on top of this. It shows how important those , traps around the country are. The traps are, by the way, cleared and inspected once every days, plus or minus day. No other finds have been reported outside the precise zone in Mount Roskill. It appears that the outbreak is undoubtedly coming from smuggled fruit, probably direct from Hawaii. There are no Mediterranean fruit fly of this species in South-east Asia. I understand that they could possibly be from Western Australia, although Hawaii seems to be the place that is being referred to.

I would like to thank the two members who have made a contribution and reply to a few questions that have been raised. I just start with the observation that for reasons of almost statutory conflict, what the member has just said is quite correct. The Minister for the Environment, if he or she were to be Minister of Conservation, would have to have so many Chinese walls in place that little would get done. I do not think there is a problem for the short period to the election in which I am holding both portfolios. I can inform the House that I am taking considerable care to see that those roles are not in conflict. There are, however, some advantages in being Minister of Research, Science and Technology and being Minister of Conservation. As is noted in the report, one of my priorities is to see that the department gets a really good long-term research strategy in place. I am strongly of the view that if we are to spend money on pest control or threatened species then we really need to have an excellent research base to underpin that, not just in terms of getting good environmental results but also in terms of knowing how we are spending our money. The other thing we also need to do, which I think is mentioned in the report, is to make progress now as a department being the lead agency for developing the biodiversity strategy. I am starting to take a close interest in this, and it really is hugely important. I think it was the member for Nelson who mentioned that the Department of Conservation's interest does go beyond the Government-owned estate. The biodiversity strategy, of course, encompasses the whole of New Zealand, or will do. The basis on which that is done will have to be very carefully considered. The member for Eden raised the question of Kerry McDonald's management review. The answer is that some interim advice has been given to me. It has really been more in the nature of briefings with consultants who are assisting the director-general with a review of this, so I am not in receipt of anything final at this stage. I think it would be fair to say that if we are to get quality conservation management systems in place, there will have to be much better line management accountability and much clearer protocols and better ability to require that things happen down the line. That, I think, will be the outcome of the review. I note that in the select committee's report, the department is reported as saying that the task will be formidable, and I think that is right. This is a very, very significant review that is being undertaken, and it is important that we get it right. I hear the member for Nelson say that the Department of Conservation needs more money. Well, yes I think it spent well on conservation, and the Government has fallen in with that; it is putting up a lot of extra money. But if the department is spending a bean more than it needs to on administration and on bean counting, then we have to ask questions. I think the sort of stewardship that I would want is a stewardship that ensures we get accountability to Parliament for the money that is spent to secure conservation outcomes, but we should not be presiding over a system that is monolithic and costly to administer. Every cent that we can free up from administrative requirements without compromising safety is a cent that can go into adding to the protection of species and adding to the removal of pests, which of course are the Government's two priorities. I think that the member for Nelson's comments would make clear to anybody listening that the Labour Party has apparently unlimited resources available for the department if it asked for them.

To suggest that only a union---no one else, no other organisation---can prevent an unequal situation from evolving is quite bizarre, but not as bizarre as members might think. I have been trawling back through the statutory history of this Chamber's predecessors in England and I have discovered that this sort of thing has been done before. I want to draw to the attention of the Committee the Test Act in , in which Parliament, at Queen Anne's behest, passed a law that said only those taking the sacrament of the Lord's Supper according to the rites of the Anglican Church could hold any office, civil or military, under the Crown. Now the Roman Catholics had been out of it for a long time, but a Roman Catholic lawyer at the time was moved to observe that surely the Presbyterians did not do anything to deserve worse treatment at the hands of the Government than any other Protestant. The parallel is absolute. We have good workers who want to go into collective agreements. They want to bargain; it is just that they do not want to use the established church. I put it to Catholic and Presbyterian members opposite, if they have got a faith, that centuries ago they were discriminated against precisely because they did not want to be forced into the established church of the day. In secular terms this is no different. The part that the Opposition proposes would say that they do not have to use the established church, that they can choose their own bargaining agent---and, guess what, their own bargaining agent, not a union, might be just as competent in securing their rights as those non-conformist preachers were in securing the salvation of their souls in heaven, years ago. Back in , it was that sort of legislation that led droves of people to leave Ulster for America. Look what happened in terms of who made it in the world! The same parallel exists here: if the established church has a monopoly in the form of the unions people will be leaving this country for Australia. That is where they will be going, because in Australia, despite all sorts of extraordinary union legislation, people can have somebody other than a union represent them in collective bargaining. That is as absurd as it is. The only sad thing is that in our political culture there is a long and unhappy history of Governments that cannot allow anyone to see the world through any eyes other than their own, insisting that they will say who we can deal with. It is most important to emphasise that this part does not suggest that people should go off and become heathens, or worship in a different religion. No, to use the religious analogy, they must stay true to the cause, they must believe in collective bargaining, they must believe passionately in the worker and the boss, and they must have meetings to negotiate. All we are saying is they should be able to choose someone in whom they have confidence. It is no answer to say: ``Oh well, go off and form a union.'' because then there is this extraordinary paraphernalia laid down by this Act. Why cannot people simply reach their own agreements? None of this would be to the prejudice of those who believe the true faith is better and want to proselytise for it.

Today we are debating a very important matter of principle. We are talking about a party that supports fairness in terms of taxes, and parties that do not believe in fairness and intend to oppose this clause. The proposal in this clause ensures that people who should be paying c tax do pay c tax on all their income, rather than some people who are investing in superannuation funds having to pay c. It is an issue of fairness, and the National Party is standing on principle and saying that people who should be paying c should pay c, not c. The parties on the other side of the Chamber, and indeed some parties even on this side of the Chamber, are saying: ``No, you should be paying, you should continue to pay more than your fair share.'' Well we are not prepared to do that, and we are standing firm on this issue, and we will go to the wire on it. The suggestion that we need to ameliorate the provision by changing the social assistance provisions is quite wrong. It would be putting the wrong incentives into the system. It would mean that people who are receiving social assistance would not be paying the correct tax rate. We cannot afford to manipulate our tax system in that way. We have to have a very clear and definable tax system. Those savers who were also receiving social assistance would see superannuation funds as a preferred investment vehicle, and that would not be appropriate.

The only thing that Opposition members have shown us over the last half-hour or so is that they are totally bereft of ideas, but they do have big voices. That is all we have heard. I give them out of for big voices and wagging fingers. But it takes more than big voices and wagging fingers to move this nation. This nation needs big ideas. The only big idea that the Labour Party has managed to come up with is its new president---and his big idea is to have a grand coalition. A former leader of the Labour Party has said that the Labour Party is bereft of ideas, and cannot communicate the ideas it does have. After listening to the debate so far, the public will merely see that that view has been confirmed. The Budget Policy Statement debate is an opportunity to pause. It is an opportunity to look left, take fright; look right, then look left again before moving on. It is a chance to look backwards and see where we have come from, but, more important, to look forwards to see where we are going. It is a reality check. The Budget Policy Statement tells a great story. It tells the people of New Zealand three key things: it spells out the Government's long-term goals and objectives for its income and expenditure, it explains the Government's plan of action that will be incorporated in the Budget, and it outlines the spending boundaries over the next years. It is a head-up display of where the Government is heading. It tells us which way the Government's antennae are facing. It shows whether the Government is focused on the future, on growth, and on being positive, or whether it is focused on looking back, on pining and whining for the failed policies of the past, and on being negative. There is no room for equivocation with this Budget Policy Statement. It has one very loud and clear message. It is a blueprint for a Government that has growth and innovation very clearly in its sights. It is a plan for setting a scene where employment and income will flourish, and where trade, social cohesion, and social opportunities will prosper so that all Kiwis can play their part in this country's future, and not, as the Opposition would have it, for some to be left languishing on the dole. This is all about participation and involvement. The Budget Policy Statement builds on a history of careful management of the economy. It sets out that sound economic and fiscal policies inevitably lead to higher and better social dividends. It profiles a society where participation is the name of the game. There is no denying that New Zealand has gone through a difficult patch, and, because the fortunes of the economy are linked so closely to the lives of people, some New Zealanders have had a pretty difficult time. This country has been put on its mettle not only because of the normal business cycle but also because of the Asian economic difficulties, the Asian crisis, falling commodity prices, and severe drought. But, by and large, New Zealanders have come through. It is clear from the commentaries that the recovery is under way. We will not get carried away with it. We will take it cautiously, but the indications are that the recovery is well under way. The restructuring of past years, and actions taken by this minority Government and previous Governments, have proven to be sensible decisions---ranging from the tax cuts, which kicked in just at the right time, through to microeconomic reform and macroeconomic stability that this Government and its predecessors have provided. The Government's past focus on reducing Crown debt has shown that it pays dividends. It has enabled interest payments to be diverted, to be reallocated. Instead of spending it as expenditure on interest payments it is now invested in health and education. Why pay out interest when we can see the benefits from investment in health and education? But let us look a bit wider than just the Government's interest bill, because, in fact, the huge change has been in personal interest bills. Interest rates are now the lowest in years, and New Zealanders are reaping the benefits. Most New Zealanders aspire to owning their own homes and those who have a mortgage are seeing huge benefits. A family with an $, mortgage is saving $ a week on mortgage repayments, as a result of the stewardship of this Government. Not only are interest payment reductions flowing through to the family's spending power but also the tax cuts are flowing through and there is family assistance targeted to those who really need it. A family earning $,, with older children and an $, mortgage, is $ a week better off. Labour has nothing to match that. That is putting the spending power, the decision-making, back in Kiwis' hands. We are all about empowering Kiwis, empowering individuals---the people who make our country tick. The National-led Government is a ``can do'' Government, not a ``can't do'', not one that will take us back to the failed policies of the past. It is one that prides itself on talking about what people can do, on empowering people, making them feel strong, and knowing that they can succeed. We are seeing the manufacturing sector lead the economy out of its difficulties. We look at the export-led recovery in Canterbury. They are leading the charge. Auckland is following closely behind. But the domestic emphasis in the Auckland market has slowed down Auckland's growth. But we recognise the importance of Auckland---not like Dr Cullen, who takes pride in stifling it, who talks about it being a crushing weight on the rest of New Zealand. Auckland is a hive of activity. It is a wealth of activity from its northern borders to its southern borders; whether it be Albany, North Shore, or the Penrose industrial edge, where companies and businesses are sprouting up more quickly than they can build the buildings. The Budget Policy Statement encourages this innovation. Unlike the Labour Party, this Government celebrates innovation. National will not tax innovators the way the Labour Party will. National is proud of Auckland, it is proud of the innovation that is being shown throughout New Zealand. It is a pity that Helen Clark seems to be picking up on the lead taken by Dr Cullen in criticising Auckland, in trying to stifle the growth that Auckland is demonstrating. She is playing down the benefits that will flow through from the America's Cup and from APEC. We know better. We know that Auckland is the engine room of the economy, together with the rest of the country. Together they go in partnership. The Budget Policy Statement highlighted seven overarching goals. We want a strong-growing internationally competitive economy. We value innovation. We place a high value on the contribution that individuals, families, and communities can make. We want to focus social assistance where it is most needed. We value our partnership with Maori. Above all, we are proud of our New Zealand identity, and this is profiled and highlighted in our Budget Policy Statement. We want to move people up the ladder. We do not want to hold them down. We cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong, and we cannot help the poor by destroying the rich. We cannot help people by doing for them what they can best do for themselves. The National-led minority Government believes in the power of Kiwis. It believes in the power of Kiwis---as individuals, in the community, and in the family. The Labour - Alliance bloc is desperate. All the deputy leader of the Labour Party could do was muster personal attacks against the front bench of this Government. He cannot bear the thought that this Government is brimming with talent, youth, enthusiasm, and experience. He is struggling to regurgitate the old arguments; he has not realised that the ground has moved. The National-led team is making a success of minority Government and it has guided the country through difficult economic times. It is delivering better opportunities for Kiwis.

Today we are debating the third reading of a Bill that has undergone a significant metamorphosis since it was first introduced by Mr Tony Steel in May under a different name, the Tertiary Students Association Voluntary Membership Bill. It is the third Bill in almost as many years and indicates the level of interest in this issue across Parliament, and indeed across parties, with the Bill first introduced by Michael Laws, then Mr Steel's Bill, and a further Bill introduced by Donna Awatere Huata. There is significant interest in the issue that this Bill addresses. It is about membership of students associations and about choice---two simple issues. The purpose of the Bill is to enable students, the intelligentsia of our society, to have a choice on whether to join a students association---an association representing their interests at their tertiary institution, whether it be university, a private training establishment, whanaunga, or whatever. If they choose to belong to an association then this Bill will enable them to do so. We have heard lots of opposition from members on the other side, that they do not believe that students are capable of making a choice of their own. They want to direct students; to impose a students association membership on them. They want to remove the fundamental right of all of us---to be able to choose to associate with whom we want. The Opposition would have us believe that students, who are able to make a decision to take out a student loan, to go to university, to go flatting, to get married, to live together, or to go overseas, are not capable of deciding whether they should join an association that represents their best interests, or, perhaps because they believe that that association may not represent their best interests, they may choose not to join. The Labour/Alliance cabal on the other side wants to control everything, every aspect of a student's life. That is something that this side of the House, and some members on the other side of the House, do not concur with. Significant change was made to this Bill during the Committee stage. Where was the voice of the Opposition on the amendments that were introduced in the Committee stage? There was not a tweet, not a sound, not a noise from the Opposition benches, from the Labour/Alliance cabal---not a whisper and definitely not a bark. Students throughout New Zealand could be forgiven for believing that there was consensus across the House on the amendments that were introduced in the Committee stage. But now we hear a few bleats from the Opposition saying that it was not a good idea after all, but it is a bit too late in the piece. Students should feel let down by members of the Opposition who now purport to stand up for their interests. The feedback is that students are pleased to be able to have the choice to decide which associations they would like to join. This is a member's Bill. That point has been made before.

If I was a permanent Wellington resident I would be worried, after having listened to the previous speaker. I would not only be worried but very upset, because we have heard minutes of reasons that the Transmission Gully motorway will not go ahead--- minutes of reasons that it is not going to happen. Wellington has waited too long for that motorway, and I congratulate Mr Dunne for introducing this bill and getting something into the House that we can debate. It is an indication to the people of Wellington and, indeed, New Zealand, that an MP is prepared to put his or her money where his or her mouth is---to put a bill into the House so we can get on with the issue. I hope this bill does go to the select committee, although clearly, if the Government does not support it, the bill will have a hard track getting there. However, there are other members in this House who could well support the bill to ensure that it does get to the select committee. The select committee has already spoken on the Transmission Gully issue. It has dealt with at least three petitions calling for the Transmission Gully highway to be progressed. More than , people have signed a petition supporting the highway and calling for action, so the select committee is well briefed on the issue. I assure the member that it will receive a positive, constructive, and timely hearing---if it makes its way to the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. However, we have seen quite clearly that the Government is not in a mood for green lights. Indeed, it is a foolish Government that thinks it can thumb its nose at the sentiment in Wellington at the moment. There is no doubt that there is significant support for this highway, and we now have something in the House that we can deal with and start to action. The Minister started off in typical style by attacking the messenger, by attacking the former Minister and by attacking the member for some of the actions he has taken in the past. That is the Minister's typical style: attacking the person, not the message. The Government has done a lot of talking, and we have read press releases in recent days about how things might start moving. But we are sick of hearing the talk; we want to hear about the action. The Minister says that the Government will make a decision on roading policy in months' time. Well, months' time! Every time that the Government gives a deadline in terms of transport policy, that deadline is put off. The Minister rubbishes the efforts of previous Governments to deal with roading issues, and progress has certainly not been as fast as it might have been. I wonder how much the Minister will borrow from the work of previous Governments in the policy that he finally does get round to delivering. The Minister talked about environmental issues, and the select committee, in considering the petitions, was very strong on that. We should get on with the job and start addressing those environmental mitigation issues, so that we do not have to wait any longer than is necessary. The select committee is keen to deal with the detail. We are not concerned that the bill is not perfect as it is at the moment. Certainly, members of the select committee on the Opposition side of the House are not concerned that the detail is not perfect. We are prepared to work on it, and the member has indicated that he recognises that change is necessary. The National Party is committed to supporting this bill. We have been lobbied long and hard by Wellington National Party members. They want to see this road built, and we want to see it built. It is great to hear that the Minister is keen to consult local MPs and to have some sort of bipartisan agreement. If he is so keen to consult and to gain bipartisan support, why does he not support this bill going to the select committee so that we can get on with it? We are dealing with something of substance, not some ethereal matter that he thinks might come forward in a few months' time. It is good to hear that the Minister is prepared to address the private sector funding of roads and tolling, and, while it may be foreign to the present Government to deal with those sorts of issues, it is certainly not foreign to us. This bill is a chance for the Government to express its support for the Transmission Gully highway project, to show that it believes in action and not just in words. We want to get on with it. We have heard lots of talk from the Minister, but there has been nothing concrete. It is time to put some action behind his words. The Minister's comment made earlier this week or last week, saying that he believes that the Transmission Gully road should be built, was followed by a series of ``buts'', and that is what we have heard in the House today. Yes, he thinks the road should be built but there are all sorts of reasons that it should not happen. He is a Minister whose ``yes'' is followed by ``but''. We saw that just last weekend, over the Virgin Blue incident, when he said that yes, we want to see competition in the New Zealand air traffic market, but there are all sorts of reasons that we will not deliver on it. We say to the Government that it should just get on with the job. Mr Dunne has delivered an olive branch to the Government. He has given it a helping hand, and the Government should not spurn it. It will be a hard job for the Government to convince the public that, by opposing the bill, the Government supports Transmission Gully. The only way to support progress on the Transmission Gully issue is to take this first tangible step of supporting the bill. Politicians are constantly criticised for just talking; here is a constructive mechanism to get rid of the talk and to start some action. Wellingtonians are sick of hearing the reasons against the Transmission Gully highway---so are Aucklanders, for that matter---and we want to see some action. The councils, the MPs, and the population of Wellington, are united---excuse the pun---on the issue. They want to see the road built. They do not want to know the reasons for not doing so; they want to see it happen. It is good to see that the public is coming in behind the concept of tolling. People are not opposed to polling, and are prepared to pay for the road if it means building it more quickly. We have heard that the officials' paper relating to this bill urged that the Government oppose it. It stated that there was discussion on Land Transport Safety Authority policy---that it was reviewing policy, and the decision should be made by the end of April. Well, that is another deadline that has gone by. That deadline has passed, as have the rail deadlines. All sorts of deadlines in relation to transport policy have passed, and we are not prepared to wait any longer. The Government should take note of the saying that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. This bill is something that it can get on with. Mr Dunne has already referred to the officials' paper. It is appalling to think that the officials tried to justify not supporting this bill because that might set a precedent for local MPs, electorate MPs---or list MPs, for that matter---promoting bills to see roads built in areas in which they are needed. As Mr Dunne pointed out, is that not what democracy is all about? It is about members of Parliament standing up and fighting for what they believe in. To attempt to justify defeating this bill on those grounds is just amazing, but, of course it is par for the course for this Government that is all about trying to stifle free speech. It is appalling that the officials were prepared to put their names to that argument. The community is well and truly prepared to see this road built. It is sick of reading headlines and it is sick of reading why we are waiting---the red-tape highway, crusaders for a safer road, highway of horror. There is huge support for the Transmission Gully road, and the Government should get on with it and take the initiative. It should follow the initiative that Mr Dunne has given to it, the key he has given to it by introducing this bill. If the Government bill catches up with this bill, then so be it. That would be great. At least it might put a bit of pressure on the Government to get its act together. But Mr Dunne has got his act together; he has a bill in the House. Yes, it has a few flaws, but we can deal with those. We should let the Government's legislation catch up with Mr Dunne's bill. If I was a betting person, I would probably put my money on Mr Dunne's bill making progress before the Government's legislation sees the light of day. I say that the priority is to deal with something that we have in our hands at the moment. Wellington needs the Transmission Gully highway. There will be huge social benefits, economic benefits, and strategic benefits from seeing this road completed. Aucklanders do not want to see any of their projects being deferred, but we want to see the Transmission Gully highway completed.

Part has two clauses. I give notice that I would like to have minutes on the commencement clause, and I would like to take a second call to deal with the purpose clause. Normally, we would have two bites at the cherry and there are two different sets of issues that need to be addressed. First, in relation to the commencement date, members will be interested to note that the bill was introduced under an expectation of urgency, in the sense that the Minister wanted it to be considered and passed within a very tight time frame. A -week time frame was given to the select committee when the bill was introduced. That would have meant that the bill would have been introduced and passed by April this year. It should not pass members' attention that that date was several months ago. The commencement date was then amended by the select committee to September . That was just over a month ago. The committee sent the bill back to Parliament on June, within the extended time frame the Minister had agreed to, and then it languished on the Order Paper for a good months. This very, very important, urgent legislation should have been passed in weeks. Although it did not languish in the select committee---the select committee worked very, very hard on it---once it came back to Parliament it sat on the Order Paper for months. Finally, the bill has come to the Committee and we see in Supplementary Order Paper in the Minister's name that the implementation date is now April . The implementation date is to be year after the implementation date that was anticipated when the bill was introduced, with a very short time frame of a -week period for the select committee process. That highlights the way in which the bill has been mismanaged. The Minister failed to recognise how the bill should have been progressed, by failing to conduct a fair degree of consultation prior to its introduction. Then, arguably, it could have been dealt with a lot sooner than it has been. I shall move on to the clause , ``Purpose'' just in case I do not get a second call, although I do hope I will get a second call. The purpose clause is very wide ranging. When the bill was introduced, the purpose clause had two main thrusts. One was to enhance the safety of civil aviation, by improving the regulation of medical certification. The second was to validate existing medical certificates and certification decisions. After extensive lobbying by a number of people, the Minister has agreed to delete, by way of Supplementary Order Paper, the validation clause, so the validation purpose within clause of the bill is now redundant. It is good to see the validation clause has been, or will be, removed from the bill. It is important that we set the record straight concerning the purpose clause. There were a number of diverging opinions in the select committee, as indeed, there are in the Committee, as to the reason and justification for the bill. The Scott-Gorman report, which reviewed the medical certification process, identified a number of flaws in the medical certification system that had been set up in the early s. That report identified an inconsistency of practice amongst some doctors and raised serious concerns. The report's view was that the director of the Civil Aviation Authority was not able to revoke certificates that had been issued by aviation medical assessors, where he considered that they had been incorrectly issued. Similarly, the director's power to remove aviation medical assessors whom he considered were not doing their job properly was not clear. It was suggested that brought the medical certification process into disrepute, or certainly caused serious concerns about the director's ability to ensure public safety through ensuring that pilots had been properly, medically certified. There was a lot of disagreement through the select committee over the Scott-Gorman report. While there may be doubts over some parts of it, I certainly was convinced that there was reason to look very closely at the medical certification process. Indeed, I accept that the director did not have the powers he needed in order to uphold public safety and to uphold his or her role as the prime regulator of aviation safety in New Zealand. However, as the Committee will find later on, the National Party believes that the Minister's response to the Scott-Gorman report was way over the top. He went for the recentralisation of the devolved system and, in fact, went too far. He overreacted to the points raised in the Scott-Gorman report and went too far. We believe that a devolved system can work, but it will be necessary to tighten up the process. One of the reasons that the certification process has not worked was that audits did not take place. The responsibility for that must fall on those who were in the Civil Aviation Authority at that time, and, in particular, on the principal medical officer. While the principal medical officer undertook paper audits of the certificates, he did not undertake clinical audits of aviation medical assessors' practices. As a result, over time there appeared to be a drift amongst the medical practice of some aviation medical assessors. There was much argument that if the audits had taken place, the issue of drift would not have arisen. Well, time has drifted on too long for that---if one excuses the pun. It was certainly identified that audits needed to be implemented, and that the responsibility for audits was with the Civil Aviation Authority. It is essential that the Civil Aviation Authority does implement an effective audit system. The potential for conducting the audits was in the principal Act; it was in the rules. The Civil Aviation Authority did not implement that process at that time. It is only in the last couple of years that audits have taken place and some of the failures of the system have been identified.

I wish to make only a short contribution to this debate. I am unashamedly in support of option A. Some odd lines of thought have drifted through this debate. This is not about under-age drinking, it is not about Sunday trading, and it is certainly not about shoplifting in supermarkets. The options diminish in liberality as we progress through from option A, which is the wine, the beer, and the spirits down to option B, which is the wine and the beer, and, finally, down to the wine by itself. The problem I have is that I am happy to be a conservative in so far as the age is concerned but not in so far as from where the stuff is sold or what is sold there. After all, supermarkets are places where we can buy those other things that people drink, like methylated spirits, varnish, and paint thinner, which still enjoy a certain level of sale to certain clientele. So, in a sense, spirits would be one of the lesser alcoholic beverages available. As I said, there is nothing worse than trying to be half a liberal. One of the earlier contributors to the debate said that she was prepared to half open the door---only half open it. Some other speaker said that the world is not quite ready for this. One of the classic contributions was made by our resident professor of law, Wayne Mapp. He described this as a progressive situation where we slowly move through things over the course of time. Well, he also managed to be progressive in the course of his speech. I would warrant he started off advocating option B, which is the halfway stage between being a chardonnay socialist and a full libertarian. He then progressed to option A, which, I think, if he has a look at the Hansard, he will find was the case. Although one could excuse that as some kind of Freudian slip one would hope that his subconscious is in better touch than the presentation he made tonight. Certainly, he may have started to talk about option B, but, indeed, he finally found his soul in option A, and I agree with him. One has only to listen to Patricia Schnauer or to Bob Simcock to hear a clear, rational explanation of this whole situation. This is all about moving into the next millennium---normalising things, having sensible, educated drinking New Zealanders. We are not talking about children; we are talking about mature adults. Those are the points that I wanted to make, and I hope that people support option A.

I would like at the outset to give some congratulations to Detective Inspector Pope in Picton for reaching the milestone of making an arrest in the Operation Tam case of the two young people who disappeared in suspicious circumstances. I am sure the other side of the House will join me in that. Sadly, it seems that those two young people are dead. I congratulate the whole Operation Tam team. Ted Cox's name was raised, and I would like to put in an endorsement for Ted Cox. I have known him since he was a young constable, a detective, and as he has moved all the way up through the ranks. He is one of those outstanding policemen who has had contact with the front line then reached a higher rank. To me it is unfortunate to hear his name used in other than reverential terms, so I would like it recorded that I believe that he is an excellent policeman. I am grateful in a way to see that the integrated national crime information system is coming to make some kind of sense. It has been recognised in the review that members---I think that is the actual figure---need not go. I think that is a very good idea. I would like to think that the Justice and Law Reform Committee assisted in leading the folk concerned to that view, and I do believe that is the right way to go about it. This whole review has had a horrific build-up, not least because it was tied up with the Fire Service debate, which attracted all manner of odium to itself. Some of that is rubbing off on to the police review. I personally tend to be terribly sensitive about anything that touches upon the police, but I must say that having now read the draft review I feel a lot more relaxed about the matter. If I have a reservation at all---and it is only fair that I mention my reservation---it is who will do the administrative work when the administrative people are gone. I trust and implore those who redesign the force to ensure that it will not be the front-line staff. I have no doubt that the system of consultation will sort that out, and that the folk making the final decisions will be well apprised of that. The ``front line'' is a term that is bandied around this House fairly liberally. The front line exists in reality, and it is also a fairly metaphysical entity in the public mind. It could be described as the thin blue line, as indeed it often is. The police in that situation are seen as avenging angels who occupy the ground between chaos and law and order. I am certain that that is the view that most members of the public have of the police. The public expects the front line to arrive, to quell disturbances to the orderly events of their lives, to restore order, then to visit upon the perpetrators of that disorder some kind of social disapproval. That is how basic it is. The front line is the thin blue line that is out there, and it is our duty as parliamentarians to keep it strong. If it is not strong, then the whole fabric of society is affected. That is not saying something in a pompous manner; it is saying something in a very realistic, basic manner. If this review releases more resources to the front line, then as far as I am concerned it is a good thing. The review touches on other matters such as the constitutional arrangement between the Minister of Police and the Commissioner of Police. As it points out, historically the Minister has been able to direct the commissioner in administrative matters and the running of the police, but never ever in terms of the operational character of the police. If that is to be altered, I hope a great deal of careful thought is given to it. The fact it is raised at all implies that someone has something in mind for it. What exactly that will be will emerge, no doubt, in the course of the consultation. I would have thought about the matter in a slightly different way. I am actually a bit of a fan of having a civilian commissioner. I do not really think that tracking one's way up through the ranks as a career policeman necessarily fits one to be Commissioner of Police. I can think of numerous occasions in the past when, if we had had a wheeler-dealer who was very good at catching resources, we might have been better off. So if it is not a career policeman who ends up as commissioner, I would not be terribly upset. I support the notion of a civilian in that position. There is a very interesting Newspeak word here, ``outsourcing'', which I take to mean the contracting out of police jobs. I am certainly not averse to that. Over the last -odd years the police have picked up all manner of almost dross-type jobs, only because they were the only ones around to do them. The police were, for a long, long time, the only -hour emergency service. They were the only ones silly enough to keep the doors open in the middle of the night, so people with all kinds of problems---not necessarily related to law, order, crime, and so on---wandered in there with things to be done. So now, years later, I think this is as good a time as any, as we move towards the millennium, to have a look at a whole range of tasks that the police perform and consider them being outsourced, which seems to be the ``in'' word. I am talking about things like prosecutions, crime prevention, scene of crime examinations, the lost and found function, and the escorting of prisoners here, there, and everywhere. There is a lot of room to move in those terms. Labour folk have a very short memory on this particular theme of out-sourcing. The Labour Government, in its incarnation-

I am directed to report that the Primary Production Committee has carefully considered the Potato Industry Act Repeal Bill and recommends that it be allowed to proceed without amendment. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The Bill was referred to the Primary Production Committee on May . No submissions were received on the Bill. The consideration and deliberation phase was completed by the committee on June . The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries acted as adviser to the committee. The background of the Bill is as follows. At a joint meeting on August the Potato Growers Federation and the New Zealand Vegetable Growers Federation recommended that the Potato Board be abolished. Because that body formerly represented the interests of potato growers, discussions were held with representatives of the Potato Board, the Potato Growers Federation, and the Vegetable Growers Federation for the replacement organisation. At the end of November the Potato Growers Federation merged with the New Zealand Vegetable Growers Federation to form the potato division of the Vegetable Growers Federation. As a consequence of that merger in the potato industry, the main crop levy regulations were revoked and the Vegetable Levy Extensions Order was promulgated with the effect that in no levies were assessed in support of the Potato Industry Board. The Vegetable Growers Federation was able to levy to meet the costs of its new division. Agreement has been reached with the potato industry that the remaining assets of the Potato Board should be transferred to the potato division of the Vegetable Growers Federation. The gathering-in of the board's assets, and the disposal of its property, before dissolution, is in hand and near completion. As arrangements are in hand, and as the potato division of the Vegetable Growers Federation is assuming responsibility for many of the board's functions, it is possible to proceed with the repeal of the Potato Industry Act , and with the vesting of its remaining assets in that body. The Potato Board, the Potato Growers Federation, and the Vegetable Growers Federation have been consulted and are in agreement with the proposed repeal. The Bill's purpose is to repeal the Potato Industry Act. It is made up of the following clauses. Clause relates to the short title and commencement. Clause will become effective on August . The remainder of the Bill will become effective on the day on which it receives the royal assent. Clause defines the term ``board'' as the New Zealand Potato Board. Clause repeals the Potato Industry Act and its amendments. Clause keeps the board in existence in the meantime. Clause requires the board to advertise its impending dissolution and to call for claims against it. Clause requires the board to dispose of its property, recover all debt owing to it, dismiss its staff, and make redundancy payments. Clause requires the board to satisfy all proper claims made against it. Clause requires any surplus funds after the payment of claims to be paid to the Vegetable Growers Federation, to be paid to or used for its potato division. Clause , which comes into force on August , dissolves the board. Clause provides that debts owing to the board on dissolution become debts owing to the Vegetable Growers Federation. The Bill fulfils the potato industry's wishes. The committee agrees with those changes, and did not amend the Bill in any way. I hope that the Bill will proceed as quickly as possible through the House.

I accept the point, but I was just trying to correct the member for Rangitikei and put him on the right road. I am sure that he will recommend to his farmers that they take appropriate action against the banks and other lending institutions that are causing them problems. The proposed new section F() in clause deals with a breach of contract. That provision is probably one of the most important provisions in the Bill. During the select committee hearings the industry as a whole was very grateful for the opportunity to present submissions. Its representatives were able to go away and discuss the various provisions with other officials. They have made constructive and helpful changes to the Bill. I applaud their actions. The point has been made in the debate that farmers will not find the Bill very helpful, yet no farmer wants a hand-out; I do not know of one farmer who does. Opposition members have said that farmers want hand-outs and no charge for the meat inspection service, but that is totally incorrect. Farmers are not bludgers, and they do not want hand-outs. They want only to pay their fair share in the industry and to keep it on a viable footing, and that is what the Bill will achieve. In conclusion, the Bill will be of considerable benefit not only to farmers but also to the people who work in the industry. Several sectors have been mentioned by previous speakers, but Opposition members should have been more constructive. However, that is the essence of the Opposition at the moment. I support the Bill, which has taken considerable time to put together. The Bill has passed through its stages not only in a constructive way but also in a democratic way. I shall build on some of the remarks made by the member for Matamata, particularly about the energy sector. The Government's approach to energy is contrary to the best advice that it is receiving---in the instance I am about to deal with---from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research has been telling the Government that, first, oil is being used internationally as though the world's supplies of liquid fuel were everlasting. In other words, international rates of consumption equate with those of the s and s, before the first oil shock, as we know it, which torpedoed the Kirk-Rowling Administration. It set off, amongst other things, a massive inflationary spiral, and put out of kilter the Government's own Budget. The Government is headed down precisely the same path, and its Budget of a few days ago is already out of date because of what has happened in the past few days in the Gulf. That is the first advice that the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research has been giving the Government. Second, it has also been telling the Government that in one geographic area---Asia---the use of energy has increased in the past years alone by more than percent. Third, the department has told the Government that it can expect to be confronted with shortages in oil supplies in the early s---indeed, so can the international community. The Government has also been told that the production of oil has peaked in non-OPEC countries---essentially, countries outside of the Middle East that have petroleum sources, including the United States, Canada, and the Soviet Union, to name three. Massive investment is needed within OPEC countries to boost sagging production. Moreover, it is said that because of the emergence of East European countries on to the international oil market as a result of recent political changes, there will be a massive increase in the demand for fuel. Hitherto those countries have secured their oil from the Soviet Union, but they cannot necessarily rely on that source in the future as their economies get cracking---it is hoped---because Soviet production is in decline. That is what the Government is being told---not by the Ministry of Energy, because there is not a Ministry of Energy. The Government dismantled it. It poked a few of the people who once worked there into the Ministry of Commerce. The Government has effectively said that it does not want to hear from specialists on those matters other than those from the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. That is the international position, excluding the crisis in the Gulf that has revolutionised the international oil scene just as happened in -. I well remember as a new Minister going into Cabinet and within days being confronted with the realities of the oil crisis of that period. As I said a minute ago, we should think about the impact on Government budgeting. We should think about what an increase in the price of fuel will do to the spending patterns of Government departments alone. There is nothing in the Budget about those realities. The next Government will have to grapple with them, as the National Government had to grapple with them years ago. With a new oil crisis one would expect a little sense from senior Government Ministers, but there has been none of that in the past few days. I shall come to some of the statements made by Ministers in a minute, but before I do I draw the attention of the House to the state of oil production in the Middle East, and, more particularly, to the place of Middle East oil reserves and production in the total oil scenario. Saudi Arabia, which is much in the news at the moment, is the world's leading oil producer, followed, in this order, by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, and then a grouping of small mid-east States. Those States are responsible for producing more than percent of the world's petroleum. If the two are brought together in the context of the events of years ago---the second oil shock, as we call it, and the lesser shock of a few years before that---that says in one sentence that although the growth strategy---the energy strategy, which was nicknamed ``think big'' at the time and is still known by that term---cost New Zealand in the immediate sense because it had to borrow money, that strategy was right for New Zealand. It was a combination of measures of considerable foresight. I want to refer again to the source within the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research that I mentioned a minute ago, and say that New Zealand was one of the very few countries anywhere in the world, and, more particularly, in the developed world, to have thought ahead to years ago and done something about the problem. I recall distinctly that in those years the National Government was persuaded finally to go down the ``think big'' road because political stability in the Middle East could not be relied upon. That was the clinching argument. The Government at the time went over the sums time and time again. I have not known such exhaustive research---checking, and counter-checking by various departments of State: Treasury; the State Services Commission; the Ministry of Energy; the Department of Trade and Industry, as it was called then; the Department of Labour, and the Department of Education, on the manpower and training sides, to ensure that New Zealand had the skilled people to carry the programme through. No major State programme in New Zealand since had applied the work, man-hours, and research that went into that programme. Every New Zealander---even people who support the Labour Party to the core---is saying tonight, although not necessarily in the open: ``Thank goodness New Zealand or a Government in New Zealand did what it did when that crisis occurred a few years ago.''. That means that the New Zealand economy can continue to function if the Gulf suplies dry up---not, of course, at the full pitch that one would desire, but New Zealand will not have to have carless days, for example. The machinery in the factories will continue to move, the machinery on the farms will continue to run, and New Zealand will not be held to ransom by thugs and bullies in countries we hear of so little until such a crisis emerges. I should have thought that at this time of international crisis two things would happen. First, the Labour Government, although anti-American in sentiment and disposition and having expressed that in tangible form in , would simply acknowledge that the free world, the industrialised countries, the democracies, and the United Nations are reliant finally on American manpower to get the world out of this jam. I should have expected the Government to say something like that, but there was not a word---there were only cheap shots. The free world is again reliant, as it has been since the attack on Pearl Harbour, on American might and manpower to get it out of a hole, but not a word has been heard from the Government. That is a shame, and people notice such things. Although New Zealanders, as I said a minute ago, do not necessarily say such things openly, they think them, and they say them to one another. The position is disgraceful. The second thing that the Government should have done was say to New Zealanders that it had to adjust its thinking on the growth strategy that was pioneered and implemented by its predecessor in Government. The Government should have acknowledged that because it gives us, as one of my collegues has just said, the sense of security that is so essential. What has come from the Government? There has been no leadership and no statesmanship. Frankly, there have been just silly comments such as that so recently made by the Minister of Finance, who said that Synfuel was an expensive mistake that would pay its way only when the price of oil reached US$ a barrel. That is an extraordinary statement when one considers, and most New Zealanders do, even if the Minister of Finance does not, that New Zealand's energy programme is saving the country $ billion in its balance of trade alone by saving on what it brings in or by permitting New Zealand to sell certain items by way of export---without taking into account the geopolitical factors that are uppermost in everyone's mind at present. People should put the security issue to one side---the intangibles---and notice that there is a saving on New Zealand's balance of trade of $ billion. Not one word was heard from the Minister of External Relations and Trade; neither was anything heard about that matter from Government members in their Budget commentaries. The Government is hopelessly out of touch. As one knows, Government members will go in a few weeks. Moving from the Budget as a background, I note that all Ministers should have---but I will bet they have not---charged their departments with revised estimates of expenditure as a result of the jump in oil prices. That is a jump of at least percent, and, as even a rudimentary mathematician would be able to say, every item of Government expenditure should be adjusted accordingly. If the expenditure has not been adjusted, Government Ministers and other Government members should explain why it has not, and should explain to the country how the admittedly unforeseen increase in expenditure will be financed in this financial year and in recurrent years thereafter. There has not been one word about that from the Government. The Minister of Finance has not come into the House to re-explain the State's financial position as a result of the third oil shock in our time. That is why the Government will go. It is unable to confront reality. Being in Government means taking the tough decisions; in the productive sector, in the critical energy sector, and in many other sectors the present Labour Government has shown only an ability to evade the real issues. The Government has had a lot of luck. I concede that in -, when oil prices dipped, the Government's opposition to ``think big'' seemed to be justified, but those of us who were in the National Government and, in particular, in Cabinet in that Government knew that the world could no longer rely on political stability in the Gulf and knew---as I said a minute ago---that, although the financing would work against New Zealand for a time, in the long run the right thing was being done. This week that stance has been completely justified. Debate interrupted.

The member for Clutha made many appropriate comments, and I do not want to add to them. I am sure that if the member for Coromandel were here he would echo those comments. During the Committee stage one aspect of the measure was not satisfactorily resolved, and that relates to the clear connection between casinos and organised crime. As we moved through the Bill clause by clause, the Minister was asked about that several times. He was quick to dispel any notion that there was a connection between casinos and criminal offending. During the Committee stage I contended that that was incorrect and produced some evidence, which I shall refer to in a minute. I was interested in the third reading speech made by the Leader of the House, in which he stated that, given the nature of the Bill, the incidence of offending would be kept to a minimum---or words to that effect. As I recall the Committee stage debate, he shifted his ground and conceded that there was indeed a connection between casinos and organised crime. Therefore this is a foolhardy and unnecessary measure---the important word is ``unnecessary''---and I shall explain why. If casinos are clean, as many people have claimed, why will all employees be fingerprinted? I cannot think of any industry in this country or in most other Western countries whose employees are fingerprinted. The employees will be fingerprinted, and the police will shoulder that burden. The problem of law and order is a real social issue at the moment, and there are many other social issues as well. I cannot understand the thinking of a Government that decides to introduce legislation that will increase, not decrease, the work-load of the already hard-pressed police. One of the reasons for the National Party having said that it has no option but to increase the number of uniformed police by nearly is the increasing crime wave---much of it serious and a lot of it violent. During the Committee stage I referred to the board of inquiry into casinos that was instituted in Victoria. That board of inquiry stated: ``Organised crime figures have historically been associated with casinos. It is recognised that gambling is a favourite target, and casino gambling, in particular, because of the vast number of unrecorded cash transactions.''. I thought that we were worried about white-collar crime in this country. I thought that many pensioners, in particular, who had their fingers burned by some high-flyers had had enough of losing their life savings. Why are we spending much time in introducing a casino or two instead of worrying about those people? That action mirrors the Government's distorted objectives and priorities. Further on in the Committee stage it was noted that Deputy Assistant Commissioner David Powers of New Scotland Yard said: ``Casino gambling is the life-blood of organised crime, because it provides an immense cash flow. It has considerable support services which can be taken over. It provides entry into the top flight of the entertainment world. It provides a secret but very efficient international banking system. It enables unlawful money to be laundered quickly and safely. It provides entry into the international hotel industry and is causing money to flow from people who are unlikely to complain, such as the compulsive gambler and naive person. Taken altogether, that is a pretty severe amalgam of criminal opportunities.''. Against evidence like that, which the House saw at the earlier stages of the Bill, I cannot understand the Government's supporting the Bill. It is irresponsible. In this instance it is not finally a matter of whether we as individuals approve of gambling; it is a matter of our public responsibilities. If members take the Bill seriously this new burden should not now be foisted upon the overworked police. For those reasons, above all others, I oppose the Bill and will vote against it.

I want to say at the outset that I am confident about the actions of the Minister of Justice. On each occasion that the matter arose in the House the Minister explained the inequity of the legislation, and I believe that he gave the House and New Zealand all of the assurances about the steps he would take.
