The functions of the Iwi Transition Agency are clearly defined in the Maori Affairs Restructuring Act : ``Section : Functions of Iwi Transition Agency---() The principal functions of the Iwi Transition Agency shall be as follows: (a) To carry out efficiently, with such modifications (if any) as may from time to time be lawfully made, each of the Department's programmes, until that programme is transferred to iwi authorities or to any other organisation or agency, or until the programme is lawfully wound up: (b) To promote the development of iwi authorities, and to transfer such of the Department's programmes as are to be ongoing to iwi authorities, taking care to ensure that the iwi authorities are fully operational and capable of carrying out the programmes in the best interests of the people they are to serve. () In addition, the Iwi Transition Agency shall carry out any directions given to it by the Minister for the benefit of any Maori or any group of Maori.''

Yes, they are. There is underachievement in education, and a look at the Department of Justice shows us that prisons are overflowing. Does the member say that that is not negative? My word, some people are not housed or getting proper food. I am talking about the basic needs of human life in this country. The member says that that is not a fact. What have we had from the Government? The Budget is a cost-cutting exercise. Cuts have been made to positive sectors. The Government should be making the negative sectors more positive. I say to the member for Waitotara that I do not think that anybody would disagree with that. We should follow that aim as a measure to ensure that we bring the economy into line, but, more than that, we should provide the basic needs of people. If we do not follow that line, we are destined for more trouble, and it seems to me that the recipe that the present Administration is following will lead to exactly that. Before the election we heard a lot of talk about racism, but it seems to have disappeared. We heard a lot of negativism about the Treaty of Waitangi. The Deputy Prime Minister, who is trying to interject, thinks that it is fashionable to talk about the treaty, to the extent that it is a founding document of the National Party. I have to say that the Minister of Justice the other day was quite open about the U-turn made by the Government on Bastion Point.

Kati ko te mea tuatahi---e Whetu kei te mihi atu ki a koe me o matua o Ngai Tahu whanui. Ara e tu mai ra te maunga o Aoraki tae atu ki te tahatai moana o te katoa o Te Waipounamu. Kati ki a koe Tipene me o matua, ka nui te mihi me te hari o te koa o te ngakau kua haria mai koe tenei kaupapa roto i te Whare nei i tenei po. Me ki he kaupapa tuatahi tenei mo tenei Whare, otira, mo tetahi iwi ki roto o Aotearoa. He kaupapa ataahua no te mea e titiro whakamua e koutou mo o koutou whakatupu, ara, i te taonga i mahia ai o koutou mahia, o koutou tupuna mai ano i te wa, a, tae noa mai ki tenei rangi. No reira ka nui te mihi atu ki a koe, otira, koutou katoa, e rau rangatira ma, tena koutou, tena koutou, tena koutou, a, kia ora huihui ano tatau. In those words I have addressed my colleague the honourable member for Southern Maori and her people who are here this evening, along with the chairman of the Ngai Tahu Trust Board. As I have said, this Bill that is being introduced is a first for the House and for the Maori people of New Zealand. I also said that it will have far-reaching effects into the twenty-first century because people have sat down and looked at where they have come from and where they want to go. In my view, this Bill will be reflected in the charters that will be considered during the select committee hearings. The charters will clearly set out the objects of the runanganui. They will set out the administration, how it will be accountable, and what it will do on behalf of its beneficiaries. As I said before, it will unleash itself from the Maori Trust Boards Act and do away with the trustee legislation of the same year so that the runanganui can set itself up as a body that has all of those commercial values, as well as the origins of the people. With regard to that aspect, the directive nature will probably be dealt with in committee hearings around the country. I want to say to the Minister that we should meet the Ngai Tahu trust board as soon as possible. It will not have wasted months for nothing without being able to come to the committee tomorrow, or as soon as possible. We should then set about looking at the regulations, looking at all those people whom the board purports to represent, and ensuring that we get from them the sort of things they have talked about, to ensure that the Bill is fully representative of the people. I believe that those are the important aspects of the Bill. I simply want to say that the Bill has its origins in the Waitangi Tribunal. It has some aspects of the Runanga Iwi Act---and I am sure that the Minister of Justice will wish that that legislation was still in place.

I support the Bills that are before the House and, particularly, the Maori Land Amendment Bill. The Minister will know the last time that a real consequential amendment took place in the consolidation of the principal Act. It is probably fair to say that the Resource Management Act heralds history, in that some pieces of legislation brought it about. This time the House has reflected a consequential amendment that was flagged some years ago when the principal Act was being promulgated and put together. Now that the Maori Land Act has been promulgated and came into force on July this year, the amendments contained in sections and A are agreed to. The question of consultation is of the utmost importance at this time. All members have had letters from the local authorities about the speed with which the Bill should proceed, because authorities want to get on with their district planning schemes. Tied up in those decisions was, of course, the question of consultation about our lakes, streams, and harbours. The question of consultation with Maori came about in that package. I believe that it is important for us to use all of the mechanisms available to us to ensure that we get a package that the country can be confident with in the days that lie ahead, because of the enormous impact that the Bill will have economically, socially, and culturally on our country. I think that we have taken the right steps and I believe that the Bill enhances that. What we are looking at in the two small amendments is the question of significant and spiritual values in the types of reserves that the Minister may want to promulgate under the appropriate section of the Act. It is because of the nature and the importance of those provisions that I wanted to raise the wider question of consultation. For example, just recently a conservation order was placed on the Wanganui River. The Minister of Conservation had quite correctly written to the Whanganui River Maori Trust Board because he was conscious of the spiritual meaning and the significance of the river to the people. The board was constituted under an Act in to take cognisance of the people's concerns before what was then the National Parks Authority. Correspondence has gone between the Taranaki and the Wanganui boards. We ought not to ignore the processes that are available to us. We should alert the Minister and the people involved that the processes are available and that they should be used so that we are not in conflict and we get a package at the end of the day that will enhance our environment and the areas that need to be conserved. I believe that our people have made a contribution to the country over many years and continue to want to do that. At the end of the day, in the debacle that arose over the Wanganui River issue the board said at the time that it was not against the orders of conservation and simply wanted to be advised and consulted to ensure that the orders were agreed to amicably between all the parties concerned. The Minister may not know that at the time that the issue was being discussed the various bodies responsible for conservation undertook to ensure that consultations took place. I thank Parliament for the opportunity of being able to talk about these issues.

Having listened to the Minister's reply in respect of the pouihi in New Zealand House, can I take it that the original agreement reached between the New Zealand Government and the late Inia Te Wiata, as the architect of the pouihi, is still in place?
Will he urge all parties involved in the current impasse over the Moutoa Gardens to use the Waitangi Tribunal process to reach a settlement; if not, why not?

I want to join with the House and with colleagues in supporting the introduction of the Bill. I believe it is timely that the Bill has come. It is at a time when this country is about to take part in a great event. We as a nation and as a people will gain from that great competition. The efforts of my colleague, who was the former Minister of Health, and who introduced the Bill back in , are to be applauded. I was part of that Cabinet and I well appreciate the trials and tribulations she had to face in this nation when trying to bring the principal legislation to where it is now. This event this afternoon characterises just how this Parliament can come together, which I think we need to do in times like this when rational discussion is required. The amendment being sought this afternoon is only a very temporary measure to allow that event to take place until the season is fulfilled. We understand that our Australian colleagues have likewise entered into the debate legislatively, and will give effect to it on the same basis that we in this nation have explored and traversed over that period of time. My interest, and it is not unknown in this House, is simply to say ``thank you'' to all those members who will support the Bill and see its passage here today. As we know, many of our people who support the code and have done for many years will, I am sure, appreciate the thought that has gone into presenting the Bill in this way, given I guess the period that we have had in the trans-Tasman relationship in the code. I think about years ago, the late Brownie Paki, who was of course the first Maori to go to Australia under the new set of rules of reciprocity, was the first Maori from this country to take part in the code as we understand it. It was there that he was honoured at that game between the British people and the New Zealand Maori team that met at the park. People like him and people throughout this nation who have supported the code are to be admired. We now see that code stretching throughout this country, back into the West Coast, into Hawke's Bay, up north, and everywhere throughout this nation. Some years ago the Prime Minister and myself spoke at the one-hundredth anniversary of the New Zealand Rugby Union in the Banquet Hall. It was said then that there was a small flow from one code to the other, and that if they did not take stock there would be a rushing tide into the league code. We now see that happening. I want to say, also, that it was another factor that gave rise to that, particularly in the Maori world. It was because of the South African issue that took place in the early s. We find that happening today, and starting to spread. I am glad that the rugby people are now trying to grasp the nettle and encourage our people to stay with that code, and to ensure that it has a long life in the years to come. But in my view we are entering a new period and a new phase of a dynamic sport for all our people. I am sure that many people in the House today will be there tomorrow to see the first game and, I am sure, all the other team games after that. I think the House is to be congratulated on the way it has come together to accept this amendment. As the member in charge of the Bill said, it is only a temporary measure until January next year, although I am bound to say that it has wide implications for our nation and for all those people who are involved.

I am extremely disappointed that this Bill has come back from the Health Committee with a recommendation that it be discharged. First, I add my congratulations to those that have already been given to Lianne Dalziel, and to those who worked to shape this Bill. I also want to add a word of respect for the Hon. Katherine O'Regan for her honesty in the way she has spoken to the Bill, and her courage in presenting it to her caucus and arguing for it. I think that the recommendation from the majority of the Health Committee that the Bill be discharged is short-sighted and it seems to me, after listening to the previous speaker, that the recommended discharge is also based on some misunderstanding. It is my view that the Osteopaths Bill, as suggested, in fact, protected the name of osteopaths, but it had no effect whatsoever on mirimiri. My understanding is that the only Act that has an effect is the Physiotherapy Act, and I would suggest that the member investigate that Act if that is the concern he has. I want to talk about the ``why'' of registration, and I want to talk a little about my history. In May I entered Wellington Public Hospital as a student nurse, and some little time after May I graduated as a registered general and obstetric nurse. That registration meant that I was safe to practise. That is what nursing registration means, that somebody has passed the necessary tests to be deemed as safe to practise. What is being given is protection to the public. People understand what the term ``registered nurse'' means. They know what being able to wear the nursing medal means. They know that it means that certain standards have been reached, and it is also a protection for the nurses themselves. That, of course, is incorporated within the Nurses Act. I want to speak a little more about that later on. I want to look at the alternative that has been presented by the majority of the Health Committee, by members on the opposite side of the House, as the alternative to the Osteopaths Bill coming back to the House with a recommendation that it proceed. Their alternative is that the Ministry of Health, which is apparently conducting a review of health occupation registration, will be developing comprehensive legislation and will provide a registration regime for a great array of health professionals. That range will include chiropractors, dentists, and nurses, but not doctors, because they have been covered by the Medical Practitioners Act, an Act, of course, on which this Bill was modelled. It talked about issues of competence, standards, training, and discipline, and in fact it was comprehensive. May I suggest that the Medical Practitioners Act and the proposed Osteopaths Act were comprehensive and were robust. What I want to challenge is this Government's ability to turn out comprehensive, robust legislation for all those health professionals listed in the report back. Looking at the Government's recent legislation I would say that it is anything but comprehensive, it is anything but robust, and, sad to say, it has a great deal of ad hockery about it. I need only talk about the biosecurity legislation, which has had a recent airing in the House. I would suggest that the resource management legislation, which has been sent back to the select committee because of disagreement amongst the coalition partners, rather than be reported back and proceeding, had very little about it that I would say was robust. I would talk about the legislative measures around the rabbit calicivirus disease---that is a legislative mess. I would suggest also, in relation to the review, that if this review of the health occupation registration follows the same pathway as the aquaculture review, it may languish for a very long time before it gets to this House, as it seems to have been on the back-burner for a very long period, prior to the advent of the Resource Management Amendment Act (No. )---and we all know about that. What really worries me is that we are throwing out a good piece of legislation for some Government ``great blue yonder'' comprehensive legislation based on some review, that in my understanding is not yet completed. It seems to me that the Government should take a good hard look at itself, take a good hard look at its abilities---and a touch of realism. I look at some of the legislation that is sitting on the Order Paper going nowhere---the Protected Areas (Prohibition on Mining) legislation, for example. A great achievement for this Bill---and it has already been mentioned tonight---was getting the opposing groups from the osteopath profession to come together through this legislation. That work, of course, has now gone for nought, as has the work of the select committee itself. It seems to me extraordinary that the select committee has put all those hours of work into the Bill, and for what? There is gross inefficiency there, I am afraid. It is also a matter of great concern that David Russell of the Consumers Institute has made very strong representations about the need for this regulation. People who consult those who call themselves osteopaths, and a variety of other health professionals, are putting their well-being literally in the hands of those people. It seems to me that the protection that the Consumers Institute is calling for---the protection that this Bill would have given---has been thrown away very, very lightly by this Government. I very much regret that Katherine O'Regan's arguments to her own caucus were not accepted. I applaud her for the effort in trying, and I applaud those members of the select committee who had the vision to see the importance of this Bill, who supported it through thick and thin, and who worked hard at it. I feel very much for those people who have suffered already at the hands of unqualified people and for those who may similarly suffer in the future, because without registration members of the public do not have that protection, they do not have the certainty that when they go to somebody who is registered they have certain standards and a certain minimum. Once again, this Government has failed abysmally the people of New Zealand. I would have to say that the Greek chorus coming from the other side of the House is contributing absolutely nothing of value to this debate. It seems to me that the member could well do some background reading on the whole issue and then make a useful contribution to legislation in this House.

It has taken a while. The point I want to make is that having taken all this time to get to this point, it suddenly appears on a day the Education and Science Committee is sitting. Like Mrs Awatere Huata, I have come from that committee. Admittedly the business of the committee is almost over for today. Nevertheless, it does suggest that the management of the House is questionable in this regard. The Bill is an important Bill. There are important issues that once again raise questions about the role of the State in education, the role of schools, and the role of parents. One of the areas in this debate that particularly looks at the role of society, as against the role of parents, is home schooling. We had some very impressive submissions from the home educators of New Zealand, but when we came to look at the substance of the Bill we came right up against this balance of responsibility between society and parents. Some amendments were made during the course of the Bill and they are in the Bill as it has come back to the House. Labour has some further amendments to make that we believe will deal with some of the outstanding issues of concern to home educators, without in any way prejudicing the education of their children. One of those relates to exemptions for students over years. We are bringing forward an amendment that makes sure that students who are over years of age and who are being home educated are not discriminated against in relation to things like health services for secondary school students, National Library access, and that kind of thing. We are also bringing in an amendment that assists with privacy matters. As it stands, the Minister could have access to sensitive, personal information in a review report. We do not believe it is necessary for the Minister to know things like names and addresses, when it comes to a report. Obviously, children who are educated at home should be subject to review, but this does not mean that personal details necessarily have to be given to the Minister. There is also a big issue about reasonableness in requiring information. I believe that there is another very useful Labour amendment here, specifying that when parents are required to provide statements about education provision there will be a test of reasonableness in relation to the form or manner that the Education Review Office specifies. In other words, it is a higher test than the Education Review Office just being able to ask for any form or manner. I believe that this test of reasonableness is quite an important one. In talking on the short title, I also want to mention the key area of access to local schools. It has been said that this Bill has some good things in it, and that is true. It has some inadequacies, as well. It does not go nearly far enough. This whole issue about whether children can get to local schools or have to go right across, say, Auckland has implications that are much wider---for example, in traffic congestion in Auckland. We were told at another select committee that traffic congestion in Auckland is much worse at the times of day and the times of the year when children travel across Auckland to get to school because they cannot get to their local schools. That implication has not been taken into account in not ensuring that children have access to their local schools.

There is one point in Owen Jennings' speech that I agree with, and one only. I agree with him when he says that the Government has bungled and has been incompetent. Beyond that, I have to say that our paths differ. There is nothing else that I can remember in Mr Jennings' speech that I agree with. However, that has been one of the background threads to this whole biosecurity debacle. The other background thread was spoken of by Mr Peter Brown---that is, the alarming lack of respect for the law, the lack of respect for science, the lack of respect for biosecurity, and the lack of respect for the rights of others. I suggest to Mr Gavan Herlihy, after hearing his speech, that when he advocates that people should be able to use illegal actions to give a wake-up call to Wellington he should think very hard about the implications of that statement. What happens when some other group whose actions he disapproves of decides to give a wake-up call to Wellington? One of the areas of bungling and incompetence that I believe the Government has indulged in with regard to this Bill is in the promulgation of the regulation that came into effect on September. It is a regulation effectively to make the illegal legal. I was so concerned about the making of this regulation that I wrote to the Regulations Review Committee to ask it to investigate this to see whether the regulation comes within the Standing Orders. The reasons given were: does it meet the objects and intentions of the Biosecurity Act under which the regulation was drawn up, and does it make unusual and unexpected use of the regulation-making powers in the Act? Most particularly, I want the select committee to look at the adequacy of the consultation process. I refer the House to question for written answer No. , lodged on September , wherein I asked the Minister for Biosecurity about the consultation process in relation to the promulgation of these regulations. I was assured of the adequacy of consultation and also that the requirements set out in the Court of Appeal decision Wellington International Airport Ltd v Air New Zealand would be adhered to. I will just read out two of those requirements, because I do not believe they have been adhered to. The first requirement is: ``Consultation must be allowed sufficient time and genuine effort must be made. It is to be a reality, not a charade.'' The second requirement is: ``It is also implicit that the party obliged to consult, whilst quite entitled to have a working plan already in mind, must keep its mind open and be ready to change and even start afresh.'' I do not believe for a minute that the Government was ready to change, and even to start afresh, in relation to this regulation. I think it is a poor regulation and that it is poor legislation. I think it is poor because it is validating a regulation that I believe is questionable. If the legislation did just this, I believe it would have to be opposed today in the House. However, clause does something else. It deems the rabbit calicivirus to have been established in New Zealand. Whether one thinks the actions that led to this are right or wrong---and in my view they are very wrong---the reality is that it does appear as though the rabbit calicivirus is established beyond retrieval in New Zealand. It is with the utmost reluctance that I support this Bill going to a select committee, purely because there does not seem to be any other choice in this regard. I want to speak also about some of the claims made in the explanatory note. I have concerns about some of the issues Mr Herlihy raised but I have different concerns. As he pointed out, the explanatory note speaks of the need for Government agencies to obtain information. I hope the select committee will examine this claim very closely, and investigate the adequacy of any of the systems set up to gain this information. The reason I say this is that a decision based on science, and what I believe to be good science, has been overridden already. It was the decision that for reasons of science the calicivirus should not be introduced. A scientific approach must be re-established if this claim is to mean anything at all. The information must be scientifically collected and scientifically organised. The second claim in the explanatory note that I want to talk about is the benefit that is supposed to be gained by having a coordinated spreading. The explanatory note talks about an uninformed and incorrect method of spreading, leading to the prospect of large-scale immunity. I say that it is too late to avoid an uninformed spread. It has happened already, because of uninformed, ill-thought-out, and irresponsible actions.

Yes, I agree with the definition: ``The term `acute care' typically equates to emergency services. For the purposes of this study the consultants have adopted a broader definition of `acute' care, which we believe is more appropriate for the study.''. Specifically, services to be included in the acute care hospital under this broader definition are everything but geriatric, accident and emergency, psychiatric, rehabilitation, long-stay geriatrics, and low-risk obstetrics. I think that that definition is perhaps a little narrow, and maybe that is where we have run into problems with the decision that has had to be made. There have been many discussions over the years and at one stage it was decided to establish this acute care hospital in Clive---which is in Hawke's Bay, for those people who have never visited the area---in deference to the feelings of Napier and Hastings. It is nonsense to attempt to settle a parochial attitude in that manner and the proposal was abandoned. A petition has been presented to Parliament by the people of Napier. If the positions had been reversed and I had been losing my hospital in Hastings I would have asked the member for Napier for his support in asking Parliament to hear this private member's Bill. It is a very serious step to close this hospital for the area. It is a big step. The hospital has been established for more than years and every avenue should be explored to make sure that this decision can be endorsed by the people of Hawke's Bay. If the member listens he will learn something. Does he want me to speak up? There should be one acute hospital facility for Hawke's Bay. There is no doubt about that. Perhaps we could have a maternity hospital, an accident and emergency clinic, and a chronic care hospital for Napier. That would go some way towards assisting the member for Napier and the people of Napier, but I still think that the matter should be heard by Parliament. Hospitals are like post offices. They are reassuring to the community. We already know what has happened to all of our post offices. If there is anything that we can learn from the Labour Government about the closure of post offices it is that it is one sure way of losing the Government benches. We have to think very carefully about the closure of hospitals. The net goes far wider than just the hospitals for Hastings and Napier. It extends to Waipukurau and Wairoa. The people in those communities would feel an injustice equally as great as that felt by the people of Napier if they were to lose their facility. That could be on the drawing-board in the future. The Hawke's Bay Area Health Board was elected by the people to make a final decision on this problem. It was elected to do the job and has engaged Booz. Allen and Hamilton Inc. to give it a very extensive report. It has opened the report to criticism and consultation and has behaved in a reasonably fair manner. However, there is still one resort the people of Napier are asking for and that is asking the House to listen to their submissions and allowing them to be considered. The problem must be resolved if Hawke's Bay is to have a quality medical service. There is no doubt that the Health vote will not grow greatly in the next few years, and those health dollars must be spent in a more targeted manner that provides the people with the best services possible. The money must be invested in one acute hospital for Hawke's Bay. However, I support the member and the people of Napier in this approach to have every aspect of the rationalisation explored. Parliament should at least give the people of Napier and the member a hearing.

The Leader of the Opposition is green, but not environmentally green; he is green in other ways. A little history may be useful. The previous Labour Government supported protection of the Antarctic environment, as Labour Governments have always done. However, the Labour Government did not previously receive support from any of the international community; it did not receive the support from the international community that is upfront on the issue at present; and it did not receive support from the Opposition. The Government was alone. In the National Government commenced negotiations on the Convention on the Regulation of Antarctic Mineral Resource Activities. The member for Remuera said that the Labour Government had set the course. However, the National Government set the course; it conceived the negotiations, and the member for Otago opened the first meeting in Wellington in . The second meeting was also held under the National Government. The policy was set by the National Government. In , when the Labour Government took office, it still desired, above all else, protection of the Antarctic environment. However, at that stage it was clear to the Government that it was critical to hold together the moratorium until some international agreement could be reached. It was also clear to the Government that the position of the National Party had not changed politically, either internationally or in New Zealand. The Government looked for other solutions. It tried to consider what would happen if other goals could be achieved. It also wanted to ensure that the convention gave sufficient clout to those who had doubts that it would be able to prevent damage. The Government looked for safeguards, and that is the way in which the convention negotiations were continued. At that stage New Zealand had to balance the probability of uncontrolled exploitation, should the moratorium expire, against a control that could be exercised under the convention. Those were the Government's only choices at that stage because of the international political environment. The change of heart of other governments did come as a surprise. However, it was a welcome surprise, and it has been useful in many respects. It simply would not have been credible for New Zealand at that stage to flip-flop its position on the convention. We had to gauge international opinion on the new suggestions that were being floated by France and Australia. I was in Stockholm at the time that France and Australia made their announcement, and I took the opportunity to speak to several Ministers from other countries, including Scandinavian countries, and the French Prime Minister, Monsieur Rocard. At that stage it was still not clear to me or to the Government that the position of Australia and France would succeed. However, it was clear that the countries interested in exploitation were running out of patience. The time of the moratorium was running out. If the convention was not acceptable and if the moratorium lapsed there was a perceived danger of uncontrolled mineral exploitation. During the past months there has been a great deal of international discussion, particularly in Paris in October . New Zealand has been very active. It has been clear that the treaty parties are in a deadlock on the issue. The New Zealand Government has done the sensible thing again: it has tried to act in a conciliatory role; it has tried to mediate the opinions; and it has put forward a sensible proposal to try to resolve the impasse. It is nonsense for Opposition members to say that New Zealand was at the head of the makers of the impasse. On the contrary, New Zealand is at the forefront of advocates of environmental protection for the Antarctic, and New Zealand was at the Paris meeting, just as it has been in the forefront of environmental protection advocates during the convention negotiations. As I said, the impasse resulted because some countries want to reserve the right to mine---they do not accept a world park---while others want only a world park. The Government is not in the camp that says it wants to reserve the right to mine. That has never been the Government's policy, although the Minister of Conservation said that it was the policy of the previous National Government. The lesson from the Paris meeting was that a new approach was necessary, and that is what the Government is adopting. In particular, much emphasis has been placed publicly in the past few months on mining and on mineral exploitation of the Antarctic. However, other issues are involved. I should like an Opposition member to talk about the other issues involved---for example, oil spillage. The Exxon Valdez spill is a clear example of what happens when a ship hits up on the Arctic. Issues of aviation use and the French airstrip are other examples. Another issue is land-based tourism. Will it be allowed to continue? Will there be any controls if it is banned? The Government's considerations are clear: protection of the Antarctic environment, and protection of the Antarctic treaty system, which has ensured that the Antarctic has been a demilitarised zone for many years. The Government does not want either of those considerations to be sacrificed for the other. The steps taken have been prudent, cautious, and sensible, and in the end they will lead to an international agreement to protect the Antarctic environment. I conclude by welcoming the Opposition on board at last on such a critical issue.

That Act enabled the diocesan board of trustees to amalgamate into one fund the large number of trusts administered by it for diocesan and parochial purposes. In , Parliament passed the Anglican Church Trusts Act, which gave the board wider powers of investment than it would otherwise have had, and the board now wants to separate the trusts that it administers into separate funds to allow for long-term and short-term investments. However, unfortunately it has found that it is prevented from doing so by the Act. That Act is considered to be superfluous, and the Bill before the House repeals it and allows Church of England administrators in the Wellington diocese to invest their money in an appropriate way. I have pleasure in presenting the Bill to the House for its second reading.

I am happy to say from the outset that the Opposition supports the introduction of the Bill. However, Opposition members are concerned that it is a bald Bill without a lot of facts and information. We will be looking towards the proceedings in the select committee. I say from the outset that science and technology are important to a nation's economy, and I am concerned that in this country over the past several decades we have not put the necessary emphasis on new technology and scientific research. If New Zealand were to match some of the technological outputs of the European and Asian nations it would be an economy to be reckoned with. Switzerland annually exports technologically based goods to the value of US$, a head of population; for the Netherlands the figure is US$,; and for New Zealand US$. The whole economy would benefit if New Zealand could obtain a tenfold growth in technologically based exports. I am also concerned about the breakdown between public sector funding and private sector funding. The Bill will set up a foundation that is based on setting priorities and allocating functions and funding to public sector research and development. Figures published over the past couple of years show that New Zealand spends about the same on public-funded research as most of the other nations in the OECD do--- percent of gross domestic product. I am worried that the private sector rate is about one-quarter of the amount spent on science, and research and development. Why is the Government not showing more initiatives to stimulate private sector spending? The Bill will do nothing about that. It will just allocate the probably realistic level of funds already provided. My first question about the Bill relates to functions, which are set out in clause . The first function of the foundation is to allocate funds for the production of science outputs. My colleague the member for Raglan has said that that definition is very narrow relative to, for example, the Medical Research Council Act , which sets out much more broad-based and laudable functions---to initiate, foster, and support medical research; to furnish information, advice, and assistance to persons and organisations concerned with medical research; and to collect and disseminate scientific information, including the publication of reports. I am saddened that such a laudable base of aims and objects for the research council has been brought by Treasury to one sentence in the Bill---that is, ``To allocate funds for the production of science outputs''. As the member for Raglan said, science cannot be treated as a sheer production line, and we cannot consider just the outputs. We have to consider long-term strategic science, the funding of it, and so on. The second function of the foundation is: ``To provide independent policy advice to the Minister on matters relating to research, science, and technology, including advice on national priorities for those matters''. I am concerned that confusion may arise between the ministry's function of providing advice and the foundation's function of providing advice. If there is conflict between the advice that the Minister and the ad hoc Cabinet committee receive from the two bodies, who will be the final arbiter? Subclause () of clause does state: ``The Foundation's advice shall be formulated after consultation between the Foundation and representatives of industry and the community.'' That is to be applauded. How will the funds be allocated? Will there be large blocks of individual money to be split up by subcommittees; or will subcouncils be set up in different sectors to allocate the money to individual projects; or will the foundation be working on a more global and macro level and allocate funds individually? Clause states that the foundation has to adhere to Government priorities. I welcome the provision that under the Bill the Government will be bound on March each year to publish those priorities, and so on. Under clause the foundation is to invite competitive proposals for the provision of science outputs---once again the rhetoric of Treasury---and to ensure that the producers of outputs attain specified standards of performance, and account for the use of the funds. That is all very fine, but I have been looking in the Bill for more specifics on the mechanism. The most important point that the Opposition can make today is to ask where the people with skills will come from and what aspects of science they will represent. I notice that the second schedule amends the Medical Research Council Act by removing the reference to the Director-General of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and replacing him with the chief executive of the Ministry of Research, Science and Technology. Could the Bill not have had more detail about the changes it proposes? The Medical Research Council has functioned exceedingly well. It would have been better for us to have used as a model the facts and figures of the way the Medical Research Council has functioned rather than Treasury's advice that we received on the Bill. The foundation is to consist of not less than three nor more than nine members. It is important to find out the qualifications the Minister will be looking for, why he will be looking for people with specific qualifications, and how sector groups will be represented. The Bill does not mention the way that sector groups will be represented, and the danger is that specific groups may be left out. The other matter of concern to all scientists will be the security of tenure of their funding. Many projects are medium-term and long-term projects for to years. Clause states that the functions of the foundation will be reviewed every years. The foundation has to review the operation of the Act and consider whether the foundation should be retained or abolished. That sounds a laudable ambition, but I would be hard pressed to find people who will sit on the foundation and decide that they should be abolished. It is sensible to review the need for amendment of the Act. However, we need to consider more specific details about the people, how they will act, how the funding will be allocated, and the security of tenure. The Bill states that the first review is to be after the first years, and from then on at not more than -yearly intervals. That could put the kibosh on some of the medium-term and longer-term funding. The Opposition and I support the move to contestable funding. It is the right move, although I am a little concerned that the figure is arbitrary. The Government has decided to move to percent contestable funding. It will start in the first year with percent, and move an extra percent each year to percent. Are those figures to be dynamically reviewed? If some great impact occurs on certain projects that are under way because of the move to percent, is it possible that that schedule could be slowed down or be changed? There have been many inquiries into science and technology and research---the Beattie report, the Stack report, and many others, which have given clear direction to the country to put itself into a good position to take advantage of technologically based exports, agricultural products, and so on. However, it is unfortunate that the Government has taken a drip-feed approach. Science and technology have taken a back row relative to many of the Government's other projects and Government business, and I am sorry that it has taken so long for those reports to be implemented.

I should like to thank the National Director of the Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, Mr Neil Wells, who was also very helpful at the beginning of the year in giving me some pointers. I pay special heartfelt thanks to one of my constituents, police officer Jim Donald, who is the owner of police dog Luke. He allowed me to use police dog Luke, which had had his shoulder competely blown away by a shot-gun, to promote the Bill in Auckland. I was delighted to take Luke round, to have photographs taken, and to use the dog in the promotion of the Bill. I thank all those people who have written letters to me over time. My in-tray has never been so inundated with letters from all round the country. The Bill has spurred a great deal of feeling, and I appreciate the letters that were sent. Some people have even sent in money---one person sent me $ for what I have done---and I intend to pass the money on to the Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. I appreciate all the messages of support. To those people who think that the Bill should go further, I say that I do not believe that the Bill I have introduced should go much further. The select committee will give people the opportunity to make submissions. I also give my heartfelt and sincere thanks to the member for Yaldhurst, who was prepared to pass round the Government caucus an album that had been provided to me by the Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, and who was prepared to provide information to Government members. I was absolutely delighted when she told me that it was the Government's intention to support the Bill's introduction. It is natural that I thank my own caucus colleagues, who deliberated very carefully on the issues, and who have finally given absolutely unequivocal support for the Bill as it now stands. I want the Bill to send very clear signals to those macho tough-guy he-men in the community who think they are real heroes if they inflict shocking and premeditated cruelty on defenceless animals that do not understand what they have done and what is being done to them. I appreciate very much the comments of the member for Whangarei when he referred to Muldoon and Spooky. Muldoon is one of the most beautiful German shepherd dogs in the country. I know that the member looks on Muldoon with a great deal of affection. I shall now tell the House, in finer detail, what the Bill does. It adjusts the fines by not very much more than the movement of the consumer price index over the period for which they have remained unadjusted. The total consumer price index movement was about ., and I have rounded the figure to a fivefold increase. In other words, a $ fine is increased to $, and so on. With the way inflation has increased over the years it will be no more than a couple of years before the fines again start to slip behind. The Bill also expands the definition of the word ``cruelty''. It gives the court the power to prevent people from owning animals. In the urban environment it penalises people who deliberately lay bait to kill domestic animals as an act of revenge, and that provision is significant. The Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals gave me examples of city people who, to get back at a neighbour because of a noisy car or stereo, laid poisonous bait and killed off the family pet dog or cat, with the comment, ``That'll teach you.'' In the documents supplied to me today by the society I read of a case that was hard to believe. It was about a husband who was having an argument with his wife on the eleventh floor of a penthouse building. When the argument got out of hand he turned round, grabbed her cat, threw it out of the window, and said, ``I hope your cat can fly.'' The cat died on impact on falling from the eleventh floor. Such behaviour is not acceptable in our society, and people who act in that way will be penalised. The raising of fines was an interesting question. The Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals also provided the example of a truck driver in Ngaruawahia who had savagely beaten a couple of dogs, locked them in a shed, and deprived them of food for an incredible length of time. When found, those dogs were emaciated, with broken limbs and broken backs. The veterinary bills were horrendous. The fine imposed on the truck driver did not even cover the first week's bills for trying to get the dogs back into shape. Time will not permit me to answer several of the questions raised tonight. I look forward to the Bill's going before a select committee. The chairman of the Primary Production Committee, the member for Gisborne, has assured me that he supports the Bill's basic thrust and that it will be given a fair hearing. I thank the member for Gisborne for that. I also want to reflect on the remarks made by the member for Timaru when he said that, in percent of cases, the Bill has to do with urban cruelty to animals. The Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals understands that if there is a drought, for example, farmers do not inflict cruelty by desire. The member for Napier criticised me for having used a sexist term in the Bill when I used the word ``he''. Maybe I did use the word ``he''. I always try to avoid sexist language, but, in relation to animal cruelty, percent of the people who perpetrate the crimes are males. I have no sorrow for having included the word ``he''. Finally, I think that this country must look towards education. We must instil in our young people a healthy respect for all living creatures. We need to see human beings as paramount, and their needs must come first, but we must not do that to the total exclusion of animal rights. The Bill gives members the opportunity to consider very carefully the issues at hand. I welcome the support the Bill has received, and I have great delight in moving its introduction in the name of Chloe, the Williamson pussy-cat. Motion agreed to. Bill introduced and read a first time, and referred to the Primary Production Committee.

This provision to award costs against the broadcaster was put in because I as Minister felt that there were a number of times when broadcasters really took a dog-in-the-manger attitude to a complaint. I think it was quite clear to a number of people from the outset that there had been a breach. Of course, as everyone realises, complaints have to go first to the broadcasters. In many cases they just held on to them for some weeks, if not months, because they had working-days to deal with them, then just said: ``No, we don't find anything.'' When a complaint finally got to the authority, the authority quite properly upheld it, and the broadcasters got a slap on the hand with a wet bus ticket. So the original clause that went into the Bill as introduced provided for a $, fixed fine for everyone who had a complaint upheld. The select committee's view was more along the lines of making it more discretionary than that, but saying that $, was not really enough for some of the bigger broadcasters, and moving it to $,. That will have two or three effects. First, it will put a little more pressure on the broadcasters to think carefully about how they handle a complaint, because if they uphold the complaint in the first instance, it does not even go to the Broadcasting Standards Authority. So if one takes a complaint to the broadcasters---if they breach some standard or code that they have agreed to; it is a voluntary code that they have agreed to and it is now mandatory that they abide by it---then they should own up and say: ``Yes, we're really sorry. That was stupid. That was dumb.'' The complaint will not even go to the Broadcasting Standards Authority if broadcasters do that, but if they want to fight on they will have to think about it. I agree that $, is not a big fine for Television New Zealand, so even if the Broadcasting Standards Authority fined the maximum possible $,, Television New Zealand will pay it out of the coffers quite easily, I assume. But I am told by the current chairperson of the Broadcasting Standards Authority, Judith Potter, that the broadcasters would take a fine of any magnitude quite seriously. It would hurt their professional pride. It would be a real smack back for them, and it would not necessarily--- I am talking about all broadcasters. Even if the Broadcasting Standards Authority imposed a $ or so fine on them, the fact that they have been fined for a breach of the code and have to pay up---stump-up with it---is a concern. I understand in the case of privacy breaches that there is a great deal of concern about having to make those payments, even though they are quite nominal. I know there was talk about pushing the fine up even further, but I think that where it is positioned right now should have the effect of forcing broadcasters to be a bit more sensible when they look at the complaints in the first instance. Secondly, I do not think many broadcasters would like to have on their record that they were fined for breaching the codes.

Cutting tariffs does not mean cutting jobs. On the contrary, while tariff reductions lead to job losses in parts of the economy being protected by those tariffs, they actually lead to job growth in other parts of the economy. Tariffs are a tax on business and families and protect local industries from international competition. As a result, they inflate the prices of goods to consumers and raise the price of inputs to business. They make it harder for our companies to compete internationally. Tariffs therefore do not create jobs. On the contrary, as tariffs are reduced, assets tied up in those businesses can be transferred to industries that are free from protection.

I thank the member. It helps councils know which of the organisations they control are subject to the special accountability regime that applies to local authority trading enterprises. The committee has fully considered the major concerns expressed in submissions on the proposed new definition. The submissions were all from councils and associated local government organisations. The submissions focused mainly on the proposed new definition of a local authority trading enterprise. All submitters expressed some concern about the types of organisations to be included in the definition, and the taxation implications of inclusion. Under section of the Taxation (Remedial Provisions) Act local authority trading enterprises will not be able to apply for charitable and district improvement tax exemptions after the end of this financial year. This legislation was passed to prevent commercial local authority trading enterprises from being exempt from tax---in order to answer the very good question from the member for Tamaki. However, if the current definition of a local authority trading enterprise were not amended, the Taxation (Remedial Provisions) Act would also prevent council-controlled trading undertakings of community benefit from seeking charitable and district improvement tax exemptions. That has never been the Government's intention, and it could threaten the community benefits that such organisations provide. The Local Government (Meaning of Local Authority Trading Enterprise) Amendment Bill---and I do intend to talk to law draftsmen about whether we can get some shorter titles for some of these pieces of legislation---excludes those council-controlled trading undertakings that are neither companies nor profit-orientated from the definition of a local authority trading enterprise. Such trading undertakings will therefore still be able to apply for the charitable and district improvement tax exemptions, as they are now. However, as the committee noted, councils are able to choose how to structure their activities. For example, rather than establishing a company to carry on a trading undertaking, a council could set up a non-company structure such as a trust. Councils need to weigh up the advantages and the disadvantages, including whether there is a requirement to pay tax, before deciding whether a company structure is always the right one. I am pleased to see that the Government has fixed a problem with the new Wellington stadium that is being built by a trust. The trust would have had problems with this legislation if it had had to go about its original funding track by having made available to it an interest-free loan for a -month period and deferring the time for settlement. The Government has removed the problem that this legislation would have caused the trust. I know that the member for Wellington Central, for example, was seriously concerned about that issue, and he will be pleased that this matter has now been addressed. I congratulate the committee on its comprehensiveness in addressing the submitters' concerns in the report. The committee, rightly I believe, recommends that the Bill should go forward unchanged.

I need to take a call because this issue in clause ZK can, on the surface of it, be quite seductive in terms of saying: ``Look, if you have a heavy truck with freight on it, or if you have a commercial bus and it is pulled over by law enforcement, for whatever reason, and the driver is found to be a disqualified driver, then it should not be that the vehicle is impounded as it would be for a private car.'' I say that on the surface of it that sounds quite seductive, but I would like to raise three or four issues with this Committee for us to think about. They are simply this. First of all, we have said in the report-back speech to Parliament that employers or operators of companies will need only to have checked in a reasonable fashion that the person is still a valid driver. I said in my Hansard speech: ``-day type check, here are the names of our drivers, are they OK?''. One of the concerns raised with me is: ``What if a driver got disqualified in Christchurch yesterday, then flew back up to Auckland, and kept driving for me? As the owner of the company, I did not know.'' This Bill will implement a whole new, sophisticated system of checking. The Land Transport Safety Authority is looking at devising very simple telephone and fax-type systems and fax-back systems. I would not be surprised if it also looks at direct telephone inquiry systems and an telephone-type thing, or even an Internet-based facility. But there are now very simple, easy ways, just as there is for checking motor vehicle registration, for checking whether the driver is valid. They will need only to have done that on, say, a -day type cycle. It fixes that problem of someone driving and being disqualified yesterday and the owner did not know about it, but that person being out there driving for the owner today. I give the Committee a caution about this. First of all, the bus or truck could not carry on even under the current laws. If the authorities catch someone driving while disqualified that person cannot carry on driving. The authorities cannot let that bus or truck go on to the nearest town and then say ``Now we will get you.'' The fact is that if a disqualified driver is driving, we have to take that driver out of the system right there and then. I accept that another driver could be brought to the scene. I want to make it clear that within police operational policy we expect all endeavours will be made to minimise the inconvenience to those who are innocent---that is, the passengers on board the bus or making sure the freight gets to a depot first.

I would like to speak briefly on Part , which is about mitigation of penalties and rights of appeal. Obviously whenever strong legislation is passed, as this is, with quite heavy penalties, one wants to have quite a few areas where there can be mitigating circumstances and rights of appeal. Lianne Dalziel raised an issue before that struck a chord with me, and certainly with others here, that in fact there may be mitigating circumstances in certain circumstances. I think they are limited to very, very specific circumstances, otherwise the suits can always find a way through---a loophole. I give a specific example. If a young couple were living on a farm somewhere in the backblocks, the woman had a serious heart attack, and the man was a disqualified driver, one would expect him to be able to jump in the car with his wife and shoot into the nearest hospital. If he happened to be called over by the police, then the mitigating circumstances would be quite clear: there was a serious medical emergency and the police would assist him. I do not think we even need to mention this, actually. One of my officials from the police here said that, frankly, in a medical emergency police would assist such people to get to hospital. However, just from the point of view of tidiness, and so that everyone can feel good about it, the amendment that stands in my name is to pick up on that, and the police are comfortable that it does not create loopholes or abuses. The amendment will be to insert after line in clause () the following paragraph (e), which will state: ``The driver drove the vehicle in a serious medical emergency . . .''. A bracket will then be inserted just for a slight explanation, because Lianne Dalziel pointed out that I clearly do not know my maternity issues as well as I should, which states: ``(which for the purpose of this paragraph includes carrying a person who is about to give birth)''. I understand that a woman giving birth is not considered to be a medical issue. I am told that midwives would take me round the back and beat the bejesus out of me if I ever said that a birth process was a medical emergency. So we will put a clarification in there with brackets around it so that we get it right. I am very happy to do that, and I thank Lianne Dalziel for raising that point.

I remember meeting the president of Federated Farmers earlier this year at a National Party caucus meeting in west Auckland. He said that the one thing about the National - New Zealand First coalition that was upsetting Federated Farmers a bit was that we were not progressing with reforms and deregulation. I replied: ``Well, that's a bit rich, Mr Bailey, because it was Federated Farmers who said not to deregulate.'' In fact an ACT member, when he was in Federated Farmers, showed up at the front of Parliament on a horse and trap with all these big pieces of paper stating: ``You must not deregulate post.'' Mr Jennings rode the horse and trap up to Parliament, and said we must not deregulate the postal services of this country. That was a bit rich coming from an ACT member, and I am delighted to say that he now has seen the folly of his ways. I am pleased to say that so has Federated Farmers. Mr Bailey stood up at that meeting of our caucus and said: ``Mr Williamson, I am pleased to say that Federated Farmers got it wrong. We got it wrong, and you should proceed to deregulate postal services.'' I said: ``Great! It's great having you on side. Join the queue; it's a long one, Mr Bailey. Three years ago the world was going to end, and there would be no New Zealand shipping. The whole place was going to crumble. Guess what? Not one of those things happened---not one.

I move, That the Local Elections and Polls (Processing of Voting Papers Before Close of Voting) Amendment Bill be now read a third time. I think this is a good Bill in terms of its indication of how Parliament can work to the benefit of the general community. It was Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers that actually wanted this Bill. They came to me earlier in the year and said they would like it done for this election, because the benefits of processing voting papers before the close of voting are quite substantial. First of all there is a significant cost saving to local authorities, arising from fewer staff being required following the close of voting. There is an easing of pressure on local resources---for example, computers---coupled with their more efficient use. Instead of all of them being needed as of . p.m. on closing day, there can be fewer of them and processing can be done over the / days before the midday closing. It also allows the meeting of the high public expectation of prompt and accurate provisional announcements of election results at p.m. on Saturday night. Everyone is glued to their radios, wanting to hear the results of the local body elections by p.m. This measure dramatically fixes that process. This Bill---originally the result of an initiative by the Society of Local Government Managers---has now been amended considerably to meet what I think are the genuine concerns of a number of people about maintaining the security of the voting process while still gaining the benefits of the initiative. A number of people were legitimately worried that if somebody were able to process the votes early and do some provisional counting, or even spot a trend that was happening, that person might be able to get hold of one of his or her mates who was a candidate and say: ``Hey look, Fred,''---or Nora---``if you spend a little bit more on your advertising, if you throw around a couple more circulars, you might be able to close the gap.'' I think the security of the voting process goes to the heart of our democracy, and it must be protected. I believe that the changes that were made, first by the committee then by the House, have significantly enhanced the security provisions. Therefore this Bill should now be passed to enable those local authorities that so choose to use these processing procedures in the upcoming local authority elections in October this year. The progress of this Bill has reflected what I think is a true partnership approach between central and local government. Firstly, as I said, the initiative came from the Society of Local Government Managers. The initiative was supported by Local Government New Zealand, the body representing the political interests of local government. The vast majority of local authorities subsequently indicated their support for the proposal, either individually or through a joint submission prepared by Local Government New Zealand and the Society of Local Government Managers. When the Society of Local Government Managers originally approached me for my support for the initiative, I suggested that it ascertain the support of other political parties. We would not have put this Bill through the Parliament if there was going to be one big, long, protracted fight. There did not seem to be any purpose in doing that. Then at the Internal Affairs and Local Government Committee cross-party support for the Bill was forthcoming. I thank all the members of that select committee. I think they did a good job in tidying up some of the provisions in the original Bill, which the Society of Local Government Managers had put forward. The select committee has, sensibly, put some better provisions in it. I would like to thank all the committee members from all the parties represented on it for the work they did. In particular, the committee achieved several things, including an appropriate level of flexibility so that local authorities have discretion as to whether to adopt the procedures, when to adopt the procedures, and to what extent they adopt particular procedures. I think that flexibility was important. The existing rights of scrutineers, particularly, to be present at the commencement of the scrutiny of the roll and following the closing of voting also needed to be protected. A minimum amount of change to the principal Act was required to achieve the necessary clarity and certainty for local authority returning officers implementing these procedures. The House has made more changes to further enhance the Bill. In particular, it has changed the security provisions by reducing to hours---from midnight on the Tuesday before the close of voting, instead of the whole days before the close of voting---the period when voting envelopes may be opened and processed but, and I stress this, not counted. I believe that it is a satisfactory outcome. It gives a balance. It meets the concerns of those people who were worried about security, and were worried about the outcome of the local election being affected, but also gives local bodies a gain in that they can use dramatically fewer resources over a longer period of time. I acknowledge the recommendation for some form of review of these procedures following the election. I hope the select committee does do such a review, and decides whether anything further needs to be tightened. It is desirable that once we know how the local authorities adopted the procedures, and how well it worked, we make any changes if necessary. Finally, once again I thank all members of the House and all the political parties who supported the legislation so far.

I move, That the House take note of the report of the Government Administration Committee on the Matrimonial Property Amendment Bill. This bill has been a long time in the making, and it still has some way to go as far as the Government is concerned. It is worth reflecting that it has been years since the Matrimonial Property Act was enacted, and years since a ministerial working-group called for a review of the Act. The original Act from its enactment contained flaws. It did not apply to de facto relationships. It did not apply to same-sex relationships, and it did not apply in the event of death. The amendment bill addresses one of those defects---namely, that the Act applies to marriages ended by the death of a spouse. Basically, the bill provides that the surviving spouse must elect, within months of the grant of administration, whether he or she wishes to take the option of the Act or the will---so they have a choice to go under the Act or the will. If no election is made within that time, then the survivor is deemed to have elected to take the option under the will, or, where there is no will, that of intestacy. The bill applies to wills made both before and after the amendment Act comes into force. The bill addresses a variety of other issues, including provisions relating to the deferral of equal sharing where dependent minors are concerned, to ensure that their well-being is taken into account. There are also attempts to defeat those practices whereby a spouse's interests are acted upon detrimentally by the other spouse through the use of such devices as family trusts. There is also an important provision that gives the sole originating jurisdiction to the Family Court to deal with matrimonial proceedings. All these matters are important and worthwhile. However, the fact remains that the bill still fails to address fundamental issues---in particular, those issues relating to de facto and same-sex relationships. Just as important is that it fails to adequately address the important question that was the subject of the ministerial working-group, which was how we address the economic disadvantage experienced by non-earning spouses. In other words, the presumption of equal division and the clean cut has, over the years, acted to the detriment of many women and their children. Therefore, it was necessary for the law to take account of changing circumstances. We had hoped there would be an opportunity to do that through this bill. From reading the report of the select committee, it is apparent that the majority decided not to take advantage of, or listen to, many of the submissions made on various issues. The Government will therefore relook at the issues raised in those submissions. We will look at the possibility of ensuring there is more extensive coverage on the breakdown of a relationship when it comes to property. We will do this by way of the introduction of a Supplementary Order Paper. I note that the former Minister of Justice had foreshadowed that a similar move would be made if he was still in charge of the bill. It is important to note, as I said, that this is a piece of legislation that women in particular have waited for, for a long time. It has therefore been a matter of concern that we have had to wait longer as the processes in this House have been gone through ever so slowly. In particular, it is matter of concern to the Government members who participated on that select committee that the bill appeared to be unnecessarily delayed because of the changes to the De Facto Relationships (Property) Bill. This Government is determined to move with considered haste to make sure that the bill more fairly reflects the concerns of those who took the time and the trouble to make submissions. In particular, we are concerned about the whole issue of economic disadvantage for non-earning spouses. At times it is difficult to realise and understand the distress that many women---and their dependent children---experience when they have performed the role and function of spouse to their husband, and then have been discarded for a newer and younger model at the very time when they are most in need of some reciprocity in terms of the partnership arrangement they thought they had entered into. These women frequently find themselves with very limited earning capacity because they have, in effect, sacrificed the development of their own skills in the marketplace to enable their husbands to be able to earn more. The matter is a complex one, and that is not denied, but its complexity does not mean it should not be addressed. There have been suggestions that it should be addressed through the reintroduction of notions of maintenance. In the past, one of the real difficulties of following this route was seen to be that it locked parties into a continuing relationship at the very time when it was important that they were given the resources to get on and manage their own lives without continuing the conflicts and disputes that had arisen from the breakdown of the marriage. The whole purpose of the original Act was to acknowledge that the contribution of women to the partnership was equal to that of the earning male. That fundamental purpose of the legislation remains at the centre of the amendment. The interests and concerns of women drove the amendment being proposed. However, the difficulty is that there still appears to be a reluctance today to accept that women who devote their lives to the well-being of their partners and children should be adequately compensated.

Clause in Part sets out clearly the objects of the legislation. They are driven by two concerns. One is the poor rate of productivity achieved under the Employment Contracts Act, and the second is the need to prepare our labour market to be able to compete globally in the future, and also the need to retain skilled labour, which has been fleeing New Zealand in the last decade, under the Employment Contracts Act. We therefore see the objects in clause as an attempt to get a better balance in the employment relationship, recognising those drivers that respect the skills and labour of people in the employment relationship, as well as, of course, recognising the contribution of employers. We were attempting to get a better balance in that relationship, and also to provide for a remedy that was more cost-efficient and more likely to produce better, win-win situations. Clause (b) addresses our international obligations. Members will note that that paragraph states ``to promote observance of the principles''. We recognise that by our continuing to make sympathy strikes unlawful, the ILO, when we submit this legislation to it, may have some difficulty with it. Apart from that, we believe that the principles in ILO Convention , under the rules of interpretation in the courts these days, can be observed. I also note that in clause the parties to the good-faith relationship must not mislead each other. That notion may be foreign to some from time to time, but is clearly understood by many. I have no doubt that there will be litigation at the outset, as there is with all legislative change, but I also have no doubt that there will be less litigation under the personal grievance clauses. Therefore, at the end of the day I would be very surprised if the compliance costs, particularly for small employers, were not lowered. I am also not surprised that those whose business is conflict have difficulty in understanding notions of good faith. One has to start somewhere, however. It is true that those who are locked in the experience of the past will have some difficulty, whether they be employers or employees, but this legislation is designed to support a new way of their being able to conduct that relationship.

The Government acts to ensure its policies are consistent with the law. Where there is a doubt as to the meaning of the law, then, depending on the facts, the Government will seek clarification of that law from the courts to ensure that in the future it acts consistently with the law.
