While we do not have the notion that it is a committee of experts, this committee does in fact come close in its representative composition of people who will, I hope, be able to adequately understand the content of the submissions, and therefore will be able to ensure a fair hearing is given. The previous speaker tended to indicate that a knowledge of the workplace was a disqualification. I note that in fact under that member's Government previously a lack of knowledge was normally a qualification for appointment. This Government believes that an understanding of what one is talking about is a primary qualification. Therefore the fact that members appointed by the Government to the committee have direct experience of the workplace must be seen as a primary qualification. Also, members appointed from the Opposition have had the benefit of being members of what some of us would also consider to be unions--Federated Farmers and the New Zealand Law Society, being but two, and, also, distinctively, the Post Primary Teachers Association. I understand that Mr Brownlee has had the privilege to be a member of a union also, which demonstrates, of course, the balance that will be on the committee. Also, I think the committee's membership is enhanced by the presence of Mr Brown, who has considerable experience of the waterfront industry. That will be invaluable when it comes to hearing the submissions. Therefore I support the motion, because the committee is well balanced. I am sorry--I forgot the Hon. Max Bradford, who has been a member of the Employers Federation and so is eminently qualified. And, of course, Sue Bradford has the advantage of having experience of being both an employer and an employee. I now want to address the issue that was also raised that somehow this committee would not give adequate time or consideration to submissions because there would not be time for consultation. I also note for the information of the House that in the preparation of the Employment Relations Bill, a considerable amount of time went into consultations with the New Zealand Employers and Manufacturers Association as well as the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions. Before the bill was tabled, meetings were held with representatives from both those organisations to brief them fully on the provisions of the bill. In the case of one organisation, I note from its public comments that, obviously, time was not sufficient for it to gain an understanding of what the bill was all about. Still, I am pleased to note that there will be adequate time for submissions. Five to weeks will be available for people to write their submissions and then present them to the committee, where, I have no doubt at all, the committee will ensure, as we will, that people are given a courteous and respectful hearing, as well as, of course, full consideration of the comments they have to make. I have also indicated to many of the employers, unions, and others with whom I have consulted prior to tabling the bill, that if there are submissions of a technical nature that will improve the operations of the bill, then, of course, they will be considered properly. I have no difficulty with amendments of that nature that are designed to make the process of good faith, mutual trust, and confidence work more effectively. I have also noted that the Opposition member, in support of the amendment, tended to indicate that there was some difficulty with the independence of the committee members when it comes to hearing submissions. My understanding is that in this House we are all representatives and we all owe our representativeness to those who elected us. If he meant, then, that independence did not come by people getting a fair hearing, then I would refute that at least on behalf of the Government members, though I cannot, of course, talk for the members of the Opposition who would be on the committee. I also note that it is important that this committee does operate as efficiently and as quickly as possible and is consistent with a full hearing of all the issues. The reason for this is that I have had many representations from people who will be affected by this legislation and want it to be introduced and passed as quickly as possible so they can organise their affairs accordingly. It is demonstrably clear to everyone that this is legislation that was promised to the electorate. A mandate was given to this Government. Therefore it is legislation that will be enacted, consistent with that mandate. People want to get on and organise their affairs. Agreements are coming up for renewal. People want to make sure that they take the advantage and the benefit that is provided by the good-faith bargaining provisions that have been provided for in the Employment Relations Bill. So that, for me, is a very powerful argument in support of the original motion that the House appoint the committee to consider specifically such employment and accident insurance legislation as may be referred to it. I have so far spoken only in relation to the employment legislation, but I also wish to make comments in support of the accident insurance legislation. It is demonstrably clear that this is legislation of a complex and specialist nature, and that already some experience has been gained in an understanding of this legislation. Therefore this committee should be supported on that ground also.

I move, That the Shop Trading Hours Act Repeal Amendment Bill be now read a first time. This bill amends the Shop Trading Hours Act Repeal Act of . The trading restrictions of that Act are retained generally, but the bill addresses one of the persistent concerns under the current Act. That concern is that while garden centres were able to trade over Easter under the previous legislation, they lost that right in , when the current Act was passed. Shops that sell plants and garden supplies are generally not permitted to trade over Easter, despite there being considerable popularity over that period, particularly on Easter Sunday, for gardening activities and supplies. The bill will remedy that situation by enabling all garden centres to trade on Easter Sunday. The main operative clause of the bill is clause , which amends the principal Act to allow all garden centres in New Zealand to open on Easter Sunday. A garden centre is defined as a shop whose sole, or principal, business is the sale of plants and/or garden supplies. Clause inserts a new section A into the principal Act to provide transitional protection to workers in newly exempted garden centres. Those employees with existing employment agreements may not be required to work on Easter Sundays, except with their agreement. Clause amends section of the principal Act to provide transitional protection for newly exempted garden centres, with the expansion of any mandatory opening times included in existing leases or other arrangements. Clause clarifies that the bill does not affect prosecutions initiated before the bill comes into force. It is recognised that the bill is a limited reform to the Act, which is in need of general reform. The current Act generally forbids retail trading on Christmas Day, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and before p.m. on Anzac Day, with some exemptions. Those exemptions, in particular, the area exemptions that were frozen in place in the legislation, have become outdated and no longer reflect current and economic reality. However, the current bill represents what was possible to achieve in the time available before Easter this year. We have focused on addressing an issue that has attracted strong public and retail support. I am pleased we have found a political consensus to advance this far. Shop trading hours is a complex issue. On the one hand there is support for retaining some trading restrictions. On the other hand there is support for retailers' and consumers' freedom of choice and the need to recognise changes and social and community attitudes in retail trade. We acknowledge there is still room to debate the scope for ways of bringing the legislation more fully into the present time, while maintaining an appropriate balance of interests. Having passed this limited reform, we need to move on to examine these broader issues---for example, the issue of whether to allow shops in regional tourist centres such as Mount Maunganui and Rotorua to open, as well. We will be taking a considered approach to this issue that seeks to set an appropriate balance between the legitimate concerns of retailers, retail employees, and the community over the cultural, social, recreational, and religious significance of the currently restricted days. I hope to bring the outcome of these deliberations to the House in the near future, and trust they will attract the same measure of support that will be accorded this bill. I commend this bill to the House.

The Hon. Paul Swain would like the public to have this mental picture of his riding into town on a white horse, throwing the books at corporate raiders, and firing bullets from his six-gun. He wants to give the impression that the New Zealand sharemarket is the Wild West. But the truth is this bill has only a very modest purpose statement: ``The bill aims to amend the Securities Act and the Takeovers Act to enable the effective implementation and enforcement of a takeovers code.'' It is a very technical bill, intended just to enable the implementation and enforcement of the Takeovers Code. I think the Minister asked himself a question, but he did not proceed to answer it: why has it taken so long to enable the Takeovers Code to be implemented? Even though the Commerce Committee was restricted to debating the technical code, I think the public deserves better answers, to enable them to understand the implementation of the Takeovers Code. It is controversial because there are many arguments in favour of it and, equally, in opposition to it. In effect, the Takeovers Code was started by the National Government in , but, being a very responsible political party, National did not pretend that it was a non-controversial issue. We did not rush into implementing the code. We have continued to receive information and have listened very carefully to the arguments for and against. One argument for the Takeovers Code is that it will ensure fairness. Some see that the stock exchange rules do not give shareholders a fair chance. They believe that the major shareholders take control and investors, ranging from substantial passive investors to small investors, might have no show. That is one of the arguments for having a Takeovers Code. Some say that New Zealand's sharemarket performance has been dismal since the sharemarket crash in , compared with that of similar countries such as the US, Britain, and Australia. They claim that our lack of a Takeovers Code might be the reason. Some would argue that Australia and Great Britain---countries similar to us---both have codes, and the fact that we are looking at closer economic ties with Australia might mean it makes sense for us to have a similar code. Support for the implementation of the code seems to be strengthening, coming from diverse groups such as the Institute of Directors and AMP. We also realise that there is a public perception that there should be more protection for small investors. Those are very valid arguments for the implementation of a Takeovers Code. But, at the same time, we must also take note that, equally, there are valid arguments as to why we do not need a Takeovers Code. Some would argue that, in effect, by making takeovers difficult we are working against the interest of the shareholders, because it is in the shareholders' interest to receive takeover bids. Some of us would agree that, in effect, a takeover bid puts pressure on management to perform in order to ensure that the shareholders continue to hold shares in the company because they receive adequate rewards. The proposed code would also raise the risk in terms of the costs of a takeover. Some would say it could lead to the protection of poor management teams and boards that deserve to be exposed. Some would say that New Zealand already has a takeovers regime in the company law and the stock exchange rules. Some would also argue that the existing rules cannot be very inequitable. One could go so far as to say that most shareholders who have already decided to invest in a company surely are aware of the existing rules, and the fact that they continue to invest in the company must be an indication that they are comfortable with the existing rules. We also hear arguments from some members of the public that New Zealand's existing arrangement puts small shareholders at risk, and is inconsistent with small shareholders voting, for example, on the recent New Zealand Stock Exchange option. The argument that share prices may go higher with the proposed code is inconsistent with shareholder voting on the New Zealand Stock Exchange option. The reason I put forward those valid arguments for and against the code is to paint a realistic picture that the public and the corporate scene are not at all unanimous about whether we need a Takeovers Code. This legislation is a technical mechanism to enable the code to happen, but whether its successful execution will lead to better performance of the sharemarket very much relies on the panel---how it exercises its discretion and power, and whether it is resourced. But let me emphasise that this bill alone will not lead to success. I would like to think the public did not see it as a panacea, and I certainly hope the Minister does not think this single piece of legislation will lead to a boom in the sharemarket. Whether investors choose to buy into a company, and whether a country enjoys a very vibrant sharemarket activity, come back to a culture, a culture that the Government is partly responsible for, a culture that people understand in the commercial world---that people should be rewarded for taking risks. I think that, particularly under this minority Labour-Alliance coalition Government, the passing of this legislation will not help to change or improve that culture, because the Labour-Alliance coalition Government intrinsically does not believe in the concept that people who take the risk of investing in a company should be properly rewarded. Until we have a Government that actually demonstrates, by not putting up company tax, by not making employment law more difficult, by not introducing more regulations to cramp the entrepreneurs of New Zealand, we do not believe that the sharemarket or the corporate sector will work any better under this Takeovers Code. On balance, we believe that this is mechanical legislation to ensure that the implementation of the Takeovers Code can take place. We support that, but we in no way share the confidence of the Minister that it is the cure for New Zealand's corporate market. In a sense, we believe that this minority Labour-Alliance coalition Government has a long way to go to restore the confidence of investors in the sharemarket.

Let me explain to Rodney Hide, the member responsible for the bill, that this has been a most frustrating process for the Commerce Committee. The Shop Trading Hours (Abolition of Restrictions) Bill was introduced into this House in , and submissions were called for by the Justice and Electoral Committee, which was in charge of the bill. Let me point out to the member who just sat down, David Cunliffe, that when he told the public that everybody was against the bill, that is not true. There were submissions received, and submitters asked to be heard. Of that number, supported the bill and opposed it. But then came the election, and the bill was transferred to the Commerce Committee in the new parliamentary term. At first, the Labour and Alliance members of the select committee absolutely refused to consider the bill, even though everyone knew that come Easter all hell would break loose, with the annual protest by garden centres over their inability to open on Easter Sunday. When we finally shamed the Government members into considering how to progress the bill, they would not hear from those submitters who had already forwarded written submissions to the select committee. The Alliance member of the select committee kept a totally closed mind on the whole bill. Kevin Campbell flatly refused to engage in any constructive debate on it. Eventually we found out that his main worry was over employees being forced to work, should restrictions be lifted. We believed that was a legitimate concern, but it is surprising he had no confidence that the much-acclaimed Employment Relations Act would stop that from happening. The sad fact was that he did not want to listen to any submitters or to consider any solution that might alleviate his fears. Apparently the Alliance did not support any change to the status quo. It was strange to learn that the Alliance subsequently caved in to Labour's shotgun, one-off legislation allowing garden centres to trade on Easter Sunday, . If the Alliance is a principled party it should have steadfastly held to its position, and should not have allowed the garden centres to open at all. As to the position of the Labour members of the committee, they simply said they would not support the bill because the Minister of Labour would come up with a perfect solution. Well, nothing happened. Easter arrived, and there was nothing from the Hon. Margaret Wilson, who is by now famous for her inability to introduce any legislation and to have it debated properly in this House. So we had, once again, the one-off, shotgun solution of allowing the garden centres to trade on Easter Sunday, . Everyone on the Commerce Committee realised and admitted that the current shop trading hours are a farce and are difficult to operate, and everybody wanted to see changes. But we were no further ahead, because those members simply refused to engage in constructive debate and to advance any arguments for or against the bill, or to suggest how to amend it. Eventually, after Easter , the Hon. Margaret Wilson signalled to us that the shape of the Government's solution to the issue of shop trading hours is for her to be ultimately responsible for considering any city or province that wants to have the restrictions on trading days relaxed. I can just imagine that the Hon. Margaret Wilson's desk will be full of applications from all parts of the regions, claiming they are tourist centres and therefore deserve an exemption from the current very messy, untidy shop trading hours regulations. Because of that, I welcome the Labour Party's sudden change of heart to a position not simply of voting down this bill but of allowing sensible, constructive debate to be engaged in by the Committee of the whole House. The shame is that the Labour Party did not allow that process to happen in the Commerce Committee, where we could have engaged the public by hearing from the submitters and seeing whether we could find innovative solutions and a way forward. The public have been deprived of that particular process. During the Committee stage, we will introduce some of the innovative suggestions from the submitters who took the time and used their resources to write to the Commerce Committee. In my personal opinion the current bill goes a bit too far, by lifting all restrictions on shop trading hours. But, from the submissions we received, there is a good level of support for a relaxation of the rules for all shops to trade on Easter Sunday, for example, in order to enable them to choose whether to open. We heard from the garden centre people, who assured us that under the current employment situation no employee would be forced to work, and that a genuine negotiation process would take place between employers and employees in terms of whether employees would work on those days. New Zealand has come a long way from about years ago, when I thought that nobody enjoyed shopping on days outside Mondays to Fridays. Nowadays we realise that -day shopping is part of the social habits of New Zealanders. Most members of the public have come to expect the freedom to choose whether to shop on certain days. For the shops, it is between employers and employees to make that decision. I also challenge the Green Party members to take a more constructive approach in the Committee stage. I find their stand of simply supporting garden centres being able to open on Easter Sunday, and not allowing other shops the same opportunity, a strange one. If it is good enough for garden centres to open, why is it not good enough for any other shops that may be engaged in selling environmental products etc. also to open? I started my speech by expressing pleasant surprise at Labour's change of stance. Labour supports this bill going to the Committee stage, but I cannot help thinking that the main reason that Labour members have changed their stern stand against the bill is that by now they have realised that the Hon. Margaret Wilson's solution is a Clayton's one. Her solution is that in future any region that wishes to seek an exemption from the current shop trading hours legislation can do so by making direct application to her office. That is simply unworkable. My cynical opinion is that maybe this particular Minister has learnt once again that her legislation is not going to work, but I do welcome that change of heart.

The lack of positive contributions from the Labour Party is absolutely astounding. However, the public should not be surprised, because the bill was introduced by the Alliance Minister the Hon. Laila Harre, who, interestingly, has already apologised to the M~aori community and said that she does not believe that the minority coalition Government has got it right. She stated in her introductory speech that the Government is not going far enough to address all the concerns of the M~aori community in terms of intellectual property. Maybe that is the reason that Labour members find it difficult even to stand to explain to members on this side of the House and the public why this bill is such excellent legislation. I particularly invite the Labour M~aori members to explain two points to members on this side of the House and to the public. First, why is it such excellent legislation, and, secondly, why is the Associate Minister of Commerce already apologising to the M~aori community for not getting it right? As a member of the Commerce Committee, I expect that this bill might come to our select committee. We want to know right from the beginning what the deficiencies are, and what we can possibly expect in terms of changes in the foreseeable future. I would also like to take up some of the criteria that the Minister herself set up as criteria for success. She said that this bill introduces clarity and certainty, and also minimises compliance costs. Let us examine that claim about minimising compliance costs. This Labour-Alliance Government repeats that phrase every time it introduces legislation. It says that the legislation will reduce compliance costs, but it never discloses the criteria for measuring by how much compliance costs are reduced. More important, it never quite grasps the business community's expectations in terms of compliance costs and rewards. The business community looks at compliance costs from three angles: the compliance cost may be justified if the reward is greater than it; the compliance cost may be the administration cost relating to it; or the compliance cost may be the actual cost of abiding with the law. In this case, if we consider the business community's interest, I have a feeling that it might think that going through an application procedure under this trademark legislation might not give it any benefit. Clause introduces a freer environment. It says that if there are applications for similar or identical trademarks, the Commissioner of Trade Marks will decide which has priority by considering who submitted the application first. If they arrived on the same day, then they are assumed to have arrived at the same time. I think a lot of people who go to the trouble of investing a lot of time and resources in developing trademarks and applying for registration of them do so because it gives them a competitive advantage. If they have no certainty that an identical trademark will be rejected, if they do not know how far the commissioner will go in allowing comparative advertising, then I believe that will make the business community less inclined to invest money in registering trademarks. During the select committee process we certainly will invite the input of a whole range of the business community, to make sure that the lack of certainty does not lead to fewer applications for trademarks. The second issue we want to examine is the claim that this bill actually introduces more clarity and certainty. I think that one of the examples I have given---the fact that the priority of applications might not restrict another applicant who submits a similar trademark---might not give the first applicant the comfort of knowing that clarity and certainty are being introduced by this legislation. Once again, we turn to the very controversial clause , ``Absolute grounds for not registering trade mark: general''. Subclause () states that the commissioner must not do a number of things. Firstly, the commissioner must not register a trademark or part of a trademark if it is likely to deceive or cause confusion. I think that during the select committee process we have to examine the criteria that the commissioner will apply to judge deception or confusion. But the second ground is even more controversial, because it states that the commissioner must not register a trademark or part of a trademark if he or she ``considers that, on reasonable grounds, its use or registration would be likely to offend a significant section of the community, including M~aori:''. I am not a lawyer, and I invite my lawyer colleagues to stand up to explain the wording of this particular provision. What does ``a significant section of the community, including M~aori:'' mean? Does it mean that M~aori in general are not included in the definition of community? I would be surprised to think that M~aori were not part of the New Zealand community. Does ``a significant section of the community,'' include M~aori, and do we add the M~aori population on top of that? I would also like to examine this definition from the Asian community's point of view. We all know that the Asian community makes up only . percent of the population. What if a trademark is offensive to all the Asian community? It would not form a significant part of the community. How are we going to address that? How about the Pacific Island community, which makes up only . percent of the New Zealand community? If a trademark is offensive to the whole Pacific Island community, does that mean offence has been taken by ``a significant section of the community,''? This bill at this stage does not satisfy us in terms of clarity and certainty. I make this request to the Minister: if she does refer this bill to the Commerce Committee, I want her to instruct the chairman of the Commerce Committee that he must act objectively. We want this bill to be examined on a very bipartisan basis. We ask him to respect the select committee process; otherwise, the Opposition will use every Standing Order available to us to ensure that this bill is examined objectively and fairly.

No, no, I did not mean to give that impression at all. We will run with campaigning at the polling booths; we will run with all of that if that is what people decide to do. Mr Mapp went so far as to say, and he can correct me if I am wrong, that to close down polling would close down free speech, and close down the information on which people would make decisions. Elections are supposed to be about the politicians of various parties, and there are plenty of us, getting up and putting our views to the public. It is supposed to be about the news media reporting those speeches and statements faithfully to the public. That is what it is about. It is not supposed to be, with due respect, about the media trying to influence the result of an election one way or another. It is true that my leader, the Rt Hon. Winston Peters, has said many times that in a country such as Britain, which has the conservative newspapers, the liberal newspapers, the socialist newspapers, the communist newspapers, and the fascist newspapers, there is then proper free speech, and it does have a balance that we do not have here. It is excellent that the Minister of Justice is in the debating chamber, because he is responsible for the administration of this legislation. Where there is reference to the Minister, it is a reference to him in the temporary position that he holds. I would like to focus on this issue of remedies, and then invite the Minister to take a call to respond to the questions I have raised. I am not referring to the Minister in the chair; I am referring to the Minister of Justice who has responsibility for this legislation. I believe that we should always be very cautious about creating or extending the jurisdiction of tribunals. That is particularly so in areas that have elements of social justice or social engineering associated with them. We are conferring on this tribunal, in its extended jurisdiction, powers that are very akin to powers that the Inquisition held so many years ago. Although it is called a tribunal, its powers are substantially the powers of a court. Within those jurisdictional frameworks it has the powers of a District Court, a High Court, and a Court of Appeal. In developing that argument I would like to draw the attention of the Committee to page of the bill, because that is where some of the remedies that are available to the tribunal are set out. They are sweeping powers. In a moment I will come back to the declarations of inconsistency that are identified as the first remedy. The second remedy is broadly in the nature of an injunction. There is a third remedy, in connection with damages, and there are provisions that run through the bill to enable issues of damages excess to go to the High Court when the jurisdiction of the tribunal has been exceeded. Section I()(d), in clause , provides the ability for the tribunal to order that the defendant perform any acts specified in the order, with a view to redressing any loss or damage suffered by the complainant. So we are talking about some unusual element of compensatory damages that is not picked up in the general damages heading. There is then a reference to the Illegal Contracts Act. But a new provision has been inserted in the bill as a result of the select committee process. It was not by the unanimous vote of the members on the Justice and Electoral Committee, but by a majority. Perhaps the Minister might respond to this. What is the scope of this new power that is being given? It is a power to make an order that the defendant undertake any specified training or other programme in order to assist or enable the defendant to comply with the provisions of the Act. What sort of training would that be? What might these programmes include? Are we involved in issues that are on the edge of the wearing of sackcloth, and the placing of defendants into stocks? Then there is the final catch-all provision in paragraph (g) of section I(), which states: ``any other relief the Tribunal thinks fit.'' So we are investing a pseudo court with huge and undefined powers. I would like to deal briefly with the power known as declarations of inconsistency. I simply note in that connection that this is a very significant constitutional shift. One could say it is a major constitutional innovation. I would say it is a major constitutional threat. It is buried deep within the legislation, and now provides an ability for the court or a tribunal to declare that an Act of Parliament is inconsistent with the right to freedom.

When the bill was reported back I spoke briefly about three areas of specific interest. In regard to the first, I was picking up a theme that Mr Eric Roy was later to offer also---that is, that on this, the last members' day of the year, time was being taken in respect of this legislation---time that might more usefully have been spent on members' bills. I raised the issue of whether this was not one of those cases that rather proved the case for us to look hard at the issue of the power of general competence---that is, an ability that would be given by this Parliament to local authorities that they could pass laws on almost any issue within certain prescribed areas. Some areas would be proscribed. They might include defence. They might touch other matters that relate to the exercise of civil power. The other issues I raised then are probably not appropriate to traverse now. However, I pick up on what the Hon. Tony Ryall said in connection with traffic congestion in Tauranga. He sees that as a serious issue in an area that he is familiar with. The costs of congestion may not have been well captured in Tauranga, but in Auckland they clearly have been. The costs of congestion in that city are estimated to be in the order of not less than $ billion a year. That is a cost born by the commercial community and, of course, by those using vehicles for private purposes. He made the comment, or I am sure would have made it if pushed, that this focus on public transport was in some measure a fad, and that public transport did not bring the relief that many of its adherents claim. For instance, it is interesting to see that the Green Party in Germany has had to rethink its position on public transport. From being passionate followers of a public transport ethos, they have been forced---in part, for political reasons---to recognise the unreality of such an aspiration. For myself the answer is not only the completion of strategic networks, whether in Tauranga or in Auckland, but associated with that the clear need for there to be an effective system of public transport. But public transport of itself will not provide the answer to traffic congestion. It is also, as another speaker has said, time to reflect again on the possibility of what in defence circles is called ``p.p.p.''---private public partnership---the ability of developers and State agencies to get together to fund significant elements of infrastructure. I would like to turn to two particular clauses of the bill and speak about their implications, perhaps with a sense of disappointment. First, I refer to clause . Mr Brownlee is to take a call and deal with some of the subtleties in this clause that, for the present, elude me. Clause is headed ``Rates of tolls'' and subclause () states: ``Different provision may be made in the bylaws---(a) for different types of vehicle''---and no one could dispute that arrangement. But then it goes on to state, in paragraph ()(b): ``for different times of the day or for different days or for different days of the year.'' In this legislation we see the start of the congestion pricing regime. The Labour Party fought long and hard against that concept. Here we see it introduced through the mechanism of a local bill. So we will likely see in Tauranga different charges for different times of the day, and an attempt to educate---it is a system of forced education---those using vehicles to gauge their trips and to set the times of those trips in order to pay less than what might be the case at other periods. As I have said, Mr Brownlee will deal at some length with the implications of clause . The other issue that I raised unsuccessfully with the select committee touched on clause , which he will also deal with. Clause is headed ``Facilities for collection of tolls''. The interesting thing about this provision is that it rules out the possibilities---which are apparent in a place like Singapore---for there to be electronic collection of tolls. If members of this House have been to Singapore, they will have seen in various parts of that city, high-level gantries, and a system of electronic charging where, from a fixed point inside the car, the car's identity is revealed and money is drawn out of, in effect, a smart card within that system. I urged, in the context of innovation, that some consideration be given in this legislation to that sort of thing. But, no, that was too ambitious for the present membership of the select committee, and instead we have gone back to a system of the manual collection of tolls from people in toll houses. So little has changed since those old days in the th, th, and th centuries where riders on horses paid at toll gates for the right of passage on public and private roads. I suggest that that is a disappointment. Whilst we see in clause the implementation of a potential congestion charge regime, in clause we have missed out on the possibility of electronic collections. Why was that possibility not left open? Finally, I say that the committee has been greatly assisted by the submissions made by the Tauranga District Council. I guess it is possible to rate local authorities on a number of measures. Tauranga District Council has so organised its affairs, made choices in respect of its senior staff, and made choices in connection with its technology, that it represents a council committed to best practice. I wish the council well in the implementation of this bill, knowing that behind it and preceding it was an exhaustive resource management process. Now we open the way for the legislation to be passed, for construction to be started, and for the Hon. Tony Ryall, I hope, to cut the ribbon on that fateful day that will see the road opened and brought into use.

I am thankful for the opportunity to speak in this debate and to follow the junior Government whip. I suggest that there is no disgrace in being a champion of the poor, the oppressed, and the disabled. That is a title that those in the Labour Government should seek, instead of seeking to throw stones at Roger Sowry, a member who has made a sincere and substantial contribution to this debate. There is nothing wrong in being a champion of the poor, a champion of the oppressed, a champion of the disabled. This report by the Social Services Committee is a further step along a route announced prior to the election by members of the present interim Labour-Alliance Government. It was on October that Mr Maharey announced that a Labour Government would dump the community wage and replace it with Labour's own work creation projects. Those projects included, members may recall, one designed to urge the unemployed to set up small businesses. Others may comment on how realistic it was to urge the unemployed to set up their own businesses; most, I suggest, would think it was laudable but naive and likely to fail. Four months earlier Mr Maharey was widely reported as saying that Labour would scrap the community wage, which he asserted concentrated on keeping beneficiaries busy---his word---in favour, he asserted, of a genuine focus on increasing job opportunities. What was being said by Mr Maharey was that in a world of choices it is better to be an idle beneficiary than one who is occupied. How can that possibly be so? There is an old line: ``The devil makes work for idle hands.'' A Government that condones idleness, and in fact funds idleness, is out of step, I suggest, with the majority of New Zealanders. We have in our community a hybrid ensemble of players. There are those who work hard and are committed to the cause of advancing the interests of this country. There are those---and Mr Sowry spoke of these people---who, through misfortune or lack of skills, are not in employment but seek to be, and they need our support. And there are those who---to follow this theme of idleness---choose a life of idleness. They are, in effect, unemployment lifestylers. This Government by its position on this bill seeks to reinforce this last group by removing the community wage and replacing it with two separate benefits. It is probably lucky I cannot hear the interjections being offered by honourable members opposite. I am happy to respond to them if they are offered in an articulate, reasonable, and witty way. The community wage is to be abolished, and to be replaced with two separate benefits: an unemployment benefit and, as Mr Sowry has said, a non - work-tested sickness benefit. It is a matter of policy as to whether idleness is desirable in a society. Certainly, I see no difficulty in a person of Mr Cunliffe's quality being put in charge of a soup kitchen. To respond more directly to his comments, I think a soup kitchen in Remuera might very well suit his style. Certainly, it would not be above him.

I am glad he agrees. It is a matter of policy as to whether idleness is desirable in a society. I do not think it is. I was intrigued and concerned to hear the Prime Minister in a television interview with Linda Clark the other day say that it was Government policy to redistribute the wealth of this society. That is truly disappointing, because the challenge, which this Government seems very reluctant to seize, is to grow the wealth pool for all New Zealanders---not be about the redistribution of wealth. There are areas in New Zealand where much work is available, but there is a real reluctance in the community to take up that opportunity. If I can just identify two areas for Mr Chris Carter---whose mouth lies wide open at the moment; the flies are hovering near it---they are the East Coast and Northland. There are truly incredible forestry opportunities in those areas of substantial unemployment. I suggest that the Government has a clear obligation to encourage the people in those areas, whose communities are riddled with marijuana, to take up that opportunity and seek gainful employment in those industries. Mr Field has said to us that working for the dole has failed. That is his view. It is not, however, supported by a respectable body of work, including work done by Stephen Ward and others. Mr Ward's seminal work is probably well known to members of this Parliament. It is really important to note, however, that under the present law it is mandatory for recipients of the community wage to be available to take part in community work, but only if directed---and I underscore those words. Mr Maharey was utterly wrong when he said in opposition to the present law that the community was being left to shoulder the burden of keeping people busy. The select committee in its majority report seems to consider that if community work is voluntary, then somehow that will restore the value of voluntary community work. Voluntary community work is immensely valuable in New Zealand. It always has been, and I suggest it always will be. We all know that a raft of organisations contribute very substantially to the community. They range across organisations like the Order of St John, the Outward Bound Trust, and the Books in Prison Trust. To the extent that the select committee has suggested in its majority opinion that somehow the value of voluntary community work has been degraded by the community wage, then I suggest it is well off the mark. Finally, it should not be the policy of any Government to encourage freeloading. The lifestyler choice of dependency on the State should not be an option. The reality is there is a group in the community that will respond---and possibly respond only---to incentives and sanctions. I suggest that those sanctions and incentives should not simply be taken away, as this bill proposes.

The long title of the Bill should accurately reflect the matters therein. I reinforce the statements made by the Hon. Dr Michael Cullen in his speech, where he talked about the remedial amendments. This Bill is not entirely remedial. Part is the section that means that it is not a remedial Bill, although there are some remedial measures in that part. But certainly clause means that this Bill moves far beyond being a remedial Bill. It does bring into the tax net another whole section of capital gain. That in itself means that this is not a simplification Bill or a remedial Bill. It is interesting that in the long title there is no reference made to simplification, although the short title makes such reference. The Government has spent much of its time in this debate arguing the benefits of simplification, but the long title of the Bill makes no reference to it. I find that really rather remarkable, because I suppose that in the long title we at last got to the stage where the truth struck home, which is that the simplifications are in fact complications for a good many people. And perhaps we could have been a little more honest with the ``remedial'' piece and said ``remedial and tax extension''. This is because clause does, of course, bring in a capital gains tax. The Alliance supports many of the measures in this Bill but at the end of the day will have to vote against the title and unfortunately, I believe, against the Bill, because it is not simply remedial. It extends the taxation regime in an ad hoc way that I believe at this point is inappropriate. The long title does not in my view reflect the Bill. It should have been more carefully constructed. About the only really accurate parts in it are the dates and the titles of at least two of the Acts it amends, although as Dr Michael Cullen pointed out, the expression in the long title, ``Inland Revenue Acts'', is a generic name for at least two other pieces of legislation, neither of which bears the words ``Inland Revenue'' in its name. All in all, the long title shows a certain carelessness in reference to what the Bill does do.

As a member of the select committee that looked at the Budget Policy Statement I want to reinforce the remarks of the chairman, Mr Tony Ryall. Comments were made that the overall effect of the Budget Policy Statement is redistributive; that it shifts upwards the wealth and income in this country. That was noted even by the Business Roundtable and the Manufacturers Federation, and they were embarrassed by the blatant shift of wealth from the poor and producers to speculators. It takes something to embarrass the Business Roundtable like that, but Mr Peters managed to out-Scrooge the Business Roundtable. It is an effort he should be proud of. I want to spend my time this afternoon dealing with the main feature of the Budget Policy Statement, the compulsory retirement savings scheme. And what a feature it is. It is like a dry lake bed: it is flat, it is undistinguished in any direction, it can be travelled at speed, it raises a lot of dust, and it leaves little impression. What was the genesis of this scheme? The Hon. Peter Dunne questioned Mr Peters regarding the make-up of the ``design team''. At the select committee the Treasurer could not name the ``design team'' even though further questioning revealed that they had been verbally briefed by the Treasurer. It took him nearly a month to recover his memory and supply the information to the committee. The confusion, the sidestepping, and the prevarication that have emanated from the Treasurer on this scheme are the result of poor planning, and, worse, execution of a shoddy, tawdry policy of deception. The deception has included calling the scheme a top-up scheme. That is what we were told---a top-up scheme for national superannuation. Now it is a replacement for national superannuation. The deception has included saying it will provide investment for New Zealand, when it is odds-on that most of our savings, in the unlikely event of this pup being successfully sold to the public, will be invested overseas. We will export percent of our income tax, and it will be done by virtue of the Treasurer, who in the past was the great opponent of privatisation and sell-off. This is a bigger sell-out than the sale of Telecom. It is privatisation on a grand scale. We gave away Telecom for $ billion. Mr Peters is planning to sell us out to the tune of $ billion a year, ongoing and in perpetuity. But the biggest deception of the lot, the granddaddy of all the various canards in this debate, is the one that says this country cannot afford superannuation in its present form. The Treasurer has had the collusion of the Prime Minister in perpetrating this confidence trick on the public of New Zealand. I am pleased that the Treasurer talked about facts in his speech. He talked about them but did not present any. I want to spend some time going through some facts and figures. Firstly, the relative cost of national superannuation is declining over time.

T~en~a koutou katoa. I stand in this Chamber today to participate in the financial review of the Ministry of Maori Development on behalf of my colleague Sandra Lee. Te Puni Kokiri has had a difficult task this year as an agent of the Crown. Its job has been to sell the Multilateral Agreement on Investment to Maori. It has set up hui around the country, which have been dubbed ``consultation hui'', but we know that these are doing no more than misinform Maori on the impact on this country of the Multilateral Agreement on Investment. It has been a difficult task because Te Puni Kokiri has been directed to run hui that have deliberately misinformed its own people. It is no more than a repeat of the fiscal envelope saga, which Te Puni Kokiri was also asked to sell. Who will forget the angry reaction, and rightly so, from Maori? However, the Government has once again failed to learn from such paternalistic ways. Once again it has asked the ministry to sell another shonky deal to Maori. It is no wonder that there is little public confidence in many of our Government departments. Running hui on the Multilateral Agreement on Investment has been a difficult task, because the Crown has no intention of bringing the debate on it to the House and then to the select committee for submissions. Mr Peters, the Deputy Prime Minister, has promised a debate in the House and said that the House will then approve it. But he is saying that we will not have a vote. I invite the Minister to tell us by what mechanism the House will approve something without voting on it. I note that the House's approval of the agreement has been sufficient reason for Dr Robin Ord up in Taranaki to say he will be a candidate for New Zealand First in the by-election. I ask the Minister to tell us how that is to be achieved. The ministry's staff, like those in other Government departments, has had to toe the Government line. Its concerns have been overlooked. What is the point of a Crown agency that is the chief Maori adviser to the Ministry of Maori Affairs, and indeed to Cabinet, if its advice is to be ignored? The Alliance understands that the department advised the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade to undertake a treaty analysis. We know that this has not taken place yet. The financial review by the Maori affairs committee of Te Puni Kokiri confirms this. The coalition Government members on the select committee also know that. The Alliance also understands that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade has continued to attend negotiations for the Multilateral Agreement on Investment in Paris. Where is the Maori input? Has the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade sent any Maori to France to put across the point of view of Maori? Will the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade now send Maori from a Crown agency along merely to push the Crown's support for this document while masquerading that it is the Maori point of view? The Alliance has been kept up to date with the so-called consultation hui for Maori, and we know that Maori have said ``no way'' to this agreement. Is this unanimous call being taken overseas? I wish to emphasise to the Committee that the Maori Affairs Committee sees two key issues for the ministry. One of them is the effectiveness of the monitoring of its policy advice. The other is its ability to monitor effectively the impact of Government policies on Maori from mainstream agencies, such as the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Those ministries must provide comprehensive data relating to outcomes for Maori. The Maori Affairs Committee notes that data protocols have already been established between Te Puni Kokiri and agencies such as the Ministry of Education, the New Zealand Income Support Service, the Ministry of Health, and the Ministry of Justice. It is high time that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade establish such a protocol with Te Puni Kokiri. Kia ora.

The Opposition spokesperson on health referred to some personal experiences, and I want to begin my speech this evening by saying that in I was overseas and I availed myself of medical services at a clinic overseas. As I came out of that clinic, I was given a piece of paper. On that paper was a questionnaire that invited me to give my opinion of the services I had received in terms of medical treatment and of the way in which I was given information about what was happening, how I was being treated, and the professional services I received. That was in , which is a significant year in relation to this Bill. I returned to New Zealand in and I availed myself of medical services in New Zealand. During the course of treatment I dared to ask what the professional was actually doing, and I received a comment: ``Oh, you are one of those.'' Receiving that comment from a medical professional in , which, one will remember, is the year after the Cartwright report came out, I consider to be an affront. I would have been pleased had the Health and Disability Commissioner legislation been in function at that time, because I would have made a complaint about being accused of being ``one of those'' when I wanted to know what treatment I was receiving. I would also at the outset praise, and make particular comment on, the people who have voluntarily worked in this area for some time. I particularly refer to the people who have been involved in patients' rights advocacy throughout this country. These people, as members know, have worked voluntarily in a great way on the contents of this Bill. A lot of the work contained in it has been done by their own efforts, and, I am pleased to say, they have actually managed to win a number of cases they have brought through the accident compensation system. This Bill was introduced, as we have been reminded several times tonight, in . I am constantly being reminded of it by people in my electorate who ask when it will be passed, when it will be through, and when it will be operative. I pay particular tribute to the present Leader of the Opposition, who was then the Minister of Health, for introducing this Bill into the House. It was introduced in response to a crisis at National Women's Hospital. Problems still exist that this Bill addresses, and they are still serious problems. Her introduction was an intelligent approach to a problem, and I pay particular tribute to her for that. As I have mentioned, it evolved from the Cartwright report. I also pay particular tribute to someone who has not been mentioned at this time, and that is Margaret Vennell. Margaret Vennell, as people will know, was No. to Dame Silvia Cartwright in the whole investigation. She has continued with a great deal of work and research in this area, and I pay particular tribute to her. What this Bill is about, to a very large extent, is accountability, and accountability in our health system. It is particularly necessary now---with the so-called changes in health and the so-called restructuring---because we no longer have elected area health boards, and this is one way of ensuring some form of accountability in the health system. I also comment on the fact that this Bill has been delayed for years. A number of urgent Bills are being delayed. I constantly keep reminding people about the real problems in this society, and a lot of them end up in the health system, such as the problems of violence, which again have delayed legislation. The member for Kapiti actually mentioned that the delays in the Bill were so that it would fit in with the new health structure, and that means it is definitely overdue and definitely desperately needed in relation to this overstructuring. I meant ``restructuring'' but ``overstructuring'' applies very, very much in this case. It has been overstructured beyond recognition. I wish to point out that health is a service, and it has been mentioned tonight that there is a power relationship between professionals in the health system. A number of professionals were read out by a previous member. The member for Kapiti kept talking about a doctor-patient relationship, but it applies not only to doctors but to dentists, laboratory technicians, pharmacists, nurses, opticians, chiropractors, dietitians, and to anyone who is working within that health system. So it is not just a doctor-patient relationship. In fact, it could be anyone who is working in an institution offering health services. I would point out that in the health system, in the way the health services are delivered, the patient very rarely has choices. Patient choices are limited because the patient does not have---I particularly use the word ``patient'' rather than ``client'', and I noticed that the member for Kapiti used the word ``patient''---the patient does not have the professional knowledge needed in many cases. The patient is, therefore, vulnerable. That is what this Bill is about. It is about the vulnerability of patients; it is about the vulnerability of people in the medical system. The patients are vulnerable, and the important thing about the Health Commissioner Bill is that patients have someone to appeal to. We mention again the lack of informed consent in the National Women's disaster--- and I stress the word not only ``consent'' but ``informed''---and the need for knowledge to be given to patients. I also mention another aspect of the relationship of the patient with the medical service---that it is often the third party who pays. It is the third party and not the patient who pays directly either through the Government or through their insurance scheme, or whatever. That makes the patient, once again, more vulnerable in the system and stresses the need for this commissioner. I am particularly concerned about the need for commissioners in our society. We have recently appointed a Retirement Commissioner. This Retirement Commissioner is in relation to the superannuation accord and deals with the problems of older people in relation to their superannuation. I am concerned, however, about older people in general and the services that we are offering to older people in our society. I asked a question of the Minister of Health recently. Did she intend that the proposed Health Commissioner would be able to exercise jurisdiction over rest-homes, both private and public, including investigations of complaints by residents and relatives? I will give the Minister's reply: ``Clause of the Bill includes licensees of aged persons homes within the definition of the health care provider. Under the Bill the commissioner and health and disability services consumer advocates will be able to investigate and resolve complaints against such persons, whether such complaints are made by residents, relatives, or some other individual.'' This particular point is in the Bill: ``A licensee of an aged persons' home licensed under regulations for the time being in force pursuant to section A of the Health Act :''. That is of particular relief to a number of older persons and their families. We have a concern. We have a concern with the restructuring of the health system. We have a concern that more and more people who are being involved in rest-homes, particularly private rest-homes, are receiving adequate care and that they have recourse to the Health Commissioner to make sure this happens. There is a concern among older people, a concern of Age Concern, that we prevent elder abuse in this society. I know of many stories, and I am continually repeating stories of people in rest-homes. I can tell a simple story of an older woman in a rest-home in Hamilton who was neglected by this rest-home. It is a simple thing. They left her teeth in. They left her teeth in so long that her son had to prise those teeth out of her mouth. I mean, it is disgusting that this happened in a rest-home. This family wants some recourse as to what actually happened. Nobody bothered to check that she had false teeth; nobody cared. This is a simple thing, but it is actually of great concern to this woman. There are many more terrible things. I can tell the House of people left on floors for hours and so on. But these things are part of the reason that we need this Bill, and I am pleased that this is in here. I hope that the code of rights, which is included in that Bill, will include recourse for these people and their families, and that the families will be able to avail themselves of the services of the Health Commissioner. I also point out something that is of very great concern to me in terms of older people, and that is where they are and what rights they will have under the code of rights. I understand in Britain, for instance, there is provision for people of different cultures to be cared for in an appropriate way for their age. This is where the Treaty of Waitangi comes in and is significant. For instance, in Britain I understand that older Chinese people are kept together because they can actually have food that is appropriate for them, and that they like. They can also speak in their own language and communicate with people. That is why it is important to have in this Bill---somebody made some comment about later on turning on the word processor and putting in certain words,and I would be happy if the word processor was put into effect---the words ``Treaty of Waitangi'', which were put right throughout this Bill, especially as it concerns older people, the care of older people, and the conditions in rest-homes. I particularly stress this. It is important---especially for older Maori people---that they have suitable and appropriate facilities, services, and accommodation. In relation to accommodation in our hospitals I know, for instance, at my particular Crown health enterprise, a hostel has been built for people coming into the hospital, both for those who are receiving services and their relatives. But it is not appropriate for Maori people. Once again that is something that has been put on the back-burner and it is going to happen next time, later, or some other time. This is where these people need recourse to a health commissioner to say that they need particular access. I once again mention access. I mention that the member for Horowhenua reported that she had been an advocate, and I find myself being the advocate, especially as our particular Crown health enterprise is trialling a new system of ensuring that waiting-lists are met. Waiting-lists relate to access. Access relates to the code of rights. I want to be sure that the code of rights does include access and it does address waiting-lists. I have a young woman, for instance, who is a student and who is actually wasting her student loan because she is constantly sick. She has been on a waiting-list for months. She needs her tonsils out. Nineteen months for a simple operation. I think they used to do it on the table when we were kids. We would get them out in a few seconds, and here she is waiting months. I know it used to happen that way. The doctor would come around and whip them out in a few seconds. She has been waiting months, losing good time at university, wasting what she says is her student loan because she does not have adequate access. I think that the code of rights needs to cover some of these cases. I will also refer to Good Health Wanganui. The member for Wanganui said that what happened is a sad case and one of misfortune. It is more than that. There should be more than one person looking at laboratory tests. There should be more than one person involved in these instances. I think that the Health Commissioner Bill is long overdue. Goodness me, if some doctor had accidentally knocked off Mr Bobbit's whatsit, and so on, there would be a national crisis. If a doctor said: ``Whoops, what has happened?'', that is what the Health Commissioner Bill is for. It is here for a code of rights, it is here to defend people, and it is here to defend people when the doctor says ``whoops''. When a doctor says ``whoops'' one is likely to lose part of one's self. It is very, very important that we have this Health Commissioner Bill and some people have a right of recourse. At least with Mr Bobbit he got his sewn back on again. Other people from Wanganui are not getting their bits sewed back on again and it is vital that we deal with these. Whether it is an accident or whether it is misfortune we cannot afford to have this type of thing happening. We cannot afford another Cartwright report and there is danger of us having one. So it is extremely important that we do not delay this Bill any further. People in New Zealand are asking for it and are wondering what has happened to it. It is very important. Auckland does not need water right now as badly as it did, but people do need the Health Commissioner Bill before more people lose bits of their bodies.

I move, That the Human Assisted Reproductive Technology Bill be now read a second time. This Bill is sometimes referred to as the ``Test-tube Baby Bill'' or now, perhaps more aptly, as the ``Dolly Bill''. It was introduced into this House in June , and I seek that it be referred to the Justice and Law Reform Committee for further consideration. I have been assured by veterinary scientists involved in the field of genetics and selective breeding of animals that we probably need at most eight fit human males with high sperm counts to maintain the present population of New Zealand. The recent international media panic over Dolly, the cloned biological replica of a -year-old Finn Dorset sheep at the Roslin Institute, Edinburgh, indicates that a brave new world of test-tube or in vitro designer babies is upon us, and that with cloning we may not need any men at all. This very reason alone is enough to convince many of the need for legislation. As one of my colleagues put it bluntly: ``Do you mean that science will do away with sex?''. For strictly reproductive purposes I think it is a distinct possibility; for recreation purposes, I doubt it. Jesting aside, there was an international outcry at the end of February this year about a sheep named Dolly. Personally, I am surprised that there was not a greater political and moral outcry in response to a Time magazine article on November recording the splitting of a human embryo at Georgetown University in Washington, DC. We were told that human twins were destroyed because they were faulty. In recent months the media have supplied us with many other sensational stories of cloning in the animal world and cloning in the human world: Mrs Blood's struggle for the right to use her dead husband's sperm without having his prior formal consent; a Californian fertility expert being the sperm donor for over children; the death of a woman in New Zealand from a stroke just days after receiving ovastimulation at a fertility clinic; the possibility of giving birth to one's own sister, or even mother; and the concern of Maori and Pacific Island people over the ownership and storage of DNA information. All these stories show that the pace of medical science and technology has outstripped ethical and legal, if not social, moral, and theological, considerations. In a Medical Council of New Zealand report by Dr Alistair Campbell requested legislation in New Zealand, not to prevent all test-tube baby technology but to establish controls and draw lines of public acceptability of modern medical practice. At present Australasian guidelines govern New Zealand reproductive technology. The second in vitro baby in the world was born in the state of Victoria, in Australia, almost years ago. In the state of Victoria considered that the guidelines we use in New Zealand were an insufficient deterrent to irresponsible scientists and practitioners. In it enacted its comprehensive Infertility Treatment Act. As long ago as the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act was passed in the United Kingdom, and there currently are calls from eminent British biologists to tighten this law. Canada, after extensive research and massive reports, introduced a Bill into its Parliament last year. In New Zealand in Geoffrey Palmer promoted the Status of Children Amendment Bill, to prevent a Baby M case in New Zealand, and to establish definitions and the rights of a legal birth mother. The legislation also protects sperm donors from paternity charges. My Human Assisted Reproductive Technology Bill, to which I referred in my maiden speech in , will do four basic additional things. It will register clinics so that we have greater access to information about current practices, and greater accountability in terms of the technologies being employed in New Zealand. It will also allow us to examine funding bases and the influence of drug companies on treatment and experimentation. It does not take a very big stretch of the imagination to realise that big money is involved in reproductive technology, and there is potential for big profits, especially if the science and technology are misused. There is a wealth of science fiction to show us how. The Bill will insist on the keeping of centralised records so that children born as a result of modern birth technologies can access their genealogical whakapapa in a similar way to adopted children. It outlaws the cloning of human beings, at least until we have had time to consider all the many and varied implications and complications of such practices. Professor Martin Johnson, Professor of Reproductive Sciences at Cambridge University in the UK, on the birth of Dolly called for international rules to ban the cloning of humans. Dr Ian Wilmut, Dolly's creator, has in recent days made the same call. I am convinced this would be a good move. The Bill bans commercial surrogacy and the sale of sperm, ova, gametes, and embryos, and establishes regulations for the time that frozen embryos can be stored, and the ownership and use of such embryos. The Bill does not include, as in Britain, sex selection for social rather than medical reasons, and perhaps it should. This may be a matter that can be considered by the select committee. This Bill is not against modern human reproductive technologies per se. I recognise the benefits in assisting infertile people to have children, where possible. The Bill does not deal with the complex matters concerning President Clinton in the United States: the right of access to modern birth technologies, and the role of the State in meeting the cost involved. I add, however, that in a recent paper by the National Council of Women its clear opinion was that children are a gift, not a right. This is an underlying philosophy to be taken into account when considering the extent of the right of access to reproductive technologies. Another major concern of women in particular is the extent to which we exercise and maintain control of our own fertility. Robyn Rowland's book, Living Laboratories, highlights the dangers of women becoming the guinea pigs of experimental scientists. The mere title of this book, based on Australasian statistical data, indicates its revealing content and the apprehensions of an academic researcher about some developing modern practices. I personally find the new American term for women as ``gestation carriers'' quite repulsive. I also recognise the very fine line between positive genetic modification to prevent inherited diseases and deformities, and genetic engineering. I have fears, and I am sure I am not alone in this, about the possible negative uses of genetic engineering, and the creation of a new, manipulative, Nazi-like eugenics movement capable of building a modern master race. This is a complex Bill about complex matters affecting the future of humanity. The people of New Zealand have a democratic right to have their say, and to set in place legislative bottom lines of acceptability in this field of medical science and intervention, a field that is exciting and frightening at the same time. We have a potential Cartwright-like calamity on our hands. We have the potential to prevent disease and deformity. We can also venture into Dr Frankenstein - like territory where, as Mary Shelley warned us, in our search to become God we may create monsters. The Bill has a wide range of support outside this House, from radical feminists, Maori, church leaders, and judges, to the Medical Council, and I look forward to support from my parliamentary colleagues across all parties. I take the opportunity of thanking all of those who have assisted with the production of this Bill: those on national ethics committees; former colleagues at the University of Waikato who organised conferences on the subject; those who have compiled reports; those who practise in this field of medicine and science; and in particular Dr Alistair Campbell, who has returned to the UK, Dr Robin Briant of the Medical Council, and Hamilton lawyer Anne Todd, who checked the draft for legal accuracy and weeded out the jargon. I also acknowledge the approval of a former colleague, Margaret Austin, and thank her for her support of the Bill in its formative stages. I acknowledge also the scientists at Ruakura research station in Hamilton who gave detailed advice and insights into modern techniques and practices; and the many people, from members of the New Zealand Dairy Board to patients' rights advocates at Health Waikato, who have shown an interest and given advice. I commend my Bill to this House and ask that the Bill at its second reading be referred to the Justice and Law Reform Committee.

I was waiting to hear about the new vision. But what did I hear? They might think that they are very clever, but anyone with an ounce of intelligence can see that what National was trying to do today was to attack Labour for National's own weakness, because everybody knows that National went to the last election with no policy to speak of. National has no policy now. I listened to Mrs Shipley speak for minutes in this House, full of an electioneering kind of rhetoric, full of slogans, and full of cliches. There was not one policy, and not one fact. I would like to hold up the nice fat volume of Labour Party policy. Mr Upton, who picked up a bit of paper on the way in here and dared to make a speech and say that he was an intellectual, cannot even read. I think that he needs Mr Creech to give him a remedial lesson in reading. I defy any other party in this House to come up with policy that is able to govern this country. We have wasted a year since the last election. Not a week goes by without some calamity, some great gaffe from members of this coalition. We have had scandals about underpants and expensive trips to Paris, we have paid out $ million on one man's ego on the superannuation referendum, we have had Associate Ministers being sacked, we have had a Minister resign because there was no consultation on her own portfolio area, we have had a Prime Minister sacked for what now appears to be no reason at all---all because there is no policy. The only reason that I can see is that Mr Simcock and his mates are getting a bit impatient about being backbenchers---Mr Simcock, who is supposed to be a constituent MP; Mr Simcock, who I believe does very few duties and spends all his time trying to stab other people in the back. Last week people believed that Mrs Shipley would be strong and that she would be decisive---she would put Mr Peters in his place. What happened? Did she have the courage to sack him? No, she did not. Mrs Shipley---who could deal to the kindergarten teachers in hours, who could whack at kindergarten teachers and take them out of the State Sector Act as a matter of national urgency, who refused to listen, who refused to call submissions, who refused to have discussion---has within days fallen right into Jim Bolger's mould and the tail is wagging the dog as it has done for the last months. When she could have shown strength, she gave Mr Peters time. What did Mr Peters do with that time? Mr Peters went behind her back, as he went behind the backs of his own team. He got the treatment he deserved from the Rt Hon. Helen Clark, who gave him, without any hesitation, short shrift. Where is Mrs Shipley now? According to McPhail and Gadsby, she is looking for a deputy---if she has not shot them all, especially in her pre-coup-bid attack on list MPs. Watch out Paul East, watch out Doug Graham, watch out Roger Sowry, and watch out Don McKinnon! Will Mrs Shipley show us a new face---a new style of leadership---and will she return women to Cabinet? Will she, as Labour did, put five women in Cabinet? Will she defy the member for Tauranga and return Katherine O'Regan---a hard-working, senior party member---to Cabinet? Will Mrs O'Regan, who is a loyal party member, be rewarded? What about the person who showed her loyalty---Mrs Fletcher? Will she return Mrs Fletcher to Cabinet? We will wait and see.

Mr Williamson says ``Only just.'', knowing that percent is about as conclusive as one can get in this regard. Another point raised is the matter of administrative costs, and that is important in any scheme of this nature. Costs must be kept down so that the beneficiaries can get the most they are eligible for. That is another point that was somewhat hidden in the $ million referendum on the recent retirement savings scheme. The last principle I want to point out is the matter of return percentages, and here we have this little bit of controversy about the argument that management needs to be more flexible, that the percent return needs to be over a wider period to allow for more flexibility. I am always suspicious of the word ``flexible'', I am afraid. We know that when it comes to employment it means no jobs, and I hope in this case that flexibility means that the people who are benefiting from this scheme do actually benefit in the way it was intended. I have been explaining to the House and those who are listening today the principles of such a National Provident Fund, which also apply to any superannuation scheme. I think that the amendments have appropriately shown that those principles are important to New Zealanders and are important to anybody who is entering into any superannuation scheme.
