It is unfortunate that that member used his very short speech to abuse personally a member on this side of the House, rather than speak to the substance of the bill. It is very clear that the effect of the bill is to impose a tax on those liable parents who are on benefits themselves. It takes money out of the pockets of families of liable parents who are on benefits. That is what we are complaining about with this bill. The National Party has no problem with liable parents bearing liability for their children. We have no problem with custodial parents receiving more money. The problem with the bill is that it takes money from liable parents, and in most cases that money will not end up in the hands of the custodial parents. It will end up in the hands of the Government. We first became aware of this measure at the time of the last Budget. At that time, I went through the Budget documents to work out where the taxes were. I said to my colleagues that a tax was hidden in the child support measure. It is called a child support measure, but it is a Government support measure. Most of the money will go to the Government, and will not show up as an increase in the money that goes into the hands of any parents, and will not go towards the support of any individual children. That is the problem with the bill. It takes from children, from families, and in most cases the money will not go towards the support of children. We support the bill, because we support the idea that liable parents should pay more. What we want to do is draw to the attention of this House and this nation that although liable parents will be paying more, that money will not be used to increase the money that goes into the hands of custodial parents. Mr Simcock, in his very good speech, drew the distinction between this system and the Australian system, where if the liable parent pays more, the custodial parent gets more. If the liable parent has to pay more, he or she can see that the money is going to pay for the support of his or her children. In New Zealand that will not be the case. In New Zealand many liable parents will have to pay more, and they can see that their children's custodial parent will not get a penny more, even though, as liable parents, they have paid more. I put it as simply as that. For liable parents who are themselves on benefits, the Child Support Amendment Bill comprises a tax, and their children are unlikely to see any of that money. The reason they are unlikely to see any of it is that the custodial parents are not working. We want to be very clear about our position on this bill. The senior Government whip appeared to misunderstand it, although I do not know why. Perhaps he was not listening. The issue is very simple. We believe that liable parents should pay for the support of their children, and we are happy for liable parents to pay more for that. But if they are paying more, and most of it does not go to the support of their children, there is a problem. We think the Government has dismissed too lightly the options available to it to make sure that the money is passed on. One of the greatest complaints I get from liable parents who come into my office is that they pay the money, but their children do not see anything of it. If there was a greater connection between the payments made by liable parents and the money received by the children for whom those parents are liable, the liable parents would not be as angry as they are when they come into my office and those of other MPs. On this side of the House, we believe that there should be a fair standard of support for children, but we think that the children should benefit from the financial contribution of their liable parents. We are also very aware that those liable parents are often in other relationships, and have other children for whom they are liable, and of whom they have custody. This bill fails to recognise that the effect of putting up the liable-parent contribution is, for many people, simply to tax liable parents, and not provide a dollar more for custodial parents. We are concerned about the approximately , parents who will be subject to a benefit cut or a tax. I put it as simply as this: in the end, if we take money away from people, and do not give that money to their children, then to say that the money is anything other than a tax is to misconstrue what is happening. The effect of this measure should be very clear. Most of the extra liable-parent contributions will go into Government coffers; they will not go into the hands of children or custodial parents. I am intrigued that no Government members took calls during the Committee stage to explain how they justified that action. Maybe the reason is that, in the end, they had closed their eyes to it. When I went through the Budget measures at the time of the last Budget, this measure stuck out as a very high, new tax. The Government is effectively taking money away from liable parents to increase Government funding. Many of the families affected will not actually see any benefit at all. Many of the fathers---as Mr Simcock says, it is generally fathers who end up as the liable parents---will not see anything for the extra contribution they make. There are a number of highly specific issues in this bill that we raised, and that are mentioned in the minority report from this side of the House. Firstly, one of the issues that is completely ignored by this bill is that a liable parent's debt to the State in the form of a student loan is not taken into account for child support assessment purposes. Where a liable parent is paying back a student loan, that financial burden is not included in the calculation when working out what money that parent has available to pay child support. That is a flaw in this bill, a flaw that the minority report pointed out, but was not dealt with. Secondly, and perhaps more important, a problem that is raised over and over again with members on this side of the House---and I suspect also with members on that side---is the issue of parents who bear a substantial part of the burden of caring for their children. They are not officially the custodial parent, because they have less than percent of the care of their children. Those parents are not treated as the custodial parent, and yet they can have substantial obligations. This bill does nothing to recognise the fact that many parents who are not officially the custodial parent bear a substantial burden of childcare. The hard-line division between custodial parent and liable parent ignores the fact that many custodial parents share the burden of care with the liable parent, and that that shared care is both a financial burden and a time burden. This bill sees things very much in black and white, and fails to recognise that reality. I would like to finish by making the point again, as clearly as I can, that for many New Zealand families on benefits, the fact that one of the parents in that family is liable for another family will mean that, under this legislation, they face a cut in the money for their households. In the end, when a cut in one's household money goes to the Government, that cut is a tax, by anyone's definition. Government speakers have failed to acknowledge that. It is very clear that when many New Zealanders have up to $ a week taken away from them, they will see it as a tax, too.
No, it is not, Mr Chairman---tempted as I am to get kicked out. You made the point that the law cannot be the law until it receives the royal assent.

I should like to ask the Minister whether the provisions were discussed with the industry before the Bill was introduced. If not, which parts of the Bill have not been discussed? The Minister took action on the controversial salmon issue only a few days ago, and he created quite a furore. Claims were made that the industry was not consulted about the steps he took. I do not want to become involved in that issue, but Opposition members would find it helpful to know to what extent the clauses have been subject to consultation, and whether agreement with the industry is identified. I wonder whether the Minister could be more specific about clause , to which my colleague the member for Timaru referred. The proposed amended section ZA()(b) provides that when a commercial fisherman has a catch in excess of his quota, but subsequently buys or leases quota that would have authorised the taking of that fish, that will be taken into account. In other words, he legitimises the fish that he has already caught. Does the word `` subsequently'' mean that days after the subsequent month is the date on which the catch must be legitimised either by the purchase or leasing of quota? Can the Minister also tell the House the extent to which unused quotas are regularly available for trading? Is it correct that they are traded every day of the week here in Wellington? I have not seen the operation, but I did make inquiries on behalf of a constituent. I found out where the individual transferable quotas were available, and what time they were up for offer. Has the Minister received any advice on whether the ruling to apply if the proposed new section in clause is implemented will persuade people to obtain their quota or legitimise their catch at the latest possible opportunity; or are there means by which they can be encouraged to do so earlier? I turn to clause , which inserts a proposed new section A into the Act. That new section replaces an existing section, and the explanatory note reads: ``...provides that, in the absence of proof to the contrary, any controlled fish found on board a vessel will be presumed to have been taken from a controlled fishery, and any gear or equipment found on board a vessel on which controlled fish are also found will be presumed to have been used in a controlled fishery''. That certainly sounds like heavy stuff. The person who is apprehended is considered to be guilty virtually from the word go, and that person has to prove his or her innocence. The fishermen are involved in a very competitive industry, and I accept that strong laws and deterrents are needed. However, the Bill seems to be the heavy hand of the State, administered through the fisheries inspectors and the ministry. Are those requirements absolutely necessary? Finally, I refer to the proposed new sections A, B, and C in clause , which cover a matter that has been controversial in recent times. The problem is essentially a South Island one rather than a North Island one, but we in the North Island observe developments with the greatest interest. How does the Minister propose, under the proposed new section A, that his inspectors will be able to enforce or certify that an unauthorised bycatch fish, or a salmon taken in contravention of the Act, shall be returned immediately to the sea with as little injury as possible? It is obvious that an inspection has not been carried out if, when a ship is apprehended, salmon is amongst the catch. Is it practical to insist that that fish must be returned immediately? Perhaps it is practical, but I would really like a picture of the extent of the seriousness of the problem of taking salmon from the sea. As we have seen from the news media, tempers are running high, and commercial fishermen are being accused of deliberately intercepting the salmon.

I do not know whether the janitor was asked to speak to them, but I suppose that that could be so, because even janitors have expectations and principles. When matters such as the stance taken by the Government towards foreign affairs and the performance of the Government from the Prime Minister down are added to the economic policies of the Minister of Finance and his coterie---they are supported by the Government caucus---it is apparent that New Zealand is on the brink of disaster. New Zealand has the highest level of unemployment since the mid-s; it has no new developments under way; it has an adverse balance of payments of more than $ billion; there is no investment in new industry; and there is virtually no investment in New Zealand for new jobs or for new products. At this time New Zealand should have a favourable balance in its balance of trade, not a deficit of $ billion. New Zealand's young people are increasingly turning their eyes across the Tasman. Indeed, it is not only young people who are doing so, but also people who have made commitments in New Zealand and bought homes. Those people are selling their homes and moving across the Tasman. Since the Labour Government has been in office New Zealanders have left New Zealand's shores on a permanent or long-term basis---that is bad news for the future of this country. What is the position, after the Government had said that it wants to restructure industry? There are now fewer jobs---many of those losses have occurred in manufacturing alone---there are fewer jobs in forestry, fewer with the Government, and there are closures of firms up and down the country. Exporters---farmers, producer boards, and manufacturers---have called on the Government time and time again to change its policies. The Government will not change them, and so it is stated in this morning's Dominion that the value of the New Zealand dollar is at a record level. The economy and New Zealanders are in the most damaging position since the mid-s, and the Government sits blindly by and follows doggedly inflexible policies that it says will lead New Zealand to the Promised Land, to a nirvana that has been promised for year after year. However, it is increasingly recognised that that result is not attainable, and that New Zealand is on the brink of disaster.

I move, That the House take note of miscellaneous business. Cabinet is in total disarray, and the people know it. Cabinet members are arguing and fighting with each other; Cabinet is disputing with the Government back-benchers; Cabinet is arguing with the President of the Labour Party; and Cabinet and Government back-bench members have fallen out with the Council of Trade Unions. The tragedy of all that disarray, except for the last point, is that New Zealand is leaderless. The country is divided and leaderless. There is a battle between the Minister of Foreign Affairs and the Minister of External Relations and Trade, and there is a battle between the Minister of Foreign Affairs and the Minister of Defence. As those battles continue it is increasingly becoming a tragedy for the country, because the work that should be done is not being done, and the decisions that should be made are not being made. Furthermore, the protection that the public expects from the laws and from the Government is not being given. The Government is in total disarray. I listened to ``Morning Report'' this morning and heard the erudite statement made by the Minister of Justice, who suggested that regulations may have to be made to govern the high seas to prevent people from taking their ships down to the Antarctic. However laudable that proposal may be, it does not bear any relationship to the Minister's real responsibilities---the responsibilities that he and the Government have stepped away from, and not faced. I refer to the fiasco in the investment world and in the financial sector, and in relation to company legislation. The Minister of Justice, in his capacity as the Minister for the Environment, is quick to talk about protecting the ozone layer, but what has he done for investors? What about the investors in the Prudential Building and Investment Society of Canterbury? He has not done one thing for them as their securities have been taken from them. That is the way the position appears today. It is appalling for the House to discover that not only did the Minister of Justice know that the building society was in trouble in November but also that he allowed it to continue advertising for funds---shades of Registered Securities Ltd! That is precisely what happened with that fiasco. Registered Securities Ltd regularly advertised for funds month after month, after the Minister and his department knew that existing investments, let alone new investments, were at risk, and the Minister did nothing. The Minister of Justice moved only when he was pushed, and that is precisely what he did on law and order. Members may recall a time when the Minister of Justice said that law and order were not problems. However, one day a public-spirited citizen in Christchurch advertised in the Christchurch Press and the Minister received coupons from throughout the country stating that the public was concerned about the Government's inadequacy in relation to law and order. The Minister of Justice moved then, but only when he was pushed into it. The sorry story of Goldcorp is the same. The Minister was approached---I approached him myself, asking him to intervene in the interests of ordinary New Zealand citizens who had been persuaded to put their money into Goldcorp---and asked to appoint an official liquidator to protect investors' interests. What did he do? He did absolutely nothing! In an answer given in the House late last year the Minister of Justice stated: ``I have received some recent correspondence from investors requesting the appointment of a statutory liquidator under the Companies Special Investigations Act . In the circumstances of this case that course is not possible, as the company is not in liquidation.'' It is strange that more recently the Minister was able to appoint liquidators, but he could not do it then. The Minister said then that, in any event, on the information that was available to him, it was unlikely that the Act could be applied. The net result was that people---many of whom were elderly, as members know---who had been persuaded by the unfairness of the national superannuation surcharge to put their money into something in which they felt their capital would be protected, such as gold, lost all of their savings. People were not much better off whether they invested---not to get rich, but to protect their savings---in Goldcorp, Registered Securities Ltd, or in the Prudential Building and Investment Society of Canterbury. Those companies collapsed with the prior knowledge of the Government, and it has done absolutely nothing. The Minister of Justice stands condemned for his lack of action in trying to protect the savings of ordinary New Zealanders. Members were told in the House today that the Government could not interfere in a building society.

I well know the Minister's attitude to the protection that we tried to give children when he was a member of the Social Services Committee. However, I do not care to bring up that matter here. The children of New Zealand are paramount, and they deserve the strongest laws to protect them, but the Government is reneging in that regard. Finally, the child protection proposals that the Opposition put before the select committee and the Committee of the whole House would ensure that there would be a team approach to resolving family problems of child abuse. The evidence that the select committee and members have is that in about percent of sexual abuse cases both parents---most are in de facto relationships---know that the offence is taking place. We believe that it is unfair to say to a family: ``You have to resolve that problem from within the family; you have to resolve it yourselves.'' The child cannot speak for himself, or, more likely, for herself. Opposition members fear that the opportunity that the House had to break the cycle of violence and abuse has been taken from us. Professional advisers---not biased advisers, not twisted people, not people who become over-zealous, but advisers who represent the community; perhaps the pediatrician, the district nurse, or Plunket nurse, or people who are surrounding and supporting a family---indeed have a role to play in protecting, first, the child, and, second, the family. The Opposition's proposals were rejected, so the Bill is inadequate, I am sorry to say, and the legislation will need to be changed. My last comment about the Bill---a Bill with which I have been associated for a very long time---is this. In order to follow arguments of cultural sensitivity the Government has weakened the protection that should be accorded a child. A child can now come under the guardianship or custody of an iwi authority. Who or what is an iwi authority? Other than the statement in the Bill that the Director-General of Social Welfare shall determine when an iwi authority is an iwi authority, that queston is not determined. Who has personal responsibility for a child who is under the guardianship or custody of an iwi authority? The changes go much further than John Rangihau recommended. He said quite properly that fono and hapu are bodies that can assume guardianship or custody, but what is the iwi? It is everyone. No one will have the specific responsibility. Under the Bill, instead of children being better protected they will be less protected.

The Bill has been before the House since December . In fact, it has been in preparation since the beginning of the decade under successive Ministers and successive Governments. The Minister himself sought a report that was published some time last year. The Bill has been completely rewritten. I am concerned that the public must have the opportunity of knowing what is in the rewritten legislation. It must have that opportunity, and the committee should sit on extra days to give it that opportunity. It is simply not fair to get submissions from up and down the country, rewrite a Bill completely, then say to the people who have made the submissions that we may tell them what is in it but that they cannot make any further submissions. It is absolute nonsense. The Minister and the Government are arrogant in trying to force through legislation without adequate consideration. After all that time, I tell the House that it should get the legislation right---don't spoil the ship for a hap'orth o' tar. Give the committee the added opportunity of sitting on the one day of the week that has been allocated to it very fairly by the chairwoman of the committee. On this occasion it is quite right that there was a total concurrence by members of the committee in relation to the need for the extra day, but we cannot force through legislation in which the country has an intense interest without proper consultation. We can do that only if we get that extra day not only in March but also during the whole of April. I do not want the legislation to carry the stamp of a desperate Minister and a desperate Government wanting to force it through without hearing the views of those who will be affected by it. The chairwoman of the committee knows quite well that the select committee went up and down the country and gave undertakings in halls and on marae that the Bill would be referred back to the people, as it was to be amended substantially. As the chairwoman and other members of the committee know, those people have a very distinct impression that they have the right to make further submissions. I am concerned that the proposal does not go far enough. An extra sitting on Friday, March, will be insufficient. The Opposition wants those additional days, and the committee may not finish even if it receives them. Extra days in June may be needed, but it is better to do that than to try to force the Bill in a way that may mean that people such as Dr David Geddes, who has been an adviser to successive Governments and Ministers for decades, will not have an opportunity to come before the select committee and make submissions.

I listened to the member for Porirua with a great deal of interest. He spoke like a winner until his last few sentences, when he gave the game away and said that a future Government would tinker with the legislation. Members must be either for the legislation or against it. However, I give the member credit for arguing strongly against the Bill's proceeding any further. My answer to my colleague the member for Tauranga, who questioned the ability of the House to make a decision---and that question has been displayed in several speeches, particularly the one made by the member for Porirua---is that taxpayers fund overseas journeys by parliamentarians so that parliamentarians can enlighten themselves and broaden their knowledge and experience. One of the things that taxpayers expect to gain from that is parliamentarians who make more measured and better balanced decisions, particularly on issues that involve a conscience vote. I think that the House is moving towards that this evening, although I do not disagree with all of the theory of my colleague the member for Tauranga on the origin of initiatives for changes to legislation that requires a conscience vote. I am concerned that the legislation before the House is the wrong Bill at the wrong time. It seems to me that the House is giving a demonstration of Nero fiddling while Rome burns, because New Zealand has a record number of unemployed, a record number of insolvencies, a record number of receiverships, and a record number of bankruptcies. For some strange reason those who are promoting the legislation seem to think that opening casinos will help to solve those problems. I believe that they will only exacerbate them. I am not a prude when it comes to gambling, but I believe that the Bill will only exacerbate the problems I have outlined. If ever members need any argument against the Bill, they should look at two or three of the clauses in the Bill as reported back. First, the new clause provides that social impact reports are required. We know that the proponents, the proposers, or the applicants for a casino licence will have to provide those reports, but it is not clear what those reports should contain. The authority would be deterred from granting a licence only if the contents of the report showed that there would be an undue detrimental effect on the surrounding area. At the time the House was about to change the law and legislate for lotto I pressed the Minister of Social Welfare many times for a social impact report on a national scale to try to measure the impact of that new medium of gambling on the whole community. My experience of the support for lotto---in particular, Instant Kiwi---is somewhat similar to that of the member for Porirua. It is unfortunate, but when one goes to some shopping malls the only queues are of people lining up to buy Instant Kiwi. That is not satisfactory, because we all know that many families are pressed for funds. Another clause that gives me concern is the new clause that provides that the Secretary for Internal Affairs shall require that applicants for positions consent to have their photographs and fingerprints taken. That is a telling requirement. It is no good for those who support the legislation to try to suggest that casinos will not introduce an element of organised crime that is entirely new to the country. I do not mean organised crime itself, but a new element of it. It has been stated time and time again by experienced police personnel overseas that, whether people like it or not, organised crime is a natural result of the introduction of casino licences and the establishment of casinos. I do not want to see that happen in New Zealand.

I support the amendment moved by the member for Rangiora. Members are witnessing the abrogation, manipulation, and humiliation of the normal parliamentary process. As the member for Horowhenua said, members of the select committee have considered the Bill for several years. Originally, she was the chairwoman of a select committee that was making reasonable progress, but after the change of Government the Government's attitude towards child protection altered. The deliberations of the committee were virtually halted, the Minister produced another discussion document, and, finally, under all kinds of restrictions placed on the select committee, an entirely new Bill has appeared. I support the amendment to have the Bill referred back to the select committee, because it is a new Bill. It has not had a first reading. Unlike the Bill introduced by the Hon. Ann Hercus, which contained about clauses, this Bill---so far unseen by the general public---contains clauses. My colleague the member for Rangiora and I pleaded with the select committee many times to discharge the Hercus Bill and allow the Minister to introduce his new Bill. Time and time again that proposal was turned down. The Minister was fearful of public inquiry into his Bill. Nothing in the Bill will smooth over the problems of ward of Christchurch Hospital. On the contrary, the contents of the Bill will exacerbate them. The Bill no longer gives the child paramount protection under New Zealand law. It offends the current legislation. It also offends United Nations conventions that New Zealand Governments have signed in the past and have attempted to honour. The declaration of children's rights states clearly that the child shall enjoy special protection and shall be given opportunities and facilities by law and other means to enable him or her to develop physically, mentally, morally, spiritually, and socially in a healthy and normal manner. In those matters the best interests of the child shall be paramount and shall be the paramount consideration. The Bill removes that protection. No longer is the interest of a child paramount. The protection for children who, unfortunately, are the members of society most vulnerable to violence and abuse is being taken away. The most travelled Minister of the Crown said that I was an old man in a hurry. It is always the Minister of External Relations and Trade who seems to be in a hurry to go somewhere. He is in a hurry to go back tonight, so he wants the Government to force legislation through the House no matter whether or not it has been considered. I invite the new Minister of Internal Affairs to intervene in the debate, to make sure that she appreciates and supports the changes in the Bill. As was pointed out by the Minister in charge of the Bill, it is concerned only with the number of members of the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council. In the third reading debate we are entitled to look at the principles of the Bill as a whole and the way they affect the principal legislation. The Bill increases by one the number of ministerial appointments. There is nothing wrong with the system of appointment by Ministers. It provides flexibility and recognition through appointments to boards and councils, and the system has been exercised with discretion by both political parties. But the matter concerns me if the system becomes an old-boy network. We do not want an old-boy network. We would not have that in a National Administration. I emphasise that the time to involve the public is when nominations are called for. There is already much legislation on the statute book that could be a model for the Government to use for all appointment procedures. The public advertising of vacancies is an integral part of a participatory democracy. The public must know that the vacancies exist, and must be allowed to make nominations, but neither the principal Act nor the amendment goes far enough. An example is the national parks and reserves legislation, which sets out in detail the way that members of boards, councils, and authorities are appointed, right back to the method of seeking nominations. I make that point either to the Minister in charge of the department or to the Minister in charge of the Bill. Does the change do anything to ensure greater public participation? I do not think it does. If, as my colleague suggested, the reason for the appointment is to include the administration of the literary fund in the responsibilities of the Queen Elizabeth II Arts Council, one might well ask whether the Minister of External Relations and Trade is entitled to participate in the debate. Does he have an interest in the grants that are made from the literary fund? Has he published a book?
